*Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* Private Notes, Scroll One.

The commentary on the text will be explained in two major divisions: first, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation. The first division has two parts: first, an account of the differing views of ancient masters regarding expansion and contraction;
second, from "Now, [I] divide... onwards, an elucidation of how the present master divides the sections and explains them. The first of these also has two parts: first, the narrative.
Next, although [the text is] obscured,
the "Small Mountain Yao" refers to the Huayan Temple on Small Mountain in Wukang County, Huzhou.
Regarding those who relied [on the teachings] within the Passes (Guān'ài), according to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) [it states]:
"[... etc. The term "etc. includes those at Mount Lu such as Longqi and others, who tasted the flavor of the Buddha’s sutras until they forgot their fatigue, and transmitted [... .
□□□ When expounding this sutra, simply divide it into one section...
[omitted] ...down to the end of the sutra. For the middle section... [omitted] ...according to the general principle, it is divided into three parts:
namely, the introduction... [omitted] ... *Note: The ellipses (□□□) represent the missing characters from the original manuscript.*
[The character] □ is where the assembly was held. By this it is verified that Master Dao’an was not [the one who] □□□□□□□□□□ it.
"Lingwei" is the name of a monastery; it is [located at] Baogao □□□□□.
Regarding the "arising" (nidāna): from the *Cunda-parivarta* up to before the setting forth of the thirty-four questions constitutes the causal origin (*nidāna*) concerning the householders.

From the *Vyādhi-saṃdarśana-parivarta* onwards constitutes the remaining momentum of the response. According to the account in the commentary on the sutra, this scripture consists roughly of four parts:
first, from “Thus have I heard” up to the parable of the old man and the youth and the exhortation to inquire; second, from [the section on] Tālavana... [text truncated].
1. From "The falling [of the hair]" (*Luo Jiaye*) onwards is the section on posing questions. 2. From "The Buddha’s praise of Kāśyapa" onwards is the section on answering questions. 3.
From the "Kauṇḍinya Chapter" until the conclusion of the scripture is the section on entrustment and circulation. This is the classification into single-person sections;
from this point onward, the citations differ.
Vasubandhu is here called Tianqin (Heavenly Relative). He composed one fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, which is divided into seven sections;
the masters of the Di-lun school rely upon and employ it.

Furthermore, regarding the mention of "chrysanthemums and orchids" within the summary of the intent: indeed, the phrasing of the sutra passages is entirely intended to lead one into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If there is no benefit whatsoever, how can one be in accord with the principle? If one accords with the four *siddhārtha* [purposes], each will cherish [their respective goals].
By opening up their respective divisions, one may respond appropriately to the needs of things.
The story of the cowherd woman adding water is as follows.
Regarding "deep currents" and so forth, this is explained by borrowing from the eight gates of the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra*.
For example, just as deep currents cause [one to sink],... [text continues].
Now, regarding the Buddha-nature in this sutra, it is as profound and weighty as...
[omitted] ...it is divided into five or seven sections.
Within these seven [sections], the first two are understandable.
Third, explaining the names: ... [omitted] ...
Regarding "the movement" (*yun*), this clarifies the path of one's own practice (*xing*). It necessarily relies upon benefiting sentient beings (*lisheng*). ... [omitted] ...
Regarding the path of benefiting sentient beings, it is therefore said that one must "await," etc. "Movement" (*yun*) signifies being in accord with what is appropriate.

From the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha) downward, all the various classes of beings were moved by the resonance of his voice and light, shaking the earth and startling their ordinary perceptions, thereby causing their great potential for awakening to be activated; hence the expression "startled into realization" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "summoned by conditions" (*en-ken-yō-shō*): when the superior commands the subordinate, it is called a "summons" (*shō*); when the subordinate looks up to the superior, it is called a "request" (*shō*).

This refers to those who, from their original ground up until before the *Lotus Sūtra*, were all part of the assembly for forming karmic connections (*ke-en*). Because such conditions exist, they are summoned by means of sound and light;
"summoning" (*shō*) means to call forth. "To cause" (*chi*) means to arrive at. It is precisely because the assembly possesses the potential (*ki*) for *nirvāṇa* that sound and light can be employed.

He summoned the assembly of invited guests, such as the shadows and echoes, to this Guṇasī mountain. He struck the resonant mechanism of the Buddha’s realization; now, rather than looking up from below to explain it from above, he need not do so.

The Buddha explains the two aspects of the bestowal of nirvāṇa in the latter two sections. First, he clarifies the fulfillment of his own practice; second, from "originally non-existent" (*ben wu*) onwards, he clarifies the completion of his merit in transforming others.
Regarding the first, it says: "The great [capacity]... the faculties were not yet fit for it, and the time had not yet arrived."
It is called a "Treasury" (*pitaka*). Next, regarding the transformation of others, [the text] explains the intent of this transformation.
The meaning is that because sentient beings were previously incapable and...
[it states] "therefore, at first, one employs... and so forth.
Those who are smeared with poison... [text missing]. Those who wash away [the poison]...
by opening up impermanence (*anitya*) as the very nature of permanence...
[text missing]. Today, for the first time, I have come to know... [text missing].
[The subject] is both identical and different. Furthermore, it is shown that [by means of] impermanence, one destroys the view of permanence.
Moreover, for the Bodhisattva, permanence is itself true permanence. All of these are cases where the beginning is identical and the end is [differentiated].
Knowing [the occasion], he waits for the opportune moment to deliver profound teachings on the intent of transformation.

With earnest and diligent exhortation, he ensures that none are sent away with lingering obstructions, so that those present may grasp the teaching without omission. He leads them away from the biased views of purity, permanence, impermanence, and the limited vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
As for "overflowing" (*chongyi*): internally, one’s own practice is filled; externally, one transforms others until they overflow.
The fifty-two assemblies all gather at Kuśinagara and all obtain the benefit of the secret treasury of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is called "full."

However, regarding the third section of the *Bichang* (Secret Treasury), which explains the five practices: the first statement, "the abyss is congealed," means that the "abyss" is profound and "congealed" is still.

The nature of the mind of sentient beings—the three virtues of nirvana—is profoundly deep and profoundly still, being primordially and fully possessed. If one does not have the five practices, how could one possibly accord with it?
Regarding "skillful means": the triad of precepts, concentration, and wisdom is itself the dharma of skillful means.
Regarding "manifesting for those who come before": "manifesting" means to reveal; it means to make the secret treasury visible. Regarding "for those who come before":
it means that from the initial mind until the final mind, everything is made fully apparent.
"Exhorting [the Master] to explain... *Sai* (pronounced *shi-yue*) means "to manifest joy"; it refers to the sign of awakening and being free from affliction.
Regarding the statement "three fingers pointing to one": [this refers to] the *Avataṃsaka*.
It is said that by practicing the five modes of conduct, a Bodhisattva attains... [and so forth].
"Exhaustless" means that these external small [elements] and so forth, having returned to the Dharma-realm, are therefore called exhaustless. By citing one, all are subsumed;
thus, these ten categories in total— [Note:

However, regarding the application of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) within the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), at the time of delusion it is solely evil, while at the time of awakening it is solely good.
Nevertheless, its fundamental principle remains [unchanging].
As for the practitioner: because they rely upon a nature that is neither good nor evil, they are able to give rise to wholesome dharmas from within the Dharma-realm;
hence it is called "pervasive and full."
"Encompassing" (kuò): the five chapters are like a bag (náng), and Buddha-nature is like the drawstring (kuò). Among the essentials of a bag, none precedes the drawstring;

among the essentials of the Dharma, none is like Buddha-nature. It universally encompasses all dharmas. Furthermore, "kuò" means to tie or bind; it means to summarize or outline; it means to level or generalize.
Regarding the five individuals beginning with Cunda, they refer to the Deer Park where the Small Vehicle was taught;
those who follow this same pattern also apply it to the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā, wherein both the provisional and the ultimate are employed together.

These four [teachings] arise as two: first, the arising of the ultimate; second, the explanation of the underlying intent, beginning with "from time immemorial. Within the first, the arising of the ultimate, there are five chapters.
This is precisely the intended meaning of giving rise to a single sutra.

"Using [the practice] because of the meaning" means that one seeks the meaning by knowing it is dependent upon the meaning; and for the sake of seeking the meaning, one knows it is dependent upon the practice and so forth.
Next, the section beginning with "Since beginningless time" explains the underlying intent. The intent is that the essence of nirvāṇa is not subject to beginning or end.
Now, the establishment of these five chapters to discuss beginning and end is entirely for the sake of [elucidating] nirvāṇa.
Regarding "the deceased": from the highest level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) down to the exhaustion of evil, they have ultimately perished.
Now, [the text] explains all of this by contrasting the transformer (*nirmāpaka*) with the transformed (*nirmita*).
Regarding the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), [the first four] are for the sake of benefiting others, while the last is for one's own benefit.
As for the meaning of "practice" (*pratipatti*), three belong to the middle [category]. One statement is... [text fragment].
