This is the method for practicing the teachings. "Totality" refers to the capacity [of the practitioner].
The square and the circle—[the former] is like a carpenter’s square, and [the latter] is like a compass.
Furthermore, shallow practice is like the square, while deep practice is like the circle. Thus, one practices in accordance with the teachings. Practice...
This accords with principle; there are fixed rules for both the square and the circle. To manifest the circle, one relies simultaneously upon two practices;
there are none that are not called the practice of Nirvana.
Regarding the statement that "the text is extensive and the matters are manifest": the five practices constitute the cause, and the ten virtues divide the fruit; both are termed "matters.
Because one enters, abides in, and fulfills these stages to obtain the twenty-five samādhis, they are said to be "manifest."
Regarding the phrase "separately as one section": although the Lion’s Roar Sūtra speaks of six statements, all of them inquire about the Buddha-nature;
however, the latter five are merely for the purpose of establishing the initial inquiry. Furthermore, the term "one section" refers collectively to the entire set of statements.

Regarding "the multitudes of sprouts" (*qunmeng*): "sprouts" refers to the initial emergence of the buds of all things. Now, by means of this single section of the text, they have become those who can follow and benefit from the opportunity for the Buddha-nature to manifest;
therefore, they are called "the multitudes of sprouts."
Regarding those who embrace evil, this refers to Sunaksatra. Regarding those who are deluded, this refers to the followers of the ten seers.
The six citations are divided into two parts in the text. First, concerning the phrase "the Great Lion’s Roar":
it means that the various bodhisattvas, like lion cubs, gathered in the śāla grove and inspired the Tathāgata, the Great Lion King, to definitively realize [the nature of] all sentient beings.
All possess the Buddha-nature. For this reason, the Tathāgata is called the Great Lion.
[Within] one's own person are the three virtues, the *nirvāṇa*, and the dharma of the Buddha-nature.
Second, the dharma of bestowing... [is] that which I bestow upon you; you, in turn, bestow it upon others—this is called...
□□□□□□□□□□ is the principle of the Buddha, for it is the function that is identical to the essence.
Next, □□□□□□□□□□□ the Buddha-nature is not five yet is five;
therefore, one attains universal realization □□□□□□□□□□□□ all principles are identical to the Tathāgata.
The practitioner is also... [text missing] ...a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who likewise appeared as a trace during their shared practice. The spiritual friend... [text missing].
“Storing away” (藏) means to excavate the treasure-trove of the various awakenings of sentient beings and bestow them [upon others].
One should know that regarding the phrase “the gift of Prajñā,” since one wishes to know wisdom through its exposition, the exposition itself is the gift; therefore, by means of Prajñā...
Regarding giving, these are the five practices of one who acts with a single purpose; that is, the five successive practices. "One practice" refers to the practice of the Tathāgata.
"Truly upright" means truly destroying the false and correctly destroying the deviant; "straight" means destroying all that is circuitous.
That which cannot be shaken or moved—Nirvana and Buddha-nature—is like empty space. Is there any falsehood in this?
That which is crooked can be moved;
"shattered" means broken, and "dispersed" means extinguished. It simply refers to the ability to break and extinguish the fetters and delusions.

Regarding the analogy of the vajra: if one were to provide a further analogy, one would liken the afflictions (*kleśa*) to a shattered vajra, which has been broken by the scraping of a sheep’s tortoise-shell.
However, a solid vajra cannot be broken by such things as sheep’s horns; furthermore, these sheep’s horns and the like may also be used as analogies for the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*).
As for the reason why there is Buddha-nature: the principle of Buddha-nature is the ultimate destination and intended meaning of the teachings and practices of Nirvana;
this is called the "reason why" (*so-yi*). It is like when worldly people head toward a certain place—they must have a specific reason for doing so before they can proceed.
Regarding the mutual [relationship] between essence and function: because there is no essence of Buddha-nature, the functions do not mutually coincide.
[This is] because they either universally possess the three causal natures.

The seventh section concerns divergent interpretations. The first [interpretation] states that [the Buddha] preached the Dharma by specifically distinguishing between the morning, midday, and afternoon;
however, this contradicts [the principle of] universal and pervasive [teaching]. That sūtra says: "In the first year, the second year... [and so forth].
Cessation. According to that teaching, because it pertains to the views of those with specific capacities, [the text] is as profound as two chapters;
it serves generally as a chapter on application. If one were to divide it specifically... [text fragment].
He draws in those with whom he has a karmic affinity from both the past and the present. "The past" refers to [the assembly of] fifty-two followers;
these, too, do not transcend people of the past and present. This is truly because those who possess the necessary affinity will inevitably arrive when summoned.

Regarding the "Brief and Extensive Gates": Kāśyapa poses thirty-four questions; the preceding [section] constitutes the brief questions, while the extensive answers to these thirty-four questions constitute the extensive gates.
From "Practice and Merit" up to "Within the Causes," the ten virtues are the differentiation of the fruit within the causes. This is why practice and the ten... [are discussed].
If both virtue (*guṇa*) and merit (*puṇya*) belong to the cause, then there is no need for prolixity;
that is to say, there is no need for the trouble of opening [the text] into two separate sections.

As for the "Master of the Stages" (*bhūmi-ācārya*), if one follows Master Baogui, he divided [the text] into seven parts based on the treatise of Vasubandhu Bodhisattva, which differs from the present [version].
The headings introduced here are largely identical [to those in the commentary]. The first is titled "The Section on the Return Demonstration of Inconceivable Supernatural Powers";

the second is titled "The Section on Accomplishing the Spiritual Lineage and Dispelling Attachments"; the fifth is titled "The Section on Entering Realization by Remaining Free from All Heedlessness";
and the sixth is titled "The Section on Sustaining through Skillful Means of Compassionate Radiance. The remainder are all the same as in the commentary.
Regarding "the doubt concerning the lineage" (*gotra*), this clarifies that Cunda’s offering of food was intended to manifest the three causes of the Buddha-nature within sentient beings.
Because there is the sense of that which can be produced and manifested, it is termed "lineage. Furthermore, it serves to simultaneously refute provisional teachings and eliminate false attachments.
Regarding the true meaning of the True Dharma (*saddharma*): the nature of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) is the true meaning.
Regarding that which is accomplished through skillful means (*upāya*): [the text here concerns] the chapter on the establishment of skillful means.
This merely refutes its functional utility. Regarding the *Siṃhanāda* (Lion’s Roar) text: [text missing].
The ten immortals were formerly certainly heterodox; now they have entered into [the path]. [Text missing].
The principle of the chapter on manifesting present utility is as follows: [text missing].
The provisional and the ultimate are termed the "Gate of Expedient Means. [In] the *Cundavarga* (Cenru pin), [it is said that]...
[regarding] what is called the general introduction (*sūtra-piṭaka*) and the specific introduction (*nidāna*). When the Buddha was about to preach this sutra...
[The phrase] "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) arises; what is thus spoken is called the "initiation" (*nidāna*).

Because this initiation is difficult to [establish] in relation to [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa, one who has received the Buddha’s transformation and wishes to transmit what was heard to future generations first addresses the assembly of the time, saying:
"Such a Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha. To establish its credibility is called the "evidence of faith" (*saddharmapratyaya*). By means of this...

Because it provides the testimony for faith and serves as the basis for the transmission of the sutra, it is called the "Testimony of Faith Preface" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-nidāna). Next, regarding the manifestation of its intended meaning:

that which was established by the Tathāgata should have occurred at that time, while that transmitted by Ānanda was transmitted to this final age; in contrast to these two positions, they are thus called the "Two Prefaces.
Furthermore, what was performed by the Tathāgata is called the "Tathāgata Preface," and what was composed by Ānanda is called the "Ānanda Preface. Moreover...
The introduction spoken by the Tathāgata is called the "present introduction. The introduction spoken by Ānanda is called the "future introduction.
Furthermore, the introduction spoken by the Tathāgata is termed the "preface to the sūtra," while the introduction spoken by Ānanda is described as the "postscript to the sūtra."

Regarding the term "teaching-gate" (*jiaomen*): every passage within this single section is none other than teaching; the teaching itself is the gate. Furthermore, this present sutra differs from the preceding four periods [of the Buddha's career].

Prior to the *Lotus Sutra*, the provisional and the real were not yet integrated; now, although it addresses the capacities of the four types of beings, all are made to know the eternal abiding [of the Buddha-nature].

Moreover, this present sutra shares both similarities and differences with the *Lotus Sutra*. Why is this? Because the *Lotus Sutra* exclusively clarifies the opening [of the three vehicles into one].
□□□□□□□ [Taking] the provisional as real is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If one takes the real as provisional, then [the application of] □□□□□□□□□ [is likewise].
The reason the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is so excellent is precisely due to the differences in the capacities [of sentient beings]; thus, the gates of the teachings differ.
□□□□□□□□□ Now, this text merely possesses the two *paryāya* (all-inclusive). The first states: "The three periods of time..."
The Path and [the rest] are the *sarvajñatā-saṃgraha* (compendium of omniscience).
Furthermore, the exhortation to believe at the end of various sūtras constitutes the *pudgala-jñatā-saṃgraha* (compendium of knowledge of persons).
The two characters "Ā" and "Oṃ" are not the *pratipakṣa-saṃgraha* (compendium of remedies). [The rest].

Regarding "the combination of [the provisional and the real]": since it cannot be explained by means of "reaching the ultimate," one must [employ] the provisional to manifest the real and use the provisional to support the real, according to the capacity of the recipient.
The assembly... [is] the principle of... [mutual] realization.

Regarding "mutually verifying one another," it means that the five meanings depend upon one another in succession, similar to the manner in which the [twelve links of dependent origination] arise in either reverse or forward order.
"Being compliant and without delusion" means that for the sake of those who will come in the future, they shall comply with the teachings and believe in the principles without any doubt or confusion.
As for the statement "capable of transmitting [the Dharma]," furthermore, that which was transmitted by Ānanda is no different from what the Buddha taught;
it is called "Thus" (tathā) because it accords with reality, and it is called "Is" (satya) because it accords with principle—this is the intent of the Tripiṭaka.

Regarding "conforming to the capacity as being suchness": when an individual enters emptiness, they share this with the *zhàng* (Treasure) and *tōng* (Penetrating) vehicles; upon entering the Middle Way, they further share it with the Perfect Teaching.
Thus, emerging into the provisional through the ten practices is what is called "conforming to the capacity."
"Contrary to the facts" refers to practicing and studying according to the sequential order; "conformable to principle" refers to the teachings discussing the central truth.

If one relies on faith, one distinguishes between the provisional and the real; if one relies on the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), for every single meaning, one first analyzes it according to causes and conditions, then judges it, and finally reveals it.
Since the current text has already performed the judgment, it corresponds to the stage of revelation. However, this is because we follow the literal meaning of the text. Therefore...
No separate section for the "Opening Text" is established.
Regarding "different yet not different": because they all enter the secret treasury, it is said they are not different. "Guǐ" (詭) means strange or anomalous.
Regarding "the fruit and retribution being manifold and mixed": this arises from the [various] fruit and retributions... [text missing].
Regarding "mutually eclipsing": the coarse eclipses the subtle; the refined eclipses the crude; and the same applies to outshining.
This is because it is viewed with the eyes of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the second [type of] giving (up to) "without distinction": through pure [giving], one brings about a superior body.
One should ask the Tathāgata about the distinctions between the present and the past. [The text continues: ... [omitted].
Those who take refuge in the place of cessation [realize] that the principle of Buddha-nature is such that all virtues return to the Dharma-body and abide in the secret treasury.
Because sentient beings are not [diverse], the Buddhas of the ten directions are one; the present Buddhas of the ten directions are one. This is... [the ultimate unity].

The squares represent the Buddhas appearing in the present. Because they initiate an influence through the formation of karmic conditions for those who are ready to receive the teaching, [the text] is arranged according to the six stages of Buddhahood (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi-buddhatva*).

The Buddhas are assigned to the number eight; the Buddhas of the eight directions constitute the eight, and when Śākyamuni, the primary teacher of transformation, is included, they are also called the nine Buddhas.
Regarding "evil and non-duality": evil itself is the secret treasury; therefore, they are non-dual.
Regarding "the fourfold assembly is not the eight Buddhas": because the provisional and the real differ and the capacities of sentient beings remain mixed, they are not the eight Buddhas.

Regarding the distinction between superior and inferior in the beginning and end: the sequence of shallow and deep is termed "superiority and inferiority. Because these merely induce the five fruits of human and celestial rebirth, one cannot yet escape impermanence and the cycle of birth and death;
therefore, they are called "transient migrations."

Regarding the Jing and Wei rivers: the clarity of the Jing is a metaphor for the correct, while the Wei is a metaphor for the deviant. The "low" (referring to the *jī* and *mǎo* constellations) refers to evil fish. In the past, turtles and fish were not together in the same water;
today, they are all together in the waters of the Great Parinirvāṇa. This serves as proof of the application of good and evil.
Those who receive and practice [this teaching] with reverence, having heard it at one time, will receive and practice it like a chief treasury minister, practicing the conduct of a Tathāgata.
The Buddha dwells in that which is the dwelling of a Buddha; the Buddha takes the great cave of *nirvāṇa* as his abode. It is precisely this that he now speaks.
Because it is the assembly at the time of giving, it is called "bestowing" (*dāna*).
Regarding the meaning of the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyakośa*) of the Western Sea: the Western Sea is a metaphor for the Secret Treasury.
Thus, the general introduction of the three points [refers to] the various sections; no section exists that does not emerge from these three points. Three...
This is the teaching (*śāsana*). Therefore, it is thus summarized... [omitted].
...Because hearing belongs to the teaching, it is contrasted with *prajñā*. Furthermore, one wishes to know the wisdom (*jñāna*)... [omitted].
The [blank] refers to the fact that when one’s capacity is matched by the principle, all accumulated karmic bonds are forever forgotten;
thus, in contrast to [the mundane], it is [the realm of] bliss. Furthermore, hearing the teaching of Buddha-nature abiding within the secret treasury, [it is] in accord with [reality];
it can purify the three delusions, and therefore it is designated as "pure."
Those who heard it together—[omitted]—manifested that Ānanda received and upheld [the teaching] without error, with sovereign mastery and unimpededness.
Thus, [omitted]... direct transmission is pure; hearsay is diluted.
This is to establish the preceding phrase and clarify that there is no error.
The sequence [of numbers] is such that each subsequent number serves as the initial term for the following.
This refers to the dharmas refuted by the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka.

As for the unification of the ultimate and the conventional: according to the Separate Teaching (pṛthagjana), one first realizes the ultimate and subsequently the conventional; it is only later, upon ascending to the stages (bhūmi), that the ultimate and conventional are unified.

Regarding the three bodies and four meanings: from the superior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the inferior response-body emerges. Because this is contrasted with the Tripiṭaka, it is said that Śākyamuni appears repeatedly and passes away repeatedly;

this refers precisely to this [inferior] body. The superior response-body corresponds to the Shared [Vehicle], the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) belongs to the Distinct [Vehicle], and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) belongs to the Perfect [Vehicle].
Although the bodies are fundamentally only three, they are spoken of as four according to the capacities of those to be taught.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha is present" (*buddhaḥ tiṣṭhati*) in the sūtra: to dwell for a long duration is called "residing" (*tiṣṭhati*); to travel for a short time is called "being present" (*tiṣṭhati*).
For example, it is said that the Buddha resided on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa for eight years preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and thus one speaks of the Buddha residing in Rājagṛha and so forth.
Now, the Buddha is for the last time present at the Twin Śāla Trees; beginning from the early morning until midnight, he preached this sūtra. Therefore, it says "the Buddha is present."
"蓑" (suó, a type of grass used for rainwear).
"Mao City" (茅城) is called Mao City in the Āgama Sūtras;
this is translated as "Firm and Solid" (堅固), meaning that wind and frost cannot alter it, and the four seasons cannot shift it—used as a metaphor for the Dharmakāya.
The substance of a diamond cannot be changed by the two types of death, nor can it be affected by the three delusions; it is firm and solid.
Regarding that which resembles the "Mutual Ceding" tree (*jiāoràng*), the *Bówùzhì* states:
"In Ānxì County, there is a tree where those that wither flourish, and those that flourish wither again; it is called the 'Mutual Ceding' tree. Now... [text fragment].
□□□□□ As when the noble and the lowly associate, because they associate with one another there is no duality.
Although □□□□□□□□□□□□, the two trees are one flourishing and the other withered.
This represents the Dharma □□□□□□□□□□□□ tree. Today, the teaching is perfected and entrusted to it.
It is a pair.
Because of this, the eight [squares]... [omitted] ...are called one grove.
Regarding "arising and ceasing": this refers to impermanence, birth, and death; as well as... [omitted] ...is called "arising."

[This is] omitted. This [category] encompasses both the two vehicles of the two teachings; if one perceives this as the arousal of the bodhicitta, it is specifically for the distinct [vehicle], while for the universal [vehicle], it refers to the bodhisattva.
Regarding the "place of the vow," it means the arousal of the universal vow and the distinct [vow].
Regarding "cultivating meditative concentration and so forth": it refers to cultivating the three trainings to fulfill one's vows; thus, the word "and so forth" is used.
Regarding "showing compassion to people": this means manifesting a physical body to preach the fourfold teachings in order to demonstrate the perfect and eternal Buddha-nature.

The "Wrestler" symbolizes the self: it manifests the sovereign power of the Dharmakāya, which possesses the strength of the Great Self, while simultaneously eliminating the affliction of clinging to a [limited] self.
The "Auspicious River" symbolizes purity: entering its waters to wash away transgressions represents the purification of the three delusions.
Regarding "being pure by virtue of having no owner": that city is so firm and secure that evil cannot invade it; furthermore, because there is no evil within that city, it can be described as pure.
Regarding "being eternal by virtue of having no owner": if something has an owner, it is impermanent; yet that which is impermanent is itself the eternal—the essence of Buddha-nature.
It is all-pervasive, like empty space; therefore, it can represent permanence.
As for the mind’s peace representing bliss: three hundred thousand people dwell together there, yet none are able to disturb it;
thus, peace is used to represent bliss.
"Form manifests purity through its delightfulness": because form is pure and because the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure, form manifests purity through its delightfulness.
"The perpetual flow manifests permanence": if there were a flow that did not flow, it would be impermanent; however, this [flow] flows perpetually without interruption.
Therefore, it can manifest the eternal. The commentary on the sutra states: "The rushing and deep flow of a river is used as a metaphor for [the nature of reality].
By means of this, it is revealed that within the midst of birth and death there exists Buddha-nature.
The essence of gold does not [change]; it is said that [this refers to] the place where Jambūnada gold is found. Among waters, this is the purest."
Do not exceed [the bounds of propriety].
That which expresses coolness is joy; it refreshes the body and delights the mind, and thus it may be expressed.
[The rest] is used to express my own self.
Regarding "the two pillars of the east symbolizing permanence":
[text omitted]. Furthermore, regarding "the two flourishing [pillars]": these two terms serve as a heading for the three subsequent phrases.
[Text omitted]. While they are distinct, they are also unified; the essence of the Dharma is non-dual. Because it is non-dual, it is explained in two ways.
Regarding the "eight Buddhas among the nine Buddhas": Śākyamuni, as the presiding teacher of transformation, is the giver, while the eight Buddhas are the assembly to whom they give;
thus, they are called "the eight Buddhas among [the nine]."
As for my statement, "I say," the intended meaning is this: if one were to discuss those who heard [the teaching] together, it would apply only to the general introduction (*sūtra-pūrva-vṛtti*).

However, here all fifty-two [bodhisattvas] have been summoned by the sound and light; they possess both provisional and ultimate aspects, and their capacity to respond to the teaching and form karmic conditions are fully complete.
For this reason, all fifty-two are equally "those who heard together. I have pre-emptively indicated this intent so that you may understand the proper boundaries.
One should know that the distinction between the two lies in wisdom (*jñāna*) and the path (*mārga*).

For example, regarding those who are blind, although the text enumerates the seven factors of enlightenment and distinguishes the two matters of place and time, they do not see them because they lack the capacity;
thus, they are said to be "like the blind."

Regarding the "Praise of Virtues": there is no separate text for the praise of virtues in this current sutra; therefore, the term "Great Words" (*mahā-akṣara*) should correspond to the praise of virtues. As for "mastery of the four Vedas":
these are (1) recitation and chanting, (2) sacrificial rites, (3) singing and hymns, and (4) the averting of calamities. One Veda consists of three hundred and twenty thousand verses (*gāthā*).
In total, there are one hundred and twenty-eight verses [per section], amounting to one thousand seven hundred fascicles. That is to say:
These are the non-Buddhist Vedas and the Buddhist Tripiṭaka of inner science; thus they receive many names.
Regarding those who are learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*): the former two teachings also belong to the Buddha as one beyond learning.

Regarding the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*): humans, devas, and those of the two teachings of the Two Vehicles constitute four; together with the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings, they form seven.
Furthermore, [the practitioners] of the two teachings... constitute three.
Regarding the assembly of those destined for certainty (*niyata-rāśi*): it is for the purpose of opening up the provisional (*upāya*) to reveal the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*).
"Not looking upward" means not gazing at the stars and constellations, and so forth.
"Not looking downward" means not performing tasks such as acting as a messenger for the state, and so forth. "Not maintaining" refers to not [maintaining]... and so forth.
□. Regarding "fearing the wolf of impermanence," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Because of [the nature of] impermanence...
one uses the wisdom of arising and ceasing to contemplate the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as being impermanent from moment to moment, like [being pursued by] a wolf.
The [blank] refers to using the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) to realize that the four dharmas within the *piṭaka* are all like illusions and transformations.
To "sustain the life of wisdom" and know that evil is not evil means to realize the emptiness of destruction.
Furthermore, there is no knower; even that which is able to contemplate is empty. "Those who fear the aggregates" refers to the destruction of the obstacles of retribution.

"All dharmas" refers to penetrating the three preceding teachings through the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), thereby maintaining a pure livelihood and emerging from the terrors of Māra and so forth.
This refers to the fact that the Dharma-realm is eternally and fully endowed with bliss; therefore, it is said that "all possess" it.
Regarding those who break the precepts and so forth: as explained below in the *Vajrakāya-parivarta*, one who breaks the precepts is also called a "mixed monk" (*saṃgha-vyāmīśra*).

Because both the non-manifestation of good and evil coexist within such a person, they are termed a "mixed monk. However, one who merely maintains the precepts for oneself while remaining ignorant of the affairs of others is called "foolish."
"Deluded monk!

Those such as Wǎn (Dàoshuān) and others are those who possess a sense of shame (*hrī*); this is a distinction made according to their essential nature. If one takes the term in its general sense, then in the Perfect Teaching (*yánjiào*), from the very beginning, those who hear the Perfect [Teaching] belong to the category of those with shame;
the same applies by analogy to the other three teachings."
Furthermore, there are four meanings. "Reality" refers to the two assemblies of those who have already produced the influence [of faith] and those who are currently responding to it.

"Having shame" refers to the two assemblies of those who are currently responding to the teaching and those who are establishing karmic connections. Moreover, "reality" encompasses all three assemblies, whereas "having shame" applies only to those establishing karmic connections.
This is because the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties is designated as either establishing karmic connections or being currently responding to the teaching; hence it is so stated.
"Or merely persons, etc. refers simply to counting either individual persons repeatedly, or counting the emptiness of the dharmas of persons;
this is the intent of the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared). "Or counting dharma-gates" refers to the six dharma-gates of the *Pratyekabuddha* (Distinct) teaching.
"Or counting the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*)" refers to the Perfect Teaching. [From... [The remainder of the text follows].
[It is] also thus. Regarding "surrounding": "sur" (圍) refers to the stationary posture; "yaou" (遶) refers to circumambulation. ... [omitted] ...
As for "reverencing with the three karmas," each instance possesses its respective dignified deportment. ... [omitted] ...
The movement in relation to the four teachings can be understood accordingly.
This is precisely the invocation; it is established by means of the sequence of [the syllables] □□□□□□□□. These are the words that constitute the "precisely" (zhengshi).
"Regarding 'responding to the opportune moment' (*kiki*): it refers to the time when the opportunity is about to open.
As for 'the Way of the Center': it signifies the Middle Way, the perfect and eternal *nirvāṇa*-dharma."
Regarding the time when the moon is full: the moon is able to wax and wane, and its function surpasses that of the sun; therefore, the full moon is taken as the symbol. Sengliang said:
"The second month is the central season of spring's harmony, unlike winter and summer, which are characterized by the extremes of cold and heat.
Previously, suffering and emptiness were taught like those extremes; now that both principles are revealed together, the full moon is chosen to represent this central harmony."
"Not waiting and not passing beyond" means it is neither before the second month nor after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; it is precisely the fifteenth day of the second month.

"Not waiting" means that when the capacity [of sentient beings] has not yet matured, one does not wait for it to do so. "Not passing beyond" means that once the capacity has matured, one does not pass beyond the time to manifest the name [of the Buddha].
Regarding the phrase "at the time of approaching [extinction]," this is explained by means of the act of approaching. "Approaching" (lin) refers to being on the verge of extinction.

When the sound emerges in the early morning, it is destined to cease at midnight; since its departure from extinction is not far off, it is called "approaching. Thus, he proclaims *nirvāṇa* to respond to the assembly that has been awakened.

"By means of the Buddha's supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)" means by means of its application. That is to say, he employs the supernormal power of the body at will (*kāya-ṛddhi*), operating without deliberation, and proclaims with a great voice everywhere.
Furthermore, it may also be said that the Buddha is the root and the supernatural power is the branch.

Furthermore, regarding the "wisdom of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-prajñā*), this is an explanation according to the teachings. Wisdom of emptiness serves as the foundation. It pertains to the Buddhas who appear through the first two teachings;
the Buddha of the distinct [teaching] is the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), while the Buddha of the perfect [teaching] is the reality-mark (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, regarding "great sound": first, it is great because its awakening reaches afar; second, it is great because it universally proclaims; third, it is great because it explains matters of great significance.
This too is capable of withstanding challenge. Now, [someone] has raised an objection based on the preceding master; his words are indeed consistent with reason.
Regarding the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*): [text missing].
These two belong to the preceding two teachings, which correspond horizontally to the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*).
"Regarding the 'summit' (mūrdhan) of □□: this refers to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) within these Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka).
Furthermore, the three [stages] of □□□□□□□□□: the summit belongs to the subsequent distinct and perfect [teachings]."
Thus, there should be no duality. [The text here is fragmentary: ...should manifest and enter into the perfect and eternal;
therefore it is said there is no duality.
To cause those who praise [this teaching] to revere and look up to it... the three titles that encompass all phenomena come forth, for the benefit of sentient beings.
It causes one to revere and look up to. "Revere" (chóng) means, according to the *Yǎyùn*, "to value" and "to be lofty.
"Truly identical" (yǔntóng) means "truly in accord. This clarifies that all Buddhas come from within Suchness; therefore, Śākyamuni is truly so.

He is identical to all Buddhas. Furthermore, all Buddhas possess the ten titles, and Śākyamuni is likewise so; therefore, he is truly the same [as them]. This inspires in others a sense of reverence and veneration.
Regarding his being the "World-Father": the World-Father is able to give birth to and nourish me; thus he is worthy of reverence and veneration. The Buddha is the one who has transcended the world.

The Father can give birth to and nourish the Dharma-body; therefore, he is worthy of veneration and respect, and is thus the Lord of the World. He is able to bring glory to my partial and perfect good karma.

Karma has its beginning and end, whereas the Buddha is the Lord who transcends the world and is able to bring glory to my partial and perfect good karma. The meaning of "Teacher" (Śāstṛ) is evident here.
In essence, these three meanings are simply that they enable us to destroy evil and give rise to goodness, allowing us to enter the Secret Treasury. There is no kinship more fitting than this.
There is no father; there is no one to revere as a teacher.
The Original Father, the Sovereign, and the Teacher—these three are all my original fathers, sovereigns, and teachers with whom I formed karmic connections.
Through their intermediate cultivation and ripening, I have today been delivered and liberated; none of this has occurred without being due to these three.
"Compassionate" (lian) means that because of loving-kindness, and because of love, one is able to bestow the bliss of supramundane liberation.
"Pitying" (min) means that because of sympathetic sorrow, one is able to uproot the sufferings of the two types of death and so forth.
Regarding the third title: A ruler is that to whom the myriad people turn; a father is that to which a son turns; a teacher is that upon which disciples rely. [They] act as a refuge.
Regarding "being a shelter for the world": just as people in the world find joy upon obtaining a house, [so it is here].
That which is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness, just like obtaining a fine house. Compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract [suffering], [and so forth].
When the mind is joyful, regardless of whether things are refined or coarse, this is termed the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*). [And so forth].
[Blank]. Those who desire *nirvāṇa*—if the Buddha were still in the world, he would be their lord, kinsman, and teacher. [Because of this...
it is therefore necessary to raise these questions.
Regarding "clarifying the four meanings in each section": this means that for every single phrase, one must interpret it according to the four teachings. "Ming" (明) signifies clarity;
it also implies dawn, representing the power of the light of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the "face-gate" (*mukha-dvāra*): a "gate" refers to the passage for entering and exiting. Here, the emission of light from the face-gate symbolizes the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
It emerges as it traverses [the mouth]. The commentary states: "Light issues from the mouth to signify the aspect of the most supreme and wondrous teaching."
The Sūtra states, "Its light is of variegated colors. If one were to analyze the scriptural text, one should first present the essence of the light; hence it says "variegated colors.
Subsequently, from "blue and yellow" onwards, it demonstrates the characteristics of the light.
Regarding "according to one's own intention": every word and every action accords with the secret treasury; therefore, it is called "self.
Regarding "according to the intentions of others": the principle of Buddha-nature establishes various names according to the capacities and circumstances of sentient beings, pervading all teachings.
This is called "following others.
To correctly express this, it precisely indicates that the sentient beings of the ten realms all enter the ocean of Great Nirvāṇa;
thus, it is named the dwelling place of sentient beings with great bodies.
"Rescuing those in the six realms" means establishing sentient beings of the six realms within the secret treasury of Great Nirvana;
this is the greatness of rescuing them.
"Purifying the six faculties" means purifying the six faculties of the two stages—the semblance and the true.

Regarding the "trichiliocosm" (three thousandfold great thousandfold world system): as explained in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, one thousand sets of four continents combined together are called a small thousandfold world system (*sāhasracūdikalokadhātu*).

When these small systems are counted up to one thousand and further combined into one, it is called a middle thousandfold world system (*dvisāhasramadhyamasāhasralokadhātu*). When these middle systems are counted up to one thousand, [it constitutes a trichiliocosm].

These are further combined into one, called a "great chiliocosm" (*mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). Because these three thousand worlds are destroyed simultaneously, they are combined into one; this is what is termed a "world-system" (*lokadhātu-kṣetra*).

Regarding the phrase "the three karmas can be known": ancient masters took the three obstructions and the three wholesome [roots] and treated them as a single section; therefore, it is said that [the meaning] can be known.
The Sūtra says, "Having seen and heard this": this refers to seeing the light and hearing the sound.
Regarding the "three karmas": there are those who, despite seeing and hearing, do not feel mental distress; and though they raise their voices, they do not weep.

Although one may clap the hands upon the head, one does not strike the chest; thus, the three karmas are not fully accomplished. One should first indicate what is unaccomplished in order to manifest what is accomplished.
The Sūtra states, "At that time, the great earth... This refers precisely to the moment of the sound and light, for it was then that the great earth shook.
Regarding mutual dependence: ignorance is the root, like the earth; views and craving are the branches and twigs, like water depending on the earth.
As for "delusion and craving": delusion is ignorance, and craving consists of both craving and views; however, only two are listed here by way of abbreviation.

Regarding "arising with surging movement" (*samudīraṇa*): the new translation renders this as "moving, leaping, shaking, striking, roaring, and bursting. Here, the old interpretation is adopted. To be light and unsteady is called "movement" (*iṭ*).

To rise from a lower level to a higher one is called "arising" (*ut*). To have uneven elevations and depressions like a rocky mound is called "leaping" (*udīraṇa*). The rising and sinking of the six directions is also termed "leaping.

To have a deep, rumbling sound is called "shaking" (*praśvāsa*). To emit a crashing, resonant roar is called "roaring" (*nirghoṣa*). To cause sentient beings to awaken is called "awakening" (*bodhana*). [The new translation...]
The clouds strike like a blow; the explosions are like the sound of fire. As for the six movements:
entering the womb, emerging from the womb, leaving home, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of the Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.

Each of these further has three types: movement, pervasive movement, and total pervasive movement. Movement refers to the shaking of the four continents; pervasive movement refers to the great [shaking].
The "thousand movements" constitute the universal movement; the same applies to the other five [elements], totaling eighteen movements. These represent the eighteen pure realms (*dhātu*).
If the six sense faculties are purified, each consists of three: namely, the faculty, consciousness, and object.
Regarding "or at one time": in other sūtras, [the events] occur either before or after; here, however, they occur simultaneously.
Regarding "to restrain": the great assembly must now exercise judgment and deliberation as to what purpose the Tathāgata’s emission of light serves.
He preached the Dharma for my benefit; furthermore, as he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he spoke thus. "To suppress" means to endure or to cease.
One should suppress and bring to rest sorrow and affliction.

A great kalpa (*mahākalpa*) consists of eighty cycles of increase and decrease. Now, within this Bhadrakalpa, up until the fifteenth cycle of decrease, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas will appear simultaneously.
If one were to request [the duration of] a great kalpa, it would obstruct this [reckoning].
"Wholesome karma is exhausted" means that limited and minor wholesome karma is subject to exhaustion. To explain this sequentially and establish the point regarding sorrow and suffering:
if one loses the primary [object of refuge], one loses the spiritual teacher; if one loses the spiritual teacher, one loses the other two as well.

Regarding those with specific affairs: they are distinguished by their physical traces and the intimacy or distance of their relationship. The Śrāvakas have forms that have emerged from the mundane net; their traces are close to the Tathāgata, and they have realized the sūtras, making them intimate.

Therefore, they are listed first. Devas and humans have forms that differ [from the Buddha] and attire that is distinct; their traces do not consist of personal service, and they have realized the sūtras only distantly. Thus, they follow.
Therefore, they are listed last. The form of a bodhisattva is not constrained by formal decorum, and their traces have no fixed location.
Since they are neither the same as the laity nor different from the monastic community, they occupy a position between the "junior" and the "senior," and thus are placed in the middle rank.
Regarding "manifestation" (*vijñapti*): Śrāvakas delight in *nirvāṇa*, while devas and humans are attached to birth and death; each has its own partiality.

The Bodhisattva neither delights in nor is attached to either, but dwells seeking the fundamental principle; thus, he stands between the two. Furthermore, the manifestation of the Śrāvaka represents the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the manifestation of the Bodhisattva represents the conventional middle way, and the manifestation of the miscellaneous assembly represents the provisional.
Moreover, understanding through phenomena resembles the teaching of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), whereas understanding through manifestation penetrates the abbreviated teachings.
To startle those who will question later: for those from outside the assembly, both their faculties and their bodies arrive [simultaneously];
for those already at the Buddha’s side, he merely summons their faculties to stir them and cause them to respond; therefore, it is necessary to summon them.
Furthermore, regarding "from many": this interpretation is inferior to the previous one which takes it as "at that time.
As for "immeasurable at that time": this refers precisely to the moment when the great voice was emitted, light was radiated, and the earth shook.
The Venerable One yielded to both sides being full. Thus the *Lunyu* says: "Hui looked upon me as a father; I looked upon Hui as a younger brother.
To say that Hui was like a younger brother means that Hui regarded himself as a son, while he revered the Master as a father.

Yet the Master declined to accept being treated as a father and instead regarded him as an elder brother, treating Hui as a younger brother. Therefore, although both sides were now full, he addressed Hui by the name "younger brother."
Regarding the first matter: furthermore, the *Chao* states, "One who generates understanding from me is like a son; one who studies after me is like a younger brother.
This also refers to a single individual.
I admire his virtuous deeds and accomplishments, rather than his years.
Since you are capable of leaving the household life—if you do not leave the household life, you shall become a Mara-king, occupying his palace and gathering his followers;
therefore, I have caused you to leave the household life.
Regarding the phrase "cleansing the three obstacles" and so forth: in the preceding text, one first cleanses the three obstacles and subsequently gives rise to the three virtues.

"Residual habits" refers here to the worldly perspective, where there is a distinction between those who have severed [the obstacles] and those who have not. "Models" refers to the generation of virtue.
Regarding "separate delusions": to treat these separate delusions is precisely the application of specific antidotes. The Buddha-dharma realm is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Since every teaching possesses the four *siddhāntas*, I shall now distinguish them according to the four teachings.

Regarding "one who has attained mastery over the mind," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One whose mind has attained excellent liberation is a person liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

One whose wisdom has attained excellent liberation is a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*). Because [the former] has not yet reached non-arising and is subject to regression, they are not praised here."
Regarding "non-arising": birth is the root of suffering, and delusion is the cause of birth. Since Arhats have severed the delusions of the three realms, the fruit of suffering does not arise;
thus, they are "non-arising. Furthermore, because the causes of affliction are exhausted and what was intended has been accomplished, it is called "already done" (*kṛtāvin*).
Moreover, they have attained the ultimate *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) and *anutpādajñāna* (knowledge of non-arising).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "departing from one's permanent dwelling place," and so forth:

in the Western Regions (India), every morning, those who first chew *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks) and rinse their mouths always do so in a secluded and private location, not within their living quarters.

Regarding "Pāṭali": in the Sanskrit original, it refers to the space between the twin śāla trees. On the day the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the people of the world wept so profusely that the entire ground became mud;
the faces of those who wailed were like flowering trees.

"Simple" does not mean shallow or superficial. The emptiness of the "City of Transformation" (nirvāṇa as a provisional resting place) is called shallow; however, what is now [discussed] is ultimate emptiness and the emptiness of nirvāṇa, and is therefore not shallow.
Sengliang said: "The various arhats know that the Buddha is eternal. Now, wishing to invite the Buddha, they seek to clarify the teaching of eternity.
This sutra elucidates permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and is free from the twenty-five states of existence; therefore, it is called 'Supreme'."
The meaning is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
As for the question regarding the ultimate: the ultimate resides in Buddha-nature; there is nothing that surpasses this.

When the sutra says "for the sake of all sentient beings," it is because they are moved by the earth; as the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings are activated, they are thus able to offer [homage].

Regarding the "Earthquake Summons," those who have attained profound realization understand that the Buddha has three summonings. Their intent is to cause the removal of the three obstructions and the generation of the three virtues, thereby manifesting the Esoteric Teachings so they shall not be severed.
It is intended to inspire a sense of urgency and resolve; thus, the entire assembly at that time each complied with the Tathāgata.
The meaning of the three invocations is precisely the sign of profound realization and understanding.
"Niyi" (尼姨) refers to a "nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*), which is a name from the Western [tradition], while "niyu" (姨女) is a designation used in this region [of China].
Regarding these three invocations: the scripture states that "also at dawn, one follows the invocation of light from below"; "the hairs of the entire body follow the invocation of light from below";
and "manifesting [the response] follows the invocation of sound from below. For the sake of taming all sentient beings, "one follows the invocation of movement from below.
This single passage of scripture fully encompasses these three meanings.
"Among the noble and holy ones" refers to the dragons among those of the previous three teachings, demonstrating that they are the foremost within these two ranks.
Regarding "the pair of cause and effect":
following this, one constantly practices and cultivates; the subsequent passage clarifies the cultivation of the cause, whereby one attains the power of mastery. The following is... [text ends]
"Attaining the fruit. This merely explains and establishes the previous meaning;
therefore, it is not used here. "Known by many people": because the river is near the city, it is known by many; this refers to the mundane world (*loka*). "Attaining merit and generating goodness":

among the eight great rivers, abandoning the small and rejoicing in the great, as well as people washing away their sins, all belong to the category of remedial application (*pratipakṣa*). This is the birth of the Buddha.
The state of non-abiding is the true principle; it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the ten meanings of the Bodhisattva: this treatise employs the Mahāyāna to refute the Hīnayāna, clarifying both the subject and the object together, such that the meaning of the Bodhisattva is fully established through the four teachings.
Now, this must also be explained by correlating each instance with the four teachings (*catur-yāna*) of the Bodhisattvas.

First, regarding the transformation of sentient beings: in the first two teachings, one merely delivers beings within the six *dharmadhātus*. In the distinct (*pratyeka*) teaching, the Bodhisattva successively delivers beings within the ten realms.
In the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) teaching, the Bodhisattva universally delivers beings throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Bodhisattva..."

One does not resolve the mind for the sake of a single sentient being, but rather resolves the mind toward Bodhi for the sake of all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm; this is precisely what constitutes the perfection of intention.
Second, regarding the exhaustive making of offerings to all Buddhas: even among the twenty schools of the Hīnayāna, there are those who permit [the practice of] the ten...
Regarding "purifying the Buddhas," it may also be said that this constitutes making offerings to all Buddhas.

Third, regarding "completely purifying all Buddha-lands": one takes up these lands for the sake of all sentient beings. Because the attainment of Buddhahood by sentient beings is not uniform, it is necessary to completely purify them.
Regarding "fourth, exhausting all by upholding all Buddha-dharmas," this is explained for now in terms of one's own practice.
Regarding "fifth, exhausting all by ensuring they are not interrupted," this is because one constantly acts as a successor to transmit the lamp.

Regarding the sixth, the analysis of exhaustion: the Dharma-realm and Buddha-lands differ in their variations of height and depth; the preaching of the Dharma also varies, being partial, complete, sudden, or gradual.

One must therefore analyze which land sentient beings utilize to attain the three stages of planting the seeds of enlightenment, ripening those seeds, and liberation. Thus, a detailed classification is required.
Seventh, complete knowledge of [the causes]: by what dharma-characteristics do the Buddhas open [the path] for their disciples?
Eighth, complete knowledge of the minds of sentient beings: discerning the differences among the minds of sentient beings within the ten dharma-realms, as well as the three non-differences.
Ninth, as for "thoroughly knowing and severing": having personally severed one's own afflictions, one must universally cause all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm to sever all afflictions.
Tenth, as for "thoroughly knowing the faculties": from the five precepts and ten wholesome paths up to the faculties and natures of the four teachings, all are thoroughly known. Now...
The text states that "purifying the Buddha-lands" refers to purifying the other three lands—the Enjoyment for Others and so forth—based upon the Land of Quiescent Light.
Furthermore, these ten meanings must arise in both reverse and direct order to manifest the mutual dependence of the ten aspects of the Bodhisattva's practice.
First is the Great Adornment: to extract suffering and bestow happiness through unconditioned compassion is itself the adornment.
Second is the relinquishing of all things: this refers to body, life, and wealth; "noble" and "lowly" refer to the primary and secondary supports [the self and one's environment].
Regarding "internal and external": one's own person is internal; wife and children are external.

As for "the four types of followers who are capable," these include those with the roots of goodness of humans and devas, up to those of the partial and limited [vehicles], and subsequently causes them all to abide in Great Nirvāṇa.

Fifth, "not grasping at 'other' and 'self': 'other' refers to the sentient beings to be saved, while 'self' refers to the mind that saves them; furthermore, this does not negate the aforementioned 'other' and 'self.
Seventh, 'unmixed mind': to practice the six perfections with a biased or limited (Hīnayāna) mind is termed defiled and not pure."
The mind. Why is this? Because it does not dedicate itself toward unexcelled bodhi or proceed toward great nirvana.

Regarding the "eight worldly activities," this refers to the Bodhisattva entering the gate of profound mystery (chongxuan) and practicing all mundane affairs in an inverted manner; such is their intent.
Regarding the statement that "the ocean-like assembly is as vast as a great collection," the fifth fascicle of that sutra says:
"At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Great Jewel Monastery (Mahāratnavyūha) between the realms of desire and form, preaching the Dharma surrounded by a great multitude.
At that moment, the great waters filled the trichiliocosm, like a vast ocean; yet within those worlds, the kingdoms, towns, houses, and mountains [remained distinct]."
The forest trees, reaching up to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), were not harmed in the slightest; they all appeared exactly as before.
At that time, immeasurable *puṇḍarīka* lotuses emerged from the water, with stems of blue lapis lazuli and leaves of pure gold, and so forth.
Then the great assembly each saw themselves sitting upon these flowers. Those flowers then emitted a great radiance, illuminating the ten directions without exception.
[Measuring] the world-systems. At that time, the great assembly addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this trichiliocosm become filled with great waters, like a vast ocean? The Buddha told Maitreya:
"Below this world-system, past as many worlds as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, there is a world named Ratnavyūha. In that land, there is a Buddha."
He is titled the Tathāgata Ocean-Wisdom Supernatural Powers (Sāgarajñānābhijña). There is a bodhisattva there named Sāgarasāgara who wishes to come here to this great jeweled pavilion;
therefore, he first manifested these auspicious signs (and so forth). It is now said that this Sāgarasāgara is none other than that very Sāgaramati.
It is merely a difference in names.
Regarding the citation of eighty kinds of Dharma-gates, the thirty-first fascicle of that sutra states:
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "To the east of here, passing through worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Ganges-sands, there is a world named Animiṣa (Unblinking). Within it..."
There is a Buddha named Samantabhadra Tathāgata. Therein dwells a bodhisattva named Akṣayamati. At that time, Śāriputra addressed Akṣayamati, saying:
"I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will explain the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattvas—how it is inexhaustible as attained by all bodhisattvas.
Son of Good Family, how is the Prajñāpāramitā practiced? How is it entered? No [other words].
Akṣayamati said: "One practices according to what has been heard and skillfully enters into contemplation. Śāriputra asked: "How does one practice according to what has been heard?
Akṣayamati replied: "The hearer possesses eighty modes of conduct, namely: the conduct of the desire to practice; the conduct of compliance with the mind;
the conduct of ultimate resolve; the conduct of constant initiation; the conduct of drawing near to virtuous friends; the conduct of freedom from pride; and the conduct of non-negligence."
The practice of respectful conduct; the practice of acting in accordance with instructions; the practice of following wholesome speech; the practice of frequently visiting the teacher;

the practice of listening with a sincere mind; the practice of avoiding unwholesome thoughts; the practice of an undistracted mind; the practice of a diligent and energetic mind; the practice of conceiving the notion of reality; the practice of conceiving the notion of medicine; the practice of eliminating all ailments;
and so on, up to the practice of attaining all Buddha-dharmas, as explained at length in the sutras.

One who skillfully enters into contemplation possesses the thirty-two marks; that is to say, they skillfully enter into the meditative concentration of upholding [the Dharma], skillfully enter into the wisdom of discernment, skillfully enter into the gentleness of mind, and skillfully enter into bodily conduct and so forth (and so on).

According to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), it cites the eighteen kinds of emptiness from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to clarify the inexhaustibility of emptiness, and the eighteen gates of inexhaustibility from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* to clarify the inexhaustibility of the provisional.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "That which is inexhaustible is neither exhausted nor inexhaustible; this is the Middle Way.

"Inexhaustible" refers to the object (*viṣaya*), and "intention" (*mati*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*). When wisdom accords with the object, the object and wisdom are designated together; hence, it is called "inexhaustible intention."
Regarding what is called "Dharma": since it is said that one must revere and honor the Mahāyāna, this refers to the Dharma that proceeds from cause to fruition.

Now, as for what is termed the "principle-Dharma" (*li-fa*), it refers to the essential substance (*ti*) upon which one rides throughout the causal and resultant stages; it is the Teacher of the Buddhas, and therefore it is revered and honored.
Regarding the statement that "nothing surpasses Prajñā," this refers to the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*), which is the principle to be revered.
As for the phrase "all dwell [therein]," the subsequent text says, "settle these sons. Since we are now explaining the term "dwelling" (*sthiti*), it is rendered as "settled dwelling" (*anusthita*).
As for "the box being large," it refers to understanding that accords with principle; thus, the box is used as a metaphor.
"Cutting three *liang* daily" is as explained in the subsequent scriptural text.
"Reaching the ocean" refers to reaching the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
The Sūtra states: "All worlds" refers to the world of sentient beings within the ten realms and five aggregates; it means to cause them all to be established within the secret treasury.

Regarding the precepts as the remedy for the defilement of transgression: this means that by upholding them oneself, one destroys evil, and by causing others to uphold them, one causes them to destroy evil.
The Sūtra says, "to liberate those who are not yet liberated. This means: if sentient beings are bound by afflictions (Skt. *kleśa*), it should be read as *jiā* (佳);

if it means that sentient beings have not yet understood the Truth of Origination (Skt. *samudaya-satya*) and one causes them to understand it, it should be read as *guǎi* (鮭). Both meanings are valid.
The "Minor Prajñā" refers to the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
According to this school, those who possess the Buddha-nature are precisely those who realize the eternally abiding person; such individuals are themselves the Buddha.

Regarding the frequent use of the "Great Chapter" (Mahāprajñāpāramitā): by means of unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*), one cultivates the perfections (*pāramitā*); thus, one is able to adorn the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
As for the merit of the six perfections: the downward transformation through the six perfections belongs to merit (*puṇya*); the upward seeking through one's own practice belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*).

Wisdom thus constitutes the two adornments (*dvaya-śobhā*). Next, regarding the concluding text on merit and wisdom, the Sūtra also states: "The expedient means of the secret teaching" refers to the provisional [manifestation] of the same essence.
These skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)—expedient means being precisely the secret—are so designated.
"Unknown to the world" means it cannot be known through worldly methods of calculation; therefore, the Ganges is used as its measure.
The Sūtra states that those who receive and uphold the five precepts should also be called "upāsakas. The Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty says:
the Sanskrit name is *upāsaka*, which here means "male lay devotee. One who receives the five precepts and is fully endowed with dignified deportment is immediately qualified [to be so called].
Because he is a layperson who has gone forth [into the religious life], he is called an *upāsaka*; this is merely an abbreviation of the text.
One who is "fully endowed" with dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) is so named only when they are entirely free from transgressions, whether gross or subtle.
Regarding those in the two assemblies who have departed from desire, they are also called *brahmacārin* lay followers (*upāsaka*) and so forth.
If one does not violate the secular laws, it is because one has a legitimate wife.

Furthermore, regarding the addition of the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), since the five precepts do not prohibit eating after midday, this means that while observing the five precepts, one further observes the eight [precepts].
This refers to the precepts.
As for those who merely take the Three Refuges, they simply direct their minds to receive the Three Refuges, doing so merely to turn away from falsehood and toward the correct path.
Those whose aspiration is to seek *nirvāṇa* are "those of limited scope," for they reach only the *pariṇāmanīya-ratha* (the temporary resting place).

If there are those who act for the sake of sentient beings—these are the bodhisattvas who emerge from the conventional—they constantly uproot suffering with great compassion and bestow the medicine of the Dharma upon others.
To be ever accompanied by the precepts means that while they engage in worldly etiquette, they simultaneously uphold the five precepts; this is what is meant.

"Constantly coexisting with the impermanent" refers to the destruction of the impermanent; when objects are seen as being like illusions and transformations, this constitutes the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*), though it is merely stated briefly here.
"Lifting the foot and setting it down" explains the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*); that is to say, all four modes of deportment are fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma.
Question: If this is the case, since *upāsakas* already possess the "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) and so forth, do *śrāvakas* and *bodhisattvas* also possess them?
The four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) constitute "non-attainment," because one has not yet attained the fruits [of the path].

Regarding the statement that the first fruit is "partial": if one divides the Bodhisattva path according to the Tripiṭaka into four parts, taking the three great aeons and one hundred kalpas as these four parts, there is no error in meaning.
However, one must not take the moment of reaching the foot of the tree and severing the fetters as the "complete" part, because the severing of the fetters is itself the attainment of Buddhahood.

Regarding the phrase "those who have severed the dust-like [afflictions]": if explained according to the intent of the intended recipients, practitioners of the Three Vehicles had already severed the dust-like afflictions during the period of the Vaipulya and Prajñā teachings, thereby attaining the name "having attained a small portion.

Now, in terms of establishing their positions and revealing the provisional to disclose the ultimate, it is only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that they truly attain such names as "having attained a small portion" and so forth.
Both the Common and Distinct Teachings must rely on the previous teachings to achieve entry.
The subsequent teaching employs provisional characteristics; this can be understood by analogy with the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).

As for why the Shared Teaching (*paryāya-yāna*) does not explicitly mention the Two Vehicles, it is because they are analogous to those in the Tripitaka Teaching and thus are not separately enumerated.

In the eighth stage of the Shared Teaching, one reaches full completion; this constitutes the fulfillment of the Bodhisattva stages, as is the case in both the Distinct and Perfect Teachings. This is because even the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)...
It is called the "Equal Enlightenment Buddha" (Samyaksambuddha); therefore, it need not be discussed further for now. Furthermore, one may also attain it through progressive advancement.
As for the "Non-differentiated Buddha," this refers to the principle of Equal Enlightenment.

Regarding each and every Dharma gate up to the "Original and Traced" (Honji-Suijaku): from the stages of the Bodhisattva grounds and dwellings upward, all possess a true original essence that can manifest as traces to transform beings.
And they lead toward actual practice. If those prior to the stages and dwellings are all substantial persons, they are led by means of expedient means.
To take one example regarding evil dharmas: if evil is divided into four parts, when evil lies dormant within the body, it is called the "unmanifested part" (amūlaka);
when one performs evil through a single karmic path, it is the "majority part" (bahula); and when one performs evil through all three karmic paths, it is the "complete part" (paripūrṇa).

Regarding the deeds performed by a minor bodhisattva: whether relying on fundamental dhyāna, or on the untainted (anāsrava), or on worldly samādhi, they give rise to supernormal powers (abhijñā); such is called a minor bodhisattva.
This refers to the initial teaching, that which was employed at the Deer Park in the past.

Regarding the contemplation of the six practices (*ṣaḍvidhābhāvanā*): the six are formed by taking the superior three cultivations and contrasting them with the inferior three cultivations. As for the term "purity" mentioned in the text:
This can be understood by following the literal meaning.
As for "Śrāvaka" (Voice-hearer): "voice" refers to the teaching. Those of the Lesser Vehicle, possessing dull faculties, attain awakening and understanding by consuming the voice [of the teaching];
therefore, they are called Śrāvakas. As for "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer): they attain awakening and understanding through conditions; therefore, they are named Pratyekabuddhas.
"That which was not previously stated" refers to what should have been explained at the end of the first fascicle.

"The bhikṣus are not so" is a counter-interrogation intended to refute [the opponent's claim]. Since the bhikṣus had already attained arhatship in the past, there is no passage extolling the former based on the latter;
how much less could this be the case for the assembly of upāsakas?

Regarding "the illness gone and the medicine perished": this refers to the principle of the Great Nirvana, which is non-eternal and impermanent, because that which treats [the illness] and that which is treated are both [transient].
Regarding "the two extremes do not receive [it]," etc.: this is the explanation within the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā of the gradual practice of the Perfect [Teaching], by means of the Great Nirvana.

Regarding the person who cultivates with a focused mind: the present sutra also fully contains these two types of practice—the person [who cultivates] and the person who constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa* while practicing the Path.
As for the two kinds of cultivation: first, impermanence remedies permanence; second, permanence remedies impermanence.

As for those who advocate "the priority of the One," they are not merely people of the past or present; their interpretation is that the refutation of permanence by impermanence occurred in the past, while the refutation of impermanence by permanence occurs in the present.

Regarding "abandoning both illness and treatment": one who realizes that [phenomena] such as permanence and impermanence are neither permanent nor impermanent—wherein both the middle and the extremes are quiescent and one perfectly accords with the wondrous principle of *nirvāṇa*—only then is this called "profound joy. This applies to every single phrase.

Furthermore, these three explanations all concern the disclosure of the provisional (*upāya*). Therefore, after each passage, it says: "Hearing the medicine of eternal abiding, one destroys impermanence and the like."
Regarding "sickness":
one who is endowed with these virtuous practices is endowed with the conduct of the Tathāgata and the virtue of the "twofold wandering," which leads toward Nirvana—
specifically, it leads into the present Great Parinirvāṇa.
"Even a single kind does not exist" means that even the principle of *nirvāṇa* should not be considered as one, let alone two or three.
"Having nothing to rely upon" refers to a standard or rule. By taking the person of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as the standard for the provisional person's method, one enters *nirvāṇa*.
This is termed the "Track.
Regarding "Great Nirvāṇa as Suffering": having realized Great Nirvāṇa and abiding in Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one pervades the Dharma-realm; the meaning of this transformation is like suffering.
That which is called a "gate" refers to medicine as the gate to illness. Regarding the passage on "the real and the unreal," it is explained in terms of the Truths (satya).

Regarding "refuge and non-refuge," it is explained in terms of the Three Jewels (triratna). Regarding "sentient beings and non-sentient beings," it is explained in terms of seeing or not seeing one's nature;
only upon seeing one's nature is one termed a "non-sentient being. Regarding "the eternal and the non-eternal," this is simply explained in terms of the permanent and the impermanent. Peace.

"Non-peaceful" (*aśānta*) is explained in terms of realization and non-realization. "Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) are explained in terms of being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).

"Abandoned" (*prahīṇa*) and "not abandoned" (*aprahīṇa*) are explained in terms of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). "Nirvāṇa" and "non-nirvāṇa" are explained in terms of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

"Superior" (*adhimātra*) and "not superior" (*anadhimātra*) are explained in terms of stages (*avasthā*). If the *Zeshou* commentary says: "Briefly, six types are cited; the first, suffering and pleasure, etc., is by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mukha*)."

1. Contemplating the phenomena of birth and death as impermanent, suffering, and so forth; and contemplating the phenomena of nirvana as permanent, blissful, pure, and self. This is the gate of the two truths:

the real and the unreal, wherein the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is real and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is unreal. 2. Taking refuge and not taking refuge, which is the gate of revulsion and detachment.
Turning toward the Triple Gem is called "taking refuge" (*śaraṇa-gamana*); being entirely free from false dharmas is called "not taking refuge. 3. Sentient beings and non-sentient beings.
This is the gate of the provisional and the real: the five aggregates are not sentient beings; it is the provisional person established upon them that is called a "sentient being.
"The five are eternal or non-eternal" refers to the gate of cause and effect: Nirvana is eternal, while birth-and-death is non-eternal. "Peace and non-peace" refers to the gate of causal practice.
Wholesome conduct is peace; unwholesome conduct is not peace. Furthermore, the untainted (anāsrava) noble ones are peace; that which is tainted (sāsrava) is not peace.

The six categories—the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)—constitute the gateway to the Four Noble Truths. The conditioned is suffering. Form-phenomena, mind-phenomena, non-form phenomena, and non-mind phenomena are all conditioned.
The unconditioned is not suffering. These arise through mutual contrast: space, cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

Cessation (*nirodha*) is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
