"To obtain life" means to obtain the retribution of life. "To obtain peace" means peace within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "To obtain discernment" means to obtain worldly wisdom so as to be able to preach the Dharma.
"Physical strength" is easily understood.

Regarding the fourth point, "the subsequent difficulty reaching the eyes": if one follows the pattern of the initial passage, which states that [the practitioner] is fully equipped to transform others, it should say, "Furthermore, they have not yet been able to cause sentient beings to be fully endowed with this heavenly state.
The latter three difficulties should all be explained by analogy with this.
"Digestion" refers to the transformation of flavors.
The Sūtra says "not eating. Cunda’s intention was this: if there were eating and digestion, then there would be the five fruits [of karma].
Since it is said that there is neither eating nor digestion, there are no five fruits. If there are no five fruits, then distinctions of magnitude and smallness are established. How could this be?
Is it said that there is no distinction?
"Ji-jiao" (pronounced *qí jì* as a gloss for *líng líng*, meaning water chestnut) refers to the "falling of the corners. To say "ji-jiao" simply means the difficulty of the corners falling away.

If one takes the small initial objection against the large subsequent [point], this constitutes the momentum of the corners falling away. If one takes the large initial objection against the small subsequent [point], it likewise forms a "ji-jiao. In the text:

There is no such power. If one were to use a minor initial objection to challenge a major initial [objection], it would constitute a simultaneous challenge; the same applies to the two subsequent aspects of the major and minor.
As for the "retinue bodhisattvas," these are those who were fellow practitioners and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in the past, acting as a retinue; they are in fact emanations.
The authority of the teaching has not yet been discussed; for now, it is said that the "retinue" constitutes the *nirmāṇakāya*.

The "Victorious *Nirmāṇakāya*" (*jina-nirmāṇakāya*) refers to the Supreme *Nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, while the "lesser *Nirmāṇakāya*" within the ten billion lands is as perceived by those of limited capacity.
Regarding the fact that the milk-rice and the light are eternally distinct: the Buddha on the lotus pedestal takes this light as food by entering it through the crown of his head;
because it is thus "crown-food," they are not the same.
Regarding the "difficulties concerning distinctions": all five difficulties are difficulties concerning distinctions.

As for the phrase "the Jing and Wei rivers are clearly distinct": what Cunda perceives is turbid at first and clear later, whereas what Mahāprajāpatī perceives is clear both at the beginning and at the end;
therefore, it is said that they are non-dual.
Regarding "auspicious grass," it is like the *māo* grass of this land.
One who possesses internal afflictions dwells in the state of being submerged in delusion; this is the body of affliction.
As for "this being the final body," from beginningless time until today, one has already practiced the bodhisattva path, yet [it has not been completed].
One is exempted from birth and death. Today is the final body; having entered parinirvāṇa, one will no longer undergo further rebirth. This is called the "final body" (paścima-deha).
As for those capable of benefiting others in five ways, they do so by means of the five fruits that still involve outflows (sāsrava).
"One who has long possessed wisdom and abandonment" refers to the characteristics of having attained enlightenment long ago, as clarified in the "Life Span" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Having accomplished the initial reception [of the fruit]" and so forth means that after the great conditions and views, one enters nirvāṇa through cessation.
How can one who possesses inferior views [claim this]? The preceding text stated that it occurs after the great conditions and simultaneously with the beginning of the minor conditions;
now, to say that the initial stage of the inferior is used to challenge the final stage of the superior is precisely what constitutes a logical difficulty.
Regarding "the body having separation and conjunction": this precisely clarifies that both the small and the large each have their own instances of separation and conjunction.

What constitutes the "separation of the small"? It is when the latter end emerges as impermanence. As for the "separation and conjunction of the large": in the previous objection, there were five points regarding the large, using the diamond as the illustrative analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*).
In the Buddha’s response, there are six points regarding the large, likewise using the diamond as the illustrative analogy. This, then, is the separation.
There are five or six [examples], but combined there are only four or five. Since Cunda did not see the four bodies, he likewise did not see the diamond-like body used as the analogy.
When it is said that "the final limit reaches equality," the sutra merely lists the final-limit body (*paryanta-kāya*); it is precisely this impermanence that is equated with the final limit.
The margins are identical; therefore, they are combined.
Although only three bodies are listed, there are only five and not four because one sees only the five great [bodies] and lacks the four small ones.

However, the "body of eternal abiding" mentioned at the beginning of the commentary is precisely the "eternal body" in the sutra, which refutes the "body of impure food. Next, the "body that is not affliction" is...
The Dharma-body. The destruction of the body of afflictions is itself the union with the body free from afflictions; furthermore, it is like a diamond and is therefore not an impermanent body.
Since it is complete with five bodies, it is said that there are only five and not four. Moreover, if one explains this according to the principle of "neither-nor" (the double negation):
That which from the beginning does not eat non-food is the eternal body (*nitya-kāya*); thus it is joined with that which is neither impermanent nor has a final limit.

That the body is neither affliction nor non-affliction, and neither dharma nor non-dharma, belongs entirely to the *dharmakāya*. It is not the diamond-body (*vajrakāya*), but rather that which serves as a metaphor for it;
thus, one departs from the five or six [bodies] and unites them into only three bodies, as cited in the sūtra. Furthermore, if the Great Vehicle refutes the Small Vehicle...

The phrase "not a non-eternal body" (非無常身) is joined with the latter half of the phrase [to form] the final body (後邊身). The phrase "not a vajra-body" (非金剛身) is joined with the [latter] half-phrase to form the eternal body (常身).
Thus, it constitutes the "great five" breaking the "small four," which is also called the "great six" confronting and breaking the "small four.
If one relies on the "double negation" (雙非), then both the great and small consist of six; this opening and closing is appropriate, and thus they are treated as four, five, and so forth.
That which is profound and yet more profound consists of four and five; this is one profundity. That it is neither four nor five is another profundity.
Furthermore, the constant subversion of the impermanent is yet another profundity. Moreover, to cite the nine fundamental aspects while transcending the provisional traces is yet another profundity.
Since both the fundamental and the trace are inconceivable, it is said that the two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction.

Regarding "entering the vajra-samādhi": the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment enters the vajra-like samādhi, shatters the final category [of afflictions], and ascends to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
Regarding "clearly seeing the Buddha-nature": seeing it with ultimate, final, and distinct clarity is what is termed "clarity."

"Knowledge and abandonment are without distinction" means that both at the beginning and at the end, one attains knowledge and abandonment; therefore, they are said to be without distinction, differing only in their timing.

"A person who is a god among men" refers to a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), who is the most excellent and superior among humans—namely, a Universal Monarch (*sārvabhauma*)—and is thus praised as such.

Heaven. There are five kinds of heaven: first, the worldly heaven (*laukika-deva*), which the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls a provisional designation; this refers to human kings who are called "sons of heaven" (*devaputra*).

Second, the born heaven (*upapatti-deva*), ranging from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Third, the pure heaven (*viśuddhi-deva*), ranging from the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the Pratyekabuddha.
Fourth, the heaven of meaning (*artha-deva*), ranging from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward through to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*) Bodhisattvas.
Sakyamuni understands the meaning of emptiness. The five types of "First Principle Heavens" (paramārtha-deva) refer to the Buddhas and Tathāgatas who have seen their nature to its ultimate limit;
this is called the First Principle. Among these five heavens, the Buddha is the supreme heaven, and is thus named the God among Gods (devātideva).

Regarding those who merely relinquish material wealth, the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "By means of compassion alone, he practiced universal giving; even when his body was mangled, he felt no resentment.

He praised the Buddha Tiṣya and subsequently [attained] unsurpassed bodhi. Regarding the six pāramitās, in these four stages, one by one and then two by two, they were cultivated to perfection in their respective order.
This refers to universal giving through a compassionate heart, extending to all things, including even one's own life and limb.

He was entirely without attachment; thus, his perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) was fulfilled. Even when his body was dismembered until not even a portion the size of a mustard seed remained, his mind harbored no resentment;

thus, his perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) was fulfilled. He did not give rise to physical actions or verbal expressions regarding the retribution for his deeds; this is called the fulfillment of his ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

Upon encountering the Tathāgata Tiṣya in the Fire-Light Samādhi (*jvālana-samādhi*), joy arose in his heart; with single-minded devotion and upright sincerity, he forgot to set down his foot and stood gazing up at him with palms joined.
After seven days and nights, he praised Dīpaṃkara Buddha with sublime verses, saying: "Heaven and earth, this world-system, the Hall of the Śakras," and so forth.
This is called the fulfillment of diligence (*vīrya*). Morality (*śīla*) subsumes patience (*kṣānti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) subsumes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);

thus, it is only through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and wisdom that [the path] is further perfected upon the Vajrāsana. Therefore, the verse says: "Next, unsurpassed enlightenment. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "This..."
These explanations are all given based on the predominance of a single moment or a single practice, and thus they are described as being "complete.

According to the true meaning, however, it is only upon attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that the four *pāramitās* truly become complete. Subsequently, at the stage of unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*), one accomplishes the two *pāramitās* of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
This refers to the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) of Śākyamuni Bodhisattva beneath the Bodhi tree, up until the thirtieth [moment].
When the three minds attain the Vajra-samādhi, it is called the accomplishment of the dhyāna-pāramitā.

Upon reaching the thirty-fourth mind and attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), one becomes fully endowed with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); this is called the accomplishment of the prajñā-pāramitā. These are merely the six perfections as practiced through activity;
they have not yet seen the dāna of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and are therefore termed "dāna without principle."

Those who have already attained thorough penetration have long since achieved the fundamental ground; yet, manifesting as being within the traces of the path, they still abide in the stage of a bodhisattva.
If one were to explain the essential teachings in detail, they are in the process of attaining Buddhahood through the eight phases; therefore, it is said that "at that time, [he was] a bodhisattva."
"Regarding 'having already obtained the Buddha-eye': while still in the stage of a bodhisattva, one has already partially obtained the Buddha-eye.
As for 'I truly do not eat,' Fayao said: 'This clarifies that although the Bodhisattva does not actually partake [of food], he manifests the appearance of partaking.

Now, his entry into nirvana is likewise a manifested appearance. Since both types of manifestation are appearances and not identical, why do you not distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles at the outset?"
As for the later views, they merely state that both [the Buddha and the disciples] were manifestations (*traces*); thus, the distinction between the Great and the Small Vehicles is not made.
This is not what we accept here. Regarding the one who received the milk gruel: in the past, there were two sisters; the elder was named Nanda and the younger was named Nandabalā.
Together they tended a thousand oxen. At one time, they milked the milk of the thousand oxen to feed a hundred cows, and then they milked the hundred cows to feed [ten].
There were ten heads. She milked one head to drink and boiled the milk of another cow to make a gruel. The gruel boiled seven feet above the ground.
When the woman saw this marvel, she did not dare eat it herself; instead, she offered it to the tree deity. The Buddha was beneath the tree, but the two women did not know this.

Upon arriving, they encountered him and immediately presented the offering. Therefore, it is said that at their first meeting, he received it directly from her mouth due to this minor causal connection.
If that is so, since the intent of the objection states that [the object] both moves and stands still, and having stated it stands still, then states it moves—
what benefit does such moving and standing still provide to the object?
"Both going and staying" means that while the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) goes, the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) stays; this "non-staying" is not easily understood.
Regarding "attaining great fame and profit": because he accepted Cunda’s offering, he universally accepted the offerings of the entire great assembly; how could the benefit exceed this?
Regarding "the five fruits should come first": it means that among all people, one first attains the five fruits.
Regarding "because of being complete": the fulfillment of virtue and the fulfillment of benefit are called "fulfillment."

"Name conjoining with phenomena" means conjoining with the Dharma-body of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), which is the principle and object of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Name conjoining with the Buddha" means conjoining with the wisdom of omniscience (*prajñā*).
"To be in harmony with the Saṃgha" means to be in harmony with the knowledge of the modes of the Path and liberation.

To praise him for having found a master is like a loyal minister whose mind accords with the sovereign's intent; to praise him for having found a teacher is because he is able to give rise to understanding.

Regarding the praise for those who have attained intimacy: their innate nature is identical in essence. This passage clearly demonstrates that Cunda’s essence possesses the three qualities of being a master (*svāmin*), a relative (*bandhu*), and a teacher (*śāstṛ*), which are imperishable.
As for "surpassing the sixth heaven": when the Brahma King first requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, it was Cunda who later requested and received [the teaching].
Because he makes offerings, he is equal to Brahmā and others.
As for the statement in the sutra that "Cunda rejoiced," there are three reasons for his joy: first, he rejoiced because the Buddha accepted his offering;
second, he rejoiced because his act of giving had brought him into the stream of the sages; and third, he rejoiced because he was praised by the multitude.

The Buddha is unstained by worldly dharmas because, as one who is himself unstained, he teaches the dharma of non-staining; therefore, it is praised that hearing [the teaching] is difficult to encounter.
Regarding "having no master, yet having a parent-teacher": when a master is present, they discipline me; when a parent is present, they can nurture and protect me;

when a teacher is present, they can provide guidance and instruction, causing the threefold perfection to unfold and the three virtues to increase. If this growth is lost, it leads to the arising of suffering and affliction.
"Benefiting through the Perfection of Wisdom" refers to the benefit of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
"Clouds arise and one attains coolness" means that from the True [Dharmakāya] arises the Responsive [Nirmāṇakāya].
Just as clouds suddenly arise in a cloudless sky and are further able to bring coolness to others, it is thus used as a metaphor for how expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) benefits sentient beings.
"Those who dispel chaos and rectify what is wrong" refers to the shaking and agitation caused by the armies of deviant spirits, which afflict and disturb practitioners.

Now, having received the illumination of the Buddha-sun, their afflictions are extinguished; they realize that the suchness of the realm of Māra is identical to the suchness of the Buddha-realm. This is like a sage ruler who dispels a chaotic age to ascend the throne of rectitude;
hence, it is called "rectifying what is wrong."
Regarding "mutually dependent": from the preceding toward the subsequent, this is due to the presence of the three prerequisites.
Regarding the "three absences of a Buddha": this refers to being born among humans, obtaining supreme benefit, and hearing the Dharma—these three are difficult to encounter.
Since these three are shared by all people and are easy to hear, they are not reiterated here.
The Sūtra says: "As for you, Cunda, now. The name "you" is called out individually. It is difficult for such a human body to exist; therefore, it is necessary to call out the name individually.
Furthermore, regarding the obstruction of others: because of your offering, the Buddha universally accepts all offerings. If you were to request that he remain, there would be none [who could do so].
To perform the final offering would result in contradicting others.
If you yourself are one who holds a spear and a shield— having requested the Buddha to remain for a long time and yet wishing to present offerings to fulfill the final act of generosity—
this constitutes a self-contradiction and a mutual conflict.

Regarding "the living": since the Dharma-body is eternally present, how can one request it to remain? Regarding "the deceased": since their faculties have ceased and they have entered extinction, how can one request them to remain?
As for the deceased, the Dharma-body is eternally quiescent; as for the living, when their faculties arise, it responds throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
That which is neither existent nor non-existent is symbolized by entering extinction between the twin trees; the same applies to abiding and so forth.

The essential meaning of the text is simply that there is both constant existence and constant extinction, and constant extinction and constant existence. By a single utterance of "extinction," the three truths are fully realized.
Those who speak of this find their words stammering, for the very substance of existence and non-existence is itself the Dharma-realm; thus, it cannot be expressed by speech.
Yet, that which preserves its own being does so because it is naturally so for all things.
Those who grasp at it lose it. If one grasps at impermanence everywhere, one loses permanence;
if one grasps at permanence, one loses the principle of Great Nirvana, which is neither permanent nor impermanent. Therefore, it is not to be grasped.
Regarding the phrase "the six kinds," etc.: the "six" refers to the fact that Cunda clearly understood he had attained partial realization of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Because he did not know what lay above them, he requested [the Buddha] to remain.
As for "restraining the lofty," this means restraining Cunda’s loftiness and quelling the expectations of those below him.
The Sūtra says: "Regarding the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*): their nature is to arise and their nature is to perish; this nature cannot be requested.
Since it accords with what is appropriate for each object, how could it be requested? Furthermore, 'nature' refers to the internal, taking the continuous flow and latent passing away as its essence.
'Characteristics' refer to the external, taking the ultimate cessation after a hundred years as its meaning."

Regarding concealment and manifestation: employing the impermanent is concealment, while employing the permanent is manifestation. Proclaiming cessation is concealment; speaking of abiding is manifestation.
That which is capable of permanence brings glory to all places; that which is capable of impermanence makes arising and ceasing manifestly clear.
Regarding "becoming another's object": because it manifests as impermanent, it becomes an object for others.
How could it be fixed as either self or other? One should rather say: how could it be fixed as self or fixed as other, such that the agent is simultaneously both self and other?
If it were to employ impermanence, then impermanence would extinguish itself of its own accord; why then would there be a need to request that it remain?

Therefore, the mention of "two functions" indicates that the essence is neither permanent nor impermanent. If one interprets this passage accordingly, one should apply the aforementioned "Buddha-realm.
How could it be that functions are established through permanence? The subsequent section discusses functions as being identical to the essence; hence, they are called the "two functions."
The Sūtra states, "The three realms are all impermanent," which explains that suffering arises solely from the nature of impermanence.
The Sūtra further states, "Destructible phenomena are in flux," which cites impermanence to manifest and establish the meaning of emptiness.

Regarding the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*): "self" is defined as sovereignty. Since one is invaded by old age, sickness, and the like, and entangled by afflictions (*kleśa*), one realizes through verification that there is no self.
As the Sūtra says, "That which is fundamentally without benefit": the impurity of the seed is the root of all impurities.
The meaning of "as in the *Śrī-sūtra*" (Ruisheng) is explained in the ninth section of the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) below.

Regarding "this shore" and "the other shore": the cycle of birth and death within the three realms is this shore, while the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Three Vehicles is the other shore.

Furthermore, the Three Vehicles constitute this shore, while the compassion that emerges from the conventional constitutes the other shore. Moreover, emerging from the conventional constitutes this shore, while entering the Middle Way constitutes the other shore.
Additionally, the sequential Three Truths constitute this shore, while the perfectly integrated Three Truths constitute the other shore.
Therefore, it is said that "crossing over is neither here nor there."
Regarding "the three truths as one truth": this is explained by taking the essence as the function; each is interpreted through the mutual identity of essence and function.
"Neither one nor three" means that essence and function are both extinguished; "both three and one" means that essence and function are both illuminated.

Regarding the statement that "the three truths are all empty," they are equally merged within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As for the phrase "and so forth," one should say: "one is provisional and all are provisional;
the provisional is itself the dharma-realm, existing only as a name."
What is meant by "requesting to abide in one 'middle' which is all 'middles'"? The middle is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which is equal and non-dual;
it neither departs nor abides. Why, then, do you again request that he abide?
Regarding the single verse on "detachment from desire": since it speaks of "contemplation," is this not provisional? As for the six difficulties being due to the Buddha:
obtaining a human body depends upon the five realms (*dhātu*), and those realms exist because they were taught by the Buddha. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one can uphold the name of Śākyamuni Buddha within one's home, the other five [difficulties] follow suit. Therefore, it is said that [they are] "due to" [the Buddha].
The Buddha.

As for those who arise from function: upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching that [dharmas] are neither permanent nor impermanent, they realize that this is the very substance of function, and thus they take leave of the Buddha.
Regarding the severance of the outflows of the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), this refers to the partial elimination of the three delusions.

As for the metaphor of the elephant and the dragon: the dragon represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which possesses great power within the water and is named after its capacity for severance;
the elephant represents equal power on land.
Regarding the phrase "extracted from beneath the deep spring": I was a lowly artisan within the city named Bā Yuànquánzhīxià (Extracted from Beneath the Deep Spring).
Having attained entry into the Grounds of Dwelling, I am now called Chù Yúnxáozhīshàng (Dwelling Above the Clouds and Mists).
"Capable of producing the goodness of beings" means giving rise to the great goodness of eternal abiding.
"The suffering of the great assembly has arrived" means that the fifty-two assemblies all made three requests; this is termed "the arrival of suffering."

Furthermore, there is no "vomiting out" [of the teaching]. Sentient beings do not weary of the Buddha, and the Buddha does not weary of sentient beings; therefore, the metaphor of "vomiting out" is employed.

As for the skillful subtlety of the Sage’s words: they are "skillful" because they accord with the capacities [of beings], and they are "subtle" (mimetic) because a single utterance accords with these two types of discourse.
Regarding the statement that "taking 'non-being' as the primary and 'being' as secondary": the original intent of making offerings is to seek the true principle that is neither being nor non-being;

this is why taking "non-being" as primary and "being" as secondary is considered a skillful means (*upāya*). Those who cling to "being" do so specifically to manifest that which is neither being nor non-being; likewise, those who cling to "non-being" also do so to manifest that which is neither being nor non-being.
There is "existence" and "non-existence"; both are appropriate to the circumstances of things, which is termed "skillful means.
Regarding the four *siddhāntas*, the first [the *vyavahāra-siddhānta*] is explained as threefold; furthermore, they can be understood by correlating them respectively with the four *siddhāntas*.
Regarding the statement "it shall be explained extensively later": in the *Śoka-parivarta* (Chapter on Lamentation), it is explained extensively that [reality] is neither permanent nor impermanent.

By citing this to reveal what is not [the case], one extensively cites its impermanence; through this affirmation of "neither permanent nor impermanent," the errors held by the two parties are revealed.
Regarding this principle and its application: the two functions belong to the phenomenal level (*dharma*), while being neither eternal nor non-eternal belongs to the noumenal level (*tattva*).
As for the statement, "That which exists is not non-existent," this restates the previous objection;
it refers to Cunda’s assertion that he exists. Why? Your claim that Cunda exists is incorrect. The non-existence of Cunda is capable of negating the non-existence of Mañjuśrī.
Because [Mañjuśrī’s] non-existence is itself non-existent, Cunda’s non-existence becomes the non-existence of permanence; thus it is said that he "returns to this non-existence.
Since Mañjuśrī’s non-existence is what is negated, this non-existence conversely becomes existence. How, then, can one challenge [Cunda] by saying he must be existent?
Furthermore, if one were to follow the direct flow of the text, it should say "the existence of Mañjuśrī," not "the non-existence of Cunda."
There is none. Thus, the "non-existence" of Mañjuśrī is precisely the "non-existence" of the former teaching;
one should not use the former to challenge the latter, thereby causing non-existence to become existence. Both interpretations are valid.
Regarding "no impairment in the profound": in Mañjuśrī’s state of being neither permanent nor impermanent, there is no diminution.
Regarding "abandoning both victory and defeat": this diminishes the Middle Way.

Regarding those who each cling to two functions: for one who clings to permanence, they know that permanence is itself impermanence; for one who clings to impermanence, they know that impermanence is itself permanence.
These are all intended to reveal the true essence which is neither permanent nor impermanent; thus both names are correct, and both are seen as being "neither."
Regarding the claim that "each has one 'is' and one 'is not'": the entity being grasped is "is" insofar as it is the cause;

however, if one is biasedly attached to permanence, one loses impermanence, and if one is attached to impermanence, one loses permanence. Thus, each may have one aspect that is "is" and one that is "is not."

One should train in this manner: observing that the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, as a skillful means for the samādhi of true emptiness, one is thus exhorted by these words.

For those who are burdened by the toil of existence—the cycle of birth and death within the three realms—the "wheel" refers to the burden of sentient beings; it is a metaphor for suffering, like the wheel of the three realms.
It revolves; it ascends and descends; it shifts and passes away from moment to moment. Therefore, it is used as a metaphor for suffering.

When the sutra says "the same as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)," it refers to the nature of impermanence. If [the Dharma King] were the same as all conditioned phenomena, he would not be the Dharma King.
The Buddha is the Honored One of the triple world because his myriad practices are perfected; how could he be the same as all conditioned phenomena?
"Venerable husband" (*zhàngfū*) is a metaphor for that which is firm, upright, and straight; it refers to the principle of the Middle Way’s uprightness and rectitude.
"Having already given rise to the aspiration" (*yù fāxīn yǐqù*)—the term "giving rise to the aspiration" refers to the stage above the level of mere names (*míngzì*).

Regarding "not yet sufficient": distant insufficiency refers to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); proximate insufficiency refers to the stages from the Grounds (*bhūmi*) and Abidings (*vihāra*) upward.
As for "the absence of the five constant fruits": the five fruits constitute the body, while their basis is like a house that serves as a dwelling place for people;
since [at these stages] the practices (*caryā*) have not yet been fully established, there are no five fruits, just as there is no household when one lacks a home.

Regarding the phrase "in principle there is no wisdom or abandonment": although the nature of principle (li-xing) has not yet functioned as wisdom or abandonment, it possesses the nature of liberation;
therefore, it is called "meaning" (yi). As for "begging" (qigai)—the character *gai* is pronounced either as *ge* or *gai*; it means "to surpass" (*qiansheng*).
That which is easily dyed by plain silk seeks tranquil wisdom within the compassion of names;
it is like plain silk that is easily dyed, being analogous to the practice of contemplation.

Those who have a superficial knowledge of names and numbers understand that the name is itself the person; they understand that the provisional is identical to the real, the real is identical to the provisional, and that which is neither provisional nor real is the reality of the corner while the provisional is the side.
This is because their names alone penetrate vertically through both the provisional and the real.
"An inn (*yìlǚ*) refers to a house by the roadside called a guest-house (*kèshè*), which serves as a place of reception (*yì*). It is where travelers scattered from various states reside;
they gather together at night and disperse in the morning. Furthermore, 'reception' (*yì*) means to welcome. A guest-house is a place for welcoming guests and travelers;
thus, it is named an inn."
The greedy person who seeks material things, though they crave them, cannot obtain them; therefore, they are likened to an empty village.
Those who burn with compassion for them are wise observers who can penetrate the nature of these evil thieves, just as a wise person feels pity for those who have encountered them.

Regarding the general explanation of the term: a practitioner of contemplative cultivation who is merely able to explain loving-kindness briefly to others, and who practices solely in accordance with the teachings, earns the name "one who explains."

Regarding "entrusting one child": Fayao said, "To explain 'entrustment' (*ji*): it means to be born by entrusting oneself to the five aggregates (*skandhas*). 'One' (*yi*) means being true and non-dual.
As for 'the compassionate teaching already manifest': one is able to use a single wondrous voice to pervade the three thousandfold world-system, reaching everywhere according to one's will."
The name is used to manifest this.

Regarding "compassion that encompasses both the supported and the supporting" (*yi-fu*): when similar compassion is perfected, it is called "supported" (*yi*) because it can destroy the pervasive delusions (*tong-huo*), and "supporting" (*fu*) because the specific delusions (*bie-huo*) are suppressed.

Now, as for the word "completely" (*xi*)—although the pervasive delusions have been eliminated, the specific delusions remain entirely; yet, from the perspective of their being completely suppressed (*yuan-fu*), it is thus named.
Regarding "alternating strength and weakness": when one is able to destroy pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), compassion alone is strong;
when ignorance has not yet been destroyed and true understanding has not yet arisen, that which resembles compassion is weak. This is called "alternating."
Regarding the phrase "carrying a child," it refers to carrying a child who practices contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
"Heading toward the city of Nirvāṇa" means heading toward the city of Great Nirvāṇa.

Regarding "encountering evil winds and rain," Master Sengsheng said: "The five desires are like wind and rain; the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are like obstructions. If one encounters evil friends..."
"Like mosquitoes and gadflies. This interpretation is too shallow.

Regarding "mosquitoes, gadflies, bees, and stinging insects": according to Dharma Master Yan’s *Jīngyīn* (Phonetics of the Scriptures), "stinging insect" (*chì*) is the name of a distinct species of insect.

If one provides a phonetic gloss, it refers to the action of the insect; thus, it is the name of a specific insect. As for why it is the name of a specific insect, [the text] first lists four types of insects: mosquitoes... [and so forth].

"Mosquitoes," "bees," and "stinging insects" are followed by the two characters for "poisonous insects" to conclude the passage; thus it says, "that which they bite and devour," thereby revealing their function.
The Venerable Rāhula also reads this as "stinging."

Regarding external karmic obstructions: these are the defilements of external evil karma that assist internal karma; therefore, they are called "external defilements" and constitute external obstructions.
It is like being swept away by water.
Regarding "the merit of compassionate mindfulness": it is because by cultivating the three types of perfect compassion, one attains entry into the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
As for "partial application," one should not practice contemplation and mindfulness in a biased or one-sided manner.

The Sūtra states, "not the same as various conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*), clarifying that the Tathāgata is not the same as various conditioned phenomena; because he is eternally abiding (*nitya*), one should not say they are the same.
The Sūtra states, "those who do not yet possess the eye of wisdom," meaning those who do not yet possess the Buddha’s eye of wisdom.
The Sūtra states: "The True Dharma of the Tathāgata" refers to the principle of the secret treasury, which is termed "True.

Regarding the phrase "extensively refuting," every single passage refutes the three former teachings; as they belong to the partial and are not the True [Dharma], who would not possess the eye of wisdom or the true principle?
Therefore, the commentary says "and so forth."

Regarding the prohibition against partial teaching: because the capacities [of the listeners] are not yet known, one may only respond with the Mahāyāna Dharma to lead them toward all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Generally speaking, from the stage of "similarity" (*sabhāga*) downward, all are capable of both partial and complete teachings according to their respective capacities.

Those who subsequently perceive the principle of the opportune means are those above the stage of partial realization (*bhūta-vidarśana*). Those who possess both "existence" and "non-existence" are also those above the stage of partial realization.

Only those who possess the two functions of simultaneous non-apprehension and simultaneous illumination are termed "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*); this refers to the realization that permanence is itself impermanence, and so forth.
This is called the "perfect teaching" (*paripūrṇa-deśanā*).

It is also for those whose faculties are suited to perceive the primary truth (*paramārtha*), as they are well-able to distinguish between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is addressed to both types of audiences.
As the Sūtra says, "One should say that the Tathāgata is identical with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)," which refers to being identical with the unconditioned state of *nirvāṇa*. This is also...
It is the same as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Regarding "the principle is quiescent yet luminous": the Dharma-body is tranquil and secure, which is called the quiescence of principle; liberation accords with conditions, which is called being without bondage.

To be luminous without luminosity—ignorance is itself clarity. This is the intrinsic, complete presence of the three causes within the nature of reality, characterized by both quiescence and illumination.
Explanation:
Regarding "the interval between the beginning and the end," the four stages in between are collectively termed the "middle path.

Regarding "being constrained and pressured by birth and death": not escaping the three realms is termed "constraint" (*ku*), and transmigrating through the six destinies is termed "pressure" (*bi*). Furthermore, it is for the sake of birth and death...

"Restrained by the oppression of afflictions, one who is humble and seeks instruction" refers to one who has merely entered the stage of names and has not yet attained the path of contemplation; this is called "humility.
To follow the principle and seek contemplative practice toward an understanding that accords with the stages of semblance and so forth is called "seeking instruction."
That which is oppressed by ignorance is that which is covered by coarse ignorance.

As for the term "suddenly arising," it refers to impermanence, which is a phenomenon that was originally non-existent and now exists; therefore, it is called "suddenly arising. Furthermore, that which burns one's own body is also called "suddenly arising."
"Neighboring truth is for the awakened. Since one who has attained semblance-understanding knows that they will certainly enter true reality, it is called "awakening.
However, regarding "abiding in white dharmas": the stage of semblance can destroy the blackness of the six realms and is thus called "white";
from the stage of partial truth upward, it is called "neither white nor black dharmas."
Regarding "clothing wrapping the body": this refers to the contemplation that penetrates the objective realm, just as clothing wraps the body.

To manifest what has been abandoned means that ultimate contemplation is perfected; because the two deaths and three delusions are forever exhausted, it is said that one "constantly dwells in peace and bliss."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts," the intended meaning is: "You are a bhikṣu who possesses the full precepts;

why do you align yourself with those of limited views? This clarifies that there is a cause for transgression in such false speech, and that one enters hell after death demonstrates the fruit of that transgression.
Regarding this passage on the thirty-two marks, Sengzong said: "They represent the fruition of retribution. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has thirty-two ministers;
these serve as metaphors to symbolize the thirty-two marks."
"Eighty times" is a metaphor for the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
"The Great Brahmā King": *Brahmā* means *nirvāṇa*, and the "King" is the Buddha; it is also equivalent to "the Lord.
The phrase "those eighty" below serves as an example to provide this correspondence. Since this passage [describes] the thirty-two marks...

Regarding the application [of the analogy]: one should state that if it were so, the subsequent examples would apply accordingly. The eighty minor marks correspond to the eighty reversals mentioned above;

the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) correspond to the wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*) mentioned above. Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "Moreover, now," the minor marks serve as an analogy for the eighteen [unique qualities], all of which are not shared with the lower stages.

Regarding the phrase "as in the text at the beginning": first, it praises the appropriateness of his teaching; second, it praises the appropriateness of his comprehension. Therefore, he utters "Excellent! twice.
As for the "eighteen unique qualities" (*āveṇika-dharma*) mentioned in the Sūtra, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 26, states:

For immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Buddha has constantly employed precept, concentration, and wisdom to purify his body and speech, resulting in two absences of failure and three types of mindfulness.
There is no loss. Because the Buddha has long cultivated his mind in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), he has well-cultivated all profound meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

His mind is not distracted, and he attains all mental actions (*manas-karman*) that proceed in accordance with wisdom; this is called "non-loss of mindfulness. Regarding the four kinds of non-differentiation:
the Buddha has no discrimination toward any sentient being; there is no distinction between near and far, and no thought of difference. He universally delivers them all with an equal mind.
Lack of discernment is called "the absence of divergent thoughts. Fifth, there is no lack of concentration; concentration is termed "one-pointed mind.

Because the Buddha does not regress or lose his realization within the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), this is called "no lack of concentration. Sixth, there is no relinquishment without full knowledge. Sentient beings possess three types of feeling:

suffering gives rise to aversion in sentient beings, pleasure gives rise to craving, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure gives rise to delusion. Regarding these three... [The Buddha is free from them].
Regarding the various types of feeling: within painful feeling, he knows that painful feeling arises as suffering, abides as suffering, and ceases as suffering;

within pleasant feeling, he knows that pleasant feeling arises as pleasure, abides as pleasure, and ceases as pleasure; within neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows it at the time of its arising, its abiding, and its cessation.

He remains constantly in meditative concentration throughout the four postures; this is called "equanimity based on full knowledge. Seventh, his desire does not diminish, for the Buddha knows the debt of gratitude toward wholesome dharmas.

Although he possesses all manner of virtues, he constantly desires to gather all wholesome dharmas and desires to deliver all beings; this is called the non-diminution of desire. Eighth, the non-diminution of vigor:
the Buddha’s two kinds of vigor—of body and mind—are never at rest as he delivers others through compassion;

yet he dwells peacefully in cessation, neither increasing nor decreasing; this is called the non-diminution of vigor. Ninth, the non-diminution of mindfulness: regarding the Buddha’s [mindfulness] throughout the three periods of time...

Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*): because they are associated with all-encompassing wisdom and are fulfilled without diminution, they are called "no diminution of mindfulness" (*smṛty-asaṃpramoṣa*). Regarding the ten wisdoms:

because the Buddha has attained all-encompassing wisdom and has perfected and brought to ultimate completion the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), it is called "no diminution of wisdom" (*jñāna-asaṃpramoṣa*).
Regarding the eleven liberations (*vimokṣa*): the Buddha possesses two kinds of liberation; the first is... [the liberation through meditative concentration].

Liberation (*vimukti*) refers to that which is associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Second, unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*) refers to the total exhaustion of all afflictions (*kleśa*) without remainder;
this is called "liberation without decrease. Twelfth, the "knowledge and vision of liberation without decrease":

regarding all liberations, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are perfectly clear and distinct, and his wisdom is immeasurable and boundless; this is called the "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
There is no decrease. In the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth [stages], all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Buddhas proceed in accordance with wisdom.
All the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Buddhas have wisdom as their foundation. Having attained unimpeded knowledge, they preach inexhaustibly;
there is nothing that does not benefit all sentient beings. Their three karmas are tranquil; this is also called the "three non-... (the three non-regressions).
Sixteenth, the unimpeded wisdom that knows the past: the Buddha’s wisdom illuminates and knows the past;
everything throughout the limits of the past—whether phenomena pertaining to sentient beings or phenomena not pertaining to sentient beings—he fully and universally knows without impediment.
Seventeenth, the unimpeded wisdom that knows the future: the Buddha’s wisdom knows the future without impediment.

The Buddha’s wisdom illuminates future worlds; throughout the entirety of the future limit, all things—whether phenomena pertaining to sentient beings or phenomena not pertaining to sentient beings—he fully knows without obstruction.
With the eighteen kinds of wisdom, he knows the present world without obstruction.

The Buddha’s wisdom illuminates the present world; throughout the entirety of the present limit, all things—whether phenomena pertaining to sentient beings or [phenomena not pertaining to sentient beings]—[he fully knows without obstruction].
He fully and unimpededly knows all the dharmas of sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "words and deeds correspond": Cunda dwells in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and speaks in accordance with his practice; therefore, it is called "correspondence."

Regarding "right view and right knowledge": right view belongs to concentration (*samādhi*), while right knowledge belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*). Just as when one internally possesses both concentration and wisdom, they enable external application;
because concentration and wisdom increase the ground [of practice], it is called "right guarding" and "right teaching."
"Permanent causes and conditions" refers to practicing the causes and conditions of permanence.
Regarding the "single word of reprimand and exhortation," in the preceding passage, Mañjuśrī merely first reprimands and subsequently rejoices.
When the Sage speaks only of his own dharma, it means that Cunda, dwelling in the stage of the ten abodes, speaks of the dharma he has personally realized; this is called "his own dharma.
If one speaks of what they have not yet personally realized, it is called "speaking of another's dharma."

"Obstructing the 'Great Latter'" means to hinder, to block, or to sever. This clarifies that Cunda raised an objection regarding the "Small Initial" while challenging the "Great Latter," to which the Tathāgata extensively replied that the two types of giving are without difference.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī and Cunda each held their own positions, failing to accord with the perfect principle;
thus, the assembly collectively set them aside. Such delusions were precisely intended to be blocked and severed for those who might later cling to the "Small Initial."

Regarding the phrase "after the Great [Perfection of Wisdom]": this refers to those who, following the exposition of the Great [Vehicle], used it to refute the followers of the Small [Vehicle] at its inception.

By causing them to cease their views and realize that the karmic fruits of the two types of giving are no different, they are identified as the "mixed assembly. The underlying meaning is that these are individuals who, after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, were further subdued by the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Those who have come to this assembly for the Nirvāṇa are called the new multitude.

As for your exhortation that I should conceal [the truth] and so forth: in this case, Mañjuśrī conceals the real while employing the provisional, whereas Cunda conceals the provisional while employing the real.
That which cannot be fully utilized is because this existence is the very substance of its function; therefore, it is inexhaustible.

That which cannot have its limit exhausted is because this non-existence is the very substance itself; its measure is identical to the Dharma-realm, and the path of language is severed, so there is nothing that can exhaust it.

That which words do not reach is the function within the essence; thus, when words fail to reach "existence," it is the essence within the function. When words fail to reach "non-existence," it is the essence within the function.

As for "setting aside the primary meaning" (*paramārtha-vyavasthāpana*): this refers to the submerging of function and returning to the essence, which is named the primary meaning. Why is this so? It is because the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa...
Since *parinirvāṇa* is neither existent nor non-existent and cannot be fathomed, it is for the time being set aside.

As for those who do not know its true nature—those who are enlightened and have attained realization understand that mutual attachments are all merely provisional manifestations of what is neither expedient nor substantial;
this is the true essence of *nirvāṇa*. The deluded do not comprehend the meaning of these mutual attachments, and thus it is said they "do not know."
Regarding "setting aside for the sake of others": one makes offerings to generate wholesome roots for sentient beings; therefore, it is categorized as being for others. Furthermore, Zezhou says:
"To rectify the discussion, [the matter] is temporarily set aside rather than permanently; thus, it is said 'let it be set aside for now.'"
The Sūtra states that regarding "fundamental seeds," giving (*dāna*) is the seed of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while the objects given are the seeds of giving.

As for the principle concerning those who involve themselves with greed, the meaning is that the Great Assembly does not enter *nirvāṇa*, nor do they require food; both [of these] should be unnecessary.
This is because of one's own greed.
Mañjuśrī’s seeing it as identical with others refers to seeing it as identical with those people who present the food.
His sealing of their reproach refers to sealing their reproach as being appropriate.

Regarding the phrase "having received the Buddha’s approval": Mañjuśrī’s intention is that you say the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has received the Buddha’s approval; I say the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) should likewise receive his approval.
Since he does not approve of me, it follows that the Tathāgata possesses a mind of attachment and aversion, and thus approves of one side while disapproving of the other.
Regarding the "simultaneous subduing" (fu-bing), the first instance of "subduing" states: "If the Tathāgata delights in you, it is not fitting that he should delight in sentient beings.

Since sentient beings are already delighted by me, why does he not delight in me? The subsequent instance of "subduing" states: "Since the Tathāgata delights in sentient beings, it stands to reason that he should delight in me.
Since he does not delight in me, how can he delight in you? Based on this, these instances of "delighting" are all partial; the term "delight" (yue) lacks any definitive meaning.
This is the sign of subduing [the opposing views].
As for the passage in the Sūtra stating, "You should not... [to] be pleased," Cunda’s intention was this: "I am speaking in accordance with the principle of the teaching;
it is that the Tathāgata is pleased with me, not that the Tathāgata possesses a mind of love or hatred and is thus biasedly pleased with me alone."
The Sūtra says, "Those who act in conjunction with inversion. It is not only your claim that there is such an inversion; my claim that there is no such thing is itself an inversion. Why is this?
Because what is considered pleasant is the cause of craving and aversion. Therefore, it is said they "act in conjunction."
Regarding the analogy that clarifies according to the text: this uses a metaphor to reveal a fault.

It shows that worldly people, because they possess affectionate attachment, may perform acts of transformation to benefit others, yet whether the task is completed or not, they suddenly abandon it to instead benefit their own kin. The Buddha has no such thoughts.
Therefore, it is in contrast to the faults that the state of being free from them is manifested.
Regarding "universally pure and pleasing": "universal" refers to viewing all things with equality; "pure" means that nothing can reach or affect it.
As for the two analogies concerning Ye-cheng (Yecheng): both are cases of those below not knowing what is above; this interpretation is correct. [The analogy of] the Cloud-Root (Yun-gen).
The meaning of the *dharmakāya* may be applied to a limited extent; all else is inadmissible.
Thus, when it is said that "all speech is exhausted," it is because speech is exhausted that it is inconceivable, and because deliberation is brought to its ultimate end that it is inconceivable.
"Various auspicious signs" refers to the nine signs mentioned in the first fascicle.

"Supporting those above and transforming those below" means that invoking the name of the Buddha is called "supporting those above," while meeting the capacities and needs of sentient beings is called "transforming those below."
The Sūtra states that it is not without cause or condition; first, it urges the offering of alms, and second, he will certainly enter Nirvāṇa—these are the causes and conditions.
As for his not having given his consent, it is truly because his compassion is so profound that he has no leisure to utter words; therefore, it is said he has "not yet consented."
To cease such agitation, one should contemplate the benefits of the Dharma. Why weep? Sorrow is of no avail; a distracted mind loses its way, which is unbecoming for a practitioner.
One should observe the body and relinquish the purposeless intent.
Regarding the six similes for emptiness: these six are all empty because they are subject to complete disintegration.
Regarding the three similes for impermanence: their substance is entirely lacking solidity, as they perish moment by moment.
The three similes for impurity: having taken a piece of overripe, rotten fruit, one finds that its flesh is entirely decayed; this is used as a metaphor.

The two similes for non-self: just as a woven cloth depends entirely on the warp and woof, with the upper necessarily relying on the lower, and none possessing independence—this is used as a metaphor for non-self.

The Sūtra says: "One who still eats mixed food"—that is, when the five dharmas such as suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and so forth are combined with the benefit of food, it kills the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body;
therefore, one should contemplate them as equal.

The Sūtra states that "the nature of all Buddhas is thus" (dharmatā). This means that according to the principles of transformation and manifestation, when the ritual forms of teaching have fulfilled their purpose, they must necessarily cease; hence it is called "thusness.
The Sūtra states that "they reach this place," meaning that they all reach the place of Lesser Nirvāṇa as well as the place of Great Nirvāṇa.
Regarding *nirvāṇa*: to know that the manifested Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) has entered extinction is called knowing *nirvāṇa*; to know that the true [body] eternally abides is called non-*nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, because they do not currently know the extinction of the Tathāgata’s manifestation, it is said that they cannot conceive of the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata;
likewise, because they do not know that the Buddha’s true body is eternally abiding, this is called non-*nirvāṇa*.

Regarding "taking a friend with him to prepare [the offerings]," the *Daohui ji* states: "Because Cunda’s conduct had not yet fully mastered the methods for arranging offerings, he took Mañjuśrī with him.
Furthermore, as for "friends": those who dwell together under the same teacher are called *peng* (companions); those who share the same resolve are called *you* (friends).
They are those who are closely knit together through cold and dampness, heat and humidity, and who understand one another in times of hunger and satiety.

The Imperial Commentary on the Śrīmālādevī Sūtra: Part Four. Now, this section clarifies the Master’s formal exposition of the latter part of this chapter.
First, regarding the term "world" (*loka*): it is so called because of the distinction between the internal and external.

Next, as for the phrase "furthermore, already-arisen goodness is corrupted": "corrupted" (*yǒu) means erroneous or deviant. If the Buddha has departed from the world, already-arisen goodness will inevitably fall into error.
"Ya-xiao:
'The good has not yet arisen' means that it is obscured; the goodness of the Buddha-nature is hidden and does not manifest.
Furthermore, 'the evil appears' means that even though the practitioner has not yet exhausted their training, the residual habits of learning have not been fully eliminated."
Regarding "those who harbor evil," this refers to the ignorance as vast as dust and sand.
Next, in distinguishing the differences, the preceding chapter follows from the person, as Cunda is a person;
the subsequent chapter follows from the matter, as the long sigh pertains to the matter.
The "opponent" in the preceding chapter refers to what the worldly call the son of a craftsman;
the "opponent on the Path" in this chapter refers to the bhikṣu who practices the threefold cultivation.
In this chapter, there is no offering, for there is only the invitation to the Dharma.

Regarding the dual requests in the preceding chapter—requesting the acceptance of the final offering and requesting the Buddha to remain in the world—the request in this chapter concerns only his remaining in the world.
Regarding the "person" in the preceding chapter, the aforementioned text states: "Out of compassion for us, we only pray that you will quickly entreat the Buddha to remain for a long time."
He benefits immeasurable multitudes in the world; this is precisely because of the great assembly that Cunda made his request.
In this chapter, the bhikṣus themselves requested that [the Buddha] remain.
As for the brief elucidation of the Buddha-nature in the preceding chapter, it was called "brief" because the permanence [of the Buddha] was revealed through such acts as the offering of food.

Regarding the discussion in the preceding chapter on the present teaching, it concerns both the Buddha and Cunda; all discourse therein pertains to the dharma of the perfect and eternal Buddha-nature within the present teaching.
This chapter fully elucidates the three types of cultivation—superior, inferior, and middling.
The discussion between two individuals in the preceding chapter refers to the discourse between Mañjuśrī and Cunda.
The discussion in the present chapter in relation to the Buddha refers to the three bhikṣus who questioned the Buddha.

In the preceding chapter, those who harbored doubts due to their attachment to movement heard that there is no difference between the two types of giving; they immediately clung to their former doubts, now constructing doubts regarding distinctions and raising the five objections.
In this chapter, which refutes attachments and eliminates doubts, the doubts and attachments concerning inferior cultivation are destroyed, and the three superior dharmas are cultivated.
Regarding the presence of both the general and the specific: among these ten differences, each one applies universally.

As for those who can discourse [on the Dharma] in the preceding chapter and in this chapter, they are likewise human beings. In the preceding [chapter], there were also matters of lamentation; in the preceding chapter, Mañjuśrī and others were also on the Path.

Now, in this chapter, how could the assembly of fifty-two not include those of the secular world? Furthermore, in the preceding chapter, there were also those who did not offer provisions, yet they went to the side of the Buddha’s assembly. Now...
This chapter also takes the Dharma as its offering. Regarding the earthquake that extends back to the preceding section:

since it is stated that "not long after Cunda had departed, the earth suddenly shook violently," this earthquake extends through two chapters. One should reflect upon the various other instances that follow to see this for oneself.
Regarding the third point, "The Arising within the Exegesis of Xinghuang," this refers to its own arising.

Regarding the fourth point, in the section "Now Explaining Below" under the main exegesis, it says "not departing from causes and conditions. This means that there is nothing that is not the movement resulting from the mutual resonance of the four *siddhāntas* (the fourfold teaching) and the path.
However, the text places "having conditions" within the context of liberation; this constitutes the *puruṣakāra* (benefit for persons).

Prajñā is the remedy; the Dharmakāya is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Hearing that these three powers are non-different yet different, one moves through the stages (*bhūmi*) and gives rise to a heart of compassion and joy—this is the world (*loka*). The same applies to the next two individuals and the great assembly.
Regarding the phrase "its meaning is immeasurable": this refers to the fifty-two assemblies of those who lead and those who are led, each and every person of whom possesses the four *siddhāntas*.
Thus it is said. One may understand how the sequence of the four lines from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* corresponds to the four *siddhāntas*.

Regarding the four matters that stop the grief of those in the city of Pāṭaliputra: these are the four passages beginning with "the realm of the Tathāgata," which appear at the end of the preceding chapter.
The term *bì* (腷) [with the phonetic gloss *fú* (符) and *bì* (逼)] means that the inner meaning does not leak out.
Regarding those that consist solely of form and sound: "moving," "arising," and "leaping" refer to form; "shaking," "surging," and "bursting" refer to sound.
As the Sūtra says, "moving exclusively": when a form moves directly, it is called "moving."

That which moves sequentially from beginning to end and throughout all directions is called "universal shaking" (*samprakampita*). That which shakes everywhere simultaneously is as described in the sutra:
regarding the Tuṣita Heaven, both the *Carmavastu* (translated as *Chamatuojie jing*) and the *Daoxing jing* (the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*) both translate it as "tranquil" (*śānta*).
The *Śāstra* (Commentary), fascicle 51, states: "Miaozu" (Exquisite Feet) is also called "Doushu.
Regarding the words [heard], they must have been the sounds within the earthquake that said, "Today the Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa," and so forth;
therefore it says, "Having heard these words..."
The Sūtra says: "That which is not fit to be consumed refers to the dharma of impermanence, which should not be practiced;

therefore, it is called 'unfit'. Regarding "lofty, perfect, and luminous": one who presides above the myriad people is called "lofty"; one whose manifold virtues are fully complete is called "perfect"; and one who has attained thorough realization is called "luminous."
The sentiments of the myriad people are clear in this:
entering deeply into the bottom of water is analogous to drawing near to those who benefit one. Water relies on the earth and relies on mountains, just as a child relies on its parents;

thus there is the benefit of having a refuge and being nurtured. If a mountain were to enter the water, the water would have something to rely upon; therefore, entering the water is used as a metaphor for relying on parents.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the color of the water is the same as the mountain": it means that because the teacher is able to provide guidance and the disciple’s understanding accords with the teacher’s intent, the analogy of "same color" is used.

Regarding "the illuminating wisdom of Guangzhai," the meaning of Guangzhai is that during the stage of causal practice there is the wisdom of "reflective illumination" (*fanzhào zhì*), which reaches fulfillment upon the completion of the fruit.
Because wisdom is stilled, there is no reflective illumination.
Regarding the "four losses," the old commentary states: "The four greats are laughable.
*Lèi* (pronounced *lěi*) refers to the notion that the mundane exists outside the real, and the real exists outside the mundane; this is called "separation" (*lèigé*).
Regarding "purifying the earth with cow dung," others interpret this as follows: the earth is inherently impure; Śākyamuni merely manifests a pure land provisionally upon this defiled land.
How is this known? It is like when Śākyamuni touches the ground with his foot, the earth immediately becomes pure, just as a spot of ground becomes pure when rubbed with cow dung.
"Perceiving sensation at the tip of a finger" means that once one has realized wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), there is no longer the wisdom of retrospective reflection;
it is like a person looking at the tip of their own finger who cannot see anything distant.
"The Tathāgata is indeterminate" clarifies that the Tathāgata’s wisdom transcends both good and evil, and is therefore termed "pure white" (*bai-jing*).
It is indeterminate.
As for "one wisdom and three wisdoms," both are able to destroy darkness. As for "three wisdoms and one wisdom," both are able to reflect back upon themselves.
That which is neither three nor one, yet is both three and one, is in every case inconceivable.

Regarding "that which is one within the three": it means that the three are identical to the one. Since all [three] are simultaneously capable of illumination, how could this be like the Kai-shan school, which holds that there is merely a single wisdom that illuminates alone?

Regarding "the inconceivability of the three and the one," Master Guan said: "There is simply a single wisdom that is naturally capable of reflexive illumination. Why is this not [the case for others]?"
To know that the three are one and the one is three; that they are neither three nor one, yet one is three and three is one.
Their essence pervades the Dharma-realm, their quiescence and manifestation are mutually identical. Therefore, it is called "inconceivable."
Regarding the "Exposition of the Old [System]": the present school’s [textual divisions] are largely identical to those of the old system; they differ only slightly in terminology and phrasing.

However, following the points of agreement, we shall rely on the ancient divisions to segment the text by tracing the sutra passages. As for the phrase "there is great hindrance," "great" (kyū) means significant.

From the beginning at the Deer Park until the end at the *Prajñāpāramitā*, whether esoteric or exoteric, [the teachings] culminate in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where the provisional means are clearly unveiled.
All see the Buddha-nature and equally enter the perfect and eternal; how could they all be termed the "arts and crafts" of the Hīnayāna?
The *caṇḍāla* refers to those of the Two Vehicles who have not yet attained the benefit that is neither eternal nor impermanent.
The Tathāgata’s relinquishing of his response [to them] is like entrusting a son to a *caṇḍāla*. Their lack of the karmic capacity for the Path is called "ugly countenance";

the Sage’s compassionate pity is called "constant love and remembrance. His exhortation and instruction in the Three Studies is called "teaching arts and crafts"; what they have practiced has reached completion, and their mastery is fully realized.

This analogy has a beginning. The Buddha’s relinquishing of parinirvāṇa and causing the bhikṣus to be afflicted by the cycle of changeable birth and death is called "entrusting to the caṇḍālas," used as a metaphor for that which has no end.
The Sūtra says: "We (up to) the prince, together with all the other sons, have received the Buddha’s instruction and training in the arts;
we have attained right view and are thoroughly proficient in them; our forms are also upright and handsome.
Attaining the fruits of the Hīnayāna is what is meant by "attaining right view"—this implies having a beginning. We pray that you will not abandon us, so that there may be no end in the future.
Regarding this, the various commentators have said: Fa-yao stated, "This analogy refers to the Buddha being fully endowed with *prajñā*. He should remain in the world to preach it for our sake;
yet his parinirvāṇa is like the realm of all phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), in which he does not speak. Now, my true concern is that he fears the Māra of Death. Why?
If the Tathāgata has not yet subdued the Māra of Death, why would he fear this Māra and abandon us to enter nirvāṇa?"
Regarding the third analogy concerning the violation of vows, Bao Liang said: "This means that the Buddha should not fail to fulfill his vows.

In the past, he made the Four Great Vows to remain within the cycle of birth and death to deliver all sentient beings. Now that the illnesses of sentient beings have been cured and I am fortunately among those who were to be delivered, yet the Buddha has ceased his transformative activity—does this not constitute a violation of his vows?"

The Sūtra says: "Therefore, there are those who harbor secret reserves. If the Buddha were not to abide [in this world] and teach me so that I might attain liberation, he would possess such secret reserves—just like that physician.
That the people have no Buddha to sustain their lives is like being before the destruction of ignorance.
To "cling to the likeness of Mañjuśrī" means that since the Buddha has already specifically instructed Mañjuśrī, I now likewise wish to cling to his likeness.
Why does the Tathāgata not instruct me so that I may become equal to Mañjuśrī? Why does he abandon us and enter parinirvāṇa? Thus...
This satirizes the Master’s intention.

Regarding the phrase "ceasing external sorrow and so forth": one should contemplate the true mark of the mind, and contemplating the Buddha is likewise so; contemplating the true mark of the Buddha, contemplating the mind is likewise so.
How can one share in the joys and sorrows of ordinary people?
Regarding gain and loss, joy and sorrow: the four favorable winds constitute gain and joy, while the four unfavorable winds constitute loss and sorrow. One should not grieve over such losses;
for in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is neither loss nor gain—how, then, could there be sorrow or lamentation?
Indeed, the very essence of this sorrow and lamentation is eternally quiescent, and therefore it cannot be pursued.

Regarding "diligently obstructing the two evils" and so forth: in contrast to the diligent contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this is called right effort (*samyakpradhāna*).

Seeing and thinking that [afflictions] have already arisen is termed "evil already produced"; by contemplating them as empty (*śūnyatā*), one causes those already produced not to arise, and thus exerts diligent vigor.

Viewing the sands of phenomena and ignorance as "evil yet to be produced," one contemplates them as provisional (*prajñapti*) and as the Middle Way (*madhyamā*), causing those yet to be produced not to arise, and thus exerts diligent vigor. One must exert oneself to the utmost.
The practice of the four samādhis truly wards off these two evils. The knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) is called "wholesome states already arisen";

because this wholesome state is easy to produce, it is said that the path to nirvāṇa is easily attained. The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are called "wholesome states not yet arisen.

One should diligently increase the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) that has already arisen, and cause the wisdom of the conventional and the middle way (*upāya-madhyamājñāna*) that has not yet arisen to be brought forth.
Because it is wholesome, there is neither sorrow nor joy; this is because the wholesome is the true nature (*dharmatā*).

As for "right mindfulness," it is to constantly contemplate *nirvāṇa*. The essence of *nirvāṇa* is all-pervasive; being pervasive, it is eternally quiescent, and is thus termed "non-thought" (*amanasikāra*).
Regarding the phrase "Whose ministerial offspring are they?": where there is a ruler, there is a loyal minister to serve him; where there is a parent, there is a filial son to return to them;

where there is a teacher, there is a disciple to attend upon them. Now, seeking right mindfulness, one realizes that the source is fundamentally dark and true, wherein both subject and object are quiescent;
therefore, "Whose ruler? and so forth refer to the responsive [aspect], while "Who is delivered? and so forth refer to the perceiving [aspect].
I (the Emperor; "zhèn" pronounced "zhí rèn," meaning "myself") say that to have no master for oneself means to lose the correct path—that is, the correct path to Nirvana.
To attain goodness means to attain the goodness of the Hīnayāna; to lose goodness means to lose the goodness of the Mahāyāna, which is like the loss of a child.
Now, regarding those who hear of "proximity to wisdom": observing the nature of the mind as it is now is itself proximity to nirvana; how could it be otherwise?
How much more so for one who has opened up both meditative concentration and wisdom? Even worldly diligence brings no sorrow, let alone supramundane concentration and wisdom.
Regarding birth-and-death and nirvāṇa: birth-and-death is impermanent, while nirvāṇa is permanent. Both accord with the essence of the Great Nirvāṇa, which is neither permanent nor impermanent.
To clearly understand these two functions: the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is itself a skillful means, and the manifestation of birth is likewise a skillful means; both are eternal.
That which is impermanent is itself eternal; all are caused to abide within the treasury of the three virtues. Therefore, it is said that this is the "dharmatā" (the natural order of things).
Furthermore, regarding what is called "dharmatā": when the conditions for response arise, they should be extinguished and return to the truth; such is the nature of all transformative manifestations.

As for the sūtra’s statement that [the Buddha] remained constantly silent: first, it was to stop the weeping; second, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas. Since they have all entered *parinirvāṇa*, why should one request them to remain?
Furthermore, as for the question "What benefit would there be in allowing him to stay?": if you yourself lack the capacity (*indriya*), what benefit would his remaining in the world provide?
Regarding "he who opens the inquiry": if emptiness and non-emptiness were necessarily not two, one should indeed question this.
Regarding "further revealing the Bodhisattva": this refers to the subsequent Kāśyapa Bodhisattva.

To ask whether that which is not empty is illness is to understand that when the conventional is realized as emptiness, it is then called the healing of the illness; the other phrases are likewise so.
Furthermore, birth and death are provisional and ultimately return to emptiness, whereas Nirvana is perfectly consummate, serene, and eternally present, and is thus "not empty.

Formerly, the three unconditioned states were taken as the permanent; now, it is clarified that wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara*) is the permanent. The remaining phrases follow this analogy. This is one teaching.
If the explanations of the teachings have not yet been clarified,
and one further opens them up for public inquiry— as in the thirty-four questions below—
then these various explanations will be faultless; whether applied to the present or the past, both explanations are universally valid.

Regarding the "three kinds" and "four kinds": the "three" refers to the preceding passages concerning emptiness and non-emptiness; the "four kinds" refer to the subsequent passage which treats the matter through four gates.
