Furthermore, within the five periods, these two *sūtras* (the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Nirvāṇa*) are interconnected, both possessing the three and the four. Up to the present, they have all been opened up, and there is nothing that is not true reality;
thus it is said, "extensively analyzed. Now, I shall further provide an explanation based on the text: namely, that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is termed "empty," while *nirvāṇa*...
The *pātra* is not empty. Furthermore, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called "empty," while according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is not empty.

If one proceeds from the perspective of ultimate reality, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is taken as the ultimate truth; thus, the ultimate truth is not empty, whereas the conventional truth is called "empty.
Because it is real, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states that false phenomena are called the "empty" [aspect of] the Tathāgatagarbha, while true phenomena are called the "non-empty" treasury.

Regarding "if it is both permanent and impermanent": birth and death are impermanent, while nirvana is permanent; furthermore, conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is impermanent, while ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is permanent.

Regarding "if it is suffering or not": Master Bao said, "If one proceeds according to the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), then from the diamond stage (vajra-bhūmi) downward, one is still said to possess suffering."
That which has already transcended wondrous enlightenment is called non-suffering. One should say that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is suffering, while *nirvāṇa* is not suffering;
the two truths are likewise so.

As for what is to be relied upon and what is not: the Three Jewels are to be relied upon, whereas external paths are not to be relied upon. Furthermore, true dharmas are to be relied upon, while false dharmas are not.
It cannot be relied upon. Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* teaches that the Tathāgatagarbha is the one reliance.
Regarding "going" and "not going": correct practice leading to transcendence is called "going," while erroneous practice leading to sinking is said to be "not going.
Furthermore, the cause is termed "going," whereas the fruit is "not going."

If one speaks of "taking refuge" and "not taking refuge": the Lesser Vehicle’s progression toward the Great is called "taking refuge," while the Great Vehicle, having no destination, is called "not taking refuge.
Furthermore, the cause involves taking refuge, whereas the fruit is without refuge.
Regarding "the eternal" and "the non-eternal," these are generally explained as being identical to the aforementioned "the permanent" and "the impermanent.

If discussed specifically, that which is unarisen is called "permanent," and that which is undestroyed is called "eternal. Furthermore, birth-and-death is not nirvana; this is "eternal. Moreover, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is called "eternal," while the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is "non-eternal."
Regarding "either interrupted or eternal": saṃsāra is taught as being interruptible, while nirvāṇa is eternal; furthermore, false consciousness is interruptible, while true consciousness is eternal.
Regarding "sentient beings or non-sentient beings": internally they are sentient beings, while externally they are non-sentient beings; furthermore, they are sentient beings by way of designation.

In reality, they are not sentient beings. Furthermore, although there are those who are sentient beings, emptiness is not a sentient being. Moreover, because non-sentient beings are free from birth and death, whereas others are sentient beings because they have not yet permanently severed [the cycle].
Regarding "existence" and "non-existence": the three conditioned dharmas are termed existence, while the three unconditioned dharmas are described as non-existence.
Furthermore, speaking in terms of persons: ordinary beings possess birth and death but lack nirvana; noble ones possess nirvana but lack birth and death.
Regarding the real and the unreal: saṃsāra is unreal and nirvāṇa is called real. Furthermore, the One Vehicle is real and the Three Vehicles are unreal.
Moreover, deluded sentiment is unreal and the Buddha-nature is real. Additionally, conventional truth is unreal and ultimate truth is real.
Furthermore, the two truths are not both real; rather, one reality is the truth.

If that which is true were not true, then birth-and-death would not be unreal and nirvana would not be real. Moreover, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is true, while the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is not true.
Regarding "if it is both extinguished and not extinguished": in relation to the Four Noble Truths, the Truth of Cessation is extinction, while the other three are not.
Furthermore, false phenomena can be extinguished, whereas true phenomena are not extinguished.

Regarding "secret" and "not secret": either the Lesser Vehicle is secret while the Greater Vehicle is not secret; or, in the Lesser Vehicle, concealing the reality is called secret, whereas in the Greater Vehicle, revealing the reality is called not secret;
or, in the Greater Vehicle, that which is profound and hidden is called secret, while in the Lesser Vehicle, that which is coarse and manifest is called not secret.
Regarding "if there are two or not two," this is discussed in terms of the vehicles (*yāna*). The provisional and the small are called "two"; the single great reality is called "not two.

If the body were to exist [and yet] not be the *dharmatā*, then according to the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), one must first extinguish the body and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* before it can be called the Dharma.
As for the nature (*dharmatā*): while the body exists, it is not called the *dharmatā*.
Now, regarding the statement that "the *dharmatā* is the extinction of dharmas," this means that the *dharmatā* is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished.
That you previously did not accept [this] and took nirvāṇa for yourself is not due to any inequality on my part.

Regarding "being free from the eight difficulties," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The four wheels crush the eight difficulties. First, the wheel of having planted roots of goodness in past lives crushes the first four difficulties.
Second, the wheel of diligently making correct vows crushes the difficulty of possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence. Third, the wheel of making offerings to the Buddhas...

It destroys the obstacles of being born before or after a Buddha. It causes one to be born in a central land within the four modes of birth. It destroys the obstacles of being born in the northern continent of Uttarakuru or the long-lived heavens.
Next, the mention of gold sand serves as a metaphor for the latter five obstacles; just as gold sand is extremely difficult to find, so too are these [five] within the cycle of birth and death.
These five matters sought are extremely difficult to encounter. The metaphor of the *tánhuā* (rare flower) illustrates the difficulty of a Buddha appearing in the world.
One should not recognize a Buddha through worldly intimacy; one should not use worldly kinship as a metaphor for the Buddha.
While such things may exist in the world, the Buddha is not like this; therefore, it is rebuked as being inappropriate.
Those who do not recognize the Buddha are, by this very fact, ignorant of the Dharmakāya; though it eternally exists without change, they fail to recognize the Buddha as their own kin.
Furthermore, they simply do not recognize the Buddha within their own bodies. Because they do not recognize him, they are not princes.

"One who does not recognize the treasure city" refers to one who does not recognize that both the interior and exterior of the treasure city are made of jewels— just as one fails to recognize the city of Nirvana,

which is adorned with the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and is fully present within this very body. Because of this lack of recognition, the body is not upright or well-proportioned.
Regarding "those who are self-obscured by ignorance": they do not recognize that their own ignorance and afflictions are like *caṇḍālas*; what does this have to do with the Buddha’s entrustment?

Regarding "the gate is not small": it is the gate of the expedient means of identical essence; because it universally penetrates all things, it is not small, and it universally encompasses [all beings].
"Never having been stingy with his possessions": "suddenly" (*hu*) means lightly.
Regarding "pointing to the mountains and so forth," it refers to giving away his body and head like Mount Vipula.
Furthermore, throughout the trichiliocosm, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where the Bodhisattva has not sacrificed his body and life; therefore, it is said "doubly."
"Much.

Such merit and virtue refers to the fact that all the aforementioned ascetic practices were undertaken for the sake of nirvana and for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings; this is what is called "merit and virtue."
As for those who lack a sense of shame (*ahrīka*), they are unable to feel shame before those of noble station.
Bound in prison, it is because they themselves lack the great capacity (*mahā-indriya*) that their superior response is not manifested; this is not the fault of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said:
"It is not that I am ungracious."

"Severe" refers to the precepts that are perfect, eternal, and complete. Because they universally prohibit all evils, they are called "severe. Because they perfectly transcend the two types of death, they are termed "perilous.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of the "perils and difficulties of birth and death"; this is precisely the proof of this point.
"Samādhi" refers specifically to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
"Píènxì" (to look askance) means to peer; it is read as *fǎngyì* in the upper tone and *wǔjì* in the lower tone, signifying a sidelong glance.

"Broadly penetrating both ancient and modern" means that by means of the great wisdom of the same essence (*tóngtǐ dàhuì*), one universally reveals that the coarseness of the four seasons is none other than the sublime.
"Renowned for broad knowledge of the past and present;

both inner and outer are treasures. Here, "inner" refers to the virtues of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), and "outer" refers to the virtues of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). Since the essence of cultivation and nature is identical, they are said to be "both treasures.
Furthermore, the provisional application of transforming others is the "outer," while the practical application of one's own practice is the "inner"; thus, the subsequent line says, "overflowing."
"Exquisite" (guī; *gǔ qū* [rhyme with *qí*]) refers to beautiful jade.
"Not weary of refuse-rags" means not regarding them as burning refuse.
"Not delighting" means not taking pleasure in the superior, wondrous, and great tranquility of the *kaṇṭhaka* necklace (*yíngluò*).
"Regarding 'you do not see the Buddha and so forth': to fail to recognize the Buddha of the eternal body, characterized by the three dots and four virtues, is called 'not seeing the Buddha.
To fail to understand the Dharma of the true, eternal, and quiescent essence, and to fail to awaken to the ultimate teaching of the Tathāgata, is called 'not hearing the Dharma.'"
One who does not attain the profound above nor harmonize with the principle below is called a monk who does not enter the ranks of the assembly.

Such a person cannot be said to be free from obstacles; that is, they cannot be free from the eight difficulties outside the boundary. The subsequent passage concerning "obstacles" (*nān*) is likewise the same.

The eight difficulties outside the realm are termed "difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) by way of principle. That is to say, [being born] as one of the three evil destinies, or in the state of no-thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), or in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) where it is impossible to generate the resolve for awakening—this is called "conforming to evil.

This applies even up to those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Furthermore, if one enters the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and the Buddha-way is forever extinguished, [it is likewise a difficulty].

Is it not the case that the three evil realms constitute a difficulty? Fourth, regarding the fixed lifespan of Uttarakuru as a difficulty: among the Four Noble Truths, the Truth of Cessation corresponds to the North;
when Śrāvakas realize cessation, they are like that fixed lifespan. Fifth, regarding the long-lived heavens:

those of the Two Vehicles are called "Pure Heavens," but if they enter Nirvana without remainder and return to the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (Paramārtha), how could they be converted? Sixth, regarding the periods before and after a Buddha.
1. Those who see the truth upon entering contemplation and perceive the conventional upon emerging from it, yet do not see the Middle Way—this is the "before and after" of the Buddhas.

2. Those with worldly wisdom and eloquence: those of the Two Vehicles who have not yet seen the Middle Way but have developed untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) are said to possess worldly wisdom and eloquence.

3. Those who are deaf, blind, mute, and dumb: persons of the Two Vehicles who lack the faculties of a Bodhisattva; though they may attain the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they do not see [the ultimate].

The forms of the ten realms are like those of the blind; the sounds of the ten realms are not heard, like those of the deaf; one cannot understand through a single voice according to the various types of beings, like those who are mute.

Regarding the "expedient means prior to the Way": that which follows the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and precedes the stage of practicing the causes is termed "prior to the Way. This refers to the state before the realization of wondrous enlightenment.
As for those who follow after the Way, your consciousness exists only in the severance of the ashes;
though there are those who precede the Way, they possess only the expedient means of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, and thus it is not the perfect cause.

The Sūtra states, "For your sake, throughout immeasurable kalpas," which refers to the manifestation of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arising during the interval after attaining Buddhahood, such as by demonstrating the relinquishing of the body and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "giving rise to wondrous goodness": it is called "giving rise to" because cultivation is initiated from the nature (*prakṛti*), thereby accords with that nature.

Regarding "vertical and horizontal": penetrating the principle through the three trainings is called vertical; the essence pervading and encompassing all phenomena is called horizontal. The subsequent three sections explain the high and broad [aspects] based on the preceding vertical and horizontal.
Regarding "the exhaustion of delusions": one should further state that the exhaustion of delusions is the exhaustion of contemplation; when contemplation ceases, delusions cease.

Those who delight in the dharmas favored by the poor do not seek the true nature of the Mahāyāna; they cherish only the small vehicle’s biased emptiness, which is like a counterfeit pebble instead of a bright moon-jewel.

They are not true *bhikṣus* worthy of offerings; they are not the ultimate *bhikṣus* worthy of offerings who abide in the Middle Way beyond the realms. They are merely those who possess the merit of the True Dharma.
He is one who is worthy of offerings within this realm; therefore, he is dismissed as "not [so].
Regarding that which is useless yet used: medicinal herbs are inherently useless, but it is solely due to the suitability for sentient beings that these herbs come to have utility.
Regarding "invited by karma": karma is like a mechanical device, and the great earth is like the Dharma-body. Responding to an invocation is like [the ripening of] past good roots.
Since past good roots have degrees of depth, the medicine administered has its own value and price. This refers to the third of the three applications.

The threefold "revolving" refers to the three aspects of the great earth, the three aspects of medicinal herbs, and the three aspects of sentient beings' utilization; these cannot be separated from one another.

It is like the Dharma-body giving rise to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), which must preach the Dharma, and the preaching of the Dharma necessarily involves the receptive capacities and conditions of sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called "revolving."
Regarding the phrase "the three meanings of the great earth" and so forth: as stated above in the passage beginning "neither arising nor having arisen," this is the union of prajñā and liberation;
the union with the aforementioned three [meanings] is likewise. "Transcendent union" refers precisely to returning to that union.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "and my sons," Master Zezhou stated: Because the virtues of the various Bodhisattvas are capable of succeeding to [the lineage], they are called "sons.
The fourfold assembly—consisting of Śrāvakas, both lay and ordained, each divided into male and female—shares the same teaching and is made to realize Great Parinirvāṇa;
this is termed the "peaceful secret treasury. What is now referred to as "my sons" refers precisely to these four assemblies; there is no need for further elaboration.
This is why the present commentary uses "center" as its counterpart.

Regarding "not understanding the concealment" and "understanding it": [the former] refers to the application of provisional means (*upāya*) not being understood as a concealment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It is like the deceptive doctrines of non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*), which they do not wish others to know and therefore keep hidden. As stated in the sutra below:
Regarding the fact that the Dharma-body is inherently present, Master Sengsheng said: "Now, illumination reaches its ultimate limit naturally, and its abiding principle is supreme.
Since the supreme cannot be equaled, it is necessarily not horizontal; since what is to be eliminated is near, there is no liberation at the lower level.

Since the lower level lacks non-correspondence, the form-body is both 'is' and 'is-not'; since it is not prior, it is also not 'transverse. Since the three absences do not depart from principle, distinguishing them is especially incorrect."
Therefore, it remains steadfast without deviation, just like the letter *i*. This interpretation does not avoid the fault of being either vertical or horizontal, as seen in other texts.
"The third is identical to the first, like a fine stroke" refers to the character for "grass" (*cao*), where the fine strokes are connected.
Regarding the "three eyes," Master Daosheng said: "Prajñā occupies the superior position; because the Dharmakāya and liberation are both without superiority, they are listed together below.
This has already been refuted as before.
The Lord of Adornment who illumines the world: with his three wisdoms, he adorns the Great Parinirvāṇa above, while below he universally illumines the capacities and principles of the Dharma-realm.
This is what is meant by "illumining while ever-quiescent" and "quiescent while ever-illumining. He is like the Heavenly Lord (Indra), who has one face and three eyes;
above, he adorns the celestial countenance, and below, he illumines the world. Because his celestial body is sublime, he possesses this adornment.
Regarding the phrase "to raise up the concise while encompassing all": the Dharma-body encompasses all bodies; Prajñā encompasses all wisdoms;
and Liberation encompasses all dharmas. It manifests bodies and preaches the Dharma, exhausting all provisional and ultimate teachings without exception. Therefore, it is said to "encompass all."
"That which cannot be seen through physical characteristics" means that it cannot be grasped by the six types of physical forms produced by those of lower stages.

"That which cannot be known through mental conception" means that it cannot be known by the mental conceptions of ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, or Bodhisattvas of the partial teachings of the lower stages.
"Pervading the ten directions" means having bodies throughout the ten realms.
"Neither broad nor narrow" means that while the various bodies are not broad, their corresponding [essence] is likewise not narrow.
"Neither knowledge nor words" means that because *prajñā* is merged with the *dharmakāya*, it is neither knowledge nor words.

"Those who cannot move their thoughts or engage in discrimination" means that those of the lower stages, the mundane world, or the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are unable to discern [this];

it refers to one who wears the broad sash. It is like the eighth chapter of the *Lunyu* (Analects): "Zi Chang was in the next room; hearing his master speak of a certain matter from across the wall..."
I feared that you might forget this, so I have recorded it here for you to inscribe upon your sash. Now, to speak truly, it cannot be transmitted through mere words.

To be able to exhaustively realize the illumination of *prajñā* such that the three truths are universally radiant—whether provisional or real, all are illuminated within a single mind—is what is called "universal radiance."
Regarding "half-full and fully complete": by citing these terms, "half" and "full," one encompasses the Buddhadharma of the ten directions and the three periods of time, leaving nothing unexhausted.
"The mundane" refers to the Land of Common Dwelling; "the supramundane" refers to the Land of Expedient Means; and "the supramundane of the supreme" refers to the Land of Reality.
Response: The Buddha dwells in the Land of Tranquil Light (Sukhāvatī), yet shines downward to illuminate the three lands.
Regarding the phrase "the flow of the Dharma-realm": it refers to the universal penetration of the spoken word, whereby all things enter the secret treasury;
this is termed "flowing forth. The teaching descends upon those below like a cascading torrent; its compassionate gathering of sentient beings is likened to the surging of the ocean.
Regarding "expounding with a single sound": in reality, this encompasses all sounds; however, speaking from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is called a "single sound.

Regarding "neither clamor nor stillness": this is neither the clamor of saṃsāra nor the stillness of nirvāṇa. Whether described as bondage or liberation depends on the provisional or the wisdom-based explanation.

As for the statement that the ten knowledges cannot [falsely] negate it: the essence of liberation pervades the entire Dharma-realm; how could it be destroyed by the ten knowledges of the Lesser Vehicle?
Regarding the phrase "for those who are dull-witted and so forth": he is like those who are dull-witted and so forth, yet he liberates others from their bonds.
Regarding the manifestation of good and evil: it should also be said that sentient beings possess evil, or [the Buddha] manifests good for them;
or they possess good, or [the Buddha] manifests evil for them, thereby subduing them.
"Though base, one must surely bestow [upon them]" means that although sentient beings may be base and evil, one must certainly bestow transformation upon them in order to deliver and liberate them.
"The mental activity of the Buddha" refers to the Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) which are not shared with the lower stages; therefore, it is said that his mind is inconceivable.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that "the adornment of the Tathāgata" refers to the purity of wisdom.

Furthermore, regarding the "purity of the six sense faculties," although it cites the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one must explain it based on the six faculties of the true stages (*bhūmi*) as described in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Regarding "including both the general and the specific": this refers to how the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* encompasses the three virtues (*triguṇa*) as well as the various differing explanations found in other sūtras;
hence it is called "general and specific.

Regarding "encompassing both phenomena and principle": the *dharmakāya* is the principle (*li*), while *prajñā* extends from cause to fruition, and *vimukti* (liberation) is the liberation of both self and others.
Both belong to the realm of phenomena (*vastu*).

Regarding "entering Great Nirvāṇa," Master Daosheng said: "The trace of the six-foot [form] is truly real only when its conditions are exhausted; it is called 'entering' because, in terms of response, it no longer manifests.
Furthermore, Master Zeshou said: "Although that which abides is eternal, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, one extinguishes the response and returns to it."
This refers to entering the nirvana of transformation and extinction (*nirmāṇa-nirvāṇa*).
A sutra states that it is like the worldly letter *i*; yet, it further says "transformation and extinction," for the letter *i* would not be formed [otherwise].
As for "not forming the Celestial Eye" (*tiānmù*): the Celestial Eye is identical to the *i*, and therefore it is omitted here.
Yet, by saying "I now," it appears as though one has only just attained enlightenment. Therefore, the commentary explains:
this is merely following what is appropriate for the occasion;
it "strips away" [the claim] regarding that which is realized. Previously, the Buddha used three cycles concerning the True Buddha, True Dharma, and True Sangha to refute me as being false.
Desiring to abandon the old, yet not having attained the new Dharma, and being uncertain whether the new Dharma is truly superior, one says that it cannot be abandoned immediately.

As for "one is false and one is true": if the former teaching were not [true], for what purpose would it have been the same as my own realization? If the present teaching were not [true], how could it be so?
I did not speak of this earlier. This is brought forward here to correspond with the meaning of the later text.
Regarding "arising and departing from here": although the three types of practitioners hear the teaching on the true and eternal, they do not contemplate true and eternal *nirvāṇa*.
They abide in a state of non-movement by clinging to limited aspirations, thereby giving rise to the conceptual understanding of arising and departing. For this reason, they are filled with anxiety.
"Sorrow.
The Sūtra says, "All are filled with grief," for two reasons: first, they grieve that the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*;
second, they grieve that they have not yet attained the flavor of the new *ī* Dharma. Although the Buddha previously said, "I have not yet attained it," they therefore grieve.

"Quickly speak" means that the Tathāgata previously spoke of the principle of the three true and eternal virtues, yet the bhikṣu mistakenly claimed that he was speaking of impermanence and so forth as the dharma realized by himself; therefore, [the Buddha] said "quickly."
"Zhuàng" (壯) is pronounced "zhuāng" (莊). It carries the meaning of solemn restraint (*zhuāngshù*). Furthermore, it simply means "magnificent" (*zhuàngcái*).
It skillfully elucidates the principle and is further able to shatter delusions; therefore, it is called "magnificent."

"Practicing this advancement" means being able to progress toward and plant roots in the higher [stages]; this is the factor of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), which is the very beginning of the virtue of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇa*).
Therefore, it is called "superior.

Regarding the mention of what comes later: the sūtra simply speaks of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and does not speak of abandoning those to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*); since the latter is mentioned, one must know that the former has already been addressed.
To sever the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the statement that "if the preceding is not gathered, the subsequent is not included," when delusion departs and wisdom perishes, the perishing must necessarily entail the perishing of delusion. The term "removal" (*chu*) extends to what follows; this means that one also removes the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*).
Regarding those who should not enter *nirvāṇa*: because they are not [absolutely] separate, they are able to enter *nirvāṇa*. This is because it concerns the adherence to principle;
thus, it is explained by way of the "double negation" (*ubhayābhāva*).
If one were not separate from impermanence, then since I am already able to destroy delusions, one should know that this principle is not non-separate.

Regarding the term "separation from that" (*tad-viveka*): another interpretation states, "If one is separated from permanence, it is incorrect; if one is not separated [from it], then by being separated from impermanence, it is permanent.
Why, then, do you dismiss it as false? Those who make such a statement find it difficult to perceive the underlying logic.
"Fat" refers to the one who praises the teaching. Since the teaching is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), "fat" is used to praise it.

Regarding the frequent use of the analogy of kinship: although the previous critique of the request employed five analogies, the majority pertained to kinship. As the first analogy in the preceding text stated:
"It is like parents who give birth to an only son, whose countenance is majestic and upright," and so forth. Since that [previous section] has already been rejected, it is not [discussed] here.

"Having acted, yet not having eliminated one side" means that although one has attained the limit of emptiness (*śūnyatā-koṭi*), one is unable to emerge into the provisional (*saṃvṛti*) and thus remains neither in emptiness nor in the provisional.
In these four similes within the text, the character "master" (*shī*) appears in each; therefore, they are treated as a single unit.
The Sūtra says: "Regarding 'emperors and kings,' the compassion of emperors and kings extends even to an entire nation, yet they still practice acts of grace and pardon;
how much more so does the Buddha’s compassion encompass all beings, showing such pity to each and every one?"

Regarding the analogy of the mantra-practitioner: even a worldly physician of meager compassion does not abandon a patient; how much more so would the Supreme Physician of the Transcendent World not fail to save us?

As for the seven outflows (*āsrava*): the outflow of views, the outflow of mental formations, the outflow of the faculties, the outflow of evil, the outflow of intimacy, the outflow of craving, and the outflow of mindfulness, as explained below.
This is explained in detail in the Sūtras.

Regarding the four [categories] of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*) and the one of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the *Abhidharmakośa* calls them the five groups (*pañca-varga*). For example, as in the section on suffering (*duḥkha*), the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) together constitute one group;
those of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*) each constitute three groups; and the four underlying tendencies of cultivation constitute one group.

Regarding the seven messengers of the universal mind (*sarvatraga-citta*), the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: first, sensual craving (*kāmarāga*); second, anger (*pratigha*); third, craving for existence (*bhavarāga*); fourth, pride (*māna*); fifth, ignorance (*avidyā*);

sixth, views (*dṛṣṭi*); and seventh, doubt (*vicikitsā*). These are also the three poisons, along with views. Among them, sensual craving and craving for existence are greed (*lobha*); anger is hatred (*dveṣa*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is delusion (*moha*). Pride (*māna*) is included within delusion. Views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) belong to the sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). When categorized according to the three realms, they total ninety-eight [afflictions].

Regarding "the person" (*pudgala*), this refers to the person who establishes the treatise (*śāstra-pudgala*). This is explained according to the Mahāyāna in its general application (*vibhāga-sāmānya*). Therefore, all four noble truths...
Tenth: Although they do not manifest, the seeds remain; therefore, they are included in general. If something manifests, it is grasped;
if it does not manifest, it is excluded. Thus, in the case of origination and cessation, each excludes three paths, while the other two exclude two.

The five gateways of contemplation are impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity. Furthermore, there are seven or eight fascicles of the *Buddha-vibhāṣā*, which state that there are fifty types of afflictions of insight (*darśana-heya*).
These consist of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) that delude and obscure the five aggregates. Regarding the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are seven:
four in the desire realm—greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—and three in the upper realms, with the exception of hatred. This interpretation is profoundly consistent [with the truth].
The Sūtra speaks of the analogy of malaria: when the Buddha eliminates my coarse afflictions (*kleśa*), they immediately cease to arise;
yet the subtle ones remain at their root and have not yet been removed, just like the recurrence of a malarial fever.
The simile of the plantain tree: the practitioner contemplates that these conditioned phenomena are impermanent, that form is impure, and that the three aggregates are non-self.

If there were a self, the Buddha would have previously instructed one to cultivate the realization of non-self; yet I have already cultivated non-self. Thus, the Buddha’s teaching on the "constant self" rejects all falsehoods. This is the comparison.
Kū replied, "I mistakenly thought you were saying that there was once a self in the past. If there were a self, why did you not speak of it then?
Why do you only now say that a self exists?
As for the three meanings, they are impermanence, non-self, and impurity.

Regarding the four *siddhāntas*: "Questioning and answering" refers to the world of people; furthermore, "initially subduing" refers to the remedial (*pratipakṣa*) teaching; furthermore, "intending to produce" refers to the production of goodness (*kuśala*);
and furthermore, "clinging to" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The explanation of these characteristics can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "receiving the praise and restating the former position": immediately after receiving the Buddha’s praise, one restates their previous position, claiming that the Buddha was indeed praising them, though his true intention was to refute them, and he first offered praise merely as a preliminary.

"Those who fall into confusion" refers to those who are deluded regarding impermanence and so forth, not knowing that by cultivating the realization of impermanence as being itself eternal, and so on.
When the Sūtra says "viewing the mountains and such," it is a metaphor for being deluded regarding the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), taking them to be false permanence and so forth.
"Contrary to the good" refers to the goodness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is explained in reference to the monks' estimation that their own dharma is superior.

If it is taken to mean "contrary to the Mahāyāna," then these monks, upon hearing that the World-Honored One now cultivates permanence, bliss, and so forth, instead claim that the World-Honored One is like a drunkard who perceives the sun and moon as revolving;
this concludes with the fault of being intoxicated. If there are those who do not cultivate suffering... [text ends]
The characteristics of impermanence, up to and including those not even called "noble," specifically refer to the cultivation of permanence, bliss, and so forth, which are not called noble.
In the subsequent passage, the Buddha uses the analogy of intoxication to address the bhikṣus: "This is your own intoxication; it is not my intoxication. This interpretation is correct.
Second, regarding being "without fault": I am one who has practiced well, free from faults such as confusion and error.
As for those who merely know the words, they cling only to the name "impermanence" without being able to comprehend the meaning of impermanence.

Furthermore, you maintain that practicing the cultivation of permanence and bliss constitutes intoxication, while practicing the cultivation of suffering and emptiness does not; how can you possibly understand the meaning of intoxication and non-intoxication?
Furthermore, while the fruit of Buddhahood is truly eternal, one reckons it to be impermanent; this is a state of great intoxication. Therefore, it is said that "one has not yet attained its meaning.

Regarding "hearing of the transformation of another": when hearing the Buddha speak of true eternity, one says it is a "transformation," claiming, "It is you yourself who transform; another is truly not transforming."
That which you deny does not deny existence. O bhikṣus, that which you have just denied is precisely the true and eternal.
You have instead denied what is truly real, namely, the "eternal" by means of the "unreal" adherence to the three types of cultivation. You have taken the "unreal" to be the truth.
Therefore, as for your disparagement of what is wholesome and unwholesome: if one were truly practicing the wholesome, they would know that impermanence is itself permanence.
You delusively claim that impermanence is wholesome practice while true permanence is not; you are like a drunken man—what record of reality do you have?
The "ten gates" refer to the ten gates of counteraction for lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) as found in the first fascicle.
The "six practices" refer to the dual cultivation of both the superior and the inferior.
Regarding those who do not know the correct cultivation of all dharmas: "correct" refers to the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
If one were to defend that [position], one should say: "The permanence and bliss of the world differ from the permanence and bliss that transcend the world;
thus it might be possible for one to be inverted and the other non-inverted. However, since the names 'worldly' and 'transcendent' are identical, how can one be inverted and the other non-inverted?
If the world were inverted, the Tathāgata would also have to be inverted."
The "uninverted consciousness-mind" refers precisely to the five sensory consciousnesses that arise simultaneously with a sudden impulse (*ābhoga*).

Furthermore, previously it was stated that the four inversions regarding emptiness serve as the basis for the four [inversions] regarding permanence and bliss; now, by citing the three inversions, the origin of the aforementioned four inversions is explained.

Regarding the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*): perception takes the grasping of the provisional as its function. One erroneously clings to what cannot be found as a real dharma, engaging in recollection, imagination, and investigation.

That which gives rise to perversion based on this is the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is capable of taking principles as its object; first through the mind’s objective engagement, it subsequently gives rise to perversion.

Regarding the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*): through the thorough examination of phenomena, one thoroughly establishes an inversion. Based on this, four [inversions] arise, which, when paired, become eight. Furthermore, the essence of the seven consciousnesses is the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*).

The false grasping of the characteristics of phenomena is called the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*). To establish a fixed reality upon the perceived conceptualization is called the inversion of view.
Moreover, the deluded thought that "various phenomena exist" is called the inversion of perception. This gives rise again to mental activity that takes objects as its conditions.

What was previously conceived as "mind" is called a perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*). To grasp at the objects of the mind as being fixed and distinct is called a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
Regarding the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth, to regard what is not the true characteristic as being truly real is called a perversion of mind.
To conceive of these as being uncontaminated is called a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*). To biasedly cling to them as being fixed and real is called a perversion of view.
The "unexcelled skillful means" refers to the Buddha’s supreme application of skillful means.

Question: There are those who hold that names exist while meanings do not, such as the externalists who cling to permanence; there are those who hold that both names and meanings exist, such as the proponents of the three superior cultivations;
and there are those who hold that names do not exist while meanings do, as in various sūtras where, although the name "nirvāṇa" is absent, the meaning of nirvāṇa is present.

"Without name and without meaning" refers to the essence of *nirvāṇa*, which should not be designated by names or meanings; thus the commentary says [at length]. "All should correspond to the four propositions" means:
the mundane constitutes two propositions; the mundane being identical with the supramundane, and the supramundane being identical with the mundane, constitutes one proposition;

these together with the mundane and the supramundane constitute the four propositions. Furthermore, the contrast between the superior and the inferior constitutes two propositions; the inferior being...

"Supreme" and "opening and revealing" constitute one phrase. "Supreme" implies "inferior," meaning it shows [the Buddha] as being the same as ordinary people; "supreme" and "unexcelled skillful means" constitute another phrase.

Regarding "one who possesses the virtues of the world's inversion": within the inversions of the world, one realizes the virtues of permanence and bliss; this is explained according to the opening and revealing.
Thus it is said.
Regarding the arising of the function of skillful means, this refers to the body’s arising of the functions of benefiting sentient beings through both permanence and impermanence.
Within this context, all phrases must be treated as two phrases by contrasting them according to their superior and inferior aspects, and as two phrases by treating them as identical in nature.

Regarding the former statement that "impermanence and so forth" [are not mutually inclusive], such a formulation is inverted and incorrect. Now, it should be understood that the question pertains to the provisional;
the question and answer proceed in sequence, and the meaning of the person [who practices] according to this order corresponds to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).

Regarding the general discussion and so forth: each and every such practice possesses three faults. These are: [the fault of] progressing through birth and death; [the fault of] desiring to abandon suffering by means of suffering;

and as for the phrase "abandoning suffering by means of suffering," it refers to the body already being suffering, yet further practicing the precepts of chickens, dogs, and the like, falsely claiming this to be *nirvāṇa*.
This is even more suffering. How could such abandonment of suffering ever be attained? Furthermore, it is because all that is practiced by non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) is a cause of suffering.
Regarding the designation of the Three Jewels: it is not merely that one possesses three jewels; rather, the three are in fact but a single jewel. The Tathāgata is the Buddha.
The Jewel: the Dharma-body is the Dharma-jewel; Nirvana is the Sangha-jewel, which is also the Reward-Buddha (Sambhogakāya-buddha) and the Response-Buddha (Nirmāṇakāya-buddha).
The Dharma-realm is the Reward-Buddha; because it is undefiled, it belongs to the Buddha.
"Not vertical and not horizontal" means that because the three are identical with the one, they are not vertical; because the one is identical with the three, they are not horizontal.
They are neither three nor one; all are the inconceivable Dharma-realm.
The Sūtra says, "That which is impure is precisely conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Master Daosheng said: "Indeed, whatever arises adventitiously is conditioned. [The Sūtra continues...
"How can this be equal to such a poisonous body? [This means that] if the Buddha were to remain in the world and instruct us, then [this body] would be destroyed.
The body is poisoned by ignorance; now that the Buddha has declared it departed, how can we continue to dwell with ignorance while practicing the holy life?
As for what is not within your sphere: when the conditions arise, he remains; when the conditions cease, he departs—yet he is eternally abiding. He abides.
Yet he is constantly departing;

therefore, it is not a realm accessible to the followers of the Two Vehicles, who cannot know the Buddha’s coming and going. Since you do not know this, you must understand that the Buddha does not come, yet is certain to follow the Buddha in departing without departing.

Regarding the "Dharma of those who remain now": "persons" refers to those who possess the Dharma; therefore, they may be relied upon as a support. When the Buddha was present, the capacity for realization resided in the Buddha;

when the Buddha had departed, that capacity resided in Kāśyapa. If Kāśyapa were identical to me in his dwelling, [the teaching would be complete]. Hexi says: "Those with minds of anger and pride"—this interpretation is superior.
Those who have practiced universally but not yet reached the goal attain the four fruits; those who have practiced partially are inferior and attain only the emptiness of one side.
Not yet having attained the Great Principle is called "not reaching the ultimate.
Regarding "by the power of the Buddha-nature," this refers to the internal power of the Buddha-nature and the external power of the verbal teachings.

If those of sharp faculties, within the various flavors preceding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, have already entered [the realization] after hearing the Buddha-nature revealed both openly and secretly in various places—even though the followers of the Two Vehicles heard the Vaipulya [sūtras]—[they do not yet reach the ultimate].
It refutes and rejects [other teachings]. Through the refinement of Prajñāpāramitā, it reaches its full manifestation in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and this present teaching.

Although one had not yet entered [this realization] in the past, those [earlier stages] served as the conditions for entry; therefore, upon hearing the teaching now, one attains awakening in that very seat.
Therefore it is said thus.
"Without deficiency" means it is like a precious jewel that does not receive dust or impurity, for it is fully endowed with all treasures.

Regarding "the place where the mind dwells": first, it directly reveals the Buddha-nature; second, it clarifies the constant [nature] which destroys the impermanent; third, it serves to reveal that the constant is precisely...
Impermanence. Impermanence itself is the simultaneous vanishing of both "not permanent" and "not impermanent," thereby entering directly into the practice of the Perfect and Supreme Dharma.
This distinction among the six stages of identity constitutes the textual essence of this sutra; it is therefore called the place where the mind is fixed.

"Those who have not yet eliminated their old attachments" refers to those who, although the Buddha has spoken with his own mouth that [the Dharma] is eternal, still regard the Buddha’s body as impermanent;
thus they entreat him to remain. Viewed in this way, their old attachments have not been relinquished.
For those who study the new *yi* (scriptures), it should likewise be said that they are for the sake of future learners; therefore, [the teaching] was entrusted to Kāśyapa. Master Daosheng said:
"The reason he entrusted it to a śrāvaka is to clarify that one must possess both understanding and practice before attaining the Way.
As the foremost in asceticism and having achieved profound realization, he can certainly serve as a model and guide for future disciples; hence the entrustment."
Regarding "reforming delusion to give rise to faith": one should reform the delusion of inferior practice and believe in the true, eternal, and real Dharma.
How can one fail to reform delusion due to attachment?
As for "seeking but not obtaining": if there is a skillful means, one will lose [the goal].
Regarding the phrase "both the year and all things are new": what do these two lines signify? Furthermore, it is a time when the myriad things open and flourish;
these five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are like springtime, capable of increasing the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) in those who travel the path.

Moreover, the blossoming and flourishing of grasses and plants serve as a metaphor for the moment when hearing [the Dharma] triggers the awakening of the spiritual faculty. Upon hearing the Dharma, there is none who does not feel joy and inspiration.
The "fruit that is delightful" refers to the fruits of human and celestial rebirth.
Regarding the phrase "not first liberated and later lost": if one had completed the bonds during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñāna, that would constitute being first liberated and later lost.
Now, following Yuan Jie’s *Dayuan*, I shall explain from the perspective of those who are fundamentally deluded.
Regarding the term "loss" (*shi*), it is an interpretation of the Middle Way: that which ought to be attained but is not attained is termed "loss."
"Those who are generally deluded" refers to all those who have not yet seen their Buddha-nature; they belong to the category of people within delusion, hence the term "generally.

"Emerging from [the crowd]" means presenting what one has understood and realized to the Buddha, hence the phrase "distinctly emerging. Master Zezhou said: "From this point onward is an analogy for the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
from the passage 'At that time, the people... onwards is an analogy for the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Regarding "reflection":
Seeking the meaning of the teachings is likened to "entering the water together. Searching for this treasure serves as a metaphor for the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Furthermore, the separate verification of the Dharma is called "competing to seize it. That which is verified—such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth—is not the ultimate truth; it is called "ordinary stones.

Because they mistake the counterfeit for the real, it is said that they "claim to have obtained it" [when they have not]. Obtaining the lapis lazuli gem represents the attainment of the Dharma, which brings satisfaction; therefore, one observes it with joy.
This serves as an analogy for those who possess skillful means and have produced the perfect faith of true permanence, and for those who are adept at contemplation. Master Zeshou says:

"The desire to feign is not the truth" is a metaphor for attaining the ultimate meaning (*artha*) while relinquishing the conventional expression (*vyañjana*). Therefore, it is said "specifically" and "specifically emerges.
This emergence refers to the realization that suffering and so forth are not the actual reality; this is called "knowing they are not true."
From this point, the parable of setting aside the false jewel to take the true one illustrates [the stage of] hearing-wisdom (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*).

From "At that time, the assembly... down to "calmly and steadily," it illustrates contemplative wisdom (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*). "Immediately thereafter" illustrates cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

Having already refuted [the opposing views] regarding the application of these three types of wisdom to the sutra, I shall now briefly describe them so that you may understand their similarities and differences.

"Those who are submerged by attachment to pleasure" refers to those attached to the pleasures of the six sensory objects within the realm, as well as those attached to the pleasure of sinking into emptiness via the two vehicles outside the realm;
these are called "the bottom of the water."

Regarding "seeking through crude contemplation": the first two teachings are both termed crude contemplation. Why? Although they destroy pervasive delusions, one has never yet heard the name of Buddha-nature.

Although, in the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā periods, one sees Bodhisattvas discussing matters that are not within the scope of one's own wisdom, these are merely instances of hidden inspiration and hidden understanding;
therefore, both belong to the stage of "identity with principle" (*li-ji*).
To know the letter means to know that permanence and impermanence are themselves true permanence; this is called knowing the letter.
To know the meaning means to penetrate that permanence and impermanence are neither permanent nor impermanent; this is called knowing the meaning.

Regarding the power of the jewel: first, it is perfumed by the internal power of the Buddha-nature; second, it is perfumed by the external power of the verbal teachings, as well as the power of contemplative practice.
By practicing in accordance with principle, one perfectly subdues the three delusions; with phenomena and principle being non-dual, it is like water becoming clear and still.
Regarding "the signifier being like the signified," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Syllables are themselves liberation; the nature of syllables is detached, and this is called liberation.
Regarding "the signified being like the signifier," one realizes that the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are precisely the three dots (*bindu*); therefore, it is said of both.
Regarding the statement that "the water becomes clear by the power of the jewel": because the substance of the jewel is pure, it causes the water to become pure;
because the substance of the Buddha-nature is suchness (*tathatā*), the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual.
Regarding the analogy of the full moon for similar pleasure: the lunar orb is perfectly round and lacks any boundary or surface, which can be used as a metaphor for pleasure;
because the moon’s radiance is bright and pure, it can be used as a metaphor for purity.
"Neither above nor below" means that the water is not above and the moon is not below. Furthermore, the moon does not exist within the water, nor does the water exist within the moon;
yet, because they are not separate but constitute a single entity, the moon in the water appears perfectly distinct. It is the same with the pearl:
it does not emerge from above, nor does it belong to the mud below; thus, it is "neither above nor below."
Regarding the comparison of the superior with the inferior: this compares the moon in the heavens to the jewel in the water.
Since the moon is neither above nor below yet possesses sovereignty, and the jewel is likewise neither above nor below, it may be equated with the moon; both serve as metaphors for sovereignty.

Furthermore, comparing the true stage (*bhūmi*) to its semblance is like comparing the moon to the jewel, thereby manifesting a semblance of sovereignty. Moreover, this semblance is compared to that which is superior...

Regarding contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*): it manifests a semblance of mastery. If a phenomenon accords with this, it is neither above the stage of transformation nor below the stage of fragmentation;
one attains mastery within the interval between subduing and destroying, which serves as an analogy for the "Self" (*ātman*).

Those who find its gateway are those who find the gateway of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). Only those with the capacity for the Perfect (yuanji) can enter; therefore, it is said that "one person" [enters].

To be "unclouded by the water of the teaching" means to fully comprehend the teaching so that it accords with the principle, and not to become obstructed by its gateway; this is called being "unclouded by the water."
Regarding "the waves of the unmoving mind": it is only when one attains the realization that the mind is itself the principle of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) that it is called "unmoving.

The Sūtra states, "then one is free from the notion of self," which refers to having severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). The phrase "then one is free from arrogance" refers to severing the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

Regarding "the function of abandoning *asmimāna* (ego-conceit) and so forth," this clarifies that the former teachings possess the function of destroying [delusions of] views and afflictions (*kleśa*) and realizing the principle.
The Sūtra asks: "What is the meaning of 'attaining entry into *nirvāṇa*'? Is it the former [teachings], or is it the present [teaching]? Is it the former, or is it not the former?
Is it the true *nirvāṇa*, or is it not the true *nirvāṇa*? Because it is not the true *nirvāṇa*, he asks: "In what sense? The Sūtra says: "Good..."
One who is able to inquire—that is, one who is able to ask about the meaning of this *nirvāṇa*—destroys ignorance by means of this inquiry and attains the vision of the Buddha-nature;

furthermore, they can cause others to destroy delusions and see their nature. For this reason, he praises them. Moreover, because they skillfully inquire at the proper time, they are able to trace back to the fundamental concentration;
thus, they now sever their own doubts.
"The king" refers to this very person. The king is a metaphor for sentient beings; "little wisdom" is a metaphor for worldly knowledge.
Regarding "clinging to false permanence and being constantly in darkness": one calculates that which is truly permanent to be falsely permanent.

Externally, they cite those among sentient beings who possess little of my majesty; these outsiders, through their perverse attachments, seek to subdue others, claiming for themselves the utmost supremacy.

Greedily drawing in followers of heterodoxy as their own, they consider this to be peace and happiness—just as a king, having intimidated the frontier tribes with his majesty, indulges in the extraction of wealth and treasures.
They take this as their pleasure.

"Yin" (pronounced *mo-jin*) refers to dullness and wickedness. It is a metaphor for non-Buddhists such as Udraka Rāmaputra and others. One whose mind does not recognize correct principle is called "wan" (obstinate);
one whose mouth does not follow correct teaching is called "yin" (dull).

The Sūtra says, "And the king does not distinguish. This means that the king does not distinguish between sentient beings who rely on either the heterodox or the orthodox for treatment; consequently, their illnesses grow increasingly severe, hence it is said he "does not distinguish.
Master Sengsheng said: "Heterodox" (*ye*) is defined as conforming to worldly sentiments. As for the fundamental principle, there is nothing that can change it. "Feng" is synonymous with "to give.
This refers to those of little wisdom who do not recognize the heterodox from the orthodox, yet are given the four requisites [of life] by him gratuitously.
Regarding "greasy and moist": those who engage in false conceptualization give rise to attachment everywhere, just like grease and moisture.
Although the various defiled things are not truly the self or sovereign, they are still reckoned as the "self" due to such persistent clinging; thus, they may also be called the "self."

"Furthermore, as for 'ignorance' (yā) and so forth": this refers to not knowing that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise from the disease of false conceptualization (*mithyā-parikalpa*). Therefore, it is said that one does not know the root source from which the disease arises.
Wind-disease (*vāta-roga*) is a metaphor for anger (*dveṣa*), because of its abrupt and violent nature. Cold-disease (*śīta-roga*) is a metaphor for delusion (*moha*), because of its sudden stupor.

Burning-disease (*pitta-roga*) is a metaphor for greed (*lobha*), because it consumes the heart. Afflictions (*kleśa*) are not merely all [physical] diseases; they are a metaphor for the eighty-four thousand dust-like labors (*aśīti-catur-sahasra-paryutthāna*).

Furthermore, the sudden and violent arising of wind is like anger (*dveṣa*); its cold nature and congealing quality are like delusion (*moha*); and its hot nature and turbid agitation are like craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
As for the passage in the Sūtra concerning "the beautiful and the ugly" and so forth: beauty and ugliness are the causes; goodness and evil are the effects.
Moreover, goodness is true milk, while evil is counterfeit milk; the same applies to ugliness.
This patient does not know sentient beings, nor does he know the former physician; this is the root from which the illness arises.
As for the king who takes leadership as his principle, the king is one with the people of the nation.

"Like one who transforms through affection" means that among those being transformed, the transformer acts as the king and those transformed act as his subjects; furthermore, the master acts as the king and those he transforms act as his subjects.
As for "one who is forcibly requested," since such a person is not a true teacher, the meaning is that they act as a teacher to sentient beings only by force.
"One whose mind does not incline toward virtue" means that although the mind lacks genuine understanding, one performs acts of goodness while actually practicing evil.
"One whose speech does not discourse on loyalty" means that the mouth is merely malicious and devoid of sincere faith.
Regarding "insufficient medicine": how could the worldly wisdom of ordinary people ever destroy delusions? This is called having insufficient medicine.
Regarding "abundant illness": the three poisons remaining entirely within both the internal and external realms constitute abundant illness.
Regarding ignorance that takes up signs as its object: ignorance is the root and taking up signs is the branch. Because this ignorance arises from the branches, it gives rise to the eight inversions.
Such a person is one who does not know the medicine; they do not even know the medicine of impermanence, let alone the medicine of true permanence.

Regarding the Buddha’s provisional teaching of a "self": the Buddha taught that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are in combination, and that there exists only a provisional self which is entirely impermanent.

Outsiders recklessly speculate on whether [the self] is identical to or separate from [the aggregates], thereby producing the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*), as well as the Vaiśyas and others who establish the four castes and eight arts.
According to the *Āgama* Sūtras, first, "knowing the nature of the illness" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s ability to know the gravity or lightness of afflictions (*kleśa*). Second...
1. Knowing the cause of the disease is analogous to the Buddha’s ability to know the causes that give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).

That is to say, the seeds and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) are the primary causes; the objects of form and so forth, as well as the false teachings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), are the secondary causes. 2.

Knowing the characteristics of the disease is analogous to the Buddha’s ability to know the characteristics of afflictions. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "A mind of greed is lowly, while a mind of pride is high."
Such are the characteristics of these afflictions (*kleśa*). Fourth, "knowing the location of the illness" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s ability to know the locus of the afflictions:
when things are contrary, anger arises; when things are favorable, greed arises; and when they are neither contrary nor favorable, ignorance (*avidyā*) can arise.

Fifth, "knowing the time of the illness" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s ability to know the time of their arising—namely, whether it be youth or old age, times of greed or wealth, or whether it be cold or heat. Or...

Whether hungry or full, various afflictions arise according to what corresponds to those states. Sixth, knowing the medicine is a metaphor for the Buddha’s ability [to teach] the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth.

Seventh, knowing the treatment is a metaphor for the Buddha’s ability to know that the contemplation of impurity treats greed, while the cultivation of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*) treats excessive anger, and so on.

Eighth, knowing the prohibitions and their transgression is a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge that when practicing the contemplation of impurity, one must not grasp at anything that accords with one's own desires or gives rise to greed.
Regarding the signs: when practicing loving-kindness and compassion, one should not grasp at signs of resentment that contradict those feelings.

The Buddha’s knowledge of the Eightfold Noble Path consists of: the Eightfold Path of the Tripitaka teachings, which specializes in treating [the views of] permanence and self; the Eightfold Path of Non-arising, which destroys the notion of impermanence;
the Eightfold Path of Immeasurability, which sequentially treats the former two; and the Eightfold Path of Non-action, which simultaneously treats the eight inversions. Now...
This is the unconditioned Eightfold Path of the Perfect Gate.
"The extinction of wholesome dharmas" refers to supramundane wholesome dharmas. "Wisdom-life" refers to the eternally abiding wisdom-life.
"Neither increasing" means not committing evil. "Neither diminishing" means that even if one is cast into the Avīci Hell or similar realms, one intends to attain the extinction of the body.
The offenses are not extinguished; the name is not diminished.
Regarding "one who does not give rise to meditative concentration": this refers to one who does not cultivate the four dhyānas, because they have severed only the dull afflictions (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Regarding "only diminishing without increasing": this refers to practicing with a mind of attachment and aversion.
Regarding "not all-pervasive": it refers to not severing ignorance and nescience, and being unable to transform others.
Regarding "all-pervasive in both aspects": a bodhisattva’s comprehensive study of the four gates is called "all-pervasive in both aspects";
yet, lacking the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness is called "lacking skillful means."
Regarding those who are free from pain and affliction: form itself is emptiness, a skillful treatment of illusion.
Although this treatment is skillful, it cannot cause those of the Two Vehicles to perceive the Buddha-nature; therefore, it is said that it cannot cure one who is destined to die.
That which is difficult to cure is the disease of ignorance (*avidyā*). It can only be cured by entering into the third contemplation;
therefore, it is said that it cannot be done all at once.
Regarding "being unable to cause it to pass": the first stage (*bhūmi*) cannot serve as the name for the second stage, and thus it is said it cannot pass beyond. This is one [point].
Explanation: One should rely on the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Nine, for the correct interpretation.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "surpassing the fundamental," the essence of the Dharma-body itself cannot be surpassed; rather, it is said to "surpass" it in the sense that the stage of wondrous enlightenment is ultimate and wisdom and severance are perfected.
Regarding the skilled physicians of today: the present sutra is exclusively the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). The Wondrously Enlightened One is the excellent physician.
As the sutra says, "coming from afar" means descending from the stage of the original Dharmakāya to manifest traces and transform the world; this is termed "coming from afar."
Regarding "the conditions for curing illness," ordinary people take impermanent phenomena as their conditions.
Regarding "consulting and receiving," it clarifies that non-Buddhists do not know to request the Buddha as their teacher; this is called not knowing how to consult.

Not knowing to listen to and hear the True Dharma from the Buddha is called not knowing how to receive. To claim oneself superior to the Buddha is called perverse arrogance; to claim the Buddha inferior to oneself is likewise so.
He became conceited with the name [he received].

Regarding "removing his crown" and so forth: having seen a corpse, a sick person, and others as he exited through the four city gates, he immediately left the household life; at first, he relied upon teachers of non-Buddhist paths.
"Sending back the horse" refers to Kṣemadatta returning to the palace and so forth.
"Six years of ascetic practice" and so on includes his reception of the teachings on the four dhyānas, the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda), and the emptiness of dharmas from him.
"Only one who clearly understands this body": the Buddha at the time of his initial realization was merely the physical body born of Queen Māyā, which is why it is called "this body.
"Still a non-Buddhist" means that he was still proclaiming the teachings of outsiders.

Regarding the statement that there is a "separate original body": it is only upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, which reveals this original nature, that one finally knows the Buddha was not a disciple of non-Buddhist paths.
As for the phrase "entering together to see the King," this refers first to external transformation (*bāhya-vinaya*).

Those who lack the wisdom that observes capacities possess only worldly knowledge; they lack the function of illuminating capacities and instead employ only their deluded minds in darkness to transform beings.

As for those who apply medical prescriptions, they do not merely employ prescriptions regarding the impermanent and the permanent; rather, even the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten wholesome actions are all [medical prescriptions].
These are the words of the Buddha, all of which are medical prescriptions.
Regarding "Wenlin" (文鱗): Wenlin refers to a blind dragon.

As for "supernatural powers like those in the *Ruiying jing* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses)": that sutra states that when the Buddha entered the cave of Kāśyapa, the dragon’s poison could not affect him, nor could the dragon’s fire.

They are not burned by fire, nor drowned in the Ganges River. They gather fruit from three directions: namely, they take *bīlakṣa* fruits from the east, *jambu* fruits from the south, and *harītakī* fruits from the west;
from the north, they take naturally grown non-glutinous rice. They know the nectar of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and are aware of its defects.

He concealed his supernatural powers; when the fire he had manifested was extinguished and would not burn again, and when he raised his axe but could not bring it down, and so forth—though witnessing these various transformations, he remained stubbornly attached to the superficial.
Thus he said, "Though Gautama may be miraculous, my Way is more authentic. The Buddha then spoke to him, saying, "You are not an Arhat, nor have you attained the Way.
Both teacher and disciple were simultaneously awakened and submitted. This is as recorded in the first fascicle of the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) and its *ji* (Notes).
Extensive citations are provided to demonstrate the characteristics of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

Regarding the "reversal of the triple refuge" (*triśaraṇa-viparyaya*): it means turning away from evil teachers, evil teachings, and evil assemblies to take refuge in the True Dharma and the True Assembly;
this is simply expressed as taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Regarding the initial seeking of the vow, the Sūtra states, "Now is precisely the right time," which refers to the moment when the five men should attain awakening.
Those who truly cherish and care for them will respond to this principle with profound contemplation, causing them to become free from attachment.

Regarding the "roots that correspond through latent affinity": past wholesome roots and even non-Wholesome roots, combined with the internal permeation of the true cause, bring about supramundane realization.
Because this awakening occurs latently in those of small capacity, it is called "latent correspondence" (ming-dui).

"Reaching the right hand for convenience" is a metaphor for the response of those with limited capacities (*hīnayāna*); "and other parts of the body" is a metaphor for the subtle, hidden assistance provided to those with great capacities (*mahāyāna*).

To clarify once more that "reaching [the capacity]" refers to a single capacity is precisely to indicate the hidden arising of a small aspiration; it is only appropriate that the initial teaching (*ādikarmika-dharma*) be applied to them.
Therefore, it is said that they do not dare to have many requests.

As for the scripture’s statement, “I pray that Your Majesty issue a proclamation,” this means that after having received transformation through the teaching, one uses that transformation to further teach and transform others, spreading the news from one to another;
this is likened to issuing a proclamation.
Those who delight in harmful matters and engage in much malice destroy the life-force of true reality and the eternally abiding Dharma-body.
"Severing the head" means severing the head of the roots of goodness of true emptiness; furthermore, among the myriad virtues, the faculty of faith is the head.
If one takes inverted views as medicine, then there will be no cultivation of the faculties—this is the meaning of "severing the head."
Regarding "resolving and severing delusions": one resolves them through the contemplation of impermanence and severs the pervasive delusions, thereby attaining true life.
Having attained this life, one will necessarily attain the eternally abiding life of wisdom; only then is it called "perpetual cessation."
Regarding those hindered by delusion from liberation: because the delusion of false permanence hinders true liberation and causes one to lose the life-force of wisdom, it is called "untimely death.
Furthermore, being hindered by impermanence from the middle way of liberation is also called "untimely death."

The "deluded person" refers to those of the Two Vehicles. The deer is a metaphor for the realm of the aggregates (*skandhas*); the horse is a metaphor for perverse attachment. To take what is permanent as real is the delusion.
The "wise person" refers to the Buddha.
The statement "this deer is not a horse" means that the heterodox view of permanence is not real.
As for those who grasp at non-existence as being "horse," although they know that the deer is not a horse, they nevertheless cling to the notion that the state of non-existence itself is the horse;
this is precisely analogous to the way the followers of the Two Vehicles cling to impermanence.
Regarding the phrase "where else could it exist": the essence of impermanence is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so, then, would it be a delusion to reckon it as real?

As for the statement that "the Buddha-fruit is impermanent," the intent is that the Buddha is the eternal body (*nitya-kāya*), whereas the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive the Buddha entering *nirvāṇa*.
This means that one is certain that impermanence is identical to what one has personally realized. Since one clings to it as impermanent, this affliction is easy to recognize.
Once the affliction is easily recognized, the true, eternal Buddha-nature can be shown, and the mind is easily opened; therefore, it is said to be "easy to see."

Regarding the phrase "namely, birth and death, etc.": Birth and death are fundamentally impermanent phenomena; moreover, they possess conditioned impermanence, which is difficult to recognize as a disease.
Since this disease is difficult to recognize, it is shown that birth and death are themselves the true and eternal Buddha-nature.
Because the Buddha-nature is hidden and its mind is difficult to awaken to, it is said to be "difficult to see."
Those who wish to die do so because they possess the potential for awakening. If such potential were absent, it should be said that they would certainly die.
As for the question in the sutra, "How should one treat them?"—it refers to the arousal of the great potential.
Those sentient beings who do not accept [the teaching] specifically refer to those who, upon hearing of the Buddha’s body of merit within the Vaipulya sutras,
the inconceivable deeds of the bodhisattvas, and the discourse on the inconceivable liberation, claim that these are not within their own capacity.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s repeated teaching: having heard the true aspect (*dharmatā*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they had not yet awakened to it; then, upon reaching the *Nirvāṇa*, they received the provisional means (*upāya*).
To "open the provisional" means that what was previously taught as real is now declared to be not real; this is precisely the opening of the provisional.

"Those who were previously used as expedients" refers to those for whom the impermanent was used to treat the permanent; these were not the ultimate truth. "Now this meaning is explained" means that the provisional [expedients] are now being opened up.
"Do you wish to deceive me? means: "Previously you spoke of poison, saying 'do you wish to deceive me? Now that you have caused it to be ingested, do you wish to deceive me?"
Yes. What was poison in the past is poison now; thus it is said, "it completes the former.
As for "he deceived me and drove me away," this refers to regarding the former physician as marvelous while claiming the new physician is not genuine; hence it is said, "he deceived me."
In this context, "the entire body is a metaphor" clarifies that all preceding passages are likewise metaphors.

As the Sūtra says regarding "the wise person who sees it": the new physician does not proclaim it with his mouth, and the old physician, though understanding the medicine, does not manifest it in his mind.
As for the statement in the Sūtra that "this is also ambrosia": this medicinal milk was originally ambrosia, yet those of the Two Vehicles who have transcended it perceive it as a poisonous drug.

Regarding "slippery grass," this can also serve as a metaphor for dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*): attachment to favorable objects is like the slippery [grass], while aversion toward adverse objects is like... [the thorny].
"Rough. Regarding "having excellent kinsmen": because the mother is excellent, the child is excellent; this shall be explained one by one below.

As for "the people of the country reaching the point of not accepting [it]": to accept the words of others is called being possessed by a ghost (*bhūta*); to spontaneously give rise to the notion that they are [possessed] is called... [being possessed].

For those who are deranged and confused, I cause them to understand the gateway of the teaching: when they see the teaching that speaks of permanence, they know it is used to treat the disease of impermanence;
