when they see the teaching that speaks of impermanence, they know it is used to treat the disease of false permanence. For this reason, I merely combine these two medicines.
To speak of the Tathāgata as "is" clarifies that the essence of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is not like the deceptive and false appearances of saṃsāra;

it is designated by the provisional name of "reality. It is described as "truth" because it has transcended emotional delusions. Its essence is without transition or change; therefore, it is called "permanent."
It is designated as the "master" because it is the source of all virtues; it is further called the "basis" because it is that which is expounded through all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
its essence is without arising or ceasing, and is thus termed "unchanging.
[The Buddha] concludes by exhorting the fourfold assembly to practice and study this.
The fourth section, the commentary on the "Chapter on Longevity," is divided into two parts.
First, the explanation of the title; second, the word-by-word exegesis of the text following the title. The first part [the explanation of the title] is further divided into three sections.

First, clarifying the reason for establishing the name; second, from "Now, explaining... onwards, clarifying how the name is manifested through its meaning; third, from "This is... onwards, concluding by returning to the subject.
Regarding the correspondence addressed in this chapter:

as for the initial mention of "the first three chapters," these refer to the three chapters beginning with the Prologue. Although they proceed from persons to matters, all of them serve to manifest permanence;

therefore, the Chapter on Longevity is placed last to encompass the preceding manifestations of permanence, for there is nothing that is permanent which is not long-lived. Thus, it follows immediately after the preceding chapter.
The distinction between "left" and "right" in the translation merely reflects the difference between Chinese and Sanskrit, as well as the distinction between superior and inferior.
Fearing that those who rely on the preceding text— specifically the lamentation of Cunda— merely speak of the Tathāgata and his permanence (*nitya*) without yet mentioning his longevity (*āyus*),
I have now stated that these two are one and the same.

Regarding the phrase "Correct Speech arises from the Permanent, etc.": these four serve as causes for obtaining the fruit of long life; therefore, it is said that the name is established based on what is obtained.
Next, regarding "the name being manifested according to the meaning," this establishes the name based on the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold principles).
"To cause one to plant roots of goodness" means to cultivate the goodness of permanence and bliss.

Regarding the phrase "the others are each as the occasion demands" within the section on the three refuges: while the thirty-four questions specifically clarify longevity, in the answers, they are granted according to the specific inquiries.
Although they are granted in this way, they do not transcend the causes and conditions of long life.

Therefore, in the subsequent entry into the textual explanation, it says: "The Buddha-dharma reaches three. This clarifies the exhortation to be complete with the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) to benefit sentient beings.

The first exhortation, "reaches," further expresses the meaning that the Buddha is identical to the world. The first exhortation [to "remove"] signifies the meaning of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*). The second exhortation is to "accept."
The lower [stage] produces goodness. The three exhortations benefit sentient beings; the "lower" refers to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
As for the phrase "those whose doubts above have been exhausted," this clarifies that the various bhikṣus' attachments to the mind regarding permanence and impermanence have already been shattered.
Having completed the profound faith that "permanence is precisely neither permanent nor impermanent," it is called "exhaustion."

Regarding "those who were silent when first exhorted": this clarifies that in the initial section of this sutra there is only the text of the exhortation, but no text concerning an inability to comply;
thus, they silently accepted the exhortation.
Regarding the core tenet of this sutra: one should know that the Vinaya is the precious treasure of this present sutra, redeeming the eternal life-force of wisdom;
it is not the primary doctrine of the sutra itself, and thus should not be spoken of in that way. Master Daosheng intended for this to inquire into the causes of long life.
Long life is fundamentally a sublime ford for entering the cycle of birth and death to save sentient beings, taking compassion as its basis. As for the salvation through compassion, it first...
The precepts and rules were established to prevent the commission of all evils, and only thereafter was the ultimate practice of goodness made possible.
Regarding the term "zhū" (諸) in the phrase "yú zhū jièlǜ" (於諸戒律), the word "zhū" does not originally exist at the beginning of the sutra;

it is likely that it was present in an earlier manuscript and subsequently entered into the text. Furthermore, one should take the following passage from the sutra as evidence: "I am now without wisdom regarding the various precepts and rules" (我今無智於諸戒律).
These words establish the meaning of this passage; therefore, the various characters are employed.

Regarding "restraint, meditative concentration, and the path": restraint refers to the prātimokṣa precepts; meditative concentration refers to the śamatha-samvara (precepts concomitant with concentration); and the path refers to the mārga-samvara (precepts concomitant with the path).

Regarding "shining upon both [truths]... reaching the conventional": this is explained by treating both the ultimate and the conventional as conventional within the context of the sevenfold two-truths.
Mingjun says: "The myriad virtues ultimately take precepts, concentration, and wisdom as their foundation. The preceding phrase cites the precepts;
'nature' refers to emptiness and quiescence, which cite concentration and wisdom. 'Nature' is the realm of the wisdom of emptiness; 'quiescence' is concentration."
"Explained in detail as above" refers to the preceding passage on your threefold training in the precepts (*śīla*, *samādhi*, and *prajñā*).
"The realm of the Tathāgata" refers to the reality of the Dharma. This clarifies that the wisdom which illuminates this realm is profound and vast, difficult to fathom;
it is called "inconceivable" because it is beyond the reach of the minds of the nine realms. It is called "incomparable" because the words of the nine realms cannot attain it.

"Being identical with the names of all Buddhas" means being identical with the Buddhas of the three periods of time; because they all ride upon the suchness (tathatā) to come and achieve perfect enlightenment, they are said to be "identical.
"All meditative concentrations (samādhis)" refers to their practice.
Regarding those who lack the three types of knowledge: because the knowledge pertaining to the lower stages cannot inquire about the three knowledges of the stage of fruition, they remain silent.
As for the Śrāvakas who are unfit to be entrusted [with the teaching], the Tathāgata exhorted them to inquire so that [the Dharma] might surely circulate;

yet these Śrāvakas were unable to assume the three roles. First, their knowledge was shallow; second, their lifespans were short; third, they lacked a retinue. Thus, they were incapable of upholding the Dharma.
Regarding "forcibly accepting an entrustment": if one forcibly accepts an entrustment, it means that the Tathāgata has lost what was entrusted to him.
As for the number "one hundred and twenty," these belong to the future; since they have entered into extinction, they are not discussed here.
Regarding "unable to abide": "abiding" simply means to dwell; it refers to being unable to cause the Mahāyāna Dharma to endure for a long time.
Regarding "ten thousand": ten thousand *liang* constitutes one *jin*.
There are one million liberations. From a single phrase, ten thousand phrases arise;
furthermore, each of these phrases has nine hundred and ninety phrases as its retinue, thereby constituting one hundred liberations.

Regarding the phrase "How can one return?": [The commentary] refutes this by stating that during the Age of Semblance Dharma (*sāṃprata-dharma*), Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet appeared;
how, then, could it be called "twenty years"? [The text continues: "Give me back my wife."

"Those who are returning" refers to those beings being transformed; when their general and specific delusions are exhausted, they attain the vision of the Dharma-body—this is the time of returning, which is to say, they have returned to me.

Regarding the Śrāvakas who falsely accept [the teachings]: Zezhou says that when a bhikṣu has no dharma-receiver to whom he may entrust the transmission for the sake of converting disciples, this is called "having no successor.
When impermanence presses upon him and his condition is said to be grave, it is called "the onset of illness. When his body perishes and returns to non-existence, it is termed "the end of life.
As for the Dharma entrusted to him, because there is no one to receive and practice it, it is said that everything is lost and dispersed.

Regarding "attributing merit": there are various bodhisattvas worthy of being entrusted [with this task]; why not entrust it to them instead of having me receive it? For this reason, he declines. Regarding "vigorous and handsome": this may also be analyzed word by word.
"Vigorous" is a metaphor for the perfection of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others; "handsome" [is likewise explained].
This is precisely like attaining the King Samādhi.

As for the parents: the mother represents the attainment of the three Real Truths (satya), while the father represents the provisional truth (upāya-satya). Therefore, the three and the one are paired with the one and the three respectively.
The Sūtra states: "Regarding all śrāvakas and others," when they were at the Deer Park, gold was impermanent;
upon reaching the Vaipulya assemblies, it was realized as eternal (and so forth).
Regarding "those who falsely attribute merit to the self": the followers of the Two Vehicles merely attain the mind of a false self;

therefore, it is said that they have well attained the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) in attributing merit. Zhezhou says: "Not exalting oneself is called the untainted mind; 'not' refers to the ego-self, which is called the Arhat-mind."
Regarding the two conditions: Tánjì stated, "First, because the śrāvakas have no retinue; second, because the bodhisattvas have a large retinue.

Sēngzōng stated, "First, they are well able to engage in question and answer, which is beneficial for the present; second, they cause the Dharma to abide for a long time, which is beneficial for the future.
Míngjùn stated, "First, they can cause the Jewel of the Dharma to abide for a long time; second, they benefit and bring peace to sentient beings. Therefore, the Commentary says:

Regarding the phrase "or those who are well able to engage in question and answer, etc., all of which appear in the preceding text": this refers to the passage above concerning how the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma should be entrusted to the bodhisattvas, and so forth.
The term "confusion" (or "error") points to the section following that on being "well able to engage in question and answer."

At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly... [up to] "...as for women. Within this assembly, there were upāsakas and others, all of whom were individuals with great spiritual capacity (*mahā-indriya*).
The Sūtra states: "As for my lifespan," lifespan is the ultimate of the fruit; precepts are the beginning of the cause. This summarizes [the meaning].
This is an exhortation to inquire by citing cause and effect.

If one obtains a questioner who accords with the capacities of the assembly and is a person with whom there is a karmic connection, then they will be able to benefit those with whom a bond is formed, those who are the immediate audience, and those in lower positions as their reflected images; the only exception being when an ancient Buddha acts as a reflected image.

Regarding the previous point: if one disregards the benefit and treats it as non-existent while claiming the meaning differs, there is no doubt that this is because the Bodhisattva’s explanation is clear. As for the statement that the Two Vehicles cannot ask about names and thus have no doubt:
the Bodhisattva is able to ask for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, whereas the Two Vehicles cannot ask, as they practice only for their own sake. Therefore...
The phrase "the meaning of the different intentions of speech and the secrets of the body, etc.
includes the "Chapter on Names and Merits" up to the "fourfold [distinction between] the heterodox and the orthodox," which refers to the "Chapter on the Four Virtues."
If one asks about "life" (mìng), it refers to the opening of the "heavenly course" (tiānxíng). To practice according to the constant principles of life is called the heavenly course.
If one asks about "discrimination" (biàn), it refers to the opening of the "brahmic course" (fànxíng). The brahmic course takes compassion as its foundation; that is to say, because of compassion—
Regarding the statement: "Asking about what is pleasure is to distinguish the pleasure of extensive learning and discernment.

Regarding "asking about returning to what is the self": the Three Refuges overturn the false self in order to reveal the true self; furthermore, because there is the precept of taking refuge, one is constant.
One practices with mastery among humans and devas; therefore, when asked about taking refuge, it is "I" who am asked.
When asked about taking refuge, one employs the discernment of the eternal to overturn the discernment of the heterodox and eternal, thereby manifesting the discernment of the true eternal.

Regarding the term "treatise" (*lun*): it refers to the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*. Regarding "the great power of the Buddha": it refers to what is stated in the sūtra, "by the supernatural power of the Buddha.
Regarding "the youth Mañjuśrī": it refers to the youth Mañjuśrī as described in other sūtras.
"Passing through the village of Tāla" refers to the reeds; it means the people of the Reed Village.
"Noble family" (kṣatriya) refers to those of the foremost rank; by the sequence of *jia*, *yi*, *bing*, and *ding*—that is, *jia*, *yi*, *bing*, and *ding*—they are the superior clans.
Regarding the "assembly of those who have attained certainty": Bodhisattvas from the stage of *bhūmi* (ground) upward are called the assembly of those who have attained certainty.
Having already attained spontaneous entry into the flow of the Dharma, they are well-able to definitively declare that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

Regarding "he himself inquired": Kāśyapa harbored self-doubt; although he was among the ranks of the great assembly, he feared he might not be the person destined for this summons, and thus he made his inquiry.
Regarding "the Sūtra caused you to rejoice": he rejoiced because it was appropriate, and he rejoiced because it accorded with his capacity.
Regarding the Buddha’s virtues and so forth: first, praising the Buddha’s virtues as majestic, lofty, and supreme; second, praising the Buddha’s assembly as pure and untainted;
third, praising the Buddha’s body as firm and solid like a diamond—this clarifies the solidity of the body—and its color as being like lapis lazuli—this clarifies the purity of the body;
fourth, praising the Buddha’s assembly for the profound and vast wisdom and virtue.

Regarding the statement that they do not speak out of self-seclusion: this refers to the vast distance between the great and the small. How could one with a small body possibly question one with a great body?
How could one with small wisdom possibly question one with great wisdom? Yet, I venture to speak these words to strike upon the Supreme Sage.

Regarding the term "jièzhě" (借者): if read from the perspective of the various additions by Kāśyapa, it is pronounced with the rising tone (*shēng*); if read from the perspective of the additions by the Buddha, it is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).
As for those who maintain both readings as permissible, this master [maintains] the latter four verses within the lingering momentum of the question; furthermore, this is also acceptable.
This question refers to the Five Practices and Ten Virtues and so forth; it is intended to simultaneously refute the two preceding schools.
As for the "Thirty-two Questions" of Emperor Wu of Liang, they are numbered according to their actual content.
Thirty-seventh: By adding the final three verses to the previous thirty-four, they are combined to form thirty-seven.
Regarding the passage "Acting as a refuge for the multitude," this refers to the section on entrusting ministers and so forth within the *Śokavarga* (Chapter on Lamentation).

"The Great Illumination of the Path of Awakening" refers to the awakening of the Buddha; that is to say, the path of the Buddha. This reveals that throughout the entire dispensation, this is the path of the Buddha’s great transformation.
Therefore, one must not attempt to cleanse it by means of the limited or proximate.
Regarding the combination of two questions: if there were thirty-two questions, they should have been combined into one;
if there were thirty-four, they would be divided into two.

As for their being divided into four, this is because the subsequent answer distinguishes them into four separate responses; therefore, it was necessary to divide them. How can this be considered a question?
The cause is "longevity and the adamantine body. The question regarding the fruit is "not harboring [a physical] body. Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one ask about the cause?
It is "attaining great, firm, and solid power," which is the question regarding the fruit. Thus, the first half [of the verse] contains both cause and fruit, and the second half is likewise.
Therefore, it is divided into four questions.
If one counts the verses such that both the introductory verse and the summary verse also consist of thirty-two [lines], then the first two verses serve merely as two questions.
Regarding the "thirty-six," this refers to taking the initial verse and adding further causal conditions to it, thus completing a total of thirty-three.

Why? Because those śrāvakas have never before heard of the "eternal. This refers to those who, having attained the minor fruits at the Deer Park, did not pass through the stages of the Vaipulya and other assemblies, but have come directly to this present seat;
thus it is called "never having heard of the eternal," and for this reason they should have doubts and raise objections. Furthermore:
Furthermore, taking for granted the explicit portion of the present sutra as the basis for the objection:

"The attachments of the śrāvakas have already been refuted" clarifies that the two vehicles, regarding the first two chapters, have already had their doubts and attachments concerning [the teaching of] permanence refuted;
this constitutes the objection.

If that were so, then the objection raised against the superior [view] would not be valid. Since it was stated that doubt arises because [the former view] serves as a condition (*pratyaya*), then that which does not depend on the superior [view] should arise from the text itself.

As for the conclusion at the twin trees (*yugma-vṛkṣa*), one should know that this refutes the previous [position] as being unestablished; that too is improper, and therefore it is refuted by means of the subsequent [point].
Therefore, it is not an ultimate discourse because the discourse does not reach the ultimate;

thus, it is not an ultimate discourse. Regarding the statement that "the permanent cannot be cultivated," the intention is this: if the permanent were primordial, its very essence would be devoid of cultivation.

If there were no cultivation at all, then everything should be permanent. Since all sentient beings have not yet attained the permanent, they ought to have cultivation. This is why one asks about the permanent.
From what cause does the fruit arise, and of what nature is it?
Regarding the cause for the myriad virtues upon the fruit, it is the cause of the myriad wholesome deeds.
As the Sūtra asks, "How does one obtain longevity? Saṅghazong replied: "One lifetime constitutes a lifespan; a long duration of such lifetimes constitutes longevity. This is the fruit of permanence."

This is not a matter of expectation; let me entrust these words to your long ears. In essence, the discussion concerns the inexhaustible mirror of wisdom, which is precisely *prajñā*. How could one possibly inquire into its cause?

The "indestructible body of diamond" (*vajra-kāya*) refers here to the *dharmakāya*. Just as the substance of worldly diamond cannot be destroyed and can sustain all things, it is used as a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*.
Its spirit cannot be shifted by the three marks (*trilakṣaṇa*), yet through myriad transformations, it can alter even the grasses.

The Master Ti of Zhezhou provides a threefold analysis of this verse. First, determining the number of questions: it has been traditionally transmitted that there are thirty-six questions within this verse.
Second, clarifying the distinctions among the questions, which are of six types: (1) General questions, also called "inquiries," such as "How can one attain long life? and so forth;
(2) Questions seeking [instruction], such as "I pray that the Buddha will reveal the subtle and secret [teachings]," and so forth.
1. The difficult question (*praśna-duṣkara*), such as when it is said that the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and so forth.

2. The critical question (*ākṣepa-praśna*), such as when it is said: "If the Tathāgata has severed the net of doubt, why did he not speak with definitiveness? and so forth. 3. The praising question (*praśaṃsā-praśna*): For example, when it is said, "The great refuge of sentient beings," and so forth.
Kāśyapa first offered praise before intending to pose a difficult challenge; therefore, although it is a praise, it functions as a question. 4. The humble question (*vinaya-praśna*).
Question: As stated in the text below, "I now wish to inquire about the aggregates (skandhas), yet I lack wisdom," and so forth.

This humble acknowledgment of one's own inadequacy gives rise to the subsequent discourse. Such a distinction seems to carry the profound intent of the *Bhrū-sūtra*, though its underlying principle was not previously manifest;

therefore, this is shown merely to instruct those who seek knowledge. The textual analysis and explanation is divided into three parts. Regarding the verses, there are two sections. First, the inquiry concerning the methods of training (*śikṣā-dharma*): How so?
Having attained proximity to the Unsurpassed Way, one subsequently inquires about and studies its practice (*caryā*). How is this known?

As in the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly" (*Mahāparṣatparipṛcchā*), before the answer concerning the study of practice is given, Kāśyapa requests: "I pray that you will explain the merit obtained within this Great Nirvāṇa.

Therefore, it is known that what precedes is the study of the Dharma (*dharma*) and what follows is the study of practice. The Dharma encompasses both principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*), whereas practice pertains only to phenomena. The Dharma also encompasses the internal...

To claim that external practice and virtue pertain only to the internal, while the Dharma pervades the three natures such that the practice can arise through the contemplation of dharmas of all three natures,

yet the practice itself exists only in the wholesome, and that while the Dharma pervades both self and others— such that another's practice may become one's own Dharma and one's own practice may become another's Dharma—
to judge it in this way is far too superficial and narrow.

Regarding "the sūtra is acceptable": each and every question therein addresses all three periods of time; however, when treated individually, they follow one specific direction, which is why it is said that "the sūtra is acceptable.
As for "acting as a basis for the communal practice," this is actually not [a statement by] an Arhat, but rather an answer from the "Chapter on the Four Reliances" regarding even half a verse.
This is because the four reliances are shown to constitute the four fruits.
Regarding the absence of a verse as a response: following this verse, it would be as if one were to ask, "If pleasure has not yet arisen, how can it be called the experience of pleasure?"
Regarding the phrase "all are called 'with remainder'": following this verse, one should have stated, "As for the severing of the net of doubt, why is it not definitively explained?
These two lines were not separately extracted within the response.

If they were combined with the phrase "why is it not definitively explained that one enters the state of non-finality," then including the preceding "experiencing pleasure," this would constitute thirteen questions; the first section, however, contains only fourteen questions.
It is simply because the actual phrase "not an Arhat" was not disclosed within the response;
thus, the few remaining fascicles—from here down to the questions of the Great Assembly—consist of only seven fascicles of sutra.

Regarding the question of why there are fewer verses later on: some ancient scholars maintained that the latter four verses were originally part of the question. However, from the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" (*Prakṛty-upāya-parivarta*) onwards, the entire sūtra serves as the answer to these four verses.
Thus, while the question is brief, the explanatory text is extensive. Judging by this, we know that these four verses do not constitute a question.
Regarding the statement that "the sutras all possess the nature of peace and bliss," Sengzong said: "That which is produced by practice must necessarily depend upon the object.
Among objects, nothing is more wondrous than Buddha-nature. The *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* is the brief [version], while the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* is the extensive [version]."

The Sūtra states: "Regarding the various aggregates (skandhas), from the Buddhas above down to those in the five realms below—those Bodhisattvas who are diligent and have attained the eighth stage or higher, who possess the three non-regressions, even these do not have this as their sphere of activity;

therefore, they cease their questioning. Now I say: the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct Teachings, whether entering emptiness or emerging into the provisional, are all unable to know it.

"All that accords with principle" refers to what is called the principle of the secret treasury. "All that has its correspondence within the primary meaning" refers to the four *siddhāntas*, as described in the preceding four passages.
"Already attained, not first attained" means that as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it was already attained; it was not first attained at the site of the Bodhi tree (Vajrāsana).

"Augmented and praised" refers to what was mentioned above: by the Buddha’s majestic empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), they are assisted by his wisdom-power, and the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the great assembly are increased.
"My eloquence and discernment" refers to the praise of his added qualities as written in the text.
Regarding the phrase "equal and without difference," Sengzong said: "This question encompasses the grand purport of the entire sutra and gathers the pivotal mechanism of the myriad practices.
Because it looks up to and propagates the intended meaning, he repeatedly praised it as 'excellent' in order to commend it. Your question and my answer illuminate the principle."
It is the same. How could the teachings of all Buddhas differ from this? Therefore, it is said that they are equal to all Buddhas.
Regarding the "partial and indeterminate teachings," ancient masters categorized the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* as partial and indeterminate teachings;

however, in the profound commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*, this view was extensively refuted. Our school does not hold such a position; rather, within each of the first four periods of teaching, there are elements of indeterminacy.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
This is precisely its characteristic.
As for those who claim this is a secret teaching (*guhyaka-dharma*), the Master’s intention is not so; rather, the secrecy resides in the Buddha himself and cannot be [limitedly] defined.

It is gathered [in the *Avataṃsaka*], yet it cannot be transmitted. That which is transmitted is called "manifest" (*prakaṭa*), whereas the "Dharma-pavilion of Expedient Means" (*upāya-maṇḍala*) is not so.
Everything from the interim period up to today is the manifestation of traces (*vyañjana*), an expedient demonstration of completion.

How can you single out the site of silence (*śānti-maṇḍala*) as the beginning? Sengzong said: "It is not only that [the Buddhas] such as Vipaśyin and others do so; they likewise share this with the Great [Buddha] of the past."
Scholar, in the past, when the *Avataṃsaka* was preached in its seven locations and eight assemblies, great beings from the ten directions gathered like clouds to discuss the meaning of the doctrine;
they too once posed this very question. Yet even there, it was not understood that the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) was merely a provisional manifestation.
Regarding the phrase "the great ocean and so forth," Sengzong says: first, it is profound and vast; second, it stores treasures. Therefore, it is called the Great Ocean of Wisdom.
Regarding "the dharma-nature as empty space": first, all phenomena are fundamentally without intrinsic nature; second, nirvana is also termed the dharma.
This nature is beyond the reach of the power of thought.

Regarding "bearing it upon one's head," Sengzong says: it means to receive the bestowed instructions and honor them by carrying them on one’s head with reverence, like a minister of that [Tibetan] treasury.
Answer: Regarding the cause of long life, it refers to how one attains the three characters; these are the causes.
If there were fixed causes and effects, such that a cause were definitively a cause and an effect were definitively an effect, then they could not be subverted.
Because they are not fixed, one can establish causes and effects that are neither fixed causes nor fixed effects. If one clings to them as being fixed, one falls into nihilism.
It is eternal.
If one says that it reveals the secret of cause and effect, this refers to revealing the former provisional secrets to establish the present Great Nirvāṇa as the cause and effect;
only then can it be called the true essence of Nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is termed the "lesser condition."
If it is for the purpose of manifesting *nirvāṇa* and so forth, this is explained according to the intention of the Buddha and the Sautrāntika school.

What is meant is that there were those who previously practiced the three provisional means, and those for whom the sutras revealed the real through the provisional; furthermore, there were those from the very beginning who maintained the precepts and protected the Dharma with the mind of the Great *Nirvāṇa*.
All of these were for the purpose of manifesting the essence of Great *Nirvāṇa*, which is neither eternal nor impermanent—this is the primary intent.
Regarding "simultaneously clarifying cause and effect": since cause and effect must necessarily exist and can be manifested, they are precisely what constitutes cause and effect;

therefore, it is said that they are "simultaneous. Regarding "expounding cause and effect through skillful means": this sutra simultaneously elucidates both provisional and real cause and effect, which is the function of the dual flow.
To manifest the true essence, it is termed "cause and effect" as a provisional teaching.

As for "leisurely composure" (*zōngróng*): by advancing and retreating with careful deliberation to attain the central mean, one dispels attachments to annihilationism and eternalism; hence it is called "leisurely composure."
Furthermore, regarding "suppression" (yī) and "examination" (àn): the true essence of *nirvāṇa* is fundamentally quiescent and by nature free from the four attachments; this is termed "suppression.

To cultivate in accordance with principle—whereby the cause is not the cause [of samsara] and the fruit manifests the true essence—is termed "examination. Cultivation in this manner is what is called the "cause and fruit" of the present sutra.

Now, it is clarified that if one posits causes based on what is inferior, this constitutes the establishment of attachments such as "self" and "other" through the mutual relation of cause and effect. If one were to formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) regarding causes alone: 1.
A cause that is a cause by its own nature, not depending upon an effect, is called the *svabhāva-hetu* (cause of self-nature). 2.

A cause that is a cause not by its own nature, but by virtue of an effect, is called the *parabhāva-hetu* (cause of other-nature). 3. A cause that is a cause due to the conditions of an effect, is called the *sādhāraṇa-hetu* (common cause). 4. [The fourth case is] the negation of these...
Because the cause is separated from the fruit, the cause is termed "the cause of the nature of being without a cause. The four propositions regarding the single fruit are likewise.
This employs the four propositions of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) to refute attachment to [inherent] nature.

Furthermore, if the cause were inherently a cause and so forth, it would merely establish the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Biéjiào), because the times of cause and fruit differ and the essence of phenomena is not integrated.

"All fall into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism" means that those who reckon for themselves fall into annihilationism, while those who reckon for others fall into eternalism; those who reckon for both fall into both extremes.
Since there is no internal reckoning, one falls into annihilationism; therefore, it is said "all."

Regarding "from the many" and "from the correct": in the preceding passage, the cause is primary while the effect is secondary; in the subsequent passage, the cause is secondary while the effect is primary.

This pattern applies to both the "many" and the "few," for cause and effect mutually constitute one another and cannot be separated. This is precisely what resolves the question: "How can one attain long life?"

Regarding "an overturned vessel," it should fully be stated as "overturned, leaking, defiled, and mixed. The present text merely cites one aspect—impurity—to serve as a warning regarding the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Sengzong said: "When about to answer a question, it is necessary to issue a warning and an injunction. For the ultimate principle (*zongchi*) is profound and mysterious."
Regarding "that which is received with a light mind": although it says "Kāśyapa," the intent refers to the assembly present at that time.
As for the meaning of the words, there are two further phrases in the treatise: "One should preach the Dharma to such a person as one who hears the teaching with a joyful and exultant heart."
Regarding this "cause that becomes karma": each instance sequentially explains the destruction of the causes of the nine dharma-realms and the establishment of the cause of the Buddha-dharma-realm.
If karma were a fixed cause, it would be a cause external to its fruit.
If karma were a fixed fruit, then a fruit external to its cause could not be the fruit of that causal family.
Since cause and effect cannot be established in such a way, they both accord with the Middle Way; therefore, they are unobtainable.
Regarding the phrase "the path of language is cut off" and so forth: it is because the cause is indeterminate that the path of language is cut off;
because the fruit is an indeterminate fruit, the sphere of mental activity ceases.

As for the "bodhisattva of diligence," this refers to the bodhisattvas of the *zang* (Treasury) and *tong* (Penetration) teachings. Those of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) know the Middle Way from their very first thought; therefore, they possess [this quality].
"Jian" (Simplified). Furthermore, although individuals prior to the stages of the *bhūmis* diligently practice emptiness and the provisional, they do not know the perfect and eternal [truth].
Moreover, "Jin Jian" (Exhaustively Simplified) refers to the humility of Zhanran;

having already consulted on the profound meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and examined the significance of the secret treasury of the present sutra, he could not forget the feelings inspired by what he had heard, and thus said "Yi Yi" (Already Done/Finished).
Regarding the phrase "supreme and without summit": vertically, it exhausts the true reality (*dharmatā*) such that its height cannot be apprehended; thus it is called "without summit.
Horizontally, it encompasses the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) such that its boundaries cannot be found; thus it is called "without limit."
Regarding "accomplishing much": it is only upon partial realization that one is said to have accomplished.

Regarding "karma that can destroy karma": this refers to the karma of emptiness. By maintaining the precept against killing and other such karmas with the mind of Great Nirvāṇa, one destroys provisional karma and enters ultimate emptiness; this is what is meant by "destroying."

"From the perspective of non-abiding karma" refers to provisional karma. This means that one realizes the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) are themselves the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).

Since the aggregates, elements, and sense bases have no abiding place, the secret treasury likewise has no abiding place. Because it is without abiding, one returns to rely upon the aggregates, elements, and sense bases in their state of non-abiding to establish the cause and effect of the secret treasury;

this is called "establishing karma. It is neither a refutation nor an establishment; because the essence of karma within the middle [state] fully possesses both negation (*遮*, *chā*) and illumination (*照*, *zhào*), it is called "correct" (*正*, *zhèng*).
The passage beginning with "Karma is thus" below synthesizes and concludes the intent.
Regarding the phrase "prior to the Way": from the moment the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is generated until the attainment of *bodhi*, all is termed "prior to the Way.

Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) constitutes the "middle of the Way," and the period following the realization of Sublime Enlightenment is termed "after the Way. Therefore, the subsequent text cites scriptural evidence to clarify the characteristics of essence and function.

"By means of the power of the jewel" refers to the realization of the essence (*tattva*). "Clarifying and purifying" refers to the realization of the function of compassion. "Great kindness and great compassion" refer to the realization of the function.
"Buddha-nature" refers to the realization of the essence.

"Personally going to the place of bondage" means that the Tathāgata’s Way extends forward in response; he responds to sentient beings just as a king turns his carriage to go to the place where they are bound.
As for the phrase "there is also the Buddha-nature," this is a statement intended to suppress pride and stimulate aspiration. Why? Because the fundamental principle of their nature is identical.

The Buddhas are inherently complete within this very essence; this is what is meant by "inducing. Although this nature is fundamentally possessed, one frequently gives rise to sinful karma and is thus unable to perceive it.
Consequently, one suppresses it and says it does not exist. Yet existence and non-existence do not possess two distinct essences; sentient beings themselves are simply Buddha-nature.
The Buddha-nature is simply the sentient being. The prince serves as the analogy for the absence of nature; because he is the prince, he serves as the analogy for the presence of nature.

Regarding "uprooting the causes of suffering" and so forth, this refers to uprooting the causes of suffering—the three delusions—of the nine realms, and bestowing the wholesome causes of bodhi within the Buddha-realm.
They uproot the suffering of the two types of death within the nine realms and bestow the fruit of the great nirvana of the Buddha-realm.

As for their function and essence: these are the functions of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). Furthermore, for practitioners of the Two Vehicles, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has non-aversion as its wholesome root for its nature;
compassion (*karuṇā*) has non-harming as its essence; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the feeling of joy; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is non-attachment. For the Bodhisattva—

Regarding the practitioner: great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and its counterparts have, in general, great wisdom (*mahājñāna*) as their essence. Furthermore, it is said that they have meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence.

As for "compassion" (*karuṇā*), it refers to the inability to rescue sentient beings suffering from the suffering of suffering; "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*), however, is able to uproot sentient beings from the three types of suffering.
There are many such distinctions in their characteristics.
Regarding "universally in relation to the Four Truths": this refers to the fourfold sets of the Four Truths.

The four great vows of non-action take as their object of resolve the causes and effects of the ten realms, the two types of death, and the three delusions. It is not merely that the four miserable destinies are addressed by the four great vows of non-action;
rather, it is because these vows universally open up all partial and Hinayana teachings, and thus they are so described.

The Sūtra says: "For those who have not yet been liberated, one speaks of the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) to cause them to practice; for those who have not yet crossed over, one speaks of the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) to cause them to cross over;

for those who have not yet attained Nirvāṇa, one speaks of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) to cause them to realize it; for those who have not yet found peace, one speaks of the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) to cause them to find peace."
The Sūtra uses such practices as these because it takes the aforementioned four minds of the "only child," the four great vows, and the three dharmas as the causal basis for its activity.
Why is it said that one gives rise to love? If there were love, there would be "self" and "other"; how then could this be called viewing all equally? This refers to their own characteristics.
"Contradiction.
"Mutually obstructing one another" means that they hinder each other.

"No difference between before and after" means that the former is function while its essence is the latter, and the latter is essence while its function is the former; this is the answer given by citing the Buddha-way.
Prior to the Bodhisattva path, essence and function are non-dual; by what means of contemplation could one say there is any hindrance?
Those who rescue from peril are rescuing those who violate the Buddha’s teachings. "Peril" refers to evil transgressions.
That "there is no harm whatsoever" is an interpretation that accords with reason and conforms to compassion.

As for the statement in the sutra that "one does not leave them unattended," this cites what is improper rather than what is correct; for a state takes cruelty as its foundation. If there are those who have committed offenses...

One must certainly assume a solemn appearance and not be lax or negligent. The Buddha, however, is not like this; toward sentient beings who have committed offenses, he regards them as his own children and does not abandon them.
Regarding the "fourteen administrators," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitation Vinaya), Volume Six of the Eighth Section on Dharma, states: "The Buddha was at Ārā..."
In the country of Āravī at that time, the monastic quarters (vihāra) had collapsed. The Buddha, knowing this, asked Ānanda:

"Why has this multi-storied monastery collapsed? Ānanda replied: "Among those who were repairing these monastic quarters, some have died, some are ill, some have reverted from the precepts, and others have gone to other countries.
The Buddha said: "As for those who have died and those who have reverted from the precepts, the tasks they ought to perform, the Saṃgha shall now undertake."

One should appoint an administrator through formal ritual (karmavācanā). Among the bhikṣus, those who are capable of acquiring much wealth and are able to accomplish tasks should be appointed for a term of six years;
if it concerns a new dwelling, they should be appointed for twelve years. Next, one should appoint an administrator of bedding and seats;
third, an administrator of food; fourth, an administrator of rice gruel distribution; and fifth, an administrator of the distribution of bowls and robes.

Sixth, appointing those who distribute medicinal substances; seventh, appointing one who knows how to prepare utensils; eighth, appointing a single bhikṣu to reside permanently and oversee the monastery;

ninth, appointing those who assign dwellings; tenth, appointing one who receives and guards robes; eleventh, appointing one who distributes robes; twelfth, appointing one who distributes bathing robes;
thirteenth, appointing one who acts as the *karmadāna*; fourteenth, appointing one who assigns duties to śrāmaṇeras.
These fourteen persons are all to be appointed by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

For example, if Dhanika has committed an offense that requires confession (*sāpattika*), yet does not see it as such, the Saṃgha may carry out a formal act of suspension for not seeing the offense (*adarśana-pratiniḥsarga-ukṣepa*) against him. The monks do not associate with him in work or residence.
[The formal acts] are performed: one motion (*jñapti*) is made, two motions are made, four motions are made. [This applies to] the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and...
Regarding all *karmas*, one must not enter or stand among the fourteen types of persons;
because they loathe me as if I were a *caṇḍāla*, it is said that one may not serve as the presiding master (*karmavācaka*) of a *karman*, and so forth, as explained at length in the Vinaya.

Regarding "defiling others' families and engaging in evil conduct," this is entirely as explained in the third fascicle of the *Ten Recitations Vinaya* (Daśādhyāya-vinaya), under the section on the eight rules.
Two bhikṣus defile others' families and engage in evil conduct; everyone hears of it and everyone knows they are engaging in evil conduct.

These bhikṣus sit together with women on the same bed, eat from the same dish, drink from the same vessel, sleep together, and consume food that has been kept overnight, yet they do not receive [the formal admonition].
They ate [in such places], and even rode upon elephants, horses, chariots, and litters amidst large crowds while playing musical instruments.
The bhikṣus reported these matters to the Buddha, who ordered that the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) be performed against them.

Regarding matters such as engaging in disputes with others, the Vinaya simply states: "If one takes pleasure in quarreling and mutual recrimination, and it is already known that this is a quarrelsome bhikṣu, he then goes to their location and says to them:
'Next, you must firmly uphold this matter and not allow others to strike at it; you must secure victory for me, and I shall assist you,' and so forth.
It does not mention going into the city to lodge a complaint. This [latter case] should likely be understood according to the *Śāstra* (commentary).
This is merely an explanation based on the essential meaning.
To cause one to rely upon a steadfast and upright person, the Vinaya states: "First, you should be instructed to live in dependence upon such-and-such a person;
second, the *cittāśraya-karman* (the ritual for relying upon the mind) should be recited (*etc.*)."
Regarding the phrase "at a later time, the householder," the Vinaya states: At that time, there was the bhikṣu Upasena Vaṇija-putra, who was accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
They were all forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), wearers of rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika), and alms-seekers (piṇḍapātika) who delighted in dwelling in open spaces.
When the householder saw these visiting bhikṣus coming and going, sitting and standing, their food, drink, robes, bowls, and deportment were all pure.
He immediately gave rise to a heart of pure reverence. Because of this visiting bhikṣu, he invited the Saṃgha to his own home for a meal the following day.
At that time, the master of the saṃghārāma said to the householder Citta, "He did not first inform me;
because of a visiting bhikṣu, he has invited the Saṃgha to his house for a meal. I am the Mātika-Mātideva of the householder Citta’s Āmra Grove."
"Householder, the householder Citta did not question me. Once this night has passed, I shall speak with this householder.
When the ground was bright and the night had ended, he took his bowl and went to the householder's residence, where he saw various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink prepared.
He spread out various multi-colored mats and asked, "Why are there no sesame *modaka* (joy-pills)?

The householder replied, "I shall now provide an illustration, as if from a commentary, for my pleasure in speaking. This was because the householder’s family had practiced the oil-pressing trade for three generations;
thus, he was making this sarcastic remark.
Regarding the eight methods: among the fourfold [set], they are: first, censure; second, dependence; third, expulsion; fourth, prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople;
fifth, not seeing [the offense]; sixth, not repenting; seventh, not relinquishing evil views; eighth, formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya*); ninth, punishment for verbal abuse.
Within the Vinaya teachings, there are only these nine methods; however, the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* contains only eight methods. The fifth is "not seeing."
Regarding this: in the Vinaya, when the bhikṣu Channa was accused of committing an offense and asked, "Do you see [your fault]?", he replied, "I do not see it.

The Tathāgata established a rule to expel him from the assembly and strip him of all benefits; because the penalty was applied only upon his admission, this is called the "offense of non-seeing" (*adṛṣṭāpatti*).

As for the "one who does not repent": this refers to Channa again, who, though aware that he had committed an offense, did not repent or extinguish it. The Tathāgata established a rule to expel such a person from the assembly.
Because it must wait for repentance before it can proceed, it is called "non-repentance.
Regarding the "constant light": the constant light is always present as one fathom, without increase or decrease; thus it is called "light."
As for the "extraordinary" (asādhāraṇa), it is because they serve as conditions that either increase or decrease, and are thus not uniform.
Some say that within the five-colored lights, one, two, or even up to five types may be emitted.

Regarding "the entire body consists of five": the emission of light possesses manifold conditions, as cited in the third commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; therefore, the note says "and so forth.
Regarding "dharmas not yet seen": these are dharmas you have not yet perceived; since you wish to see them, I shall now explain them for you.
Regarding "severing the evils of the four abodes": the four abodes are afflictions external to the essence [of the mind]; therefore, they are metaphorically compared to neighboring kings.

Regarding "those who feign intimacy while lacking compassion": this refers to those who see others committing evil yet do not discipline or investigate them; such people who dwell together with them feign intimacy while being devoid of compassionate pity.

Regarding the initial mention of the king and his ministers: the king represents the Buddha, and the ministers represent those who transmit the Dharma. To cause those who have not yet generated the aspiration [for enlightenment] to generate it is called "giving birth";

to cause those who have already generated it to bring it to fruition is called "nurturing. Whether born or nurtured, they are collectively termed "sons. That their capacity for the Way is unimpaired is called "handsome";
that their consciousness masters cause and effect is termed "wise."
The "three roots" refer to the superior, middling, and inferior.
Regarding the "four groups," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are two for the laity and two for those who have left the home life, making four groups in total.

Alternatively, by including the assembly of Śākyas and the assembly of Brahmās alongside the two groups of those who have left the home life, one arrives at four groups. Bao Liang says: "If there are two [groups], they are the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs."
The bhikṣuṇīs; third, the śrāmaṇeras; and fourth, the śrāmaṇerīs.
Regarding the "three types," the partial faith refers to the three vehicles (the three teachings), while correct faith refers to the Perfect Teaching (the One Vehicle).

As for the "entrusted teaching," Zezhou said: "There are those who have committed the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or slandered the True Dharma—these are the three kinds of offenders."

Regarding the *yifa* (monastic regulations), one who has been expelled for disciplinary offenses may die [during the process]. Among his disciples, there may be those who have committed minor offenses of the ten evil deeds;
these too must be punished, and this is called "the remaining one son. One must certainly undergo severe punishment to purify oneself from the assembly of the wicked.

This was spoken according to the Buddha’s original intent: "Even if I lose three sons, I shall never harbor resentment. Furthermore, the *Chaowuji* (Record of Transcendent Awakening) states: "Suppose even three sons..."
"Regarding 'until they are brought to fulfillment': this is a metaphor for the three groups, such as the nuns and others, who may retreat due to disciplinary punishment;
whereas for the single group of bhikṣus alone, one must apply rigorous discipline to ensure they fulfill the three trainings. Sengao said:

"This clarifies that the Tathāgata entrusted the fourfold assembly of disciples to those who propagate the Dharma, instructing them with the mandate of the three fulfillments. Even if the [other] three groups of disciples were entrusted to propagate..."
To claim that one does not attain the Way because the treatment [of faults] is incomplete, or that there remains a group of people who are not treated simply because they are few—
such interpretations are all refuted within the *Śāstra*. Therefore, I have set forth this [explanation] so that you may know that such interpretations do not accord with the intent of the Sūtra.
Regarding the phrase "having attained the first shift of the immeasurable," one shall soon hear that [the Tathāgata] abides within the secret treasury of the shift.
How could great merit exceed this?

As for the phrase "it is not that the son does not think," it is not so with the Tathāgata; there is no one other than this son who is "not the son. Thus, he brings about the fulfillment of equanimity.
The same applies to those who do not achieve [this] for others.
As for "even one who attains immeasurable merit," before long they shall realize the provisional nature of the teachings.
You who take the fruit to be the cause—why have you seen the Buddha? Because he entered parinirvāṇa as a condition, you perceive him as impermanent.
Regarding the fruit: if the fruit is impermanent, is the cause likewise so?
There are those who maintain that within the continuity of the world, as long as a single lifetime has not been severed, it is termed "permanent."
That which is not conditioned by enumeration refers to the unconditioned state of cessation through non-discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which is eternal space refers to the unconditioned state of space (*ākāśa*), which has non-obstruction as its essence.
That which exists inherently means that form itself is emptiness; being devoid of any relative opposition, it is called "inherently existent" (*mūla-sat*).

The Buddha answers regarding the fruit of long life: the previous response addressed how one attains the three characters [of the name], while the present response specifically addresses the two characters "long life.

When it says "the Buddha-treasure is eternal," it clarifies that the single essence of the Buddha-treasure is eternal; subsequently, it clarifies that the same applies to the other two treasures as well.

Regarding "the earth and empty space": within empty space there are those who travel through the void; likewise, those on water and land, as well as humans and devas, all possess the existence-body (*bhava-skandha*), the intermediate-state body (*antarābhava-skandha*), and a lifespan.
This is illustrated by the eight great rivers, all of whom shall become Buddhas, just as rivers inevitably flow toward the ocean.
Regarding "able to emerge from the realms of humans and devas": if humans, devas, and others, being deluded regarding the permanence of nirvāṇa, are born through defiled dependent origination,

whereas the Buddhas arise from the essence to manifest function— this is pure dependent origination— and thus enter into birth-and-death in order to lead sentient beings of the nine realms into the ocean of great nirvāṇa,
they are therefore said to be "able to emerge."
Regarding the Anavatapta Lake: its name is established based on its presiding deity. This is translated as "Free from Affliction and Heat," while its secondary name is "Cooling.
It is called the Lake Free from Affliction and Heat because the dragon king resides within it.
Regarding the emergence of the four rivers, the sūtras do not speak with uniformity. Some say there are eight, while others say there are twenty rivers;
each has its own justification. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: from the silver ox-mouth in the east emerges the Gaṅgā River; from the golden elephant-mouth in the south emerges the Sindhu River;
from the lapis lazuli horse-mouth in the west emerges the Vakṣu River; and from the crystal lion-mouth in the north emerges the Sītā River.
Regarding the many rivers:

as for the "eight rivers," when the Buddha appeared in the eastern mountains, there were thirty-five thousand rivers that all people saw clearly; these were taken as metaphors for the great rivers of other regions.
Furthermore, there are great and famous rivers known to all, which are also taken as metaphors. Together with the previously mentioned [rivers], they are said to be eight.
In other regions there are small rivers that lack great renown and are unknown to all; therefore, they are not mentioned here. This is why eight are spoken of.
As for the statement that there are twenty, it is as explained in the Āgamas: forty *li* outside the lake, each of the four rivers branches out into four further rivers.
In total there are twenty [rivers]. Following their respective directions toward the ocean, they traverse the clouds.
The retinue of the Gaṅgā consists of four further rivers: first, the Yamunā; second, the Sarayū; third, the Aciravatī; and fourth, the Mahī.
The retinue of the Sītā also consists of four: first, the Vipāśā; second, the Ilāvatī; third, the Śatadru; and fourth, the Vitastā. The retinue of the Vakṣu...
There are also four: first, Bana; second, Vitara; third, Mingsha; and fourth, Guangzhongpo Siduo.
The retinue of Siduo also consists of four: first, Salili; second, Vimola;
third, Dubanti; and fourth, Bisoupobo. These constitute the twenty.
Regarding "Brahmins and others": the term "others" includes all devas and humans, as well as lay practitioners (*upāsaka*). All of them are transformed by the Bodhisattva.
This clarifies that during the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), he bestows all life; the merit of this transformation returns to the one who transforms.
Therefore, upon reaching Buddhahood, it becomes eternal.
Regarding "from the basis of non-abiding": the secret treasury constantly causes all things to abide nowhere. It fully encompasses the life-span of the nine dharma-realms;
this life-span of the nine dharma-realms, being without abiding, pervades the secret treasury. Because these two dharmas are in essence non-dual, they are able to universally establish all phenomena.

Regarding the exiting and entering of meditative concentration: if one speaks of exiting from concentration and entering into concentration, this merely accords with the meaning of previous teachings.
Now, in the Great Nirvana, both exiting and entering are the Dharma-realm; because its essence pervades all of space, it is praised by means of emptiness.
The Sūtra states that the Tathāgata is likewise the foremost in lifespan among all sentient beings; this refers to the meaning of "emergence.
The intention behind this emergence is precisely to lead all sentient beings into the ocean of the eternal life of Great Nirvāṇa, which is called "the ability to enter.
Therefore, the metaphor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) is employed.

If the lifespan of the Tathāgata is as described in the sutra, it is because of the four aforementioned dharmas. Sengzong said: "This is to respond to the capacity [of the audience] and fulfill their request.

Regarding the passage in the sutra stating that one should not form the notion of exhaustion: if one does not give rise to the notion of the Tathāgata’s extinction, for what reason is this request made?

Can he not abide for one eon and so forth? Since it is verified that the Buddha’s request to remain produced the perception of the extinction of arising and ceasing, how much more so in the case of the two [other] circumstances?
Even those of external paths who possess the five supernatural powers can extend or shorten their lives at will, abiding for one or two eons;
how much more so for the Tathāgata, who has already attained eternal life, yet cannot abide for one eon and so forth?

The Sūtra indicates that those things described as being like poisonous trees are all indeed poisonous trees; they must subsequently be boiled away forever. Therefore, it says, "seeing them, one abandons them.
Regarding the objection concerning the two teachings: both possess what is spoken of, and that which is spoken of is precisely the teaching itself.

Regarding the point that "the two principles are not different": Kāśyapa’s intention is that if the Tathāgata and the non-Buddhists were both born together and ceased together, one would know that the principle realized by him was no different from that of outsiders.

Regarding the heretics who steal the teaching of permanence: during the time of the True Dharma, there were still the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), and for that reason, outsiders were unable to steal it;
it was only in the Semblance Dharma (*pāriyānika-dharma*) that they did so.
As for the subtlety of the Buddha's principle: the Dharma-body is subtle and wondrous; it is not something seen by ordinary eyes, nor is it something conceived by the mind. This is called...
Regarding "non-manifestation" according to external heterodox principles: from the primordial darkness (*ādi-tamas*) arises intellect (*buddhi*); from intellect arise the twenty-five *tattvas*.
After twenty thousand kalpas have passed, they return once more to the primordial darkness; this is called non-manifestation.
Regarding the Buddha’s recognition and leading back [of sentient beings]: for those of great capacity, they have already been recognized and led back within the *Avataṃsaka*;

for those of small capacity, he subsequently provides the teaching of the Small Vehicle, reprimanding and purifying them, so that it is only upon reaching the present sutra that they are finally recognized and led back.
Regarding "the various forms": although forms are diverse, they belong to a single group; likewise, although the teachings are diverse, they all expound the same principle.
"Not anticipating the human or celestial realms" means not anticipating the bitter fruits of human or celestial existence, nor the contemplation of suffering of the two vehicles.

Regarding "the person who propagates the sūtras benefits themselves": this refers to a person who propagates the teaching in accordance with the Dharma. Although they speak it for others, the others do not accept it;
because it is the final age of the Dharma, it remains as mere words and names, resulting only in benefit for oneself.
Regarding the absence of women: Unsurpassed Bodhi takes great compassion as its foundation.
Since outsiders do not seek unsurpassed Bodhi, they must likewise lack such compassion; yet there is the benefit of attaining it.

Regarding those who admire the profound principle: this refers to the admiration within the capacity [of the practitioner]. Why? Because they rejoice in the name of "eternal bliss," they inquire about the meaning of admiring the profound principle.

That which is not based on the foundation of permanence cannot serve as the basis for permanence; it is only by upholding the precepts with the mind of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* that one is fit to become the root of permanence. Anything inferior to this—
Everything other than this is not [the Way].
"Lacking concentration, wisdom, and skillful means" refers to the perfect, eternal concentration, wisdom, and skillful means. Zhezhou said: "Direct observation is called 'gathering';
lateral investigation is called 'shaking. Worldly goodness that merely leads to rebirth is called 'the difficulty of obtaining the gruel.'"
The analogy of the whey (*maṇḍa*) to humans and devas is as follows: when the essence is refined, it becomes clarified butter (*sarpis*); the remaining liquid is whey.
The intention is that even what is discarded from the curd cannot be obtained, let alone the curd itself and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "arising from views such as self and person": among the sixteen types of views, the ninth is the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

This refers to the arbitrary conceptualization of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and naming them "self. The fourth is the view of person (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*), which conceives of the self as the practitioner.

The seventh is the view of the knower (*jñātṛdṛṣṭi*), which conceives of the self as the five sense faculties that can perceive the five objects. The eighth is the view of the seer (*darśakadṛṣṭi*), which conceives of the self as the faculty and object that can see forms and give rise to [false] views.

1. The view of origination (*samutthāna-dṛṣṭi*): the view that calculates the ability to produce sentient beings, as when parents give birth to a child. 2. The view of nurturing (*poṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi*): the view that calculates "I am able to nourish others.
3. The view of the aggregates (*saṃkhyā-dṛṣṭi*): the calculation that "I possess the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements."
5. The view of the experiencer (*vedaka-dṛṣṭi*): reckoning that "I" shall experience the retribution of future bodies. 6. The view of the agent (*kāraka-dṛṣṭi*):

reckoning that "I" am able to create the retribution of future lives. 10. The view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*): collectively grasping the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and naming them a "sentient being. 11. The view of a life-principle (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*):
regarding the life-force as something that must quickly continue, fearing its rapid interruption. 12. The view of a doer (*kartṛ-dṛṣṭi*): reckoning that "I" am capable of having [objects].

13. The view of a life-span (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*): calculating the duration of a single lifetime. Although one usually calculates that the time of illness is most critical, there is fear that the continuity [of the life-force] might be severed or that the single lifetime might be too short.
14. The view of an agent (*kārayitr̥dr̥ṣṭi*): meaning that [the self] drives and urges [the body] by means of itself.

15. The view of an experiencer (*vedayitr̥dr̥ṣṭi*): meaning that suffering and pleasure arise from oneself. 16. The view of an originator (*utthāpayitr̥dr̥ṣṭi*): causing [the self] to be reborn again.
The realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is called "arising" because it is seen [as such]; thus, the word "etc. is used.
Regarding the loss of the wholesome roots of humans and devas, Sengliang says: "Those with many false views are able to sever their wholesome roots; thus, both humans and devas lose them."

Regarding the phrase "the rest are those of the semblance-dharma and the final dharma," Master Daosheng said: "The Buddha’s scriptures cause people to attain the three dharmas of precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
these are fundamentally the paths for attaining Buddhahood. Those who seek worldly pleasures and lose the fundamental [purpose] are what is meant by 'the rest'."
Regarding "adding water": the Sūtra states that the term "person" (pudgala) refers to non-Buddhists who cling to a self; this is the water of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

"Brahmā" refers to non-Buddhists who worship Brahmā; they reckon that Brahmā can produce the world, yet he is not the cause of production—this is the water of the view of rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Alternatively, reckoning Brahmā as eternal is the water of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Īśvara refers to the non-Buddhist practitioners who worship Īśvara. They also reckon him to be eternal and capable of producing the world;
this is likewise an extreme view characterized by attachment to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
"Atoms" refers to the tenets of the Lokāyata and Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists. They maintain that the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal and capable of producing the world;
this is also an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and a form of asceticism regarding rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Regarding the "nature of the world" (*jagat-prakṛti*): the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists reckon the *pradhāna* (the primal cause) to be the nature of the world; they also reckon it to be eternal and capable of producing the world.
This is also a form of the extreme view of attachment to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

"Rules" refers to the non-Buddhist adherence to the precepts of dogs, cows, and so forth, or the adherence of ordinary persons to specific ascetic practices for liberation, as well as the meditative concentration-precepts (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*) which they believe can attain *nirvāṇa*. As for "concentration," it may be...
These four dhyānas and eight samāpattis are either the tainted (sāsrava) samādhis of ordinary worldlings; they are not the path to nirvāṇa, yet they are grasped as the causal path.

These are either the "prohibitive and acquisitive" [practices] of outsiders, or the mundane wisdom of outsiders, or the wisdom arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation of ordinary worldlings.
Since these are tainted, they are not the path to nirvāṇa; to grasp them as the path is likewise a form of śīlavrataparāmarśa (clinging to rules and observances).

"Taking up water" refers to those who attain liberation through external paths. This means that when practitioners of the six practices of the non-Buddhists suppress their afflictions and sever the lower-tier afflictions, they realize the fundamental stage (*mūlabhūmi*) following the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
this is termed "liberation. However, it is not true liberation; to regard such a state as liberation is the "grasping at water."
The realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the clarified butter of the suffering of birth and death; it is not truly nirvāṇa.
It is a mistaken calculation of the non-Buddhists, and is likewise the water grasped by views. These types of attachments and views arise in conjunction with craving, pride, and ignorance.
All these are collectively termed "adding water and milk.

There are those who practice a small portion of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), observing the ten wholesome paths of action and the eight precepts, while also making offerings to their parents and others;

all such things exist within the Buddha-dharma as its constituent dharmas. These are but a small portion of the power of the Tathāgata’s unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*). Because they rely on this practice and its fruit, they are designated as "small."
Regarding the Brahma-faring:
those who take refuge in the Three Jewels do not know that taking refuge in the Three Jewels as being of one essence serves as the constant cause.
Since they neither recognize the cause nor recognize the fruit, it is said that "in reality, they do not know."
Regarding "pervading the six great cities": if we base this on the refutation of outsiders, it begins from the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras where they were successively driven away;
for now, I shall follow the final explanation.
As for "the extinction of tainted wisdom reaching nirvāṇa," this refers to the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), by which tainted wisdom is severed and exhausted.
One attains nirvana through the principle of cessation; one does not take non-analytical cessation as nirvana, because analytical cessation is merely the absence of conditions.
Both of these types of knowledge pertain to both the superficial and the profound.
Since there is already the duality of right and wrong, it is like how untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is not itself *nirvāṇa*; therefore, wisdom does not abandon wisdom.
If the Path were able to bring about cessation, then the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment would merely be able to lead to cessation rather than being cessation itself;

thus, they are not *nirvāṇa*. This raises the objection regarding the sequence and depth of the two types of wisdom. Now, I shall cite three masters who merely resolve this by eliminating the abandonment of wisdom.
Regarding the passage that uses the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to challenge the body: "uses" means that by negating the nature of phenomena, one challenges the present *dharmakāya*.
As for their mutual challenges: if the body exists, one should not speak of the nature of phenomena; if one speaks of the nature of phenomena, [the body] should not [exist].
To speak of "having a body": how can it be that the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is non-existent while the body is existent, such that they result in mutual contradiction?
Regarding the four bodies (*kāya*) up to the point of being "unresolved": one speaks again of the "existence of the body" and again of "the *dharmatā*"; therefore, they remain unresolved at present.

Regarding "the Heaven of No-Thought" (*asaṃjñisattva*) and so forth: this raises an illustrative example. This heaven is located within the fourth *dhyāna*, depending upon the Bṛhatphala (Great Fruit) devas;

it is a distinct, superior region that serves as the place where the retribution of the Heaven of No-Thought is experienced. There are non-Buddhist practitioners who, having cultivated the meditative attainment of no-thought (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), are born therein.
Upon their initial birth, they possess perception (*saṃjñā*); subsequently, perception ceases, and for five hundred great eons (*mahākalpa*), they remain without thought. There is no... [text ends].
It is held that the beings in that realm definitely possess ten bases (*āyatana*), namely the six sense organs and four sense objects, excluding the two objects of fragrance and taste.
Question: Since those gods are unable to produce speech and lack inhalation and exhalation, how can there be sound? Answer:

Because external winds must strike various parts of their bodies to stimulate the internal body and thereby produce sound, they definitely possess [these ten bases]. This is also the case when their life is about to end.
If one conceives that thought arises again, they will slander *nirvāṇa* and ultimately enter hell. The Buddha now raises this point:

at the time when that thought ceases, there is only the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), but there is no thought upon which the aggregate of form depends, nor is there any thought that serves as the objective condition for the elevation of form.
Regarding "arising from the fetter of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*): because there is still a mind present, afflictions arise; this is termed the "fetter of craving.

As for those who have not yet reached [the state of non-conception], they lack the mind of perception and possess only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which sustains the retributive life-force so that it does not cease.
This is like one who has come from outside; they are praised as being in the "state of succession" (*upapadya*).

Regarding the statement "one should not formulate [objections] such as 'cessation' and so forth": one should not formulate the objection that while the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) ceases, the body does not cease.
Why? Because the Tathāgata arises by reason of conditions and ceases by reason of conditions; he leads all sentient beings to the state that is neither cessation nor non-cessation.

How can you unilaterally formulate objections regarding arising and cessation? Master Sengzong said: "How much more so, since the Tathāgata is the ultimate subtlety—how could he be something that can be known? Formerly...
To point to solitary extinction as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is provisional rather than ultimate.
In the Sūtra, it is said that there is no difference between them: the Buddha is the Dharma and the Saṃgha; the Dharma is the Buddha and the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha is the Buddha and the Dharma.

Thus, if one speaks of arising and ceasing, this constitutes a notion of difference. These three dharmas are of one essence and lack the three distinctions; therefore, they are called "without difference."

Its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is that its essence is eternally abiding; therefore, it is said to have no characteristic of impermanence. Because it is not subject to being displaced by the three delusions or the two deaths, it has no characteristic of change.
These constitute the three aspects of the single Buddha-body. Taking the sense of awakening and discernment as the Buddha-treasure (*buddharatna*);
