because its essence contains nothing that is not Dharma and is endowed with all merits, it is called the Dharma-treasure (*dharmanatna*). Its essence does not separate from things and is necessarily in harmony with principle; thus it is named... [the Sangha-treasure].
It is called the Sangha-jewel.
If one practices these three dharmas as distinct entities, it should be known that such a person does not achieve pure refuge.
Since they claim the Buddha-jewel is not yet ultimate, how could they possibly obtain the full precepts? If one relies upon the eternally abiding Three Refuges, then...
This refers to the attainment of the full complement of precepts.
Regarding the "purity of the three refuges" mentioned in the sutra, this refers to the single essence of the three refuges.

As for the phrase "if [it were] like the four seasons of the past," this merely indicates that the time had not yet arrived and thus could not be spoken of; it does not mean that this refers to the refuges of the Hinayana.
One may observe the precepts yet fail to achieve accomplishment. If one hears this present sutra, a śrāvaka must realize the Buddha-nature;

only then will their taking of the precepts be complete. If they do not know this, their observance of the precepts remains incomplete. This is why the ten seers, having first attained the minor fruits of the path, only then entered the secret treasury.

It should be understood that regarding those who have already attained: if one speaks in terms of the transformed mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*), one may say they have already attained it; however, if speaking in terms of the conditions of sentient beings (*pratyaya*), one cannot say they have attained it because the time has not yet arrived.

As for the passage "The Tathāgata is also like this," because there is a constant dharma (*dharmatā*), it accords with the preceding cause of the tree, clarifying the single essence of the *dharmakāya*.
Because it is eternal, there is a refuge; it is as if a tree and its shadow were conjoined. This clarifies that the distinct substance of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is also eternal;
thus, it is said not to be impermanent. This concludes by summarizing it as eternal.
Regarding the statement that the Sūtra says [the Buddha] is not like the various devas and so forth, the intended meaning is as follows:

if the Tathāgata were permanent, he could serve as a refuge for those who are impermanent. However, since the Tathāgata is impermanent, for an impermanent person to take refuge in an impermanent Buddha would not constitute true refuge.
Regarding the passage in the sutra that speaks of a tree without a shadow: the tree is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*, and the shadow is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Since the *dharmakāya* is eternal as a single essence, the *nirmāṇakāya* is likewise eternal. Why, then, does Kāśyapa raise the objection that the *nirmāṇakāya* is impermanent? Sengzong said: "The traditional interpretation [is as follows]."
The tree is a metaphor for the true *dharmakāya*, and the shadow is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya*. While this was convenient for the preceding text, it is not convenient for the objection.
Now, when it says "there is one to whom one may go for refuge," it correctly states that the wondrous existence of the ultimate fruit is eternal; thus, there exists the quality of being a refuge.

If this quality did not exist, the meaning of "refuge" would also be destroyed. Therefore, Kāśyapa raises an objection based on the shadow, wishing to show that there is no one to whom one can go for refuge.
This interpretation results in only a single dharma being established with two meanings. It should instead be explained according to the principle that they both exist eternally.
Sengliang said: "The stars and moon have light, and the trees have dark shadows; however, because these are subtle, they are not seen by the naked eye."

The Dharma-body is likewise; it is not that which you perceive. Just as in the sutras it is said that if parents are each different, they cannot produce a child, whereas through their union a child is born—this is illustrated by the usual analogy—if there were no such principle of a child, it would necessarily be impermanent.
That which acts as frost and hail within the sutra is intended to shatter the view of impermanence and cause the arising of the constant view and the understanding of permanence.
*Da niepan jing shu ji*, Fascicle Two.
Completed copying on the second day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Shōhō era; collated once against the original manuscript.
Private Notes on the Commentary to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, Scroll Three.
The text of the "Chapter on the Vajra-body" is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the title; second, the word-by-word commentary following the text. The first part is further divided into two sections, the first of which is the explanation of the title.

Next, regarding the intent behind the successive descending and ascending inquiries: as for the initial reference to the "Vajra-body," Master Sengsheng said, "Both 'longevity' and 'vajra' refer to the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) form.
Longevity is the outward manifestation of response; the vajra is the internal reality of illumination.
Since the essence of this real illumination is perfect and complete, it is not limited by spatial direction."
Regarding the four meanings of "Vajra," they can be understood by correlating them respectively with the four *siddhāntas*.
As for the "fundamental basis of the world": among gold, that which is most excellent is called "gold-essence" (*kāñcanagarbha*), which is the lowest grade of *vajra*.
"Jing" (pronounced *jū* with the *shèng* rhyme;
meaning "vigorous") refers to that which is proposed having no predecessor. This means that all that is proposed is shattered, leaving nothing [intact].
That its color is indeterminate is a metaphor for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Because it is indeterminate, it is able to serve as the basis for all things.
The dharmas that pervade the dharma-realm cannot be entered unless they are fully encompassed; therefore, it is said that they are "difficult to perceive.

Next, regarding the two sections within the exposition of the intent: first, the formal presentation of the intent; second, the citation of ancient authorities, beginning with "There are some who say... The first section [the formal presentation] further has three parts:

first, the formal presentation of the intent; second, "If one takes the general [perspective]... which clarifies how the substance of the dharmas interpenetrates to constitute the Three Truths; third, "Now, following the specific [perspective]... and so forth.

Regarding the intent of the "Chapter on the Conclusion": when it is said at the outset that "one meaning applies universally," this means that each of the remaining thirty-three answers should be cited individually to establish the significance of the initial "Long Life. Therefore, it is so stated.

Regarding "Perfect Pervasion" (Yuántōng): the Dharma-body being without deficiency is called "perfect" (yuán); its universal encompassing of all phenomena is called "pervasive" (tōng). Furthermore, its essence being omnipresent is called "perfect," and its being without obstruction is called "pervasive.

Next, regarding the passage in the "Mutual Pervasiveness" section that says, "If one takes 'pervasive' as the name," etc., this means that having departed from the general to produce the specific, it answers the thirty [questions].

Question: Therefore, it is said that there is no lack of distinct meanings. By synthesizing the distinct, the general is formed; since nothing is not longevity, it is said that there is no lack of pervasive meaning.

Next, in the exposition of the ancients, there are two parts: first, the formal analysis; second, "Furthermore, others clarify... and below, the re-explanation. The first part also has two sections. First—

The preceding section provides a historical introduction; the subsequent section clarifies the following by providing the formal explanation. Within this, the phrase "the first has already been briefly explained" refers to the five [qualities] such as eternal life, which were already briefly explained in the *Cunda-parivarta*.

Regarding the "four characteristics" (up to the point of) "discrimination": these four characteristics pertain to verbal action (*vākkarman*); therefore, they are discussed in contrast to permanence. As for their grouping:
the thirty-three questions are subsumed within the first question; there is nothing that is not [included in] long life.

As for "if [the text] were scattered," this means departing from the general to produce the specific, and distributing [the points] throughout the various answers; all of this is intended solely to manifest the meaning of long life and eternal abiding.

Next, in the second part of the re-explanation, there are two sections: first, the narration of the ancient views; second, "now then" (jin ze) and below, the actual explanation. Within that, it says "withered forest."

Regarding "entering extinction": entering extinction within a withered forest signifies the manifestation of the Middle Way through the non-duality of both [extinction and existence]. Entering extinction within a flourishing forest signifies the manifestation of the conventional through the simultaneous illumination of both.
The section on the East below [the first] uses the non-duality of withering and flourishing to manifest the Middle Way.

The statement "flourishing is itself the Real" below clarifies that illumination is simultaneously quiescence, thereby manifesting the inconceivable Real. The statement "withering is itself the conventional" below... [clarifies that] quiescence is simultaneously illumination, thereby manifesting the inconceivable conventional.

"Quiescent yet illuminating" reveals the inconceivable conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "The three truths are identical to the one truth" further explains that the aforementioned "flourishing" is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"The one truth is identical to the three truths" further explains that the aforementioned "withering" is itself the conventional truth.

The two subsequent lines concerning "differentiation" clarify the non-differentiation and further explain the aforementioned Middle Way, manifesting its dual aspects of negation and illumination. The final section, beginning with "the realm of all Buddhas," concludes the intent and manifests the Buddha-nature.
The substance of the objective realm is fused; the three truths are mutually identical. This is beyond the conceptual deliberation and verbal expression of the three teachings and nine dharma-realms.
Neither the two deaths nor the three delusions can invade or destroy it; therefore, it is metaphorically likened to a vajra.

Next, regarding the explanation: first, it is said that "the previous question contains two [aspects]. Within the previous question, the upper and lower [levels] mutually contain two layers of cause and effect.
The causes and conditions for long life were already answered in the preceding chapter; now, the single layer of cause and effect pertaining to the *vajra* is further elucidated.
"All are dharmas and all are metaphors" means that each and every body is metaphorically represented by the vajra and so forth.
By citing what was seen, it clarifies that Kāśyapa raised an objection based on literal traces, which was then resolved through the wondrous explanation.
"Shattered into śarīras" means that they should indeed be shattered into śarīras.
Next, regarding the formal answer, according to the outline of the commentary, there are six sections: first, indicating the characteristics of the single and double counts of the phrases;

second, "Now, as for the ancients... and below, presenting the ancient interpretations; third, "At Tiantai... and below, clarifying the interpretation of the present master; fourth, "In my private opinion... and below, distinguishing the author's own supplementary views.
Explanation: Fifth, from "Since ancient times" onwards, the first four teachings are presented to demonstrate the distinctions between the shallow and deep levels of the hundred negations.
Sixth, from "Based on the sutra" onwards, the text is annotated to reveal the characteristics of the three truths.
The phrase "sometimes one exists and one perishes" expresses the characteristic of single-line [verses].
As for "not perishing moment by moment," although they enter nirvana, this is not like the impermanence of the two vehicles, which involves moment-by-moment extinction.
"Non-body is body": this single phrase distinguishes the two bodies of existence and non-existence. "Non-body" means the body has perished; "is body" means the body exists.
Next, regarding the statement in the older commentary that "it is not the body prior to the Vajra [mind]," the ancients said: "Prior to the Golden Mind, one still belongs to the state of non-being."
Because it is eternal, it is called "non-body.
Those who take this to be a "good body" do not correctly grasp what is good; [it refers to] the body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*).

Regarding that which is formed through causes and conditions: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the cause, and the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the condition. From these, kalpas arise, employed to accommodate [sentient beings].

This is appropriate for the nature of things. Furthermore, sentient beings act as the cause and the Dharma-body acts as the condition; through the causal conditions of resonance and response, the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya) arises to transform sentient beings.
Therefore, it is said that they "mutually accomplish" one another.
"This emptiness is devoid of emptiness" clarifies that while the body of the Dharma-pervades all of space, it is not identical to space.

Third, regarding the three types of fourfold propositions (catuṣkoṭi) within the present masters: the single fourfold proposition is the same as the method of propositions found in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the preceding statement concerning "non-": the preceding non-statement does not form a proposition by being paired with "is" and "is-not.
It may also be used independently with "non-non" to constitute a fourfold formulation (*catuṣkoṭi*); the same applies to "is-is."

Furthermore, regarding the principle that the simple comes first and the compound follows: one should first complete the fourfold proposition (catuṣkoṭi) concerning "the simple" and "that which is not the simple," and only thereafter construct the fourfold proposition concerning "the compound" and "that which is not the compound."
Regarding the four "negations" (*fei*) within the four types of assistance, what are the four phrases of "not yet knowing the negation"?

Now, when we speak of "negating the body," the three collections (*piṭaka*) and the hundred negations serve as the objects of negation. The comprehensive negation (*tōng-fēi*) negates the [first] collection; the specific negation (*bié-fēi*) negates the preceding two;
and the perfect negation (*yuán-fēi*) negates the preceding three. Only in this way is the ultimate of the negating subject revealed.

Regarding "excluding the characteristics of one dharma": this means excluding one body and one dharma; as for the various bodies manifested externally, they all exist in such a way because they respond to sentient beings.

As for the fifth point, that the intent is not yet fully revealed within the *yōkyō* (teachings according to capacity), it means that the hundred negations (*hyakuhi*) have not been distinguished as belonging to which specific teaching.
No. The meaning of the present scripture’s statement that it is "not a sign" (a-lakṣaṇa) is as follows:
regarding the distinction between the shallow and the profound, the provisional is shallow while the real is profound.
As for "being endowed with the hundred blessings," this refers to having destroyed the hundred non-attainments (aprāpti) and thereby attained the hundred blessings; therefore, it is so designated.
"Superior among the superior" means that within the superior of the superior, it is yet more superior.
"Those who possess existence and so forth" refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) which are constrained by the causes and effects of the twenty-five existences within the three realms.
Therefore, it is said that "existence exists. This statement is made to generally refute the *āgama* (Tripitaka) teachings.

Regarding the "poisonous vessel unfit for storing food": this refers to the vessel of impermanence, which is unfit for storing the food of non-arising (*anutpāda*) and eternal abiding (*nitya-sthiti*).
To consume [that food] would be to kill those who abide in non-arising and eternity. "Falsehood" (*mṛṣā*) is a refutation of the *āgama*.
That which is empty cannot be grasped as empty; it is that which cannot be destroyed by either false emptiness or analytical emptiness, because it is the emptiness of the non-arising of marks.

Regarding the sequential realization of the truths, one first realizes emptiness, then the conventional, and finally the middle way; the same applies to their relative superiority and inferiority. Attaining the stages (*bhūmi*) is considered superior.
"One within the immeasurable" refers to the teachings prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).
"The one within the immeasurable" refers to the teachings upon entering the stages in the Distinct Teaching.
"Neither one nor immeasurable" means that both are absent; "not different" means that both are manifest.
Evil is itself the Middle Way, which also signifies the opening of the provisional. This opening of the three preceding teachings allows them all to enter the Perfect Teaching (the *yuanzong*).
Furthermore, regarding "the emptiness of the hundred blessings," it should properly be stated as "how much more so within the conventionality of the hundred blessings.
In the *Liutie wen* (Six Categories of Texts), the scripture says, "not the body of humans or devas. The commentary on the scripture states:
"Although one manifests the reception of human or deva bodies for the sake of transforming sentient beings, the mind has no grasping or attachment; this is what is meant by 'spontaneously arising.'"
It is not a body subject to fear, for although there is the terror of birth and death, it has attained the four fearlessnesses.
It is not a body sustained by mixed food, for it is not nourished by the four kinds of nutriment, but sustains itself through the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna.

Regarding the statement that "the body of the Tathāgata is not a body, yet it is a body": the True Body (dharmakāya) is not subject to arising and ceasing, nor is it something accumulated through grasping; therefore, it is "not a body.
The Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) is neither born nor unborn, and neither has form nor is without form; therefore, it is "a body."
Regarding "neither arising nor ceasing," the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: Because the Buddha-body has no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), it does not arise;
because it has no posterior limit (*aparākoṭi*), it does not cease; and because it has no intermediate state, it does not abide.
"Not accumulated and not cultivated" means that it does not consist of the accumulation of many dharmas, for it does not depend upon cultivation.
"Immeasurable and boundless" means that the Dharma-body pervades everywhere; how could there be any limit or boundary?
"One who has no footprints" refers to abiding in the non-localized samādhi.
"Without knowledge and without form" means that through great awakening one is without knowledge; the wondrous image is formless, for the Dharma-body is formless, having transcended all marks.
Regarding "ultimately pure": it is purified by the simultaneous elimination of both [extremes].
Regarding "without movement": the Dharma-body is conventionally quiescent; who could move it?

Regarding "no sensation, no practice" up to "conditioned phenomena": because the stages are fulfilled, there is no receiving. This is because one has already emerged from the three types of wisdom. As for "receiving"— *Note: The provided text appears to be a commentary on a verse concerning the ultimate purity and immovability of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), explaining that such purity arises from the dual negation of extremes, and that the dharmakāya, being inherently still, cannot be disturbed. It further clarifies that at the fulfillment of the stages, there is no longer the "receiving" associated with the three types of wisdom (śrutamayī, cintāmayī, bhāvanāmayī prajñā).*

This is the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Practice is the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*). Because the Tathāgata has abandoned cultivation, his illumination is quiescent and still;

because he abides in the state of realization, he does not "practice. Because he does not dwell in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), he does not "abide. "Activity" (*kriyā*) is karma; "flavor" (*rasa*) is passionate attachment (*tṛṣṇā*);

"mixture" (*miśra*) is the poison of hatred. Since the nature of the Tathāgata is pure, it is said that these do not exist. Furthermore, "flavor" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), and "mixture" refers to the fruit [of suffering]; they are not [present in the Tathāgata].
As for "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*), it does not conform to any numerical categories.

It is "not karma" because it is free from further results; it is "not a result" because it is free from remaining results—meaning that it has eternally severed the cause and effect of maturation (*vipāka*) within birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

"Neither proceeding nor ceasing": "proceeding" refers to saṃsāra, and "ceasing" refers to nirvāṇa. This is because the Buddha perceives that all of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are identical within the single suchness (tathatā).

Regarding "neither mind nor mental factors": because they do not grasp at the characteristics of association, nor at the general or specific characteristics of objects—wherein the mind-king grasps the general and the mental factors grasp the specific—the Buddha-mind has no attainment; therefore, it is said to be "neither."
"Inconceivable and eternally beyond deliberation" means that it cannot be measured by the three vehicles or the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
"Without consciousness and detached from mind": that which manifests through discrimination is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); that which can produce future existence is called "mind" (*citta*).
Now, because it is without discrimination, it is not consciousness; because it does not produce future existence, it is not mind.

Furthermore, "not being separate from the mind" means that although there is no conceptual discrimination, there is nothing that is not known. Moreover, because it is the mind of *tathatā* through the noble wisdom of self-realization, its mind is "equanimous":
it is called "even" (*sama*) because it is free from high and low; it is called "equal" (*samatā*) because it is free from superiority and inferiority. Furthermore...
It makes no distinction between enemy and kin, for it is like empty space.
Regarding "neither existing nor yet existing": because the Dharma-body has no form, it does not exist; yet because it also manifests through transformation, it also exists.
There is neither going nor coming, yet there is both going and coming. Since there is no form, who goes and who comes?
Manifesting forms within the six realms, one appears to go and come;
yet, being neither destroyed nor extinguished—because one is free from the four marks—one is not destroyed, nor even severed, for the essence is not of the future.
Therefore, it does not emerge into the present, nor does it perish and enter the past.

It is neither a master nor a master; the Dharma-body is wondrously transcendent—what could it rely upon, and what master could it have? Yet, as the Way reigns over the three thousand worlds, it is said to be "also the master."

"Neither existent nor non-existent" means it is not existent because it does not conform to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), and it is not non-existent because it does not conform to the great void (*mahā-ākāśa*).

"Neither cognition" up to "neither word" means it is neither applied thought (*vitarka*) nor sustained thought (*vicāra*), because the application of speech through *vitarka* and *vicāra* has already been severed. It is not a person.

Because it is not a celestial being, it is not a name; because it should be designated as a human or celestial being, it is not a non-name. Furthermore, because it is free from the characteristics of coarse and subtle mental states, it is neither applied thought (*vitarka*) nor sustained thought (*vicāra*).

That it is neither in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) nor not in concentration means that because the mind ranges over the myriad objects, it is not in concentration; yet because it is tranquil and unmoving, it is not not in concentration.
Regarding "concentration":
it is "invisible" because it is not perceived by those on the ten stages; it is "clearly seen" because it is seen by one in their final existence.
"Having no dwelling place (up to) a house": in reality, there is neither a place nor emptiness; yet because he constantly dwells within the five realms of existence, he is also "in a house.
"Neither darkness nor light": because he penetrates and discerns the three periods of time, there is no darkness; because he manifests in accordance with ordinary beings, there is no light.
There is no [state of] non-quiescence up to [the state of] quiescence. Because the body is divided and the form dispersed, blazing forth in response to phenomena, there is no quiescence;
yet because it is eternally tranquil and perpetually in meditative concentration, it is also said to be quiescent.
This "non-existence" (until) "extinction" means: it is non-existent because there are no twenty-five realms of existence; it is non-acceptance because there is neither clothing nor food;
it is non-extinction because merit does not increase.
"Purity up to the absence of dispute" explains the preceding phrase: because there is neither "is" nor "is not," there is no dispute.
"The sūtra says 'no place of dwelling'" means that nirvāṇa is the true abode where there is no extinction.
"Neither grasping nor falling": because there is no further seeking, there is no grasping; because there is no retreating, there is no falling. "Neither dharma nor non-dharma field":
it is not dharma because it has severed the marks of tracks and signs; it is not non-dharma because it is a transformation person (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*). It is not a field because it has severed speech;
it is not a non-field because it is a worthy recipient of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*).
Regarding "the inexhaustible (up to) exhaustion": it is called inexhaustible because it is not exhausted throughout successive kalpas; that is, because it is precisely non-exhaustion.

"Emptiness is apart from all exhaustion" means that it is emptiness because it is without nature and without marks. "It is apart from emptiness" means it is apart from emptiness because it is apart from impermanence and selflessness.
"Detached from non-permanence (up to) extinction": because it transcends speech, it is not permanently abiding; because it transcends all marks, it does not perish moment by moment;
being free from defilement, it is without impurity and thus does not undergo extinction.
"Without words (up to) 'the speaker'" means to sever the five sensory objects.

"Nor is it cultivation (up to) 'measurement'" means that because there is nothing to be advanced, it is not a cultivated accumulation; because there is no mutual dependence, it is not a matter of weighing and measuring.

"Neither identical nor different" means that they are not identical because their square and circular forms correspond to distinct appearances, yet they are not different because their true nature remains unchanging.
"Not an image (up to) adornment" means that while it is wondrously transcendent of all marks, its marks transcend the world.
"Neither brave (up to) tranquil. Because he has subdued the four māras, he is not afraid; because there is neither stillness nor non-stillness, there is no tranquility.
"Without fever (up to) appearance. Movement and stillness are of one essence, and their characteristics are difficult to perceive.

Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata delivers [beings] because he has attained liberation": although in this way he brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to extinction (nirvāṇa), in reality there are no sentient beings who attain extinction.
The remaining phrases should be understood by analogy with this. This explanation is provisionally attached to the "hundred negations" of the Tripiṭaka teaching;
it serves as the object negated by the three subsequent teachings in order to reveal the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-artha*) of the present sutra.

Furthermore, regarding "entering and exiting simultaneously": because the entry is not fixed as an entry, one is able to exit immediately; because the exit is not fixed as an exit, one is able to enter immediately.
Because of this simultaneous exiting and entering, two thousand [eons] are accomplished.
"Because there are those who attain the fruit": this response further asks by what causes and conditions one attains the phrase of great, firm power;
it clearly explains the power of attaining the fruit because of the cause.
"This gives rise to what follows" means that it initiates the subsequent request for the Buddha to provide a detailed answer.
Third, regarding the exhortation to practice: since there is no way to achieve realization without being exhorted to practice, he exhorts them once more.
"Guarding the indestructible" means that by taking the indestructible dharma as the cause, one attains the fruit of the indestructible, eternally abiding dharmakāya;
thus it is said, "taking a corresponding cause. This refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

The Sūtra states, "those who do not receive the five precepts. This passage should be understood as possessing two meanings. First, there are those who entirely do not receive the five precepts, doing so from the outset for the sake of protecting the True Dharma.
Second, considering the intent of the scriptural text, since it says they do not cultivate dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), this does not mean they have not received the precepts;
rather, they did so from the outset to protect the Dharma, and thus do not fully observe the various minor transgressions regarding the dignified deportment associated with the five precepts.
The first [explanation] holds that it was for the purpose of protecting the Dharma; thus, one may carry a knife and so forth. Both interpretations are valid.

Regarding "abandoning the matter": the seven branches of body and speech constitute the "matter. Now, to carry a knife and so forth while lacking dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*) is called "abandoning the matter."
Regarding "upholding the principle": the Great Teaching elucidates the principle; this is called "upholding the principle.
Regarding "nameless practice": although one may be able to maintain the precepts, such nameless practice cannot protect the Dharma.
Regarding "each being unable [to protect]": this forms four permutations (catuṣkoṭi), and for that reason it is recorded here.
As for "the Buddha and the King of Seon-yeo" (Sireṇa): the Buddha is the Dharma King, while the King of Seon-yeo is a human king; both kings are each capable of providing protection.
"Peaceful in former times" refers to the period when the Buddha was in the world and during the era of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
"Peaceful both now and formerly" means that if today the Great Dharma can circulate without hindrance, one likewise should not carry weapons or the like.

The Sūtra says: "Regarding the 'protection' [of the Dharma] up to the 'pure bhikṣu': although one may uphold the precepts without transgression, if one does not protect and uphold the True Dharma, one still cannot be called a pure bhikṣu."
Regarding the question concerning the abandonment of principle: Kāśyapa’s intention was that only a bhikṣu who dwells in tranquility is truly called a *saṃgha*.

If one who carries a sword or holds an arrow acts as a protector of the Dharma, such a person is merely a shaven-headed layman (*gṛhapati*). Since the Vinaya contains explicit prohibitions, it is necessary to raise this question. As for the meaning of the Buddha’s response:
if one acts as a protector of the Dharma, protecting the True Dharma, only then is one said to uphold the precepts. Your objection [is thus refuted].
This is not so. When the sutra speaks of "various teachings," it refers to the provisional (upāya) dharma. How is this known?
Because it does not definitively state that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; therefore, we know these are provisional.
The statement in the sutra regarding the "ninefold division of the scriptures" refers specifically to the nine divisions of the Mahāyāna. How is this known?

Because it states that they are "able to roar the lion's roar and explain extensively," which means excluding the three categories of nidāna (causal origin), avadāna (parable), and upadeśa (treatise).
Regarding the sūtra’s statement on "benefit and peace": it is only when one establishes sentient beings within the ocean of nirvāṇa that they can truly be called "at peace.

Regarding the sūtra’s statement from "not [merely] observing the precepts" up to "attaining a name": it should rather be stated that those who neither observe the precepts nor protect the Dharma receive the title of "shaven-headed layman."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says "the remaining forty years," etc.: at this time, when the Dharma is about to perish, it is precisely the time for protection.
Prior to this, there was no need for the protection of the Dharma; for this reason, the merit of protecting the Dharma is great.
Regarding the second point, "establishment through mutual dependence": because of sublime bliss there is no anger, and because there is no anger there is sublime bliss.
As for the statement that the King was the first [disciple] in his previous life, the *Ṣaṭ-khaṇḍa-nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The King was the second disciple;
Bodhivaṃśa (Jiǎodé) was the first disciple. The claim that the King was first is likely because he was born in that country earlier.
The bhikṣu is the second reliance. Because he has attained renunciation, his status is profound; thus, he attains the second reliance.
As for the Mahāyāna śrāvaka, because they have realized the Great Dharmakāya through hearing the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they manifest as being small.
Those who attain the name of Śrāvaka are like one who draws upon stone.
Those of the Hīnayāna who understand the Tathāgata as impermanent are like one who draws upon water;
as soon as they draw, it merges back, vanishing and dissolving moment by moment. For this reason, the analogy of drawing upon water is not adopted.
Regarding those who still possess the virtue of a teacher, [Kāśyapa] asked with a sincere intention: "Is he fit for the rank of a teacher, or is he unfit to be a teacher?
Fayao said: "He follows and protects [the Dharma], yet his outward traces appear to violate the precepts; thus, there is fear that he lacks the virtue of a teacher.
To clarify that this person’s virtue of upholding the precepts is unimpaired and that his path as a teacher is even more flourishing, Kāśyapa posed this question."
Regarding the repeated question concerning those who personally observe the precepts: this inquiry arises from the preceding text on killing or harming.
If a *dharmapāla* bhikṣu personally observes the precepts yet is without companions and alone, how can he travel about to teach and transform others?
Regarding those who encounter powerful conditions: although they understand the Vinaya teachings, they must rely on the power of laypeople (*avadātavasana*) to be able to protect the Dharma together;
therefore, these are called "powerful conditions. The same applies to the understanding of the Sūtras.

As for the passage in the Sūtra concerning "mixed monks" (*miśra-bhikṣu*): because both wholesome and unwholesome non-informative actions (*avijñapti*) coexist in such a person, they are called "mixed monks.

However, those who merely maintain the precepts themselves but do not know the *poṣadha*, do not know the *karmavācanā*, and do not know the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*) are called "foolish monks" (*mūḍha-bhikṣu*).
Regarding "purity": it is difficult to destroy by virtue of these two conditions: first, not seeking fame; second, not violating the laws and regulations. As the Sūtra says:
"If they are śrāvakas," this refers fundamentally to those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) śrāvakas.

Regarding the six kinds of fivefold dharmas clarified in the Vinaya, the first fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), "The Seven Dharmas," states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"From now on, it is permitted that one who has accomplished five dharmas and has reached ten years or more [of seniority] should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple (*sahavāsika-śiṣya*).

These five are: first, maintaining disciples; second, those in training (*śaikṣa*); third, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); fourth, divine understanding; fifth, instruction and admonition; sixth, service."
As for their application: the present sutra clarifies only one type of fivefold dharma, namely those pertaining to spiritual understanding; therefore, it differs from the list provided in the Vinaya.
The fivefold dharma of spiritual understanding refers to the clear comprehension of these five dharmas.

Regarding the four matters that are equal to the Vinaya: the Vinaya states that (1) one knows what constitutes an offense, (2) one knows what does not constitute an offense, (3) one knows when an offense is light, (4) one knows when an offense is heavy, and (5) one knows how to recite the Prātimokṣa.
Because these are extensively explained as the benefits of study, it is said that they are "slightly different" [from the other categories].
Regarding "teaching according to the occasion": in this sutra, the Bodhisattvas, in order to subdue sentient beings, do not select specific times or places;
they preach as soon as the opportunity arises. Therefore, it is called "teaching according to the occasion."
"Knowing the weight of what is visible" means knowing the characteristics of whether the four classes of people have transgressed or not.
"The Buddha enters among ordinary beings" should be understood as the Sage manifesting identity with sentient beings;

there are those who reveal their origins spontaneously and those who wait for others to reveal them, such as Master Fu (Fu Dashi), who relied upon the ascetic Śaṇavāsa to reveal his origins—this is precisely an example of this. It is for the sake of benefiting all things.
However, it is not that he himself does not know;
rather, one who is actually experiencing [the sensation] up to the point of intense pain should be asked: "If you are actually experiencing pain, how can you enter hell?

One should understand that it is precisely by realizing the dharma of non-pain that one is able to manifest entry. If one says there is pain, it should not be realized. This should be explained in five parts.
The *Baichenghu jing* states that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifests five hundred bodies here to teach and transform sentient beings.
Some wicked bhikṣus say: "Maitreya Buddha should manifest five hundred bodies; I am also one of them," and thus they do not require verification.

Regarding the practitioner of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it is stated within that contemplation on the purity of upholding the precepts: "To prevent and restrain is the meaning of 'precept' (*śīla*); contemplation is likewise so.

The three contemplations are called "that which prevents," and the three delusions are called "that which is prevented. Such prevention extends its meaning throughout the entire *dharmadhātu* and is not restricted merely to body and speech.
Furthermore, in the *Vinaya*, there is "extinction" (*nirodha*), because it extinguishes all non-proper actions of body and speech. Moreover, regarding the *Prātimokṣa*...
Furthermore, "reciting" (sūtra) refers to holding the text in mind through oral recitation.

Furthermore, "vinaya" refers to weighing the gravity [of offenses], distinguishing between what constitutes a transgression and what does not; this is the explanation of the name based on the Vinaya. First.
All of these are to be viewed as the contemplation of the mind. The meaning of the three delusions is explained extensively in that text.
Regarding "knowing the *sopadhiśeṣa* [nirvāṇa] and so forth," this refers to knowing *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the concluding praise: "The Buddha-dharma is immeasurable" concludes the preceding section. "The Tathāgata, moreover... and so forth constitutes the praise.

"Eliminating the evil and heterodox views of his disciples" refers to those who give rise to false views, such as not believing in cause and effect, who have transgressed from the monastic community to enter among the laity, or who have become followers of external paths;
these are termed "those who have gone astray. "Deliverance" (yueji) refers to saving them.

Regarding the other two sets of five dharmas, the Vinaya states: first, knowing the dharma of renunciation; second, being able to act as a preceptor (upādhyāya); third, being able to act as a master of precepts (karmavācanā-ācārya);
fourth, being able to know the dharma regarding the reliance on a teacher (niśraya-ācārya); and fifth, being able to know the dharmas that obstruct the path and those that do not obstruct the path.
This is the fifth set of five dharmas concerning instruction.
Regarding the six matters that employ five methods, the Vinaya states: first, one is able to teach disciples the pure precepts; second, one is able to teach the Abhidharma;
third, one is able to teach the Vinaya; fourth, when disciples are distressed by another region and cannot find joy there, one causes them to come [to this place].
If one is unable to do so oneself, one may bring [the disciple] through the power of others. Regarding the five disciples, if they are ill, one should be able to provide for them;

if one is unable to do so oneself, one should be able to cause others to provide for them. When these five dharmas are accomplished and ten years have passed or more, one should confer the full ordination upon a co-resident disciple.
These are the remaining two sets of five dharmas.

The "Chapter on the Merits of the Name" is divided into four sections according to the commentary text: first, the explanation of the name; second, the explanation of the merits from the phrase "Furthermore, this... onwards;

third, the discernment of similarities and differences from the sixth fascicle onwards; and fourth, the word-by-word exegesis from the phrase "Regarding the text... onwards. Regarding the initial statement, "Those that are the same," it refers to the names.
The two characters are both designations for the essence of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they are said to be "the same. To be "different" means to be distinct from these two characters:

that is, the name (*ming*) refers to the essence (*ti*), while the word (*zi*) indicates its qualities (*de*). Master Shanxian said: "That which explains the essence is called the name; that which marks the qualities is called the word."
These characters are named "Mahāparinirvāṇa. The name is itself the character. "Merit" refers to its functional significance.
Relying upon the expressive names, the expressed meaning is established; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of Names and Characters."
The subsequent explanation of the merits (*guṇa*) consists of two parts: first, the explanation of the merit of the name; second, the praise and explanation of the merit of the characters.
Regarding the phrase "excellent speech" (*vāk-suvibhakta*) in the text, Bao Liang states: "The superior, middling, and inferior modes of speech are combined into a single excellence.

This is intended to clarify that *nirvāṇa* is the most supreme and preeminent among all modes of speech, and is therefore called 'superior speech. The untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) constitute 'middling speech.'"
To speak of the suffering and impermanence of birth and death, up to the nature of the true cause (*samyag-hetu*), constitutes the "inferior discourse.

If these three types of discourse are all taught without contradicting the Dharma, they are called "excellent. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 83, states: "The superior discourse is also excellent" refers to the excellence of the beginning;
that is, because joy arises at the time of hearing it. "The middle discourse is also excellent" refers to the excellence of the middle; that is, [the excellence of] practice.
At that time, there is no grasping and no suffering. Because one dwells in the practice of the Middle Way, remaining far removed from the two extremes, even the subsequent words are excellent;
this refers to the ultimate excellence, as it is free from all defilements.
"Excellent in meaning" refers specifically to its discourse on principle.
"Its phrasing is also excellent" praises the teaching as being superior in its expression of that very principle.

"Pure and complete" means that the vehicle's essence is fully sufficient; since the essence of this sūtra alone clearly explains the sufficiency of cause and effect, it is said to be "pure and complete."
Furthermore,

regarding "complete in excellence": within a verse, its meaning may be complete, such as a single verse from the *Himavat* which simultaneously encompasses both the meanings of permanence and impermanence.
"Pure" means that the principles and teachings of this sutra are authentic; because they are able to eliminate all signs regarding both cause and effect, it is called "pure.
"Brahmacarya" means that the words and patterns of this sutra can give rise to the *brahmacarya* of the practitioner.
The "Vajra Treasure Store" refers to the perfect fruition of nirvana as elucidated in this Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
It is fully endowed with all merits and is not like a solitary extinction or mere liberation; it is, therefore, likened to a treasure store.
Regarding the statement that "Kaisan combines [the categories] into eight": he combines the upper, middle, and lower levels of Yecheng into one;

thus, there are only eight. As for the current reliance on the seven similes: the sequence of the seven similes is assigned to the seven types of goodness, as can be seen from the textual structure. The first simile clarifies the "Great" (Mahāyāna) and so forth.

Furthermore, these seven similes do not go beyond the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold truths). Within the text, there are two layers; in the first layer, the longing [for worldly things] is eternally severed.
This is like having eaten milk gruel and requiring nothing more. Next, from "Furthermore, this is the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) downward, there are three [levels].

These are then sequentially assigned to the three [audiences], such as those for whom the teaching is intended (*pudgala*), with only the "worldly" (*loka*) being omitted. If one speaks of the three [truths] as distinct, that constitutes the meaning of the worldly;
thus, the fourfold purpose (*catuḥ-prayojana*) is complete.

Next, regarding the gate of the bodhisattva within the merits of the syllables: because a bodhisattva practices in accordance with the dharmas cultivated by all Buddhas, it constitutes the gate of the bodhisattva.
Third, regarding the distinction that there is neither "this" nor "that" within the midst: a single form and a single fragrance are none other than the ocean of Great Nirvana.
Within this, the true marks of the Way do not fall into the flow of "this" or "that. It is only because those who enter it are unequal that the designation of "flowing toward that" arises.
Regarding "one question and three answers": above, the question was simply how one reaches the other shore;
in this chapter, however, the answer is given through three points—namely, the other shore, this shore, and the middle stream. Therefore, it is said that the response exceeds the original question.
In the fourth section, the explanation of the text, the Sūtra says: "words and phrases. This refers to the Mahāyāna sūtras as established upon sound (*śabda*).
However, there are two kinds of "text" (*vyañjana*): first, text as sound; second, text as written characters (*rūpa-akṣara*).
Here, it primarily refers to text as sound, while also encompassing text as written characters. As for "name" (*nāman*), it designates the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*).
"Phoneme" (*vyañjana*) refers to names such as "form," "sound," and so forth. "Phrase" (*pada*) denotes the differentiation of phenomena;

it refers to explaining that form and other aggregates are tainted, suffering, conditioned, impermanent, empty, selfless, and so on, as well as explaining the distinctions of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*, such as permanence, bliss, and so forth.
"Sentence" (*vākya*) signifies the completion and fulfillment of the expressed meaning. "Letter" (*akṣara*) refers to the syllables themselves, which serve as the basis for names and phrases.

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Names (nāman) express intrinsic nature; phrases (pada) express distinctions; and phonemes (vyañjana), which are the same as syllables (akṣara), serve as the basis for these two.
For now, I shall cite the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to elucidate the scriptural text.
Furthermore, regarding "being able to return to the root": receiving and upholding *nirvāṇa* is the root; subsequently returning to this [state] is therefore called "returning to the root.

Regarding "the fruit being distinct from the wholesome": the myriad wholesome acts (*kuśala*) should be at the beginning, and the myriad virtues (*guṇa*) should be at the end. Since virtues are accomplished through wholesome acts, why would there be an eon of virtue?
Therefore, it is said that "the fruit is distinct from the wholesome."
Regarding that which is not produced by conditions: all phenomena produced by conditions are impermanent, and the same applies to the cessation of those conditions.
This has been fully explained according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* as cited in the first fascicle.

The commentary on the "Chapter on the Four Marks" is divided into three parts: first, a brief explanation of the title of the sutra; second, from the question "I pray that the Buddha... onwards, an explanation through questions and answers that resolves doubts;
third, from the section on "oral secrecy" onwards, an exegesis of the text itself. Regarding the initial statement, "by means of the four kinds of marks," [it refers to] the Mahāparinirvāṇa...

"Parinirvāṇa" is the general term; the four characteristics are its specific divisions. By setting aside the single nirvana and opening it into these four characteristics, the secret treasury of nirvana—both its analytical distinctions and its unification—is revealed and can be seen with clarity. Therefore, it is said to be "manifest."
Furthermore, regarding "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*): its meaning is that of a sign or marker; it is also called "manifest.

Next, the resolution of doubts is divided into two parts: first, the arising of the question; second, the formal explanation following the "former interpretation. Within this, there are again two sections: first, the presentation of the former interpretation; second, the formal explanation beginning with "Now, I clarify.
Regarding the first, there is first the presentation, followed by the refutation beginning with "This meaning... The initial section states: "There is no understanding."
As for "liberation," it is only when one enters the realm of nirvana without remainder that true liberation occurs; this is solitary liberation.
Therefore, when the dharma-body and prajñā exist, there is no [conventional] liberation.
Regarding "mutually obscuring": in the past, impermanence obscured permanence; now, permanence destroys impermanence. This destruction is termed "obscuration," and this is what is meant by "mutual.
Regarding the three dots of impermanence in the past: these are the three dots arranged both vertically and horizontally.
What was previously described as conditioned liberation refers merely to liberation with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-vimukti*).
That which takes the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) of superior wisdom as its object is still, in fact, the mental ground of expedient wisdom taking [an object]; this is designated as "liberation.

From the perspective of the Mahāyāna, this remains merely a phenomenon of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); therefore, it is said to be "the mental ground capable of [taking an object]."
Regarding the phrase "the past and present mutually establish one another": the past establishes the present, and the present opens up the past, thereby revealing the true path to *nirvāṇa*.

Next, regarding the statement in the "Refutation" section that "all four positions obscure the true principle": a "gate" (*mukha*) is so named because it enables passage; yet each [position] clings to its own means of passage. It does not...
It accords with the correct principle; therefore, it is called "covering" (*āvṛti*).

Regarding the simultaneous resolution of these points: the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) serve as mutual remedies, for the four propositions themselves are the principle. All must be compared with the ancient authorities and resolved together, so that they may reach the ultimate correctness.
What is this ultimate correctness? It is what is called the "esoteric" (*guhyaka*).
The formal explanation is twofold: first, a brief explanation; second, a further detailed explanation.

Regarding the initial statement that "the four phrases are entirely mutually inclusive," this means that three phrases encompass one phrase, and one phrase encompasses three phrases, and so forth; hence it is so stated.
Regarding the subsequent statement that "it is neither self nor other," the ocean of the Great Nirvāṇa does not pertain to self or other; therefore, it is said to be "not."
One who proclaims what they have personally realized is called a "speaker. Because one speaks of what has been realized in order to benefit others, it is termed "speaking.
That which is eternally without anything proclaimed is called a "speaker"; this means that to speak constantly of non-speaking is termed "having nothing proclaimed."
Regarding what was previously called the *dharmakāya*, it refers to the fivefold *dharmakāya*.

In the third of the three explanations within the text, it says that "oral secrecy" (*mukhamitha*) means that one characteristic is identical to four characteristics, and four characteristics are identical to one characteristic;
being neither one nor four, yet both one and four—this is termed "secrecy."
As for the "one characteristic": correcting oneself is itself *nirvāṇa*; correcting others is likewise so, and being able to skillfully understand accordingly is also like this.
Regarding the four characteristics as one characteristic: although there are four kinds of functions, they constitute only the single Great *Nirvāṇa*.

The scripture states, “analytically revealing and instructing” (*vibhajya-saṃdarśana*). This first indicates its underlying intent. If one were to follow the literal sequence of the text, it should read:
“In the Mahāparinirvāṇa, there are four aspects of meaning analytically revealed and instructed. These “four aspects” are named according to that which they signify.
Sengzong said: “Regarding ‘self-correction’ (*svayaṃ-samyak*): first is correct practice, acting in accordance with the Vinaya; second is correct understanding, discerning comprehension.”
That which is eternally *vajra* for the Buddha is itself impermanent. Second, "correcting others" means causing people to receive the scriptures in accordance with one's own understanding.
Third, "being able to respond to questions" means being able to cause others to attain realization; thus, one can answer difficult questions. These constitute the three aforementioned matters.
This is because of a thorough understanding of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Regarding the Tathāgata: if one explains the Tathāgata according to the former Hīnayāna, he is called "Tathāgata" because he arises in response [to sentient beings].

If one explains the Tathāgata according to the Mahāyāna, wisdom accords with the object is called "Tathā" (Thus), and the object giving rise to wisdom is called "Āgata" (Come). Therefore, it is so named.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s “correctly perceiving all conditions (pratyaya) up to their objects”: the ten realms, the five aggregates (skandha), and so forth are called "all conditions.

Furthermore, whatever is perceived within the four modes of conduct—the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya)—are none other than conditions; they are all objects of perception (ālambana). Therefore, it is said that he correctly perceives objects. Moreover, this...
The principle of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) pervades the past; there is nothing that is not a matter of causes and conditions.
To illuminate the realm of causes and conditions means to illuminate the three thousand realms within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), which is itself the true reality (*dharmatā*).

To illuminate the realm of causes and conditions and thoroughly comprehend that causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is called "seeing all causes and conditions. Furthermore, to thoroughly comprehend that ignorance (*avidyā*), as the cause, is itself the true reality.
When [the conditions] act as causes for one another, it is only then designated as "view.

Regarding the statement that "the true mark (*dharmatā*) is not a cause, etc.": taking the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as self and ignorance as other, one investigates through the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), finding that all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is by revealing the true mark in this way that it is called "view. Furthermore, the true mark being non-causal is precisely ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, it does not reside in conditions either; this is the inconceivable provisional. The two phrases "unshared" and so forth constitute the Middle Way, wherein both are simultaneously negated and simultaneously illuminated.
To realize the true reality (*dharmatā*) in this manner is what constitutes seeing.

To illustrate the profound by means of the shallow: a bhikṣu’s perception of fire is a shallow matter, yet it serves as a metaphor for the realm of the former Buddhas; hence, it is said to "illustrate the profound.
Furthermore, although the mass of fire is shallow, when analyzed, it constitutes an inconceivable realm that is no different from the previously perceived conditions of causes and effects.
Therefore, this serves as an illustration for what precedes it.
When the Sūtra says, "a bhikṣu sees fire," this refers specifically to a bhikṣu of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), whose meaning extends throughout the Mahāyāna gates.
"Observing the body in the same way" means that by refuting the four attachments and accomplishing the three truths, one is then called "right view."
Regarding "one who embraces fire to burn the body": with an inconceivable and wondrous body, one casts oneself into a wondrous fire; therefore, one does not engage in false speech. Sengzong said:
There is another causal condition recorded in the *Kušāstra-sūtra* (枯樹經). The Buddha was walking with a bhikṣu in a desolate place and saw a hollow, burning tree stump.
He immediately asked the bhikṣu, "Can this tree be embraced? He replied, "It can. The Buddha asked again: "Suppose..."
"There is someone who is pressuring you to declare that the Buddha is impermanent. If you do not speak, he will embrace this withered tree; what would you rather have happen?
The World-Honored One embraced fire and died. His case and yours are essentially the same, so it can serve as proof."

Regarding the statement that "one treasure should also be opened": the ancients saw that their own rectification and the rectification of others share the same meaning as self-awakening and awakening others;
thus they raised this question to ask whether it might be permitted.
Regarding the differences between the teaching gates: the four marks and the three jewels differ in their pedagogical approaches and cannot be treated as a single uniform rule.

Is it not because for those in the world-stage, one preaches the dharmas of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements as distinct and sequential worldly phenomena, rather than being fit yet to preach that the aggregates are impermanent?
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktāgama* (or *Saṃyukta*) provides only the benefits appropriate for the world-stage.
Regarding those who [believe in] no-self and impermanence: for them, he taught impermanence in the Deer Park, whereby they became noble ones (*ārya*) of the Hīnayāna.

Once they had entered the state of sainthood, this was called the benefit of producing goodness. Having obtained this benefit, they subsequently entered the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā to extensively refute the Hīnayāna;
this was called the benefit of remediation (*pratipakṣa*).

Now, regarding those who nourish an infant: that which is before the chest is called the "infant" (*ying*). One places [the child] before the chest and nourishes it with milk; therefore, it is called an "infant.

As for "containing the *sū*," the former [character] (pronounced *hù gàn*) refers to feeding mouth-to-mouth, which is termed "containing"; when the mouth itself contains [it], it is pronounced in the level tone (*píng shēng*).

The character *sì* (pronounced with the *cí* and *lì* finals; meaning "to feed") in the *Shuowen Jiezi* is composed of the radical "person" (*rén*). The common vulgar form is written as this [character for] *sì*. Furthermore, to place jade in the mouth is called *hán* (to contain), which is equivalent to "giving.
That compassion is the root of goodness refers to unconditioned compassion (*wúyuán cí*). This is analogous to a beginner who has faith in the world.

For example, regarding those who rely on hearing the Dharma for their own sustenance: if they hear of the world as a source of self-sustenance and thereby manifest signs of joy, this further becomes a sickness.
To excessively praise the world so that others become attached to it is precisely what is called a sickness.

How much more so for those who consume coarse or soft food while praising the world; this still obstructs the path of progress toward cultivation, let alone the three subsequent [types of] perversion.

As for those capable of being refined through切磋 (qiē-cè, i.e., critical examination and polishing), those of the Two Vehicles who have already attained minor fruits come to enter the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna]; they fear being rebuked and broken by Vimalakīrti.
Hearing the Great [Teaching] without slandering it, the capacity for perfect realization is secretly awakened; through being "cut and polished," one becomes a vessel for the Way.
As for the woman who silently contemplates, this reveals the aspect of correcting others, for she enables those who receive the teaching to attain understanding and awakening.
If one does not first eliminate the disorder of the "thought-seed," how could one awaken to what is constantly taught? This is what is meant by a "virtuous and upright person."
The four traditional interpretations do not present any significant obstacle; therefore, they are not refuted here.
For example, regarding the "transformed boy" (*huàtóng*), he is like the novice who received the precepts previously mentioned.

The sutra says "transformed and dissolved" (*xiāohuà*); the character *huà* is pronounced with the level tone (*píngshēng*), meaning "completely dissolved. If it were pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), it would be confused with the term for "magical transformation" (*biànhuà*).
Therefore, it is not to be used.
Regarding the passage where a woman addresses the Buddha, Sengzong says, "This is the word of the Buddha. Baoliang and Zhixiu both say it is the word of the woman.

"Unable to serve as an antidote" clarifies that such small persons are only fit to give rise to wholesome states; they are not yet capable of entering the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings for the purposes of antidotal counteraction or subduing.
To say they are "unable" is precisely a form of analytical discrimination.
As for the statement in the Sūtra, "then one does not provide sufficient [medicine]," it means that if both types of medicine are obtained, they are already sufficient for treatment;
just as even hard food can be digested, how much more so the inherently soft ghee, which should be provided in abundance?
The Sūtra says, "One whose merit is already complete" means that having already attained the benefit of generating wholesome states, their merit is said to be complete.
Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, "He preaches the six flavors," Master Sengzong said: There are three conditioned [flavors] and three unconditioned [flavors].
The function of suffering is to transform into pleasure, just as vinegar can transform sweetness. The reason all phenomena undergo flux and transition is due to the urgency of impermanence.

Therefore, it is like the taste of salt, which can render that which is not sour salty. The statement of "non-self" is contrary to human sentiment because it implies a lack of sovereignty, just as the taste of bitterness is unpleasant to people.
"Pleasure" (sukha) takes delighting oneself as its meaning, just as the taste of sweetness is what people relish.
"Self" (ātman) means to exercise control with freedom such that nothing can obstruct it, just as the pungent taste permeates and awakens [the senses].
The eternal principle is profoundly serene; it is a single mark without differentiation, like the lack of distinction in a bland taste.

To use the fire of the wisdom of constant understanding to burn the fuel of the delusions of the eight inversions, thereby sustaining the life of wisdom—this is metaphorically called "food. This, too, is but one approach.
To interpret the current passage on "counteractive measures" (pratipakṣa) as being entirely definitive is not quite correct.

Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "afflictions as fuel" and so forth: all afflictions that arise within the cultivation of wholesome states (*kuśala*) and within the process of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are termed "fuel.
The wisdom capable of counteracting [these] within the cultivation of wholesome states and within the process of antidotes is termed the "fire of wisdom.
By means of these three, one fully accomplishes the food of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is the Nirvana characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Regarding the phrase "ordinary beings and sages combined": this means that both mundane and supramundane ordinary beings and sages possess both the actual phenomena (*dharmas*) and their metaphors.
Furthermore, regarding the flavors from sweet, pungent, and bland up to the flavor of retribution: these arise from the same names in both the heterodox and the orthodox [teachings].
However, if they are grasped by ordinary beings, they are subverted by the three [characteristics] such as impermanence.
There is a specific intention here: the supramundane three samādhis sublate the mundane three samādhis. This applies both to the present and the past;

throughout all five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], the Great Vehicle is used in every instance to sublate the Small Vehicle, thereby constituting a complete system of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*) that leads directly into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

It is for this reason that its application is said to be so vast. Furthermore, in order to clarify the scriptural text, the six [samādhis] are combined into three: the mundane three and the supramundane three.

For example, it is also said that there is a distinct meaning here: that the "Small" and "Great" vehicles were established in the past. This refers to the relative relationship between the Small and Great vehicles within the entire body of teachings throughout a single lifetime of the Buddha;
thus, the Fourfold Benefit (catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu) is not exclusively restricted to the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, since this present sutra elucidates both the provisional and the ultimate simultaneously, the Small and Great vehicles together may constitute the Fourfold Benefit. Therefore, it is called "universal" (tong).

Regarding those households that possess the Buddha: if one contemplates the household of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as being entirely eternally abiding, it is then called "possessing the Buddha.
As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "All phenomena are without arising; all phenomena are without cessation. If one can understand them in this way, the Buddhas will always manifest before one."
Zhixiu said: "Virtue is established by relying on faith; it takes faith as its home.
When this virtuous mind takes the eternally abiding as its object of focus in every thought-moment, then the eternally abiding Dharmakāya will always reside within the home of faith."
The Buddha raised this question without a fixed method because no one else was able to ask it; thus, the Buddha raised it himself.
"Without a fixed method" means that he set forth this question by transcending all established patterns and formal structures.
"Other cases are likewise" means that the other five perfections are analogous to this.
Regarding the first point, "not knowing them," this explanation primarily clarifies the virtues of the donor. The subsequent explanation clarifies the virtues of the recipient.
Master Zong says: "Now, it is easy to give material wealth, but difficult to give one's reputation; therefore, the explanation here proceeds by way of reputation."
What is meant is this: suppose there is a person who maintains the precepts and is of few desires and easily satisfied.

Now, the original intention of this donor was to manifest that such a person’s virtue does not reside in the relinquishing of wealth. Therefore, in the midst of a vast assembly of people, he offered what was not accepted by him.
Since he did not accept it, from the perspective of the multitude, the one who refused was praised for his reputation of having few desires and being easily satisfied.
This is to make it manifest. As for "the giver," it means the reputation for being able to practice great giving is made prominent.
Regarding "rejoicing without obstruction," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva rejoices in the merit of others—just as when a person selling incense, a buyer, and a bystander all three gain benefit—the merit of rejoicing is therefore vast."
To explain this through skillful means (upāya) is equivalent to granting life; therefore, one obtains great merit.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the reason the primary argument regarding the giving of alcohol was raised first as an answer is that it serves to introduce the subsequent prohibition against eating meat; thus, the giving of meat is placed at the beginning.
The Sūtra says, "the sound is heard throughout the world. The *Yinwen* (Inquiries on Sounds) states: "When the crane cries in the nine marshes, its sound is heard in heaven";
thus, it is called "sound-hearing" (*yinquen*). The present case is likewise: when one's own name reaches another, it is termed "heard" (*wen*);
once the other has heard it, it is also termed "heard. Thus, although it is the same character "heard," it is pronounced with two different tones.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "those who eat meat," etc., this restates the previous explanation—that those who do not eat meat—brought forward as a question:
"If one should not even give to those who eat meat, how much less should one give to those who do not eat it?
This is because those who do not eat meat possess great merit."
"All shall become Buddhas" means that all sentient beings are future Buddhas.
Regarding "impurities of semen and blood," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The bodies of all sentient beings are formed from the semen and blood of their parents;
therefore, they must not be eaten."
Regarding the phrase "all are portions of others' life-sustenance": whatever objects one receives are all portions that support the lives of others.
As for the scripture stating that eating meat is not permitted, why was it permitted in the past but not permitted now? What harm is there [in its previous permission]?
The first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is that of Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). Those who eat meat cannot enter this first stage.

Now, killing and harming violates Great Compassion, while consuming [meat] violates Small Compassion (*maitry-ālpa*). Because one attains the great through the small, Small Compassion is the seed of Great Compassion.

It must be said, "For my sake," meaning that one may eat without hesitation. However, if one says, "Bring me meat for my sake," then one must not eat it, regardless of whether the animal was killed specifically for him.
A monkey that resembles a human should not be eaten because it belongs to the same category.
A snake that resembles a dragon should not be eaten because dragons bestow kindness upon humanity by sending rain at the proper times, thereby bringing the five grains to maturity.
Regarding the "nine types," Liang said: "There are three instances of 'not seeing': namely, the joy before eating, the joy at the time [of slaughter], and the joy after [the meal]—these two joys.
Likewise, there are three for each of 'not hearing' and 'not doubting. Zong said: "The three within 'seeing' are: seeing when life is being severed, and seeing after the slaughter and dismemberment.
The three within 'hearing' are: hearing when it is being slaughtered, and hearing when it is being dismembered. The three within 'doubting' are: doubting whether this was done for my sake."

Yes. This extends even to doubting the preliminary and subsequent applications (*pūrvāpara-upāya*). Regarding the preliminary and subsequent applications: before the act of killing, one gives rise to the mind of application;
after having killed, one gives rise to the mind of rejoicing.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra which states, "I also do not say that fish, meat, and so forth [are permitted]," the Buddha’s intention was this:

His previous teaching that one may eat meat was merely a temporary, expedient teaching intended to accommodate the capacities of certain beings. How can you use such a temporary statement to challenge his ultimate teaching?
The Sūtra states that "it must be dyed with a discolored color"; this is a supplementary citation regarding the precept on the possession of robes.
The Sūtra states that "sesame oil and the like" are all fatty substances; therefore, they may not be possessed.

Regarding those such as Tāo (pronounced dǎo; one who devours wealth is called tāo) and Tiè (pronounced tiě; one who greedily eats is called tiè): "Naked" refers to those who are inferior, while "Tāo and Tiè" refers to those who are excessive.

When the Sūtra says "each has [its own]," it means that for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, the consumption of meat must be prohibited and severed; it is not the same as the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), which is why it says "each has.

When the Sūtra speaks of "different intentions," it refers to observing the capacities of beings and applying the appropriate medicine according to what is suitable for them, temporarily permitting the eating of three kinds of meat. Therefore...
This refers to "different intentions. Master Sheng said: "There are two kinds of afflictions: those arising from intention (*manas*) and those arising from perception (*saṃjñā*).
To cease according to one's emotional attachments is called 'arising from intention. When what is craved has no limit, it is called 'arising from perception.
Therefore, partial restraint diminishes the intention, while total restraint diminishes the perception. By eliminating the greedy intention, one fosters compassion."
Regarding "because of the three kinds of external [meat]": although one sees, hears of, or eats the three kinds of meat, one further conceives them as being among the ten kinds of meat.

Furthermore, one must abstain from the ten kinds; once the ten kinds have been abandoned, one again conceives them as being distinct from the ten kinds, namely all other meats. Therefore, it is necessary that all [meat] be completely abandoned.
The Sūtra says, "All are terrified. Zhi Xiu said: "A person who harbors no intent to harm beasts will likewise not be harmed by them.
This is why one may pluck a tiger’s throat-throat bone from among the mountains and become intimate with soaring gulls upon the sea. However, if one has already eaten their flesh..."
How could it possibly harm them or cause their eternal extinction? It is because one hears of its harmful influence that fear and thoughts of resentment arise.
As the sutra says, regarding "pure food": even the food obtained through alms by Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas is not yet considered pure enough to be consumed.
The Sūtra says: "The *gǔ* (pronounced *gōnghù*; meaning to nurture poison) and the *chū* (pronounced *chìyú*) trees.

Regarding the "Three Piṭakas" up to "causes and conditions": causes and conditions are a dharma-gate of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, they are dharmas produced by causes and conditions;
therefore, they belong to the teaching of causes and conditions.
First, regarding the "preliminary conditions" (*pūrvaprayoga*): this refers to the preparatory stages prior to receiving the precepts. Regarding the "precept-substance" (*śīla-dravya*):

immediately after the three *karmavācanas* have been completed, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) arises; this is what is meant by "the characteristics having been received. This refers to the manifestation of the characteristics.

According to the present text, this is precisely intended to inquire about the meaning within the context of the "conformity" (*anuvartana*), not the meaning within the context of the "reception" (*upasaṃpad*). There should be two interpretations.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "Why was it not for Prasenajit?", one should ask: "Why was it not for the fourfold assembly?
For why did [the Buddha] ask King Prasenajit about the profound and subtle meaning of the rules established all at once (sudden precepts), rather than asking about the precepts established gradually?
