The King replied: "Regarding the five coins, if one steals up to five coins, the offense constitutes a capital crime. For those who have left the household life, if they commit such an act, their offense should result in immediate execution.
In matters of adjudicating crimes, [the standards for] renunciants always coincide with those of the sovereign."
The Sūtra states, "Or it is said that [the teaching] is profound. Master Zezhou says: In the past, for the sake of the Persians, impermanence was taught and designated as shallow;
today, permanence is taught and taken as profound.
Alternatively, it is called "offense. When the Tathāgata first appeared in the world, before the precepts had been extensively formulated, it was called "non-offense";

once the precepts were extensively formulated, it was termed an "offense. Master Baoshou said: "The Sūtras are taught according to the capacities of beings; the Vinaya is established only in response to specific conditions. Thus, their modes of exposition differ, which is why we inquire now.
The Abhidharma seeks the nature and characteristics [of phenomena]; although there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna in their methods of teaching the Dharma..."
This is established as definitive; therefore, it is not questioned.
As for "the precepts being the constant of the Mahāyāna," this refers to what is called "precepts" as maintained by the mind of the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
Regarding the question on "falling," it asks about the offenses that are prevented, which can cause sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth.

Therefore, it is called "falling" (*pāta*). As for the Vinaya and the Prātimokṣa, they are so named because they are capable of preventing [transgressions]. That which is capable of preventing [transgressions] is the teaching; this is what is called the Vinaya.

Regarding those who are content with their livelihood and pure in their sustenance, this is not a formal etymological explanation of the name *Prātimokṣa*; rather, it clarifies the precepts in terms of the mind that functions through their application.
This is the meaning. The Dharma of the Śrāvakas takes few desires as its practice. If one follows few desires, then all that one does will daily increase in merit.
By citing few desires, the precepts are clarified. Because one possesses the precepts, one achieves dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Because one accepts nothing for personal possession, it is called "pure livelihood" (*pariśuddhājīva*).
Next, the response regarding "falling" (*pāta*) is as follows: the meaning of "falling" is general, for it applies to both light and heavy offenses.
As the Sūtra says, "falling into the hells, even unto Avīci": among the eight great hells, Avīci is the lowest.
Therefore it is said: "up to and including. Such karma is necessarily grave, leading to retribution in the *Avīci* hell; thus it surpasses a torrential rain.

Having heard this, the following explains the state of falling into wrong intention. Cultivating the practice of distancing oneself from faults and not committing natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) is called "firmly upholding the precepts.

Avoiding prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*) and distancing oneself from them is called "not violating the rules of decorum" (*ābhisamācārika-śīla*). Cultivating and accumulating the lower cultivation of the practice of distancing oneself from attachment [is as follows].

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "detached from body, speech, and so forth," Master Zezhou said: "This clarifies detachment from natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Now, it is clarified that this does not pertain solely to natural transgressions.

Regarding "entering the precepts" (*jiejie*): "entering" (*ru*) means to accord with or follow. The Vinaya texts of the five schools establish the prohibition of grave offenses as "entering the precepts."
Refraining from the fault of negligence is called "entering into dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*).
Regarding the "excellent meaning of the profound sūtras": clarifying the teachings of the sūtras refers to concentration (*samādhi*);
because it is the opposite of evil, it is called "excellent meaning," which refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Prohibiting the acceptance of impure things" refers to the one hundred types of impure objects.
"All wholesome [states]" means that all signs of the wholesome have been completely severed. "Ziman" (滋漫): the character for "man" (漫) is pronounced as "man" (慢);
it means to overflow or spread diffusely. If the character is read with the tone of "wan" (萬) at the end of the phrase "if like fruit," it means to trail or extend like a creeping vine.
The ten wholesome paths as an analogy for the sudden teaching (*dun-jiao*) is as follows: in the *Avataṃsaka*, the bodhisattva precepts are established all at once.
This is because the ten wholesome paths are the primary wholesome dharmas; the superior merits are the wholesome dharmas of practice; and their essential meaning is the dharma of principle.
Regarding the opening and closing of the sudden and gradual [teachings]: this refers to the bestowal of the gradual and sudden, and the convergence of the gradual back into the sudden.

As for the scripture’s statement, "one who is able to preach the Dharma," etc., it means that the path of resonance and response intersects; it is not a response without being elicited, nor an elicitation without being responded to.
The secret treasury shared by our fellow practitioners is entirely inconceivable.

That it is "neither one nor four" refers likewise to the nature of the mind in a single thought-moment, the Dharma of Great Nirvāṇa; it cannot be categorized as one or four, and thus it is said to be "not."

Regarding the Three Jewels as a single essence: just as one characteristic is identical to four characteristics, and four characteristics are identical to one characteristic, they thus attain the same category.
Now, as for "wondrous existence" within Nirvana: attaining the twenty-five sovereign samādhis is termed "wondrous existence."

Now, regarding that which serves as the teacher and the Dharma within Nirvana: the wondrous principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and the land of eternal tranquil light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*) are that upon which it relies.
As for "all being based on the Buddha’s intention": although those of limited capacity perceive only the small, the Buddha’s intention is eternally real.
"One should not say they are identical" summarizes the meaning of the preceding five objections and refutes them; thus it says "should not.
Regarding "that which is abandoned and that which is attained," this clarifies that the afflictions abandoned by this sutra are far-reaching, and the eternally abiding nirvana attained is vast.

Regarding "extinguishing existence and extinguishing its fruit": extinguishing existence refers to extinguishing within the twenty-five states of existence; extinguishing the fruit refers to extinguishing the retributive body (*vipākakāya*).
Now, as for the Buddhas present within this Nirvana, they are said to "possess all Buddhas" because they are fully endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Regarding the "three apparent difficulties": the phrasing in the sutra is elliptical; it implies that "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the "existence of suffering," yet the text is not explicit.
Therefore, they are called "apparent. The passage beginning with "Furthermore, like that iron... follows immediately thereafter.
Regarding the worldly wisdom that severs delusions, Sengzong said: "The iron atop a chisel may serve as a metaphor for the ordinary person who suppresses the fetters;
even if they reach the Peak of Existence (naivasamjñānāsamjñāyatana), the fetters will arise again later. The Buddha is not like this; [the fetters] never arise again."
Regarding "the further arising of distinct delusions": once the coarse delusions have been severed, the subtle delusions manifest; this is what is meant by "arising.

Regarding "not being the same as the two extremes": ordinary beings have the extreme of emptiness belonging to the Two Vehicles. Based on the preceding two difficulties concerning permanence and impermanence, the question and answer are formulated.

Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata (up to) being born again": the intended meaning is that if the Tathāgata, having already entered extinction, were to exist within a "sublime existence" (*sūkṣma-bhava*), then such a sublime existence would constitute being born again.
To be born again is to be identical to ordinary beings in their impermanence.
The Sūtra says, "That which has ash. Although ash exists, it does not revert to wood. The Buddha is wondrous existence (*miao-you*); he does not revert to impermanence.
Regarding the phrase "named as arising later," this specifically refers to things such as a broken jar, used as proof that after the afflictions have been severed, one is "named as arising later."
By means of realization, one negates [the conventional] nirvana.
As the Sūtra says, "it burns those sentient beings": it burns the two types of delusions—general and specific—of ordinary persons, and it burns the specific delusions of the two vehicles;
therefore, it is called "all."

The Sūtra states, "Wandering among the flowers of awakening. Flowers are objects of mental appreciation; they are analogous to the permanence, bliss, self, and purity that constitute the dharmas realized by the Buddha—namely, the flowers of bodhi.
Thus, the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) says, "There are the flowers of the Buddha’s samādhis."

This is to refute the claim that [the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra] is exclusively for the noble ones (ārya). As the subsequent text states: "This Great Nirvāṇa can establish great benefit," and so forth—all such things are performed by the noble ones.
Why, then, does Kāśyapa raise the objection, saying, "The Tathāgata’s afflictions (kleśa) are not yet exhausted," and so on?
To reveal the mystery of the Dharma-body means that being able to manifest the bodies of the nine realms within the Dharma-body is called the "mystery of the body.
To reveal that the bodies of the nine realms are themselves the Dharma is called the "revelation of the mystery of the body."

Regarding "manifesting various bodies": these constitute the bodies of the nine realms. Both their differentiation and their integration are termed the "Secret Body. As for "one object being concealed" and so forth:
when [the teaching] has not yet been proclaimed, the three secrets are all concealed. Only when the four marks are proclaimed does the "Secret Speech" open.
Although the Secret Speech has opened, the body and mind remain concealed. Why? Because they have not yet been proclaimed, they are called "concealed. Regarding "hidden and manifest":
When the body is opened, the secret and liberation are still hidden; thus it is said, "each opens [the others]," etc.
Regarding the phrase "only covering what has been opened," the intention of our school is this: when covered, all are covered together; when opened, all are opened together. Why?
Because at the very moment the mouth is opened, the body and mind are both opened; it is simply that the text does not repeat itself, which results in the appearance of a sequential order.
Regarding those who do not understand: "not understanding" means it should be concealed.
As for what else could be understood, the refutation says: if one does not understand when the mouth is closed in secrecy, how can one attain understanding when the body and mind are opened?
Regarding the Sage’s art of affairs: the Buddha employs the great function of non-calculation. Why then would one attempt to explain this through the art of affairs?
The term "art" (shu) refers to the superficial applications of outsiders; therefore, it is not permissible.

As for the phrase "how could it not be due to causes and conditions": for the time being, following the established views of the ancients, their meaning reaches its full depth; every single instance is nothing other than the mutual resonance of the Way of response and stimulus.
Therefore, it is called "causes and conditions."
"Wondrous wisdom" arises precisely from the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñā); only through this can such function exist.
Regarding "the immeasurable cannot contain even a single mote of dust": the immeasurable is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Outside the immeasurable, there is not even a single mote of dust;
furthermore, the mote itself is the dharma-realm. Outside a single mote, there is no other mote. Thus it is said.
Zhuang Zhou was one who attained realization of the fundamental nature; that is to say, he internally realized that the body is empty and illusory.
Therefore, he was able to perceive in this way his own self as a butterfly, and to see himself traveling to the ends of heaven within a dream. The one of ultimate virtue is the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "initially as in the text": my own conviction that the Tathāgata has crossed the great ocean of afflictions is precisely an acceptance of this intent;
however, because those words leave something unsaid, a further inquiry arises, namely, to elicit the opening of the Tathāgata’s secret of the body (*kāyaguhyaka*).

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "If the Buddha has already crossed over," etc., the intent of the objection is as follows: If it is said that he has already crossed over, why did he again take Yaśodharā?
Since he has now taken her, he must therefore not have severed his afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Sūtra says, "You should not," using this phrase as a heading for what follows: "You should not say for what reason Yaśodharā was taken in marriage;
you should not say she was truly born [of her]."
The Sūtra states, "One who can establish the great purpose," clarifying that the Buddha abides in Great Nirvāṇa, manifesting bodies throughout the ten realms.
His great functioning pervades the Dharma-realm, boundless and inexhaustible in its successive layers. How could he merely be capable of receiving Yaśodharā and giving birth to Rāhula?
Furthermore, the eight subsequent sections all describe the characteristics of the great meaning.

Regarding the general mention of "bodhisattvas," Liang says: because they have seen a small portion of the Buddha-nature, they are said to be "dwelling" [in the stage]; this uses the lower to illustrate the higher.
"Transcending cause and effect" means simply transcending that which pertains to the causal stage.
As for "nirvāṇa being the cause," it is because the bodhisattva practices the cause in view of the fruit; therefore, nirvāṇa is that in which the person on the causal stage abides.
The Sūtra says: "I have long dwelt... up to "...manifestations. This refers to two types of manifestation: first, manifesting as a trace following the path of the original Buddha;
second, arising from the Dharma-body to manifest as a response, such as being born in a royal palace and so forth.
As for the term "wondrous" (*miao*) used in the translation, it signifies that the sun is able to dispel darkness; this is the internal illumination of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "the elephant king newly born," Sengliang said: "In India, when the elephant king is born, he immediately takes seven steps upon leaving the womb."
Knowing this to be the Elephant King, the Bodhisattva first manifests the marks of a Sovereign King in the world.
As for manifesting the transcendence of the six realms, he has not yet transcended the two vehicles; how then could he reveal the secret of the Buddha-body?
"Corresponding to the seven factors of enlightenment" is an explanation of taking up [the practice].
"The west is the direction of autumn" means that when all things reach autumn, they wither and fall as if dead.
"The north is the left" refers to Uttarakuru, which is superior among the four continents.
Regarding the directions: in India, the east is considered the beginning; the west is the end; the north is the left; and the south is the right.
Traveling east signifies the beginning—first, it indicates the infant stage; second, it clarifies the head of the Path to demonstrate mastery.
Regarding the "discrimination of other births": this refers to [the Buddha's] manifesting renunciation and so forth here in Jambudvīpa in the past; therefore, it belongs to another birth.

As for "using the previous intention to challenge the subsequent": this means using the previous statement from the section on verbal secrecy—namely, the intention that "like a scattered spark of fire, it is extinguished forever"—to raise an objection.
These are various manifestations.
When the Sūtra says, "The Dharma-body eternally abides," "abides" refers to wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara-sat*).
When the Sūtra says, "You should not now raise such an objection," the Buddha’s intention is to say: "I have merely borrowed a lamp-vessel for a moment..."
This serves as an illustration. You should not now challenge the analogy used by others.
When the sutra says "like the extinguishing of a lamp," it means that the causes and effects of the afflictions of the segmented realm have merely been exhausted;
like the extinguishing of a lamp, there still remains the body and wisdom. This is not the Great Nirvana, but rather a Lesser Nirvana.
The Sūtra states that one who does not come repeatedly is so called because "coming" refers to being born in a higher realm and then falling back down;
furthermore, within the Form Realm, there is also one who comes only once and not repeatedly, namely the *ūrdhvasrotas* Anāgāmin.
"Those who do not arise from the two extremes" refers to Bodhisattvas from the stage of *bhūmi-pratiṣṭhita* (dwelling on the stages) upward.

Regarding the "opening of the three karmas" at the end of the *Catur-lakṣaṇa-parivarta*, this explicitly clarifies that while the secret of mind (*mantra-guhya*) is primary, it is simultaneously endowed with the other two [secrets].
The "treasury of all awakenings" refers to the secret of the mouth; the "wish-fulfilling jewel" refers to the secret of the mind; and the "hidden treasury" refers to the secret of the body.
"Seeing a small portion of Buddha-nature" refers to what is perceived from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward.

Regarding "neither manifest nor secret": this refers to the thorough realization of the true nature (*dharmatā*), wherein there is no longer any need to speak of opening [the teaching] as being "secret.
As for Nāgārjuna’s specific intention in naming the *Lotus Sūtra* "secret," it means that once [the teaching] has been opened, there is nothing external to it—this is what is called "secret.

If one were to claim that "secret" refers to the sūtra itself, then all sūtras would be equal in this regard; how could it apply to the *Lotus Sūtra* alone? Therefore, it is said that [this interpretation] universally applies to all sūtras.
Therefore, this "non-existence" is precisely the absence of a secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*).

The Sūtra states that the "secret treasury" (the character *mi* is pronounced as *zàng* [tsang] with the *gang* [gang] tone; hereafter there are three more instances of the character "treasury" with the same pronunciation, though the phonetic glosses for various sūtras all provide this explanation).
Regarding the initial passage, "As the text says," Kāśyapa probes the Buddha’s intention, stating that there is only the "profound teaching" (mi-shuo) and no "hidden treasury" (mi-zang). Why is this?
Because in the past, when the capacity for the teaching of permanence had not yet been awakened, he taught the doctrine of impermanence while intending it to point toward permanence;
how could there be anything secret therein?
Those of base arts employ illusions; what they produce merely allows others to see it, but does not allow them to obtain it. The Buddha is not like this:
he constantly vows that sentient beings shall share in what he has attained. How, then, could this be called "concealing"?
Regarding the next nine similes, Master Zhezhou says: First, it clarifies that the Tathāgata’s speech has no concealment; therefore, there is no secret treasury.
Second, because his mind is free from stinginess, there is no secret treasury. Third, because the Dharma is without deficiency, there is no secret treasury.

Fourth, because there is nothing owed or borrowed, there is no secret treasury. Fifth, because his compassionate love is profound and heavy, there is no secret treasury. Sixth, the roots of evil have died out...

Because it is exhaustive, there is no secret treasury. Because the sevenfold speech is free from error, there is no secret treasury. Because it is appropriate for the various transformations of the eightfold assembly, there is no secret treasury.
Because the rain of Dharma moistens all equally, there is no secret treasury. This, too, is merely a single approach consisting of words.
The Sūtra says: "The secret treasury" (the character *zàng* [藏] below has sixteen occurrences;

all share this pronunciation) is like a person who does not seek goods from the debtor, but rather from the owner. For example, if a person wishes to recover property, they ought to go to the one holding the property;

if they do not see him and instead seek it from the owner, they will have no recourse when they wish to return. The Buddha is likewise: he truly bears the burden of delivering sentient beings from the world.
Regarding the wealth of the Dharma, he constantly desires to return it; however, because sentient beings do not accept its meaning, they ought to bear the burden.
The scripture states that there is "only one son," which is a metaphor for the śrāvakas taught by the Buddha Tathāgata, who are called "the one son."
"Affectionate mindfulness" is a metaphor for the great compassion of the true aspect.
"About to go" is a metaphor for being about to approach the gate of Buddha-nature.
"Teacher" is a metaphor for the Dharma, which is that upon which all Buddhas take as their teacher.

"Desiring to cause those who receive instruction to cultivate and study the Buddha-nature" means that those who fear not achieving success quickly are likened to those who fear they may not yet understand the meaning of the Buddha-nature.

"Seeking to bring them back immediately" is a metaphor for bringing back the Śākyamuni of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), who first taught the Small Vehicle and subsequently taught the Great Vehicle.
Regarding the question-and-answer format within this text, there are two aspects to it: namely, the questions and the answers.
The Sūtra states: "That which is called the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging existence" refers to a wondrous reality that remains unchanged both now and in the past;
therefore, it is said to exist eternally.
"Impermanence is universal" refers to the two truths that encompass the ultimate (zhen).

If those who are "received" [into the higher vehicle] open up the ultimate to reveal the Middle Way, it is termed "permanent. If they are not so received, all things ultimately revert to annihilationism (huaiduan).
It is called "impermanence.

As for the scripture’s statement regarding the "descending of the great rain of Dharma," both at the beginning and at the end there is a great rain; yet the three types of grasses and two types of trees each receive benefit according to their own nature, which is not the fault of the Dragon King.
Regarding the former [passage] where "the powerful one" (*quan*) was briefly cited as a metaphor for the King to explain impermanence:
the *Sūtra* says that "its traces cannot be sought. Sengzong remarked, "This means both body and wisdom have perished. This, too, is an ancient saying and thus should be set aside.
The subsequent commentary states: "It is near to Bodhi; Nirvāṇa has no location or direction. Its reality transcends the reach of ordinary sentiment."
This means it is difficult to investigate. There are a hundred such verses; who could possibly understand them?
To illustrate "accumulation" by showing what is not accumulated: first, one cites material wealth and treasures as things that are accumulated.
Since the Śrāvaka Saṃgha and others do not accumulate such things, they are called "without accumulation."
Furthermore, regarding "no accumulation" (*asaṃcaya*): both the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas possess this term. To explain it according to the Dharma:

what is meant by the two schools not accumulating worldly treasures is called "no accumulation. The untainted ultimate truth, which inherently possesses the merits of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), is called "accumulation.
However, the sutras clarify only that not accumulating worldly wealth is termed "no accumulation. If one were to take [the meaning] out of its proper time...
Realization is termed "accumulation. Only when one attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity is it termed "non-accumulation.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva attains non-accumulation in both the mundane and supramundane realms, it is called "non-accumulation."
"Regarding 'there is no pleasure and so forth,' this clarifies the unconditioned Four Noble Truths.
'Because there is cessation, there is no suffering' means that there is no suffering of the two deaths, the three sufferings, or the eight sufferings.
'This is the realization' refers to the traces of the Dharmakāya; it is wondrously transcendent and difficult to seek, yet it manifests extinction by relying upon great liberation."

Furthermore, regarding the impossibility of seeking its boundaries or depths: this means it is boundlessly vast and bottomlessly deep; there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm, and therefore it cannot be sought.
To explain briefly by means of three points: vastness is the Dharmakāya; being free from blemishes is Prajñā; and reaching the destination is Vimukti.
Therefore, these three points are used as metaphors for them.
Regarding the accomplishment of essence and function: the *dharmakāya* is the essence, while *prajñā* and liberation are the function.

Furthermore, the three causes of the rational nature (*li-xing*) inherently possess essence and function, yet they reside solely within the principle (*li*). Moreover, within cultivation (*xiu*) there is also essence and function; their full perfection resides exclusively in cultivation.
Furthermore, within function there is essence—function that is itself essence—and within essence there is function—essence that is itself function. Why?

It is for this reason. Because each of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) individually possesses the three dharmas, their essence and function are mutually integrated, such that both self and others are fully perfected.
Here, one’s own practice is the essence, while transforming others is the function. Furthermore, if one’s own practice lacks function, one’s own practice is incomplete;
if transforming others lacks essence, there is nothing for others to realize. Only when both self and others are fully provided for can it be called "complete perfection."
Regarding the etymological interpretation according to names: while the Great [Vehicle] is vast and extensive, we shall follow its etymological explanation for now;
it cannot be said that this is a "great" [state] in relation to a "small" one. Here, it is neither great nor small, and thus there is no mutual dependence.
"What is valued in the True Dharma" means that what is valued is abiding eternally in the True Dharma.
"A single person possessing eight qualities" refers to: first, fewness of desires; second, contentment; third, seclusion; fourth, diligence; fifth, right mindfulness.

Sixth is right concentration; seventh is right wisdom; eighth is non-proliferation (*aprapañca*), meaning that fewness of desires is the path while much desire is not the path, as explained at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Four Reliances."
The Sūtra says, "being free from all sores and blemishes. This refers to the simultaneous cessation of both cause and effect upon death—whether after three or two lifetimes.
This general term is the counterpart to that general term. Xinghuang merely offered a speculative interpretation of the principle.

Since *nirvāṇa* is a general name for the West, one should likewise establish "Great Parinirvāṇa" as its general name. While translating that *nirvāṇa*, one uses specific terms [for its particular aspects].
"Distinct. As the text raises the objection, this refers to Xingxing (興星), who challenges the interpretation of the preceding masters.
By explaining the particular as distinct from the general, he clarifies that the Sūtra is "without blemish" and so forth; thus, he explains the general term *nirvāṇa* through these three meanings.

The Sūtra says, "To extract the poisonous arrows" means to extract the poisonous arrows that are the causes of the three delusions; it means to apply the secret, wondrous medicine of the three virtues.
The Sūtra says, "To cause them to leave suffering behind" means to cause them to leave behind the suffering of the results of the two types of death.

Furthermore, regarding their mutual manifestation: logically, one's own practice should inherently include the practice of transforming others, and the practice of transforming others should inherently include one's own practice.
As for the locus of accomplishment, it refers to the truth of the principles realized.
The six realms and the four types of noble beings further clarify the ten realms; they do not exceed these six realms and four noble beings.
However, sentient beings who require subduing must have the karmic conditions arise before they can be tamed.
Regarding those among animals who are most fearful: they have forever abandoned the five fears.
Regarding their constant freedom from hunger and thirst: they always sustain themselves with the food of Great Nirvāṇa.
Regarding "those who have no affairs of humans or devas": humans and devas take the three sufferings and eight sufferings as their affairs.

As for the passage in the Sūtra that says, "one who possesses faith," Bao Liang states: from the point where one is able to give rise to even a single thought of goodness, up until the establishment of the primary faculty of faith, all are termed "cured.
Now, however, [the term refers to] the stages from contemplative practice (*guanxing*) upward, such as the stage of partial realization (*fenzhen*).
All are termed "already cultivated.

Regarding those who maintain that the fruit of Buddhahood is always possessed of form (*rūpa*), it should be understood that the mind is a formless form; this is termed the "form of the fruit of Buddhahood.
To simply say "it is form" is an imprecise statement.
The Sūtra says: "That which is not form. The Master [Hui]zong said: "What is now meant by 'the Śrāvakas are not form' is that they do not manifest forms within the six realms of existence.

It is for the sake of sentient beings that it is said they are 'not form. In the former teachings, it was only stated that they relinquish their bodies and undergo total extinction, without mentioning the three matters."
Since these three things do not exist, there is no material body (rūpakāya) that manifests as a responsive form; therefore, it is said to be "non-form" (arūpa).
To serve as the two conditions [for cognition], the essence of the Dharma-body is neither form nor non-form, yet it manifests forms and so forth for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding the question of how [the subtle form] can abide, it is difficult to refute those who falsely cling to the teaching that there is no form in the formless realm (*ārūpya*).

To cause the Buddha to explain to followers of the Two Vehicles that they do not entirely lack form, the Buddha uses the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as an analogy; he states that while there is indeed a subtle form, it is described as being "without form."
The Sūtra states that even the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception possesses form (*rūpa*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies this doubt by declaring that Bodhisattvas with the faculty of the nose perceive the fragrance of palaces in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Furthermore, the *Āgama Sūtras* state that when Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa, the gods of the form and formless realms shed tears like a fine spring rain; likewise, when Jambudvīpa [the Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa, the gods of the form and formless realms [shed tears].
Standing to the front side—this is translated as "also color.
Regarding the extensive explanation of liberation (*vimokṣa*), Sengliang said: "The preferences of sentient beings differ; therefore, liberation is praised extensively.
It clarifies that there is no suffering not exhausted and no bliss not complete, matching their dispositions and fulfilling their aspirations, thereby attracting them through manifold means."
Regarding the number of heads: if one merely counts those who have attained liberation, there are likewise eighty-four;
as for the ninety-seven or ninety-eight, this is by adding the thirteen masters who have attained liberation, which likewise results in ninety-seven.
As for those points that are briefly inexplicable, they do not accord with the meaning of the present sutra’s text; therefore, they are not employed here.
Regarding "Numinous Stone" (Lingshi): it is located in Huangyan County, Taizhou.
As for all ten thousand dharma-gates, according to principle, every single phrase is complete with ten thousand dharma-gates by means of the dharma of liberation.
Each and every one is mutually adorned, mutually pervasive, and mutually complete, forming a hundred thousand dharma-gates. What is here called "ten thousand" refers to a single phrase.
Regarding the terms "horizontal and vertical" up to "without blemish": when the three or two deaths are simultaneously extinguished, it is therefore called "without blemish."
Regarding those who reach the state of liberation: each and every phrase traverses the Dharma-realm horizontally and penetrates True Suchness (tathatā) vertically;
thus, both horizontally and vertically, they all arrive at the principle of liberation.
That which is complete and without deficiency possesses the single point of liberation; only when it possesses all three points can it be called "fully endowed.
Regarding the statement that it can only be described in terms of the vertical: this means that it can only be realized through the illumination of the perfect mind.
It pervades the Dharma-realm horizontally and exhausts the principle vertically; how could it ever be exhausted by paper or ink?
"Because of insufficient power" means that one's intellectual capacity is inadequate.

"Broadly [explaining] the above 'without sores or defects'" means that every sentence in the sutra accords with the meaning of being without sores or defects. The same applies to the two [sections] below that broaden the above.
If one examines the text in relation to its meaning, the correspondence is very clear.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that speaks of "being far removed" and so forth: each of the one hundred phrases must be explained according to the four teachings (*catvāraḥ śāsana-dharmāḥ*) in order to reveal the perfect teaching (*pariniṣpanna*).

For example, the phrase "far removed from all fetters" refers to the essence of liberation (*vimukti*), because it is free from the wounds and sores of the two types of death and the three delusions (*trividha-kleśa*).
Furthermore, that which was previously bound is the great suffering of birth and death;
that which realizes liberation is the great bliss of Great Nirvana. Birth and death possess ten thousand entanglements; Nirvana possesses ten thousand stillnesses.
Liberation from birth and death means that the myriad entanglements are themselves *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, within each and every phrase there should be five points:
first, the enumeration of names; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion; fourth, the identification with the Tathāgata; and fifth, the further analysis of what is difficult to understand.
Moreover, the number of these elements in the text is not fixed: some begin without an end, some end without a beginning, and some lack a middle.
There is no fixed sequence of beginning or end. Within the exegesis, there may be an explanation consisting solely of the dharma, or it may include both the dharma and a simile.

Similes may be either concordant or inverse. Regarding concordant similes: "Liberation is also like this. Regarding inverse similes: "Liberation is not like this. In the pairing of dharma and simile, the order is not fixed;
sometimes the dharma comes first, followed by the simile and then the application (*upanaya*), while at other times the simile comes first, followed by the dharma and then [the application].

There may be a *nigamana* (conclusion), or there may be only the application of the principle (*dharma*) followed by the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) without a conclusion; or there may be only the illustration followed by the principle without a conclusion.
Since the structure of the text is not fixed, these cases are shown here first so that they will be easily understood when the actual texts are reached.
The Sūtra says, "That which is void and non-existent": because one realizes this voidness and non-existence, one becomes free from all fetters and afflictions (*gaṇḍa*).
The Sūtra says, "It is precisely the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)," referring to the unconditioned dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Because one realizes the unconditioned, one is thus void and non-existent, and free from afflictions; these [terms] are successively adorned by the subsequent phrases to culminate in the supreme freedom from afflictions.
The same applies to the "Extensive" and the "Liberation. Thus, each single phrase is adorned with a hundredfold expansions.
As for what the Sūtra calls the "Eternal Dharma" (*dhruva-dharma*): "Constant" (*chang*) signifies that which is unchanging, immovable, and majestic;
"eternal" (*heng*) signifies that which is ever-present and unalterable. These are also synonymous terms, referring to that which remains eternally so throughout all days.
The Sūtra states: "If there were a self, it would be the view of permanence; if there were no self, it would be the view of annihilation. This omits the third phrase.
Regarding the fourth phrase, "non-self," the Sūtra says:
"One should only sever attachment to birth-and-death (saṃsāra), for the notion of 'self' arises erroneously. This attachment must be severed.
Indeed, the Buddhist scriptures do not cease from this principle.

As the sutra says: "That which is called 'not empty of emptiness' refers to the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity as the first reality; furthermore, liberation from all sufferings is the second reality.
This is what is meant by 'not empty of emptiness.'"

The Sūtra states: "Regarding 'emptiness of emptiness' (śūnyatā-śūnyatā): the liberation conceived by the Nirgranthas is a single emptiness consisting of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
furthermore, it is not liberation because its essence is impermanent, which constitutes a second emptiness; moreover, it is not liberation because it is termed 'nothingness' (akiṃcanya)."
"Non-action" refers simply to non-action itself.
"From here to there" means going from this place to that place, or reaching the other shore from this shore.
Although there is no "this shore," the two phrases regarding the superior and inferior [levels] are established.

Regarding "the fruit being severed in one part": when Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) severs one part, it immediately enters Wondrous Enlightenment (prabhāsvara-bodhi); this is termed "the fruit being severed in one part."
Regarding the statement that "all are neither severed nor not severed": it may be because wisdom is non-dual.
To explain by way of non-severance: impermanence is itself permanence; thus it is neither permanent nor impermanent. Permanence is itself neither permanent nor impermanent;
therefore, it is said to be "neither."
"To depart from birth and death outside of principle" means to depart from the birth and death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-utpāda-nirodha*).
The Sūtra says, "to sever all marks (*nimitta*). Greed is the root of bondage; "marks" refers to the objects of greed.

Greed and that which is greedily clung to bind one to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). All afflictions arise from this, and thus the succession of births and deaths, as cause and effect, is inexhaustible.
Because greed is eternally severed, [the afflictions] are extinguished in succession, resulting in universal liberation.
That which is "one and yet three" (and so on) up to "three and yet one" is likewise the identity of impermanence and permanence, and so forth.
"Distancing oneself from the hunt (up to) 'those who are near' means simply distancing oneself from birth and death.

'The frightened pigeon (up to) 'the one who fears' raises the shallow to reveal the profound; this is because Śāriputra’s unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*) was not yet perfected, due to his reliance on the distinct entities of the Triple Gem.
Regarding the "distinct entities of the Three Refuges" mentioned previously, the text concerning the three prostrations is that [passage].
Regarding the "four māras" mentioned in the sūtra: these refer to the four māras each within and without the realms.

Regarding the "inexhaustible" mentioned in the sūtra: because nirvāṇa is eternal, it is inexhaustible. In the text, from the passage "By following [this], one attains peace and happiness" onwards, the characteristics of the seven dharmas are proclaimed precisely to clarify their single essence (*ekakāya*).
Kāśyapa merely cites the three distinct essences of the past to challenge the present.
Because they are one essence and three [aspects], it is said that "raising the three makes the one difficult.
Thus, that which is neither wondrous nor precious is not the principle of Buddha-nature, and therefore is not wondrous; it is not the One Essence of the Triple Gem, and therefore is not precious.
Regarding "three in substance but one": the Sūtra says, "One thereby knows the Buddha-nature and the certainty of Nirvāṇa," which proves that the substance is one.
Regarding "the names and meanings are both different": this proves a distinct essence; it means that while there is one, there are also three in their distinct aspects.

The Sūtra states: "Dharma is called non-awakening (*abodha*). Dharma takes the sense of "guiding and maintaining" as its meaning; that is, it guides and gives rise to understanding in sentient beings, which is not the meaning of awakening.

Regarding "emptiness is called non-virtue," Zezhou says: "It is not the performance of virtuous acts within the practice of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. This refers to the emptiness of the *dharmatā*.

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Its essence is subsumed under the ultimate good (*paramārtha-kuśala*). Master Baoshou stated that it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*); therefore, in relation to the Buddha-dharma, it is termed "not good" (*a-kuśala*).
The Sūtra states that *Prajāpatī* was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. After the Buddha had fasted for seven days, his mother passed away; *Prajāpatī* [then] nursed him with her milk.
[The King] raised [the child]. After the Buddha had left the world, Prasenajit changed his chest-plate and wove a golden-threaded robe with his own hands.
He waited for the Buddha to return to the palace, intending to offer it to him. When the Buddha later returned to the kingdom, Prasenajit then presented it as an offering.

The Buddha then said: "A gift given out of affection does not possess great merit. One should instead make offerings to the Saṃgha. Because the Saṃgha possesses the Three Refuges, I now cite this example."
The distinct entities of suffering are fully present in the Sangha;

breaking down the former distinction, it is explained that there are three [aspects], which means destroying the previous notion of separate entities and causing one to enter into the present single entity.
When the Sūtra says, "This matter is not so," although the phrasing regarding "no arising and no ceasing" is the same, its meaning is entirely different. It is empty.

"Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) is established as a name in relation to the investigation of form (*rūpa*); "liberation" (*vimukti*) is designated in relation to the departure from obstacles. Since their respective objects of reference differ, it is said that [the two] are not the same.

As for the Sūtra stating, "Metaphors are employed for the sake of transforming sentient beings," this means that for the sake of those with specific conditions, one speaks of either one or three; such is the nature of the Tathāgata.
Originally there are not two.
As for the statements that there is "one" or "three," the intent is that one might speak only of one, or speak only of three;
or speak only of three, or speak only of one. Why then do you provide these two kinds of explanations? If you provide an explanation of three, that is impermanence.

Regarding the phrase "sometimes definitively explained" and so forth: this clarifies that the Tathāgata acts as the condition. He may explain [the relationship] as being of one essence, or he may explain it as being of distinct essences.
Yet, within the Tathāgata, there has never been duality. It is like a person who harms his mother: regarding the single body of the mother, he may incur an offense, or he may not incur an offense.

Regarding the fourth section, the "Comprehension," the sūtra fully summarizes three meanings therein. "The place where the Tathāgata reaches" summarizes the meaning of the aforementioned "place of liberation.

"Life-span" (āyus) summarizes the meaning of the aforementioned "vastness and breadth," for the Tathāgata takes constancy as his life-span, encompassing all horizontally and penetrating all vertically.

"Vitality" (jīvita) summarizes the meaning of the aforementioned "absence of sores or defects," for the Tathāgata takes wisdom as his vitality, illuminating and penetrating the three delusions and the two deaths.
Because of these sores and growths, the three meanings have been explained extensively; therefore, I now fully receive this essential purport.

Regarding the "Four Reliances" chapter, according to the commentary text, there are four sections: first, the explanation of the title; second, from the question "As for the Tathāgata... onwards, the questions and answers that resolve doubts; third, the old...

The section "Elucidating" below distinguishes between the different stages and practices elucidated by ancient and modern scholars. The phrase "From 'dividing this'" below begins the word-by-word commentary.
The first part explains the title based on the four *siddhāntas*. From the words "The number four" onwards refers to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly perspective).

Because the minds of beings develop a desire for joy based on the distinctions between self and others, it is called "benefit. Next, from the words "Answering the previous question: What is... onwards refers to the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the individual perspective).

Based on those who have attained the Dharma of the Great Person, the mind rightly gives rise [to realization]; therefore, it is said that they "have attained. From the third section, "Furthermore, from the past," onwards, this is the counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*).
Regarding those of the past who were mixed with both the true and the false—meaning people mixed with demons—one must externally rely on the Four Noble Truths of the Deer Park to discern them.

Now, the reason the Dharma is said to be "mixed" regarding the Great and Small Vehicles is that it involves hearing the Great and adopting the Small, using the Great to subvert the Small, and using the Great to open the way for the Small;
for these reasons, it is termed "mixed. This is precisely the wondrous antidote found in the present sutra.
Fourth, regarding the phrase "furthermore, from the past based on the first principle below":
to abandon this and resort to that is for a person to seek the Dharma externally, as if abandoning this to resort to that.
Now, this sutra reveals that the impermanent person and dharmas are neither permanent nor impermanent; this is the principle of Buddha-nature. Therefore, there is nothing to be abandoned.
Next, regarding the resolution of doubts, it says that one must not create images of the Tathāgata. After the Buddha had passed into nirvana, Māra Pāpīyas was also able to create them;
this is why he was able to produce images of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the general discussion of the "all-encompassing agent": as explained previously in the context of liberation, abiding in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi and manifesting various displays constitutes the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
As for its specific presence within the four fruits of the path, the practice of the transformative way becomes easy.
"Those who are Tathāgatas by virtue of being Tathāgatas" refers to the Buddha manifesting himself in person while in the world.
"Those who are Tathāgatas as the four reliances" are those who should see him; for their sake, he temporarily assumes that form.

Regarding the four reliances as being for the four reliances: the four persons act as mutual high and low positions; that is to say, when the fundamental is low and the trace is high, or when the fundamental is high and the trace is low, and so forth.

Regarding "the four fruits being the four fruits": the provisional four fruits are taken as the actual four fruits; this also refers to the mutual relationship of superiority and inferiority among these four persons.
Regarding "the four fruits cannot serve as the four reliances": this distinguishes the actual four fruits, which cannot serve as the four reliances.
As for the statement that "uniting them results in being a Buddha," this is because they are contained within a single body.
Regarding the initial point of "uniting according to the Dharma": the former teachings merely required one to rely upon the Dharma.
In the third section, "Distinguishing the Ancient and the Modern," it states: "The thirteen minds refer to the stages from the Ten Abidings up to the third practice.
The seventeen minds refer to the stages from the Ten Abidings up to the seventh practice."
Regarding those who initially possess afflictions: because their afflictions have not been exhausted, they lack ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, regarding those who possess *nirvāṇa*: the fourth reliance (*niśraya*) is the culmination of the causal stage; although subtle afflictions still exist, it is nonetheless called the ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding those who possess only afflictions in the future, all four reliances apply, because they partially subdue, partially sever, and partially realize nirvana.
Only at the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) is it termed "nirvana of contemplative practice."
Regarding the claim that the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* is "perfect" (*yuan*), this is based on a semblance of perfection; for the time being, let us grant it as such.

As for the forty stages of mind collectively constituting the four reliances (*catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāni*): the ten abodes (*daśa-vihārāḥ*) constitute the second reliance, and the practices and directions (*caryā-pratipannaka*) constitute the third reliance.
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) constitute the fourth reliance; conversely, the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) serve as the first reliance.
Only by correlating this with the scriptural text can one understand the meaning of "distinct" and "equal. One should know that the four reliances refer to the persons who lead others.

Since they have not yet entered the ultimate reality from the provisional stage, those among the led who attain entry into the ultimate reality do so either by leaping over stages or by following a gradual sequence; therefore, the principle of the four reliances must apply to each respective stage. Thus, they remain [in these stages].

The stages of practice (*pratipatti*) differ in their depth; however, those who initially rely upon the Bodhisattva path all abide within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). The sutra text itself states:
"There are people appearing in the world who possess the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*"; this is called the first [stage]. Their position is thus fixed."
Regarding the initial reliance on being merely a disciple: this is first determined by the nature of possessing afflictions.
As for the intermediate case where one is both teacher and so forth: in relation to those below, one is a teacher; in relation to those above, one is a disciple.
In the commentary on the fourth entry, it says: "Regarding the 'heading and praise,' the text fully praises both the person and the Dharma.
"Not allowing other conditions" means not permitting Māras, externalists, or those of the Two Vehicles to cling to impermanence, nor allowing wicked bhikṣus to cause disturbance.
Regarding "establishment" (pratiṣṭhāpana): it means that when the guiding principles of the True Dharma (saddharma) are collapsing, one is able to rectify, sustain, and establish them.

Regarding "abiding": it means causing the True Dharma not to be interrupted, which is called "recollection" (anusmṛti). Furthermore, when the mind does not forget, it is called "recollection of the True Dharma."

These three phrases concern the virtues of one's own practice. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "For a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, what is called 'transforming others' is itself one's own practice.
The present four reliances are likewise so.
The Sūtra says, "Those who find peace and happiness among humans and devas," because the devas come among humans to listen to the Dharma. Sengliang said:
"In the final age, the universal Dharma is not the domain of the śrāvakas."
As for their being paired with bodhisattvas, it is simply because they have left the household life through the correct Dharma-eye of the śrāvakas that they are so paired.
Although bodhisattvas may conceal their traces within the secular stream, they remain pure and untainted; in measure, they are equal to arhats.
One must not say that those who possess the state of afflictions (kleśa) have either universally severed them;

for while universal afflictions no longer arise as active manifestations, and particular afflictions, having been suppressed, likewise do not arise as active manifestations, they still possess the nature of particular afflictions, which is termed "possessing the nature of afflictions.
Regarding the four stages of Saṃghabhadra’s system, these range from the application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) up to the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma).
The thirty minds prior to the stages (bhūmi) are all paths of suppression; they have not yet attained true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).
This also serves as a general proof for the stage of the first reliance (*prathamāśraya*). Now, to provide a definitive judgment: while the names are common, their meanings are distinct.

Furthermore, it is said that although those of the three levels of worthiness (*trayaḥ pūrvayogāḥ*) suppress both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa- and jñeya-āvaraṇa*) so that they do not manifest, they have not yet realized outflow-free wisdom and are unable to sever them.
As for the seeds [of affliction], it is only upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*) that one is able to sever the seeds of affliction; therefore, it is said that "one possesses the nature of affliction.
This is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).

According to the Shared Vehicle (*tonggongshe*), since the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) manifest as the forms of the two vehicles within the supramundane body, both the Great and Small Vehicles are present.

Hong’s classification based on the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) is the most convenient; for it is the stage where the three vehicles study together, as it encompasses the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect teachings.

If one follows the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Mahāyāna, this is judged according to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, which clarifies that a person of the Perfect teaching has the principle of transcending to ascend to the ten stages in a single lifetime; hence the detailed commentary.

According to the Mahāyāna classification, this accords with the Mahāyāna of the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-śāsana). At the stage of the seventh bhūmi, when one is in the common position of the three vehicles, even the outflows (āsrava) are exhausted;
therefore, one does not return to the triple world.
If the seventh stage is taken as the third reliance, then the eighth and ninth stages— whereby one retains delusions to sustain rebirth and forms pure land affinities with sentient beings—
are taken as the fourth reliance.
If one examines this in detail regarding the "Perfect" (yuan) stage, as in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) mentioned above, each position serves as a triple basis.
That which precedes the stage is the first basis; hence the note says "and so forth."
However, as for the phrase "the substance remains," ignorance is an affliction of the same substance; therefore, it is said that "the substance remains.
Regarding the two trainings of precepts and wisdom, meditative concentration necessarily exists between them; these are the two gates of the vehicle and the precepts.

Regarding the "Eight Awakenings of the Great Man": the Buddha is a great man, and the Bodhisattva also attains the nature of awakening; being no different from the Buddha, these are called the Eight Awakenings of the Great Man.
The passage cited from the *Śāsanāntara-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Final Teachings) draws upon the small to enumerate the great.
Regarding the "eight persons": the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are the causes for patience. The Master [Dao]xuan says: "The stage of the eight patiences is the rank of the noble ones (*ārya*).
To say now that this is not the 'eighth person' refers, for the time being, to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of the nature-stage (*gotrabhūmi*) as the primary basis.
This master also judges according to the stages common to the three vehicles.
"Once the distinct delusions are eliminated," it means the aspect of the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is complete.

"In accord with the Dharma" means the aspect of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) is manifested. "Attained through the path of cultivation" means the aspect of the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is fulfilled.
Regarding the "minor difficulties concerning the stages": first, the ancient explanations are incorrect; thus they are termed "minor difficulties.
Furthermore, the commentary states that not yet having attained the second and third [stages] constitutes the difficulty.
The four types of patience (*kṣānti*) are also one approach, yet they are not entirely appropriate; therefore, they are not employed here.

This is because using the former to exclude the latter proceeds from the shallow toward the deep, whereas using the latter to exclude the former proceeds from the shallow [to the profound]. Master Fǎyáo said:
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are categorized into three dwelling places. From the first stage up to and including the sixth stage, one has not yet emerged from the defiled lands of the triple world;
this constitutes one dwelling place. The seventh stage is the second dwelling place, situated between the two perfections, being neither pure nor defiled. From the eighth stage upward...

When the conceptualizing mind is completely exhausted, it is called a Pure Land and constitutes a single dwelling place. This second type of person has not yet attained the dwelling places of the seventh stage and above;
in meaning, this resembles the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*), but it is likewise not accepted here.
"One who will certainly attain the fruit" refers to one who shall attain the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the two ancient interpretations [up to] "the one who understands": the former cites what is inexplicable to manifest that the present [interpretation] is explicable.
Regarding the compilation according to the *Ekottarika* (Increasing by One), this refers to the compilation by Dharmottara; the Master [Vasubandhu] now relies on this as the correct interpretation.

As for "those who are alike in being with effort," these two are alike in that their cultivation-obscurations (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm have not yet been exhausted, and thus they are merely termed "with effort" (*sābhoga*).
The third [category], based on having already abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm, is termed "without effort" (*anabhoga*).
Furthermore, if one were to take the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*) as a single abode, this would again contradict the established order.

Based on the distinction between the form and formless realms, two bases for the stages are established. Since the form and formless realms are divided into two, the first two fruits should likewise be divided into two bases.
Yet, these two scriptural passages themselves combine them into a single base; how then can the form and formless realms be divided into two bases?
Regarding the scriptural passage on "adventitious afflictions" (*āgantuka-kleśa*) and so forth:

for those of the Hīnayāna who seek these two fruits [of stream-enterer and once-returner], since they have not yet abandoned desire, the active afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are termed "adventitious," while the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are termed "ancient."

[The practitioner] is still unable to be free from them. For one who has attained the third fruit (anāgāmin), the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whether arising from views (*dṛṣṭi*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā*), are forever exhausted.

If one were to say that they still exist, it would be impossible. The Master [Hui-kuang] says: "Afflictions outside the three realms are considered 'old,' while afflictions within the three realms are considered 'guests.

This is based on the distinction between the root and the branches. Now, the Master [Zhiyi] comprehensively treats the three delusions as illusory; however, these [afflictions within the three realms] can only obstruct the branches.
The meaning of this fundamental principle is likewise the same.
Regarding the statement that "now the Dharma-body is revealed" and so forth: in the past, according to the provisional teachings, the *śarīra* relics of the fragmented body obscured the Dharma-body;
now that it has been revealed, these very relics are themselves the Dharma-body. Therefore, it is said: "This body of mine now..."
This refers to those who "circulate," meaning they teach and transform beings everywhere there are those with the karmic conditions to be reached.
As for the statement in the sutra, "Furthermore, one attains Bodhi," this refers to the Bodhi of the ultimate fruit.
"Severance" (dàn; *túguǎn* pinyin) refers to the analysis of the substance of phenomena having already been separated.
Regarding "attaining what the Buddha has attained": in certain sūtras, the term "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*) is designated as "Equal-Enlightenment Buddha.

Therefore, the fourth reliance is called "attaining what the Buddha has attained," which is also the ultimate limit of partial attainment within the causal stage. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states: "The causes and effects of the triple world..."
All [others] are termed "other. The merits of wisdom and abandonment are all termed "one's own benefit. Because one’s own benefit is fully perfected, one becomes a *arhat* (*yìnghuà*).
Furthermore, Huìlǎng said: "The severing of all afflictions explains 'slaying the thief'; the attainment of one's own benefit explains 'becoming an arhat';
and that which has been done is finished explains 'non-arising' (*anutpāda*)."

Regarding "if one wishes to become a Buddha, one becomes one immediately": upon a single turning, one enters the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). However, this is not undertaken for the sake of transformation, but merely for the purpose of converting others.
Regarding "reaching the ultimate merit and sublime function": these four types of persons all accord with the ultimate principle and abide in the four stages of reliance (*catur-āśraya*);

this is called "ultimate merit. Because they possess the function of subduing Māras and restraining outsiders, it is called "sublime function. They do not require instruction from Bodhisattvas, as they are naturally able to realize and penetrate the realm of Māras.
Because it is thus, there is no need for instruction.
When the Sūtra says, "I now do not rely on the Supreme Person," the meaning is this: the Buddha previously told Ghoṣila that Māra can manifest as a Buddha and so forth;
I now simply obtain what I need by examining the Dharma itself. Why should the World-Honored One require me to rely on a person? Therefore...
It is said that he does not rely [on them].
When the sutra says, "You should examine," it means to have him examine according to the sūtras and dharmas of the Hīnayāna.

In the past, the Tathāgata once taught the Four Noble Truths to Kuśira; he realized the first fruit (srotāpanna). After the Tathāgata had departed, Māra came to confuse and disturb him, and transformed—

He manifested the body of a Buddha and addressed the elder, saying: "I ask you whether your exposition of the Dharma is exhaustive. Beyond the Four Noble Truths, there exists yet another truth: the truth of a divine self (ātman).
The elder investigated thoroughly and found no such principle to be true. He then went to invite the Buddha, who immediately instructed him:
"If Māra manifests as a Buddha, you must examine and verify him."

Having understood this, one should subdue [the mind]; yet, regarding those who inquire and observe, there is no fault in their questioning. Next, one should cause them to rely on the teaching and observe with actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
If even toward the Buddha one must rely on the wisdom of faith, then regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, which ought to be accepted through faith, one must still further observe it. Why?
How much more so for others?
Regarding "stealing from a dog," this follows the six-fascicle version; "stealing" and "dog" are distinct. This means that both the thief and the dog enter the Dharma-house of the Mahāyāna.
Now, when a dog intends to commit theft, it must see that there are no guards outside and that there is the darkness of night within.

For this reason, they are able to enter. It is the same with Māra: when there are no virtuous friends or spiritual teachers externally, and ignorance covers the mind internally, Māra is able to cause confusion.
Now, regarding "ignorance as the night": it refers to the arising of ignorance, which acts as a demonic disturbance, analogous to entering at night.
The commentary states: "The wisdom of hearing is lowly, hence it is likened to a servant. Within the slight light [of this wisdom], one examines the reality or unreality of the demons;
by the power of the five fetters, the demons depart immediately. However, the Master here takes the stages of the noble ones (ārya) and the sages generally.
Subduing the two kinds of Māras does not pertain exclusively to the stage of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Regarding the "five corpses": as in the case of Upagupta, who entered the universal application of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) through the supernormal power of *rddhi*, and by means of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) of the desire realm, transformed himself into a putrid and decaying corpse to bind the King of Māra;
he then used a putrid and decaying dog-corpse to pierce the belly and break [the bonds].
A chest-cloth of the Mara’s head is used, with the head of a dead dog covering the crown of the Mara’s head. From the dog’s mouth, worms and pus flow out;

following the sweat from the Mara’s forehead, they stream down into his nose and mouth. The front paws of the dead dog embrace the Mara’s forehead, while the hind paws of the corpse-dog embrace the Mara’s neck.
Stinking, rotting dead snakes wind around his neck and cross over his chest to serve as a necklace, extending around his arms to his hands.
It is like a ring or a bracelet; a dead person encircles one’s waist, and a dead pig is tied to one’s feet (and so forth).

Regarding the five kinds of impurity, the first fascicle’s record cites the "Contemplation in Five Gates," which refers to the contemplations of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and impurity.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "One may also draw near to Great Nirvāṇa," this is spoken with a specific intent:
it means that by employing the mind of Great Nirvāṇa to subdue [the māras], one will then draw near to Great Nirvāṇa and dwell in the Secret Treasury. Why rely on others?
Furthermore, relying solely on the Buddha, as taught in the *Ghoṣila-sūtra*, one should examine the māras by means of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
It is sufficient. Why rely on another person? This explanation correctly elucidates the intent of the sutra.
When the sutra says, "it is not otherwise," it means that if one possesses the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) of a Mahāyāna bodhisattva, one need only rely on the Dharma to attain [realization].
My own view is likewise. However, for śrāvakas, one must necessarily rely on another person to obtain the method for subduing Māra.
Although they are devas, those who possess flesh—regardless of whether that flesh is seen by devas as coarse or subtle—are merely the colors of dependent origination perceived together.

Although Bodhisattvas possess flesh, for those whose six sense faculties are purified, this physical body born of parents is termed "flesh"; it is through their practice and realization [that they transcend it].
Because he has thoroughly penetrated the principle, he is able to be identical with Suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the analogy of "valiant and courageous" for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), Master Zezhou says: "The Buddha possesses fearlessness, and is thus called 'valiant and courageous.
His Ten Powers (*daśabala*) subdue heterodox teachings, which is termed 'majestic and fierce.'"

The four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) being like a bow is like an empty bow; it causes one to rely on the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārga*) to subdue that which is called "name" (*nāma*) through skillful means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-prajñā*) is like a bow, the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-prajñā*) is like an arrow, and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) is like a spear and so forth. It is also said:

"Holding the bow with cultivated concentration (*samādhi*), grasping the arrow with practiced wisdom, one raises the staff-path of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the long hook of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the snare of divine mantras (*vidyā-mantra*)."

The *Suo* states that when the sutra speaks of "beholding humans and devas," it expresses pity for those who do not see their Buddha-nature and lack the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, likening them to something light and weak.
Māra is one who lacks wisdom; lacking the wisdom that illuminates principle, he does not perceive the Buddha-nature, and for this reason he is timid.
The Sūtra says "he calls out" (hū): "calls" means to summon them; it is called "calling" because he fears others [will do so].

Regarding the mention of the "five truths" and so forth: in addition to the four truths, they postulate a truth of a divine self (ātman); in addition to the five aggregates (skandhas), they postulate an aggregate of a divine self;
and the same applies by analogy to the nineteen elements (dhātus) and so on.

As for the sūtra’s statement that one “should not give rise to sorrow or fear”: through the Great Contemplation of the Perfect *E*, one realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) of the realm of Māra; therefore, there is no sorrow or fear.
As for the sūtra’s statement that one “causes them to be subdued”: one subdues them by relying on the three trainings of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
One who hears that the realm of Māra is suchness (tathatā) understands deeply and penetrates the principle; seeing Māra as immediately Buddha, it is thus called "suchness.

Regarding those who internally ride the Mahāyāna, Sengliang says: first, because they have accumulated merit to its profound source; second, because by the power of the Mahāyāna sūtras, they are naturally able to subdue Māra.
The Sūtra says: "One obtains the *agada* medicine and perfects the wondrous contemplation of the letter *I*. This is likened to the *agada* medicine [which cures] the realm of *adharma*;
it is neither two nor distinct from the Buddha-realm. Therefore, it is said that one does not fear anything. This is explained by correlating it with the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*).

"Bie" (with the phonetic gloss *fangmie*) means that one's nature is prone to much anger and wrath. If it is written as "bi," it refers to an affliction (*ābādha*), which is not the intended meaning of the text.
Furthermore, to wish to destroy another's goodness is called "bi" (corrupting); to wish to ruin another's goodness is termed "hai" (harming).
Alternatively, "those who practice the arts" refers to those who do not recognize the true art.
"Śrāvakas returning to their origin" refers to those who have attained the original mind of the Śrāvaka and so forth.
As for the scripture stating "they create obstructions," it means they no longer cling to impermanence and the like, which would obstruct the Great Dharma of perfect permanence.
The Sūtra states: "Those who possess such power" refers to those who practice the Mahāyāna. "Possessing the power of Māra" refers to those whose physical form is like that of Māra.
"Satiated in virtue" means when one's merit is thick and the Path is abundant.
"Having neither physician nor medicine" means there is no physician because the Buddha has passed into extinction, and there is no medicine because the True Dharma is declining and weakening.

Regarding the statement that there are those who are prolix and those who are concise: those with great capacity and profound [understanding] are prolix; those with small capacity and shallow [understanding] are concise.
As for the forty years of upholding the Dharma: Kāśyapa [upheld it] for twenty years, and Ānanda for twenty years; thus, they constitute forty years in total.
As for those who flourished and passed away thereafter, this also occurred within the subsequent eighty years: flourishing during the first forty years and passing away during the latter forty years.
To claim that those capable of synthesizing the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were also those incapable of such synthesis is not entirely accurate.
The statement that "those born on the day Kāśyapa Buddha attained the Way" is likely an error, or perhaps it was spoken in reference to his succession.
As for the claim that "Kāśyapa is the eldest son": because all the Buddha-dharma was entrusted to Kāśyapa, he is called the eldest son for this reason.
The Sūtra says, "Those who eat only millet" refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), who praise only the Arhat as supreme.
The Sūtra says, "those who undergo karmic retribution" refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles, who undergo the karmic retribution of the "ash-like cessation" (the extinction of afflictions).

The Sūtra states, "These are people of merit" (up to) "those who have not heard. This clarifies that those of the Mahāyāna, from the *Avataṃsaka* and other scriptures onward, have never heard such names as impermanence, suffering, or emptiness.
The non-glutinous grain is used as a metaphor for the permanent because it is the staple food of the local people.

Rock honey is used as a metaphor for the self (*ātman*): when it needs to be firm, it is firm; when it needs to be soft and cold, it becomes so; when it needs to be warm, it becomes soft. This is employed as an analogy for the self.
To seek that which possesses existence, or to seek the path of the Two Vehicles, is called "seeking existence. This is because one does not perceive the Buddha-nature.
As for the interpretation regarding "one who understands through skillful means," this explanation is not correct and is therefore not accepted here.
The present "Explanation of the Great Practice" (*Daixing xun*) refers to the practice-dharma of the Mahāyāna, which instructs and leads others to cultivate and study it. Sengzong said:
"The Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances extensively transcribed Mahāyāna sūtras and circulated them in that region, so that at once they were transformed by the teaching;
it was as if the entire nation were eating together."
The Sūtra states that the "immeasurable bodhisattvas from other directions" refers merely to those with the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) of bodhisattvas.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra which says, "In that land there are vajras and so forth," it means that the Great Dharma resides within people, just as vajras exist within the earth.

Sengliang said: "As for the dissemination of the Sūtra, when it is in the earth, the earth is noble; when it is in people, the people are honored. This refers to one who has attained realization regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
This is precisely the Buddha-nature. All phenomena arise from this Dharma; thus, all present phenomena are entirely adamantine.
As for the King’s arrival at the deep mountains, this borrows the phrasing of the preceding passage to establish the meaning of the present context.
Regarding the depth and shallowness of the planted causes: first, one praises the intent behind the manifestation and exposition of the Four Reliances that transcend the world.
Regarding the division of the subtle hairs: ten *sī* (fibers) constitute one hair (*vāla*).
By means of each word and phrase, one explains immeasurable meanings, such as the "Hundredfold Liberation" and so forth.
Regarding those who proclaim this guide: it is not easy to propagate the Way that has been lost.

As for that which unfolds and rolls up the universe: when unfolded, it fills the entire Dharma-realm; when rolled up, it resides in nothing more than a single thought-moment within the nature of the mind, even as small as a speck of dust.
Thus, the eternally abiding secret treasury is revealed and proclaimed before the assembly, so that it may encompass the Dharma-realm and bring benefit.
"May it cause those who hear it for eternal kalpas to achieve their fruition. If it were not for the power of the Four Reliances, how could an ordinary person of feeble capacity accomplish this?
Sengzong said: "Nothing is transmitted without virtue; nothing is planted without causes. This shall cause the assembly of the present age to yearn for the Way and cultivate its causes."
The character 藂 (pronounced jù) is glossed as "light.
