Regarding "those who destroy the true precepts during the turbidity of life": this refers solely to those who destroy the precepts through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
As for the "five kinds of Dharma-preachers," these are combined into one category for the purpose of upholding [the teaching], yet they constitute five [distinct types].

Regarding the "Nine Rivers": this section of the sūtra precisely clarifies that it is difficult to give rise to faith, difficult to give rise to understanding, and difficult to possess complete understanding.

Sengzong said: "From the mention of the *Sītā* River up to the two *Gaṅgā* Rivers, these are the causes for the listeners; from the three *Gaṅgā* Rivers up to the eight rivers, these are the causes for the speakers.
This is also one perspective, yet it does not clearly reveal the distinctions in depth between the four reliances (*catur-yoni*).
The Ganges River is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length; it is forty li wide at its broadest and ten li wide at its narrowest.
Measuring down one cubit into the mud, one obtains ten thousand hu of sand, the grains of which are as fine as flour.
Regarding the fourth point, "those who always follow from delusion": this is because their delusions are many and their understanding shallow.
As for the example of one who has risen to the rank of Grand Marshal (*taifu*) and so forth: since these are offices that proceed from shallow to deep, they are easy [to attain].
The position of Chancellor (*xiangsheng*), however, is a special office that bypasses the regular sequence; therefore, it is difficult.
Regarding "first relying on the person to exhaustively fathom the Buddha-dharma": first, relying on one who is able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata is called "exhaustive fathoming.

As for "what opens up the Buddha-dharma," the nine *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* generally correspond to this initial reliance; it merely establishes the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) for Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).
Because it is [merely] the Dharma, it is not the perfect Buddha-dharma of the present sutra.

Regarding "encouraging merit to prevent transgression": this causes those who have already slandered [the teaching] to refrain from slandering it; causes those who have not yet had faith to give rise to faith; and causes those who already have faith to progress further.
As for those who neither possess understanding nor faith and do not slander, they simply belong to the category of merit. Master Sengzong said: "Encouraging..."
Regarding the meaning of faith: since the power derived from the conditions of hearing this sutra is not shallow, how could one not give rise to deep faith?
As the sutra says, "A wooden head on a banner" means that it has no further use.
Regarding the mutual citation of one side: for both self-cultivation and the transformation of others, both must be present to constitute complete self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
"The Sūtra-śeṣa" (the remainder of the sūtra) refers to the "stages of the ten abodes," because its interpretation is identical to that of the ten abodes.
Regarding the transverse exposition of the three retributions: for the time being, looking from one birth toward another birth is termed "transverse.

Regarding the vertical exposition of the three obstructions: likewise, for the time being, considering the sequence of the three obstructions as they evolve from prior to subsequent stages is termed "vertical."
"To be near Bodhi" means to have already drawn near to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of Bodhi.
"To examine and warn" refers to clearly discerning the causes and effects for those who believe or slander [the Dharma].

Regarding the four reliances as being of great benefit: because the merit of widely proclaiming the four reliances is vast, they must be venerated. Liang said: "This clarifies the etiquette for honoring one's teacher.
The virtue of the four reliances is truly worthy of reverence; as it can engender goodness in people, it is appropriate to offer them worship."

Regarding the question that it "contains two meanings": the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) are such that their traces are obscured and cannot be distinguished individually. When the Buddha was about to speak, Kāśyapa posed the questions.
As for the inclusion of various matters, this is as explained by Hexi (Dharmakṣema). Furthermore, Dharmapāla also does not go beyond the two gates of the vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*).
This person who is fully endowed should be provided with offerings; this is what is meant by "simultaneous.
Regarding the principle of the heavy superseding the light: if one does not begrudge even the superior heavy [offering], how much less so the light?
If one follows the ancient dharma, then according to the fixed standards of the Hīnayāna teachings, one ought not to pay homage. Are these two principles merely differences of intention?
Or do the two intentions contradict each other?
The Sūtra states: "A bhikṣu who upholds the precepts... [down to] 'that which is transgressed. This refers to one who, by means of worldly etiquette, violates the person who has broken the precepts;

thus it is called a transgression. However, within the text, there are only two meanings: paying homage to those above and maintaining the precepts while paying homage to those below. If one takes the distinct points according to their meaning, all three meanings are fully present.
Regarding the passage in the sutra that says, "Also in other sutras," it is stated in former scriptures that [the teachings] are contradictory. Daolang said: "Two teachings cannot both be real;
one must necessarily be true and the other false. Though one may maintain the precepts oneself, if one does not rectify those who break them, one will not save the Dharma when it is about to perish;
such a person is not my disciple. If one does not even correct those who commit the most serious transgressions, how much less should they be worthy of veneration?"
Regarding the principle that "the text is brief while the meaning is expansive": the text merely states, "He spoke this verse for the sake of a bodhisattva. This constitutes the brevity of the text.

Since it specifies "for the sake of a bodhisattva," it thereby grants permission to bodhisattvas; by using this to refute [the objection] regarding the act of holding [the precepts], it establishes that those of higher status pay homage to those of lower status, and that those who have left the household life pay homage to laypeople—this is what is meant by the expansiveness of the meaning.
Regarding the "doubts of the three threes": the doubts concerning the three concentrations, the three difficulties, and the three fetters are all dispelled.
However, in responding to this specific point, one must uphold the ritual and refute the single [opposing] position.

Regarding what was stated above: it refers to the passage in the aforementioned sutra where the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when such sutras as these and the True Dharma are about to perish," and so forth. This is that text.
"To increase what is non-Dharma" means that when the dharmas of greed, hatred, and delusion increase, it is called "non-Dharma.
As the Sūtra says: "All noble ones remain hidden"; this means that when the Buddha-dharma is extinguished, all noble ones completely withdraw into seclusion.
As for those who cause others to be turbid, one should cause those turbid people to become non-turbid.

For those who have not yet obtained the opportune moment, the moment is not yet appropriate for correction; rather, one should harmonize with their turbid radiance so that the Great Dharma may be proclaimed and spread widely.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances all first act in conformity and later differ; they manifest as breaking the precepts and manifest as holding false views.

These are shown as being drawn forth [by the teaching]. All are taken according to the capacity and opportunity of the individual to be guided and brought to maturity; once they have entered the perfect and eternal state, the power that draws them forth ceases.

Thus, even those who break the precepts are called "those who break [the precepts]" by virtue of their name alone; it does not mean that they perform acts of breaking the precepts through the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*).

"Having explained those who uphold and those who violate [the precepts]" refers to the meaning of a preceding passage. Two interpretations must be provided: first, an interpretation regarding upholding and violating;
second, an interpretation regarding the opening of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. "The Crown Prince" is also called the "Eastern Palace" (Donggong) and is further termed the "Deputy Second."
Master Sengsheng said: "Examining antiquity, there are practices that are truly worthy of veneration; it is only because people have not yet recognized them that they are called 'young' or 'immature.

From this point downward, he [the Master] will lead from the led, refuting the heterodox to enter the orthodox, such as using impermanence to refute permanence, and permanence to refute impermanence, and so forth."

All must pass through the Dharma-gates employed in the teachings of the five periods; until one reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* to enter the reality [of the ultimate teaching], one uses these to resolve such passages as that concerning the "youth.
Regarding the term *caṇḍāla*, Master Sengzhao said it means "to harm"; it refers to that which harms the life-force of wisdom.
The Sūtra says: "Mù" (mound) means "to take. As for those like trees, these are persons of inferior capacity who cannot discipline those who have broken the precepts;
they merely undergo birth and death within [the cycle] themselves, just like a tree.
Those of middling capacity are likewise.
Regarding "exercising authority" and so forth: when guards and patrols prevent virtuous people who uphold the precepts from entering, it is called "exercising authority.
When they perform the duties of those who maintain the precepts while themselves violating them, it is called "performing merit."
Regarding the "drum tied for seven days," Huilang said: "Knowing that the bhikṣus cannot be restrained by force, he wished to govern the Saṃgha according to the Vinaya.
If there were those with offenses, he would have the Saṃgha informed through the seven methods for settling disputes."
Those who have long been noble are those whose conduct has long been lofty and strict; they are the families of pure practice (*brahmacarya*).
When a sovereign abdicates the throne of the state, there are always books of abdication, along with golden chests and jade seals.
To "seek a *karmavācanā*-master" means to seek a person who maintains the precepts.
"Half the kingdom" refers to those who collectively oversee monastic affairs, being like half a kingdom.
Regarding "Udāyin and others," the third fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) states: "Regarding the matter of strife, why [is it] by three?"

The settling of disputes is as follows: wherever there is a dispute involving signs of contention or verbal quarreling, this matter should be entrusted to a *tāla-vṛtta* (a monk of upright conduct), who should receive it and settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching. Such a settlement is called "settled.

If one is unable to resolve this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, it should be relinquished and entrusted to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha, moreover...
If [the dispute] cannot be settled, at that time the Saṃgha should, within the assembly, appoint two *āvāsika* monks through a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to resolve this matter.
There are ten qualities by which a monk should be qualified as an *āvāsika* and appointed by the Saṃgha: he knows the place where the dispute arose and its origin;
he is well-versed in disputes; he is able to analyze disputes; he knows the causes and conditions giving rise to disputes; and he knows the meaning of disputes.
They skillfully extinguish disputes and, having extinguished them, ensure they do not arise again. They maintain pure precepts, possess extensive learning, and possess great wisdom;

thus, the Saṃgha should appoint these two, Riṭa and Uvāha, to settle the matter through a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation), in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
Therefore, this is identical to the case of the regular monks and the entire Saṃgha.

Regarding the statement, "Long hair signifies compassion," Liang said: "Hair grows on the human head; it is considered beautiful when long. Life occupies the foremost place among virtues, and constancy is regarded as supreme.
The general meaning is the same.
"The king was greatly delighted" refers to a temporary joy; before long, he will abandon the heterodox and return to the Right Path.
"He does not see anything to be loathed" refers to the anger of one who truly practices and maintains the precepts.
As for my "abandoning the ways of the household," it means that while I should have remained in the great response, I instead went toward those of lesser capacity.
Acting as a being who breaks the precepts, I first conformed to evil dharmas while secretly revealing the True Dharma, serving as their *karmācārya*.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra beginning with "The Former King" and ending with "the medicine": the "Former King" refers to the Cāṇḍāla king.

Originally, he summoned the Master, boasting that he possessed the immortal medicine of the Thirty-three Heavens and inviting him to share it. The Master requested a young boy; however, the boy said, "I am one who has broken the precepts.
Below me resides the wondrous medicine of the permanent abode (saṃgha), which we have not yet shared. Thereupon, the Cāṇḍāla king immediately treated him as his livestock.

Regarding "pure things," there are textual explanations concerning fame, profit, and offerings; therefore, it says, "I truly do not know. [Daosheng] said: "That which was possessed by the former Buddhas as the 'Eternal Dharma' is called the 'Medicine of Immortality.
It is stored within the Sūtra-piṭaka. Because its cultivation and study differ from others, it is called 'not shared,' meaning that one should not be stingy regarding it."

Regarding the assembly that has broken the precepts: because the great capacity within the assembly that broke the precepts has been secretly awakened, it causes them to maintain [the precepts] within the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), so that the Buddha-nature may be freely revealed and explained to them.
The Sūtra says, "Those who heard the King's words" indicates that their great capacity for awakening had been secretly activated.
The Sūtra says, "They immediately took it and returned home," which demonstrates that the secret treasury originally exists within the five aggregates; hence, it is called "taking it back."

Regarding those who undergo rigorous discipline according to the Vinaya: it is not yet appropriate for them to practice the subtle contemplation of the true nature (*dharmatā*). For now, they should rely on the teachings of the Hīnayāna Vinaya to perform repentance with utmost sincerity.
This is to first employ the contemplation of impermanence as an aid to perfecting the investigation of the True Dharma.
Regarding "phenomena and principle": one first employs the contemplation of impermanent phenomena to establish the principles of impermanence, permanence, and so forth.

As for "those of middle capacity who awaken," this uses the analogy of the king to represent those of middle and lower capacities; it does not mean that the king’s own body entering the path serves as the metaphor for awakening.
The Sūtra says, "It is like a dead man. This means that once false views have been shattered, the great capacity [for enlightenment] awakens in the darkness; hence it is said to be "like death.
The passage in the Sūtra establishing the original crown prince below serves as a metaphor for the opening of the provisional (the *upāya*).
The "Lion Throne" refers to the place where the Lion King sits; how could it be ascended by a jackal?

As for the phrase in the sutra, "one who masters the principles": "sutra" refers to the beginning and end, while "principles" means systematic organization. It signifies using the beginning and end to organize those of heterodox views, causing them to return to the correct path.

Regarding "thoroughly determining through discernment": in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), once a grave offense has been committed, there is no further possibility of repentance; therefore, it is called "determined.
As for the sūtra's statement that one does not lose the dharma of a brāhmaṇa, this means one does not lose the dharma of a brāhmaṇa’s dignified deportment.
The Sūtra states, "the remaining householders," which praises those who observe the precepts at the middle or lower levels.
The Sūtra states, "if one is able to expel them," because one can skillfully cause them to abandon error and enter into the correct path.

Regarding the term "miscellaneous items" (*shiwu*) mentioned in the sutra: *shi* means "mixed" or "various," and it also implies "accumulation. Thus, what the sutra permits one to possess are precisely the eight impure things;
these constitute the "miscellaneous items."
"Defiling the Path" means defiling the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
"Defiling Dignified Conduct" refers to the specific names listed in detail in the *Sujāta-upāsaka-sūtra*: first, maintaining fields and houses; second, planting and cultivating roots and sprouts;
third, storing up rice and millet and seeking profit from the boundaries of one's land; fourth, maintaining male and female slaves and subjects; fifth...
1. Raising herds of livestock; 2. Accumulating gold, silver, money, and treasures; 3. Accumulating ivory and various precious large couches, cotton mattresses, and wool carpets;
4. Accumulating all kinds of copper and iron cauldrons and pots. By accumulating these eight types of things, one defiles pure precepts;
therefore, it is said that they "defile one's dignified demeanor."

If one deviates from this teaching, and if one does not first act in conformity with others and later differ from them for the sake of causing others to reform their evils, repent, and enter the Great [Vehicle]—
if one does not do so, then there is fault.

The Sūtra says, "By those who are without pride": the Bodhisattva originally has no transgressions, yet manifests as if performing repentance; therefore, it is said that this is not called breaking the precepts.
The Sūtra says, "Speaking by concealing the true aspect": this refers to the provisional teachings found in former sūtras.
The Sūtra says, "Like those in the Second Heaven. This means that just as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven serve Śakra, so too is the case here. Regarding "dikes and embankments" (*tī-táng*):
the precepts are like dikes and embankments, while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are like water.

If there were no Four Reliances (*catur-niśraya*) to bring about the transformation from evil to good in the world, then the dike of the precepts would be destroyed and the waters of concentration and wisdom would be exhausted. [The characters *tí* (pronounced *cháng chóu fǎn*; meaning "obstructing") and *táng* (pronounced *dù jí fǎn*; meaning "embankment")] refer to the [damaging] leaking of the dike. It is precisely...
The character "lin" (林) may also be pronounced as "lin" (呼), though here it follows the reading "suǒjìn" (所禁).

As for the statement that "if one does not repent, one loses [the precepts]," the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) are likewise subject to repentance; this is done in order to lead those who practice according to the truth.
"I am like the main rope. Liang said: "I am the one who guards the precepts; this is a distinct matter for those of the Vehicle.
Once the main framework is established, all practices are thereby set forth.
As for the 'distinct record,' it is as explained in the ten sections of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*."

The Sūtra states that there are four kinds of persons: those who follow the four reliances (catur-niśraya) appear outwardly like evildoers, yet are inwardly matured while remaining outwardly immature;
pure bhikṣus who maintain the precepts are matured both inwardly and outwardly; and those who are inwardly born of evil are bhikṣus who are immature both inwardly and outwardly.
It is like a foolish, ordinary person who, when appointed as an administrator, does not recognize those capable of receiving and managing people;
failing to distinguish between the worthy and unworthy among the Sangha, they treat all alike in providing offerings, thereby unable to serve as a field of merit for others.
The Sūtra says, "One who recites 'shi' (market). Daoliang explained: "A market is a place for trade; it is a metaphor for the household of a donor.
It carries the sense of mutual support, whereby [the goods] are divided to provide offerings for the Saṃgha."
The merit arises from the requester; this is analogous to selling.
"Various medicines (until) not distinguished" means that those who have broken the precepts are difficult to distinguish.
When the Sūtra says "one should rely on the four dharmas," it should be stated as "in the past, one should rely on the four dharmas. "Liangwu" refers to lying on *pú* grass.
One does not eat the *yǔn* or *ruò* grasses for mats. Because these grasses resemble the inner [seeds], they are not eaten.
Regarding those of the past who were impermanent, although they were indeed "releasing" [the past], each and every one of them was consistent with the four dharmas explained in the present sutra.
It is precisely because those of the past were impermanent that they still received the dharma of impermanence; they did not rely on the person, and thus they did not rely on [the person].
The Dharma; the same applies to the other three.
If speech were to give rise to attachment, even speech from the past would not be called "attached. This is because it is viewed in light of the Great Dharma of the present;

therefore, while the meaning of the body of the past is termed "attached," its essence is without attachment. The lower meaning of the past Dharma is the True Truth (*satya*), which is non-attached within its own respective sphere. If...
To have expectations regarding it is itself called attachment. If it were not attachment, why did the two selves not advance directly to the place of treasure in the past?

Now, the essence of the Dharma is free from attachment; attachment arises from the human consciousness. That which is attached was previously the conceptualization of impermanence, arising and ceasing.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) cannot see the nature; therefore, it is called "attachment.

As for "understanding through wisdom" (*jñāna-vimukti*): that which was formerly able to destroy the afflictions of the four abodes is called "wisdom. If it cannot see the nature, even this wisdom is called "attachment.
Now, if analyzed from the perspective of discrimination, it is also termed "consciousness"; thus, that which is able to see the nature is "understanding through wisdom."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "These four dharmas, etc.," the Buddha formerly commanded reliance upon four kinds of dharma and not reliance upon persons.

Yet it is said that he only commanded reliance upon persons and did not mention reliance upon dharma. Is this reliance upon dharma or reliance upon persons? Therefore, please provide a comprehensive reconciliation of these points.
The Sūtra says, "Relying on the Dharma. This clarifies that there is no distinction between the Dharma of the past and the present.
In the past, there was no person apart from the Dharma; today, there is likewise no Dharma apart from the person. The Dharma of the past is precisely the Dharma of the present.
Therefore, it is stated that the Dharma of the past is itself the person and the Dharma of the present; hence it is said, "The Dharma is the Tathāgata."
The bonds are further resolved by relying on wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom is able to know phenomena (*dharma*) and discern their depth and shallowness; therefore, one must rely on wisdom.
As for the statement that "the ancients have already broken [them]," "breaking" means opening.
Regarding the non-duality of person and dharma: the Tathāgata is the dharma-nature of nirvāṇa, and the dharma-nature is the Tathāgata.
This is so even within the stage of mere names; how much more so in the stage of reality—how could there be duality?
If one attains awakening, this is explained according to the revelation of the provisional (*upāya*). For what reason?

If one already understands that even impermanence is itself the ultimate equality, how much more so can the non-duality of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-advaya*) be eliminated? Furthermore, it is not only that the former teachings are the secret treasury; persons themselves are also the Tathāgata.

Regarding the praise of virtues: when the words of the sūtra reach this point, one should first say, "Thus, these four persons," and only then may one say, "If one says that the Tathāgata is impermanent," and so forth.
When the sūtra says, "This person... [up to]... esoteric speech," this is a semblance understanding; it is able to pervade all with a single sublime sound.
Regarding the phrase "and able to preach" in reference to the three thousandfold world system:
one who is not swayed by gain or offerings means that even if such a person receives offerings, upon hearing another say that the Tathāgata is impermanent,
they will ultimately never believe or accept it, nor will they be led astray by that other person.
The Sūtra states, "This is called the definitive meaning," because it fears that future generations might harbor doubts; therefore, it definitively demonstrates it.
The Sūtra states, "Do not rely on the words," because in the past, there was no substantiality to the Three Jewels, and thus one did not rely [on them].
That which is not weak or inferior is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Since the Dharma-body is the adamantine body (*vajrakāya*), it is without weakness or inferiority.

That which is fulfilled is liberation (*vimukti*). Just as when the causes are perfected and the fruit is full, one is able to manifest bodies and preach the Dharma in all places to discipline sentient beings.
Furthermore, while this specifically corresponds to liberation, according to principle, "fulfillment" applies universally to the other two virtues as well.

Regarding the arising of the faults of ordinary persons: the Buddha taught expedient sutras, which ordinary persons do not understand; consequently, they give rise to the faults of attachment, grasping, and frivolous ornamentation.
Therefore, these [sutras] cannot be relied upon. Furthermore, the various treatises are the words of heterodox paths and false views.
"Ornamentation" refers to worldly speech that is devoid of meaning.
"Insatiable greed for seeking" refers to the speech of bhikṣus who follow the letter [of the teaching] while engaging in wrong livelihood.
As for the phrase in the Sūtra, "furthermore, they proclaim," this refers to speech that slanders the Dharma while conforming to one's own desires.
In the world of famine described below, one who speaks of slander regarding the precepts according to the occasion is a true wise person;
this refers to one who has partially realized True Wisdom. This also applies to those at the stage of "name-and-character" (nāma-rūpa), as mentioned above.
The Sūtra says, "In accordance with one's own mind," referring to the secret treasury of the mind of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), which reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate,
wherein one dwells securely in the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) with unimpeded sovereignty.
The Sūtra further says, "If it is said that the Tathāgata enters the Dharma, or if it is said that the Tathāgata abides in his own secret treasury-dharma through the conditions of transformation."
"The middle" refers to the teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). "Discerning the tenets" refers to discerning the tenets of the preceding five pairs.
The passage from the Sūtra beginning with "Thus, these four reliances... up to "...should be known through realization" concludes that one should rely upon these four reliances.
The Sūtra states: "Named 'Radiance' (Guāngmíng) below. It is the complete possession of the Three Jewels. Radiance is the Buddha Jewel;
invincibility is the Dharma Jewel; and the Tathāgata is the Sangha Jewel.

"Furthermore, as for the two kinds of summations (*saṃdhi*): this clarifies that the first [summation] relies on the meaning (*artha*) and the teaching (*dharma*), explaining only the present without reference to the past;

therefore, the third [summation] is performed. It does not rely on the words (*vyañjana*), but returns to the first summation which relies on the meaning—this is relying primarily on the meaning and slightly on the words.
Now, the intention of contrasting the present with the past is fulfilled. The second summation is performed, which does not rely on the person (*pudgala*), but returns to the first."
The text relies on the Dharma and relies on the person; the meaning is complete when the ancient and the modern are contrasted.

It is solely because the two passages within the summary section are intermingled that they result in a division into two parts. Furthermore, because the passage relying on the Dharma does not have its own distinct heading, it must be stated that both reliances provide a joint explanation.

The Sūtra states regarding those who fall into Avīci: because provisional teachings cannot cause sentient beings to transcend the transformation-death (pariṇāmi-śarīra), they instead cause them to fall into the pit of the three unconditioned states (asaṃskṛta); this is termed "falling into hell."
"Those who must possess [an item] through two conditions" refers to the fact that for the other three matters, its use would constitute an offense (*pātayantika*).

First, the "pure gift" (*viśuddha-dāna*) must never be omitted; hence it is said there are "two conditions. Furthermore, this present sutra should fully possess four conditions before it can be considered definitive (*nītārtha*).

Even if one were to exclude the single matter of having no donor (*dānapati*), the remaining three must necessarily be complete. All must state "for the sake of establishing the True Dharma" before one may possess such items. Zhezhou said:

1. One should observe that if a disciple possesses heavy items belonging to donors (*dānapati*), the Tathāgata prohibits them; if they have none, he permits their possession. 2. Although there may be no donors, if it is a time of abundance, he prohibits them;
if it is a time of scarcity, he permits their possession. 3. Although it may be a time of scarcity, if one does not act for the sake of protecting the Dharma, the Tathāgata prohibits it;

if one acts for its protection, he permits their possession. 4. Although one may act for the protection of the Dharma, if one does not perform the ritual of "purification" (*viśuddhi-dāna*), the Tathāgata prohibits it; if one performs the purification, he permits it.
It is permitted to keep [them]. Among these four, that which is prohibited by the Tathāgata is called "heavy," while that which is permitted by the Tathāgata is called "light.
These four dharmas are those upon which one should rely.
Regarding "obstructing the internal and external": the fleshly eye sees the internal, while the divine eye sees the external.
When the Sūtra says "that which is the dharma-nature," it refers to the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the meaning [from] "unchanging" on down, it refers to the meaning of the dharma-nature. "Wisdom" is the wisdom of the Buddha. It is like the *ālaya*... [etc.]
The *ālayavijñāna* is termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) at the causal stage, but is termed "Great Perfect Wisdom" (*mahāvaipulyajñāna*) upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood.
Regarding "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*), both that which is expressed and the expressions themselves within the Mahāyāna are termed "definitive."

The "Chapter on the Perverse and the Authentic" consists of five sections according to the text: first, the dual introduction; second, the dual explanation beginning with "Next, the perverse demons..."; third, the indication of the scope of the response beginning with "This chapter...";

fourth, the brief restatement of the textual intent beginning with "Relying on..."; and fifth, the formal explanation of the text beginning with "The text as...". The subsequent dual explanation further divides into two parts.

First, the heterodox is explained; next, the orthodox is explained below. Regarding the initial passage: first, the heterodox faction envies the orthodox, and Māra disturbs the true path, thereby deluding beginners.
Therefore, it is appropriate to discern their characteristics, establishing names based on what they signify. "Weightiness" (*gurutva*) and so forth refer to evil causes;
the "four miserable destinies" (*catur-gati*) and so forth refer to evil effects.

Regarding "perverse worldly people": those who, upon the causes and effects of the twenty-five states of existence, further give rise to causes of suffering and fruits of suffering, are therefore called perverse worldly people.
As for "practitioners of the past": if it is said that the Tathāgata truly practiced asceticism in the past, this is the teaching of Māra. If it is said...
To manifest the practice of asceticism in order to transform sentient beings is what the Buddha taught. Regarding the "gradual" practitioner:
such an individual, while in the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), first discriminates the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Having entered and abided therein, they destroy the conventional;

then, having already entered and abided in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they subsequently enter the provisional (*prajñapti*) rather than remaining in emptiness. They discriminate within the provisional until the final moment of mind in the tenth stage of dedication (*daśama-praṇidhāna*), at which point they finally abandon the two [extremes].
To seek the Middle Way within the extremes, it is said that one "discriminates between distinct categories," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "also the māras of samādhi" and so on, as stated in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) of the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of māras: first, the māra of elimination, because it gives rise to various forms of grasping; second, the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*)."

1. Because of the defilement of birth; 2. Because of the obstacle posed by the demon of karma (*karma-māra*) which prevents [the attainment of] liberation; 3. Because of the demon of the mind (*citta-māra*) which gives rise to arrogance;
4. Because of the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*) which abandons the place of birth; 5. Because of the demon of the celestial beings (*deva-māra*) who are self-indulgent and arrogant; 6.

Because of the demon of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-māra*) which constantly clings to that which is grasped; 7. Because of the demon of meditative absorption (*samādhi-māra*) due to long-standing attachment to its flavor; 8. Because of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Because Māra gives rise to a mind of attachment. Tenth, because the Māra of the wisdom of the Dharma of Bodhi never abandons [the practitioner].
Because it is abandoned, it is called "equal" and so forth. There is a distinct teaching of the "Middle Only," which is the solitary, pure True Suchness that lacks the conditions and causes.
The non-fusion of the primary and the secondary is called ignorance.

Next, regarding the explanation of the "four perversions" within the primary [reality]: having already cited this present sutra to establish their characteristics, there is no need to further cite scriptural passages to re-demonstrate them;
it is sufficient that the overturning of perversion is itself the correct. Furthermore, the essence of the four perversions possesses its...
These two directions thus constitute two meanings. What are they? Based on the side of those such as the icchantikas, it is termed "evil and perverse.
Based on the side of adhering to what is correct so as not to allow people to leave the desire realm, it is termed "adherence to correctness. The remaining three cases are analogous.
As for the root of the various forms of heterodoxy (*mithyātva*): evil and heterodoxy are the objects observed by the latter three [perfections], and thus they belong to their root.

As for "ascending purity": this refers to the goodness of humans and devas, which is free from the turbidity of sinking into the four miserable destinies; furthermore, it gives rise to worldly goodness, hence it is called "ascending purity."
Regarding "deviant and partial": that which can destroy the causality of the six realms is called "true and correct.
Regarding "deviant and gradual": that which can overturn the reality of the middle and the extremes is called "square and upright."
Regarding the fifth explanation of the text, the Sūtra states: "One should rely on what is heterodox. This means that these four types of persons are able to subdue the four Māras;
thus, one should rely on what is heterodox as something not to be relied upon. This constitutes a question that arises from the preceding section.
Regarding the "next four reliances" mentioned above: this refers to the section on the four reliances that has not yet been reached.
As for "for the sake of the four assemblies and the four fruits," it means that Māra transformed himself into the likeness of these four reliances.
"To harbor malice within" means to destroy the bodhicitta.
"To harbor sinister schemes within" means to obstruct practitioners so that they cannot leave their realm and be born together with the gods.
Regarding the five aggregates of outflowlessness (*anāsrava-skandha*): Māra is able to transform them into the appearance of the five aggregates of outflowlessness.

One should observe them as the five aggregates of outflows, the five aggregates of wholesome phenomena, the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the five aggregates of the peerless (*asama*). Thus, one causes Māra’s deceptions not to prevail.
Regarding the two types of confused practitioners: if one speaks of taking seven steps in each of the ten directions, it is pronounced as "ping" (平).
If one speaks of former ascetic practices, it is pronounced as "qu" (去) with two tones, both of which are applicable.

Regarding the statement "non-arising arising": if one says that the Tathāgata truly arises, this is the teaching of Māra; if one says that for the sake of sentient beings (the *kai-en*), the Tathāgata does not arise yet arises, this is the teaching of the Buddha.

[This refers to] the act of boasting with empty chaff—using soft words to deceive others—and making grand, empty claims. (Note on terminology: *Fǔ* [pronounced *fù*] refers to a cooking vessel; its belly is large and it has handles. *Qiū* [pronounced *qī*] refers to a similar vessel;

it is open and lacks handles. *Bǐ* [pronounced *pí*] refers to appearance; it means using a compliant physical demeanor to deceive people. If *pí* is interpreted as "harmony," then *kuā* refers to speaking in great, boastful terms.)
Regarding the sixty-four arts, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states:

"The four Vedas contain the methods for treating illness, the methods for warfare, the methods for astrology, the methods for sacrificial rites to the gods, and the methods for song, dance, debate, and inquiry.

These and others constitute the sixty-four kinds of worldly crafts and skills. Prince Śuddhodana studied these extensively and was widely learned; if he knew such matters, it would not be considered extraordinary."

This is difficult [to establish]. However, within this present sutra, from the section on "spells for healing the body" (*kāya-cikitsā-mantra*) onwards, their characteristics are also briefly enumerated; it is simply that the number is incomplete.
As for the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*) together with their activities (*karman*), when the causes of the marks and the fruits of the marks are discussed in combination, they total sixty-four.

The Sūtra states that there are eighteen types of "doubting persons," ranging from those who rely on incantations to those who engage in painting images; these constitute the characteristics of the eighteen doubting persons.

The Sūtra further states that for committing a *duṣkṛta* offense, one will suffer for eight million years; this refers to the case where Maudgalyāyana asked about the commission of a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Just as a lifespan of five hundred years in the Heaven of the Four Kings corresponds to a fall into hell,
so too does a lifespan of eight million years in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven correspond to the present sutra; this is merely a difference in the conditions for those who rely upon the two vehicles,
the Great and the Small.

Regarding the phrase "conditions and causes, etc.": one should employ the condition of clear realization (*parijñāna-pratyaya*) so that the condition and clear realization together manifest the true nature (*dharmatā*).
As for the scriptural passage from "the ninefold canon" to "heterodox views," the intent of the question is as follows:

If, as the Buddha stated above, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet this has never been heard mentioned within the ninefold canon, and since it was not previously taught there, how can it now be said that they possess it? Is this not a contradiction?

"Not committing a *pārājika* offense" means that once one has awakened [to the error], one should repent; this refers to repentance through self-reproach (*citta-vinodana*). "Praising [the act] incurs guilt" means that it should not be considered a transgression.
"The 'Great' also serves as a prohibition" means that among the five primary colors, true red is prohibited. Master Bao says: "This refers to the Great..."
It is fully adorned, yet even this is insufficient; one should say "Mahālaṅkāra.

The Chapter on the Four Truths is divided into two parts according to the commentary text: first, the explanation of the title; second, from the text below, the explanation of the content. The first part also has three sections, the first of which demonstrates...

The response to the text follows, next describing the refutation of the three [positions]. Now, the correct interpretation of this section is clarified below. Next, the two positions of the Old [Commentary] are described:

first, it clarifies the differences between the two explanations of the present and the past; second, under "The Old [Commentary] again," it clarifies that there are differences regarding the principles and facts of the discernment of the truths across the five periods.

The first of these [two] also has two parts: first, the narration of the Old [position]; second, under "Now, the question," the raising of objections through inquiry. Regarding the first passage, Sengzong says:
The Four Noble Truths are the objects illuminated by wisdom. From what was taught at the Deer Park up to that of the *Lotus Sūtra*, there are great differences in their stages.
According to this teaching, the perfect and complete realization of the eternally abiding, wondrous cause necessarily relies upon the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way.
However, without an object, there would be no means to discern wisdom; therefore, the Four Noble Truths are cited to clarify the characteristics of the cause.
This interpretation is also refuted by the present commentary regarding the statement that "only those within the realm [are affected]. The refutation states:

"If the Path and Cessation can destroy what is within the realm, how is it that all four Truths are equally outside the realm? It further asks: "When you say they are 'outside the realm,' what do you mean by 'outside the three realms'?"
If it is said that "transformation" (pariṇāma) emerges, then only outside the triple world can it be called "wholesome.

Next, regarding the refutation of the "in-between," the statement that "the immeasurable also does not emerge from transformation" mostly refers to those at the stage prior to the ground (*bhūmi*) in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyākaraṇa*).

Regarding the statement that "the three are conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are conditioned and contaminated (*sāsrava*); the path (*mārga*) is conditioned and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);

cessation (*nirodha*) is unconditioned and uncontaminated. Since they thus possess both [conditioned and unconditioned] aspects, to designate them exclusively as "finite" (*pramita*) is logically untenable.
There still remains that which is subject to the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāma-vaiparītya-jarāmaraṇa*).

Since one is thus driven by this transformative death and rebirth, it is not the case that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fails to possess the three characteristics; rather, it does not preclude the continued existence of suffering (*duḥkha*), its origin (*samudaya*), and the path (*mārga*).
Next, the five periods are distinguished into two parts: first, the presentation; second, the refutation beginning with "Now, as for the question below.
Regarding the initial mention of the "five periods," it does not include the *Avataṃsaka*, and furthermore, it places the *Prajñāpāramitā* before the *Vaipulya*, as seen in other texts.
Regarding those who refute based on principle: they argue that within the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras there are also those newly entered who obtain small benefits;
since this is clearly a fact, how can you categorically judge it to belong solely to principle? Therefore, [your argument] cannot be used.

Regarding "entering contemplation (up to) the cessation of signs": beginning from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the stage of the highest mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one gradually takes as an object the untainted principle of tranquility, thereby causing the marks of the Four Noble Truths to vanish.

Next, regarding the refutation of the middle position, it says: "This has already been challenged as before. Since the transformation has not yet been eliminated, how can one perceive the nature? Therefore, it is refuted in the same manner as the previous [extreme].
If it were not of finite measure, one should have said: "If it is neither of finite measure nor of infinite measure. Why was the Middle Way not presented?
Since its essence does not emerge from its substance, it is verified that there is no separate principle.
Third, regarding the "Buddha-nature as the true mark" in the formal explanation: both of these pervade all places.
Regarding "being able [to understand] the four matters": this means that awakening (*bodhi*) is itself affliction (*kleśa*), which is named the Noble Truth of Origination;

nirvāṇa is itself birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), which is named the Noble Truth of Suffering; realizing that afflictions are themselves awakening is the Noble Truth of the Path; and realizing that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa is the Noble Truth of Cessation.
Awakening is the fruit of wisdom, and nirvāṇa is the fruit of abandonment; these are thus the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Therefore...
It is said that "the mind rejoices" means that explaining the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is precisely the clear realization of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Regarding "within the impure," this refers to true wisdom within the nine realms of the impure accumulation truth (samudaya-satya).
Regarding "within cessation": the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) of the Two Vehicles is precisely the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
That the Tathāgata appears in the world to preach this unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) reality is as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*:
"It is solely for the sake of the one great causal matter that he appears in the world. This is the true realization.
"Those concealed aspects now revealed" means that what was previously concealed is now revealed.

"The ointment of milk obtained through washing" means that formerly the impermanent was applied as the permanent; now, the revelation of the impermanent as being truly permanent is like the meaning of washing away the medicinal ointment of impermanence.

Regarding the statement that "in the two commentaries on the text, there is only [the matter of] sequence," etc.: there are only minor instances of non-sequence within the Chapter on the Truth of Cessation, which will be evident from the text itself.
As for "one is four": the one truth is the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Regarding "suffering due to lack of understanding": from the animal realm up to the stage prior to the Ground (bhūmi) according to the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna), all are caused by not knowing the realm of the Tathāgata—that suffering alone exists and has no reality.
This is thus "suffering in both senses" rather than [the noble truth of] suffering.

The Sūtra says, "Furthermore, there are those who do not know," and so forth. By citing their ignorance, it demonstrates the perfection of knowledge; this is precisely what is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

As for the statement that "the one is suffering but not a truth": ordinary beings possess only suffering and lack the truth, and because they do not perceive the Buddha-nature, it is said that [their experience] is not real.
Second, regarding "suffering is the truth": this clarifies that the Two Vehicles represent a discourse rather than reality, because they have not yet seen the Buddha-nature.
Third, regarding "neither suffering nor discourse": this refers to the stage of the Bodhisattva, which is used here to explain the fourfold true discourse of the present chapter.

The Sūtra states: "One should know that such a person... [up to] 'is afflicted by suffering. They will inevitably fall into the evil destinies; these are the fruits of the three miserable realms (triyāṇi). To transmigrate through birth and death is the fruit of humans and devas.
They increase the various fetters (saṃyojana) and further give rise to the causes of suffering, undergoing much affliction. Furthermore, they crave the fruits of suffering.
Alternatively, the former may be the fruit of fragmented existence (paricchinna-bhava), while the latter is the fruit of transformation (pariṇāma-vaśika-bhava); thus it is said, 'either the fruit.'"

The Sūtra says: "There are those who are able to know... up to the two characters [“know” and “see”]. Master Zhezhou said: "Knowing the permanent is seeing with the eyes; hearing the permanent is seeing with the ears.
'Permanent' refers to the permanence of the Dharma; 'abiding' refers to the abiding of the retribution."
The Sūtra states that those born in the heavens who have not yet attained contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) are "near" to being born in heaven;

those who subsequently attain liberation are "near" to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and "far" from the ultimate fruit (*phala*). This applies to all three lower truths (*satya*). Zeshou says: "In the former case, they are born in heaven because they have 'seen through hearing' (*śrutadṛṣṭi*);
in the latter case, they are said to be 'liberated' because they have finally attained 'realized vision' (*sākṣātkāradarśana*)."
The Sūtra says, "Truly practicing suffering. "True practice" refers to self-realization and entry [into the path], while "great benefit" refers to transforming others.
The Sūtra says, "If one does not know": this cites ignorance in order to manifest knowledge.
The Sūtra says, "one who does not give rise to true wisdom. This means that because one does not give rise to the understanding of the causes [of suffering], one lacks true wisdom.

The Sūtra says, "by these causes and conditions. This also refers to how, due to the causes and conditions of accepting impure things, one fails to see the Buddha-nature and wanders through the two types of death and so forth.
Furthermore, "not attaining birth in the heavens" means not attaining the reward of the flowers (the immediate fruit).
"And not attaining true liberation" means not attaining the fruit-reward of *nirvāṇa*.
As the Sūtra says, "If one can know... up to "...they are not different": from beginning to end they are not different; phenomenon and principle are not different; cause and effect are not different.
This is different. One who understands it in this way may be called a follower of the Noble Discourse (*ārya-śāstra*).

As for what the Sūtra calls the "Truth of the Cessation of Suffering" (*duḥkha-nirodha-satya*), it should rather be called the "Truth of the Cessation of the Accumulation of Suffering" (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodha-satya*). However, by mentioning only the fruit of suffering, one knows that there is a cause;
therefore, it is not stated in full.
The Sūtra says: "Those who are my disciples—if they are not thus, they are not my disciples. The Sūtra speaks of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
these are the Three Jewels as a single essence (*ekakāya*), which serve as the objects of focus (*ālambana-viṣaya*).

One cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) within this realm of the Three Jewels, attaining complete and thorough knowledge of each and every aspect. Liberation (*vimukti*), which is eternally abiding and unchanging, is likewise the goal toward which one proceeds.
Regarding the statement, "That is to say, cause and effect are both eternal, truly bound, and [only] extinguished by the Path":

if this passage were intended as a summary of the Four Noble Truths, it should have been divided into two parts at the beginning of the formal explanation—first the correct principle, and second, from "True Vision" onwards, the non-summary.
However, since each Truth here follows the same pattern of six textual units, such a division is unnecessary; yet, even if one were to divide them, there would be no fault.

The Chapter on the Four Perversions consists of two parts according to the text: first, the explanation of the title; second, the formal explanation of the text below. The first part further has two sections: first, a general explanation;

second, a specific explanation of the "perversions" alone. Regarding the initial statement, "furthermore, it reveals the meaning of 'alternatively' (*vā*)," this cites the passage from the *Śokavinodanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Dispelling Sorrow) that returns the blame.
O monks, this chapter is established to clarify the characteristics of inverted delusion; thus it is said, "furthermore, it reveals.

Furthermore, whereas the preceding section cited the objects to illustrate wisdom, this section clarifies delusion to reveal its resolution. Next follows the detailed explanation, which naturally consists of six parts.

Within that, there are two sections: first, the enumeration of headings; second, the explanation beginning with "First," and so forth. This section further contains two parts: first, the demonstration of the characteristics; second, the passage beginning with "Since the Buddha appeared in the world."
The following clarifies the causes for the arising of perversions. Regarding the first point, "lao-long" (羅籠) refers to being bound by ignorance itself and thus lacking self-mastery;
hence the term is used.
"Views, perceptions, and grasping" refers to the arbitrary conceptualizations of ordinary people and non-Buddhists concerning the self, the body, and so forth.
"Adherence through views" refers to seeking nirvana in a perverted manner, taking non-perception as the ultimate goal.

"The frantic and the perverse" (the character *jù* is pronounced *miàn* and *qù*; it denotes being swift, lame, or urgent; its correct form is written as *juàn*, which is identical to the preceding character).
Regarding the term "numerous": whenever the mind deviates from principle, every such instance serves as an example; hence it is called "numerous.

As for the statement regarding the inverted truths (*viparyāsa-satya*): they are established as inverted through the causes and conditions of delusion, whereas they are explained as truths through the causes and conditions of understanding.

Next, the explanation of the causes for [this misconception] is divided into two parts. First, the causes are explained; second, from "When the Buddha first appeared" onwards, the methods for establishing treatment are explained.

Regarding the first point, "clinging to the words while losing the meaning": outsiders cling to permanence, bliss, self, and purity, yet they merely obtain these names without grasping the principle of permanence and so forth.
The followers of the Two Vehicles cling to impermanence and so forth, yet they do not know that impermanence itself is bliss, self, and purity.
This refers to the principle that all things are impermanent and so forth; hence it is said that "the intent is established.

Regarding the subsequent statement in the *Zhizhong* (Treatise on Curing) that "it pervades both before and after," this means that whether it be a Buddha of the past or a Buddha of the future, all first employ the remedy of impermanence and the like.

Regarding "the absence of perverted views where there is no truth": one penetrates the nature of the path of birth and death as being equivalent to nirvāṇa, and further penetrates [the truths] such as impermanence.

As for how these are mutually established: it is through the understanding of perversion that the truths are established, and it is through delusion that perversion is established, as explained in the sutra itself.

Regarding the statement that "the four categories are established through mutual integration," the intended meaning is as follows: it is only by employing all three categories together that the cause of wholesome karma is established;

hence, they are called "correctly wholesome. When the capacity for accomplishment fully brings about the cause of wholesome karma, these three categories serve as the "accomplisher" (*sādhana*) and the category of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) serves as the "accomplished" (*sādhya*).
Because the accomplisher and the accomplished are discussed in combination, they are referred to as "four categories."
If one recognizes only the person who enters, one ought to recognize both the person and the entry.

Just as when one fully understands the inversion of the truths (*satya-viparyāsa*), if one recognizes only the person, it constitutes recognizing the correct while failing to recognize the false; if one recognizes only the entry, it is like recognizing the false while failing to recognize the correct.

"Boat" (*hang*) refers to the conventional (*samvṛti*); "person" (*ren*) refers to the false (*mithyā*) and the inverted (*viparyāsa*). One should understand that "boat" is for the sake of the "person," and that the "person" is the boat made of gold.
Just as when one understands the inverted to be the conventional truth, one is then said to possess full knowledge.
Next, in the formal explanation, the Sūtra states: "If there should be those who say that by not cultivating emptiness and stillness one attains long life," Rāṣṭrapāla asks:

"The preceding passage stated that abstaining from killing, eating meat, and so forth are the causes for long life; why now is the cultivation of emptiness said to be the cause for long life? He replies:
"The causes for a Buddha’s long life must consist of the simultaneous cultivation of both merit and wisdom. The preceding passage was based on merit."
This text is based on the *Hui* (Wisdom) commentary; each relies on its own specific gate, and thus they do not contradict one another.

This is the third volume of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra-Private-Notes*, transcribed on the first day of the fifth month in the summer of the fourth year of the Shōhō era, based on the manuscript of the monk Jōshin.
Private Notes on the Commentary to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Four.
Commentary on Fascicle Six. The commentary on the "Chapter on the Nature of the Tathāgata" consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the title; second, the word-by-word exegesis following the response. The first part contains nine sections. First: [The text continues with the specific doctrinal analysis.]

1. The formal explanation (*samyak-vyākhyā*). 2. Next, "The various masters... and below: Refuting the ancient [interpretations]. 3. "The people of the third stage... and below: Narrating the explanations provided by the people of that stage. 4. Fourth, "Furthermore, in the treatise...
and below: Judging the errors. 5. Fifth, "Now, to clarify... and below: Re-explaining to manifest the essential meaning of the title. 6. Sixth, "In response to an interjection...

and below: Resolving doubts. 7. Seventh, "A certain master... and below: Describing the sequence of the arising [of the text]. 8. Eighth, "However, this chapter... and below: Presenting the text of the correct answer. 9. The person of the treatise.

The following is an ancient commentary. It consists of two parts: first, an explanation based on the nature of the fruit; second, an explanation based on the nature of the cause, beginning with the passage "Furthermore, as for the Tathāgata...

Regarding the first point, the phrase "in agreement with the three periods of time" means that all Buddhas arrive at the realization of perfect enlightenment by riding upon the path of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-mārga*).
Therefore, it is said they are "in agreement with the three periods of time"; "not different" refers to the world itself.

Regarding the practice of citing the beginning to indicate what follows: "the beginning" refers to the Tathāgata, who is none other than the subsequent Bhagavān. To speak precisely, he is designated as such because he proclaims the ten epithets for the sake of producing wholesome states in sentient beings;
therefore, this belongs to the category of *puruṣakāra* (human effort).
"Destroying all divergent views" refers to destroying the divergent views of the three vehicles and non-Buddhists; therefore, it belongs to the category of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
Furthermore, the first meaning of "the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) as presented below is easily understood.

Next, regarding the initial passage of the explanation based on the nature of the cause: the Buddha and sentient beings are different in terms of cause and effect, yet by showing their difference, their sameness is revealed; therefore, it belongs to [the category of]...
The world. Furthermore, regarding the "root of the fruit" (*phala-mūla*), the lower [part] refers to humans; this is an explicit mention of the hidden principle of the arising of goodness.

Moreover, regarding "nature-principle" (*dharmatā-yukti*) and below, it refers to the remedial application (*pratipakṣa*). It exalts the excellence of the Tathāgata-nature and abandons the inferiority of the nine dharma-realms, causing them to enter into the single nature;
therefore, it belongs to the remedial application. The term "Tathāgata" in the text applies generally to the first meaning (*paramārtha*).
Regarding "revealing [the truth] to people according to [their capacity]": because one rides upon their potential to benefit sentient beings, it is called "revealing to people.
Next, the refutation of the ancient [view] has two parts: first, the introduction; second, the meaning. Both are refuted below.
The initial statement that "those who can avoid suffering and seek happiness" is precisely what is refuted by this very remark. Why? Because the essence of Buddha-nature is all-pervasive;
how could there be "this" and "that"? Now, that which is "this" and "that" is entirely impermanent, and therefore does not possess the meaning of "nature."

Next, regarding the statement in the "Refutation" (Pòzhōng) section, "not by means of mind, spirit, and so forth": since the six dharmas and so on will be explained in their own context later in the text, they cannot be used to explain this present chapter; therefore, they are not employed here.

Regarding the three sections of the commentary on the "Stages of the Sequence" (Kramabhūmi), there are first the introduction, second, the brief refutation beginning with "This meaning is not so," and third,
the concluding judgment beginning with "I privately say," which serves to expose the error.
"It is not that there is no single side" means that the masters of the treatise are not without understanding the meaning of the distinct teaching; therefore, it is called "a single side.

Furthermore, while the aforementioned masters conceived of the mind and spirit as six dharmas, they only attained one side—either the internal or the external. Now, Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external, yet it is both internal and external;
for this reason, the ancient explanations are not employed.
Regarding the four judgments on errors, those who rely exclusively on the "inherently existing" (benyou) establish only the direct cause (zhengyin), lacking the conditions for development (yuanliao).
Those who rely exclusively on the conditions for development merely speak of the six dharmas of the sentient being's mind and spirit; thus, they belong to the conditions for development.
However, because the direct cause lacks substance when divorced from the conditions for development, it cannot be employed.
Regarding that which accords with the fruit: since the future fruit does not extend back to the cause, it is not employed here.
It is like those blind men touching an elephant; each obtains only the tail or the ear, thereby missing the true body of the elephant.

In the fifth section, the "Explanation of the Title," it says: "How could it be that there is only a single dharma? This refers to those who rely exclusively on a single dharma [claiming] that such-and-such is the Buddha-nature, while asserting that it does not fall under the following four propositions.
If one grasps the meaning of the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold purposes), then these four propositions may be explained interchangeably, and all will be universally applicable to the *pitakas*.
Below, it is clarified that within the "Gate of Existence" (*youmen*), the benefits of the four *siddhāntas* are fully present.
Because there are those who sever [the truth] by means of existence, for the sake of generating the principle of the correct view of annihilationism, the Buddha-nature is taught as "existence.
Because there are those who destroy permanence by means of existence, the Buddha-nature is taught as a true, eternal, and wondrous existence to refute arbitrary conceptualizations.
Those who hold the view of permanence belong to the category of those for whom this serves as an antidote.
From "Awakening to Buddha-nature" down to "is not existent," it clarifies that Buddha-nature is the principle that is penetrated, while the four gates are the means by which it is penetrated;
therefore, it is said that "Buddha-nature is not existent."
It is like a person asking about a bridge. As stated in the third fascicle of the Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra:
"In the past, when I was a bhikṣu, there was a householder who established a great assembly for almsgiving.

For all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, and the lowly, he provided whatever they required—precious jewels, clothing, food, and drink. At that time, because I was poor, I went to the site of the assembly."
On the way, he saw a great bridge. Upon that bridge, he saw a great multitude of people hurrying back and forth.
At that time, among the people was a wise man who, with his own foolish mind, asked those people:
"By whom was this bridge made? From where does it come? Where is it now heading? From what forest were these timbers produced?"
"By whom was it cut? By which elephant was it carried? Is this wood a green pine or a white pine?
Having thus answered seven thousand eight hundred questions in succession, the wise man then said to me: "Fie, foolish śramaṇa! Householder, I invited you to simply walk along the road;
you would have reached the assembly and found satisfaction. Why do you now ask these things in vain?"
"Such matters as these bring no benefit to the body. Fie upon you, deluded śramaṇa! Go now quickly; I shall speak with you again later.
When I heard this, I went immediately to where I had previously eaten until it was completely exhausted and all my wealth was gone. Having seen this, I was filled with distress.
"Bound by roots, boasting and arrogant—what suffering this is! Returning to the bridge, I saw the wise man.
The wise man asked me, 'Why are you so haggard? Is there something highly inauspicious? I replied, 'I have been asking useless questions;
they have caused me to truly lack food, drink, and wealth. The wise man said to me, 'Being a śramaṇa is of no benefit to your person.'"
In principle, one should not ask [questions], but should contemplate all phenomena. Regarding that which is beneficial for the body, it is appropriate to ask: "What constitutes benefit?
This refers to neither praising oneself nor disparaging others, but contemplating the Dharma of equality. Having thus benefited oneself, one is further able to benefit others.
At that time, ninety billion gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven heard the wise one’s teaching and resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta. Therefore, one should...
Knowing the Buddha-nature: all four gates may be used to enter the Way. The various schools’ biased attachments are like those questions. Regarding the bridge being both hidden and manifest:
from the stage of names (*nāma*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), both meanings are present.

For instance, within the stage of names, because there is understanding, it is called "manifest"; because one has not yet seen [the reality], it is called "hidden. Within the stage of contemplative practice (*darśana-bhāvanā-mārga*), because there is contemplation, it is called...

It is called "manifest" because it has not yet been realized; it is called "hidden" because it is seen only in a semblance. It is called "manifest" because the true nature has not yet been realized; it is called "hidden" because it has only been partially realized.
It is called "manifest" because it has been partially realized; it is called "hidden" because the final stage has not yet been reached.
"Both external and internal" refers to the passage in the sutra that follows this [section].
Regarding the six points for resolving doubts, the principle may be discussed in conjunction with this: because the nature (dhātu) exists within the afflictions, it is called a "storehouse" (garbha).
This does not at all discuss those who are deluded; it speaks from the perspective of the fundamental purity of the principle-nature (*li-xing*).
Regarding the differentiation of the six paths within the seven aspects of arising, one should say:
as for those in the ten dharma-realms who incur offense by destroying the aggregates (*skandha*), they incur offense because they destroy the delusory aggregates with a delusory mind.
Those that exist today are those for which contemporary families employ this principle.
Regarding the eighth point, which indicates the location of the text of the direct answer, Sengliang said: "The answer states: 'How does one perform wholesome karma, O Great Sage?

Now I shall explain it extensively. This refers to the causes for the two fruits of the *dīrgha* and *vajra* [samādhis]. Above, the cause was briefly clarified; therefore, [the text] employs compassion."
"Protecting the Dharma is the foundation. Since it is now explained in detail, [the text] proceeds from the Three Refuges up to the Ten Stages. Fayao said:
'The Buddha-nature is the direct cause (hetu-pratyaya), while wholesome karma is the contributory cause (pratyaya). Therefore, these are cited to demonstrate cause and effect.'"
Regarding "the beginning of karma and the end of its nature": if one were to judge this based on the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, it could not yet be called the "end.
Now, however, we follow the question posed by the Bodhisattva. Since he asks, "How does one perform wholesome karma? this constitutes the beginning of the inquiry.
Since he further states, "One is able to see the nature that is difficult to see," this constitutes the end of the inquiry. Sengzong also makes this same judgment.

The ninth section, "Relating the Ancients," contains two parts: first, the relation; second, from "Now, to clarify" onwards, the formal judgment. Regarding the initial statement, "Since there is no self," this refutes the provisional self (*prajñapti-ātman*).
Since it is said to be provisional, there is no true self (*bhūta-ātman*); therefore, it asks, "Who is the driver?"

In the subsequent "Correct Explanation," it says, "unable to perform wholesome deeds. This clarifies that in the stage of the Innate Nature (*prakṛti*), one is not yet capable of performing wholesome deeds.
"Grasping and emerging from the treasury" clarifies that in the ultimate stage, wholesome deeds are no longer required; however, they must be performed during the intermediate stages.
Regarding the "four phrases in the middle": these refer to the four [phrases] within the intermediate stage.
If one analyzes them according to the four phrases, one obtains four sets of four phrases; furthermore, the six stages are condensed into the names "hidden" (*yin*) and "manifest" (*xian*).

The "hidden" does not require the ultimate stage (*jiujing ji*), while the "manifest" does not require the four intermediate stages. Each stage possesses both the hidden and the manifest, as follows: [The text continues with examples illustrating how each stage contains both aspects.]
The fourth phrase mentioned previously refers to the essence of wholesome karma being neither hidden nor manifest.
Next, entering the text for its explanation, regarding the phrase "arising from the category of the four inversions": because of those prior inversions, one does not perceive the Buddha-nature.
From this question it arises: Is there definitely a self, or is there definitely no self?
If there were definitely a self, then all sentient beings should have already attained Buddhahood;
why is it that today they all remain within the twenty-five states of existence and cannot escape from them? Therefore, it is said: "If there is, it is not [truly] existent."
Regarding "one must not speak": this is because of the illness of self-attachment and the view of self; due to this illness of self, one cannot speak of the Buddha-nature.
Regarding "resolving doubts": expounding the two kinds of teachings is precisely what resolves these doubts.
The Sūtra says: "As for 'I' (to) 'all possess it. Now, the Tathāgatagarbha, the self, and the Buddha-nature are identical in essence but differ in meaning.
Possessing the eight kinds of mastery, they constitute the meaning of "self. When one rides upon the path of reality, one is called a Tathāgata; this is because [the nature] is unchanging.

Regarding the statement that "all possess Buddha-nature," this means that permanence, bliss, self, and purity constitute Buddha-nature. This is because the cause possesses its own fruit, and the fruit also possesses its own fruit.

As for the scriptural passage stating that they are "shrouded by afflictions," this refers to the obscuration of the realization of the Self; it does not mean that a separate view is produced and remains obscured throughout an eon.

Regarding my speaking of it as being "due to conditions": if sentient beings possess the four *siddhāntas*, and their capacities and needs dictate that they will only attain Buddhahood in the future, I speak accordingly.
"Quǐn" (pronounced *qǔ* with a level tone;
meaning urgent or constrained) refers to a lack of the causal conditions and resources for attaining the *sarvajñatā* (all-encompassing wisdom). Therefore, it is called "lacking conditions."
There is that which possesses the power to produce; it is the power capable of producing the understanding and practice [of the Path].
This nature is "inclusive" because each and every one of the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements is none other than the Dharma-realm of the three truths;
hence it is called "inclusive. Sengliang said: "One who finds a treasury of gold will necessarily become wealthy. If one sees the Buddha-nature..."
Thus, one attains Buddhahood.
Regarding this "universal transformation of the nature": it means that every single form and every single fragrance is none other than the Dharma-realm of the secret treasury of the three virtues;
hence these words are spoken.
Regarding "family members" (*jīnrén*): the master and his dependents constitute the family.
Being collectively deluded regarding principle, they are called those who lack knowledge. Zhezhou says: sentient beings within the twenty-five realms of existence are called "family members.
Because people possess degrees of superiority and inferiority, they are termed "great" or "small. Sharing the same failure to understand their own nature, they are called those who lack knowledge.
The term "only bodhisattvas" refers to the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka. The same applies to "only śrāvakas.

Since the proponents of the Śāstras maintain that, in addition to the three vehicles of the Tripiṭaka, there exists separately a common stage of the three vehicles, they employ the terms "only bodhisattvas" and so forth.

Regarding "The Bodhisattva Chuyi is the Great One": the Bodhisattva Chuyi’s meaning encompasses both the *zang* (Tripitaka) and *tong* (Shared) vehicles as they emerge into the provisional (*chujia*). [The practitioners of these vehicles] are both unaware [of this].

As for the scripture stating, "At that time there was a strange man," Zhezhou says: "The 'strange man' is a metaphor for the Buddha; it encourages the cultivation [of the path], for the Buddha transcends the common world."
Therefore, he is called a "different person. One who skillfully understands the method of cultivating and manifesting the nature is called "knowing the expedient means.

To instruct by means of the Dharma is called "speech. A woman encourages him to sever his obstacles and causes him to benefit others through goodness; this is called "hiring someone to clear away weeds."
Regarding "taking conditions as the power of transformation," this means that the Buddha-nature is explained as the power for me to transform others.
The Sūtra states, "skillfully knowing expedient means," which refers to the skillful manifestation of the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the scripture’s statement, "I now hire you," Sengzong said: "This is merely a metaphor for what is intended.
