Regarding the scripture’s statement, "I know the skillful means," it means that because one possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), one is certainly able to expound extensively.
The Sūtra says, "One does not even know oneself. Sengliang said: "Matters concerning one's own body are near; matters concerning another body are distant.
If one does not even know what is near, how much less so that which is distant?"
The Sūtra says, "I am now truly capable. Master Daosheng said: "The principle cannot be suppressed;
only I can know it. The Sūtra says, "Digs it up. Master Daosheng said: "To remove the covering of fetters and delusions is 'digging'; to perceive the Buddha-nature is 'digging it up.'"
Regarding the statement "likewise lamenting," that also possesses two illnesses and two medicines.
That parable which is manifest demonstrates the three inferior practices already accomplished;
this parable which is hidden reveals that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The woman is a metaphor for the previous Buddha; the subsequent Buddha likewise practices the Dharma of the former Buddhas.
As for the passage in the sutra stating, "This woman was distressed," etc., the physician and the mother serve as metaphors according to their respective meanings.

They are taken to signify the sense of nurturing wisdom and understanding, just as a mother nurtures her child. The physician’s role in treating afflictions carries the same meaning; there is no other distinct purpose.

Regarding the phrase "the flavor of suffering due to non-self," this refers to sweet mixed with bitter being collectively termed "bitter"; it likewise contradicts the characteristics of true permanence.
As for the scripture stating that "one who uses a bitter flavor as an ointment," Master Daosheng said: "The teaching of non-self is not something the world relishes. For...
"It is the taste of bitterness. Sengzong said: "One should say that the physician applies medicine; yet it is called 'mother' (mǔ) to signify that there is no distinct substance.
When the sutra says 'it cannot be touched again,' 'touching' (chù) refers to the name for defiled attachment. Since all things are impermanent, they are called 'untouchable' (bù kě chù)."

Regarding "the dependent origination of the true self": this clarifies that the great capacity [of the practitioner] has been darkly activated and its manifestation is ultimately never received; therefore, it is said that "once the false self is removed, the medicine of non-self is discarded.
This means that when the illness of the self is gone, the medicine of non-self is no longer required.

Regarding the scripture’s statement, "I have finished washing": it means that since illnesses such as permanence (*nitya*) and so forth no longer recur, one does not further apply the medicine of impermanence (*anitya*);
hence it says, "finished washing.

Regarding the scripture’s statement, "gradually returning to food and drink": this refers to those of the *vaipulya* and *prajñāpāramitā* who possess great capacity, whose latent potential has awakened in secret, and who have attained realization as distinct individuals (*bipartite persons*).
Therefore, it is said that they gradually return to drinking.
Regarding the distinction between persons: the nine realms are different. Regarding the universality of the Dharma: Buddha-nature is non-dual.
As for the distinction between persons such that they are not Buddhas: sentient beings who possess only Buddha-nature have as yet not attained virtues such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Therefore, it is said that they are not "virtues.
Since there was no distinct person in the past, and the person of today is no different from the person of the past, the nature of impermanence is itself permanent.
To whom, then, did this permanent dharma belong in the past?

The Sūtra states that "one should not give rise to fear. This means one should not feel apprehensive toward the Vaipulya teachings, nor should one harbor a mind of fear regarding the non-acceptance of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtras does one realize that [the Buddha-nature] was already possessed; therefore, it is said that it was previously "not obtained."
It is not that one universally proclaims "non-existence. If a self existed, it would not undergo transmigration through the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Since it is observed that beings transmigrate through birth and death, we know by inference that there is no self.
Regarding "those who begin with birth and end with death," one may verify that the distinctions of impermanence and so forth also raise this same objection.
As for the twelve objections consisting of six pairs: first and last, one; distinction, one; victory and defeat, one; cause and condition, one;
suffering as fruit and suffering as condition, one; forgetfulness, one; place, one; and difficulty, one.

Regarding "present function": in the present, there is only the function of impermanence; since there is no evidence of a permanent function, one knows that there is no permanence and no true self (*ātman*).
As for "there should be neither arising nor ceasing": arising is the beginning and ceasing is the end.

The preceding analogy concerning "gaining and then losing" clarifies that the Buddha’s response is twofold. Regarding the first part: one gains because of the originally existent principle of nature, yet loses because of encountering conditions that give rise to delusion.
The subsequent analogy concerning "losing and then gaining" begins with the passage from "From the Snowy Mountains" onwards.
Regarding "no loss" (and so forth): the principle of Buddha-nature is not subject to gain or loss; it is only through the resolution or failure to resolve delusion that one speaks of gain and loss.
Therefore, the commentary states (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "the royal palace," Zhezhou says: it is a metaphor for the Tathāgata. The trichiliocosm is the realm transformed by the Buddha, and is thus called the royal palace.

Ordinary sentient beings have the nature of delusion so strongly reinforced that they are likened to wrestlers. Because their minds possess the Buddha-nature, it is said that there is a vajra-jewel between their eyebrows.
Regarding the scripture’s statement that “one does not know it at all,” Fayao said: "The head of delusion destroys the forehead of right faith.
Once right faith is destroyed, how could one know of the Buddha-nature? Although one does not know it exists, the ultimate principle remains intact, like a pearl hidden within its skin."

The Sūtra states: "Because of the pearl entering the body. This means that by means of the pearl, one attains the stage of the Two Vehicles, and eventually achieves the perfect, eternally abiding Great Nirvāṇa.

Regarding the term "the capacity directed toward the Buddha," there are both general and specific capacities for this "capacity" (ki). That which is direct is called "specific"; that which is indirect assistance is called "general."
Regarding "lost" and "not lost": it is lost because it has entered the skin; it is not lost because it remains stationary.
As for "the future fruit existing in the future," although sentient beings have not yet attained it in a future life, it is fully present, just as a reflection appears externally.
Regarding "the Buddha’s wisdom silently illuminates": being submerged within the skin is "silence," while manifesting as reflections on the outside is "illumination.
That the delusions are slight is called "skin"; this is a metaphor for the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
Regarding the sūtra’s statement, “the mind harbors alarm and so forth”: hitherto, one has perceived only that one's own body is impermanent and impure.
Today, suddenly hearing that this very body is of the nature of eternal abiding—clearly and distinctly revealed like a bright mirror—one perceives that impermanence is subject to change;
thus, a sense of wonder arises.
The Sūtra states that those who cannot draw near to a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) are unable to draw near to a spiritual friend of the True Teaching;
therefore, they do not perceive the Buddha-nature, as illustrated by the following examples.

Yet, there is nothing that is not accomplished. Because of non-recognition, one instead conforms to arising and ceasing, which contradicts non-self; thus, it is only when one perceives the true self that non-self is truly established.
As the Sūtra says: "Those who do not know the state of non-self" means they do not know that non-self is fundamentally the true nature.
One who makes such a refutation is intended to realize the true self within non-self; thus it is said, "one does not even know oneself," and so forth.

The reason for losing the principle is that one is shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, although the Buddha-nature exists, sentient beings do not see it, which is what is meant by "losing the principle."

"Confusion and delusion intermingled" refers to instances where the arising of annihilationism refutes permanence, or the arising of permanence refutes annihilationism, and so forth; this is called "intermingling.
Regarding "attaining a portion at the outset," it means that from the stage of names and above, one attains the name of "attainment. Gao said:
"It is like a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage who, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, is able to see a small portion of the Buddha-nature clearly, though its principle remains profound and remote."
When the practitioner hears this teaching, they know that beneath the nature of afflictions lies the Buddha-nature.
The bamboo tube (tǒng) and the wooden bucket (tǒng) serve as the primary metaphors for this.
Regarding the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*) of the ten stages: by receiving the teachings and practicing them, one begins from the first stage and above to cultivate and realize it.
Because the cause accords with the Dharma of the three virtues of the resultant stage, it is said that "the cause receives the fruit."

Regarding those who have been born in the past: the Buddha, having cultivated the causes of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in various places throughout the past until they reached maturity, now enables these sentient beings as well to cultivate the causes and realize the fruit.
Furthermore, receiving the teachings and practicing them encompasses the intermediate four stages (*catur-yoga*).

The Sūtra states: "That which is the time for this medicine" refers to the power of the causal conditions being fully perfected, which is termed "ripening. Furthermore, because principle is manifested through conditions, it is called "medicine.
When it manifests within the aggregate body at the time of ripening, it is said to "emerge from the earth. When it resides in the mind of practice, it is called "assembling the wooden cylinder.
When one realizes and accords with the fundamental nature, it is called "the true flavor."
Furthermore, regarding "collected within wooden tubes": in principle and in teaching, it is "collected" (*cita*) because it can clearly manifest the correct name.

As for the analogy of the six flavors representing the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍgati*): if taken individually as analogies, bitterness represents suffering, sourness represents impermanence (*anityatā*), saltiness represents selflessness (*anātman*), sweetness represents pleasure, pungency represents the self (*ātman*), and blandness represents permanence (*nityatā*).
These may be applied according to their respective meanings throughout all contexts.

The Sūtra says: "True flavor... like the moon. This means that being unmixed with the false constitutes the true nature (*dharmatā*). It must reside within humans and cannot be shifted or altered, as if it were fixed in place.
Its perfect luminosity is without partiality; thus it is metaphorically compared to the moon. Regarding the statement "neither male nor female," it refers to the nature.
For those of indeterminate faculties, and furthermore for those whose faculty-nature belongs to the formless realm, the Sūtra states that there are indeed those who commit killing.
Although Master Sengsheng held that the five aggregates are subject to destruction, the Buddha-nature is not; thus, while one may harm the five aggregates, one does not damage the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, it is called "killing. It cannot be said that there is no harm, meaning that there is no unwholesome karma.

As for the statement that the six dharmas are merely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), this refutes fixed attachments; the same principle applies to the inability to calculate [the self] through the spirit (*ātman*).

Furthermore, as for the previous objection: although this passage may seem to resolve the delusion regarding the fixed existence or non-existence of intrinsic nature, it actually obscures the principle of the existence of intrinsic nature;
therefore, it cannot be employed [as a proof].

Regarding the statement that "there is that which abides and that which does not abide": the essence of Buddha-nature neither abides nor does it not abide; rather, it causes the nature of sentient beings to be both abiding and non-abiding.
As for the claim that this contradicts the preceding and following passages: those passages all clarify that ultimate purity is neither internal nor external.
The "stones, sand, and so forth" are metaphors for killing within the five aggregates of the six realms of existence.
Regarding the teaching that buddha-nature produces both good and evil: not only does the arising of good depend upon buddha-nature, but the arising of evil likewise depends upon it.
The Sūtra says: "Do you now wish to know [the meaning]? This asks whether one wishes to know the true meaning of the secret treasury within the bodies of sentient beings. The Sūtra says:

"The delusions have the poison of the eye, giving rise to [suffering]," etc. Baoliang says: This further clarifies that while the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings constitute poison for some, they do not constitute poison for others.
This is the meaning.
As for "mutually forming one another through repetition," it simply means that poisonous medicine becomes nectar, and nectar becomes poisonous medicine.
"Injuring, destroying, and breaking" refers to the destruction of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

"Entering into principle and generating goodness" refers to the fulfillment and manifestation of the body of wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*). "Destroying evil" refers to the fulfillment of the body of abandonment-virtue (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Regarding the fact that each section has its corresponding application and analogy: within these three lines, each contains both an application and an analogy.

Regarding the analogy of the three truths: in terms of the three teachings, a Bodhisattva who relies on the perfectly interfused three truths shall avoid the bonds of Māra by realizing that their own body is the single essence of the Three Jewels; thus, the realm of Māra is itself the realm of the Buddha.
Furthermore, there is nothing else that can bind them.
Regarding "skillful discernment": it means discerning that returning [to the Buddha] in the past was provisional, while returning [to the Buddha] now is the reality.
As the Sūtra says, "This is my own nature," meaning that this nature does not require one to abandon oneself and return to another.
If the Buddha were to abandon me to return to another, that would be to discard the root and follow the branches, which is not true return. Therefore, he exhorts us to understand this deeply.
Regarding the nature of one's own future fruition:

the principle of goodness consists of the Three Jewels as a single entity; this is the ultimate limit of the goodness of principle. It is the division of the perfection of wisdom and virtue that destroys evil.
Regarding "poisonous medicine": it refers to the fulfillment of the portion of severed virtues; thus it is said that the two [aspects] possess only attainment.
Furthermore, "my nature" refers to the causal nature (*hetu-bhāva*).
"Possessing Buddha-nature" refers to the resultant nature (*phala-bhāva*). One who necessarily possesses such an understanding has truly entered the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*).
The scripture states, "As for the verses I have spoken," which refers to what precedes; "if one can contemplate them with true discernment" refers to the following two lines of verse.
Regarding the phrase "initially not accepting either," this means: "I now do not know either of these. This refers to not accepting the distinct entities of the Triple Gem.

Furthermore, regarding the unified Three Jewels of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), [the text] again states that one takes refuge collectively. Kāśyapa says: "The Buddha said, 'I too take refuge in the Three Jewels,'" and so forth.
As for the Buddha's refusal to allow [external] refuge, his intention was solely to have them take refuge in the unified Three Jewels within their own bodies.
One's own wholesome karma cannot be transferred to another.

Regarding the initial general statement that "one does not know": since the Three Jewels may be either true or false, when one now wishes to take refuge and perform wholesome karma, one simply does not know the true object of refuge; therefore, it is said that one "does not know."
Regarding the phrase "How does one take refuge in the Buddha, etc.": Because the Buddha can eliminate fear, he is called "the Consoler. Because the Dharma can sever doubt, it is called "Sovereignty.
Because the Sangha is a field of merit, it is said to be "Unsurpassed Benefit."

As explained in the previous section on the four characteristics, it is as stated in the concluding summary of one hundred phrases at the end of the lower fascicle of the "Chapter on the Four Characteristics" (*Caturlakṣaṇa-parivarta*) in the *Vimukti-mārga* (*Text on Liberation*).
That is to say, because all sentient beings fear birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the various afflictions (*kleśa*), they take the three refuges (*tri-śaraṇa*) and so forth.
This refers to that which lacks prior appointment and reflects itself; it cannot reflect its own Three Jewels.
As the Sūtra says, "The karma of sentient beings is likewise": when sentient beings create good or evil karma, they will inevitably experience the corresponding good or evil fruits.
It is also like a child in the womb who will certainly be born before long; likewise, if one cultivates wholesome karma, one will certainly behold the Three Jewels as one's own body.

Therefore, it is said, "it is also thus. Master Zhezhou says: "The Dharma is used together with the analogy that the true nature of the Three Jewels within the bodies of sentient beings can produce future fruits;
this is called the 'karma of sentient beings. Because it is like the presence or absence of a child [in the womb], it is said to be 'also thus.'"
If one causes them to return to the present, it means that the distinct entities of the Mahāyāna are in fact a single entity.
If one causes them to return to the future, it means that sentient beings shall attain the single entity of their own bodies.
The Sūtra says, "Because they do not know. If one returns [to the Triple Gem] without knowing, then the return is not accomplished; therefore, such a person remains within birth and death.
The Sūtra speaks of those who are "provisionally named upāsakas"; if the three refuges are not accomplished, how can they be real?
The Sūtra states, "Regarding you among the bodhisattvas," which applies to those both prior to and within the stages (bhūmis).
As for the fourth [Buddha] of the Bhadrakalpa, this is Śākyamuni.
The seventh Buddha likewise refers to Śākyamuni. In all cases, not only are the names identical, but their original manifestations throughout the ten directions are also equal.

Response: The Sūtra states that Śākyamuni is "capable of writing" (néngwén) and "capable of Confucianism" (néngrú). This praises his mastery of Confucian principles; it indicates that Kāśyapa possesses the merit of propagating the Dharma.
As for the Sūtra’s mention of taking refuge in the Holy Sangha, this refers to upholding correct understanding to demonstrate the path of goodness to others.
"Why not use the 'correct self' to overturn the 'false self'? This constitutes a mutual challenge that brings forth the characteristics of the two gates of counteractive measures.
As for the 'right path,' the three refuges are the right path leading to the Buddha."
Regarding the phrase "all that exists is non-existent": this is because the three delusions and two modes of death have both been exhausted.

Regarding the phrase "the three are hidden as one essence during the period of concealment": the Three Treasures, which are of one essence with all sentient beings, reside entirely within the principle of nature; therefore, it is called the "period of concealment."
In the past, one had to rely [on others], but now that the teaching of *nirvāṇa* has arisen, there is no need to rely on Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Regarding the attainment of the Dharma and the Saṃgha: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) possesses the meaning of awakening and illumination, and thus constitutes the Jewel of the Buddha; this same nature possesses the meaning of providing a track for the arising of understanding in sentient beings, and thus constitutes the Jewel of the Dharma;
the harmony of object and wisdom is the Jewel of the Saṃgha. Question: For what reason must one cause [others] to take refuge in themselves?
Is it not permitted to take refuge in the other two [Buddhas] because one’s own body is the One Body? Answer: It is because one might forget that one’s own body is the One Body;
therefore, taking refuge in another is not allowed.

As for the "condition" (*pratyaya*): it is the condition of the principle of True Reality (*tattva*). This corresponds to the First Noble Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the former teachings within our present school.
Regarding "conditioning" (yuan): practicing in accordance with the capacities [of beings] corresponds to the *puruṣakāra* (human effort) cause;

responding to conditions corresponds to the *pratyaya* (objective condition) cause. Regarding "causes and conditions" (yin-yuan): in the past, merely following along with worldly causes and conditions corresponds to the *adhipati* (dominant) cause.
Regarding the "intention of counteracting" (*pratipakṣābhiprāya*):

if one interprets this passage by correctly employing the intention of counteracting, it is not without meaning that the other three [intentions] are implicitly understood as being beneficial. Therefore, the commentary states "and so forth."
The Sūtra states: "If one wishes to accord with worldly dharmas, because the teachings of the present age have flourished, one must take refuge in the single essence (ekakāya).
In the past, it was merely a matter of acceding to worldly conventions, employing skillful means to guide and lead others toward the distinct essence (prthakkāya)."

The Sūtra states, "Within my own body," because the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in the three aspects. Thus, by citing the Buddha-body, it reveals the body of sentient beings;
being of one essence, it is no different from that of the Buddha. This is precisely to cause sentient beings to conceive of their own bodies as stūpas and temples;
the same applies to the Dharma and the Sangha.
Regarding the question of whether the body possesses the Dharma and the Saṃgha: this asks about the essence of the single Truth by way of its distinct aspects.
To say that the body possesses the Dharma and the Saṃgha means that hearing the Dharma constitutes the Jewel of the Dharma, and becoming a renunciant constitutes the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
One who can expound this Dharma speaks of the presence of the nature of phenomena within one's own body; this is the Jewel of the Dharma.
To be able to constantly remember, uphold, and contemplate it is the Jewel of the Sangha.
"He still takes refuge in us" means that he still takes refuge in our single essence (*ekatva*). Why do you not take refuge in yourself?
Within your own body there is this single essence; why do you take refuge only in another, separate essence?

Furthermore, since "he still takes refuge in me" refers to taking refuge in one's own self as "me," how could it be that I do not take refuge in my own body, which is my single essence? This is the interpretation based on this [text].
This is also convenient.
When the Sūtra says, "I shall proceed in sequence," it indicates to sentient beings the characteristics of the Three Jewels as a single essence (*eka-rasa*).

As for "not daring to take this as a precedent": because the Three Jewels as a single essence are not elucidated in the *Dvaya-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-dvaya-śāstra*), one does not dare to apply it as a precedent. [The Lotus Sūtra...]
It is said: "A true śrāvaka was formerly false, but now is truly real. This constitutes the meaning of the skillful means of "becoming one body," whereby they are spoken of as "others.
As for those who manifest as a single body through transformation, having themselves attained oneness with the One Body, they are able to act as a single-body refuge for others.
Because they dwell [together], it is called "I.
Regarding the phrase "the entire body," this refers to the whole being.
As for "not being in contradiction," it means that failing to realize that identity is precisely the meaning of the Saṃgha (the harmonious assembly).
Regarding the formulation of these distinctions: you should not now treat them as identical, like those born blind who do not see the single essence.
Those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the state of a sage and those who have not yet attained it are both described as being like ordinary beings with respect to their own bonds (*saṃyojana*).

As for the distinction: because the timing was not yet appropriate, they were taught separately; this is to lead toward the single essence. Regarding the analogy of the "great general" as the manifesting cause (*vidyotana-hetu*): the great general...

A valiant hero who can defeat powerful enemies to bring peace to the nation is like the *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause); that is, *prajñā* (wisdom) which universally sweeps away the three delusions to illuminate the principle.
The Crown Prince, who is likened to the *samyak-hetu* (correct cause), is one who shall succeed to the royal throne to govern the state;

this is like the *samyak-hetu*, which is the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) that pervades all places and constantly benefits sentient beings. The Great Minister, who is likened to the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause), is one who assists [the ruler] internally...

This accords with the intent of the Master. Externally, it reaches out to the common people to assist the state, like the "conditioning cause" (pratyaya-hetu). Internally, it is liberation that assists the realization [of Buddhahood] to manifest the true nature.
As the Sūtra says, "One should not give rise to an inferior mind," meaning one should not be like the śrāvakas who do not know that all are of one essence.
It is as with the former king. The meaning is that the prince should not give rise to inferior thoughts; because he acts like his predecessor, he is able to achieve the succession of the throne.
The great king serves as a metaphor for the first among the three ministers, who represents the correct nature (*samyaktva*) and subdues all other ministers.

The analogy of the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*) is like a subordinate official; the analogy of the "supporting cause" (*ālambana-hetu*) is like a foundation. Therefore, it is said that it is likewise so.

When the Sūtra says, "I demonstrate three matters," "demonstrate" (*darśana*) means to manifest, revealing distinct entities to transform sentient beings. Furthermore, "demonstrate" means to point out;
it points out that within the single essence of sentient beings there are three meanings. This is why the commentary (*ṭīkā*) employs the term "to indicate."
The latter explanation is correct as the definitive interpretation.
As the Sūtra says: "One of firm strength" refers to one who, when directing [their power], severs their own single body and can sever the net of doubts regarding distinct entities.
To illustrate this with an analogy, it is like a sword.
"Not taking a separate entity" means not taking its former separate entity.

"That which has already been established by another" refers to that which has already become a single entity at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*); since this has no bearing upon me, I do not accept it. Upon what, then, does it depend?
I fear that those who lose sight of their own single essence will end up being the same as the Small Vehicle or non-Buddhists.
As the Sūtra says: "The Greatly Valiant" refers to those who know that within their own bodies there is the Buddha-nature and the single-essence Three Jewels; all such persons are called valiant.
Regarding the sūtra’s phrase “the locus of pure practice”: its essence is the object of contemplation for the perfect observation;
therefore, it is called a "locus. Regarding the sūtra’s phrase “extraordinary matters”: the essence of the Triple Gem transcends the nine realms of existence.
What was not previously taught is now being proclaimed; hence, it is praised as extraordinary.
The scripture states, "One should also realize and know," which refers to the author himself stating, "I too shall realize this secret treasury.
Regarding the phrase "the true refuge for those below who are deluded," it means causing others to all enter the secret treasury; hence the commentary says "and so forth."
Regarding the praise of the Buddha-nature: this is the praise of how that which is currently hidden within the minds of sentient beings is of one essence with that which shall become manifest;
it is non-dual from the Buddha. Therefore, it is praised by way of its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
This is because the aspect of the unity of my own self and that of sentient beings—the marks and signs of their hidden and manifest states—is made clear.
Those who are deluded regarding the "deviation from the mean" do so because they deviate from the Middle Way and are shrouded by the three delusions.

Regarding this "existence that is not the Way": if one definitively calculates existence or non-existence, it is not called the Middle Way; only when one transcends both existence and non-existence is it called the Middle Way.
The Sūtra says: "If I were to abide," those who hold to eternalism would say that there is a divine self (ātman) abiding within the five aggregates; this is called "the abiding of the self.
This is precisely an eternal dharma that does not escape suffering. Because non-Buddhists proclaim that the divine self is eternal, they describe it as an eternal dharma according to their own views.
Since the five aggregates are suffering, for the self to abide within the aggregates is to be called "not escaping suffering."

If there were no self, this would give rise to the view of annihilationism. One who holds the view of annihilationism asserts that there is no self even as a conventional designation for the cycle of birth and death;
since they claim there is no self, they likewise assert that there is no true self even in nirvana. Consequently, their practice yields no benefit and provides no nourishment.
Therefore, it provides no benefit.
The Sūtra says: "If one speaks of suffering, it belongs to the category of annihilation because suffering is subject to change.
To say it is both eternal and annihilated: it belongs to the eternal because there is illusory pleasure, and it belongs to the annihilated because it is oppressed by suffering."
One does not know who it is that should hold such a view; since no such person is seen to exist, it is said that "it is unknown.

Regarding "seeing the faults of those who have abandoned through seeing and cultivation," this means that upon seeing the faults in the practice of others who have abandoned [defilements] through seeing, one immediately cultivates the view of permanence for oneself; the same applies to cultivating permanence.
The *Yi* says: "The sun goes and the moon comes; the moon goes and the sun comes. The sun and moon push against each other, and brightness is produced.
Cold goes and heat comes; heat goes and cold comes. Heat and cold push against each other, and the year is completed. That which goes is contraction; that which comes is extension.
Through the mutual resonance of contraction and extension, benefit is produced. The inchworm contracts in order to seek..."
This is an elaboration. His intention clarifies that they naturally form a pair.

Now, by discarding one and adopting the other, it is like the case of the caterpillar facing the "non-self" (anātman). Since the third phrase already states "non-self," the fourth phrase should state "cultivating the remainder."
That which is the "self of dharmas" (dharmātman) is precisely what is called the Tathāgata’s secret treasury. To say now that "dharmas are permanent" is an error.
If "permanence" were to apply universally, this interpretation would be problematic; for if the other five [characteristics] are all universal, why should permanence alone be so?

The Sūtra says that those who cultivate other dharmas experience suffering; this means that while birth-and-death is fundamentally the Dharma-body, the followers of the Two Vehicles and others merely interpret it as suffering.

The Sūtra says that those who cultivate other dharmas experience bliss; this refers to the very extremes being the Middle Way, the Buddha-nature, and the great goodness of the [following] four phrases.

It is likewise so. In the commentary (*śū*), because the intention is to reveal that the Middle Way is supreme, it provisionally distinguishes the principles of the extremes and thereby elucidates the Middle Way.
The Sūtra says, "and the dharma of the fruit of right liberation. *Jin* (津) means "to pass through" or "to communicate."

Regarding "the Middle Way is clearly distinguished": the sutra states that the Middle Way is far removed from the two extremes; this is precisely what constitutes the characteristic of being clearly distinguished.
Regarding "even the foolish do not doubt": if this interpretation is taken as correct, one should say, "even the foolish themselves do not doubt."
How much more so for the wise, who would not give rise to doubt?

As for those who have reached the state where all views are rendered light and easy, when the fool hears of the Middle Way, it increases their sharpness, just as consuming ghee (sarpis) brings lightness. Why is this?
Because they see the benefit and awaken easily; "light and easy" refers to the meaning [of the path]. Furthermore, this was originally the conceptualization of various views.
Now, when a person hears of the Middle Way—the non-dual Buddha-nature—and attains understanding therein, it is like taking ghee (*sarpis*): it is light and easy.
Later, this understanding becomes the true ghee;

as for its being a "good medicine," the Buddha-nature possesses the power and function of fearlessness, capable of destroying the extremes of nihilism and eternalism, and is thus called a good medicine.
"Furthermore, attaining lightness and ease" means that within the midst of [the extremes of] annihilationism and eternalism, one perceives the Buddha-nature; this is termed "lightness and ease.
Regarding the "deluded mind," if explained according to the six-fascicle version, it refers to the meaning of the "foolish person who has no doubts" mentioned in the preceding text.
Regarding the statement that "conditioned phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent," this reveals the wondrous existence of the Middle Way as the non-duality of existence and non-existence.
As for "differing from non-duality": there is no separate duality that comes to differ from non-duality, nor is there a non-duality that comes to differ from duality.
One should know that duality is non-duality, and non-duality is duality; it is neither dual nor non-dual.
As for the "three aggregates," they are the three: form, mind, and that which is neither form nor mind.
The same applies to the earth and wind elements: the lower breath (*apāna*) treats disorders of the earth element, while the upper breath (*prāṇa*) treats disorders of the wind element.
Furthermore, the upper breath treats heaviness and sinking, whereas the lower breath treats emptiness and suspension caused by wind.
A sick person with an unskilled physician is like those of the Two Vehicles who do not know that the Buddha-nature is precisely this.
That which is first visible corresponds to the Tathāgata, who is like a skilled physician; knowing all afflictions, he is like one who understands what is wholesome and knows how to eliminate them.
His partial manifestation corresponds to his skillful application, while his opening and revealing correspond to his providing restorative care.
Regarding that which should not be clung to with attachment: the Buddha-nature is like empty space; one should not give rise to attachment toward it.
As for "existence" signifying "non-existence": existence refers to the wondrous existence whose essence is identical to empty space.
As for the principle that it is not non-existent: true, good, and wondrous existence has a nature identical to space; it cannot be definitively characterized as the non-existence of annihilation.
To speak of it with such certainty would be false speech. It ought to be able to emit light, preach the Dharma, and manifest power and fearlessness.
Why is this so? If [the self] were definitively existent, it should manifest in response when subjected to analytical investigation; since there is no such response, it is not definitively existent.
Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), Master Sengzong says:
"The fault of [the self being] identical with form is like that of the Sāṃkhya; the fault of [the self being] separate from form is like..."

The Vaiśeṣika school calculates that the single self (*ātman*) is neither identical to nor different from [the aggregates], like the Vātsīputrīya; the practitioners of the Path hold the view of annihilation;
and the non-Buddhists calculate that everything is non-existent. These are all contrary to the former [view] and are all matters of dispute.
The Sūtra states that the "seed of Buddha-nature" takes "generating" as its meaning. Since one possesses the three causes of Buddha-nature, one will necessarily attain Bodhi;
how then could it be called impermanent?
The Sūtra says that provisional names are not real. Now, whatever is expressed in words is merely a provisional name and should not be grasped as fixed.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; it is neither definitively existent nor non-existent.

Regarding the "clarification of delusions through dialectical contrast," this refers simply to the opposition between the ignorant and the wise; the universal principle is that object and wisdom are non-dual.
First, the mention of ignorance is intended to clarify the Middle Way by means of the non-duality of karma and delusion. Sengzong said:
"The essence of birth and death is empty, being without duality or distinction from the very beginning; the essence of nirvana is suchness (tathatā), likewise originally without characteristics."
This is the principle of realizing the true mark of all phenomena through consciousness; it accomplishes the practice of the Middle Way.
To explain it in this manner is clearly to establish duality rather than non-duality.
Next, regarding the "practice of knowing consciousness": this clarifies non-duality by means of karma and suffering.

The Sūtra states, "White dharmas and black dharmas," which refers to the two dharmas of good and evil. Sengzong says: "This encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) to clarify cause and effect."
The Sūtra states: "One should cultivate all suffering. Suffering is precisely the Dharmakāya; how could ordinary beings [attain] worldly pleasure?
Regarding the phrase "interpreting the suspended finger as Prajñā," it is because within Prajñā, non-duality is most clearly elucidated.

Therefore, regarding the citation from the "Profound Chapter" (*Gambhīra-parivarta*): in that "Chapter on the Lamp Wick" (*Pradīpa-vartika-parivarta*), it is clarified that neither the preceding flame nor the succeeding flame can burn the wick, yet the burning of the wick does not occur apart from these preceding and succeeding flames.
This was already stated in the previous text; it is not unique to this instance. Here, it is explained again to clarify the nature of error.

That which is not based on the sūtras cannot be established as a formal thesis (*dharmamukha*). Generally speaking, that which arises from causes and conditions to produce curd is the establishment of a thesis;
if one says that curd is produced neither from itself nor from another, this is the refutation of a thesis. For what reason is the fundamental [position] not established?
This is refuted; therefore, two gates are established.
The Sūtra states, "Even so it is with the *amṛta* (clarified butter)," meaning that at the top of each of the five flavors, there is both one that is correct and one that is incorrect;
hence it says, "it is likewise."

Regarding the statement that "there should be no similarity in the continuity," this refutes the theory of self-arising (*svataḥ-utpāda*). Self-arising refers to a phenomenon that exists in isolation;

with what, then, could it be similar? Now, the substance of curd resembles milk, yet it arises as a continuous body subsequent to the milk. Since its continuity depends on another, there is evidence that it does not arise from itself.
Therefore, the claim of self-arising is merely a superficial assertion.

If one calculates that [the effect] is produced from something else, then the body [of the cause] should be destroyed; for instance, when milk becomes curd, the characteristics, flavors, and so forth are all different at different times.
Thus, the meaning of "production from something else" is not established.
As the Sūtra says regarding the prior existence of the characteristic of curd: because the nature of curd already exists within the milk, it subsequently produces the curd; this is what is meant.
"Self-arising.

Regarding the "six stages," these six are determined as the attainment of *amṛta* (the essence of ghee), and thus they are called "fat and rich," serving as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Another sutra further states:
"The arising of clarity" refers to the severance of afflictions through the distinct arising of the light of wisdom; this pertains to the intent of the gradual teaching (*anupūrvika-deśanā*).
The claim that "delusion and wisdom, as well as understanding and realization, are not mutually identical" contradicts this explanation.

Now, regarding those who cultivate the conditions of the object and the cause: since these aids are broken down first and severed before the subsequent stages, how can it be said that understanding and realization are merely shallow and superficial when they are clearly elucidated at the outset?

Regarding "previously determined": it refers to being determined that there is the nature of curd within milk, or being determined that there is no nature of curd. Since I did not understand this, I asked:
what is the meaning of saying it is called "arising"? If it already existed previously, it would already have arisen; why then do you speak of it [as arising]?
From the causal conditions of milk, the substance of curd arises. Yet, when examining milk through the lens of these causal conditions, one finds that milk lacks the inherent nature of curd.
If it were so, then grass should also exist within milk; indeed, the seeds of grass should likewise exist within milk.

Regarding the first, "investigating through analogy" (*yanpi*): it refers to investigating whether [a thing] definitely exists or definitely does not exist, and so forth; hence it is called "investigating through analogy.
The Sūtra states, "One cannot definitively say... (up to the word) "...curd. The two characters "cannot" (*bù kě*) govern the following two sections.
The Sūtra states, "That which does not produce a rabbit's horn. A rabbit's horn is definitively non-existent; it exists only as a name.
However, curd within milk is not definitively non-existent. Therefore, one must know that it is incorrect to say, "There is definitively no nature of curd within milk."

Regarding interpretation by principle (*yukti*): it means that all phenomena of dependent origination are merely provisional designations; the essential nature (*tattva*) is fundamentally true and eternal, and is therefore called "interpretation by principle.
Furthermore, it refers to interpretation based upon the principle of the Path (*mārga*).
Regarding the "power of the merit of sentient beings," since the speech of sentient beings is manifold, it is explained according to three types.
As the Sūtra says, "curd is produced from causes and conditions": fermented starter, warmth, gruel, water, and so forth serve as the causes and conditions.
The Sūtra says, "the taste of cow [milk]"; this refers to the taste of milk.
The Sūtra says, "when this milk has ceased": once the body acquires fermentation and warmth, it transforms into curd; this is what is meant by "having ceased."
Regarding the character *láo* (pronounced *láo*), that which stirs it with substances—such as various tree sap and so forth—is thrown into milk and is called *jiào* (ferment).
This does not refer to the yeast used for brewing wine; rather, it is merely using the character *jiào* to explain the scripture.
If one uses the character *láo*, this is the character *qīng láo* (clear labor); *liáo* (lì jiù fǎn, meaning to fly high).
Regarding the meaning of "opening and transforming" (*kai-ten*): it is similar to the aforementioned process of transforming ignorance (*avidyā*) to eliminate ignorance and attain clarity (*vidyā*).

Furthermore, it is precisely the transformation of ignorance itself that becomes clarity; this is identical to what was stated in the preceding text. Therefore, it is called "opening and transforming."
The Sūtra says, "Though they are equally salty," which is a metaphor for how all sentient beings, though equally shrouded by ignorance,
all possess the water of the supreme and wondrous Buddha-nature.
As for the analogy of the elimination [of impurities]: within salt water there naturally exists water of eight virtues that is not mixed with the salt.
When the sutra speaks of "various virtues," these virtues are an analogy for the Buddha-nature; the poisonous weeds are a metaphor for ignorance.
Regarding the phrase "kṣatriyas and so forth" in the Sūtra, it should be stated that sentient beings of the nine dharma-realms are all shrouded by afflictions and thus do not see their Buddha-nature.

Regarding the passage from "the four elephants" to "and so forth," according to the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), there are four types of elephants: first, the *utpala*; second, the *padma*.
Third is Triśaṅku; fourth is Puṇḍarīka—these are the four colors: blue, yellow, red, and white. Furthermore, first is the Padma elephant;
second is the Utpala elephant; third is the Kuvalaya elephant; and fourth is the Puṇḍarīka elephant.
When thunder occurs in the heavens, if a *padma* flower pattern appears upon the ear, it is described as the *padma* elephant;
the same applies to the other three.
Third, regarding the statement "this elephant": its explanation is the same as the second interpretation.

As for the sutra’s phrase "increasing the dharma-body," the essence of the dharma-body does not increase; rather, it is because sentient beings ultimately possess varying degrees of depth [in their realization].
It is named "Increase.

Regarding the second answer, "Able to See What is Difficult to See," Sengliang said: "In the preceding section on the Three Refuges, it was clarified that the nature of the self possesses Buddha-nature;
this seemed as though there were a divine 'self'-nature that constitutes Buddha-nature. Now, it is explained extensively that Buddha-nature is neither existent nor [non-existent]."
It is free from the two extremes; abiding in the Middle Way, there is no characteristic to be grasped. Its nature is profound and mysterious, beyond the comprehension of those of the Two Vehicles;
even the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes still perceive it only dimly—how could it not be difficult to see?
Those of shallow practice and limited learning are bodhisattvas prior to the stage of abiding.
As the Sūtra says, "The Buddha-nature is extremely profound, extremely profound," meaning that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, and afflictions are themselves bodhi.
It is the ultimate depth. Therefore, the text again establishes the discourse on the "Extremely Profound.
The Sūtra asks: "What is meant by 'extremely profound' (yāvat praveśaḥ)? What are the characteristics of Buddha-nature?
Why is it invisible and yet so difficult to enter?"

Regarding the presentation of the ten analogies as a whole: when one contemplates the ten analogies in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, they correspond to the ten vehicles of contemplative methods (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna-dharma*) of *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

The first analogy corresponds to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*); thus, the single truth and the three truths—namely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—are called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
The Sūtra says, "Pointing with one finger. This means that for each [point], one must ask, "Do you see it? Sengliang said:

"The golden probe (*kanabhi*) is a metaphor for the various sūtra teachings; the single finger is a metaphor for the various sūtras of the Three Vehicles. These speak of three nirvāṇas, yet their true intent is to reveal the one eternally abiding nirvāṇa.
The text is obscure and its meaning subtle—this is like the single finger. The second finger is a metaphor for the *Lotus Sūtra*, which shatters the two [conceptions of] nirvāṇa."

The teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, though its meaning was revealed, was not yet fully clear—this is likened to two fingers. The teaching of the Buddha-nature as eternally blissful, as proclaimed today, is likened to three fingers.

Even those who have seen it only slightly have already reached the end of their lives; having reached the end, they will experience the fruition. Once the principle is unobstructed and the teaching has been heard, one immediately sees it.

At the beginning, because his power was slight, it was difficult to explain; thus, although he showed [the teaching], it was not fully understood. For this reason, the Sūtra states that a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages sees the end but does not see the beginning.
As for the refutation of the three types of patience (kṣānti) in the Commentary: the single thought of quiescent extinction resides only in the Buddha; therefore, it is excluded.

Furthermore, the explanation from the first ground through the tenth ground is based on the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). This analogy is explained here according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) from the perspective of the Single Truth (Yidi).

Regarding "deluded about non-self": in the former teachings, one was confused regarding non-self, asserting it to be the ultimate reality and failing to realize that non-self is precisely the truly eternal self;
hence, it is said to be "deluded about non-self."
The Sūtra speaks of "geese and wild geese in space. Because space is obscured by ignorance, one perceives the geese and wild geese of the Buddha-nature.

To realize this is identical in meaning to the aforementioned "seeking that which is above. If one possesses the upward-seeking [aspiration], one must necessarily possess the downward-transforming [activity].
The Sūtra says, "For example, like a drunken man. This is because one is intoxicated by ignorance; thus, one does not clearly perceive the distant path of true permanence.

This is identical in meaning to the principle of settling the mind. By means of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), one settles within the Way of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). If there were no tranquil illumination, how could one perceive the Way?
The Sūtra says: "One who wanders everywhere seeking water" refers to one who, oppressed by the thirst of ignorance and driven to delusion, fails to see the clear water of the Buddha-nature.

This is identical in meaning to the principle of "universal refutation. Only by universally refuting the wilderness of the two deaths and the three delusions can one finally glimpse, even slightly, the white cranes of the Three Truths.

The Sūtra says, "Traveling afar... to the great ship. This is because, while dwelling in the void, one does not clearly see the Buddha-nature; the watchtower represents the principle of understanding this [nature] in terms of what is passable and what is obstructed.

It is identical in meaning to the guide. If one does not recognize what is passable and what is obstructed, how can one traverse the five hundred yojanas and reach the watchtower of the Buddha-nature to discern its right and wrong?
The Sūtra says, "wandering throughout the night. This means that by wandering through the night of ignorance, one perceives the Buddha-nature of the three virtues and realizes it;

this is identical in meaning to the *mārga-varga* (the Chapter on the Path). The *mārga-varga* is the gateway through which one penetrates the Buddha-nature of the three virtues, just like wandering throughout the night.
The Sūtra states: "Those constrained by royal affairs" refers to those who, though bound by the affairs of ignorance, perceive the ox-herd of the Buddha-nature.
This is identical in meaning to the "auxiliaries to the Path. Since one attains vision through others, is this not indeed an auxiliary to the Path?

As for the scriptural passage asking, "Is this a worm?", it refers to the worm of ignorance perceiving the dust-like clarity of the Buddha-nature; this is identical in meaning to the subsequent stages.

By upholding the precepts with the mind of ultimate reality—practicing one [virtue] and ceasing one [vice]—one ascends from the shallow to the deep through the distinctions of the six successive stages.
The Sūtra states, "Regarding these oxen and so forth": this refers to those whose vision of the Buddha-nature is obscured by the ox of ignorance.
This is identical in meaning to "patience" (kṣānti). Those who possess patience are like oxen and others that quickly become compliant.

The Sūtra states: "As for the Bodhisattva who has exhausted all views": because of the ignorance regarding the images of devas and so forth, one exhausts the views [of these] to clarify the true nature of the Bodhisattva.
This is identical in meaning to "being free from attachment. Being free from attachment to these similar deva-images, one exerts oneself to perceive the true image of the Bodhisattva.
The Sūtra asks: "How can the fleshly eye see? This question is posed with reference to those whose six sense faculties are purified;
however, in reality, it applies to ordinary beings as well.
The scripture states, "Those who follow the sūtras" refers to those of the Hīnayāna.
Among them, there are those with discernment who maintain that while consciousness does not exist in the two realms of emptiness and form, there nonetheless exists a subtle consciousness of its own.

Regarding those who possess perception: this is not the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), nor is it the non-perception of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
rather, they possess their own subtle perception. This explanation is given from the perspective of the same realm (*dhātu*).
Regarding "the ordinary person within the principle": this refers to a person who practices the internal path based on the Buddha's teachings.
As for "a prince rich in the wealth of the Dharma": the noble path of the Bodhisattva is likened to a prince, while the ordinary person lacking virtue is likened to a pauper.
"Mutual interaction" means that the resonance and response open one another; this is called mutual interaction.

"Going and returning" means that when the capacity of the beings of the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū corresponds to the teaching, it is called "going. When sentient beings regress from the Great Vehicle and undergo transmigration, it is called "returning.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva’s own body regresses from the Great Vehicle, his textual manifestation also ceases its transformation; this too is called "returning. Therefore, it is said to be "going and returning."
The Sūtra says: "There is one who possesses a fine sword. That which is the true self abiding eternally is called "possessing one"; that which is sovereign and delightful is called "fine.
To sever delusions is metaphorically likened to the sword; that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are forever exhausted is called "pure, wondrous, and supreme."
Regarding the phrase "holding a knife," it means that the body relinquishes its response. "The Dharma follows all" means, in its sense, "carrying it away.
As for "the knife being secret through the stimulus-response," when the stimulus arises, the response fades;

when the response ceases, the stimulus comes and goes imperceptibly, such that the stimulus remains unknown—its meaning is like a flight that is not manifest, which is termed "secret" (*mi*). [The character *mian* (讇) is pronounced as *yǎn* or *yán*.]
The "Explanations of the Classics" refers to the existence of authoritative teachings.
As the Sūtra says, "There is no such sword within my treasury," this means that within the treasury of the Small Vehicle’s ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there is no "my sword."

Regarding the five expedient means (*pañca-upāya*): the five cessations (*pañca-vinodana*) are merely antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). As an initial gateway, one employs the five cessations to counteract afflictions so that one becomes capable of practicing the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);

therefore, they are excluded [from the count]. Furthermore, by combining the general and specific foundations of mindfulness into one, and adding the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*), there are five.

Regarding those who were "intimate and close": if explained according to the underlying intent, this refers to those who previously established the *dharmas* of measurement under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
The explicit meaning of the current text clarifies that they had previously received the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, they are described as "intimate and close."

Regarding the statement "not yet wishing to refute this heterodox view": it clarifies that although followers of the Hīnayāna have come wishing to refute this heterodox view, the karmic conditions are not yet suitable.
As for the phrase "only clarifying non-self": the wording here is concise; it simply states "non-self" and "not perceiving a self at all," as if using the blade of a knife.
Regarding the true mark (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), before the teachings on non-self (*anātman*) and so forth were expounded, the Sūtra states that "the King laughed loudly at that time.
Saṃgharāja Liang said: "The teaching concerning the twin trees is the true mark."

The "Chapter on Words" (Mojishin) treats the text in two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the text itself. Regarding the first part, there are four sections: first, a brief explanation of the title;

second, the opening of the esoteric [teachings] and the subsequent citation of old [commentaries]; third, the refutation beginning with "Now, to clarify that..."; and fourth, the detailed explanation beginning with "Now, based upon...," which is categorized as follows:
The three truths (trīṇi satyāni) manifest that written words possess the function of embodying the three truths. Regarding the first, "words" (*wén*), Sengzong said:

"Above, the causes and effects have been extensively explained, as has the extensive circulation [of the teaching]. However, since the principle (*lǐ*) and the words (*wén*) together constitute the essence of the sūtra, this chapter extensively explains the words.

The two metaphors of the bird and the moon extensively explain the principle and the words; thus, both aspects of the sūtra are complete without deficiency. Zhixiu said: "By means of the fourteen vowels..."
The manifestation of the perfected principle is termed the "full letter" (maṇḍalākṣara); the manifestation of the unperfected principle is termed the "half-letter" (ardhākṣara).

This also follows the precedent of ancient scholars. The second and third [sections] are as in the text. The fourth, the extensive explanation, is further divided into two parts: first, an explanation based on the three truths;

second, the integration and detailed unfolding of the three truths under the headings "the letter" and "the non-letter. The first part has three sections. The first section concerns emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which can extinguish the half-letters.
When one half is opened, it is immediately full, and because there is no longer any characteristic of being "half," it is called the "extinction of the half. The subsequent passage states:
"The half-syllable (ardhakṣara) is the provisional basis for all scriptures and books;
it is the root of literary expression. From this single nirvāṇa flow forth the half-syllables and so on; when these various scriptures and the like are opened, [they reveal the full reality].
This is the perfect and eternal, which is called "revealing the secret.
Thirdly, regarding the phrase "if one understands," it refers to the Middle Way.

That is to say, by means of the character "is" (即) and the character "not" (無), one subsequently integrates and clarifies the three truths. Furthermore, there are three parts: first, the conclusion; second, the analogy; as follows.

The analogy clarifies the opening. In each of the three "one" characters, beneath the first "dharma," the character "non-being" (wu) signifies emptiness. This "non-being" is itself the provisional nature of the character.
Furthermore, "also" and "immediately" below signify the simultaneous negation of both; "fully endowed" and "below" signify the simultaneous illumination of both.

In the subsequent analogy, there are again two parts: first, the actual illustration; second, the explanation that establishes the characteristics of the three truths, beginning with the phrase "one is itself the manifold.
In the first part, both together constitute a single vessel of emptiness; in the second, the manifold does not lose its conventional nature.
The third is also called "the various [teachings] of the lower and middle.

Next, regarding the explanation in the text, the phrase "as previously explained" refers to the passage beginning with "one says it is the fundamental [truth]" and continuing down to "purely the Great Dharma of Nirvana, named 'recognizing the return'.
This meaning is based on first losing [the truth] and subsequently recognizing it; therefore, it differs from the "opening of the provisional" (kai-kwên).
Regarding the subsequent explanation: it simply states that these are the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*).
"Not recognizing" does not mean first losing [the truth] and later recognizing it.
"Not giving" does not mean first providing skillful means and later bestowing [the truth] within the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Why? Because everything is fundamentally [thus].

Regarding the Great Parinirvāṇa Dharma as the fundamental basis of principle and text: the small serves as the great foundation. Because one enters the great by means of the small, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"These ninefold teachings of mine are taught in accordance with sentient beings; entering the Mahāyāna is their fundamental purpose. This is precisely the proof.
The Sūtra states: "That which is dharma is non-dharma. Here, "dharma" refers to the full [vowels], while "non-dharma" refers to the half [consonants].

This means that by opening up the half and clarifying the full, one follows the characters from the side; specifically, it refers to the twelve vowels entering into the thirty-four characters beginning with *ka* and *kha*.
Regarding "the characters following the sounds": this means that the thirty-four characters beginning with *ka* and *kha* are all produced by following the twelve vowels beginning with *a*.
For example, *ka* and *ga* are obtained by following the vowel *a*;

Regarding the statement that "Nirvana" consists of fourteen phonemes, this does not include the final two characters, as their forms are no different from those at the beginning.
The four characters *he-li-xi-li* constitute the two words of the Western [language]. When the characters *li*, *xi*, and *li* are added, they then become four characters.
For this reason, there was an error among the ancients regarding *lu*, *liu*, *lu*, and *lou*; this has been deeply established.
This is the fault of the translator. As for the chapter on words (*śabdavarga*), unless it is transmitted through direct oral instruction, its meaning can never be understood.
*Ka kha ga gha ṅa; ca cha ja jha ña; ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa; ta tha da dha na;
pa pha ba bha ma.* These five groups of five, totaling twenty-five characters, are called *vyañjana*. This is one name.

There are multiple meanings for the prefix *sva-*: first, the meaning of "not yet formed"; second, the meaning of "formed"; third, the meaning of the male and female faculties; fourth, the meaning of "sauce" (*sāṃgraha*);
fifth, the meaning of "fragrance and taste," and so forth. However, its general significance is that it functions as a third-case (instrumental) suffix to provide differentiation.
When these twenty-five syllables are not yet joined with the preceding vowels, they are merely "half-syllables" (*ardha-akṣara*) and are unfit for utterance.

The twenty-five characters beginning with *zhào yě luó pó shè sǎ suō hē lán chā* (the final two characters are not included in the count), together with the eight characters below, totaling thirty-three characters, constitute the first chapter.

All must be pronounced with the rising tone (*shǎngshēng*), and one must not allow the characters to fall into the level, departing, or entering tones. For example, as when employing the sixteen melodic tones (*yunshēng*).
When these are assigned to the thirty-three [syllables], the first foot-character is divided into sixteen variations.

However, in current secular practice, when beginning to instruct children, many do not follow this method; thus, for the four characters *he-li*, *qi-li*, *li*, and *li*, there are only twelve distinctions.
If one were to establish sixteen, there would likewise be no fault, as these four rhymes are employed.
These instances are not many; therefore, people do not preserve them. As for the "twelve sounds," they refer to:

*ka* (short first syllable, long second), *ki* (short first syllable, long second), *ku* (short first syllable, long second), *kī* (long first syllable, short second), *go* (long first syllable, short second), *ga* (both sounds short, with the character *ge* [箇] pronounced with force and exhalation).
These twelve characters—such as *ka* and so forth—are all suitable to be initiated in this manner, and each may be called by following the other in pairs.
Furthermore, one must insert the particle "zi" (子) within two characters and thereby determine their length. Of the remaining thirty-two characters, all may begin from this;
in total there are thirty. Now, the twelve names constitute the second chapter. To fully comprehend the discourse, there are eighteen chapters in total.
However, if one masters a single chapter through calligraphy, one’s knowledge of characters will be roughly sufficient, and one may gradually study the remainder. Nevertheless, based on this—
The meaning of the *Zhixiao jing* (Sutra on the Elimination of Intentions) is largely complete.
As the sutra says: "One who can protect and uphold the Great Nirvana," the Eastern King Dhṛtarāṣṭra protects permanence and impermanence;
the Southern King Virūḍhaka protects pleasure and non-pleasure; the Western King Virūpākṣa protects... [the self].

"I am without self. To the north, the Pure King Vaiśravaṇa protects what is pure and what is impure, not permitting outsiders to take its branches and leaves, nor to cut, fell, or destroy it, and so forth.

Regarding what is called "letter" (*akṣara*): in Sanskrit it is *akṣara*, which in this land [of China] is translated according to its meaning as "inexhaustible.

Its meaning of permanence is identical to that of *nirvāṇa*. For this reason, Emperor Wu of Liang [established] four [categories]; Kai-suan [established] the same five [categories] as the "Oasis" (as previously stated);
and Zang-yang added the "ability to produce," making fifteen in total with the previous "producing. Therefore, [this] is not tenable. Sixth, the "Excess of the City-Governor."

Regarding the "same adornment" (tóng zhuāngyán) and the statement that "the former twelve [vowels] and so forth" were used by those west of the Hexi region: if it were not for the explanation provided by Yìjìng, one might still rely upon this interpretation. Why?
Because the twelve vowels—*ru*, *liú*, *lú*, *lóu*, and the preceding ones—are taken as fourteen sounds.

Regarding the second point, as for what is called "speech" (*vāk*): multiple syllables (*akṣara*) together constitute a word (*pada*), and two words constitute speech. Therefore, it cannot yet be employed.

That which has not yet been completed is called "half," meaning that when the preceding vowel is brought forward to be joined [with the following consonant], it is merely a half-syllable; hence it is said to be "not yet complete."
This means that because the twelve characters beginning with "A" penetrate all other characters, each single character fully possesses these twelve;
it is for this reason that they are said to be "complete.

Regarding the absence of "prolongation" (*āyāma*) and so forth: in the preceding text, there is no drawn-out *anitya* (impermanence) that combines to form the complete character *nitya* (permanence), as in [the following example].
The four characters previously cited as being excluded as "fruits" (results) are those not practiced by the ignorant and young;
they are like the four characters *he-li* and so forth mentioned before, which the ignorant and young generally do not study.
While this may be granted, there is no basis for claiming that the two characters *lu-lou* are not studied by the ignorant and young.

Regarding the phrase "heavy child" (*chóng tóng*) mentioned in the Sūtra, the first character is pronounced with the third tone (rising tone), while the subsequent characters follow the phonetic momentum of each syllable and are all pronounced with the third tone.

Regarding the phrase "transcending sounds" (*chāo shēng*) mentioned in the Sūtra, the nine characters beginning with *nà luó* constitute these transcending sounds; this means that the five vocal registers (*wǔ yīn*) are fully present throughout the mouth.
The sound of the parrot is called "transcending sound.

A sutra says: "Though one dwells within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, one is not identical to these six dharmas; yet, while abiding in principle, one does not depart from the six dharmas.
It is only by means of these five [aggregates] that one can truly see one's nature."

The Sūtra states: "Therefore, as for the meaning of the 'half-syllables' (*ardhakṣara*): if explained by way of flowing forth from the fundamental essence, then the primordial *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is the 'full-syllable' (*pūrṇakṣara*), and that which is fundamentally full is the 'half-syllable.
Furthermore, this fundamental half-syllable serves as the basis for the mundane world.

If, however, one proceeds from the derivative back to the fundamental, then mundane writings, records, and so forth are the 'half-syllables,' while the fundamental half-syllables are the 'full-syllables,' and these fundamental full-syllables [are the ultimate reality]."
Although the nature of dharmas (dharmatā) fundamentally involves mutual dependence, its essence is non-dual.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the "half-syllables" up to "afflictions": although the half-syllables, in terms of ultimate truth, are entirely ignorance and specific delusions.
Therefore, the "half-character" (*ardha-akṣara*) is the root of affliction. Xingyun said: "Half-persons" refers only to those who dwell in a state of insufficiency;
they are all likewise "half-persons.
To further clarify the meaning of the "non-character," Sengliang said: "The aforementioned 'root of all wholesome dharmas' refers to the person."
It is also the foundation for the Tathāgata. The Buddha’s awakening is without teacher and is not encompassed by letters; it is called "separation from words.

As for the question, "Does the nature lack the meaning of 'no-words'?"—the heterodox, the eternalists, and the two vehicles possess only names with words, yet beneath those words, they lack the meaning of the eternal and blissful.

The "Bird Simile" chapter is divided into two parts according to the text: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the text itself, which follows below. The beginning of the text further divides into two: first, a brief explanation;

second, a detailed explanation following the "Old Interpretation. The first of these again divides into two: first, citing the interpretation of Hexi; second, providing the formal explanation starting with "Now, furthermore. Regarding the first: [Text begins]... "First, it says..."
Regarding "the True and the Responsive": the eternal is the True, and the impermanent is the Responsive.

As for the analogy of the moon’s concealment and manifestation: concealment symbolizes the impermanence of the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya), while manifestation symbolizes the permanence of the True Body (dharmakāya). Fayao said:

The Dharma-body is profound, subtle, tranquil, and dark, transcending the realm of sight and hearing; thus, it is hidden from the emotions. To see the six-foot form and call it the ultimate is to regard it as manifest.

Those who penetrate both the permanent and the impermanent, and penetrate the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, realize that these are precisely the permanent and the impermanent, yet they are neither permanent nor impermanent.

Therefore, it is called "concealment and manifestation. Fayao said: "In the past, impermanence was taught so that one might attain permanence. Since the attainment of permanence depends upon impermanence, how could they be separated?
Thus, they together constitute a single holy state; this is called 'common holy practice' (saṃvṛti-ārya-caryā)."

The Refutation states: Generally speaking, that which is called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) refers to two practices being observed simultaneously. Since the present and past bodies are distinct, how can they be termed "common practice"?

Regarding the reliance on the Two Truths or Three Truths: although the sutras clarify only the characteristics of the Two Truths, they do so by means of the inconceivable, wherein the Two Truths are themselves the Three Truths.
Therefore, I have provided an explanation of the Three Truths based on this underlying meaning.
Regarding "one teaching encompassing all teachings": this refers to the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), which universally subsumes and universally opens up all other teachings.
Next, the detailed explanation of the text is divided into three parts. First, in the account of the old [interpretations], it says: "These constitute two categories, forming two pairs.
This could also be understood as two distinct types forming two pairs, with the metaphors for the two modes of circulation also being applicable.
Regarding the question within the questions concerning *sāla*: in the preceding inquiry, it was asked, "What is the noble practice shared with the *sālakalyāṇī*?
As for *śarī*, it refers to the white heron and the vulture.
Next, regarding the brief explanation of the "Han" [section] below, it is provided to demonstrate the correct meaning.

As for the statement in the *Xiang* [section] that they are called "the two flows": this means that what ordinary beings cultivate is termed "the practice of the two flows," while what sages engage in is termed "the function of the two flows."

The three questions constitute the section on "Questioning the Ordinary and Inferior" (*fanxia wenda*), which refutes the erroneous to reveal the correct; this is divided into three parts: first, the question;

second, the refutation of other interpretations; and third, the present explanation. Regarding the first [the question], there are two sub-sections: first, the question that initiates the inquiry as the truth (*satya*) for explanation.

Next, the explanation following the interpretation of others is provided. First, the intent of the question is as follows: "The simultaneous flow of body and speech constitutes common practice with ordinary beings;
the permanent and the impermanent constitute common practice with ordinary beings; the impermanent constitutes common practice with ordinary beings;

and the permanent constitutes long-standing common practice with the noble ones. Furthermore, a fourth alternative cannot be established; if one were to establish it, it would be identical to the above cases.

Next, regarding the second section on the interpretations of others within the main text, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the interpretations of others; second, the re-statement of their errors under the heading "Furthermore, according to one school.
The first part also has two sub-sections: first, the presentation of the other's view; second, the refutation of that erroneous analogy under the heading "This should not be so."
Regarding the initial statement, "merely recognizing gold and so forth": gold is a metaphor for the permanent (*nitya*), while brass is a metaphor for the impermanent (*anitya*).
Next, the two points are restated: first, the errors are set forth; second, the subsequent refutation is clarified.

Within the third section, the formal explanation states that "flying together and resting together" means that when power (*bala*) is identical to principle (*li*), it is called "resting together"; when principle is identical to power, it is called "flying together. The Two Truths are themselves the Middle Way.
The "dual cessation" (*shuangxi*) refers to the two truths being called "dual movement" (*shuangyou*). It is the same for that which is neither of the two.

Furthermore, permanence and impermanence being called "neither permanent nor impermanent" is named dual cessation; "neither permanent nor impermanent" being called "permanent and impermanent" is named dual movement.
