Moreover, placing all sons within the secret treasury and my own entry therein is also called dual cessation.
Regarding "the male and female also being accomplished": two birds are one bird, and one bird is two birds; only then is it called "wandering as a pair. Regarding "horizontal and vertical":
a single practice encompassing all practices is horizontal; each individual practice being in accord with the secret treasury (hizō) is vertical.
Furthermore, the six stages of realization (*rokujisoku*) in their varying depths are vertical, while each stage universally encompassing all phenomena is horizontal.
"Common practice with the ordinary" refers to that which all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) practice in common; this is the dualistic flow.

"Common practice with both the ordinary and the noble" means that when ordinary beings contemplate impermanence (*anitya*), what they perceive as permanence is entirely the permanence of the *nirvāṇa* of the noble ones (*ārya*).

When noble ones contemplate impermanence, what they perceive as impermanence is entirely the birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) of sentient beings. Why is this so? Because the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is non-dual. If...
Generally speaking, when an ordinary person contemplates the self as either permanent or impermanent, it is not called "wandering in both. It is the same for a sage.
Only when one realizes that the essential nature of both the ordinary and the sage is non-dual can it be called "the common practice of the ordinary and the sage."

It is neither ordinary nor holy, yet it is practiced by both; both ordinary and holy beings are in accord with the secret treasury of the principle that is neither eternal nor impermanent, for it does not belong to either the ordinary or the holy.
As for the missing phrase "practiced by the holy together with the holy," it is as previously explained regarding persons and dharmas: the sixth [stage] is *niṣpanna* (perfected) nirvāṇa.
This is because people’s attainment of the Dharma varies according to its depth or shallowness.
Next, regarding the explanation of the text, it says that within the section on synthesis, "it is merely an abbreviation.

The text only mentions the three [characteristics] of "this is suffering," "impermanent," and so forth, but does not mention "this is suffering and pleasant," "impermanent and eternal," or "non-self and true self. Why were these abbreviated?
This is to reveal the identity of phenomena, meaning that suffering is itself pleasure, and so forth.
When the Sūtra asks, "What is this suffering, impermanence, and so on? what is the intent of the question?
Is it asking whether suffering, impermanence, and the like move in tandem like a pair of *kalaviṅka* birds?
The previous frequent refutations of perversion refer to the *Śoka-parivarta* (Chapter on Lamentation), which constantly subverts the notion of impermanence.
As for the phrase "only within birth-and-death are there views such as difference," this refers to forming divergent views and interpretations regarding birth-and-death.
Specifically, the two vehicles regard birth-and-death as suffering and so forth, while the Bodhisattvas regard birth-and-death as permanent and so forth; this is termed [perversion].
These are different dharmas. When their essential natures are fundamentally identical, they are said to "move together.
To use this to manifest impermanence is to borrow the "permanence" of the world’s temporary lack of change to clarify the meaning of permanence within the world.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "You should not now" up to "the speaker," it states "should not" because what he previously heard was incorrect.
As for the question concerning "a single rebirth," its meaning is as follows: when observing Kāśyapa at that time, it appeared as though the Tathāgata was identical to all other things;

thus, it seemed like a question regarding the absence of truth (*avitatya*), yet in reality, it was not without truth. However, the Buddha subsequently manifested the characteristics of how it is not without truth.
Regarding the current inquiry concerning sorrow, grief, and so forth: this expresses the intent of the question. As Kāśyapa will later raise an objection by drawing out the implication:
"If there is no sorrow or grief in nirvāṇa, why did the Buddha state in other sūtras that the Tathāgata also possesses sorrow and grief?
If he possesses sorrow and grief, does this not mean he is impermanent?"

Regarding the scripture’s statement, "Directly by means of conventional truth... [up to] 'constant,'" the Buddha's intention was that he previously borrowed the conventional [world]—using the temporary constancy of this fruit as a metaphor.
How could it be said that the Tathāgata is merely identical to this fruit?
The Sūtra states: "Although there is a body of afflictions, it is entirely Buddha-nature; therefore, it is said to be as if non-existent.
The Sūtra says, "For example, like a nugget of gold," which also refers to this [nugget]. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "this ore-nugget" (pronounced *pǔmù* or *pǔjiǎo*, homophonous with *pǔ*).
These five metaphors are all partial analogies (*fen-yù*), unlike the analogy of waves and water. Why? Because one must melt the nugget to obtain the gold.
Gold exists within its ore; if this were used as a metaphor for their dual movement, it would not fully capture the meaning.

When the Sūtra says, "For example, like the various rivers flowing into the sea," this too is a partial metaphor. It is by entering [the sea] that they become salty, and thus there is no sorrow or grief.

That which possesses a self is the true self. That which possesses sorrow and grief is the non-self. Having heard that there is no-self in the world, the Sūtra speaks of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) and so forth.
First, it clarifies that in the state of no-thought, existence cannot be definitively established;

yet, below the state of no-thought, non-existence cannot be definitively established. This meaning is concluded below: because there is no fixed location, and although there is no-thought, there is still life-span. Therefore [it is said].
It has no fixed location; the Tathāgata’s sorrow and grief are likewise. There is no conceptualizing compassion, and in reality there is no sorrow or grief.
Yet, for the sake of sentient beings, they arise spontaneously. Therefore, it is compared to the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva).

The Sūtra says, "relying on branches and so forth. This means that the spirit dwells in dependence upon the combination of the tree; thus, it cannot rely exclusively on a single branch or joint, which clarifies that it is not [inherently] existent.
Although there is no fixed location, this reveals that it is not non-existent. The Buddha-dharma is also like this.
Regarding the application of the analogy: while the absence of sorrow and grief is applied to the presence of a self, it is applied below to the absence of a self.

As for that which is spoken of within the state of non-existence: the Tathāgata possesses neither conceptualization nor deliberation, yet through the invocation of sentient beings, [compassion] arises spontaneously; this is the sense of "equality."

Regarding the mention of sorrow and grief: first, there is sorrow because of great compassion; second, there is sorrow as a skillful adaptation to circumstances. In the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is impartial, there is actually neither sorrow nor joy;
therefore, it is said that this is spoken according to the underlying meaning.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra beginning with "a mote of dust" up to "is established": even empty space cannot be established upon a mote of dust, let alone a house.
Furthermore, although a house is not fixed, it must rely on emptiness and must depend on ground and space to be established.
Regarding the scriptural statement, "Because the nature has no abiding": just as empty space does not receive material objects, the nature of a house does not abide within space;
hence it is said that "the nature has no abiding.
Regarding "the illness is permanent": this refers to the illness of [the view of] permanence.
"One who wanders in peace" refers to one who dwells in Great Nirvāṇa while universally traversing the Dharma-realm. Zézhōu says: "The metaphor of the two birds represents the Buddha-Tathāgata.
When the five turbidities increase, it is called 'midsummer. When afflictions and consciousness flourish, it is called 'the rising of the waters.

The Buddha selects the True Dharma to transform people and cause them to dwell [in safety], which is like selecting a high plateau; they do not reach [the depths]. This interpretation, based on the arising of inversion, is consistent [with the meaning].
Regarding the scriptural passage concerning "both permanent and impermanent" and so forth, it should further state: "named the foremost permanence and the foremost impermanence," and so on.
As for the scriptural expression "the place where death stinks," "stinks" (neng) functions as a demonstrative particle; it refers to the location where the fruit of death is manifested.
The Sūtra states: "Those who lack the divine eye cannot see the true self; only those who possess the true divine eye of the World-Honored One can see it.
As for the phrase "how does one reach the terrace of wisdom? it means that by ascending to a height, one sees what lies below. Thus, we know that the Tathāgata possesses sorrow and grief.

The "Chapter on the Simile of the Moon" is divided into two parts according to the text: first, the explanation of the title; second, from "Now, dividing... onwards, the word-by-word commentary. The first part consists of six sections:
first, clarifying how the two similes complement each other to manifest the meaning of the title; second, the explanation by the Master of Hexi; third, the question and answer... [and so forth].

The intent of the commentary’s questions and answers is as follows: 1. From "Fourth, Emperor Wu... onwards, it cites the calculations of the Confucian masters to clarify the mutual relations between heaven, earth, the sun, and the moon.

2. From "Fifth, the Long River contains... onwards, it demonstrates what the True Teaching clarifies to distinguish it from Confucianism. 3. From "Sixth, this chapter... onwards, it demonstrates the meaning of the text of the response.
Regarding the first two points, they are as the text states. Third, within the explanation of the intent, it says "two questions and one answer," as stated above: ...as mentioned above.

Regarding the two questions—"How can one attain vastness? and "How can one attain equality?"—the response using the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) in a single chapter answers one while implicitly answering the other.
As for the question, "How can one attain long life," this constitutes a double-layered cause-and-effect response.

As for the statement that "in the Hexi [version] there is only a single phrase," although the chapter contains three thematic meanings according to the Hexi tradition, they constitute a single point; it consists merely of one question and one answer.

Regarding the remaining two lines, there is one question and two answers in one case, and one question and two answers in another; such structural force is rare in the text, which is why it is said they are "easily understood.
However, the Master’s intention is that all thirty-four questions are fixed as consisting of one question followed by one answer.

Regarding the moon’s waning and waxing: waning represents concealment, while waxing represents manifestation. Manifestation is a metaphor for the True Body (dharmakāya), and waning is a metaphor for the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya).
Regarding the lengthening and shortening of its function: lengthening is a metaphor for manifestation, and shortening is a metaphor for concealment.

Regarding the stars' removal of misfortune: "auspicious" is a metaphor for the manifest, while "inauspicious" is a metaphor for the hidden; this is discussed according to what is appropriate. Zhezhou says: "The preceding section clarified the Buddha's determinate karma.
Now, regarding the application of [karmic] influence, three metaphors—sun, moon, and stars—are used to clarify the application of the Buddha’s two types of karma: body and speech.
What is now clarified—the two modes of activity and their manifestation or concealment—is none other than the three karmas. It is appropriate that they not be divided."
Second, it contradicts the scriptural text.

Regarding the moon’s inclusion of the sun and stars: the moon is able to undergo waning and waxing; at night, both are observed together, and their function as luminaries is identical. Therefore, the moon is able to include the two.

The *Sishu yinyi zhong* states: "The term *bǐ* (pronounced with the *bì* rhyme) refers to the sun and moon moving transversely; this means they travel from east to west. As for *zhú* (pronounced with the *sàn* rhyme), it refers to the same. "Moving transversely" simply means traveling in an east-west direction.
Regarding "circling around heaven and earth": it means disappearing from above the heavens and circling below the earth.
Regarding "the practitioner of the corners" mentioned in the *Wuyin Zhengjiao*: it refers to one who has fallen into the practice of the corners.
Next, regarding the explanation of the text, as for answering the three questions: although there was only one question above, it contained within it three questions;
therefore, three are now answered.
As for "turning spontaneously," this means that it is set in motion by the karmic power of sentient beings.
The "supporting wind" (dhāraṇa-vāyu) supports [things] in mid-air. The "dwelling wind" (sthiti-vāyu) causes them to remain and not fall downward.
Regarding those who commit theft, the Āgama Sūtra says: There was a person who stole melons and cried out, "Alas! Alas! Moon, do not rise!"
"Wait until I have stolen the melons; whether you come out or not, I shall not be pleased to see you.

Regarding the "three times" as the fundamental inclusion: according to the Buddha-dharma, only three times are established. Although three times are established, the twelve [divisions] formed by multiplying them by four are identical to the system of four times.

This does not exclude those who dwell like thieves (*caura-vāsin*). In the Buddha-dharma, the autumn season is not established as a time for ordination. If one were to exclude those who dwell like thieves, one should ask: "At what time did you receive the precepts?
If they say it was during the autumn, they are identified as dwelling like thieves. In the Western Regions, four seasons are originally established among the laity;

since they have not yet entered the Buddha-dharma, they do not know the temporal limits established by the Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, according to the Vinaya, one may not enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*) during the summer.
Regarding the offense of *ti* (defeat): if one does not observe the rains retreat (*anvāsa*) during spring or winter, one incurs the offense of *ji* (grave).
As for "spring and autumn being the same," it means that the duration is identical because the cool air is the same; therefore, the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is not established [for those seasons].
Regarding the phrase "its manifestation removes the old and so forth": when this extraordinary star appears, it signifies the passing of a king and the accession of a new one;
therefore, it is said that the old is removed and the new is spread.
Regarding the phrase "having passed through the ear once" in the sutra, Fayao said: "One initiates the merit of a single hearing and ultimately relies upon this wisdom;

all evils are eliminated. This does not mean that afflictions are exhausted simply because the sutra has once passed through the ear; rather, it correctly demonstrates that the function of this sutra is to extinguish evil.
The arising of goodness is equal to the Dharma-body.

The "Bodhisattva Chapter" is divided into two parts according to the text: first, the explanation of the title and its intent; second, from "Now, as for... onwards, the entry into the text for detailed explanation. The first part also has three sections. First: [The text continues with the specific commentary.]
First, Tǎng answers the intent [of the question]. Second, he explains the meaning of "Bodhisattva" and below to clarify the significance of the title.

Third, from "Now, Hexi... onwards, he judges the merits and faults. Regarding the initial statement that "there are thirteen [questions] above": the offense of *duṣkṛta* (突非), the non-response of the Arhat, and Māra Pāpīyān are combined into a single question;
thus, there are only thirteen. However, in the commentary on the "Yaṅzhèng" (耶正) chapter, it is explicitly opened up into two: the body and the voice.

The answers are fourteen; if the Arhats are included separately, there are fifteen. If one follows the previous classification where the initial practices are divided into four questions, then there are thirteen, making sixteen in total.
Nevertheless, whether expanded or contracted, the general principle ultimately takes fifteen as the fixed number.
If the preceding section has thirteen, then the Bodhisattva Chapter must have thirteen answers, while the Mahāsannipāta Chapter should have eight.
Question:
The Buddha-activities clarify the principles of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as the dharma that is neither permanent nor impermanent.
What follows below clarifies the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, it belongs to the power of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding the answer to questions twelve through seventeen: the intention of the ancients was that although the great assembly asked [twelve questions], he answered only six.

Next, in the explanation of the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" (up to the fourfold classification), this is specifically for the purpose of including those who have already resolved their minds and excluding those who have not yet generated the aspiration.
Those who have attained the name of "Bodhisattva" are not included among these four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); therefore, they are listed first.
Regarding the threefold offering of power: it is also said that the offering of grass, the offering of lighting lamps, and the offering of honey-molasses constitute the three offerings.
Having already made the vow, he declared, "In a future life, I shall attain Buddhahood and shall also be named Śākyamuni."

Those attendant disciples who all share this "empty faith" (kūshin) do so by realizing that within the Tripitaka itself there truly exists a dharma-body characterized by solid obstruction and dependent origination;
yet they believe in it with a mind that understands it to be like an illusion. Therefore, it is called "empty faith."
Regarding "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*): this wisdom has not yet attained what arises first; it is like shallow water, hence "dry.
One who does not fully encompass the Dharma cannot first measure within the one, nor can they measure even a single part within that one.

Furthermore, such a person cannot encompass the wisdom of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) which explains the eightfold dharmas of cause, effect, delusion, and principle; therefore, it is called "not foolishly regressing."

Regarding those who do not include all sentient beings: only those individuals who enter the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and give rise to the resolve [for enlightenment] are called Bodhisattvas;
those prior to the ten stages of faith who have not yet given rise to the resolve are not included by this teaching.
Regarding the Buddha-nature faculty: the first three teachings are merely the Dharma of Bodhisattvas; only the Perfect Vehicle (Vimalakīrti’s Round Teaching) is called the Buddha-Dharma.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva Vehicle alone does not encompass the Perfect Wondrous Enlightenment. As for the statement that "those who hear [the teaching] are immediately Bodhisattvas": sentient beings are already superior [to those of the three vehicles];
even one who calls himself a Buddha is still termed a sentient being—how much more so could one not be called a Bodhisattva?
Regarding "having rationality as the cause": having rationality as the cause means that the light of the teaching on nirvāṇa serves as the seed of bodhi.
One who understands this is called a bodhisattva who has not yet generated the resolve [for awakening]. Furthermore, it should be known that the skin is what receives [the teaching].
Those who are perfumed by the light of the Nirvāṇa teaching serve as the cause for Bodhi and are called "Bodhisattvas who have not yet resolved their minds.

Those of the *icchantika* nature and those of the three previous teachings, from the perspective of their state before transformation, do not receive or attain anything upon hearing [the teaching]; they are likewise called "Bodhisattvas who have not yet resolved their minds.
Furthermore, those of the direct, perfect vehicle (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) nature are also called "Bodhisattvas who have not yet resolved their minds."

Regarding those who turn from slander toward faith: when one turns away from delusion regarding the principle of nature upon hearing the teaching of *nirvāṇa*, and this transforms into the realization of its names and meanings, it is called "arousing the bodhicitta.

How could such a person fail to comprehend the essence of the sutra? Now, this sutra, through the teaching of the perfect, eternal, and true letter "I" (*i*), exclusively elucidates the *amṛta* (clarified butter) of the Buddha-nature.
This is taken as the core principle; therefore, no other interpretation can be made.
Regarding the statement in the "Threefold Judgment" that "this answers four questions," from this point until "is defiled by illness," there are only four questions.
"Not being defiled by illness" means that because of the vision of the nature [of reality], one is not defiled by illness.
For this reason, he answered all the questions, consistently manifesting the single meaning of the Buddha-nature.
As for those who lack eyebrows and eyes, the perfectly constant Buddha-nature elucidated by our Master today is identical to that of Hexi, like two faces that are the same.
However, the skin distinguishes each answer as being individually different, thereby manifesting the Buddha-nature; it is like a mask equipped with eyebrows and eyes.

Next, regarding the passage within the text that says, "Praising the sutra while answering incidentally": because the light of the Great Nirvana teaching universally touches all sentient beings, it serves as the cause for their bodhicitta;
this is what is meant by "praising the sutra. This Great Nirvana teaching can express the rational nature (*dharmatā*) of all sentient beings.
Since nirvāṇa arises from this rational nature, one attains the name "Bodhisattva"; this is what is meant by "answering the question. However...
This is merely a brief designation as "lateral.

For those whose roots of goodness are slight, this refers to the very emergence of the signs of bodhicitta that has not yet been formally generated. Since I am now using this interpretation for my explanation, I do not reject it.
The Sūtra states: "Although sentient beings may lack the bodhicitta, the light of the Nirvāṇa teaching permeates their inner minds, acting as the cause for bodhi.
This refers precisely to those bodhisattvas who possess the fundamental nature but have not yet awakened the resolve.
Regarding the phrase "before this chapter": it means that the production of good occurs in the present, while the cessation of evil is described in the preceding text; hence, it is called "before.

Regarding the end of the previous chapter: at the conclusion of the *Candraprabha-parivarta*, following the passage "For example, when the sun rises," there are ten lines of six characters each beneath the word "mist";
these constitute the text on the cessation of evil.
Next, regarding the refutation of the contrary view: if it is claimed that when the light of nirvana enters the pores, one obtains the cause for bodhi, this meaning is not tenable.
Why? For that which is called a "cause" must be achieved only after one has undertaken practice; therefore, it is not yet possible to claim that one obtains the cause merely by receiving the light.
Regarding the objection concerning observance and violation: this refers to the fact that there is already a distinction between those who observe and those who violate [the precepts].

As for the meaning of the Sūtra’s statement, "For what reason does it speak of the four reliances?"—if it were said that all sentient beings develop the aspiration for enlightenment upon hearing the light of *nirvāṇa*, then by using only this light, all sentient beings would have already developed that aspiration. Why, then, does the Tathāgata, after his parinirvāṇa, further cause...?
The four reliances transcend the world; do they not punish evil and reward good?
One who resolves to accumulate merit must practice as an individual, passing through countless eons before finally attaining the cause of enlightenment.
The Sūtra states that those who are icchantikas are excluded because they possess the three obstacles: namely, failing to perceive cause and effect is the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa);

claiming that there is no cause and effect is the obstacle of karma (karmāvaraṇa); and the accumulation of evil throughout successive lifetimes, which has now resulted in the state of an icchantika, is the obstacle of retribution (vipākāvaraṇa).

Regarding "great merit" and "great matters": only those with the root-nature (*gotra*) of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*) are able to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and the like; this is called "great merit.
Hearing this sutra constitutes the causal condition for Bodhi, and one thereby attains the fruit of Bodhi.

This is precisely the convergence of the path of resonance and response—the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) within the treasury of Great Nirvāṇa—and its cause and effect; this is called a "great matter."

Regarding the passage in the sutra that says "the immeasurable Buddhas, etc.," this refers to those who have truly developed [the aspiration] but whose illumination is not yet uniform, such as Liaozhuan and others.

As for the necessity of expedient means (*upāya*) and why they do not fall into the three evil realms: the sutra states that those who fall into the three evil realms are in the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxingwei*) where the body has not yet severed delusions;
because their observance of precepts is lax while their vehicle is urgent, they consequently suffer regression.
The Sūtra states: "If there are those who hear this Great Nirvāṇa... [up to] "...those who possess bodhi.

This precisely clarifies that even those who have not yet resolved their minds to attain awakening—namely, Bodhisattvas by virtue of their inherent nature (*prakṛti*)—receive the name "Bodhisattva" because they have heard the Sūtra. The Sūtra serves as the cause for their bodhi;
upon realizing this, they are transformed into what are called "Bodhisattvas by name. As it says in the Commentary: "Those who hear the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* are Bodhisattvas by name."

Furthermore, let us not explain this from the perspective of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) upon hearing the sūtras. Therefore, excluding the rational-nature bodhisattva (*dharmatā-bodhisattva*), the analogy of applying ointment to a wound represents the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*):

the medicine merely permeates the skin and gradually removes the affliction. The analogy of applying it to the eyes so that the eyes can see their objects represents the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Therefore, regarding the analogy for the wisdom of cultivation:
while the Kai-shan school uses only nine analogies, our Master [Jizang] provides ten. The preceding diamond analogy represents the ability to destroy all things;
the subsequent diamond analogy takes its essence as being like honey that does not admit external defilements. Thus, these two are distinctly separate.
The "essential path" refers to the beginning of the path to Bodhi.
"To open the eyes for future generations" means to open the eye of the secret treasury for those people of the world.
Regarding "the ten each in both the inverse and the direct order": following the ten in the direct order proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, arising from ignorance. And so forth.
Regarding the icchantika: if one commits the ten heinous acts, one is then provisionally designated as an icchantika. This arises from the "attainment" (yi-zhi);
this was previously clarified in the fourth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.
The second [of the two] consists of clarity regarding repentance and protection. As it says in that same [text] among the ten [points]: "The second clarifies [the path] by way of the wholesome.

Regarding 'repentance' (sāṃghāṭī), this is the seventh [point]: to repair past transgressions. One must not permit the commission of offenses through the three karmas (body, speech, and mind) day or night;

rather, one should now exert oneself unremittingly with a wholesome body, speech, and mind. This is not like moving mountains or filling rivers and seas; it is by means of this that one overturns those [transgressions], even if the three [karmas] were previously indulged in with license."
Regarding the "mind of karma":
the Sūtra states that "level and broad" (*yítǎn*) means "level" (*yí*) is even, and "broad" (*tǎn*) is expansive.
As for the "boundary of birth and death," it refers to exhausting the origin of beginningless offenses; this is precisely the boundary of the boundless.

Regarding "reaching the place reached first": this means exhausting the realm of future offenses until they are finished; only upon reaching the patience (*kṣānti*) that arises first is one said to have "reached the place.

As for the "monkey" mentioned in the sutra: the monkey is a metaphor for an icchantika; the moon is a metaphor for nirvāṇa; the water is a metaphor for the appearance of existence; and the "good water" is a metaphor for bodhi.
Although the icchantika hears the names of nirvāṇa and bodhi, they ultimately cannot attain them. It is like...
That was a monkey. The account of its origin is as stated in the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi. In a secluded place, there were five hundred monkeys wandering through the forest.
They came to a *nyagrodha* tree where there was a well. Beneath the tree was a well, within which..."
When the reflection of the moon appeared, the monkey leader saw it and said to his companions, "The moon has died today and fallen into the well.
We must go together and retrieve it, lest the world remain in the darkness of the long night. They then deliberated together, saying:
"How can we get out? The monkey leader said, "I know the method for getting out. I will grasp a tree branch, and you must grasp my tail;
by linking ourselves together in succession, we can then escape. Thereupon, the monkeys did as their leader had said, grasping one another in turn.
Before they reached the water, the monkey became heavy; the branch broke, and he fell into the well and died. At that time, the tree deity spoke this verse:
"These foolish apes, a crowd of deluded ones following one another, only bring suffering upon themselves; how could they save the Moon of the World? The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The monkey leader at that time was Devadatta. Those who were his companions are now the group of six bhikṣus."
Kāśyapa, it was at that time that we once followed one another and experienced various afflictions; now it is just the same.

As the Sūtra says, "It is like ashes covering fire": because fools see only the present and not the future, they fail to see that the fire of the cause and effect of Buddha-nature is covered by the ashes of prior clarity, and likewise, the fire of the cause and effect of the mundane world is also covered.

Regarding the statement that "evil does not receive its retribution immediately": this is because the retribution for an icchantika is one to be experienced in a future life rather than in the present life; thus, the retribution lies in the future.

Since the character "not" (不) is placed above the subsequent phrase, it clarifies that within the prose section, just as milk becomes curd, the same character "not" should be placed above the subsequent phrase in the verse as well.
It is like the line concerning milk: it is not the case that milk becomes curd immediately.
The Sūtra says that those who are "without eyes" see only the present and do not see the future. They do not perceive the path of the Arhat;
for while an Arhat is able to sever future birth and death, this person does not perceive it.
To raise again the point of what is incorrect: to slander the great on account of the small is precisely that which is incorrect.
When the Sutra says "casting it into turbid water," it refers to the turbid water of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings.

The Commentary states: "First, the constant [contemplations] up to the eight kinds" means that first, the five [contemplations] of suffering, emptiness, and so forth, are the causes for the actual contemplation;

the three [contemplations] of understanding and so forth are the semblance contemplations. Combined, these constitute eight. They eliminate the eight kinds of afflictions: the four inversions, the three poisons, and the equal-proportioned [afflictions].
The Sūtra says, "surpassing the eight kinds of arts. Sengao said: "This principle is complete and the power of its merit is superior; therefore, it is said that they are surpassed.
As for not repenting the past: if one's prior evils are many, one must use purgative medicine."
The virtue of permanence (*nityatā*) is likened to the incense: just as the medicinal incense permeates the entire body, the essence of the virtue of permanence is pervasive.
The virtue of bliss (*sukhatā*) is likened to the medicinal pill: because the pill provides nourishment and restoration, it serves as a metaphor for bliss.

"Showing the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms" means pointing out the three miserable realms as places of retributive suffering, thereby causing [beings] to resolve their minds [on liberation].
As for "this teaching must be abandoned," it refers to "words" because they forget the principle expressed by the teaching; thus, "abandoning" is explained in the sense of liberation.

The mother is a metaphor for the scriptural teachings. The mother is fundamentally the source; it is only by relying slightly on the teachings that one practices. Thus it is said, "Give me my mother's medicine," as explained in the commentary.
"The practice of the ten stages is fulfilled" means passing the ten months; this is a metaphor for the fulfillment of the ten bhūmis.
Pride is "dry" while craving is "low"; these are used as metaphors for dryness and moisture. The *Chao-wu ji* states:

"A Bodhisattva of the first stage possesses great compassion, and therefore does not grasp at nirvana—this is called 'pushing away the dry. Possessing great wisdom, they do not dwell in saṃsāra—this is called 'removing the moisture.
This interpretation is the same as that of Xinghuang.

It eliminates the extremes of eternalism and nihilism. As for "those who possess various inversions," this refers to the elimination of the eight inversions through the removal of ignorance; thus, the lack of distinction regarding the great essence is also eliminated.
Regarding the scriptural passage on "feeding with milk," *bù* (餔) refers to food that is masticated within the mouth.

The analogy of smearing the drum refers to "attachment. The drum smeared by the teacher represents the sentient beings who are the recipients of transformation receiving the teachings; this is called "attachment to the teaching.

Zhezhou says: "New poison" is an analogy for the Great Drum of Principle and Teaching, because the principles newly expounded by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas serve to support and perfect the teachings. Therefore, it is so described.

[The character for "disease" (病) with 帶 added below] (pronounced *zhú lì*): The "upper edge" (*qí*) refers to the seat; the "lower edge" (*xià qí*) refers to the various intestines, as it is the origin of the *sāi*.
The "previous answer regarding the removal of hindrances" refers to the preceding passage on the elimination of the three hindrances.

Regarding the phrase "the previous [is] the Dharmakāya, the body of the Sugata": it is because the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas secretly bestows its grace upon one's own practice that [that practice] can be brought to fulfillment.

Furthermore, "Sugata" (逝) is derived from the sense of "going" (往); it refers to the power of the [Buddha’s] manifestation of passing into extinction, which causes one's own practice to reach fulfillment.

The Sūtra says: "If one obtains a favorable wind," this is an analogy for practicing and attaining the hearing of the Great Nirvāṇa Dharma; thus, one swiftly reaches the *samyak-saṃbuddha* (Sakyam) shore.

Regarding "the single essence [of] many," this refers primarily to the fruit-realized person—the Three Jewels in their single essence. This is because it pertains to the realization of the ultimate stage of fruition.

The character "shi" (釋) means "to explain" or "to clarify," while "di" (地) refers to the "stages" (*bhūmi*). Previously, this was merely a partial attainment; now, it refers exclusively to the ultimate fruit. As the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata’s esoteric words are difficult to understand. For over forty years, he had never revealed them. The Tathāgata is eternally present and undergoes no change;
it was only upon arriving at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* that he finally revealed them. This is what is called "esoteric" (*mi*, *guhya*).
Regarding the phrase "like the four non-constants": these refer to the four [truths] of impermanence, suffering, and so forth.
"Each has its own intent" means that the Mahāyāna teaches permanence in order to refute impermanence and the like; this is the primary intent of the present text.
The Buddha taught a single Dharma that wise ministers understand well: permanence is impermanence, and impermanence is permanence;

arising is non-arising, and non-arising is arising. These are the Buddha’s esoteric words. How could one establish conceptual characteristics to refute and explain them? Therefore, they are not employed here.
Now, to cite one matter: this refers to an explanation based on the Dharma.
When the Buddha speaks of "arising and ceasing" and so forth, it is precisely through these four interpretations of the single dharma of arising and ceasing that one is called a "wise minister.

This is an explanation based on the Dharma according to the teachings (*yào jiào xià zhī fǎ*). As for the explanation based on the gates (*yào mén*), it refers to the gates of the teachings that enable penetration; therefore, there are two such explanations.

[This is] different. The six-volume *Yanqi* (Salt Vessel) is the same as this [text]. First, it clarifies the virtue of immovable bliss; second, the virtue of signless purity; third, the virtue of eternal [bliss];
and fourth, the virtue of the self of Buddha-nature. These correspond respectively to the four gates, and they should also be explained individually.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning the *pāṭala* tree and others: these three trees collectively serve as metaphors for the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

At the time of its decline and extinction, they fail to understand the esoteric language; the constant rain does not fall, and the eternal realm cannot be attained. The parching of both land and water serves as a metaphor for the absence of the wholesome states of humans and devas.
The Sūtra says: "Sentient beings of meager merit encounter this degenerate age; this is what constitutes meager merit.
Due to evil bhikṣus, the Dharma is rendered devoid of majestic power.

The Sūtra further says: "Alas, how perilous! Those who do not understand the subtle, secret, and hidden treasury of the Tathāgata will inevitably fall into the three miserable realms and wander therein."
Since there is no longer any turning back, it is called a "great peril.
As for the statement that "that which was obstructed is now opened," this meaning does not exist in the sutra; therefore, such an interpretation is unnecessary.
When the sutra says, "At that time there was a person," it is a metaphor for one who receives instruction and seeks the Dharma.

Regarding "other forms of knowledge and vision": apart from the objects of cognition and the cognizing wisdom, those that are encountered in a general sense are called "other forms of knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, employing contemplations such as impermanence to assist right observation is termed "auxiliary," and thus categorized as "other."
Regarding the phrase "The 'Good Man' section below corresponds [to the following]," Sengao said: "From 'Good Man' to 'Delicious Food' corresponds to the first addition;
from 'Water' to 'These Various Evil People' corresponds to the second addition; from 'Citing the Previous' to 'Companions' corresponds to the third addition;
and from 'Receiving and Keeping' to 'Water and Milk' corresponds to the fourth addition. Tanchen said: "Stop; take only the conclusion."
Adding the middle and the last to the first makes three additions; adding the first to the middle and the last makes four additions.

As for the statement that it must rely on the [two] truths: the eternal principle of Nirvāṇa is truly ineffable, yet it is explained by relying on the two truths, just as adding two portions of water.
Regarding the sūtra’s presentation of two phrases: these two phrases in the sūtra are explicit. As for the other two phrases:
women do not know the Buddha-nature; they are merely "women. If women and men were to know the Buddha-nature, they would then be called "men.
These two additional phrases are fully explained so as to complete the fourfold set of propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the dual explanation of arising and ceasing: when the Great Dharma is granted a place, it is called "arising"; when it is not granted a place, it is called "ceasing.
Therefore, the reference to Kaśmīra and other regions is precisely the manifestation of these characteristics.
Regarding the inclusion of the "upper opening" [passage]: it is called "inclusion" (*kian*) because the text of the response and question is brief.

However, this constitutes the preliminary presentation of the intent of the doubt prior to the response and question; the text is divided into two parts. First, the formulation of a doubt to solicit an explanation. From "For what reason...

onwards, the next section presents the intent of the response that includes the answer. The first of these sections has two parts: first, the formulation of the doubt and the posing of the question; second, [the subsequent response].
The section "Resolving Doubts" at the end of the Hexi [commentary] begins by asking: "Why were his doubts not resolved? The intention is this:
from the beginning until now, although Cunda has heard what the Buddha has taught, why have his doubts not been resolved? Why must he now be made to voice them again?
Next, regarding the resolution of doubts, it says that "the two persons constitute the branches. This is not as [it would be] if one were to say, "only the benefit remains.
Next, within the "Raising" section, there are two parts: first, the presentation of what was heard; second, from "Now, raising... onwards, the explanation of the words.
Regarding the phrase "suspended [in time] yet identical with principle": it is because Kāśyapa’s original question coincides in advance with that of Cunda.
Thus, while the Buddha resolves Cunda’s doubts, Kāśyapa’s difficulties are resolved in anticipation.
Regarding the citation of the verse up to the phrase "no difference": it should be stated in full that "difference is itself no difference;
no difference is neither difference nor no difference. Only then will the doubt of Kāśyapa be resolved.
This single verse appears four times; the following is the fourth instance where the Tathāgata provides an explanation, which is divided into four parts:
first, indicating the intent of its appearance; second, presenting alternative interpretations from below the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*; third, the formal explanation beginning with "Now, however...";
and fourth, describing the interpretation of Master Guṇamati, starting with "As for Master Guṇamati... The first section is as follows.
The Sūtra states: "That which originally existed but now does not" refers to impermanence that originally existed and impermanence that now no longer exists.
"That which originally did not exist but now exists" refers to the Buddha-nature that originally did not exist and the Buddha-nature that now exists.

These two phrases address Cunda’s doubts regarding their distinctness. Why is this? For Cunda had previously used the past to challenge the present, and used the present to challenge the past; the Buddha then...
By means of the latter half [of the text], one submerges the views of differentiation. Why? That which originally existed and now does not exist—this has no basis.
That which originally did not exist and now exists—this also has no basis. Therefore, these two phrases are cited, and by means of "non-differentiation," the doubts of Cunda are resolved.
This is why Zhan’an provides an interpretation of each individual phrase in terms of the Three Truths and so forth. Furthermore, it should further be stated:
Regarding the statement that "the past is impermanent and the present is impermanent": this is because both the present and the past must realize the nature (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, the past is impermanent, yet in the present there is no impermanence, for impermanence itself is the principle (*li*). Moreover, the Buddha-nature existed in the past and exists in the present, for this nature is non-dual.
Furthermore, it is possible to establish the distinction between the three periods of time as having dharmas; however, when one forgets [this], the three periods [are lost].
There is no such thing as a dharma that exists [without cause]; this is impossible.
"The general meaning is the same" means they equally manifest the sense of being undifferentiated within the One.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also for those below," it refers to the three explanations of the faculties (*indriya*) transmitted down to the twenty-sixth stage, which is considered the lowest level of root-nature (*mūla-gotra*).

In the subsequent alternative interpretations, both the establishment [of a position] and its refutation can be seen. Regarding the statement in the refutation that "this is precisely what Cunda doubted":
from the perspective of the correspondence between the preceding and succeeding *Vajra* [sūtras], this is precisely a matter of distinction; how does it differ from Cunda’s doubt?
This is not the intended meaning of the verse. The meaning of the verse is that the identity of Cunda and non-identity is precisely non-differentiation;
therefore, it says, "It is impossible for dharmas to exist throughout the three periods of time. If they were not identical, that would not accord with the intent of the verse.
This is the present that was the past. This means that today there is no "past" Prajñā; for what reason?
These two phrases still refer to the state prior to the Vajra-mind, and are not the Prajñā-Vajra-mind of today.
The latter is also a distinction. How can it be called non-differentiation? When the three vehicles reach Nirvana, this is precisely non-differentiation, identical with the Pure [Dharma-nature]. A.
It can resolve doubts regarding the statement that "afflictions and so forth exist inherently. This would mean that one attains nirvana by destroying afflictions, which is yet another distinction;
how then would this differ from Cunda’s [position], and thus fail to resolve the doubt? The same applies to the claim that "nirvana does not inherently exist."
"Those whose doubts and difficulties remain as they were" refers to Cunda’s lingering doubts and Kāśyapa’s persistent challenges.
"The perfection of both essence and function" refers to the functional operation of cause and effect, such as that which existed originally but is now absent.

Furthermore, regarding that which "should also be hidden and not manifest": today the body is manifest and no longer hidden; yet, as for what was separately hidden in the past, it should not be able to become manifest.
This distinction, moreover, has nothing to do with resolving the doubt.
"The Tripiṭaka Master" refers to the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
Regarding the phrase "birth and death have no beginning," this explains the second line: "that which was originally non-existent now exists.
Regarding the phrase "Nirvāṇa has a beginning," this explains the line: "that which was originally existent now does not exist."
Regarding "delusion is extinguished while the Path remains": in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one must first destroy the afflictions before attaining *nirvāṇa*;
this is thus impermanent and pertains to both the present and the past. Śākyamuni is the present, which is to say he was originally non-existent and now exists.
As for "extinction" (*parinirvāṇa*) being "presently non-existent and future," this means he was originally non-existent and will now exist, because Maitreya is destined to become a Buddha.

Regarding the statement that "there are three which can be categorized as three": it is precisely because difference and non-difference do not interpenetrate in their essence that difference and non-difference both constitute distinct categories; therefore, this [position] is not accepted here.
Now, to clarify that this is not so, the Master below explains in contrast to the ancients:
"Opening three without losing one" means that within the One Buddha Vehicle, one distinguishes three.
"Uniting one without losing three" refers to the expedient means of identical essence; therefore, what originally existed is now absent, and when differences are unified, they are non-existent.
Regarding the phrase "there is no difference": fundamentally non-existent yet now existing, the absence of difference is itself difference. Therefore it is said, "this is possible.

As for the statement, "the existence of dharmas throughout the three periods of time is possible," this is for the sake of conforming to the ritual of transformation; for the sake of conforming to the capacities and needs of beings;

for the sake of establishing the provisional based upon the real; for the sake of leading others into the real; for the sake of the simultaneous circulation of both [provisional and real]; and for the sake of preserving the cause and effect of the past and the present.
Therefore, what is the reason? If there were no cause and effect, sentient beings would already be Buddhas; what need would there be to cultivate the path?

Thus, cause and effect are established to lead beings to the ultimate state. Now, Cunda’s doubt specifically takes the former distinction between the causes and effects of the Three Vehicles as his objection.
The Buddha now answers with the non-differentiated yet differentiated cause and effect, thereby dispelling Cunda’s doubt. Hence it is said:
That phenomena exist throughout the three periods of time is possible;

that the impermanent is permanent is impossible. Where there is difference, there is no difference; where there is permanence, there is impermanence; where there is no difference, there is difference.
That which is neither permanent nor impermanent—that phenomena exist throughout the three periods of time—is impossible.
Regarding "the object and wisdom are neither object nor wisdom": difference is itself non-difference; therefore, they are neither object nor wisdom. Non-difference is itself difference;
thus, while being both object and wisdom, they are neither object nor wisdom. It is impossible for there to be any phenomenon existing throughout the three periods of time.

Regarding "cause and effect versus non-cause and non-effect": the essence of the self (ātman) is neither cause nor effect; yet it can still give rise to the designations of "self," "person," "cause," and "effect.
This is, for example, like the distinct characteristics of object, cognition, and clarity.
"Originally existing is simply existence" refers to the phrase "existence. "Now non-existent is simply non-existence" refers to the phrase "non-existence.

Furthermore, it is said that the first half [of the verse] represents existence, namely the two characters "originally existing," while the second half represents non-existence, namely the two characters "now non-existent."
Regarding the "two schools": this refers to the two schools of the present and the past, or the two schools formed by the lack of integration between the former and latter halves [of the teaching].
Within the third section on the "Correct Explanation," it says: "The one truth is precisely the three truths. This clarifies that this is originally a distinction within the realm of identity (*ji*).
Why then do you cling to the minor distinctions of the past to challenge the major distinctions of the fundamental [teaching]?

Regarding the statement that "the three truths are one truth," they are now eternally without distinction. Why, then, do you challenge this by forcing it to conform to the former Small Vehicle’s distinction of impermanence?
It is precisely because a single phrase is itself the three, fully present from the outset, that the doubt concerning their differentiation is resolved.

Regarding the phrase "that which is impermanent is itself permanent," etc.: because Cunda’s fundamental attachment was to the notion that the past was impermanent, [the Buddha] resolved his doubt by means of the teaching on impermanence and so forth.
As for the question, "How can this difficulty not be dispelled?"—it refers to the dispelling of Kāśyapa’s objection.
Regarding "what doubts are not yet removed": this refers to the removal of Cunda’s doubts.
From "one existence and all existences" up to "the world," this constitutes the differentiation of the non-differentiation of the three truths;
it explains the difficult points concerning the definitive distinctions made by Cunda and others, and therefore belongs to the category of the world (*loka*).
As for the antidote (*pratipakṣa*): the non-existence of the one reality serves as the antidote to the former existence of the distinctions among the three vehicles.

That is to say, because it exists, there arises the excellence of the power of the conventional and the ultimate; because it does not exist, there arises the excellence of the principle of the Middle Way.
Furthermore, because it exists, there arises the excellence of the power of the three vehicles; because it does not exist, there arises the excellence of the principle of the One Vehicle.
"Each one fully possesses four" means that each and every one is complete with the four phrases; thus, the characteristics of the four *siddhāntas* are easily understood.
Regarding the interpretation of Master Guanding of the Fourth [Patriarch], there are two parts: first, the exposition; second, the concluding judgment beginning with "This interpretation...
In the first part, it says that the three phrases "bring forth what is not correct," meaning that "there is no such place" serves as the basis for the negation.
"Non-existent now" means that while there were afflictions originally, they are no longer present now.
"That which is non-existent can be made to exist" refers to the Buddha-nature that exists now.
"Not the original of the present" means that the primordial origin is not the same as the original of the present; the original of the present is precisely the One Reality.

"This present is not the original" means that the present of the present is not the original present. That the original present lacks Buddha-nature, while that which causes it to have Buddha-nature constitutes this meaning;
therefore, the present and the original are not the same. These are all interpretations by others. Zhezhou says:
"In the immeasurable kalpas prior to the past, the Buddha had a body of birth and death, which is called 'originally existent. At that time, the impermanent Dharma-body was spoken of as..."
Now it does not exist. Regarding the past immeasurable kalpas ago, when there was no prior dharma-body, this is called "originally non-existent" (*benwu*).

At that time, there was a body of birth and death, which is described as "now existent. If one discusses this from the perspective of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, they possess a body of birth and death in the present, which is called "originally existent," while the impermanent dharma-body is said to be "now non-existent. Furthermore, regarding...

The present impermanent *dharmakāya* is called "originally non-existent" (*mūlato 'bhāva*). Because there currently exists an impermanent body subject to birth and death, it is said that "to claim there are dharmas existing in the three times is impossible.
This statement merely refutes the opponent's fixed definition; it is insufficient. To be complete, one should say:
"To claim that dharmas do not exist in the three times is also impossible. If we speak in terms of the Buddha, the Buddha originally possessed birth...
It is impossible that the body of death should exist eternally throughout the three periods of time; such a thing cannot be.

Now, as for the fundamental dharma-body which has been severed and separated from [the body of death], it is impossible that it should be eternally non-existent throughout the three periods of time; such a thing cannot be. Therefore, the Buddha has now attained it.

If one discusses this in terms of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, it is impossible that their original bodies of birth-and-death should exist eternally throughout the three periods of time; therefore, they must necessarily be eliminated and severed.
That which was originally non-existent cannot be the eternally abiding Dharmakāya; it is impossible for it to be eternally non-existent throughout the three periods of time.
Therefore, one must certainly cultivate and realize it. For this reason, there are distinctions among Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
If one explains it in this manner, doubts and difficulties remain as they were. Observing the commentaries currently in wide circulation, such is the case.

As for the remaining [points], they are therefore recorded here so that one may know their similarities and differences. Looking up to encourage future students as a profound cause, the Master’s current interpretation encompasses the essential spirit;
it resolves difficulties and dispels doubts, truly conforming to the intent of the Sūtra.
Regarding the karmic retribution of sentient beings: it is the retribution of the true cause of Buddha-nature that has existed since beginningless time.
As for "never having entered realization": the essence of the Great Nirvāṇa is such that it neither enters nor exits.

Regarding these hypothetical statements: although there may be no Buddha in the world, because the teaching of *nirvāṇa* still exists, it is impossible for those of the two vehicles who have attained the lesser *nirvāṇa* not to ultimately abide in the great *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said that "in reality, this is not so."
The Sūtra says, "It is called 'Existent Good' (*śubhāsti*). The Great Parinirvāṇa is the ultimate good dharma; because it is a wondrously existent dharma, it is named "Existent Good.
The Sūtra says, "Only one Buddha appears [in the world]. Sengzong said: "Perfect understanding is difficult to stabilize, while the inversion of permanence is easily produced. There is..."

The Buddha of Skillful Extinction does not manifest constantly; his response to the rare and excellent capacities of beings is such that he appears in the world but once. When they turn away from his transformation and lose their opportunity, many kalpas pass.
How then could he preach the Great Vehicle’s fundamental teaching? He only uses the stages of the Three Vehicles to lead them forward;
thus we know that the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle are expediently bestowed and are not ultimate.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra concerning "nature and characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): since characteristics exist apart from nature, how can they be identical or different?
The ninth [verse] answers the above question. Within the inquiry, it says: "Just as when pleasure has not yet arisen, how can it be called 'experiencing pleasure'?
By means of this half-verse, it assists in establishing the various meanings that are indestructible.

The Sūtra says: "Those who wish to protect the True Dharma internally protect the eternally abiding and indestructible Dharma. Those sentient beings who receive it shall later become its indestructible retinue.
As for 'seeking them out and finding none,' this means that there is only a provisional name; because one investigates and finds no substantial entity, one does not recognize [them as real]."
"Hands and feet" refers to not recognizing the color of one's own hands and feet.
Below this is the tenth note. Regarding the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly," the text is divided into two parts:

first, the explanation of the title; second, the entry into the textual commentary starting from the beginning. The first part further consists of two sections, the first of which is the formal [explanation].

Explanation of the Title. Next, regarding the number of questions posed by Dharmatara of Hexi: first, concerning the subject matter asked by the great assembly, it is seen that from each and every pore of Śākyamuni, various transformation Buddhas emerge;
each leads a multitude of fifty-two followers and accepts the offerings of Cunda and others.
They then question one another: "What merit and virtue does Cunda possess, such that a small amount of polished rice suffices for so many?"
The assembly is thus named. Regarding the title "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly" (*Mahāsāṃghika-paripṛcchā-varga*):
Master Guan (Guṇabhadra) states that because Kāśyapa questioned the unconditioned great assembly, it is titled the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly.
Master Zezhou says: "What has preceded this extensively clarifies the causes of bodhi; from here on, the following clarifies the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata."

This is the cause for [the title] *Pan* (Varga/Chapter). Because it was requested by the great assembly (*mahāsāṃghika*) and discussed through their inquiries, this title was adopted; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly.
Next, regarding the statement that it "also answers the question concerning the removal of illness," this refers to answering the present question by means of a leap-over [or indirect] response.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "After Cunda had passed," it refers to his kinsmen in the city of Vasiṣṭhā.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning "various radiances," these refer to colors such as blue and yellow mentioned previously, as well as others.
Regarding the further emission of various kinds of light: it was for the purpose of universally receiving the offerings of the great assembly that he emitted these various lights;

this is the underlying intent. Furthermore, according to the path and dharma of the ancient Buddhas, one does not eat after midday. At such a time, the body reaches a state where even speech cannot be uttered;
therefore, he emitted light to manifest his intention.
The Sūtra states, "those who carry robes and alms bowls"; these are the assembly that does not offer provisions.
The Sūtra further states, "each and every pore," which refers to all those in the assembly that does not offer provisions as well as the fifty-two assemblies;
therefore, it is called "immeasurable."
Regarding the scripture’s statement that the Buddha himself accepted Cunda’s offering, Sengzong said: "The Dharma-body is formless; how could its manifested transformations differ?
That the Buddha himself accepted Cunda’s offering was merely a demonstration that there is a person who makes the request, thereby revealing the distinction from those who lack prior vows."
The Sūtra says regarding the food consumed: there was neither the meager coarseness of Cunda’s offering nor the abundant excellence of the great assembly;
therefore, it says, "there was no distinction.

The Sūtra asks, "To whom was the offering made? For if there were no Buddha to receive the offerings, how could the practice of *dāna* (generosity) have been fulfilled after his parinirvāṇa? Therefore...

Regarding this praise, the Sūtra states that "the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus. This means that they come when the capacity [of sentient beings] arises and depart when that capacity declines; hence it is said to be "thus.
As for the Sūtra’s statement that "immeasurable kalpas have already passed," this is clearly explained at length in the *Niyatāniyatagotrastotra* (or *Juryōbon*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding the scripture’s statement, "to dwell forever in a place of peace and security": the text means that one has already abided within the secret treasury of the three virtues; this is the "place.

Regarding the scripture’s statement, "having heard this, you should practice it": one should constantly contemplate *nirvāṇa* while practicing the Path, thereby bringing the final stage of giving (*dāna*) to fulfillment.
Regarding the thirteen verses, Sengzong said: "There is no explicit textual indication [for this].

One should simply eliminate the four verses at the beginning and the four verses at the end, and take the general meaning of the central verses to clarify that the Buddha’s Dharma-body is perfectly complete and, though manifesting in response, is not extinguished.
The first four verses serve as preliminary metaphors; the final four verses are intended to bring peace and stability, so that one need not feel grief or distress."
The Sūtra says: "Suppose there were crows and owls," referring to six pairs. Within these six pairs, each is preceded by a verse that addresses a question and provides an answer;
the obstructed text is visible therein. The Sūtra says:
"Only then will they enter parinirvāṇa. The Buddha’s intention was this: as for the various birds mentioned above, they shall become like close brothers.
When I enter nirvana, my body cannot be obtained [as a physical relic] in the manner of the relationship between brothers. This proves that I have never entered nirvana;
why, then, do you say that I have entered nirvana?

Regarding the statement that "the seven-leafed [tree] is extremely foul-smelling," Master She said: "The lack of fragrance in the seven-leafed tree may be used as a metaphor for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). The fragrant scent of the *pāṭalī* flower may serve as a simile for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The poisonous fruit of the *kalu* tree is a metaphor for the body of afflictions (*kleśa-kāya*), while its extreme sweetness when fully ripened is a metaphor for the body of permanence and bliss (*nitya-sukha-kāya*)."

Even if foul-smelling flowers were to emit fragrance and poisonous fruits were to turn sweet, this would mean that only good arises; if only good arises and no evil exists, the Buddha’s transformation would then come to an end.
Since this body has not yet reached such a state, how could it ever be eternally extinguished?

Regarding the Buddha-fruit as "mystically merging with the Real": although it is said that merging with the Real does not depart from penetrating the Real, if merging with the Real can still emerge [from it], then the Real itself must be something other than what it is.
One should therefore challenge this by asking: upon emerging, what realm does it illuminate, and what delusions does it sever?
The Sūtra says: "There is no one who is deluded. Although afflictions exist, they are as if non-existent; therefore, it is called "absence of delusion.
The Sūtra says: "This is a *caṇḍāla*. This means "a slayer," for he slays the bodhicitta. To harm the life-force of wisdom—what crime could exceed this?
To attribute the "great assembly" to the preceding phrase is merely one interpretation; it is not entirely correct.

As the Sūtra says, "receiving my offerings alone," the Tathāgata’s inconceivable nature reaches each individual according to their own mind. When one thinks of others, they remain deluded on their own.
The scripture states, "It is like a medicinal tree. This refers to the body that extinguishes evil.

It also serves as an answer to the question regarding "separation. While the secret text is extensive and should be treated as primary, the other two texts are abbreviated; thus, they are designated as "secondary" (or "concurrent").
"Concealment" (*chādana*) refers to both the state with remainder (*sa-upadhiśeṣa*) and the state without remainder (*an-upadhiśeṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "all sūtras" (*sarva-sūtra*) mentioned in the scripture: these sūtras encompass both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna;
thus, both the states with and without remainder apply to both vehicles, as will be explained below.
Regarding the two types of recipients and the three kinds of sinners: they are accepted because they are able to reform their evil ways and protect the Dharma.

As for the passage in the Sūtra from "upholding the precepts" to "distinctions": [the interlocutor asks], "Whether one upholds the precepts or violates them, both are acceptable. Since giving and praising are likewise the same, what further distinction could there be?
I do not understand this now; I pray that the Buddha will explain it for me."
Regarding the statement in the sutra, "except for one person," the Buddha did not explicitly say he excluded them.
This was intended to startle and awaken sentient beings of that time; for if they were to ask later, [the Buddha] would clarify that it is not only the icchantika who is excluded.
One must also distinguish those whose minds incline toward *icchantika* (those who lack the potential for enlightenment).
As the sutra says, "I do not yet understand," meaning they do not know how it is that one becomes a person who has broken the precepts; therefore, it says "not yet understood."
Although it is not identical [to that], for the time being, it is stated according to what is manifest in speech; it is unknown whether the internal mind is inclined toward it.
For this reason, it is said to be "not identical.
The Sūtra states: "If one commits the four pārājika offenses... as far as the True Dharma," meaning that within a single lifetime, one commits the four pārājikas and five [pārājikas] in succession.

[This is] contrary [to the truth]. One must necessarily slander the True Dharma to be called an icchantika. Although some may commit the four grave offenses and so forth, they do so because they believe in cause and effect;
those who slander the Dharma do not believe in cause and effect, and for this reason they are called icchantikas.
The Sūtra asks: "What is the meaning of what is called 'breaking the precepts'? This means that merely breaking the *vinaya* (disciplinary rules) is termed "breaking the precepts.
Furthermore, is there something else specifically transgressed that is termed "breaking the precepts"? As I do not yet understand this, I ask: "What is its meaning?"

Regarding the six wonderful medicines: the repentance methods for the Lotus Sūtra and the Vaipulya sūtras of our own tradition all first employ the ten minds of the direct and reverse order as their procedural method.
These six medicines here are largely identical to those; they may also be used interchangeably with them.
Third, regarding the protection of the True Dharma: this corresponds to the vow among the Four Great Vows that "the Dharma gates are boundless.

One should know that those who practice repentance must first resolve to attain Bodhicitta; if one does not resolve their mind toward enlightenment, then their transgressions will not be extinguished.
If one does not seek the higher [enlightenment] while transforming those below, success will not be achieved.
Regarding the fifth, "penetrating the characteristics of offenses," this means contemplating that the nature of offenses is empty and quiescent.

Regarding "generating the mind to protect the Dharma," this means protecting places where the Buddha-Dharma exists so that it is not severed, and establishing it in places where the Buddha-Dharma does not exist.
This enables one to manifest [the truth]. Hexi says: "To bring forth the resolve and penetrate transgressions" refers precisely to the repentance of non-arising and the cessation of slander;
contemplating the true mark while seated also accords with these six intentions.
Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "For example, when the sun rises," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that it can remove the dark and obscured minds of icchantikas.

As for "bodhisattvas of shallow practice," these refer to bodhisattvas in the stage of worthiness (*bhadra*) according to the three previous teachings; upon hearing the *Nirvāṇa*, they give rise to the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhigama*).
The Sūtra states that those who are "naturally evil by nature" are so called because they have not yet undergone repentance; their nature is termed "evil.
The Sūtra states that they "attain birth among the devas"; this means they attain birth among the *paramārtha-devas* (the devas of ultimate truth).
It is like one who sows a broken seed; though they themselves possess no virtuous seeds, they are able to cause others to produce them.
Regarding the previous statement that "all [giving] is practiced," the interpretation that the word "all" refers only to this constitutes an incomplete (sāvaśeṣa) explanation.
If it is said that the three vehicles obtain different rewards, then that is the definitive (bhūta) explanation.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning Rājagṛha and so forth: In the city of Rājagṛha, there was an upāsaka who previously questioned the Nigaṇṭhas regarding the merit of giving.
The Nigaṇṭhas replied, "Giving to me brings merit, but giving to the Buddha yields no reward. Hearing this, the upāsaka found it to be unjust and went to question the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately answered him, saying: "All acts of giving are only to be praised."
He sighed. Upon hearing this, he was filled with joy and gave rise to a heart of faith and reverence; for this reason, the Tathāgata spoke this verse.
As for the passage in the Sūtra stating, "It is also for the sake of the Bodhisattvas... the secret treasury," it serves to certify the meaning of "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*).
Even the Bodhisattva, the hero among men, who embraces those who uphold the precepts and abandons those who violate them—all of these pertain to the meaning of "without remainder."
The Sūtra states that "a small portion" refers to all [non-Buddhist teachings] because there is still a remainder [of error].
Regarding the ninety-five types [of heterodox paths] and so forth: the ninety-three paths are both in name and substance false.
Although the two names *Sūtra* and *Abhidharma* are correct, their substance is erroneous; therefore, they are called the "ghosts of the *Sūtra*" and the "ghosts of the *Abhidharma*."
This refers to those who actually practice the Two Vehicles, excluding the two types of manifested beings (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The sūtra’s mention of the "fourth eightfold precept" refers to one who possesses and further maintains [the precepts] through division.
That which is neither cause nor fruit is the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); it is called the "Right Path. Therefore, it is said that it is "neither cause nor fruit, yet eternal."
Dharmas such as joy and so forth are gates of universal penetration, termed "aids to the Path.

As the Sūtra says, regarding sentient beings with equality: where there is differentiation, there is no differentiation; hence it is called "viewing with equality. Where there is no differentiation, there is differentiation according to what is appropriate;
thus, it is spoken of in an intentional (ābhiprāyika) manner.
As for the scripture stating, "I only pray that you will stay for a short while," it means: The Buddha is the most supreme among the Three Jewels;
why do you not remain long in the world to benefit us? Furthermore, when the Buddha accepts offerings, he must enter *nirvāṇa* by the power of his resolve and cannot be stopped.
Therefore, please stay for a short time to wait for the three people to arrive.

Regarding the statement that manifested traces must be impermanent: when the capacity [of the audience] ceases, the response should withdraw and the manifested traces should likewise perish; what, then, is there to be wondered at?

The Sūtra says, "At that time, the great assembly gave rise to the bodhicitta. This was their repayment for having heard the Dharma, as well as for the grace of the Dharma and the arousal of the mind.
Therefore, they made offerings again.
Regarding the "Lame Hare" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: In the twenty-sixth fascicle, within the explanation of the non-diminution of diligence (*vīrya*), it is said:
"In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a great forest where many birds and beasts lived.

A wild fire broke out, burning from three sides simultaneously; only on one side was there a body of water as a barrier. The animals were driven to their extremities, with no way to escape for their lives."

In that time and place, he became a large-bodied, powerful deer. He spanned one bank with his forelegs and braced the other bank with his hind legs, allowing the various beasts to tread upon his back as they crossed.
His hide was completely worn away; yet, through the power of his compassion, he endured it until death.

After [the others] had passed, a single rabbit arrived. His strength being utterly exhausted, he exerted himself by all means to endure [the weight] so that the rabbit might cross. Once it had crossed...
Having turned his back [on the teaching], he fell into the water and died. Those who were previously saved are now these disciples;
the last one was Rāṣṭrapāla.
Fascicle Seven: Chapter on Manifesting Illness.

The commentary on the text is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the title; second, from "Next, according to the text, it is divided into four" onwards, the entry into the textual explanation.

The first part has two sections: first, recounting the traditional interpretations; second, from "Now, all... onwards, the formal explanation. Regarding the first section, there is further [content]: Sengzong said:
