Furthermore, it is easy to cultivate compassion (*karuṇā*) in the first dhyāna; it is easy to cultivate sympathetic joy (*muditā*) in the second dhyāna; it is easy to cultivate compassion in the third dhyāna; and it is easy to cultivate equanimity in the fourth dhyāna.
These are the bases for cultivating the four immeasurable concentrations (*apramāṇa-samādhi*). However, in the present text, only a single instance is listed.
As for the claim that "the vessel is the object," this is the interpretation of another school.

Although there are two types of people—those who cling to views and those who cling to craving—the person clinging to views may be either sharp or dull, and the same applies to one clinging to craving;
therefore, all four must be present. How could there be only two?
Regarding these three joys, some say it is the joy of the unattainable; some say it is the joy of the four continents;
others say it is the joy of the Brahma Heaven; others say it is the joy of the heavens; and others say it is the joy of the triple world.
The present text first bestows the most sublime and wondrous bliss among humans and devas, and subsequently bestows the bliss of the Great Nirvana of the Three Truths.
Regarding the three grades of bliss bestowed upon the three types of superior persons, all are granted the highest bliss; for the three grades of middling persons, all are granted middling bliss.

Furthermore, among these nine grades of bliss, each preceding grade is shallow, becoming gradually deeper as one proceeds toward the subsequent ones; it is only upon their full accomplishment that they attain the ultimate.
Second, it is because it is not yet appropriate to grant them all at once.
To take the three grades of happiness and grant them across the nine types of objects: there are nine types of persons, and there are twenty-seven grades of happiness. How so?

For example, when first entering meditative observation, those who are "superior relatives" obtain all three grades of happiness; those who are "middling relatives" have already obtained two grades—the inferior and the middling.

Regarding happiness: those of inferior intimacy receive only inferior happiness; this is why they enter the second stage of contemplation. Those of middling intimacy grant them superior happiness, while those of inferior intimacy grant them middling happiness;

it is only upon entering the third stage of contemplation that those of inferior intimacy finally obtain superior happiness. Within the text, although there are three grades for those of neutral status, only the inferior and middling grades are explicitly mentioned;
the cases of the middling-superior and the middling-middling are analogous. Regarding the entry into the unwholesome state, only the superior grade of enmity is mentioned.
The cases of the intermediate enemy and the inferior enemy are analogous.
Briefly stated, there are four categories: the three types of relatives constitute one category, and the enemies constitute three categories; together they form four categories.

As the Sūtra says: "World-Honored One, for what reason is it that when Bodhisattvas attain such vast and immeasurable minds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they are not yet called 'Great Loving-Kindness' (*mahāmaitrī*)?
Furthermore, as the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states: "To bestow happiness upon the people of one world-system is called 'vast' (*vipula*);
to bestow happiness upon the people of the four continents is called 'great' (*mahat*); to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings of the ten directions is called 'immeasurable' (*aprameya*)."
Regarding the first passage, "the one who sings": because it is cultivated through a sequential mind, it is difficult to accomplish.

Or, when the compassionate one is strong and the other weak, individuals sever delusions sequentially; since even Bodhisattvas prior to the stages have not yet perfected the "compassion based on sentient beings" (*sattvālambanā maitrī*), how much less so in the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]? Therefore, it is called "weak compassion."

Regarding the second point, the manifestation of greatness: each passage must be explained by correlating it with the four types of mind attained by a bodhisattva dwelling on the stages (*bhūmi*) and abodes (*vihāra*), for only then will it accord with the intent of the text.
The Sūtra says, "A bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage"—one should know that the preceding sequential loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has not yet entered the first stage.

It is not [yet] great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). If one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), one realizes it identically with the Perfect [Teaching]. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Only a Bodhisattva of the First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*) is then called 'Great Compassion.
Because the realization in the Separate and Perfect [Teachings] is the same, they are listed together."

Regarding the phrase "only seeing the true marks and so forth": although those of icchantika nature are not the great enemies of bodhisattvas, they oppose the Buddha-dharma and are thus termed "great evils.

Bodhisattvas who practice the perfect cultivation with the threefold compassion of the one mind—from the stage of the name (mingzi-wei) upward—see only that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are without distinction, being identical in nirvana, continuing in this way until the very last single grade [of the final thought-moment].
Ignorance (*avidyā*). To constantly provide for and deliver others from it is precisely what is meant by "not seeing its faults.

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) as described in the text: when one employs the three types of compassion with a single mind to provide for and deliver others, such that each [object of compassion] does not perceive any fault [in oneself], this kind of compassion is precisely what is called "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*).

Regarding "the two [meanings] within equanimity (*upekṣā*) as well," one should have first stated "joy" (*muditā*). However, this is merely an abbreviation in the text. One feels joy because one sees that the person before one has truly become free from suffering; it is the same when they obtain happiness.
One feels equanimity because one sees that the other has fundamentally become free from suffering; it is the same when they obtain happiness.

These constitute joy and equanimity, both of which possess these two meanings, as explained in the sutra itself. Furthermore, regarding the two passages on loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) in the sutra, loving-kindness is raised... [text ends].
By removing suffering, one manifests the bestowal of happiness; by means of compassion (*karuṇā*), one brings forth the bestowal of happiness to manifest the removal of suffering.

Therefore, it is said that one "also removes suffering," and so forth. The Sūtra states: "There is nothing to protect. If sentient beings have not yet attained happiness, the Bodhisattva constantly protects them.
Now that they have attained ultimate happiness, there is nothing further to protect; only then is it called "Great Equanimity" (*upekṣā*).

The Sūtra says: "From 'sacrificing one's own happiness' downward, taking what one has realized and bestowing it upon others so that they may become like oneself constitutes 'great relinquishment' (mahātyāga).

Regarding the root of the six perfections: taking the single mind and the three types of compassion as the basis for the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) six perfections, one realizes that the five [perfections] beginning with giving are non-existent.
It is not the dharma-realm that is called "complete.

As for the fundamental nature of its own characteristics, it is simply the sequential progression of one's own practice. By penetrating the immeasurability of the world and perceiving the true reality of dhyāna, one accomplishes the three types of universal compassion within a single mind;
this is termed "Great Immeasurability."

Kaishan (Kai-shan) claims that what is called "real contemplation" (*shiguan*) is so named because others see it as a refutation; however, this current explanation is not adopted. Regarding the "refutation of the objection":
from the phrase "removing what is unbeneficial" up to "that which arrives," this constitutes the refutation; there is no further objection below this point regarding reality.
"Contemplation through mental construction" (parikalpa-bhāvanā) is derived from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and explained extensively in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the concession (*anujñā*): if it were not the ultimate bliss, it would be a concession. Those various subsequent objections [refer to this].

Regarding the "refutation of objections" (*codyaparihāra*): the intent of the refutation is that one fears the World-Honored One might reply, "In the causal stage, one merely wishes for them to have it, but they have not yet actually attained happiness.

Thereupon, one refutes this by saying: "If, in reality, they do not attain happiness, how can it be called the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)? Next is the objection based on the Buddha’s own words;
following that is the objection concerning the lack of actuality; and finally is the concluding objection.
First, regarding the praise for his prohibition: "You are of inferior rank, yet you are able to stand before me without fear or trepidation and prohibit the practice of loving-kindness;
this is truly courageous and brings no benefit, and it is for this reason that I praise you."
The Sūtra says, "And may they share their joy with those [beings]. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is asked:

"If all the merits of a Bodhisattva’s practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are shared with sentient beings, and they have already been given to sentient beings, how will the Bodhisattva then achieve unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)?

The answer is: During the causal stage (*hetu-kāla*), the Bodhisattva merely intends to give them universally; it is only upon reaching the fruit (*phala*) that he is able to give them everywhere. Why, then, does the Sūtra say 'may they share'?"
Regarding that bliss, the Sūtra states that "the lineage of the noble ones" (āryagotra) is identical to the "lineage of the Tathāgata" (tathāgatagotra).

The Sūtra further states that one does not equal even a single instance of the cultivation of loving-kindness; this refers to loving-kindness based on sentient beings (sattvālambana-maitrī), let alone that based on phenomena (dharmālambana) or that which is objectless (anālambana).
Regarding the objection that it is merely conceptual: the compassion practiced by those of the Two Vehicles has not yet attained its true reality and is therefore termed "conceptual."
The Sūtra asks: "How is this known? That is to say, how is it known that the Tathāgata’s practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is not false?
It is said that it merely causes those who see him to undergo a transformation, but that this is not a definitive transformation; rather, it only causes a temporary transformation.
Such an explanation contradicts the text of the present Sūtra and cannot be relied upon.
As for what one master says, it is precisely the interpretation of the Great Master.
One should know that there are those who are sentient beings yet are not sentient beings. This is truly because the sentient being and the environment (the dependent and the correct) are non-dual;
thus, they can transform into one another, and all such transformations are real transformations. This is the definitive teaching.

That which can cause sentient beings [to attain this] is simply because, from the beginning, the sentient beings' reliance on the primary and secondary realms is non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual;
they are identical with Bodhi and undifferentiated in the three aspects. Therefore, they can be transformed.
If even non-Buddhists can transform their bodies into stone until the end of the kalpa, how much more so for those who have realized true Nirvana—would they not undergo eternal transformation?
Those who do not realize this actually transform sentient beings into non-sentient beings, yet they remain entirely unchanged;
likewise, they transform that which is insentient into that which possesses sentience.

How much more so when compassion itself is the Tathāgata? This distinguishes the fruit and the dharma as non-dual: compassion is itself Buddha-nature, and this distinguishes the fruit and its nature as being entirely one.

Regarding the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vedanīya*) of sentient beings, the Buddha-nature is precisely all dharmas; it is established that the nature of the fruit depends entirely upon the retribution.
As the Sūtra says: "One should know that the four immeasurable minds of a Bodhisattva consist of the three types of compassion within a single mind, which is called true contemplation."
However, regarding "meritorious virtue" (puṇya): the four minds are simply what is meant by "Brahma-merit. Therefore, while they can merely suppress afflictions, they are not called "severing" them.
As for "prajñā": it refers to the single mind and threefold wisdom that completely sever all afflictions, which differs from the judgments of past scholars.

Regarding those who can serve as the root of goodness for the Three Vehicles: since the one mind and the three types of compassion inherently possess the goodness of humans and devas, how much more so the Three Vehicles?

As the Sūtra says, "those who definitely dedicate [their merit]," the five perfections are the contributory causes (*pratyaya-hetu*), while Prajñā is the revealing cause (*vibhāvaka-hetu*); only then is dedication fully accomplished.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The mind of dedication is like a hot drill;
there is nothing that reaches it without being scorched and destroyed. The mind of dedication is likewise:

not even a single hair’s breadth of a root of goodness fails to be bestowed upon sentient beings, establishing them within the path to Bodhi. Because one dedicates [merit] by means of the four ultimate minds, one attains [the result]."
It is the foundation for the following eight matters; therefore, it is called "comprehensive.
As the Sūtra says, "not giving rise to arrogance" means not conceiving arrogance toward those who receive [offerings] or toward others.
"Not hoping for a reciprocal reward" means not hoping for a present recompense from another person.
"Not deceiving others" means giving exactly as promised with genuine goods.

The Sūtra says: "Whenever one practices giving" refers to the time of cultivating objectless [compassion]. At that time, the characteristics of a Bodhisattva’s giving involve forgetting all three factors;
therefore, it says "not seeing," and so forth. One might give to those who uphold the precepts and not give to those who do not;
one might give to such fields [of merit], give to spiritual friends, give to those who are vessels for the Dharma, or give on auspicious days.
Regarding "the place": it is appropriate to give to a pure monastic community (*saṃghārāma*). One should give when there is famine, but not give when there is abundance.
Those who discriminate in this manner are all not Bodhisattvas.
As for the arising of stinginess, it is due to the observer. Regarding why stinginess arises, Zhezhou says: "The arrow is a metaphor for the beggar; because of him..."
To beg is to arouse the disease of stinginess; this is called being struck by a poisoned arrow. That the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas personally benefit such a person is called being their kin.

To cause that person to break away from the disease of stinginess and abide securely in wholesome dharmas is called "desiring to establish them in peace and security. To slander this is to misrepresent it.
To hear and seek the Dharma of giving is called the "physician of life.
To teach the recipient to rely on the Dharma of giving and to dispatch the seeker is called "extracting the arrow.
As for the discrimination of signs, it refers to discerning which person is worthy of receiving a gift and which person is not.
Regarding "what is the arrow": this refers to the discrimination within a mind of stinginess regarding the objects to be given;

it employs the metaphor of an arrow to represent this discrimination, which does not contradict the previous [use of] the barb (the character *zú* is pronounced as *jiāng mù fǎn* or *qī zòu fǎn*; here we follow the former pronunciation).
Regarding the fact that there are eight layers [of vows]: although there are one hundred and forty [vows] in the *Avataṃsaka*, they are all single vows applied individually.
In this present sutra, within a single vow, numerous vows are fully contained; by fulfilling that one vow in such an expansive manner, it is only then termed "equal compassion" (*samacitta*).
Therefore, the present sutra says: "When giving food, etc."
The Sūtra states: "Regarding all those who bestow food, it is because of the Bodhisattva’s gift of food that they obtain the supramundane food of Great Nirvāṇa;
this is truly brought about by the firm arousal of their vow."
The Sūtra states that "water of eight flavors" refers to the River of Great Nirvāṇa, which is endowed with eight qualities: first, permanence; second, constancy;
third, peace; fourth, coolness; fifth, freedom from aging; sixth, freedom from death; seventh, freedom from defilement; and eighth, bliss.
Regarding the scriptural passage that says, "attaining one sweet flavor," and so forth:

as stated in the *Caturlakṣaṇa-parivarta*, it first says that suffering is explained as a sour flavor, impermanence as a salty flavor, non-self as a bitter flavor, pleasure as a bland flavor, self as a pungent flavor, and permanence as a light flavor.
With afflictions as the fuel and wisdom as the fire, through these causes and conditions, the food of nirvāṇa is accomplished. This clarifies that nirvāṇa is without suffering and possesses only...
Because it is blissful, it is said that there are no six distinctions.
The Sūtra says: "One who gives a vehicle obtains the immovable through movement. This means that one is conveyed from the cause to the fruit;
therefore, it is called the "Vajra-throne vehicle" and so forth.

The Sūtra states that [the merit] is shared with sentient beings; this sharing occurs at the time of fruition, based on the vow made at the time of the cause. As stated in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra:
"Regarding the four-inch space on each side," when the Tathāgata puts on his robes, they remain four inches away from his body.

In the *Mahāsannipāta*, it is stated that those who regard the observance of precepts as something deficient are at fault. This is because the followers of the Two Vehicles abide in the precepts yet fail to perceive the dharma-realm of the precepts; thus, they are established as being in error.
The Sūtra says: "One who gives bedding and mats, by virtue of giving what the world relies upon, attains the secret treasury of the three virtues, which is the reliance of the supramundane."
Regarding the bed upon which the Buddha lay,

the Sūtra states: "Those who offer lamps, by virtue of offering the lamp of the world’s illumination, shall attain the supramundane single mind and threefold wisdom, which universally illumines the great radiance of the Dharma-realm."

"Those who are of the three vehicles" refers to the three vehicles within the first two teachings. Because the essence of unconditional great compassion (*anālambana-mahāmaitrī*) is endowed with both the provisional and the ultimate, it serves as the basis for the three vehicles.

"The original impurity and the inhalation and exhalation of breath" refer to the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana-citta*). The first is for sentient beings with excessive anger.

1. To teach sentient beings who are attached to desire the practice of the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*). 2. To teach sentient beings who are attached to form the practice of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). 3. To teach ignorant sentient beings the practice of the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*).
4. To teach sentient beings whose minds are discursive the practice of the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-gaṇanā-bhāvanā*). 5.

To teach sentient beings who are attached to a self the practice of the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātu-vibhaṅga-bhāvanā*). Although there are these five gates, their essentials are of two kinds: first, the contemplation of impurity; second, the counting [of the breath].

Regarding "breathing" (*ānāpāna*), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The entry into cultivation requires two gates: the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
For those in whom desire and discursive thought (*vitarka*) predominate, practicing in this successive order is precisely what is meant."

Regarding the present mention of the "two gates of ambrosia": the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) are the essentials for the gate of *nirvāṇa*;
therefore, only these two are cited. Furthermore, the first two teachings constitute the gates of ambrosia, while the latter two teachings are the ambrosia of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Regarding the scriptural passage on impermanence, arising, and ceasing, Zhezhou states: "Impermanence, arising, and ceasing constitute the contemplation of the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna (mindfulness of dharmas) in terms of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

The four *smṛtyupasthānas* are [contemplations] in terms of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), namely: contemplating the body as impure, contemplating sensation as suffering, and contemplating the mind as impermanent."

Regarding the observation that "dharmas are without self" and "form is suffering," etc., Zezhou says: "For now, this is explained with reference to the aggregate of form; the other four aggregates can be understood by analogy with form.
Those [other aggregates] are also merely listed by name without explanation. Later, in the section analyzing names, it says: "According to the Abhidharma, the first four..."
They exist within the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*); up to the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the latter three exist within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, these seven all reside within the stages of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*).

Regarding the three objects of contemplation (*trīṇi vipaśyanā-sthānāni*): according to the *Abhidharma*, contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) is called the three objects of contemplation;

this contemplation belongs to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). According to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, contemplating that phenomena (*dharma*) are impermanent (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and without self (*anātman*) is called the three objects of contemplation;
this contemplation belongs to the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśala-mūlāni*).
The sūtra speaks of the eight liberations, as explained in detail in the twenty-eighth sūtra below.
Regarding the three interpretations of "non-contention" (*araṇā*), none of them transcend the Lesser Vehicle and thus fail to escape contention; therefore, they are not employed here.
Regarding "the clarity of the realization of emptiness": it is as Subhūti’s realization of the clarity of emptiness.

As for the phrase in the sutra, "and the various supernormal powers," this refers to the supernormal power of the body at will, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of past lives, and the exhaustion of outflows;
hence the term "various."

Regarding the statement "observing both existence and non-existence": if one observes them simultaneously as being both existent and non-existent, how can this be called "neither existent nor non-existent"?
The reference to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* is intended to cite scriptural evidence for the mutual fusion and identity of the three truths.

Regarding the four propositions of provisional names: to penetrate that existence is itself emptiness, non-existence is itself the provisional, both existence and non-existence are themselves the simultaneous negation and affirmation, and all these are merely names.
These four *siddhāntas* (universal principles) adapt to the timing and the capacities of beings to lead them into the reality;
therefore, they are not frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Regarding "dependent states": small states depend upon large states.
Regarding "all meeting at one court": those who follow the proper order and those who do not all meet at one court, thereby establishing the ultimate honor.
The Private Notes on the Commentary to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Five.

*Nirvāṇa Sūtra* Commentary Notes, Fascicle Six.

In the second chapter on the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*), there is also a "provisional" [teaching]. However, within the Sūtras, the three minds constitute a common bond for a single stage, while the mind of equanimity constitutes an independent bond for a single stage;
both teachings are thus. Yet, this is merely provisional. In the definitive sense, it is not so. Why? Because a single child...
It is endowed with equality, and equality is likewise endowed with the single child. The essence of the two stages is identical; they should not be divided into two.
As for "the phenomenon being identical to the principle": it is only through the realization of the equality of emptiness that this function arises.

Regarding those who mutually support one another through affection: from the initial stage of abiding, they attain a partial realization of the correspondence with objectless compassion (*apratigha-maitrī*), viewing all sentient beings as if they were their only child.
For this reason, they are collectively established in a single fruit.

Regarding the brevity of the text: the text for the first three minds should include the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), and the text for the mind of equanimity should include the other three minds.
This is also a case of mutual manifestation: the single beloved child alone already possesses emptiness and equanimity;
equanimity, in turn, already possesses the single beloved child. This thus uses the level to manifest the uneven.
The second [view] says "the eighth stage" (bhūmi); it is unclear which teaching's eighth stage this refers to.
The third says "the first stage"; this mostly refers to the first stage of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
"If one transcends" means to leap directly into the eighth stage.
If one does not reach [the goal], we now clarify the fruits of the Separate and Perfect Teachings; these should not depend upon the Ground of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching.
Regarding "extreme love directed toward the mind": love is the resolve of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), and the culmination of great compassion is exclusively focused on the mind.
"The child is not within me" means that "love" is the loving mind, while "the child" is the object of love; therefore, it is said to be "not within me.
To provide a clear conclusion:
at the end of each section, it is stated that this is called "supreme love" and is termed "the only son. This is precisely [the meaning].
This concludes the preceding section.
Regarding "the person who has resolved to study": although the Dharma of the initial stages of the Separate and Perfect Teachings is perfectly interfused, the person is not yet free from attachment.

Regarding "the actions of body, speech, and mind": these actions of body, speech, and mind arise upon the basis of the five aggregates; because one has not yet attained the three secrets, [these actions persist].
There is nothing that is not evil.
One who saves [others] from verbal transgressions will have no faults in body or speech; as for the mind, it is naturally free of them, and thus it is omitted here.
The Sūtra says, "to abandon and end at last," which is an analogy for when the roots of goodness of sentient beings are completely exhausted.

The Sūtra says, "Inducing and instructing with skillful words. This means that one first bestows the teachings of humans and devas and so forth to gradually guide them, leading them into the ultimate perfection; hence these words.
Regarding the general analogy for rescuing [beings from] cause and effect: falling into hell and the like is the effect, while the performance of good and evil deeds is the cause.

As for what Zhijia does not understand: it is like the five similes the Buddha previously cited, all of which concern those dwelling in the stage of supreme love and the stage of regarding [others] as an only son;
yet later it says, "He kills a brāhmaṇa. The meaning of this is extremely profound, and therefore I do not understand it.
Some say that regarding the "five difficulties": the first difficulty, the objection concerning the killing of a Brahmin, is divided into three, while the second and third together constitute two;
thus they form five.
The Sūtra says: "In the past, when he was a king, if he had not practiced the bodhisattva path, he might have killed guests. This would contradict the bodhi-mind.
The path of the Bodhisattva is contrary to a mind of mere compassion. How, then, can it be called "abiding in the stage of regarding all beings as an only son"?

The Sūtra says, "If one does not attain [this stage]," the underlying intent of which is this: if one has not attained the stage of regarding all beings as an only son, then killing should cause one to fall into hell;
yet if one does not fall into hell, then one should not be taking life. Thus, he challenges [the opponent] from both sides.
"To fall short of the disciples" means to fall short of Subhūti.
As the Sūtra says regarding those who attain the ten powers in their present body: "In this regard, one commits a grave offense and does not repent."
Regarding "those who immediately attain Buddhahood," I likewise do not act as a cause or condition for the afflictions of sentient beings.
As for "there being further many matters," within the text there are six matters in total: three in the first part and three in the latter part.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning "the ash of khadira wood," Saṃghavarman said: "It burns for six days before it is extinguished; it is hard, sharp, and injures people.

As for the fact that it was all entrusted to Kāśyapa, it was because Kāśyapa had heard of it, so [the Buddha] entrusted it to him to test ignorant people of future generations, making them say that the Tathāgata truly reviled and truly killed.

Regarding the scripture’s statement that "wisely bestowing [benefits] upon sentient beings" and so forth: it is because one cultivates the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) to their ultimate perfection with the great true mind that each and every one attains longevity.
If the perfections were not perfected, one would only attain a long life by refraining from killing a single being.
The Sūtra says, "Whether banished or killed," meaning that it is better to avoid injury to one's body; thus, parents may even kill [the child] themselves.

When the Buddha replies, "It is possible," the intent of the Buddha’s answer is this: because the state of the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) has not yet been attained, it is a difficult matter, and therefore [the child] must be driven away.
To dispatch evil persons and destroy delusions without fault—this refers to those who kill when they perceive the opportune moment;

this interpretation is correct. Furthermore, one must exercise leniency regarding what constitutes the appropriate stage [of realization], while ensuring that the mind intent on protecting the Dharma remains present.
If both were not emanations— if both the Rishi and the youth were actual beings— then since the youth had died and his place of rebirth was not seen,
how could the Rishi and the Brahmin see their place of rebirth? Therefore, this cannot be judged by a single uniform standard.
As for the principle residing therein: now, one must allow for the middle way by employing both provisional and real interpretations to discern the capacity of the recipient.

The provisional serves to lead toward the real, and the real follows the provisional; furthermore, the provisional manifests as identical to the real. If it is not yet appropriate to reveal the true identity (*yǐjì*), one must ultimately not say that it is merely provisional.
Moreover, the primary intent of the present text is this: even before attaining the stage of fearlessness (*abhaya-bhūmi*), one is still able to destroy delusions. Why?

How much less could one who has entered the stages fail to attain it? Therefore, these two passages do not contradict or obstruct one another. How is it that the ancients provided an interpretation of them as being contradictory?
The Sūtra says, "If one harms one's *upādhyāya*. Outsiders refer to their original teacher as an *upādhyāya*, and they also regard the *upādhyāya* as...

They are the parents of the supramundane. While parents in this world possess the heavy debt of the kindness of nurturing, regarding the offenses of persons, even according to the calculations of outsiders, there are superior, middling, and inferior degrees of offense.
Regarding the mutual clarification of "taking away" and "bestowing": it is "taken away" because there is no fixed principle; it is "bestowed" because one obtains retribution.

The Sūtra says that "one who knows skillful means" knows the capacity and knows the timing; they accord with what is appropriate for the provisional and the real, and adapt to the sentiments of sentient beings so that they may enter the Real.
This is called knowing skillful means.

The Sūtra states: "As for those who eat human saliva and spittle," it refers to Devadatta, who, having cultivated the *uṣmagata* stage of contemplation, attained the higher realms and transformed himself into a small child, sitting upon King Ajātaśatru’s lap and so forth.
Regarding the "four flavors," the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states: "The first is precept; the next two are concentration; and the last is wisdom.

This subsequent passage provides an interpretation based on the Four Noble Truths, which accords with the meaning. Furthermore, there are two similes within the sutra, both of which are as they appear in the text.
That which produces the flavor of suffering refers to the transcendence of the two types of death; this is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
"Emptiness and equality" refers to the very substance of the earth.
"Knowledge and vision" refers to the capacity for knowing and seeing. "Being quiescent yet illuminating" means that quiescence is emptiness and equality, while illumination is knowledge.

Seeing emptiness is itself equality; seeing existence is knowing and seeing reality, which is itself equality; expedient means is itself knowing and seeing. The same applies to phenomena and principle. Regarding the fruit of equality:
equality itself is the fruit, hence it is called the "fruit of equality. Furthermore, emptiness is that which is realized through the holy life (*brahmacarya*); therefore—
Emptiness is the drawing forth of the fruit.
As the Sūtra says, "One can enter into cessation at the seventh stage. The *Daśabhūmika-parivarta* of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

Vimukticandra asked, "O Son of the Buddha, at which stage of the Bodhisattva has one not yet been able to enter into cessation? Vajragarbha replied, "At the sixth stage, one has not yet been able to enter."
"Extinction. Now abiding in the seventh stage, one is able to enter extinction in every thought-moment, yet does not realize extinction.
That this Bodhisattva accomplishes inconceivable actions of body, speech, and mind is the very proof of this.
This passage still belongs to the provisional teaching (*biejiao*) concerning the path of instruction; therefore, it shall not be used here.

Regarding "the principle is the same while the capacities differ": the single [nature of] a child refers to the capacity for function (*neng-yong*), whereas emptiness and equality refer to the essence (*ti*). Therefore, it is said that their capacities differ.
As for "emptiness of beings" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and so forth, the text provisionally distinguishes two types of emptiness from the perspective of the object (*suo-yi-bian*).

However, speaking in terms of ultimate reality, once one has cultivated through the great true mind, these two types of emptiness are then called the Middle Way; furthermore, the essence of the Middle Way itself possesses both types of emptiness.
Regarding the use of emptiness as an analogy: it illustrates the twofold emptiness of dharmas produced in prior lives.

As for the eighteen kinds of emptiness clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 34, provides an extensive explanation of their characteristics. Now, relying upon that, I shall briefly analyze these eighteen kinds of emptiness.
First is internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), which refers to the six internal sense bases; the eye is empty of self and what belongs to self (*anātman* and *anātmiya*).
The eye is empty of dharmas. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also thus. Second is external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*):

that is, the six external bases are empty of self, empty of what belongs to self, and empty of form-dharmas. Sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects are also thus. Third is internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*):
that is, within the twelve internal and external bases, there is no "mine" and no internal-or-external dharmas. Fourth is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), which means:

By means of emptiness, one refutes internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness; thus, these three emptinesses are refuted. Therefore, as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*:

"There is only the sickness of emptiness, and even this sickness of emptiness is empty. This is called the "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Regarding the five great emptinesses, they are the so-called emptiness of the characteristics of the ten directions.
Therefore, it is called "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*). It is empty because the ten directions are boundless. Sixth is "Emptiness of the Ultimate Meaning" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*):
that which is the foremost among all phenomena is called *nirvāṇa*. Within *nirvāṇa*, there is likewise no mark of reality; this true emptiness is precisely the Emptiness of the Ultimate Meaning.
Seventh is "Emptiness of the Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): conditioned phenomena are those produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions, namely the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*), etc., conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are now empty for two reasons.

First, they are empty because the self (*ātman*), what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), and any permanent characteristic or immutable nature cannot be found. Second, they are empty because the characteristics of conditioned phenomena are themselves empty;

they are neither arising nor ceasing, and they are non-existent. There are eight kinds of emptiness regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). As for "unconditioned phenomena," it is so named because they are...

Causes and conditions are eternally neither arising nor ceasing; they are like space. Therefore, while currently attending to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one speaks of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

If conditioned phenomena cannot be apprehended, then they do not exist; the absence of anything to which one might cling within the unconditioned is itself the emptiness of the unconditioned. Ninth is the emptiness of the ultimate (*atyanta-śūnyatā*):
this means that by using the preceding eight types of emptiness to dismantle all phenomena until they are ultimately exhausted and purified, it is called "ultimate. If there were no...
All phenomena (*dharmas*) likewise lack ultimate existence; how could one be attached to them? This is called "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

Tenth is "emptiness of that which has no beginning" (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*): all worlds, whether sentient beings or phenomena, have no beginning. Since it is impossible to find a point where ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) can be broken off, this is "no beginning.
Within this state of no beginning, there is no attachment; therefore, it is called "emptiness of that which has no beginning. Eleventh is "dispersal..."

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This refers to the fact that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are a mere conglomeration. If someone were to use wisdom to analyze and dismantle them part by part, then both the "person" and the five aggregates—along with the preceding dismantling—would all be found to be non-existent.
This is called the emptiness of dispersion (*vibhava-śūnyatā*). There is also the emptiness of the twelve natures (*dvādaśa-dhātu-śūnyatā*).

"Nature" (*dhātu*) means that which exists inherently and does not depend on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). If it depended on causes and conditions, it would be called a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Now, as for all phenomena...
In the middle [of these], all are without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because their nature cannot be apprehended, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

Thirteenth is the "emptiness of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). All phenomena have two kinds of characteristics: first, general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), such as impermanence and so forth; second, specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), wherein although all phenomena are impermanent, each possesses its own distinct characteristic.
For example, earth has the characteristic of solidity, and fire has the characteristic of heat. Such are the two types of characteristics.

All are empty; therefore, they are called "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Fourteenth is the "emptiness of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), which refers to the phenomena such as the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

These enter into various categories: all phenomena possess the characteristic of existence, the characteristic of being known, the characteristic of cognition, the characteristic of conditionality, the characteristic of predominance, the characteristic of cause, the characteristic of fruit, the general characteristic, the specific characteristic, and the characteristic of dependence. All of these are empty and lack any substantial reality. Therefore, they are empty.

14. The emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). 15. The emptiness of the unobtainable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*): because all phenomena and their causes and conditions are ultimately unobtainable, it is called the emptiness of the unobtainable.
16. The emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*): when a phenomenon is said to be "non-existent," it means that it has ceased;

since there is no cessation [of that which is already non-existent], it is called the emptiness of non-existence. 17. The emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*): this refers to all phenomena arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions.

That which exists is now entirely empty; therefore, it is called the emptiness of existing dharmas (*bhāva-śūnyatā*). Eighteenth is the emptiness of non-existent and existent dharmas (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Because one cannot grasp the characteristics of non-existent and existent dharmas, it is called the emptiness of non-existent and existent dharmas. This is also because one contemplates the emptiness of non-existent and existent dharmas.
It is designated as "emptiness. Furthermore, the ninety-second [fascicle] states: "The nature of these eighteen kinds of emptiness is itself empty;
that is, the emptiness-maker is also entirely empty. Since these two sūtras mutually clarify this point, they may be cited as being identical.

Alternatively, regarding the discussion of the seven emptinesses: the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* merely enumerates seven emptinesses. First, the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), because [phenomena] do not arise through self-nature, other-nature, or both combined when analyzed.
Second, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and does not arise.

Third, the emptiness of non-action (*anabhisamskāra-śūnyatā*), because the aggregates (*skandha*) are fundamentally real. Fourth, the emptiness of action (*abhisamskāra-śūnyatā*), because the combination of the aggregates and sense bases is devoid of "I" and "mine. Fifth...
1. The emptiness of the unobtainable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*): because all phenomena are falsely conceptualized and are thus ineffable. 2. The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*):

because the self-realized noble wisdom is free from faults and habitual tendencies. 3. The emptiness of that (*tad-śūnyatā*): within that emptiness, there is no sinking into extremes, nor is there "this" or "that."

This is also merely a combination of the eighteen emptinesses into seven. However, because the intent of that sutra differs slightly from that of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, one knows that the seven emptinesses of the *Laṅkāvatāra* mostly pertain to the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings.
Since the three [emptinesses] within "self-realization" are free from faults and habitual tendencies, they are taken up with ease;

they extend somewhat into the *Pratyekabuddha* (Distinct) and *Bodhisattva* (Perfect) teachings. The *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* pertains exclusively to the three teachings of the Mahāyāna gate.

Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the extensive teachings on emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth: those Prajñā texts clarify that emptiness sweeps away all marks; thus, they extensively elucidate emptiness precisely by using emptiness to manifest Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
In the present text, however, the focus is exclusively on clarifying Buddha-nature, thereby manifesting it through its very nature.

Regarding the eleven kinds of emptiness: in each textual passage on emptiness, it is stated that the eternal, blissful, self, and pure, as well as the Three Jewels and Buddha-nature, constitute the essential substance that performs the emptying, while parents and so forth constitute the objects that are emptied and destroyed.

Regarding the emptiness of mutual non-existence (*itaretara-śūnyatā*): when the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) is taught, there is no emptiness of the external (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*); when the emptiness of the external is taught, there is no emptiness of the internal. This applies to all five [remaining types] as well;
this is called the emptiness of mutual non-existence.
Regarding the statement "emptiness as it is in principle": its nature is inherently empty; thus it is so called.
As for the phrase "because cultivation proceeds gradually": since these eleven kinds of emptiness possess no degrees of depth or shallowness, how can one explain them in terms of such gradations?
The statement that "the eleven emptinesses all serve to destroy afflictions" also possesses this meaning; however, it does not accord with the present text. Zhezhou says:
"The preceding ten are 'emptiness of characteristics' (xiāng-kōng), while the subsequent eleven are 'true emptiness' (zhēn-kōng).

To clarify the meaning of emptiness within the phenomena grasped by deluded sentiment is called 'emptiness of characteristics. To discern the meaning of emptiness within the true consciousness is termed 'true emptiness. Furthermore, [he continues:]...
The first ten objects are empty; the final one, wisdom, is empty.
Regarding the objects: when sought according to reality, there is no dharma outside of the mind; all dharmas are the very substance of the true mind.
Regarding "knowledge of tranquility" (*śāntajñāna*): The *Dilun* states that the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as it is described is called "self-knowledge.

Furthermore, among the preceding ten [categories], the first eight use ignorance to break through the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). The ninth uses delusion regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to break through emptiness.

The tenth uses that which is neither existent nor non-existent to simultaneously break through both existence and non-existence; this is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Moreover, within the first eight, the first seven...

It clarifies that sentient beings and phenomena are empty because they lack marks (*animitta*); the latter [of these two] clarifies that sentient beings and phenomena are empty because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

That which lacks the nature of emptiness within the provisional middle of causes and conditions is called "emptiness of no-nature" (*abhāva-śūnyatā*). Within ultimate emptiness, there is no name for causes and conditions;
this is called "emptiness of no-marks" (*animitta-śūnyatā*). However, the intent of this sutra is that each textual passage on emptiness clarifies the Buddha-nature as the three truths.

The interpretation of the essence of emptiness merely as "the dharma of arising" and so forth does not grasp the intent of the sūtra. Therefore, this [passage] is cited to make known its similarities and differences.
Regarding the phrase "is consistent with the text," it simply states that the text lacks the expression "mutually non-existent.

Although this may accord with the underlying principle, it fails to first set forth the characteristics of internal emptiness and external emptiness; since the internal and external are not clarified, the fault lies in merely stating they are "mutually non-existent" while attempting to establish a correspondence.

Regarding the point that "it is logically correct": although this is logically sound, it is not convenient in terms of the textual structure. Why? Because the text currently distinguishes between phenomena and their respective emptinesses as being different;
it merely states that when explaining external emptiness, one should analogously understand internal phenomena.
If one were to rely solely on this analogy, the textual characteristics would remain undifferentiated; therefore, it cannot be employed.
The Sūtra states that "internal emptiness" refers to the absence of parents up to material wealth, which constitutes the object of emptiness.

Subsequently, from among these internal phenomena, the essence of that which performs the emptying is not raised. Furthermore, when explaining internal emptiness, there is no external emptiness as its counterpart; it is simply termed "internal emptiness."

When explaining external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), that which lacks an object to be emptied by internal emptiness is itself termed external emptiness; therefore, these two types of emptiness are combined into a single section.
In the eighth fascicle of the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), the explanation of the "Peaceful and Joyful Conduct" states: "Non-inversion is internal emptiness."
Within, there are no six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of "self" or "mine," and thus one is not inverted. Being unshakable means that externally one is not moved by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Being non-retrogressive means that both internally and externally are empty, because the twelve sense bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are empty. Now, in this sutra, the first two types of emptiness have their characteristics explained together, making them difficult to discern.
Therefore, I shall cite them here as an illustration to clarify the characteristics of the two types of emptiness in the present text.

If one were to treat them as mutually dependent, others would say that it is only by depending on internal emptiness that external emptiness exists; if there were no internal emptiness, external emptiness would likewise not exist.
Therefore, it is said to be "easy to see."
Regarding "combined into a single emptiness": this refers to the single emptiness of equality (*samatā-śūnyatā*).

As the Sūtra states, "internal and external emptiness," it first sets forth the objects that are empty, and subsequently, from the passage beginning "there is only the Tathāgata," it sets forth the essence that performs the emptying.

Regarding the scripture’s statement that "conditioned phenomena are empty": first, it presents the objects that are empty; next, from the middle and lower sections, it presents the essence that performs the emptying.

Regarding the scripture’s statement that "unconditioned phenomena are empty": first, it presents the objects that are empty; next, from the four [categories] beginning with the Buddha, it presents the essence that performs the emptying.
As for "initially breaking through and clarifying non-existence," this refers simply to the breaking through of beginningless birth and death, which is termed "beginningless emptiness.

Since this initial breaking through is actually without a beginning, it is called "non-existence of non-existence. That which has a beginning is precisely beginningless emptiness; the beginning is itself non-existent.
The *Fahua shu* states: "Not arising" means that when one seeks the original beginning within beginningless emptiness, it cannot be found; this is called "beginningless emptiness.

The Sūtra says, "beginningless emptiness," meaning that the beginninglessness of birth and death is that which is empty. Following the phrase "all are entirely," from "empty and quiescent" downward, the essence of that which performs the emptying is brought forth.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that "nature is empty": first, it clarifies the essence of that which is able to empty; second, it indicates the objects that are to be emptied.

As for the phrase "breaking nature to explain emptiness-nature": others [the opponents] break the attachment to the four types of nature by means of internal causes and external conditions, thereby attaining the emptiness of nature.

In our current interpretation, however, we take the dharma-nature as the "self" and ignorance as the "other," thereby establishing the four types of nature; these four types of nature are then broken.
This is called "emptiness of nature.

When the sutra speaks of "emptiness of non-existence," it first presents the object that is empty; subsequently, from the passage beginning with "when the bodhisattva contemplates," it presents the subject that performs the emptying.
The "foolish person" is a metaphor for the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); the "poor person" is a metaphor for those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
Regarding the meaning of "neither": within the discussion of the eight non-manifestations (*aṣṭāvyākṛtadharmāḥ*), this now shares the same meaning as that which is neither arising nor ceasing.
"Returning to non-existence" means emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Having no eyes" means there are no real dharmas. "Having no master" means there are no provisional names (*prajñapti*).
The Sūtra states, "There is karma and there is an agent," which refers to the teachings of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha).

To "provisionally rely on existence to clarify non-existence" means that realizing non-existence is precisely the Middle Way, the Buddha-nature; hence the phrase "provisionally relying on existence," and so forth. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states:
"Contemplating all phenomena as empty, according to their true aspect, is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)."
Regarding the phrase "the Immortal Zhi and others" in the Sūtra, the term "others" includes minor Bodhisattvas and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
As for "both of these are empty," it means that both prior existence and non-existence are empty.

"This is this" refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*); because it discriminates through skillful means, it is said "this is this. Real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) has emptiness as its essence; therefore, it is said "not this.
Now, to further formulate three propositions for critique, one challenges the third master who merely establishes the object and the wisdom. This applies to the first three teachings.
All cases are like this; therefore, it is said that this is still merely partial.

If one applies "emptiness of emptiness" (kōng-kōng) downward, then using the Middle Way emptiness within Buddha-nature to empty the objects and wisdom of the three previous teachings is only then called "emptiness of emptiness."
"All dharmas" means that the objects and wisdom of the three teachings are all empty.
"The essence of wisdom is not empty" means that the essence of the wisdom capable of realizing emptiness is not empty.
"In principle, there is no simultaneous illumination" means that while objects may be dual, wisdom is singular.

Regarding the meaning of "simultaneous illumination and elimination" being knowable: although wisdom is non-dual, it is able to eliminate the attachments to existence and non-existence regarding both the object of emptiness and the subject that is empty;
therefore, it is called "emptiness of emptiness.
As for those who value the untainted emptiness and so forth: if one values the untainted, one will disparage the tainted; thus, there will be a disparagement of the non-existent.
It is called the mutual emptiness of names; hence it is termed "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

The phrase "the substance of the two emptinesses is further destroyed" refutes [their substantiality]. The passage "since all phenomena are quiescent" correctly elucidates the essence of the emptiness of emptiness.

"All phenomena are quiescent" clarifies that the objects of emptiness are empty; "the essence of the wisdom of emptiness is also empty" clarifies that the subject which performs the emptying is likewise empty. Hence it is called "emptiness of emptiness."

The scripture states, "that which is attained is empty emptiness," which serves to distinguish [this from other forms of emptiness]. Since the followers of the Two Vehicles also attain the samādhi of "repeated emptiness" (gongō-zanmai), it is necessary to distinguish between them.
The scripture speaks of "great emptiness" (daikū); one should say that only when referring to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the like is it properly termed "great emptiness."
Regarding their mutual manifestation: Nirvana is that which is empty, and Prajñā is that which empties. That which empties is itself that which is empty;
that which is empty is itself that which empties. Therefore, it is said that they manifest one another.

Regarding "emptiness of ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*): for the time being, it is designated as "emptiness of ultimate truth" by way of its contrast with the objects that are empty. This one reality is the truth of all things;

the emptiness of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-śūnyatā*) is likewise so. That is to say, this inconceivable conventional [truth]—each and every instance of this emptiness—is explained by way of the perfect fusion of the three truths.

Regarding the statement "one does not see a primal ancestor": if there were a primal ancestor, there would be that which is capable of giving birth; if there is that which is capable of giving birth, then there must be subsequent progeny. Why is this?

Because emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is itself the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the middle (*madhyama*); the provisional is itself emptiness and the middle; and the middle is itself emptiness and the provisional. Therefore, there is no primal ancestor.

However, the commentary (*śāstra*) lacks an explanation for the phrase "nothing whatsoever exists" (*asarva-asti*). It should state: the three truths are all quiescent; this is called "nothing whatsoever exists."
As for "the true is itself the middle": there must be a "middle" within the true for the meaning of "round" to be established.
As for "this is this": because the Middle Way illumines both [aspects] simultaneously, it is said that it "immediately possesses" emptiness and the provisional.
To illuminate only one truth is not identical to the Middle Way of double negation.
As for "it is because it is empty," this does not mean that emptiness itself possesses the provisional; therefore, it is called "it is, it is."

Regarding the phrase "because it is provisional, it is not [that thing]": the provisional itself is the possession of emptiness. Furthermore, the inconceivable provisional is able to be the non-exclusive provisional.
If one takes that which is easily understood—namely, emptiness—itself as being the provisional, then it is said to be "not that."
If they appear as pairs, they explain internal-external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārthaśūnyatā*).

If they appear singly, they explain internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhāśūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*).
If there are three, it is an explanation based on the Three Truths. If there is one, it explains the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
As the Sūtra says, "the ground of empty space and so forth," this refers to abiding in the True Emptiness of the Buddha-nature at the First Stage—the emptiness of the Tathāgata.

Regarding "separating from before and attaining after passing through the sūtra": within the sūtra, there is first an explanation of the Dharma, followed by two similes and their two corresponding applications (*yoga*).

Both first clarify the separation from attachment regarding oneself and others, and subsequently clarify the attainment of the stage (*bhūmi*). In the first simile, it clarifies that emptiness does not receive anything; in the second, it clarifies that emptiness accommodates and receives everything.

Furthermore, the former simile clarifies that while possessing the characteristics of defilement and purity, its functional capacity is manifest; the latter simile clarifies the characteristic of accommodation and reception.
This reveals its functional capacity.

Regarding the extensive discernment of knowledge and vision: since knowledge and vision are already vast, they verify the realization attained; the essence of emptiness, which is equality, pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Therefore, it is through extensive vision that its essence is revealed.
"Being quiescent yet illuminating" initiates the four subsequent passages. In each instance, knowledge and vision are entirely in accord with the principle of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the phrase "first, knowing the thirteen dharmas," etc.: this clarifies that because the internal mind is pure, one is able to know and see; thus there are four [aspects].
Discriminating the external application:
The Sūtra says, "both seeing and knowing. "Seeing" refers to the fulfillment of the five eyes; "knowing" refers to the perfection of the three wisdoms within a single mind.
"Practice is precisely the mind" refers to the contemplative mind of the four teachings.
"Object" (境) refers to that which is observed throughout all four teachings.
"Nature" (性) refers to the fact that the essential nature of the ten realms remains unchanged. "Phenomena" (相) refers to the differing external appearances of the ten realms.
"Causes and conditions" refers to the differing responses and stimuli of the four teachings.
"If it is the minds of sentient beings," this refers to the differing discriminative minds of sentient beings within the ten realms.
"If it is the faculties," this refers to the differing faculties and conditions of the four teachings.
Regarding "meditation" (dhyāna), there are differences between the meditations of the internal and external realms.

Regarding "vehicles" (yāna), there are the human and celestial vehicles, the three vehicles, the nine vehicles, and so forth. Furthermore, when the provisional is established based on the ultimate, the three vehicles differ from one another.
The opening of the provisional and the revelation of the real is the single Buddha-vehicle alone.
As for "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), there are different types according to the four teachings. Furthermore, there are those who are "good spiritual friends" and those who are "demons.
Regarding the observance of prohibitions, this refers to the ten precepts.
Regarding the giver, there are four types of practice in giving that differ from one another, namely: the vast, the foremost, the constant, and so forth.
As for the statement in the sutra, "knowing yet not seeing," it means that the bodhisattva knows sentient beings but does not see their Buddha-nature.
*Bián* (pronounced *biyuán*) refers to weaving thorns to form a *lán*; one encircles oneself with it while sitting or reclining.
*Lǚ* (pronounced *lìzhū*) refers to a cloth woven from animal hair; such a headcloth is called *lǚ*.
The Sūtra states: "If one is able to practice *dāna* (generosity)," referring here to the four teachings of *dāna*.

Thus we know that "common practice" (*sādhāraṇa-caryā*) refers to the methods of the partial and the perfect, the sudden and the gradual, which are practiced in common by both ordinary beings and sages; this dharma is therefore called "common practice."
Thus we know that regarding the fruit, within the text there is again "entering darkness from darkness" and "entering darkness from light"; these are the fruits of unwholesome delusion.
"Entering light from darkness" and "entering darkness from light" are the fruits of supramundane awakening.
The Sūtra says, "One who cultivates the mind" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata both sees and knows": "sees" means seeing for oneself, and "knows" means knowing others; it does not mean not knowing or not seeing.
"Reaching the mundane" refers to the provisional emergence from the profound (*míngchū jiǎ*).
The Sūtra states: "The Bodhisattva knows that there are seeds; this constitutes a knot. However, the text does not separately open up this passage concerning the knot.

When the Sūtra speaks of "that which is known by the five eyes," it should rather say "the three knowledges" (trijñāna). That the term "eye" is used here is because the eye is employed to manifest knowledge;
knowledge and the eye are identical in nature. As for the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, it consists of verses of varying lengths.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "not named a Bodhisattva," this refers to one not yet named a Bodhisattva of the Ground of the Equality of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-samatā-bhūmi*).

As for the claim that this is an interpretation intended to dispel attachment, such a person is already a Bodhisattva of the [first] Ground; what further attachment could they have that would require it to be called "dispelling attachment"?
As for the term "ground-support" (*bhūmi-dhara*), each and every one of them is spontaneously capable of sustaining.
Regarding the causes from the past: this refers to the causal practices for the lifespan as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
When the sutra speaks of "practicing conventional truth," it refers to the inconceivable conventional truth.

When the sutra states that "one must use gentle speech," gentle speech is employed through the gate of gathering and sustaining (*saṃgraha-vastu*), while harsh speech is employed through the gate of subduing.

Second, "opening up the former expedient" refers to the opening that permits [the practice of] giving. Third, "revealing the present reality" means that the sutra cites the former, incomplete [teachings] for śrāvakas in order to reveal the present, complete [teachings] for bodhisattvas, as stated in the preceding text.

Regarding "that which has already been distanced": this refers to the third major section, which clarifies the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). First is the question, followed by the meaning of the text of the answer.

To summarize the essential intent, the preceding sutra states: Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can know in such a manner, what benefit does he obtain? The Buddha said, "Good son, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can..."
Thus, by knowing this, one attains the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge; hence it is said within the "Chapter on the Brahma-faring.
As for the Sūtra’s statement, "And you have asked again," the Buddha praised you because your question was appropriate to the needs and capacities of the audience.

Regarding "perversion and non-perversion": first, the four perversions within and outside the realms are explained; the subsequent nine [sections] likewise explain them by way of the internal and external realms.
"Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna" refers to a distinction based on the teachings (*śāsana*). "Vaipulya and Tripiṭaka" refers to a distinction based on the scriptural divisions (*nikāya*).
The Sūtra states that there are eleven divisions, excluding the Vaipulya division.
Regarding "true emptiness and birth-and-death," this refers first to the two kinds of birth-and-death:分段 (pariccheda) and 變易 (pariṇāma).
The Sūtra says, "If it is the wheel of birth-and-death," it means being turned by the wheels of these two types of death.

Regarding the five views: although these five views exist within the realm [of the threefold world], for those of the Two Vehicles and others, they are entirely the five sharp faculties outside the realm.
Therefore, it is said that prior to this, all are called people of false views.

Regarding "Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles": this distinguishes the Two Vehicles by way of their path; the path of the Two Vehicles is the path of the illusory city, whereas for Bodhisattvas, it is the path of reality.
This is because the Two Vehicles constitute a Mara to the bodhicitta.
The Sūtra states, "Those who forever wish to sever the paths of the two vehicles. This refers to severing the paths of the two vehicles as well as the partial path of the bodhisattva.
The Sūtra further states, "As for your hearing and so forth," this is because they all likewise attain the equality of emptiness.
"Directly as a linguistic convention": his intention is that when one says "at this" while referring to this tree, it is merely a matter of linguistic usage.
Second, "seeing the opening": his intention is that one might say "that" while referring to this, or say "this" while referring to that; therefore, he says "neither."
Regarding the "brief indication of the fixed locus": this refers to expressing the Buddha’s intended meaning.
When the Sūtra says, "Originally there were immeasurable afflictions," it means that from time immemorial the Buddha has possessed immeasurable afflictions.

Because he possesses these afflictions, at the present time when he is at the Deer Park, he does not possess the Great Parinirvāṇa; it was originally non-existent, and it was non-existent during his time as a youth.
The Mahāyāna cultivates and perfects the prajñā of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). At present, while in the stage of a small vehicle, there are only afflictions (*kleśa*).
If there were a śramaṇa who claimed that the dharmas existing throughout the three periods of time are non-existent, this would be impossible.

That is to say, both the original afflictions and the present afflictions are not subsumed within the three periods of time, because for the Tathāgata, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding "original existence": I originally possessed a royal palace and received a body born from the union of father and mother;
now, I lack the subtle Dharma-body of the Mahāyāna Vajra, possessing only the fivefold Dharma-body of the Hīnayāna.
Regarding "originally non-existent": my body originally lacked the body of the Great Vehicle with its thirty-two marks.
Now, while at the Deer Park, I have only a body that seeks clothing against the cold wind and seeks milk for a feverish illness.
If there were any śramaṇa who could eliminate the dharmas of the three periods of existence, such a thing is impossible.
As for those who existed from the beginning: when I was formerly at the Deer Park, I possessed only the contemplations of impermanence and so forth;
even now, while in this stage, there is no Mahāyāna bodhi.

Regarding "originally non-existent": because one has not originally seen the Buddha-nature, one currently exists in the stage of an ordinary person (bāla) and thus encounters the impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure phenomena that exist throughout the three periods of time.
By this analogy, it is known that the ordinary person is originally existent.

Regarding those whose minds were devoted to ascetic practices: because they practiced only the meditative concentration of asceticism during their earlier stages, they claimed this was the path to Bodhi;
consequently, in the past, they were unable to reach the ultimate goal of destroying the four Māras and the eight Māras, being able to destroy only a small portion of the Devaputra-māra.
This is because their physical aggregates (skandha-kāya) still persist.
Regarding those who originally lacked the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā): in the past they had no practice of the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) six perfections, but only a mind of asceticism.
Therefore, in the present, they do not attain the unsurpassed bodhi of the Mahāyāna. This can be known throughout the three periods of time.
"When I formerly possessed a body that consumed various foods" refers to the body that received the milk-rice and so forth. "In the past there was no Mahāyāna or boundless Dharma-body;

originally there were no thirty-seven factors of enlightenment" means that in the past there were no unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the like—this is the meaning.
Therefore, there is only a body sustained by mixed food; in the past, there was no boundless body of the Mahāyāna, as can be known throughout the three periods of time.

As for those who fundamentally possess a mind of attachment to attainment, they merely have the meditative mind of the Two Vehicles focused on the True Truth (*satyadharma*), which is termed "attachment."
As for those who now attain the samādhi of emptiness: in the past, they lacked the fundamental Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
there were none who reached the Middle Way. In the past, they possessed only the mind that compiled the truths, but lacked the true meaning of the Mahāyāna Middle Way.
The three periods of time can be perceived.
That which has existed fundamentally until the attainment of Bodhi—what was originally intended to be explained as the Great Vehicle’s Bodhi—is called "fundamentally existent" (*benyou*).

Because the faculties of sentient beings are dull, it cannot be explained immediately; this is called "presently non-existent" (*jinwu*). That which has fundamentally lacked sharp faculties is called "fundamentally non-existent" (*benwu*).
"Present existence" refers to the three types of skillful means practiced in the past, which are termed "present existence. The three time periods can thus be known.

When I previously stated that [the fruit] is not attained within three months, this was said during my time at the Deer Park; it was a provisional teaching regarding the present. As for the detailed exposition:
Because sentient beings were incapable, the Mahāyāna was not taught in the past; thus, the Vaipulya sūtras did not originally exist.
As for Mañjuśrī, in former times it was only said that the Tathāgata is impermanent, which is termed "non-existent now," though he can be known throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, every single phrase must state: "It is possible that dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time. Why is this so?
The opening of the assembly to bestow the fruit of its own causes, and the introduction of the perfect and eternal through the ritual of transformation, are as clear as a deer in a meadow.

However, if one says that such a state does not exist, then the six stages would vanish; for both understanding and delusion are nothing other than the Dharma-realm, though they are simply not subsumed within the mundane world.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the second half [of the verse]: in each of the eight sections, starting from "If there were a śramaṇa...
and so forth, this explains the second half, namely that "there is no such possibility.
As for "existence and non-existence in the past": both existence and non-existence in the past are impermanent. Why? Although it is said: "Now... [the text continues].
If there were only *nirvāṇa*, it would merely explain the meaning of the distinction in the first half [of the verse]. How could it resolve Kāśyapa’s objection or dispel Cunda’s doubts?

This "it is indeed so" (*naiḥsa*) refers to the reality that exists now. Although the explanation provided by Xinghuang captures the general sense, it still does not achieve their mutual identity (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Nevertheless...
The statement, "However, this is not yet fully understood," means that it is therefore not employed here.

As for the phrase, "Sentient beings perform only good, evil, and so forth," this clarifies that ordinary beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas all only attain the meaning of the distinctions in the first half [of the teaching].
Mañjuśrī, how is it that one fully attains the four propositions? The three truths are identical to the one truth;
the one truth is identical to the three truths—this is the attainment of the first half [of the verse]. That which is neither three nor one is the attainment of the second half.
Furthermore, being one while being three, and being three while being one, yet neither three nor one—it is possible for such a person to benefit sentient beings.

Furthermore, if one interprets the verse as follows: that which originally existed is the conventional; that which now does not exist is the ultimate; and that which is not subsumed within the three periods of time is the middle.
Moreover, that which originally did not exist is the ultimate; that which now exists is the conventional.
Regarding the four gates within the Middle Way that are not subsumed under the three periods of time: if these four gates are categorized according to the Three Truths,

the True corresponds to Emptiness, the Conventional corresponds to Existence, the simultaneous illumination of both corresponds to the Total (Zhao), and the simultaneous negation of both corresponds to the Universal Inclusion (Wangyouwangwu).
"All dharmas" explains the first half-verse by means of establishing the provisional based on the ultimate.
