"Each and every one of them" refers to the fact that each attains the specific meaning of the first half-verse of the former teaching;
thus, it should be known that the statement "there are [dharmas]," etc., explains the first half-verse. "All for the sake of benefiting" explains the second half-verse.
The Sūtra says, "Briefly equalizing," and so forth. To take the One Vehicle as the Three Vehicles and to bring the Three Vehicles back to the One Vehicle is called "briefly equalizing.

Furthermore, as stated in the preceding text regarding the twelve links of dependent origination: to collectively name them "conditioned" is called "extensive explanation," while to briefly state that within the single category of the conditioned they are divided into twelve is called "broad explanation from the brief."

Regarding the phrase "the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*) and so forth": this refers to a comparative analysis of the gravity and the nature of transgression or non-transgression by contrasting the ten *pārājika* rules of the Bodhisattva precepts with the four grave offenses of the Hīnayāna.

Furthermore, it contrasts the minor stains (*laghu-mala*) of the Bodhisattva precepts with the thirteen [offenses] and below of the Hīnayāna, distinguishing between what constitutes a formal transgression and what does not.
For example, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, stealing four *kārsāpaṇa* coins from a person through three means is defined as a transgression.

What is a *pārājika* is explained as a *sthūlātyaya* in the *Caturvarga-vinaya*. Regarding the explanation of the four grave offenses (*catur-guru*) as *sthūlātyaya*, if one reverses the preceding [conditions], it constitutes an offense.

As for the explanation that there is no offense and so forth, it is like the eight impure items: if stored during a time of scarcity, there is no offense; if stored during a time of abundance, it constitutes an offense.
Regarding the statement that "a light offense is declared heavy" and so forth: in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one who wears white robes commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), yet it is not noted;
instead, it says one commits a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, one who wears white robes commits a *dukkaṭa*, yet it is not noted.
The offenses of *thullaccaya* (grave transgressions) all take birth and death as the upper half of the world. True reality is the lower half of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
There are times when the upper half is the lower half; sometimes, regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), the lower half is the upper half.
All other cases follow this same principle.

That all conditions give rise to views of existence and non-existence refers to the first half [of the verse]. If one perceives the Buddhas as being neither other than nor identical to the Dharma-realm, they are not subsumed within the three periods of time.
As for the statement in the Sūtra that it is called both "the Path" (*mārga*) and "Awakening" (*bodhi*): "Path" is the Sanskrit *mārga*.
Just as among the Four Noble Truths there is the Truth of the Path, here too the Bodhisattva is called the Path. How do these two differ? Generally, they are one;
specifically, *mārga* is the path of the cause, while *bodhi* is the path of the fruit. For this reason, two distinct names are established.
Regarding the phrase "though the eternal Way is attained, etc.": the eternal Way is precisely attainment without attainment; this attainment of non-attainment alone is called the "Great Attainment.
Although the Two Vehicles attain it, it is impermanent.
Regarding those who perceive according to the categories of the sutras: they see the real as the provisional, the provisional as the real, and that which is neither provisional nor real.
If even such semblances are not false, how much less so that which is clearly understood? How could that be false?
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "Seated, the Tathāgata fully knows and awakens," Zhezhou says: first, in terms of practice; second, in terms of stages. Regarding practice:

hearing-wisdom (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is "knowing"; seeking through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is called "awakening"; and the realization of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is termed "seeing. Furthermore, hearing and reflection are "knowing."

Cultivating contemplation and attaining clarity is called "seeing" (*darśana*); realizing and harmonizing with it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*). In terms of stages: that which precedes the [ten] stages is called "knowing"; the first stage is called "seeing";

and from the second stage upward, repeated contemplation is called "awakening. Now, we clarify the six levels of identity (*ṣaḍ-vidha-bhāva*) to elucidate the principle of knowing, seeing, and awakening to the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
In the "Chapter on the Holy Life," there are three questions regarding those who share the world. These two instances of "hearing" are both correct hearings and not difficult expressions. Why?
First, for the sake of Śāriputra, it was taught that the world possesses knowledge and vision; the Buddha likewise possesses such knowledge and vision. Is this definitely so?
If it were truly so, how would this differ from the world?

As for the question of why those in other worlds do not know [this]: the intent of the question is that since the World-Honored One, like those in the world, possesses the four great elements, wears robes, and partakes of food, why is it that worldly people do not know, see, or perceive [him]?
For what reason does the World-Honored One alone possess such knowledge, vision, and perception?
"I do not understand this now; I pray that the Buddha will explain it for me. Thus he asks, "What is its meaning? which summarizes his two questions.
When the Sūtra says, "is called a Bodhisattva," it refers to those who are Bodhisattvas by name alone.
The Sūtra states: "Not awakening to the twelve divisions [of the teachings]" means not knowing that the twelve divisions contain the Buddha-nature;

not knowing that the twelve links of dependent origination without action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) are the Buddha-nature of the three virtues; not knowing that the eight inversions are the permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
not knowing the four truths without action; and not knowing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without action. By taking these various dharmas as causes, one attains bodhi.
Taking *nirvāṇa* as the fruit—worldly people do not know this at all.
If one can know it, such a person is a bodhisattva who practices in accordance with [the truth].
Regarding the passage concerning "Brahmā and others," Master She said: "Brahmā is the lord of the first dhyāna; Maheśvara (Īśvara) is the lord of the fourth dhyāna."
The "eight" refers to the hand-guarding celestial lords who protect the world.
"Nature" (prakṛti) refers to what the Sāṃkhya school calculates as primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti). "Time" refers to the calculation that time gives birth to all things.
Regarding "atoms" (*paramāṇu*): this refers to the Lokāyatas and Tīrthikas who assert that subtle atoms produce coarse resultant material phenomena, both virtuous and non-virtuous;

and the Vaiśeṣikas who maintain that wholesome and unwholesome actions produce the sensations of suffering and pleasure. Each of these schools maintains that their respective conceptualized entities are the causes of all things.

He is called the Lord of Creation. To regard the end of the world as ultimate is a view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). To hold that the first dhyāna and so forth constitute reality is the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
This is the mistaken understanding of what is known, seen, and realized in the world, taking it to be correct.

Those who falsely speculate on annihilationism (*uccheda*) or eternalism (*śāśvata*) and provide explanations of "no beginning and no end" fall into the view of eternalism; those who provide explanations of "having a beginning and having an end" fall into the view of annihilationism.
This is incorrect. It means that these are entirely externalist views, and their meaning is identical to this [point].

Second, regarding that which is neither mundane nor supramundane: the essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa does not properly belong to either the mundane or the supramundane; therefore, it is said to be "neither.
When the Sūtra says, "They are not called non-mundane," it means that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are termed "non-mundane."

The first half-verse is as explained previously: it is the same as the ancient masters' judgment that the Buddha possesses great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and is able to bestow upon sentient beings the great, true bliss;
therefore, he is praised. The subsequent verse praises his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):
because he is able to uproot the causes and effects of suffering—the two deaths and the three delusions—he is praised for this.
That which joy abandons is the ultimate abandonment of suffering.
That which joy attains is the vision that sentient beings have obtained great, true bliss.
Regarding the praise of great equanimity (*upekṣā*): since sentient beings have already ultimately abandoned suffering and attained great bliss, I therefore relinquish them. Thus it is said.
It is said that [the practitioner] neither dies nor is born.

Regarding "taking precepts as the foundation": *brahman* has the meaning of purity. If one lacks precepts oneself, how can one transform others? Furthermore, both sitting meditation and walking meditation take precepts as their foundation.
Although the text mentions this here, the intended meaning must apply to the beginning [of the practice].
If one lacks ethical discipline (*śīla*), there is no fundamental basis for transforming others; this is because such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
As for the phrase "it is logical that it should be so," it means that since a bodhisattva exists within the world, they ought to be indistinguishable from worldly people in their lack of realization.
The Sūtra states, "This is what is called a worldly bodhisattva. This refers to a bodhisattva in name only. That they do not entirely coincide [with ordinary beings] is due to three points:
first, they share the same worldly knowledge and views; second, they differ from worldly knowledge and views; and third, they are able to know that which transcends the world.
Therefore, it is said that they are not entirely identical. The mention of only "two" is a brief omission of "concentration.

As for the sūtra’s statement that one is "not moved by the four winds," this means being unmoved by the eight winds (aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ) both within and outside the realms; the same applies to the four inversions (catur-viparyāsa).
The Sūtra states: "That which is known, seen, and realized by this bodhisattva" refers to a bodhisattva at the initial stage of the worldly path (*laukika-prathama-citta*).
The Sūtra further states: "up to those who have attained clear understanding" refers to bodhisattvas who have attained the equality of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samatā*).

Regarding Nanda: as explained in detail in the fourth fascicle of the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation) within the section on rebuking the five desires, he was unable to follow [the practice] from beginning to end;
this case has a beginning but lacks an end when compared to the preceding four.
Regarding "impurity": this is the opposite of the four types of impurity mentioned previously; thus it is called "in contrast to the former.

As for "contrasting with the former's lack of beginning or end," the first precept here contrasts with the third [of the previous list], which was "not ultimate. The second precept here contrasts with the first [of the previous list], which was "existent.
The third precept here contrasts with the second [of the previous list], which was "indeterminate regarding sentient beings. This is as stated in the text.

Regarding the phrase "not the five precepts and so forth," it should rather be stated as "the five precepts, the ten precepts, and so forth. To cultivate these with the mind of the Great Nirvāṇa is what is called "non-precept";
it differs from the definitive mental adherence to them held by those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary worldlings.
The Sūtra states that "it arises spontaneously. This refers to the state described in the preceding passage: from the mind of joy, there spontaneously arises a mind of rapture and bliss;
one becomes tranquil and immovable, attains concentration and liberation, perceives the Buddha-nature, and realizes Great Nirvāṇa—all arising spontaneously.
Such a person is one who has already entered the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*).
The Sūtra says: "One who holds a bright mirror" refers to one who, relying on the teachings, cultivates the precepts until they are luminous and pure;
thus it is said that the reflection of the face appears spontaneously for such a person whose contemplative practice has progressed.
The Sūtra says: "As with the farmer below, by means of the purity of precepts, there arises the virtue of generating the wholesome;
likewise, as with the lighting of a lamp below, by means of the purity of precepts, there lies the merit of extinguishing the unwholesome."
The Sūtra states, "By means of purity," and so forth; the subsequent text is abbreviated. It should be understood in full as previously described:

a mind free from regret, joy, delight, and tranquility, up to the point of seeing the Buddha-nature and attaining liberation and nirvāṇa. Both the illustrative passages and the applications of the analogy must follow this same pattern.

The Sūtra says, "Seeing one's own facial expression": this means knowing for oneself that one is a person who has violated the teachings; therefore, seeing one's own facial expression, one is not pleased.
The Sūtra says, "The mind then becomes joyful": this should rather say that the mind of one who has broken the precepts is sorrowful and distressed.
The five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*) are the faculties of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.

It is said that grief exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) because one has not yet attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and is thus agitated by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm; therefore, suffering and grief exist in the first dhyāna.

This is because within the first dhyāna, while the eyes see forms, the ears hear sounds, and the body experiences tactile sensations, there is no perception of odors or tastes; being disturbed by these three [sensory objects], there is suffering and joy.
In the second dhyāna, one attains detachment from the three types of sensation present in the first dhyāna; therefore, joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*) persist in the third dhyāna.

Although there is joy in the second dhyāna, it still involves detachment from suffering and entails agitation and instability; thus, the third dhyāna is designated as the sensation of pleasure. Although there is pleasure in the third dhyāna, it can cause the practitioner’s body and mind to become submerged in it;
for this reason, the fourth dhyāna is able to relinquish both suffering and pleasure, thereby realizing the state that is neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha*).
It is appropriate.

Regarding "now being the same as the factors of dhyāna": this refers to the five factors of dhyāna—vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and citta-ekāgratā (one-pointedness of mind). In this context, joy is shallow while bliss is deep.
As the Sūtra says, "that which is called 'superior' is bliss," because bliss is the dharma of the superior fruit; therefore, it is termed "superior."
Regarding the "five factors of assistance," one attains liberation from the six kinds of five factors of assistance. That which is called "nirvāṇa" refers to Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Within this sutra, terms such as "faith" and the "five views" must all be interpreted deeply in order to accord with the present text.
The term "vowei" (猥) means "evil."
"Those of no use" refers to those who lack the utility for humans or devas; having lost the status of human or deva, they lack the utility for receiving the Path.
"Those who run as servants" refers to bodhisattvas acting as their messengers, commanding them to read, uphold [the teachings], and so forth.
Now, regarding those who admonish teachers of men: since they are individuals who protect the Buddha-dharma, they must maintain the precepts and not violate them.
To rebuke those who seek existence refers to seeking within the twenty-five realms of existence; because this arises from the mind, it belongs to the category of mental karma (*manas-karma*).
"One who does not seek karmic retribution" means that while sitting for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi, one does not seek the fruits and retributions of the nine realms;

only then can one be called "profoundly discerning. "There are none who do not request [instruction]" means that if there are those of sharp faculties who value the Dharma, it is unnecessary to wait for them to request it; one should act for their sake.
Regarding the "uninvited friend": for those of dull faculties who treat the Dharma lightly, one must wait for an invitation; therefore it is said that matters must accord with the timing.
From the phrase "if one wishes to receive and uphold" up to "the Buddha-nature has ten names," these are called the Ten Knowledges (daśajñāna).
Following this, the next section exhorts the purification of the mind. The scripture states: "That which is called Buddha-nature.
The term "Buddha-nature" (foxing) is used in its singular sense; for the time being, it refers to the primary nature. As for the "Secret Treasury," it possesses the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the "essence and substance of the *nirvāṇa* school": the Great *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra is its substance, while the teaching of Buddha-nature is its school. "School" (*zong*) means "honored" (*zun*).

This is not the "sectarian" aspect of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) and other practices, which constitute the essence of the school; rather, it is the function of liberation. As for "hearing even a single verse," this refers to the teaching.
Regarding "the three karmas being pure," this is precisely what is fully elucidated within the text.

Regarding the "ten recollections" (*daśa-anusmṛti*): the *Āgama-sūtra* states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus, "You should practice ten dharmas, and you will then achieve supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), eliminate all signs of distraction, and reach nirvāṇa.
First, the recollection of the Buddha; continuing thus up to the seventh, the recollection of cessation (*virāga*). Eighth, the recollection of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).
Ninth, the recollection of the impermanence of the body. Tenth, the recollection of death. You should practice these well."

Regarding "the essence of mindfulness is tranquility": this means that the mental activities and perceptions are stilled; one's disposition is careful and discerning, free from sudden outbursts or violence.
Constantly focusing the single mind, one always seeks skillful means to enter samādhi. By maintaining uninterrupted mindfulness, one spontaneously attains nirvāṇa.
The eight recollections and mindfulness of breathing consist simply in counting the breaths, knowing them to be long or short, and knowing them to be cold or hot.
By discerning the inhalation and exhalation and recognizing the length of the breath, one eliminates all distracted thoughts and thereby attains nirvana for oneself.
Regarding the ninth, mindfulness of the body (*kāyānusmṛti*): one focuses exclusively on the thirty-six components of the body—hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, and so forth.

One contemplates: "What constitutes the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element of this body? All are produced by father and mother. From where did they come? For whose sake were they created?
One considers these six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): where will they cease upon death at the end of this life, and where will they be reborn? Thus, one brings oneself to *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding "death through ten recollections": this refers to focusing one's mind exclusively on death. One contemplates passing away from here and being reborn there, wandering through the various realms of existence (*gati*) without the life-force pausing for even a moment.
The faculties scatter and perish like rotten grass, and one attains *nirvāṇa* by oneself. In the *Āgama*, this pertains only to the Hīnayāna;

in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it belongs specifically to the Mahāyāna. Now, I cite the small to illustrate the great: while the object of recollection is no different, the contemplation itself varies in its skillfulness or clumsiness.
Regarding the eight recollections (*aṣṭānusmṛti*): based upon the six recollections, one further adds the recollection of death and the recollection of inhalation and exhalation.
For those who possess the terror of destruction, it is taught that even at the initial stage of the mind, by practicing these six recollections, they may sweep away their terror.
Yearning for the fruit while practicing the cause, they request the protection of the three realities to guide them, so that their own person may become one with the Triple Gem.
One quickly attains its manifestation; therefore, one recollects the Triple Gem.

Regarding the statement that "the heavens have near fruits" and so forth: the immediate retribution (*puṣpavipāka*) is proximate in the heavens, while the distant result is the fruit of Great Nirvāṇa with no further rebirth (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Although this [proximate fruit] is near in the heavens, the heavens are not what is desired; therefore, one must look toward the distant goal. Furthermore, it is not permissible to be exclusively [focused on the heavens].
If one contemplates only the *paramārtha-devas*, it will again fail to be universal; therefore, one must contemplate them together.

As the Sūtra asks, "How does one practice the recollection of the Buddha?"—the practice of recollecting the Buddha possesses four intentions, the first of which is to cause the aspiration for Bodhi to be established.

First, it is for the sake of seeking the supreme object. Second, it is to cause those who aspire to the fruit to practice the cause; thus, one does not dwell on the fruit, but subsequently contemplates the cause so as to fulfill the practices for enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*).
Third, it is to cause them to understand according to reality that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-dual.

Fourth, it is so that the Buddhas may grant their protection, provide guidance, and bring about awakening for the sake of delivering sentient beings, enabling them to swiftly realize the virtues of a Buddha.
Therefore, there is no separate recollection of the Buddha.
Regarding the ten distinct titles: names such as Śākyamuni and Maitreya are specific designations, whereas the ten titles beginning with "Tathāgata" are general appellations.
Distinct titles are established because the manifested aspects must be differentiated; general appellations are established because their actual virtues are identical.

To summarize the aforementioned virtues: the World-Honored One summarizes the ten titles above; because he is fully endowed with these ten titles and is honored by the world, he is called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).

As the Sūtra says regarding the "Ten Powers" (*daśabala*): it means that by means of the Ten Powers he subdues the celestial Māras, and by means of the Four Fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) he overcomes the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), like a great lion.
"Title" (*hào*) refers to definitive exposition.
"Great Śramaṇa" refers to the ability to extinguish evil. "Great Brāhmaṇa" refers to the purity of all practices.
"Great Purity" refers to ultimate purity regarding the three obstacles and two deaths.
"Invincible" means that all virtues are perfected.
"One whose crown cannot be seen" means that he transcends all worthies and sages.
"Free from fear" means that he is eternally detached from the five fears. "Unstartled" means that nothing can cause him alarm or offense.
"Immovable" means that the mind is always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Solitary and without companion" means there is none equal to it.
"Self-awakened without a teacher" means clearly perceiving one's own mind through awakening that does not depend on another.
One of swift wisdom knows that the Dharma is steep and sharp, for they can know all dharmas in a single thought-moment.
One of great wisdom knows that the Dharma is profound and vast. One of keen wisdom possesses clear vision.
"Profound wisdom" refers to the depth of that which is known.
"Wisdom of liberation" is named as such because it is pure through having emerged from obstructions.
"Unshared wisdom" is so called because it rises far above others and is not shared with those who are inferior or base.
"Extensively universal wisdom" is so called because it benefits all beings with impartiality;
"ultimate wisdom" is so called because it reaches the final, perfect consummation; and "wisdom-treasure" is the summary of these qualities.
He is the elephant-king among men because of his great power of endurance;
he is the ox-king among men because his gait is even and his movements are worthy of observation;
he is the dragon-king among men because he raises the clouds of compassion and pours down the rain of the Great Dharma.
He is called a "hero among men" because his marks and signs are majestic and he is honored among men.
He is like a "lotus among men" and so forth because his nature is pure and cannot be defiled by the two types of death.
The "Teacher who Tames and Governs" is so called because his wisdom benefits beings and can transform their minds.
He is the "Great Donor" because he bestows the Dharma-wisdom upon others.

The preceding passages were all abbreviated; here, they are fully restored by explaining each of the seven virtues individually to elucidate the various qualities mentioned before, thereby providing both an extensive and an abbreviated treatment.
Because their meanings are equivalent, I shall now briefly explain the significance of these various names.

Regarding the scripture’s statement, “by knowing the various natures of sentient beings,” this was previously explained within the section on knowing the noble and the humble by way of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*).
Using this as verification for what preceded, one knows that what preceded was appropriate.
To understand according to suchness (*tathatā*) means that understanding in accordance with the principle is called "suchness.

To speak according to suchness means that speaking in accordance with the principle is called "coming" (*āgata*). To speak of what I have understood is called "suchness"; to understand what I have spoken is called "coming."

It is called "coming. The Sūtra states: "As for the four māras," it should rather say "all eight māras. Regarding the explanation based on the character *jiǎo* (foot): when pronounced with the level tone (*píngshēng*), the character *xíng* (to practice) means "fulfillment";

when pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), it means "exhaustion" (*pí*, with the phonetic *jiè*). Regarding the explanation based on the character *zú* (foot): when pronounced with the level tone, it means "satisfaction"; when pronounced with the departing tone, it means "affliction" (*bì*, with the phonetic *jiè*).

Regarding the "five aggregates" and so forth: the five aggregates and the like are the effect; the five worldly desires are one cause. Although there are six [categories] in the world, they do not transcend cause and effect.
Regarding those who open the way to severing delusions: one who has something to be severed is called a "Superior Being" (sopadhi-śeṣa);
one who has nothing left to be severed is called a "Supreme Being" (anuttara).
As for the "Deer-headed Man," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Formerly, the King of Vārāṇasī entered the mountains to hunt and saw two deer.
There were five hundred herds, each with its own leader; one was the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni and the other was the Bodhisattva Devadatta.
When the leader of the deer saw that the King was slaughtering his flock, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion and went straight before the King, kneeling and addressing him:
"For the sake of a minor matter, you have caused these deer to suffer death all at once. If they are intended for your meal, they should be assigned in turn."
The King approved of his words. Thereupon, the two lords each assigned the order of execution.
When it was Tissa’s turn, there was a doe among the herd who said to her lord, "It is my lot to die; however, I am pregnant. My offspring has not yet reached its time to die.
I beg you to grant me justice so that the living shall not be treated as the dead and the deceased may receive their due turn. The King grew angry and said, "Who does not cherish their own life?"
Next, the mother deer went there alone and thought to herself, "My king is merciless; he has unreasonably become enraged.

She then went to where the Bodhisattva deer-king was and reported the matter in detail. The Bodhisattva King said, "I alone shall take his place. He then personally delivered himself to the gates of the king's palace.
When the people saw him, they were astonished that he had come of his own accord and reported the matter to the king. The king, too, was surprised. The king—
The King asked, "Are the herds of deer all exhausted? The Deer King replied, "Great King, you are benevolent and compassionate; no one among your people commits offenses against me.
There is always an abundance of fodder, so there is no time of depletion. However, that mother deer returned and informed me. Out of pity for her, it would be improper for me not to act.
If I were to neglect her and fail to rescue her, I would be no different from wood or stone. [The King said: "This body..."

"In time, one will inevitably escape the calamity of death. To compassionately rescue others from suffering and calamity is a merit of immeasurable extent. If a person lacks compassion, how are they different from tigers and wolves?
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately rose from his seat and spoke in verse:
"I am truly a beast, though my name is 'Human-Headed. You, O Deer, though you are a beast, are named 'Deer-Headed. It is by reason that a person is a person."
To not define a person by their physical form is precisely the point at issue.

Regarding the *jāmbuka* (jackal), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, states: "For example, a jackal dwells among the trees in a forest, relying upon lions, tigers, leopards, and the like for its sustenance.
When there is a lack of meat and time passes in vain, it leaps over the city walls in the middle of the night."

He entered a person's house seeking meat but found none. He fled to hide and fell asleep, unaware that the night had passed. Terrified and at his wits' end, he first intended to rise and leave, fearing he would not escape;
yet, staying where he was, he feared the agony of death. He then feigned death, lying upon the ground. When people came and saw him, they [mistook him for a corpse].
One person said, "I need the jackal's ears," and immediately cut them off. The jackal thought to itself, "Though it is painful to have my ears cut off, at least my body remains.
Next, another person came and said, "I need its tail. It thought again, "This is but a minor matter to be cut.
Then another person said, "I need the jackal's teeth. The jackal thought to itself, "Those who take me are becoming more numerous; should they take my head as well..."
There was no way out. He rose from the ground and, exerting all his strength with supreme courage, opened [the path] and traversed the scriptures until he achieved self-deliverance.
The mind of the practitioner seeking liberation from suffering and hardship is likewise so. Not to practice when young is like losing one's ears;

not to practice when old is like losing one's tail; not to practice when ill is like losing one's teeth; how much more so when one reaches death, which is like losing one's head—this is the very proof of it.
Regarding the differences between the two: others say that in Sanskrit it is *bhagavān*, which here is translated as "World-Honored One" (*shìzūn*).
"One who has destroyed the afflictions" means one who has destroyed the afflictions to ultimate exhaustion.
"Merit" refers to being fully endowed with the fruit that accords with the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Skillful discernment" refers to spontaneously discerning the phenomena of the dharma-realm as real; it is the teaching that bestows the provisional, reveals the provisional, and manifests the real.
Regarding "a good reputation": it is when one is praised throughout every direction for all beings within the ten realms, causing those beings to enter the ultimate from the provisional;
only then is it called a "good sound. To merely preach the three teachings does not yet qualify as a "good" [reputation].
The Sūtra says, "Great Wisdom Giver": the Tathāgata benefits sentient beings by making giving his foremost practice.
The Sūtra says, "one who has vomited out the female organ": because he has long since destroyed the karma of a woman, it is said that he has "vomited" it out.
Regarding the "three further turnings" up to the point of "merit": it is for the sake of fulfilling merit. Giving with wisdom fulfills merit by destroying the karma of womanhood;
furthermore, because the fourth [turning] possesses great merit that is unsurpassed, it also belongs to merit.
The Sūtra states: "Elder" refers to a senior who possesses virtue; an "elder" is one with such qualities.
Regarding the fifty-four minds, each is explained in relation to the Buddha-mind. It is only when one is free from the minds of the nine lower realms that they constitute the cause of Buddhahood.
This refers to the absence of an agent who acts with a specific purpose; because the mind has already reached fulfillment, one abandons both extremes.
These two abide eternally in the Middle Way.
Regarding "unspecified through understanding," it is spontaneously specified. Regarding "unspecified as karmic retribution," it refers to the pure-unspecified (*śubha-avyākṛta*).
Regarding "one who does not seek retribution": the three causes are fully developed, spontaneously accords with the ultimate, and seeks no retribution within the nine realms.
As the Sūtra says, "one who has no mind of speech": if one knows that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, this is called "much learning."
"Having no fixed attachment" means having no mind that clings to permanence as fixed.
The Sūtra says that one who contemplates the Dharma possesses three intentions: first, to cause them to constantly contemplate the true path of practice without any other thoughts;
second, to cause sentient beings to attain the wondrous fruits of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa; third, to deliver sentient beings and establish them [in these fruits].

The shore of nirvāṇa; for it is the dwelling place where all Buddhas roam and reside. Furthermore, in the sūtras, every single phrase of the Dharma first presents the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the phenomenon, followed by its functional capacity (*kāritra*).

For example, [the passage] "That which is not form (*arūpa*) cuts off form" refers to the essential nature of the non-form dharma. "It can cause sentient beings to cut off form" refers to its functional capacity.
"That which is not karma" refers to the essential nature of the non-karma dharma. "It cuts off karma" refers to its functional capacity, which can cause sentient beings...

This refers to the severing of karma through birth. The remaining phrases follow this pattern. Within the text, the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are fully demonstrated by means of three categories of doctrinal gates (*dharmamukha*).
The Sūtra states: "That which the Buddhas have taught" refers to the teaching that expresses [the truth].

"Obtaining the fruit in the present" means that those who have attained perfect fulfillment constantly contemplate *nirvāṇa* from beginning to end while practicing the Path, without any change. This is contemplating the principle of cause and effect; it is both one and yet many.

Birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) carries the meaning of transcending and ascending through the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Even if many lifetimes elapse, because the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) does not change, it is called "attaining the fruit in the present.

The *Tripiṭaka* Bodhisattvas also, based on the aspect of unchanging contemplation and regarding the birth-body of parents within the realm of segmented existence (*prādeśika*), attain Buddhahood by severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*) through thirty-four moments of mind;
this is called attaining the fruit in the present. In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), from the seventh stage onward, they retain their afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten and sustain rebirth.

Although they take birth in various places, they form pure land affinities with sentient beings; by attaining perfect enlightenment within a body born of moisture, they are said to have attained the manifest fruit.

Those of other capacities still practice in stages, where each successive stage involves a shift in contemplation that may involve regression, such that it takes many kalpas for their cultivation to reach completion.
Therefore, it is not called "attaining the fruit in the present.
As for the Sūtra’s question, "How does one recollect the Saṃgha? the Sūtra contains three meanings:

first, to cause one to realize that the principle of the mind-nature is such that the teacher above and the disciple below are in harmonious accord, being non-dual and without distinction; second, to cause one to practice in accordance with the Dharma, thereby accomplishing the conduct of Bodhi.
Third, it is for the sake of delivering sentient beings by causing their minds to become pliant, equanimous, non-dual, and eternally unchanging, thereby realizing the state of a true *saṃgha*.
As the Sūtra says, "The Buddhas and the noble *saṃgha": those from the Buddhas downward are called the noble *saṃgha*, such as Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and others.
The Dharma-Buddha is not the Saṃgha; rather, it is by citing the Buddha that the characteristics of the Saṃgha are revealed.

The Sūtra says, "those who practice in accordance," which refers to the correspondence with the wisdom of destruction (prajñā), wherein the higher [truth] merges with the lower, achieving the function of perfect harmony.

The Sūtra says that "vast, universal, and boundless" refers to being able to bring sentient beings of the nine realms to merit and cause them to enter the ultimate perfection; only then is it called the "superior field.

That "the perfect Saṃgha is the upright Dharma" means that mindfulness of the Saṃgha is the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Dharma is the Saṃgha; only then is it called "upright. [End of] previous section.
The monks of the three teachings are circuitous and biased; they cannot be called upright. What, then, is meant by "recalling the precepts"?

Such recollection may possess three aspects: first, to realize the nature of the dharma of the precepts; second, to serve as the cause for purifying the buddha-land in order to deliver sentient beings;
and third, to seek the unsurpassed state of a bodhisattva. Because one possesses these three intentions, it is necessary to practice this recollection.
Regarding the precepts:

when the sutras state that "the precepts are unbroken" and so forth, this clarifies that the bodhisattva takes the two hundred and fifty precepts of the Hīnayāna and, by means of the mind of the Great Nirvāṇa, cultivates each and every one of them as the dharma-nature of the dharma-realm; thus they constitute the bodhisattva discipline.
Thus it is said, "without confusion," and so forth.

Regarding the sūtra’s statement, "skillfully cultivating expedient means" and so forth: the Buddhas have skillfully cultivated these until their fruits are already perfected, while Bodhisattvas skillfully cultivate them so that the fruits may be swiftly fulfilled; therefore, they are praised.
Some claim that what is called "unmanifest precept" (*avijñapti-śīla*) refers to the unmanifest precepts of the Hīnayāna; thus they cite the three explanations from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
As for the statement that there is no such thing as "unmanifest matter," the *Mahāsāṃghika* clarifies that the unmanifest precept takes the mind alone as its essential substance (*śīla-tattva*).
That form which is not characterized by resistance does not belong to the body nor to the mind; it is invisible and non-obstructive form, which constitutes the unmanifest (avijñapti).
It is merely a conventional form arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions.

The Dharmaguptaka school holds that the essence [of the precepts] consists of that which is neither matter (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), and thus it is subsumed under the fourteen factors dissociated from thought (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

This accords with the view of the Saṃmitīyas. However, this present sutra takes the nature of the mind as the essence of the precepts; therefore, it says that because the mind is free from delusion, the precepts are also free from delusion.
Since they are neither mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*) nor material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), the preceding passage is cited to prove that they are neither of these two categories.
The Sūtra says, "Like the great earth," and so forth. Just as the great earth can give birth to all things, so too can the precepts give rise to the dharmas that resolve the three types of disputes.
A ship can carry one across; a necklace can adorn; a noble clan is honored among men; the great ocean contains many precious jewels;
lye can remove impurities; a house can provide universal shelter; a sword can cut through everything; and a bridge can span across all.
"Deliverance. A skilled physician treats them everywhere; wondrous medicines are applied everywhere," and so forth.
The Sūtra says that those who have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* know their Buddha-nature and temporarily take the small fruit to rest the two vehicles.
Therefore it says, "I too have a share. As for the fivefold mindfulness of giving, it is simply the mindfulness of relinquishment. There are three great meanings: first, for... [text ends]
1. By bestowing [the gift] upon the Dharma-realm, one accomplishes the supreme dāna. 2. By universally gathering sentient beings through giving, one creates the conditions for a pure land;

for if one does not practice wise giving, one cannot adorn the fourfold assembly. 3. By taking giving as the cause for bodhi and nirvāṇa, one causes the fruits of bodhi and nirvāṇa to be swiftly fulfilled.
The Sūtra says that those who practice closely are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the Buddhas have already perfected their cultivation, while the Bodhisattvas are currently completing it.
Regarding the "four groups" mentioned in the Sūtra, there are two lay and two ordained groups; alternatively, they consist of devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās.
The Sūtra states that "that which can eliminate present afflictions" refers to the practice of giving, which destroys the mind of present stinginess and greed;
this is called destroying present afflictions. As for the thorough severance of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is through wisdom that they can be cut off.
Regarding the *Saṃpuṣpita* (Miscellaneous Flowers): it extensively clarifies how the partial and the perfect encompass all causes and effects;

thus, it is called "miscellaneous goodness. Regarding the "Recollection of Devas" (*devānusmṛti*), there are three intentions: first, to take the various devas as the object of contemplation; second, to recollect the devas so that one may share in their status, thinking, "I too am the same as them";
and third, by contemplating the various devas, to perceive the *paramārtha-deva* (the ultimate deva). Furthermore...
With compassionate thought, one reflects that the various devas of the three realms do not know impermanence and do not perceive the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).

Therefore, this illuminating reflection is called "recollection of the heavens" (*devānusmṛti*). Furthermore, one recollects the heaven of the Buddha-nature, which is the great, true, and ultimate principle;
for this reason, it differs from others who merely recollect the heavens of future fruition.

Regarding the establishment of distinctions according to meaning: although the name "heaven" (*deva*) is one, the various heavens of the three realms and the Heaven of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*) are established;
hence it is so said.
Regarding "decline due to lack of propagation": because there are wicked bhikṣus and a degenerate age, the twelve divisions of the Great [Dharma] [are diminished].

As for the statement that it "does not equal Nirvana," there is indeed this meaning. Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the various sections [of the teachings] were still characterized by a mixture of provisional and ultimate meanings; therefore, they did not equal it.

Regarding why it is superior because it accords with the capacities of those present: first, while a Buddha is in the world, he reveals the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional means, thereby benefiting sentient beings according to their specific capacities; thus, it is superior. Second...

This is because, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were those who realized that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding; for such individuals, both the precepts and the vehicle were urgent, and they were of a disposition capable of manifesting the ultimate through the provisional.

Therefore, they are superior. As for the claim that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is not necessarily found among the twelve divisions of the canon, establishing it as such merely makes it superior to the twelve divisions of the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Section on the Ears.
Regarding the scripture’s statement that “the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, etc.”:

this teaching elucidates the Three Jewels as a single essence (*eka-rasa*) and the Bodhisattvas who practice according to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and proceed toward the ultimate goal; for this reason, all are termed “inconceivable” (*acintya*).
The Sūtra asks: "For what reason is it further said that a bodhisattva is inconceivable? It may be granted that a bodhisattva is a human being;
yet in what way is there anything inconceivable about them?"

Regarding those matters of the human world that are entirely unfathomable: just as people cannot fathom ghosts and spirits, even those who are superior among men cannot fathom the affairs of those below them; how could this not be called inconceivable?
"That which cannot be contemplated as one, two, or three" means that it cannot be contemplated as a single one, a single two, or a single three.

It must be taught by means of objects (*viṣaya*): for those of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha*), conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) must first be aroused by conventional objects before their wisdom can become clear; therefore, it is called "teaching by means of objects."
"Not arising from the realm of persons" means that the dharma of the non-duality of the perfect and eternal realm and wisdom is inherently present from the beginning;
it does not come into existence only through its being elicited by the persons of the Two Vehicles or by distinct mundane objects. Therefore, it is said to "not arise from the realm of persons."

That which is identical to the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is as follows: the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) of birth and death are the objects for downward transformation through these two [practices], while *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi* are the fruits sought upward;
therefore, it is identical in intent to the arousal of the mind.
Those of the two vehicles who know only the limited portion of the segmented [existence] perceive only the impermanence, arising, and ceasing of the segmented;
they do not see that it is like an illusion or a transformation, nor do they see the nature of the self.

Regarding "the conventional is itself the true and the middle": the conventional refers to the three thousand [worlds]. Since the three thousand are themselves the true and the middle, it is said that one does not weary of them.
"The middle is itself the true and the conventional" is called "not departing. Benefiting sentient beings is what is termed "not departing."
"Peace of mind and identical intent" means that because the three wisdoms accord with the three truths, they are identical in meaning to the sense of "peace of mind.
"Like the bliss of nirvana" refers to the bliss of Great Nirvana.

Regarding the obstacles to the three truths: the three delusions and two deaths obstruct the three truths. Why is this? If one is deluded regarding bodhi and nirvana, it is called "obstruction" (sai-da);
yet, that birth-and-death is itself nirvana and that affliction is itself bodhi—this is called "pervasion" (tsū). Therefore, it is said that they are identical.
It is also like the Great Compassionate One. This is identical in intent to the analogy of the dwelling provided for those who have resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment]:
"Now these three realms are all mine; the sentient beings therein are all my children. Furthermore, they come when conditions arise and depart when conditions cease.
Although there is coming and going, it does not transcend the Dharma-realm; therefore, by means of the Middle Way, it is called "returning."

Regarding the practitioner of the three truths: they transform themselves and others by uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness, taking compassion as their foundation; thus it is called "practice. Regarding the realization of the three truths:
the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are themselves the bodhisattva path; therefore, this is identical to the "concordant realization" (*sābhāsagati*).
Regarding the "stages of the three truths," this refers to the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya*) within contemplative practice.

As for "the immeasurable within the one": "one" refers to a single thought-moment; "immeasurable" refers to the three thousand [realms]. These three thousand are themselves emptiness and themselves the middle.
Therefore, it is said that "within the immeasurable, there is one and so forth.

Regarding the teaching of the three truths, this refers to the teaching of the dual flow. What is meant by "establishing the provisional based upon the real"? It is that the permanent is itself impermanent.
This serves to remedy the inversion of regarding the impermanent as permanent; by opening up the provisional to reveal the real, it shows that the impermanent is itself the permanent.
Thus, because it is not a false view regarding impermanence and so forth, one realizes permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, its meaning is identical to that of "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*).

Regarding "the womb cannot produce": it means that for a person at a stage of similarity, the womb of the parents cannot produce [them], because they have attained the sovereign function corresponding to that stage.
As for the retribution of the three truths, it refers to the retribution of the three truths in their state of similarity. The ninth and twelfth passages are identical in meaning.
Regarding "intention": as for "speaking" and "silence," silence is obstruction while speaking is penetration.
Regarding the three truths and the three karmas of body, speech, and mind: the destruction of these three karmas through the three truths is identical to the universal destruction [of delusions].

The Sūtra states, "Therefore, this wisdom," and so forth. That which is entirely subject to arising and ceasing is [conventional] wisdom; it is called "incapable of distancing itself," meaning there is neither subject nor object.
One never says, "I have destroyed the afflictions," because one has realized that the essence of the three delusions is entirely the Dharma-nature. Therefore, it says "never."
It is not said that they are destroyed. This refers to the detachment from the craving for similar dharmas (*sādṛśya-dharma-tṛṣṇā*).
"Those who have not yet entered and abided" refers precisely to those who are similar [to those who have entered] but have not yet entered the stage of the first dwelling (*prathamavihāra*).
Regarding the phrase "the former ceases and the latter arises," this is the ancient masters' interpretation of the passage concerning "different arising and different ceasing."
Furthermore, regarding those who disparage wisdom: they claim their own goodness, saying, "I act on behalf of the Bodhisattvas," yet this is not so.
Ultimately, they do not harbor the thought, "I possess wisdom capable of destroying delusions. Therefore, it is said that there is nothing to rectify or replace.

Furthermore, from "arising" down to "inferior," it explains that there is neither capacity nor object. Again, from "if arising were permanent" downward, it further refutes the ancient objections regarding the necessity of existence:
if there must be existence, is this existence existent or is it non-existent?
Regarding the "double objection": if this sutra exists, then the five practices must exist; since the five practices exist, how can they subsequently be extinguished and disappear?
Regarding the "general explanation": answering by way of many general points across various contexts is termed a "general explanation."

This refers to "original existence. When the Buddha was in the world, the Dharma did not perish; this is called "original existence. When the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, it is called "present non-existence.

This is precisely extinction within non-extinction. Furthermore, in the past, the Hīnayāna held that what perishes is called "original non-existence," whereas now, the Mahāyāna maintains that in reality there is no extinction, which is called "present existence.
It is illogical for a dharma to exist throughout the three periods of time; thus, it is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished. Furthermore, this is the principle.

In reality, there is no arising or ceasing because they arise through conditions. Because it is the catalyst for attaining the Way, one proclaims cessation; thus, it is said that while there is no cessation, there is cessation.
The Sūtra states: "External dharmas" refers to the Dharma of teaching; "internal dharmas" refers to the Dharma of principle.
Regarding the statement in the sutra that "the heavens have no cessation of realms," these heavens refer to the celestial stages of the sages of the various teachings.
As for "now the Buddha distinguishes in response," this means the Buddha is now distinguishing [the truth] in response to Kāśyapa.
As for the sūtra’s statement that “the faculties are not non-existent,” this refers to the five faculties such as faith being non-existent [in their absence].
The passage beginning with “If the Buddha first descended” clarifies the initial enlightenment as perceived by those of lesser capacity at the Deer Park;
furthermore, the passage beginning with “Next, good son” clarifies the initial enlightenment as perceived by those of great capacity at the Place of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa).

Regarding the phrase "first, the interpretation of the meaning" (*arthaviniścaya*), if one were to explain it: in all cases, one must state that although there may be an interpreter of the meaning, if there is no donor (*dānapati*), it cannot be obtained;
although there may be a donor, if it is done for profit, it cannot be obtained; although it is not for profit, if strife arises, it cannot be obtained;

although strife does not arise, if faults are spoken of, it cannot be obtained; and although faults are not spoken of, if various [unauthorized] explanations are given, it cannot be obtained. This is precisely the sign of the extinction of the Dharma.

Regarding the sixth type, those who speak in various ways: they fail to comprehend the diverse capacities of their listeners and instead extensively cite divergent doctrines. Unable to harmonize these views, they engage in mutual refutation and affirmation;
this is like the contemporary lecturers on the Vinaya, who merely cite at length the various schools without being able to synthesize them, resulting only in disputes.
This is a sign that the Dharma and its methods are in a state of decline.

Regarding the scriptural passage stating, "Some say there is a self (*ātman*), etc.": for instance, the Vātsīputrīya school asserts that there is a self, whereas other schools assert that there is no self.

Regarding the statement, "Some say there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), etc.": the Sarvāstivāda school asserts that there is an intermediate state, while the Mahāsāṃghika school asserts that there is not.

Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the claim that "some say there are three time periods" and so forth: the Sarvāstivādins maintain that the three time periods exist, whereas the Ekavyavahārikas maintain that the three time periods do not exist.
Regarding the phrase "some say all exists" and so forth: the Sarvāstivādins maintain that all exists;
the Ekavyāvahārikas maintain that all does not exist.

Regarding those who claim that sentient beings have a beginning and so forth: the Mahīśāsaka school asserts that they have both a beginning and an end, while the Sautrāntika masters assert that they are without beginning and without end.

Regarding those who claim that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth: the Mahāsāṃghika and Mahīśāsaka schools assert that they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for the remaining schools, some assert that these are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding those who claim that the Tathāgata underwent the practice of illness and suffering, the Sarvāstivādins say he was ill and practiced asceticism for sixty years,
whereas the Mahāsāṃghikas say he did not.
Some say that the Tathāgata did not permit [the use of] ten kinds [of items] for bhikṣus, as explained in the "Chapter on the Four Marks" (Caturlakṣaṇavarga).
Others say that he permitted nothing at all; this is the teaching of the Mahīśāsaka school.
The Sūtra says: "The world is empty. Because the Buddha would soon enter nirvāṇa and Kāśyapa did not further inquire of him, he repeated the words: "The world is empty! The world is empty!"

Regarding "extinguished yet not extinguished": this indicates arising and indicates extinction; both serve to uproot [delusions] and lead [beings] toward the Perfect [Teaching], thereby performing great benefit.

The passage on "pure purity" concludes the text; the passage on "neither pure nor impure" is uniquely marvelous. Within the passage on "pure purity," it is the explanation of the "double negation" that constitutes this point.

In the "Chapter on the Holy Life" (Brahmacarya-varga), King Ajātaśatru is a true evildoer. One must truly employ skillful means to lead him, using the provisional to guide toward the real; thus, both intentions are simultaneously fulfilled.
As for Nandi, he was the son of Sūdra, appearing as one who had committed various offenses.

Regarding the fact that Emperor Wu of Liang did not see [the scripture], Wang Yi said: "Since this concerns the Brahma-conduct (brahmacarya), it should only expound the dharmas for generating purity and goodness;
it should not expound the dharmas of heterodoxy and evil. This proves it is a spurious work."
The Sūtra says "the charioteer," meaning one who advances and controls.

The Sūtra says "the mind feels remorseful heat"; this refers to when the obstacles to desire have been removed and the great capacity for awakening has been activated. At the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the obstacles were not yet deep and the capacity had not yet been activated.
"The mother anoints with medicine" means that the mother anoints him with worldly medicine; though she anoints him, it does not cause him harm or destruction.
"The evil conditions" refers to these six ministers, who are the conditions for extinguishing evil and distancing oneself from it.
However, among the teachings of the six ministers, there are points that accord with the Buddha-dharma. There are also those who calculate the workings of karma;

although their words may be similar, they essentially claim that killing is without sin and without retribution. As for the extensive textual passages [of this kind], these were composed by those of expedient means to demonstrate [the truth] to future generations.
In order to cause people to recognize the characteristics of the Dharma, this teaching was given: "Nirvana is like an antidote to poison.
When good people hear of the Great Nirvana, they are able to diminish their evil; thus it is called "ambrosia" (amṛta).
When evil people hear the wholesome Dharma, they instead give rise to even more evil; thus it is called "poison. Now, King Ajātaśatru is likewise; although he has been exhorted by the wicked...
To not follow evil is what is called "ambrosia" (*amṛta*).
Regarding "morning-white" (*zhāobái*): it is called "morning-white" because one becomes white in the morning.
As for the passage in the Sūtra concerning Pūraṇa and others, Kumārajīva said: "Kāśyapa's mother was of the Pūraṇa clan; 'mother' is her family name. This is the calculation.
"All dharmas are like empty space, neither arising nor ceasing. Zhaò said: "According to this person, all dharmas are annihilated like space;
there is no way of ruler and subject, father and son, loyalty and filial piety."
Regarding the phrase "inferior karma" in the Sūtra: inferior karma refers to actions performed with an inferior mind; when created with a superior mind, they constitute superior karma.
Regarding "Makkhali" and so forth: Kumārajīva stated that "Makkhali" is the name and "Gosāla" is the mother's surname; he [Makkhali] maintained that sentient beings...

"Sin and merit have no causes or conditions. Sengzhao says: "As for those who calculate regarding sentient beings, they hold that suffering and pleasure do not arise from causes and conditions, but occur spontaneously.
Regarding "Saṃjaya and others," Kumārajīva says: "Saṃjaya is a name; [the others are] Vairāṭīputra and so forth. This is according to the *Jiyao jing* (Sūtra on the Essentials)."
Birth and death continue through incalculable kalpas; yet, by proceeding spontaneously, one naturally reaches the end of suffering. Zao said: "In calculating the Way, there is no need for seeking.
It is like a ball of thread unwinding on a high mountain—it stops when the thread is exhausted. What need is there for seeking?

The present sutra states that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings arise from causes in previous lives; there is no cause in the present, and the future fruit is not identical to the waves [of the present].
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that "one immediately attains liberation," this refers to reckoning the first dhyāna and so forth as liberation.
As for Ajita and the others, Kumārajīva said: "Ajita" consists of the characters *A-ji-duo*; "Kambala" refers to coarse clothing.
They regard what is not a cause as a cause, such as the coarse practices of plucking out their hair or fumigating their noses with smoke; they take these various ascetic penances to be the path.
Zhaò said: "Through ascetic penance in this present life, one attains eternal bliss in future lives."
Regarding "Kātyāyana" and so forth: Kumārajīva said, "This is the name of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). That person manifests himself according to circumstances;
if someone asks whether something exists, he answers 'it exists,' and it is the same for 'non-existence' and so on. Sengzhao said, "Kātyāyana is his clan name; the rest are his given names."
They reckon that all phenomena are both existent and non-existent.
As for the scripture’s statement regarding "whether internal or external," they reckon that the waters of the Ganges can extinguish the two ailments of body and mind.
Regarding "Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and others": *Nigaṇṭha* is his clan name, while *Nāta* is his mother's name; they reckon [in terms of] transgressions and merits, suffering and pleasure.
All [consequences] stem from previous lives and must inevitably be repaid; they are not like the present [life], for according to their reckoning, there is neither cultivation nor the Way.
After eighty thousand kalpas, one will naturally attain liberation. These six teachers are all naked and claim to be omniscient beings;
their reckonings do not go beyond such views as whether the effect exists within the cause or does not exist within the cause.

"Opening for those who go against [the Way]" means to reveal and instruct them. This refers to provisionally demonstrating skillful means to lead those who are inclined toward evil toward the ultimate reality.
"Solidly reviving" means that those with chronic illnesses who should have died are treated and all are cured; this is termed "solidly reviving."
As for the scripture’s question, "Great King, do you sleep in peace?", it was asked because [the Buddha] knew that the king could not sleep in peace;
wishing to awaken the king and let him know of the person who possesses the foremost peaceful sleep, he thus made this inquiry.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "The body is free from all evils," the King’s thought was: "I am possessed of the four transgressions of body and speech, and my mind is full of doubt;
because of this, my body and mind are tormented by feverish distress. How can I obtain peaceful sleep?"
Regarding the bodhisattva who attains peaceful sleep, there is only one sentence in the sutra that is exclusively for the bodhisattva, which states: "For the sake of all sentient beings.
All other sentences pertain to the cessation of evil.

As the Sūtra says regarding "if it is for oneself" and so forth: "If I now act for my own sake—that is, for the peace of my own body and out of desire for palace ladies and female musicians—by what means can I attain peaceful sleep?"
It does not mean that [the Prince of the Eastern Palace] himself; for as long as the Crown Prince has not succeeded to the throne, the myriad people cannot attain peace and security.
Furthermore, while the successor has not yet been established, one cannot sleep in peace—not because one cannot sleep in peace during the time of being the Prince of the Eastern Palace.
If one follows the preceding explanation according to the *Shu* (Commentary), it is correct; if one interprets the *Jing* (Sutra) text, the latter explanation is consistent.

Regarding the passage "looking up from below": since the lower section lacks the five virtues and the text does not mention associating with virtuous friends, one can verify that the upper section possesses these five virtues.
Thus, the reason for declining to speak is that, out of humility, he does not claim himself to be the king's virtuous friend.
The Sūtra says that "white dharmas" (śukla-dharma) refer to attaining goodness from evil—that is, committing a transgression is a black dharma, whereas deriving good from it is called a white dharma.
The Sūtra also says that there are parents and so forth; those who lack a sense of shame do not see the existence of parents and so forth.
Your Majesty now speaks of their existence because you possess a sense of shame. Why do you not go quickly to the presence of the Buddha?
The Sūtra says: "The evil wealthy one. When the king previously committed offenses, he was called the evil wealthy one; that the king now feels shame and remorse is the wealth of a virtuous person.
Regarding "speaking of one's transgressions to others": to reveal them is the expedient means of repentance (*pratideśanā*).
"Because it was not yet determined" means that the king was not yet willing to acknowledge [the truth] immediately.
Regarding the "kāmalā disease" mentioned in the sutra, this refers to leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).

As for the initial presentation of the skilled physician, the text contains two intended meanings: first, praising his own practice; from "O Virtuous One" (*bhadanta*) onwards, praising his benefit for others.
The first section also has two parts: first, praising the virtue of abandonment; second, from "possessing the ten powers" onwards, praising the virtue of wisdom.
Regarding the first point, "awakening without a teacher," this refers to the Mahāyāna awakening without a teacher, which differs from that of the Hīnayāna.

Next, from "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*) downward, there is the praise of altruism, which also has two parts: first, the praise of the altruistic mind; second, from "Rejoicing" (*anumodana*) downward, the praise of altruistic practice.

Within these practices, both physical and verbal actions are included. For example, the praise of the Buddha’s physical practice is like a calf following its mother; next follows the verbal action (*vākkarman*).
Regarding "knowing the proper time": it refers to being skillfully adept at discerning the conditions and opportunities for bestowing medicine and so forth.

"Truthful speech" means being free from false or deceptive words. "Pure speech" means being free from impure speech. "Sublime speech" means being free from coarse and harsh language. "Meaningful speech" means being free from speech that lacks purpose or benefit.
"Discourse on the Dharma" (*dharmavāda*) means being free from discourse that is not the Dharma. "Single discourse" (*ekavāda*) means that one's speech is non-dual.

Furthermore, "truthful speech" (*satyavāda*) and "pure speech" (*viśuddhavāda*) clarify the absence of false speech. "Exquisite speech" (*praṇītavāda*) clarifies the absence of harsh speech. "Meaningful speech" (*arthavāda*) and "Dharma-discourse" (*dharmavāda*) clarify the absence of frivolous speech;
speech that benefits others is called meaningful speech, while speech that accords with the Dharma is called Dharma-discourse. "Single discourse" clarifies the absence of divisive speech.
The Sūtra says: "If you cannot reach this place, I request that Your Majesty do not harbor doubts.
The Sūtra further states: "Even if there are those of the Two Vehicles among the assembly of Bodhisattvas who reach here, they all know the eternally abiding Buddha-nature;
for this reason, they are all called the assembly of Bodhisattvas."

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says "whether existent or non-existent," etc., this indicates that [the Buddha] knew the King possessed the faculties for the two truths, three truths, and so forth;

if he hears this Dharma, he will be able to cure the ailments of his own body and mind. Furthermore, it is explained as the two truths, which is to say that the three truths are subsumed into the two truths:

"existence" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), and "non-being" refers to nirvāṇa; "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*) refers to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), and "without-outflows" (*anāsrava*)...

This is the truth of cessation and the truth of the path; that is to say, the conditioned and untainted [factors] complete these four truths. These characteristics are equivalent to the two truths and so forth.
As for the eleven kinds of form, they refer to the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*).
Regarding "form is not form, nor is it non-form": others say this refers to the dharma of "acquisition" (*prāpti*) among the fourteen dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
As for the fourteen kinds of form, they refer to the five sense faculties, the five sense objects, and the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind.
As for the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): if one establishes a Middle Way as something distinct from form and mind and speaks of it in this way, it merely constitutes conventional truth.

Why? Because although it is said that the Middle Way has no substance since both extremes are abandoned, one further posits that which abandons and that which is abandoned; thus, it is called conventional truth.
"Self-inflicted and self-received" means that when one personally practices the breaking of the provisional to enter the empty, this is called "self-received.
"Self-inflicted and received by another" refers to the Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas who emerge from the provisional to manifest as earth, water, fire, and wind,
as well as providing the primary retribution and administering medicine, thereby bestowing various texts for the sake of others' enjoyment.
The pattern of the text is such that all phrases within the sūtra are explained by means of the three truths. If it is a vehicle, it is the vehicle of the ultimate truth;
if it is not a vehicle, it is the vehicle of the mundane truth of humans and devas.
To "disparage the present" does not mean to disparage King Ajātaśatru.
As for the passage in the sutra that says, "He replied, 'Kauśika,' and so forth," the Buddha answered him by following the sequence from the end [of his inquiry].
Regarding the phrase in the sutra, "arising from doubt," it is because Kauśika originally harbored doubts concerning his own life.
Therefore, it is said that "those born from doubt" are indeed as taught by the Buddha.
When the sutra says "Mahāmaudgalyāyana," this cites the disciple to manifest the teacher.
When the sutra says "Great King, even animals see the Buddha," this cites a lower class of beings to illustrate the human race.

The Sūtra says: "Great King, when the World-Honored One had not yet attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi... This cites his causal practices to illustrate that the power of his resultant virtues is likewise great.
The Sūtra says: "Great King, there was a wilderness ghost... This reveals the Buddha’s compassion that universally delivers all beings.
The Sūtra says, "Even the disciples of the Tathāgata possess such qualities as these. This cites the disciples to illustrate the Master by way of comparison.
The Sūtra says, "I pray that you will reflect well upon this. Regarding the thirteen matters mentioned above, I pray that Your Majesty will carefully reflect upon them;
they shall certainly not be false.
The Sūtra states that it is "judged as appropriate for the wise" to preach the Dharma to women who are extremely wicked and lewd. Furthermore, "judged" (pan) means "half.
It refers to obtaining a mate and uniting with them, rather than [merely] experiencing the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

The *Brahmacarya-varga* (Chapter on the Holy Life), in its fifth sutra, states: "I shall now [remain] until I abide in the world. This has two aspects: first, it applies generally to all who do not yet know that he abides eternally;
second, it specifically concerns the King, who does not yet know that he abides eternally. The reason for abiding in the world is to cause the extinction of evil and the arising of good.

Regarding the assembly at the Twin Trees: the fifty-two groups have already heard that [the Buddha] is eternal; they know extinction as non-extinction, and the World-Honored One has eternally known this.
Therefore, it is necessary to speak of his "abiding."
The esoteric words of the Tathāgata are: first, for King Ajātaśatru who committed the parricidal offense; second, for all those who have committed the five heinous crimes;
third, for all sentient beings of the conditioned realm; fourth, for those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature; fifth, for the assembly led by Ānanda and Kāśyapa;
sixth, for those who, due to being possessed of afflictions, do not see the Buddha-nature; and seventh, for the ladies of the royal harem.

The assembly is entirely for the purpose of extinguishing evil and generating roots of goodness so that they may see the Buddha-nature; thus, the proclamation of remaining in the world and the proclamation of entering extinction are likewise so.
Because this is not something known by Kāśyapa and others, it is called "esoteric speech."

Regarding the statement that "the sūtras are also not fixed": my current intention is that one must refer to those of the Perfect Teaching (yuan) from the first stage (chuzhu) upward to be designated as "unconditioned sentient beings" (wéi zhòngshēng).

Furthermore, generally speaking, those from the stage of "name-only" (míngzì) upward who have heard the teaching of eternal abiding—even up to those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (děngjué)—who hear this name are unconditioned sentient beings.

Those in the previous two teachings who have not yet received the Perfect and Eternal [teaching] all belong to the conditioned (yǒuwéi). As for the Separate Teaching (bié), their knowledge of the Middle Way is for the time being the same [as the previous].
[This] is a comprehensive inclusion. If one examines the essential nature [of these states], they are all alike conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) prior to the stages [of the Bodhisattva].

Regarding "deep and shallow" or "distant and near," this refutes the various former masters who definitively judge the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) based on the fixed positions of the stages; according to them, the *vipaśyanā* stage is "distant."
Those who have now resolved [to attain enlightenment] are near [to it]. It cannot be definitively established that this has been accomplished.

The Sūtra says, "By means of the eight worldly dharmas," which refers to the eight winds (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*). Before the King had resolved his mind, he was constantly defiled by these eight dharmas. What are they?
The four unfavorable conditions for killing his father-king and the four favorable conditions for coveting the royal throne and worldly pleasures. Furthermore,
Following afflictions is contrary to the Buddha-nature. Furthermore, because one is defiled by the eight worldly dharmas, transgressions are not extinguished and wholesome qualities do not arise.

If one can resolve to generate the aspiration for enlightenment and perceive the Buddha-nature, then transgressions will be extinguished and wholesome qualities will arise. Moreover, the eight heterodoxies constitute the eight worldly dharmas.
Regarding the concluding praise: having observed that the preceding six stages are all words of intentional meaning (*saṃdhābhāṣya*), he offers this praise for the four inconceivable stages.
As for the first, "governing the body": because the mind is not at peace when the body is not at peace, one first governs the body in order to bring peace to the mind.
The four preceding sections discussing "light" clarify the functional efficacy of the light;
the final section explaining "Moon-Love" (Candrakānta) distinguishes the essential nature of that light. Furthermore, Jīvaka recognized the samādhi into which the Buddha had entered.
It was evident that he was no ordinary man.
When the Sūtra asks, "Whose light is this? the King’s thought was: "This must be the light of insentient things such as the moon in the heavens;
it should be the light of a human being. This is why he raised the question.
