The Sūtra states that "this light has no root. "Root" (mūla) is defined by the sense of being able to produce [something]. Since the Middle Way Dharmadhātu lacks both producer and produced, it is called "rootless.

The Sūtra further states that it is "neither hot nor cold," meaning it transforms the king’s body so that he may attain refreshing coolness; however, the text of the Sūtra clearly elucidates the Middle Way.

Regarding "radiance," each instance is explained by means of the double negation of the two extremes: "not permanent" refers to the extreme of existence (*bhava*), and "not ceasing" refers to the extreme of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The remaining phrases are to be understood accordingly.
The Sūtra states that it is "truly ineffable," because light is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which cannot be described or perceived.

Regarding the passage from the Sūtra beginning with "By what causes and conditions... up to "light": the King’s intention in asking this question was whether this emission of light serves to extinguish his sins or not.
Regarding "advancing or retreating": retreating refers to the six destinies; advancing refers to Bodhisattvas at the six stages (*ṣaḍvihāra*).
As for the "seven expedient means" (*saptopāya*): the two vehicles of the two teachings constitute two; the three types of Bodhisattvas, together with humans and devas, constitute seven.

Regarding those among the seven sons who give rise to rebellion: now, within the seven stages of expedient means, if there are those with perfect capacities whose faculties are awakened, I immediately respond to them, causing evil to be extinguished and goodness to arise, so that they may perceive the Buddha-nature and abide in Great Nirvana; this is called [responding to] the sick son.
The mind thus becomes biased and heavy, differing from the judgments of the ancients.
One who truly understands the "sixth stage" (ṣaṣṭhī bhūmiḥ) should be one who corresponds to the sixth of the ten dwellings (*daśavihāra*) within the distinct [path of] dwellings.
One who understands the "sixth mind" refers to the sixth mind within the distinct ten faiths (*daśaśraddhā*).

Regarding the six points as they appear in the text: first, the analogy of blooming and being bright represents the arousal of the bodhicitta. Second, the ability to cause all those on the road [to see] represents practice (*caryā*).
This constitutes the pair of arousing the mind and cultivating practice. Next is the pair of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*):

gradual increase represents the virtue of wisdom, while decrease represents the virtue of abandonment. Third is the pair of extinguishing evil and generating good: removing the affliction of greed represents the extinguishing of evil.
"The taste of ambrosia gives rise to goodness;
it extinguishes the transgressions of the mind. From this point downward, each question and answer reveals the manner in which the Tathāgata responds in secret to benefit sentient beings.
Furthermore, in each question and answer, the icchantika is compared to King Ajātaśatru, so that the king may [attain] liberation limb by limb.
He is superior to the icchantika because the King possesses the five virtues and is capable of generating the resolve for enlightenment.
Jīvaka’s intention was this: "In the three periods of time, one may search for even the slightest bit of goodness in an icchantika and never find it;

yet the Buddha still feels compassion for them and does not abandon them through his hidden response (*mṛtyu-pratibhāsa*). How much more so for a king who now possesses the five virtues—why does he not quickly see the Buddha to have his mind-disease treated?"

Regarding the icchantika who has severed the roots of goodness: they have severed past goodness and, based on the present, lack goodness; since there is also none in the future, the goodness of the three periods of time is thereby rendered entirely extinct.
As for those whose faculties and conditions respond to the Buddha: they are established as having the conditions that respond to the Buddha.
Regarding those icchantikas who possess grave evil: on top of their manifest evil, they further deny the existence of cause and effect; this is what is called "grave evil.
As for the phrase "severing all present and future goodness": while it is true that future goodness cannot actually be severed, one speaks of "severing the future" based on its current absence.
Regarding "slight good from the past": because the five precepts observed in the past induce the present retribution-body, it is called "slight good.

Regarding "discarding one and taking one": this refers to seeking principle through the mind—turning away from existence toward non-existence; turning away from non-existence toward both; and likewise turning away from both toward the dual.

It is not merely turning away from the single to enter [the other]; rather, it fully turns away and fully enters, repeatedly turning away and repeatedly entering. That which transcends words is termed "discarding" (śeṣa).
"Taking one and rejecting the other. Furthermore, they cling to existence and thus destroy non-existence, or cling to non-existence and thus destroy existence, and so forth.
The analogy of the high mountain refers to those who have lost their precepts; just as a mountain can produce all things, so too the precepts are the foundation of all virtues.
Once the precepts are lost, all virtues perish together.

The trees are a metaphor for those who have lost their meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Just as trees depend upon mountains, so too does meditative concentration arise based upon ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Furthermore, "dhyāna" (meditation) is called a "branching forest," and the tree is used as a simile for this.

Regarding the "four vehicles": the elephant serves as a metaphor for the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*); together with the preceding three vehicles, they constitute four. Regarding the "two extremes":
the extreme of annihilationism (*uccheda*) and the extreme of eternalism (*śāśvata*)—namely, annihilationism destroying permanence and eternalism destroying annihilation—are called the two extremes.
"To be foremost in faith alone" means to uphold the solitary precepts; these precepts are the place of refuge and reliance, like a head resting on a pillow, seeking peace therein.
"Seeking no good rebirth" means that among the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), one finds nothing at all that is wholesome.
Regarding those who wear leaves as clothing: although they wear these garments, they cannot avoid being naked; thus, this is a metaphor for shamelessness.
Moving from the trigram Kan (☵) to Li (☲) signifies clarity; it is an analogy for the manifest commission of evil.

Regarding "the roots and conditions that evoke the Buddha": this refers to a hidden resonance with the Dharma-body through the power of unconditional compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*). Internally perfumed, it forms a spiritual capacity (*tanka*), which is what is meant by "evoking.
As for the analogy of "relatives," it simply means that this very body is regarded as virtuous.

Regarding the phrase "only by means of evil do they evoke [the Buddha]," the intention of our school is that evil also serves as the karmic condition (*ki-en*). Because evil reaches its ultimate limit, it is able to evoke the Buddha;
therefore, it is said that they "invite medical treatment for their illness."

"With the head covered in dust" means to be shrouded. The five abodes [of ignorance] are like dust; furthermore, giving rise to icchantika views and repudiating cause and effect is like having the head covered in dust.
This is explained by way of the relative gravity [of the offenses].
Regarding those who rely on and await a response: although there is no response in the present, it shall be fulfilled in the future.
As for the initial contemplations and so forth, these are all dark contemplations and dark permissions. Furthermore, regarding the twelve types of self-view:
Regarding the fourteen truths appearing in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, its thirty-sixth chapter states:
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the fifth stage knows as it truly is: 'This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering;

this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. He skillfully knows the conventional truth and skillfully knows the ultimate truth."

He knows the truth of characteristics; he skillfully knows the truth of distinctions; he skillfully knows the truth of establishment; he skillfully knows the truth of phenomena; he skillfully knows the truth of arising;

he skillfully knows the truth of the exhaustion of outflows and non-arising; he skillfully knows the truth of the successive accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages, up to and including the truth of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
This bodhisattva causes sentient beings to rejoice according to their mental inclinations.

Therefore, one knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by penetrating the single true nature (*eka-lakṣaṇa*). One knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by awakening to the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena.
One knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*) by comprehending the distinctions among the various states (*avasthā-prabheda*) of all phenomena.

One knows the truth of establishment (*vyavasthāna-satya*) by skillfully discerning the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). One knows the truth of things (*vastu-satya*) by awakening to the suffering and affliction of body and mind. [One knows] the various realms of existence (*gati*)...

Because there is the continuity of birth, one knows the Truth of Birth (*jāti-satya*). Because all feverish afflictions are ultimately extinguished, one knows the Truth of the Knowledge of Exhaustion and Non-arising (*kṣaya-anutpāda-jñāna-satya*).
Because non-duality arises, one knows the Truth of the Knowledge of Entering the Path (*mārga-praveśa-jñāna-satya*).

Because one perfectly awakens to all modes of activity (*ākāra*), one skillfully knows the successive continuity and accomplishment of all Bodhisattva stages, up to the Truth of the Accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom. By means of this...

This is known through the power of the knowledge of faith and resolve, not through the power of ultimate knowledge. Because those who are icchantikas lack the power of faith and resolve and deny the existence of these roots of goodness, they are said to have severed their roots of goodness.
As for the scriptural passage, "Though one goes away, what benefit is there?": even if one were to encounter auspicious signs along the way, what further benefit would there be?
Regarding the phrase "the Way responds and intersects with the Path" (*ganying daojiao*): it carries the meaning of the intersection of the Way.
The two children are a metaphor for the mutual destruction of nihilism (*uccheda*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*). Furthermore, their self-exaltation is likened to throwing one's head down;
their mutual injury is likened to pulling each other’s hair. Bricks, stones, swords, and staves all serve as metaphors for nihilism and eternalism, which mutually destroy one another.
That which is discarded by the sages is picked up by the icchantikas.
That the śramaṇa is a solitary practitioner signifies that the icchantika lacks the roots of goodness for transcendence and fails to constitute a responsive capacity.
Because the Buddha constantly desires to manifest his birth [in the world] yet the sentient being lacks such capacity, he is thus represented as having no companion.

As for the scripture’s statement, "going to the place of illness": although an icchantika lacks roots of goodness from the three periods of time, through the power of unconditioned compassion (apratihata-maitrī), one responds to them in secret;
thus, one seeks their roots of goodness with meticulous care. Therefore, it is said that one "goes to the place of illness."
Regarding the subsequent contemplation of the past: one further examines whether there has been any goodness from time immemorial.
Briefly stated, those who lack patience will give rise to anger upon hearing others speak of the causes and effects of the supramundane; thus, they are fully possessed of the three poisons.
Regarding "the bones and joints are the body-faculty": this means that when seeking goodness within the body, mouth, nose, and so forth, none is found.
Regarding "excretions and urination being obstructed": the bodily characteristics involve mutual harm and are contrary to the proper way; this is termed "obstruction."
The "obesity" is a metaphor for the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Because one reckons a self throughout all twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), it is called "obesity.
The Sūtra says: "Inquiring after those who tend to the sick," referring to icchantikas whose capacity for awakening is rooted in evil.
Regarding the question of what the intention of one who tends to the sick is: is there any root of goodness that can be aroused, or is there none at all?
As for "the faculties and conditions being opposed," this means that regarding the faculties and their corresponding conditions, none of them possess any goodness.
Regarding "the fierce and violent": this refers to the mundane and supramundane sharp and piercing evils.

When the Sūtra says, "perceiving the body as fine and soft," etc., it uses silk and cotton to illustrate the evil of the body; or when it says, "hard as stone," etc., it illustrates the evil of speech and mind.
Therefore, it is said that one sees only the three poisons.

The Sūtra says: "Thus it is not fixed" (up to the words) "as for those who die. This means that in the future, when they are in the darkness [of the intermediate state], there will surely be the occasion for their awakening;

therefore, it is said to be "not fixed. Regarding the phrase "that which is not prescribed by the Buddha's teachings": since the capacity for the Path has not yet been perfected, it is not appropriate to manifest [the truth] prematurely.
One should allow them to give rise to views such as eternalism or nihilism, as well as unwholesome actions of the three karmas; therefore, it is said, "do not prohibit them."
The Sūtra says: "Regarding these two awakenings: first, hearing that Kāli was entering prison; second, hearing that Cāṇūra saw the Buddha and his offenses were eliminated.
Although he heard these two accounts, his mind alone remained undecided.
To "render the indeterminate determinate" means that if the nature of the offense were fixed, it could not be eliminated by a single act.
Because the nature of the offense is not fixed, the Buddha possesses the wisdom capable of eliminating it; since he is certainly able to eliminate it, it is said to be "rendered determinate."
The Sūtra states: "Those who look up and behold the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and so forth—merely by contemplating the Buddha’s body, one has already extinguished immeasurable heavy offenses;
how much more so when hearing the Dharma?"
The Sūtra speaks of eight kinds of sounds. The *Brahmayu Sūtra* states: first, the most excellent sound, which is pure and elegant;
second, the easily understood sound, wherein whatever is spoken is clear and easy to comprehend; third, the harmonious sound, whose volume is moderate;
fourth, the soft sound, which is gentle and pleasing to hear; fifth, the unerring sound, which is free from mistakes or errors; sixth, the non-feminine... [text continues]
The sound is majestic and resonant. Seventh, the voice of wisdom is free from hesitation or timidity. Eighth, it is deep and far-reaching, like the roll of thunder.
Although these are not listed separately in the present sutra, they are identical to those sounds mentioned there; therefore, they are cited here.
The Sūtra says, "One should bind the mind," and so forth. These twenty matters are for the sake of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

by relying on these phenomena to observe and subdue the mind, one reaches the phenomena and perceives the principle, thereby accomplishing wondrous contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇā*). Furthermore, the present text clarifies that the primary and auxiliary practices must be cultivated in conjunction; thus it is said.
The Sūtra says: "Regarding this body of mine, within it there have not yet arisen any untainted roots of goodness.
The Sūtra says: "Those who have not yet attained discipline" refers to those who have not yet subdued [the mind] through contemplative practice.
The Sūtra says, "There is no place where one does not fear. The three miserable realms are places of fear.
Regarding the phrase "one who lacks the wisdom prior to the Way": here, the first stage (*ādikṣānti*) is taken as the Way itself.

The Sūtra says, "It is difficult to obtain freedom from the [eight] difficulties. This means that by attaining true *saṃgha*, one becomes proximate to separation; by separating from the [coarse] divisions of existence, one attains the Middle Way, and only then can one truly distance oneself from the eight difficulties.

The Sūtra further says, "There is not a single dharma capable of obstructing it. This refers to the fact that as long as there is not yet a single wholesome dharma within one's person, nothing can obstruct the twenty [difficulties].
The fifth is the enmity between cause and effect.

As the Sūtra says regarding those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*): "There has never been one who, without the seed-wisdom of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-jñāna*), could cross over the perilous path of the five heinous crimes.
This passage specifically refers to the person of the King.

The Sūtra states that "birth and death have no limit. When the contemplation of non-arising is perfected, one enters the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), at which point one begins to perceive a portion of the end of birth and death.
It is only upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) that one fully exhausts its limits.
The Sūtra states that "one who does not perform any karma" means that since no wholesome karma is performed, it is called empty and non-existent.
The Sūtra further states that "arising from long-term clarity" and so forth refers to the fact that transgressions arise from the mind and are extinguished by the mind, just like a single hand.
Whether turned face down or face up, neither leaves the hand; birth and death are likewise: they cease because of ignorance.
As for the four perversions being the path of affliction, these twenty matters do not transcend the three paths; all are objects of contemplation.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, those who contemplate the mind in succession, having extinguished the three marks, [cultivate] concentration, wisdom, diligence, and precepts.

The explanation of the preceding matters of contemplation is concise in both text and meaning; therefore, it further elaborates upon the wondrous contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*) to shatter clinging attachments and cause one to awaken to the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Those who obstruct entry into the Way, though they cultivate non-arising, yet further cling to these four [extremes], thereby turning it back into arising and ceasing.
How can they enter the perfectly wondrous Way?

The Sūtra says: "If all dharmas have no fixed nature, for one who understands this meaning, even though all dharmas have no fixed nature for sentient beings—who at times commit evil and at times perform good—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas likewise at times manifest entry into birth and death."
At times he manifests entry into the truth; therefore, it is said that there is no fixed [nature].

As for "being luminously clear": if one does not practice cultivation, yet claims to universally deliver all beings through non-arising, while merely saying that there is no father, such a person is one who possesses great shamelessness.
Regarding the four great elements encompassing the ten material forms: the four great elements, as the formative agents, encompass the sense faculties and their objects;
the sense faculties and their objects, as the formed, in turn encompass the four great elements.
The Sūtra states: "Great King, in the past you did not command anyone to kill. This was merely a skillful means of granting leniency;
for the King’s mind feared that his retributive intent (*vipāka-citta*) would remain unbroken, and thus he spoke only of such things as "cutting off a foot" and so forth.
To blend together the minds of the high and the low: the Buddhas are "high," while the king’s two karmas of speech and mind are "low.
By merging these two states of mind and seeking the non-existence of sin, how can one calculate that killing one's father is necessarily grave? Therefore it is said:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no sin; why do you alone claim to have sin?"
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that "one may also obtain good fruits": because he killed a rishi in the past, he was killed today;
because he made offerings to a corpse, he has attained the first fruit [of the path] today. Therefore, it is said that one may also obtain good fruits within the present life.
"Acting lawlessly in both vertical and horizontal ways" means to act with unrestrained license, committing various unrighteous acts.
As the Sūtra says: "Among my disciples... those who violate the precepts," the Buddha also temporarily grants them leniency of mind.

"If among my disciples there are those who are deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or beset by intense suffering, their violations carry no guilt; this is because they lack their fundamental [right] mind."
The reason it is said that "not speaking now" is more serious than death is as follows: the intention is not to say that one values death or regards death as a grave matter.
Rather, when a person commits a grave offense—such as killing a human being—they commit a grave offense; whereas killing an animal constitutes only a light offense, a *dukkaṭa*, or a *pācittiya*.

Regarding the offering of food: as it is said, "This food—superior in color, fragrance, and flavor—is offered to the Buddhas of the ten directions," this is a secondary citation used to explain the term "etc.
(等). Therefore, it is called a separate discussion.
Regarding those who destroy their stagnation at extremes and lose the principle: they lose the principle of the Middle Way.
As the sutra says, "Nirvana is not existent," and so forth; the essence of Nirvana is neither existent nor non-existent, yet there is also Great Nirvana.
The scripture states, "Although it is not existent," and so forth. This concludes the preceding discussion.
Regarding "although it is neither existent nor non-existent, there is shame and remorse": if one kills, one incurs transgression; this properly concludes by returning to the King.

The Sūtra states: "Receiving the retribution of the fruit" [is] followed by a passage that temporarily employs the two heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism to demonstrate that the Great King is free from these two errors.
Furthermore, the subsequent passages all serve to show why those who cling to the two extremes fail to attain the Middle Way;
thus, the previous citation of the existence of the Middle Way in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* was intended to shatter their error of being stuck in one-sided extremes.

To say that "experiencing the retribution of results" is termed "existence" (*bhava*) clarifies the essential nature of karma; because this essence attains its fruit, it is the view of emptiness held by those who hold nihilistic views.
The Sūtra says: "Those with the view of existence" refers to those who constantly and dogmatically cling to the view of existence. "Those without the view of existence" refers to...
This refers to those who calculate [existence] through annihilation and deny the existence of karmic retribution.

As for the passage in the Sūtra stating that "those with the view of permanence" (up to) "are not existent," this merely refers to a falsely imputed permanence and does not refer to the Buddha’s true permanence.
Therefore, it says they "fall into the view of non-existence and permanence. Nevertheless, the conclusion below states, "although it is not existent."
"It is not non-existent, yet it is also eternally existent. One who holds the view of permanence is certainly a person who maintains the view of eternalism.
To exhort one to cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and so forth is precisely to exhort one to cultivate the contemplation of non-arising and so forth.

The Sūtra says: "I have now only just come to know... up to "...even the shallowest. This should fully be understood as taking impermanence (*anitya*) in opposition to permanence (*nitya*), and so forth, as the object of contemplation;

however, the text mentions only one side. The Sūtra says: "Knowing all phenomena... up to "...as non-self" (*anātman*). This also mentions only one side; it should be completed by [taking] permanence [in opposition to non-self].
These four pairs constitute the contemplation.
"The King’s initial resolve" refers to the resolve for practice undertaken for one's own sake.
"The King’s repeated resolve" refers to the resolve for the purpose of transforming those below.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "one immediately attains what is slight and thin": this means that because they have not yet been entirely eliminated, they remain merely slight and thin.
As for the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, it refers to the *Ajātaśatru-kaukṛtya-vinodana-sūtra*.
Regarding the meaning of the five repentances: once one has heard the Dharma, both oneself and others must fully possess these five; only then will the ritual of practice be perfected.
As Maitreya said in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*: "Śākyamuni only attained the Way after diligently practicing austerities;
I, however, now sit and cultivate the practice of bliss. By diligently performing the five repentances during the six periods of day and night, I shall attain the realization of the Way.
This is precisely such an example.
The Sūtra states that the four kinds of māras among sentient beings do not exceed the four [views] such as heterodoxy and permanence, nor the four such as impermanence.
The Sūtra further states that the great assemblies of all Buddhas are adorned; if there were no bodhicitta, the assembly would not be dignified or beautiful. Why is this?
It is because the bodhicitta mutually adorns one another; when seeking enlightenment above and transforming those below, and when cause and effect are fully perfected, only then is it so named.
Regarding the Buddha and his assembly:
it is like those who enter the Binṭa hell; whether they must enter or not based on their karmic retribution, their transgressions are nonetheless not extinguished.
As for the passage in the sutra that says "like the *Saṃpuṣpita*," Zeshou states that according to the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*, the *Saṃpuṣpita* is none other than the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Furthermore,
the "Chapter on the Practice of the Infant" refers to the practice of the Tathāgata, which is the perfect infant.
Regarding the two transformations, the great and the small: the "small" refers to the Tripitaka of the Lesser Sages, while the "great" refers to the Mahāyāna gateway.
Zhezhou said: "One cannot manifest the infant-like mind through arising and abiding; one cannot manifest the infant-like body through going and coming;

one cannot manifest the infant-like mouth through speech. Examining his commentary, it is not that he lacks this intent; however, it ultimately does not equal the explanation of the present Master, which accords with the scriptural text.
The general purport is as follows:

When the sutra speaks of "that which is not yet fully understood," it means that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas manifest as if they have not yet fully understood; this is also to say that there is no speaking while speaking, which is termed "not yet fully understood."

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "Names and things are not uniform," it is like the case of worldly infants, who may be called "Gēniáng" (歌孃), with both characters pronounced with a heavy tone.

Sentient beings are likewise: for some it is appropriate to teach permanence, for others impermanence; for some it is appropriate to teach all at once, while for others it is appropriate to teach gradually.
The Tathāgata, through his skillful means, accords with their varying capacities—deep or shallow—and causes them all to enter the ultimate. Therefore, it is said: "Because of the shallow..."
This is understood.
Regarding the "infant who delights in and loathes," this is an explanation based on the opening of the provisional (*upāya*).

As for taking the character *he* (和) as the primary focus: *he* is shallow while *po* (婆) is deep. Why? Because the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka [vehicle] require three great aeons (*kalpa*) and one hundred kalpas.

To practice while remaining prostrate before the delusions is called "Great" [Mahāyāna], yet one has not yet attained the untainted (anāsrava) state; therefore, in this present text, the term *p'o* (Pratyekabuddha) is contrasted with *yen* (Mahāyāna).

Regarding the phrase "not committing great perversions (*mahā-viparyāsa*) and so forth," this refers to the practice of the individual (Pratyekabuddha), who directs his mind toward the ultimate fruit and does not abide in the perversions of the two extremes.
"Seeing the path as the attainment" refers to its realization.

"Cultivating the nine grades progressively" means that the bodhisattvas of the aforementioned distinct teaching cultivate loving-kindness by first bestowing happiness upon those who are superior and close, and then upon those who are inferior.
Up to the ninth grade, it is only then called the accomplishment of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

If one were not to distinguish this through the perspective of the delusive, there would be no way to emerge [from the stages], because it is through the completion of practice that [the result] is attained.
Regarding "ceasing from weeping": only upon reaching the ultimate fruit do the myriad practices finally cease; prior to that point, all are termed "weeping.
Reaching far into *nirvāṇa* refers to the ultimate fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the third, the single summary: first, the two paired headings of the noble practices; second, the sequential and non-sequential practices; third, the paired explanations; fourth, the non-dual practices;
and fifth, the single summary of these five practices.
Fascicle Nine: The Chapter on King Virtue (Guṇarāja-parivarta).

The initial commentary on the sub-commentary is divided into two parts: first, a preliminary clarification of the similarities and differences regarding the virtues of practice; second, the explanation according to the text. The first part is further divided into two.

First, the ancient [exegesis] is presented; second, the present [exegesis] follows with the formal explanation below. The first [section] also has two parts: first, the presentation of the ancient [view];

second, from "Now, as for... onwards, the brief refutation. Regarding the first, it says: "The one and two virtues extensively practiced by the sages" is because the two virtues are contrasted with the single practice.
It is called "extensive" (*vipula*) to manifest the characteristics of the perfected virtues of cultivation. Thus, each single practice possesses both virtues.
The same applies to the grand and magnificent essence; however, it is merely that the latter two practices are less convenient for direct correspondence.

Regarding the point that "the substance is one while the meanings differ": it may be granted that the substance is one; however, it is not so regarding the commonality of their being wholesome causes.
Why? Is the cause prior to the stages (bhūmi) the cause for the stages above, and is it a wholesome cause of the universal (pariniṣpanna) type or the partial (prādeśika) type?

Finally, regarding the claim that "the ultimate limit of study" refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), which is called the "ultimate limit of study" because it marks the completion of the path of learning—this too is now refuted.
For what kind of teaching does this "ultimate limit of study" belong?

Regarding "feeling the subsequent fruits of practice": this refers to the bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), whose gradual cultivation and study do not yet accord with perfect interfusion;

therefore, it is necessary to break through them. Furthermore, the terminology of "habitual causes and habitual fruits" is mostly found in the provisional teachings (*upāya*), whereas [the terms] "holy fruition causes and holy fruition fruits" pertain to the ultimate reality.
Regarding the statement that "the golden mind constitutes the essence": others, seeing that the sixth merit involves entering the Vajra-samādhi, claim that the golden mind constitutes the essence.

This is refuted by asking: since [the practitioner] realizes this at the first stage (bhūmi), why would the golden mind alone constitute the essence? Furthermore, do the remaining merits not also have an essence?
Regarding "adorned with praise and encouragement": it means that one is adorned with ten virtues and encouraged through five practices so as to cause practitioners to cultivate and study them.
Next, in the section on "refuting [the opponent]," it says: "The stage of a bodhisattva" refers merely to the attainment of the distinct stage of a bodhisattva.
Regarding "where there is no exhortation": in every instance following the exposition of the practices, there is an exhortation to cultivation; why then would it be unique to the ten virtues?

In the second section, the "Correct Explanation," it states that the "first three noble practices" refer to the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*), the pure practice (*brahma-caryā*), and the infant-like practice (*bāla-caryā*).
This also refers to the "realization" (pratyakṣa) sections that follow each practice; these may span one, two, three, four, or five pages.
Since the "Celestial Practice" (devayāna) is what is to be realized, yet the extant text contains only three lines, it is said that "the text is brief."
It is not that the ten merits are not clearly cultivated; this is indeed true cultivation, which is the practice of the heavens.
As for the initial address, it is directed toward the one who proclaims and inspires the Teacher; therefore, he addresses him first.
That the Dharmakāya is noble means it is the ultimate in loftiness; that it is precious means it is all-pervasive.
The Dharmakāya pervades all places and is the most honored and noble among the three bodies; how could anything exceed this?
The Virtuous King is one who has attained liberation. He manifests emanations and disperses reflections to subdue beings everywhere and liberate all capacities; thus, he is like a king.
Furthermore, according to the actual nature of the Dharma, this chapter should be titled "The Ten Meritorious Qualities. However, it is now titled according to the person to whom it was addressed;
therefore, it is said that the chapter title is derived from the person.
The reason names are not listed individually is that the sutra contains only the sequence of ten virtues, but lacks the specific names of those merits.
The sutra states, "One who practices such a Great Nirvana," wherein *nirvāṇa* is the fruit to be realized and the *sūtra* is the teaching.
By practicing the five practices according to the teaching, one attains the fruit of nirvana; hence it is said that one attains ten matters of merit.

As for why only nine phrases are retained: if the eight characters beginning with "rare" (*āścarya*) were included, they would constitute ten phrases, and one could likewise attain the wisdom of discernment (*pratisaṃvid*).
"Neither difficult nor easy" means that the wisdom of discrimination is difficult to produce, while the wisdom of nirvāṇa is easy to attain;
the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way cannot be known by these two types of extreme wisdom. Therefore, it is said to be "neither difficult nor easy," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that because it is formless, it is not characterized by marks: since form and mind are coarse and superficial, they must be negated.
Regarding "without limit and without center": this is precisely the center within the limits; therefore, it is not a center existing outside of the limits.
Regarding "cutting off the four," these refer to the dharmas of the four propositions and the hundred negations; as they are all subsumed within the mundane world, they must be negated.
Regarding "repeatedly stating": when speech is exhaustive, stating a previous matter once and then a second time is called being exhaustive.
Now, since the ten virtues individually do not establish the meaning of "pervasive," they are not employed here.

First, regarding the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and so forth, we shall now refute [the opponent's view] based on the sūtras. According to their perspective, there is something that is not heard; this refers directly to the wisdom derived from hearing.

How can these [three types of wisdom] be of benefit? How do they correspond to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*)? Regarding the correspondence of the latter three with the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), the textual formulation is most inconvenient.
If the three wisdoms merely suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*), how can they sever doubts and so forth?
"The first is the root" means that all dharmas take hearing the teaching as their root.

"One cannot even attain equality" is a refutation; its intent is to say that the true realization of entering the stages through the practice of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is identical to that of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
It is still not accepted today. Fearing that it would obstruct the guidance of the teaching, how could one employ the three types of wisdom—distinct, shared, and common—to provide an explanation?
Therefore, it is not accepted here.
The text clarifies that this is the third error: how could one compose an explanation based on the distinct, shared, and other [categories]?

The phrase "the text states that the civilizing [teachings] do not hear the lower" refers to the fourth point: because the three types of wisdom arise only by hearing from others, [the lower teachings] are not [capable of this].

The phrase "the text states that the civilizing [teachings] are inconceivable" refers to the fifth point: the three types of wisdom in the first three teachings are all dharmas that can be conceived and deliberated upon.
In the *Bunmei Himitsu* (Secrets of Civilization), Part Two, it states: "The sixth [section], 'Now the Ten Virtues,' concerns the three virtues that are realized.

Since the *Jingei Hihō Kyō* (Sutra on the Secret Dharma of the True Self) itself declares, 'The secret treasury of the Tathāgata,' how can one provide an exoteric interpretation of it through the three types of wisdom?"

"Civilization is perfectly complete," etc. (Section 7): The hearing, contemplation, and cultivation of the three preceding teachings are dharmas that are one-sided and deficient, lacking in perfection.
"Civilization is startling," etc. (Section 8): The three wisdoms of the two vehicles are ordinary dharmas; since they were already attained in the past, how [could they be marvelous]?
Now, hearing this, are you not even more startled and amazed?
The text states that there is no difference below [this point]. The ninth [section] on the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) concerns the dharmas of differentiation.
The text states that the Middle Way below [this point]—the twelfth [section] on the Bodhisattva’s three types of wisdom—is the dharma that exhausts the two extremes.

Regarding those who do not hear of the characteristics of the ultimate cause: if one considers the ten virtues in relation to the preceding five practices, they are called "fruition-verification" (*phala-sākṣātkriyā*);

yet in relation to what follows, as they have not yet reached the ultimate, they remain causes for *nirvāṇa*. As for the "heavenly practice" (*deva-caryā*), it is not heard [as such]; rather, hearing while verifying the principle is itself the practice that is the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
How can the ancients have consistently explained this solely as the ultimate fruition?

As for those who practice and realize this: by relying on the true cultivation of celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*), they realize the truth stage by stage. This is the "unheard" of wondrous awakening; it is the "hearing" of the arising of understanding.
Upon entering the first *vihāra*, true realization unfolds, and they see all Buddhas everywhere. Their respective bodies and lands mutually interpenetrate and merge;
the teachings of the lands and the teachings of the atoms are inexhaustible, yet a Bodhisattva can comprehend them all in a single thought-moment. This is...
Regarding its characteristics:
it is not that those who do not understand other aspects would thereby destroy the preceding passage on the three types of wisdom.
To briefly enumerate the three types: the essence of the Great Nirvana is non-hearing; the three truths are what is realized, which is hearing.
Therefore, it is explained by way of the three truths. Thus it is said: "not hearing what is heard. This is the realization of the Way, the single mind of the three truths.
For this reason, it is stated in all cases that this is not shared with the Two Vehicles.

Furthermore, regarding "not realizing the conventional": the practitioners of the Two Vehicles destroy the conventional arising from conditions of the six elements, yet they cannot emerge from emptiness into the provisional to possess the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Although they realize the true, they cannot, within that truth, fully embody the Middle and the Provisional as the ultimate destination.
"Correct praise" refers to the correct praise of the single mind as the three truths.
When the Sūtra speaks of the "nature and characteristics of the Three Jewels," it means that the single-substance Three Jewels are endowed with the four virtues;
furthermore, "nature" is the single-substance Three Jewels, while "characteristics" are the Three Jewels of manifestation.
The scripture states, "All Buddhas... [are] eternally abiding. This cites the profound to illustrate the shallow.
It is because Bodhisattvas equally realize the secret treasury (guhyagarbha) as do all Buddhas; thus, by citing the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas are made manifest.

Regarding the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata: having mounted the path of reality to attain perfect enlightenment, this is "coming without coming," which corresponds in meaning to the initial nirvāṇa—meaning that what is realized and entered is itself the end without being an end. "Not going" corresponds in meaning to the final [nirvāṇa].
Thus, the beginning and the end constitute a single pair.
In each and every matter, there is nothing that is not the Middle Way. All twenty phrases are dharmas that are negated by the two extremes.
Why is this? First, "neither existent nor non-existent" does not negate the Two Truths; "neither conditioned nor unconditioned" [does not negate them].
It does not refer to the Four Noble Truths—the conditioned truths of suffering and its origin, and the unconditioned truths of the path and cessation.
Nor does it refer to the distinction between the outflowing and the non-outflowing, nor to the realization versus the non-realization of truth.
"Neither form nor non-form" means it is not the mind associated with form.
"Neither name" means it is not the designation of the four aggregates. "Neither non-name" means it is not the aggregate of form.
"Non-characteristic" does not refer to the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. "Not non-characteristic" does not refer to the ultimate truth.
"Neither existent nor non-existent" does not refer to the existence of the twenty-five states of being, nor to the emptiness of the twenty-five states of being.
"Not a thing" means it is not the objects of the six sense organs, nor the hidden or manifest sensory realms. "Not not a thing" means it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Neither cause nor effect" means it is not the cause and effect of the two states of birth-and-death: the fragmented (*paricchinna*) and the transformative (*pariṇāma*).
"Non-contingent" means that to depend upon the contrast between the ultimate and the conventional is called "contingent.
"Not non-contingent" means that when one realizes that which is beyond extremes is itself the Middle Way, it is then termed "absolutely non-contingent."
"Neither light nor darkness" means it is neither the clarity of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) nor the darkness and delusion of the three obstacles.
"Neither emerging" means it does not merely emerge from the triple world like those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and so forth.
"Not non-emerging" means it is not that one does not move or emerge from the vehicles of humans and devas.
"Not permanent" means it is not the false view of permanence held by those outside the path, such as bodhisattvas who have emerged into the provisional.
"Not non-eternal" means it is not the non-eternality of the two vehicles' stagnation in emptiness.
"Not annihilated" refers to the stage of severing delusions. "Not non-annihilated" means it is not the stage of not severing delusions.
"Neither beginning nor end" means that it does not involve the external calculation of a primordial beginning in darkness, nor an end after eighty thousand kalpas of extinction;
this is precisely the negation of the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Regarding the phrase "it is not the past, etc., and the rest should be understood in the same way": the nine subsequent merits are likewise so.

As for "hearing what was never heard before" and "all externalists who are versed in the scriptures": formerly, outsiders claimed their own [teachings] were ultimate, yet the two vehicles did not know this;
now they finally come to know that [the truth] does not exist [in their systems], and that within *nirvāṇa* there is the inconceivable dharma of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The Sūtra mentions the four Vedas. The Commentary by Master Zezhou states: "In foreign lands there were four great masters of treatises.
First, Vyāsa composed the Four Vedas, also called the Vedas; this is translated as 'Treatise on Wisdom.
One is the Ṛgveda, which clarifies the methods for fire rituals and repentance; second is the Yajurveda, which clarifies the methods for giving and sacrificial offerings; third is the Atharvaveda..."
The *Abhidharma* is the vidyā that clarifies all methods of combat. The *Samaya-vidyā* is the vidyā that reconciles disputes and conflicts between different nations.
Because it brings about knowledge of these births, it is called the *Jñāna-śāstra*. The second master of treatises is Pāṇini, who composed the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra*.
This is known as the *Abhidharma* (Theory of Enumeration). It clarifies all phenomena such as sounds, names, phrases, and syllables. The third master of this school is named Kapila;
he is the sage of the Yellow Head who composed the *Sāṃkhya*—which here means "enumeration"—and this is the name of the treatise he produced.

Within that treatise, twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are analyzed; its function pervades the great elements, and it takes the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence through enumeration. The twenty-five truths are as follows: [list follows].
The fourth master is named Ulūka; he is the sage Kapila, who composed the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra.
This is titled *Paramārtha-prakāśa* (The Illumination of Ultimate Truth), concerning the meaning of the six categories (*ṣaṭ-padārtha*). It is explained as previously stated.
Regarding the three fundamental non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*): all that is conceived by outsiders does not exceed two types of gods and three types of sages.
As for the two types of gods, they are Maheśvara-deva and Viṣṇu-deva (also called Vairiṇa-deva or Vairūpa-deva;
this is translated as "Pervasive Victory," "Pervasive Distress," or "Pervasive Purity"). The *Āgama* states that these are gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
This is the highest heaven of the Third Dhyāna.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "As for the Śubhakṛtsna (Universal Purity) Heaven, its inhabitants grasp conch shells and hold wheels;
they ride upon garuḍas and possess great supernormal powers, yet they mostly cause harm. At that time, people, fearing their majesty, came to revere them accordingly... (and so forth).
Maheśvara is here translated as "Mahādeva" (Great Sovereign). He is the deity at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
He has three eyes and eight arms, rides a white ox, and holds a white fly-whisk; he possesses great majestic power capable of overturning the world.
Taking the World-Honored One as the basis for his transformation, his full details are as cited in the tenth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* commentary.
Regarding the three sages: the first is Kapila, translated here as "Yellow-Headed" (Huang-tou), because his head was like the color of gold.

He taught one hundred thousand verses of sutra and also the Sāṃkhya treatise; "Sāṃkhya" means "calculation" (shu). His method employs the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) to clarify that the effect exists within the cause, taking the concept of "One" as its fundamental tenet.
The second is Uruvilvākāśyapa, translated here as "Uruvilvā-sage" (Xiu-liu-xian). This man would hide in mountain valleys during the day...

He composed scriptures and traveled about at night preaching the Dharma to convert others; because he was like that bird, he received this name. His teachings also consist of one hundred thousand verses.

He is also called Vaiśeṣika, which here means "Incomparable" (*anirjita*). He maintains that the effect does not exist within the cause, and he takes the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) as his fundamental doctrine.
The third is Kṛṣaka, which here means "Asceticism" (*tapasvin*); he took mathematics as his holy dharma and composed scriptures. He also...

There are one hundred thousand verses. As for the Nirgranthas, these people sever the fetters and take the six obstructions and four turbidities as their doctrine, asserting that the fruit exists within the cause, that it does not exist, and that it is both identical to and different from the cause.

Regarding the six obstructions, as stated in the *Upāyahṛdaya-śāstra*: first, the obstruction of ignorance regarding non-perception; second, the obstruction of delusion; third, the obstruction of experiencing suffering;
fourth, the obstruction of the exhaustion of life; fifth, the obstruction of nature; and sixth, the obstruction of names and phrases.
Regarding the four turbidities—namely, hatred, pride, greed, and flattery (and so forth)—the sūtra enumerates all four great masters, whereas the commentary mentions only two.
While correctly explaining the sūtra text, it states: "In the *Lesa-sūtra*, they are similarly omitted and not mentioned;
therefore, three [masters] are cited in full to explain the sūtra and the commentary. Thus, the four masters are used to elucidate both the sūtra and the commentary.
Regarding the reckoning as "both one and two": this refers to the dual reckoning of the preceding two [positions]. Therefore, it is said that they are roughly the same as those two people.
When the Sūtra says, "Never having heard it before," this means that although it was not heard previously, one now comes to know it through this very sūtra;
because it is heard now, it is said that it was not heard [before].
The Sūtra states: "The meaning of the profound mystery has not been heard; now, because of hearing it, [I have attained it].
To explain the causal conditions: listening and receiving [the teaching] is the condition for realizing the fruit; the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is the cause for realizing the fruit.
Regarding the threefold exposition, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "The three wisdoms are actually present within a single mind;
their allocation to three distinct persons is merely for the sake of ease of understanding.

This synthesis was made precisely because they were presented through three metaphors—wherein the mirror does not equal the torch, nor does it equal the sun—and thus appeared to follow a sequential order that required reconciliation.
Regarding the scriptural passage stating that "it causes those of the two vehicles [to attain] the Buddha-way": what was previously unseen is now finally seen;
this is termed "remote.
As for "passing through the four dharmas," the first emphasis can be seen in the preceding sutra text. From the words "Good son, listen well" onwards is the second emphasis.

There are four dharmas. That is to say, "name" and "meaning" constitute one pair. From "Furthermore, good son" (*atha khalu kulaputra*) onwards, the third section on practice and understanding constitutes one pair.
From "Good son, bodhisattva" (*kulaputra bodhisattva*) onwards, the fourth section on dharma and meaning constitutes one pair.

"Severing doubt regarding external treatises" means severing the doubtful arguments of others outside [the Buddhist tradition]. It is also called "separation," because it causes oneself and others to be free from the net of doubt in the mind.

Regarding the mutual clarification of "before and after": because one internally realizes [the truth], one severs doubt; because one severs doubt, one internally realizes. Furthermore, what "before and after" could there be?
Regarding the doubt that the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* is an inversion of impermanence (*anitya-viparyāsa*): this refers to the initial phrase in the sutra expressing doubt regarding the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*.
Next, concerning the clarification of the inversion of permanence (*nitya-viparyāsa*): this refers to the phrase in the sutra expressing doubt that the Buddha is permanent.

These two constitute one pair. Together with the third, fourth, and fifth [points], they form three single phrases; combined, these constitute five phrases. While such a correspondence is presented, it is not entirely satisfactory.
This is merely based on my own interpretation; it is convenient for explaining the text.

However, as for the principle that "the Buddha-nature must be fully enumerated," one should state after the preceding sections—which raised doubts regarding terminology and the eight inversions—that once doubts are severed and the mind is extinguished, one is then able to realize that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Applying this passage to the preceding context, [the meaning becomes clear].
Therefore, it is said that they clarify one another.
As for what the Sūtra calls "the four [views] such as permanence," these eliminate doubts regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
As for "whether life or non-life," these eliminate doubts regarding the sixteen types of speculative views.
If one asks whether "sentient beings" or "non-sentient beings" refers to those who see the Buddha-nature, they are called non-sentient beings; this removes doubts regarding provisional designations.

If one asks whether it is "ultimate" or "not ultimate," this removes doubts concerning the provisional teachings that have not yet been fully revealed or realized. Therefore, the preceding text asks: "What is..."

They are called "ultimate" and "non-ultimate," meaning that which has a remainder and that which is without remainder. Furthermore, regarding other worlds and so forth, there is the removal of doubt concerning the past and the future;
that is, doubt as to whether there will be retribution in the future, or no retribution, and doubt as to whether there was a cause in the past, or no cause.
If there is existence or non-existence, it removes doubt regarding the two truths. If there is dharma or non-dharma, it removes doubt regarding attachment to the teachings.
If there is good or not good, it removes doubt regarding the human realm, the heavens, and the three miserable destinies.

Regarding the next section on provisional designations (*prajñapti*): however, there are five different types of speculative views (*parikalpa*) within the sūtras. First, one harbors doubt regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), not knowing which among them is the self (*ātman*).
Second, one harbors doubt regarding the self in relation to the six faculties, beginning with the eye’s ability to see, not knowing who it is that sees, and so forth, up to who it is that knows.

Third, one harbors doubt regarding the self in relation to form, sensation, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*), which comprise the five aggregates, not knowing who it is [that experiences them]. Fourth... [text fragment]. Fifth... [text fragment]. Not knowing who it is [that constitutes these].
1. Receiving retribution; 2. From the four form realms to the lower aggregates in other worlds, one harbors doubt regarding the self, not knowing who will go to the next life;
3. Regarding the dharma of non-arising, one harbors doubt below the cycle of birth and death, not knowing whether it has a beginning and end or is without beginning or end.

Regarding "having a beginning and having an end" as the heterodox: it calculates the first of eighty thousand kalpas as the beginning and that which follows the passing of eighty thousand kalpas as the end.

Regarding the two chapters on the "straight" and the "crooked," they are interrelated; within the crooked there are further two: first, the crookedness of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and second, that of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Regarding the passage "seeing an old man" and so forth: the *Śrī-mālā-devī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (translated as *Ruìyìng jīng*), in its first fascicle, states that when the Prince reached the age of fourteen, he requested the King’s permission to go out on an excursion to observe human affairs.
The King ordered his attendants and the hundred officials to escort him; they then set out from the eastern city gate.
The Lord of Devas transformed himself into the body of a sick man, emaciated and haggard, leaning against the doorframe while gasping for breath. The Prince asked, "Who is this person?
His attendants replied, "He is a sick man. "What is meant by 'sickness'? they were asked.
They answered, "Generally, those who are sick contract this illness due to wind, cold, heat, or chills. The Prince said, "How bitter is this suffering! If I were in his place..."
Even those who enjoy the pleasures of food and drink in wealth and status may lack moderation; they too will surely fall ill—how does this differ from that?
Next, as he rode out through the southern city gate, the Lord of Devas again transformed himself into an old man. The Prince asked, "Who is this person?"
The charioteer said, "An old man. "What is meant by 'old'? He replied, "His years are advanced, his faculties are matured, his form has changed, and his complexion has faded;
there is but little life remaining. Therefore, he is called 'old. Next, they drove out through the western city gate. The Lord of the Devas again transformed himself into a dead man.
The Prince asked again, "Who is this person? The charioteer said, "A dead man. "What is meant by 'dead'? He replied, "Dead..."
This means "exhaustion. When one's lifespan—whether long or short—is exhausted and merit is spent, life ends and the breath ceases; the spirit then departs, and such a person is called a "dead man.

Next, he proceeded to observe and went out through the northern city gate. There, the Lord of Devas again transformed himself into a śramaṇa, wearing dharma robes and holding an alms bowl, walking while looking at the ground.
The Prince asked, "Who is this? His attendant replied, "A śramaṇa. "What is meant by 'śramaṇa'? [The attendant] answered:
It is said: "I have heard that the Way of the śramaṇa is thus. The Crown Prince said: "Excellent! Only this is truly refreshing. This is as explained at length in the sūtras.

Regarding the "reliance on existence and non-existence," it simply means relying upon the non-existence of existence to discuss both the "neither" and the "both-illumination," thereby clarifying the inconceivable.
This discusses the Three Truths.
"Profound and yet more profound" means that both the preceding explanations of cause and effect are inconceivable; hence it is said to be "profound and yet more profound.
As for the meaning of "hearing what is not heard" mentioned in the Sūtra, it simply means "not hearing while hearing. This was a mistaken understanding by King Devarāja.
What does "not" mean? It means that if one has not heard, one should not say that one has heard; if one has heard, one should not say that one has not heard.
Therefore, this constitutes a mistaken understanding.

Regarding the initial refutation establishing the two [alternatives]: if a phenomenon is definitively existent, the refutation of hearing establishes its arising; if a phenomenon is definitively non-existent, the refutation of not hearing [establishes its non-arising].
It is established as cessation. If a dharma is heard, there is no non-hearing; if there is non-hearing, there is no hearing.
How then can one say that what was not heard is now heard? Therefore, it is called "not heard."
Regarding the statement that "one attains this but not that which is non-one": since arising and ceasing are distinct, one cannot establish the single meaning of "hearing" and "not hearing.
As for the scriptural passage, "hearing what was not heard," if you intend to refute it, you must observe that "not hearing" and "hearing" are manifestly different;
how then can the World-Honored One say that "hearing what was not heard" constitutes a single meaning?
First, regarding the establishment of two through fixed determination: since "not hearing" and "hearing" are distinct, we know there are two fixed determinations.

It is illogical for these fixed determinations to be one. How could one observe that "not hearing" and "hearing" are different, yet claim that "not hearing while hearing" constitutes a single meaning?

In general, the repetition of three analogies is still an illustration based on the Dharma. "Arriving, yet not departing" clarifies that what was previously called "not hearing" is definitively "not hearing.

"Arriving, yet not arriving" clarifies that what was previously called "hearing" is definitively "hearing. This is also like the passage beginning with "once born," which functions as a reverse clarification:

since birth has already occurred, it is definitively born and cannot be born again; this clarifies that what was previously called "hearing" is definitively "hearing. If one were to say "no... [the text continues].
"Arising is itself non-arising. This clarifies that what was previously stated as "not hearing" definitively means not hearing and not attaining.

Furthermore, it says "hearing what was not heard" and "having attained what was not attained," which is the same as the phrase "having arisen, it is not arising. "Not attaining what was not attained" is the same as the phrase "non-arising is non-arising.
One should know that "hearing what was not heard" has two meanings. How then, World-Honored One, can one speak of "hearing"?
Is that which is not heard a single meaning?

Within a simile, there is nothing that is not a single simile; however, if within a simile the phrase "it is also thus" is lacking, this constitutes a difficulty in establishing it as a single [simile].
Thus, it cannot be considered one.
Regarding "conceding the objection": what is meant by "conceding" is the first point, namely, granting that there is both non-hearing and hearing.

When the Sūtra speaks of "Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes," it is a counter-interrogation. If one says that ordinary beings have not yet attained the state of a Bodhisattva, have not yet attained Nirvāṇa, and have not yet seen the Buddha-nature;

As for those who have attained it, even though Bodhisattvas have already attained it, they are still said not to have attained it. Since there is thus a distinction between the ordinary person and the sage, we know by verification that "not hearing what is heard" refers to their being one.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that says, "The Tathāgata in the past," and so forth: if he heard it from another, that would constitute hearing; how then can it be said that he did not hear?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that he had "no teacher": having no teacher is equivalent to not hearing. How then can it also be said that he heard? This is a contradiction.
"Hearing" and the "basis of hearing" constitute these two. Why, then, is it said that "not-hearing" and "hearing" are of one meaning?
Regarding the "tying together of the two verticals": since the ordinary seat is not the same [as the Buddha's], we know these constitute two distinct dharmas.
As for these dharmas, first the verticality of the Buddha-fruit is tied together, and next the verticality of sentient beings is tied together.
Regarding the subsequent objection, its intended meaning is as follows: if even form (*rūpa*) is sometimes invisible, how much more so could there be anything in *nirvāṇa* that is not heard?
As for "obstructed internal form," all phenomena of form are of three types: first, visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*), which refers to that which is seen by the eye.

Regarding form (*rūpa*): first, there is that which is visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*), namely the forms perceived by the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body; second, there is that which is invisible and resistant (*anidarśana-sapratigha*), namely the forms within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are non-manifest (*avijñapti*);

third, there is that which is invisible and non-resistant (*anidarśana-apratigha*), namely the forms within the sphere of mental objects that are non-manifest. Of these, the first is visible, while the others are invisible;
therefore, it is called "delusive."
Regarding the Buddha’s clarification concerning illusion and so forth: the Buddha answers by means of illusion, emptiness, and the illusory nature of the provisional.

Therefore, he says: "You now well understand that all phenomena are like illusions and so forth. Within this passage, the meaning of the Three Truths is complete; the Buddha’s true intent is to state that all phenomena are entirely like magical transformations.
Why, then, do you cling to fixed characteristics and raise such objections?
This constitutes the response to the praise. A question was raised according to the capacity [of the audience]. Once the doubts of the assembly had been dispelled, the Buddha first offered praise.
From the words "O virtuous son, now you... onwards is the answer. It is not that blue and so forth are not heard; it is that blue and so forth are seen while being heard.
"To answer concurrently" means to answer both the "not-hearing of hearing" and the "hearing of hearing.
Generally, these three answers are as follows: the four propositions concerning illusion and so forth—namely, "not-hearing of hearing" and so on—are one answer for those of superior faculties.
The four propositions concerning the arising of arising are one answer for those of middling faculties. The third is the answer to King Devarāja’s request.
This is one answer.

Regarding the phrase "for those of inferior capacity who have come" (and so forth), it refers to such things as "not coming yet coming," "not releasing yet releasing," and so on; thus the Sūtra says (and so forth).

The Sūtra states: "It is not that what is non-blue sees blue; it is not that what is non-blue hears blue; it is that what is blue hears blue. This is why it is called a "wondrous response" (śubha-pratyuttara).

Regarding the phrase "the essence of this light, etc.": making [appearances] such as blue and so forth is the essence of the light; seeing blue, yellow, and so forth is the function of the light. From the perspective of the True [Nature]...
The arising [of this light] should also be understood in the same way.

"All destroy fixed characteristics" means that, incidentally, it destroys the King of Virtues' doubt regarding fixed attachments; because this light does not belong to causes and conditions, it possesses no fixed characteristics.
The Sūtra states: "Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are mindful of the Dharma-Buddha. This entire passage describes the essence of light;
therefore, it is said in each instance that it is eternally abiding (*nitya*).
Regarding "the four Bodhisattvas' own refutation and establishment": the four Bodhisattvas personally refute ignorance and establish their own Bodhisattva-lamp.
Regarding that which should be understood through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): that which is profound is silence and thus not heard; conventional truth is speech and thus is heard.
One should follow what is spoken, adapting to what is appropriate for each being.
Regarding how [the Buddha] remained silent and was unable to answer below: it possesses the fourfold intent of the *siddhānta*. It demonstrates that the Buddha-way is identical to the world;

it is the intent to generate goodness in those of this land; it is the intent of remediation to eliminate the evils of this land; and it is the intent of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to cause them to see their nature and attain the Way.
Regarding this Buddha’s “raising” of that bodhisattva: "raising" (jǔ) means to awaken (jǔjué) or to cause to arise (juéfā).

As in the sutra, at that time the World-Honored One asked Mañjuśrī, "By what causes and conditions does this radiance exist? Mañjuśrī then explained that the name of this radiance is "wisdom," and so forth.
It is through this dialogue that the bodhisattva arrives; this is precisely the sign of being raised by the Buddha.

Regarding the statement that "the three *siddhāntas* are also taught": within the Perfect and Eternal [Dharma], there are the benefits of the three *siddhāntas*, yet the *prātimokṣa* rules of discipline are not taught as a remedy, because they merely support the Eternal.
Furthermore, concerning the question-and-answer [method] up to the point of "indeterminacy": the method of question and answer is such that, in all cases, one asks those below about those above.
The current text, in which the Buddha questions and the Bodhisattvas answer, merely accords with what is appropriate for sentient beings; therefore, it is said to be "indeterminate.

This refers to the "human and side" [categories]. Previously, when Cunda and Mañjuśrī debated with the Buddha regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this was the "human and side.
Setting aside the conditioned and unconditioned for a moment, it reveals the True Dharma as being neither eternal nor impermanent.
Thus, this Dharma is not peripheral.
As for what constitutes a peripheral [inquiry] regarding this Dharma: it is when one does not hear the correct discourse on the Dharma, yet instead asks about matters of past and future.
For this reason, it becomes peripheral. However, although the question may follow a peripheral course, the response has already transcended the periphery.
That which is precisely what it is: the phenomena of the past and future are "hearing that which is not heard," yet people do not lean toward them.
This refers to the Buddha questioning the Bodhisattva and providing the answer, as well as the Bodhisattva questioning the Buddha and providing the answer.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "coming for the sake of arrival," this means coming by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Regarding "coming for the sake of non-arrival," this means coming by way of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Furthermore, it is called "coming" because there is no coming;
it is called "coming" because there is coming and going.
The Sūtra says, "Even arriving, there is no coming. This clarifies that what comes is itself non-coming.
Furthermore, it says, "Not arriving, there is also no coming," which clarifies that even non-coming is unobtainable.
The Sūtra says: "If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were permanent, they would likewise not come. Permanence is itself non-permanence;

if it were not impermanent, then even if it were impermanent, there would still be no coming. Impermanence is itself permanence; thus it is neither permanent nor impermanent. This is why it is said in all cases that they do not [come].
Therefore, it is said that with respect to the preceding object, there is no coming. Furthermore, as for "coming here from there," these sentient beings are the objects;
they come for the sake of these objects.

As for the subsequent eight sections: the first, "there are sentient beings," refers to karmic retribution; the following section, beginning with "pride," refers to the causes based upon that [retribution].
Cause and effect constitute a pair. "When clarity comes" refers to non-coming. Third, regarding "taking up and practicing":

from below, both those who grasp at existence and those who do not grasp at existence—so long as they have not yet seen the Great Truth—are termed "taking up and practicing. Fourth, "if one sees the Tathāgata" and so forth refers to the two vehicles seeing coming and going.
Fifth, "not hearing of Buddha-nature" and so forth refers to the ability to destroy [delusion] and clarify coming and going. Sixth, "if one sees the Śrāvaka" and so forth...
7. "If one sees the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" and below, this explains coming and going by means of names;
because the Two Vehicles' *tathatā* (True Reality) also possesses the names of the four virtues, yet their essence is different, they must be distinguished and excluded. 8.
"If one sees the Tathāgata" and below, this explains coming and going by means of the double negation (*ubhayābhāva*).

In response to those who have heard [the teaching] from the Noble (Gao-gui): one awakens and thus does not hear; one is deluded and thus hears. The same applies to the fundamental and the phenomenal (ben-ji):
from the perspective of the ultimate essence (li-ti), there is no hearing; through clear realization and vision, there is hearing.
The Sūtra states, "Setting aside this matter for now," meaning that the matters of the past and future are set aside.
"The radiance abides in its source" means that at the place of the Buddha Pūrṇacandraprabha, he also posed the three pairs of questions,
just as King Devarāja does now.
As for those who have already heard extensively, they have completed their extensive hearing.
Those who realize this through internal awakening—realizing the principle—is called "not hearing"; seeing it clearly is called "hearing."

"Each thought-moment increases clarity" means that in every thought-moment, one's renown increases. To be constantly in accord with the principle of nature is what is called "that which has not been heard.
As for the scripture’s statement, "You now wish to exhaust [all things]," etc., I have long since realized this.
Regarding your desire for an end [to your doubts]: I am able to skillfully explain that what you previously could not speak of was because the conditions were not yet met;

now that the conditions have finally matured, you have encountered me. As for my statement regarding "all doubts within," this refers to the great doubts concerning the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the manifested, specifically regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Those who have already broken [the fetters] but have not yet eliminated them are now being pulled out so that they may see their Buddha-nature.

Furthermore, for those in the final age, he teaches the provisional while retaining the real to manifest the real and eliminate doubts regarding both the provisional and the real; therefore, it is said that he "is able to skillfully pull them out."
For those who wish to cross the great river of birth and death, I can act as your pilot of the vessel of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*).
Regarding those who conceive the thought of [the Buddha] as their parent: first, there is a natural affinity; second, we were once bound by a great karmic debt.

After falling back from the Great Vehicle and wandering through the five realms of existence, it is now that the provisional is opened and the real is revealed, whereby one finally realizes that our natures are identical in principle. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This is the reality..."
"I am truly your father; my son," thus it is said that one gives birth to the heart of a newborn child.
Regarding those capable of contemplating wise giving: as the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "The great chariots made of the seven treasures, numbering immeasurably, were bestowed equally upon all his sons.
Now it is likewise: the Buddha-nature of the True Dharma is universally revealed without partiality.
If one gives rise to this text, there will be no doubt because it can exhaust the ocean [of afflictions]. Because there is no doubt, one perceives the nature.
Because one perceives the nature, one crosses the river of the two deaths. Because one has crossed the river, one realizes the nature.
Because one realizes the nature, one obtains the Great Vehicle and travels through the four quarters, proceeding directly to the site of enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "appearing as the six perfections": the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not preach the Dharma in vain; all [teachings] are attached to specific dharma-gates.
Since the Buddha’s intention is difficult to fathom, it is explained here by way of the six perfections, and thus they appear as such.
Regarding the vow of diligence: if one lacks diligence, how could one possibly exhaust the ocean of ignorance?
Regarding the vow of the precepts for deliverance: if one lacks ultimate precepts, how can one possibly uproot the poisonous arrows of transgression and defilement?
"High and noble is likewise so" means that because Prajñā perfectly illuminates the Dharma-realm, it is represented by "high and noble.
"A single phrase or half-phrase" refers to the fact that the cause of awakening (*bodhi-nimitta*) is the proximate cause for Buddhahood and Nirvana; hence these words are spoken.
Regarding "hearing and not hearing as the causal condition": "hearing" refers to cultivation. Upon entering the first stage (bhūmi), there is a partial accord with principle;
this is termed "not hearing. Therefore, it is called "hearing and not hearing."
Regarding the statement that "not hearing" is the true cause (*samyak-hetu*): the true cause of the rational nature (*li-xing*) is fundamentally "not hearing.
Since the nature is manifested through cultivation and attainment, it likewise does not require hearing. Therefore, the true cause pertains to both "not hearing" and "hearing."
