The text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the entry into the text for exegesis following the chapter heading. The first part is further divided into two: first, the direct explanation.

Title. Next, [the commentary] explains the intent of the "Chapter on the Grounds" (*bhūmi*). This section has three parts: first, a summary of ancient views; second, a concessive refutation beginning with "It is not that...";
and third, the formal explanation beginning with "Both of these... Regarding the intent of the second part (the concessive refutation):

although the title is indeed established from one perspective—that of the Bodhisattva—it cannot be taken as absolute. Within the third part (the formal explanation), there are two further sections: first, stating the intent; second, [the detailed exposition].

What follows is the sub-commentary. This commentary consists of three parts: first, an explanation based on the literal meaning of the text; second, a clarification through questions and answers to resolve doubts;
and third, an explanation established by correlating [the text] with the four *siddhānta* (fourfold) Dharma-gates. Regarding the first point, "capable of roaring immeasurably":

The Buddha is one who has realized the fruit and benefits those at the stage of the cause; therefore, it is said that he "can roar," and so forth. Next, the resolution of doubts is divided into two parts: first, the formulation of the doubt;
second, the answer which follows as the explanation.

The character for "eye" (目)—[the phonetic is *yǐ*, using an archaic form]—is a semantic compound (*huìyì zì*). The character for "teacher" (*shī*) [pronounced *sōulèi* as a fanqie; the five verses state: "a teacher wears a cloth headband, hence 'teacher'"].

Within the "Threefold Explanation of Accomplishment," it says: "As for the 'world' (*shìjiè*), because there are differences between teacher and disciple, as well as the three karmas and the six stages of realization (*liù jí*), it belongs to the world."

Regarding "becoming a person": "son" (zi) serves as the "provision" (zi); it is also "compassion" (ci). Because of the provision, one's own goodness arises; because of compassion, the goodness of others arises. As for the "antidote" (duizhi):
it remedies the fact that the three previous teachings were unable to provide definitive certainty. [The teaching that] all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature was established in the world;

whereas previously, during the stages of the distinct teaching (biejiao) and before the stages of the ten grounds (dibian), although this was known, it could not yet be definitively proclaimed. Therefore, the three teachings are all considered [preparatory].

Regarding the "object of treatment" (*pratipakṣya*): as for the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*), it refers to the Master occupying the highest position among the assembly and exhausting the source of Buddha-nature; therefore, it corresponds to the ultimate truth.
As for the title containing many meanings: it contains the meaning of the Master’s sixth [stage], which is the manifestation of Buddha-nature through the four *siddhāntas*.

Next, the explanation of the two [points] within the "intention" section consists of two parts: first, the citation of the ancient [view]; second, the current clarification and subsequent explanation. The first part, again, has two sub-sections: first, the formal citation;
second, the brief refutation beginning with "Now, all... and so forth.

As for the statement that "it was not spoken by the Bodhisattva," this clarifies that the Bodhisattva is merely one who is capable of questioning regarding Buddha-nature; one should not designate the questioner as the speaker.

It is because of the questioning that the teaching occurs, yet the speaking resides with the Buddha. The Buddha speaks to enter into the realization of Buddha-nature in order to answer the Bodhisattva’s questions.
For this reason, one must not follow [the title] exclusively; to do so would cause the title of the chapter to deviate from its true meaning.
As for this, it may also be understood as being discordant.

Next, regarding the phrase "all belong to the revealing cause" (*jñāna-hetu*) within the textual commentary on the section concerning categories: the myriad virtues (*kuśala-dharma*) belong to the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
This is because, by means of being able to reveal and understand the myriad virtues, those myriad virtues are then able to assist the True Principle (*saddharma*). Therefore, the myriad virtues...

Regarding those belonging to the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), as for the existence or non-existence of their nature: one correctly takes existence as the nature of the fruit (*phala-bhāva*) and the nature of the fruit-of-fruit (*phalaphala-bhāva*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "sentient beings," one also takes the existence of sentient beings as the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding "existence and non-existence": these two phrases are taken as the nature of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*). There is only the twenty-five realms of existence (*bhava*) as the adverse objects.

Furthermore, regarding "giving rise to wisdom": it is the wisdom that contemplates these repeatedly; because the wisdom manifests from the objects and the objects manifest the wisdom, it is called "giving rise."
Regarding the causes and effects of habitual practice: the first phrase takes "existence with cause" (*sahetu-bhava*); the subsequent phrase takes "existence with effect" (*saphala-bhava*).

As for the three phrases: taking "existence with activity" (*sābhisaṃskāra-bhava*) as the causal condition for retribution, and taking "existence with retribution" (*vipāka-bhava*) as the resultant fruit of retribution.

Regarding the nature of cause (*hetutva*): one takes two causes as the "nature of cause" (*hetutva*) and the "cause-of-cause-nature" (*hetuhetutva*). One takes two fruits as the "nature of fruit" (*phalatva*) and the "fruit-of-fruit-nature" (*phalaphalatva*).
As for "relying on activity without an agent": "activity" refers to the act of performing; therefore, it belongs to the nature of cause.
Regarding the eighteen cultivators, it is sufficient to rely on the preceding list and its numerical categories.
As for their similarities and differences: "similarity" means they do not transcend the Buddha-nature; "difference" refers to the various meanings mentioned above.
This is thus being the same yet not the same, and not the same yet the same.
However, this does not yet constitute grasping the essential meaning. Although the exhortations and inquiries cite eighteen points, their intent lies in the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

If one were merely to follow the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* and separately exhort [the interlocutor] regarding the "Lion’s Roar" (*siṃhanāda*), making it a separate question, how could the Buddha-nature be revealed? Therefore, this does not yet constitute grasping the essential meaning.
"General exhortation" refers simply to the exhortation to inquire about the Buddha-nature.
"Solemn exhortation" means that one must specifically inquire so as to cause the assembly to obtain benefit.
As for the phrase "addressed the Buddha," these three characters still belong to the scribe of the scripture; they should not be placed at the end of the preceding sentence. Taking [them]...
These three characters form the latter clause.

Regarding the conformity to the literary style, the analogy of the *dharmakāya* refers to a body constituted by such qualities as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*).

Regarding "the ground is itself ethical discipline" (*śīla*): if ethical discipline is not pure, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not manifest. Ethical discipline is the foundation of all wholesome qualities;
it is like the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), which arise in dependence upon the precepts.
The Sūtra states, "Desiring to destroy those who are not lions": this means that the three previous teachings are all incapable of performing the lion’s roar.
The Sūtra states, "Desiring to cause the dwelling place to be pure": this refers to the secret treasury of the three virtues being untainted by the three delusions.
Regarding the "pointing out what is not [the case]": this is not something that can be accomplished by those of the two vehicles, non-Buddhists, or ordinary worldlings.

As for the previous mention of "pointing out what is not [the case]," it refers to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others; prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, they were all unable to provide a definitive teaching, and thus it is said to be "not [the case]."
Regarding the first three questions, "questioning the dharma" refers to posing questions based on the teaching; "questioning the person" refers to posing questions based on the individual.
First, "questioning the nature of the fruit" means that when others see something as existing and ask what constitutes Buddha-nature, this is termed questioning the fruit.
Next, regarding the inquiry into the nature of causes: for what reason is that which is perceived [as existing] designated as a "cause"?
As for the subsequent dual inquiry: permanence, bliss, self, and purity apply to both cause and effect.
Now, as for bringing later individuals to inquire about the preceding dharmas: first, one brings all sentient beings to inquire about the essence of the principle of Buddha-nature;

next, one brings the bodhisattvas of the ten abodes to inquire about the meaning of the partial Buddha-nature; and finally, one brings the Tathāgata to inquire about the name of the ultimate Buddha-nature.

Furthermore, by taking these three types of persons and applying them across this single dharma, the inquiries are universally applicable. How is it that the essence of the Buddha-nature of sentient beings [is defined]?
How does a bodhisattva abide in the essence of buddha-nature? What is the essence of a buddha’s buddha-nature?

Since the essence of buddha-nature is identical, why is there further differentiation in terms of depth and shallowness? The same applies to the meaning of “buddha-nature” and the designation “buddha-nature” for others.

Regarding the initial inquiry into the essence of the Buddha-nature as principle (*li*): because it has not yet manifested the functions of the conditions (*yuán*) and the causes (*liǎo*), it is termed "essence" (*tǐ*).
When speaking directly of *prajñā*, one simply says *prajñā* and does not call it *pāramitā*; therefore, it belongs to merit (*fú*).

If one were to maintain the precepts for an entire eon in a pure land, it would not equal the merit of being free from anger and obstructive thoughts in this land from dawn until the time of the midday meal;
therefore, it is said that the merit [of the latter] is superior. Thus it is.
"Those who honor wisdom" refers to those who merely admire and look up to the wisdom of the ultimate fruit (*atyanta-phala*).
Regarding "Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes up to those of the Shared Teaching": here, the "abodes" (*vihāra*) are that which relies, and the "stages" (*bhūmi*) are that upon which they rely.

Because Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage of the Shared Teaching are identical to the Buddhas of the Shared Teaching in being able to manifest the eight aspects of enlightenment (*aṣṭākāra-abhisambodhi*), it is said that the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are like [the Buddhas].
The Buddha. Thus, that which Bodhisattvas share with the Buddha belongs to the adornment of wisdom (*prajñā-alaṃkāra*); from the ninth stage downward, all belong to merit (*puṇya*).
Regarding the interpretation of this passage, the intent is as follows: this section of text still describes the past; therefore, it is interpreted through two perspectives—present and past.

In the past, hearing the "constant" (the *nitya*) required discussing the "secret entry. This teaching was for those who were not yet fixed, intended to lead those who were not yet fixed into [the path].
Therefore, it is said that those of sharp faculties and so forth [attain this].

If this is already the case for the very lowest, then why could the *Tripiṭaka* bodhisattvas and humans and devas—who had already secretly attained non-arising prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*—not also do so?
As for the *Sāmānya* and *Viśeṣa* bodhisattvas, as well as the humans and devas of the two vehicles, how could they not be capable?
Regarding the phrase "If I were equal to [the Buddha] in the two adornments," the intent of the objection is as follows: If I were endowed with the two adornments, I too should be able to answer;

and if the Buddha were endowed with the two adornments, he too should be able to question. Since both parties would be equal in these two respects, the dynamic of question and answer could not be established; therefore, it is said that this is not the case.
"It is not a 'one and two' within a 'one and two'" clarifies that the present twofold adornment is not a 'one and two' characterized by differentiation;
rather, it is a 'one and two' that is non-dual in essence, and furthermore, it is a 'one and two' that transcends both one and two.
It is not like the fixed attachment to "one and two" held by ordinary beings.
This is also what is meant by "speaking about the ineffable.

It is analogous to how, in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, thirty-two bodhisattvas spoke about the ineffable, while Mañjuśrī responded with the ineffable within speech, and Vimalakīrti remained silent—this being the ineffable within the ineffable.
Now, [the Master] is fully endowed with the two adornments, just like those thirty-two bodhisattvas.
This is not a matter of speaking about speech; it does not share the characteristics of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.
It is because both "one" and "two" are simultaneously absent that the Lion’s Roar is illumination while being absence, and the Tathāgata is absence while being illumination.

Thus, the Bodhisattvas are granted the simultaneous absence, and the Buddhas are granted the simultaneous illumination. Although these are granted separately, it is for the purpose of manifesting their mutual absence.
It illuminates while being without the act of illumination.
If there were no "one" or "two," the intention is that one must first have "one" and "two" before they can both be simultaneously negated;
if there were no "one" or "two," there would be no phenomenon to negate.

One who does not perceive the limit of emptiness is so called because the limit is itself the center; thus it is termed "the vanishing of limits. Because the center is itself the limit, it is termed "the vanishing of the center.
When both center and limit are quiescent, their essence is the Dharma-realm, devoid of dual characteristics; only then is it termed the "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The Sūtra says, "and that which is non-empty. This also refers to the Middle Way, which is empty while being non-empty.

As for "neither before nor after," this refers to the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), which follows the truths of the ultimate and the conventional; thus it is termed "shallow and deep.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), however, both are present within a single mind.
"Those who are not [empty] of the prior and posterior" refers to the sovereign, namely the sovereign of the two extremes.
As for "this being a case where the names are identical": the followers of the Two Vehicles take the departure from annihilation and permanence as the Middle Way;

the Bodhisattvas take emerging into the provisional realm to accord with capacities as the Middle Way; and ordinary beings merely take what they practice as the Middle Way. These three types of people are all not [the true Middle Way].
The Buddha-nature and the Middle Way share the same name, yet their essences are eternally distinct.

As the Sūtra says regarding "the practitioner of suffering and pleasure": for those of the Two Vehicles, practicing asceticism to destroy the suffering of birth and death is termed "ascetic practice."
Attaining a minor nirvana is called "practicing for pleasure.

Regarding the phrase "lacking the meaning of perfect universality": these three types of persons do not perceive the principle of the Buddha-nature, the Middle Way, and the Dharmadhātu as being perfectly pervasive.
Since it has already been stated that the result [is attained], this now explains the term "nirvana" within the sutra.

Regarding the knowledge that this fruit arises from causes and conditions: the realm of buddha-nature serves as the causal nature (*hetu-svabhāva*), and the possession of the wisdom capable of contemplation serves as the causal cause (*hetu-hetu*).
From these two causes, the two fruits arise.
Regarding the "Middle Way": the following explains the two characters for "middle way. All of this clarifies the two characters for "seeds" (*bīja*) in the sūtra.

Why? Because the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*) are manifested through the causal seeds of the Middle Way, and furthermore, the Middle Way is manifested by means of the seeds of these four natures.

Regarding that which can produce two causes and two fruits: by means of the seed of Buddha-nature, it can give rise to the two causes—the conditional and the perfect—and accomplish the two fruits—bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, regarding how this seed can manifest the Middle Way: by means of the seeds of the two causes—the conditional and the perfect—it can manifest the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is said that they are "mutually [dependent].
Furthermore, regarding "seeds," these refer to the seeds of the three causes within the three paths. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The six sense bases, the seven consciousnesses, and so forth, constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata. This differs from the definition of seeds established in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

As for the question of what to do with these passages: it is precisely because the sutra speaks of "nirvana," again of the "middle way," and again of "seeds" that, were one not to rely on the present explanation, these texts would be extremely difficult to interpret.

Furthermore, regarding "auxiliary" (*pārśva*) and "principal" (*mukhya*): for the time being, these names are established in relation to the meanings of the "contemplating subject" (*ālambaka*) and the "object contemplated" (*ālambana*).

Moreover, it should further be stated that the Buddha-nature is the auxiliary cause as the seeds of the conditions and the immediate antecedent; the other two [the *tathāgatagarbha* and the *dharmakāya*] may be understood accordingly.

Second, regarding "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*), others say this refers to the phrase in the treatise: "neither arising nor ceasing. Third, regarding "annihilation and permanence" (*uccheda-śāśvata*), this refers to the phrase in the treatise: "neither annihilated nor permanent. However...
The discussion of the "eight negations" does not correspond with the present text; therefore, this explanation shall not be employed here.
Regarding "neither identical nor different": the fruit is non-different, while the cause is not identical.

Regarding those who shall attain the supreme fruit: that which they conceive as "permanent" is their supreme dharma. Because they form this conception, they shall attain the supreme fruit in the future;
therefore, it is said that they "are able to attain" it.

When the supreme Bodhisattva perceives according to reality, they clearly see that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear to those who hold the view of impermanence as they appear to those who hold the view of permanence; this is precisely seeing them according to these two principles.
"Rather, it is above both sides. This phrase explains the scriptural passage: "For what reason? Because it is supreme.
This refers to the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), which transcends the two aforementioned groups: ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists.

The Sūtra states that regarding the fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of birth and death: ignorance (*avidyā*) is the fundamental limit of the past; craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is the fundamental limit of the present.
Furthermore, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*) are themselves the three paths, which are termed the "fundamental limit."
Regarding "two causes flanking one fruit": the text explicitly clarifies that this refers to the five fruits of the present, which constitute the Middle Way capable of destroying birth and death;
it simply states that two causes flank one fruit.
As for that which is called the Middle Way, how can it destroy birth and death?
The Sūtra states that the Dharma of the Middle Way is precisely the cause and effect of the three paths of sentient beings; this itself is the Dharma of the Middle Way.
The Sūtra states, "like a poor person": this refers to the poor among the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Regarding the "prior and posterior errors" mentioned [in the text]: ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are the prior error; the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) are the posterior error;
and the Bodhisattvas occupy the middle position, which is termed the "middle. This concludes the third section, the formal explanation of this chapter.
Regarding "neither impermanent nor discontinuous": the two vehicles do not perceive the Buddha-nature as impermanent, blissful, self, and pure;
thus, they lack the dual causes of wisdom and severance. They cannot take the cause belonging to the stage of the cause as the "cause of the cause" (hetu-hetu).

Nor can they take the object of observation belonging to the stage of the observing wisdom as the "object of the cause of the cause" (hetu-hetu-viṣaya); it is merely a single cause. Only the observing wisdom itself can be taken as the cause of the cause.
Wisdom arises from causes; therefore, it is called the "cause of causes. It cannot be [attained] through the fruit of the fruit-house; the fruit of the fruit is likewise so.
That which is attained through the fruit of the cause-house is given the name "fruit" because it is able to observe the object of observation. If one observes the present...
The fruit of nirvāṇa is termed the "object of the cause of causes.
That which is merely a cause refers to the twelve links of dependent origination; because it is the object of the rational nature that is to be contemplated, it is termed a "cause."
Regarding the statement that "the nature of the object is not a cause," this means it is not a cause of a cause.
However, where the analogy diverges from the principle (*dharma*), the principle employs two factors as causes, whereas the analogical text treats a single matter as two causes;
the same applies to the two results. Here, we take only those cases where both the principle and the analogy possess two causes and two results, such that their names correspond.
To provide an analogy:
the same principle applies to the two fruits. Nirvāṇa is a fruit in its own right; with respect to wisdom (*jñāna*), it is further called the "fruit of the fruit" (*phalaphala*).
Furthermore, it is the fruit of nirvāṇa. Since nirvāṇa is a fruit in its own right and yet acts as a fruit [for wisdom], it is therefore named the "fruit of the fruit."

Regarding the scriptural statement "this is the cause and this is the fruit": the wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination serves as the cause for *nirvāṇa*, and is thus called "the cause.
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the fruit of this wisdom, and is thus called "the fruit."
Regarding the nature of conditions, there are two types. From this category of cause, two causes are derived; from this category of fruit, two fruits are derived.
That which is neither cause nor fruit is called the "correct nature" (samyaktva).
Regarding "combining conditions to form the correct": this means that the two aforementioned "combinations" are further subsumed into a single textual unit.
Regarding "the correct has no further number": since the correct is precisely the absence of correctness, how could it be a matter of numerical quantity?

The Sūtra states: "That which is without knowing and without seeing" means that there is neither a knower nor an object known, and neither a seer nor an object seen. The objective realm is itself wisdom, and wisdom is itself the objective realm;
they are non-dual and without distinction. Therefore, it is called "profound."
Regarding the extensive explanation of the profound: each of the six gates clarifies the twelve links of dependent origination, which is precisely the Middle Way and Buddha-nature.

Although ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, and even partial bodhisattvas possess it within their own being, they are unable to perceive it; only the Buddha understands it with perfect clarity.
Therefore, it is called "profound."
The Sūtra says: "Although there is no recipient, it is not eternal; yet because there is karmic retribution, it is not annihilated. Although the recipient perishes, this is called non-eternality;
that the fruit does not perish is called non-annihilation. There is no deliberative cognition, thus it is not eternal; because it exists through the convergence of conditions, it is not annihilated."
The Sūtra states that there is no beginning or end because the twelve links of dependent origination revolve through the three periods of time like a whirling firebrand;
thus, there is neither beginning nor end.
Furthermore, one should also perceive a "beginning" to some extent, meaning that when one [link] is severed, all are severed; therefore, a beginning can be perceived.

Regarding the statement that "the beginning and end are now mutually revealed and concealed": this clarifies that for a bodhisattva, one speaks only of "seeing the end. This refers to the severing of afflictions by means of applied contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*);
alternatively, it may refer to the "end" as being either the interpretation or the very last [moment].
"The beginning was profound obscurity" is explained by taking the initial and subsequent stages as a reference. Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes merely sever the end of ignorance at its inception;
they have not yet perceived the primordial source of the subtle ignorance that is identical with the Dharma-nature. Therefore, it is said to be "profoundly obscure."
Regarding "the ignorance that shatters the source in the Ten Abodes," this refers to the first shattering of a single stage.
"The future fruit does not arise" means that the fruit of transformation does not arise; that is to say, each and every stage possesses its own corresponding future fruit.
To find it easy that self-nature is non-existent means that it is easy to realize that the present twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
To exhaustively investigate the twelve links of dependent origination as being unstained yet stained, and having no beginning, is difficult; therefore, the Bodhisattva perceives only their end.

I maintain that what is said regarding "that which is abandoned at the first stage" refers to the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). This is explained by way of contrast, based on the fact that one first abandons a single grade [of defilement].
However, in the Sūtras, it is taught for the sake of convenience by taking the completion of the entire category as the final point.
Regarding the phrase "beginning to sever": the Bodhisattvas of the first stage and the ten stages are all those who have begun to sever [the afflictions].
Thus, one knows that those in the stage of the worthy (śaikṣa) have not yet seen [the truth] prior to these distinct stages.
The Sūtra states that a "p'o-k'u" (柏毱) is a leather ball; when struck by others, it has no autonomy. Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are likewise:
they are constantly borne along by the wheel of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), transmigrating through the three realms (*tridhātu*) without end.

The three categories, such as those previously defined as "those whose practice is fixed in bliss" and so forth, are as follows: those whose practice is fixed in bliss are Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the provisional;

they are discussed here as being on the ground [of the mundane], seeing [the truth] but not yet clearly. These are the individuals who enter via the Distinct Teaching (biejiao), and thus cannot be entirely identical [to the previous category].
For the time being, we maintain that they are the same as before only in terms of their pedagogical path (*shèndào*).

Regarding the claim that from the perspective of the Ten Abodes it is "not seen": this too cannot be said to be "already seen" at the First Abode. How then can it be called "not seen" when viewed from the subsequent stages?
As for "one single bodhi," there is no distinction in bodhi; how then can it be called "not seen" when viewed from the Ten Abodes? If one says...
If one does not perceive the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and so forth, there ought to be a separate, distinct bodhi.
As for the sūtra’s statement that it is "the emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), this means that the essence of buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) is itself empty;

it is not the same as the "emptiness of the ultimate truth" among the eleven kinds of emptiness. In those [eleven], the emptiness is called the "ultimate truth," and thus it is termed the "emptiness of the ultimate truth."
Regarding the five Buddha-natures: these five do not transcend the three causes. Thus, it is also appropriate to conclude that Buddha-nature consists solely of the three causes.
To address this very objection, it is as stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*: "The Buddha perceives thirty [kinds of impurities] within the bodies of sentient beings."
Endowed with the two marks and the eighty minor characteristics, sitting in the full lotus posture—
this statement made by the Buddha regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* not employing the cultivation of the path is precisely what constitutes the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda’s challenge.

However, while the preceding section merely clarifies the Buddha-nature, the following section excludes what is not it. If one says that the Buddha-nature exists within the present, this is the correct explanation.
To say "it is complete by relying on conditions" means it relies on the conditions of the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature).

Regarding "the offense is not present": because the primary cause is manifest in the present but not yet revealed, it is called "not present. For sentient beings, that which is manifest is called "not future" (non-present).
If one understands this intention, one may say that for sentient beings, both the "presently existing" and the "to-be-existing" are possible. Why? Because of the present.
Because [the fruit] exists, it is realized only when the conditions for the future are complete; thus, there is no contention.
Regarding the attainment of the fruit by way of conditions: sentient beings, due to delusion regarding conditions, have not yet seen [it] and are not yet fulfilled.
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, however, attain it through the conditions that destroy delusion; therefore, there are distinctions such as the various stages (bhūmi). Thus it is said.
Regarding "that which is insufficient for functional use": that which has no use at all is called "insufficient," and that which possesses only partial use is also called "insufficient.

As the Sūtra says: "Although there are no [real] aggregates, elements, or sense-bases of hell," this means that although sentient beings do not yet possess the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of a Buddha.
"In the future, one will certainly attain the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) of a Buddha.
As for the scriptural passage stating, "That which existed originally is now non-existent," the intent of this verse is as follows:

the Lion’s Roar raises the objection that there is originally no distinction, thereby challenging the Buddha's assertion of distinctions. In response, although distinctions are spoken of, the three truths are fully present; therefore, it is said that dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time.
There is no such possibility.
As for that which both differs and does not differ: the upper half differs, while the lower half does not differ. They are neither identical nor different.
This concludes the integration of the three truths in the lower section, returning to the purport of the verse.

Now, regarding the prose commentary (*dīrgha-pada*), the text is divided into two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, a further explanation based on the subsequent section, which again correlates the fundamental and the derivative to establish the fusion of the three truths (*tri-satya*).

The first part is further divided into two: first, the statement of the intent; second, the explanation beginning with "If [one considers] birth-and-death... The explanation itself is further divided into three:

first, the explanation of the upper half-verse and the phrase in the prose commentary concerning the existence of the three times; second, [the explanation of the phrase] "Although birth-and-death... and so forth.
The two truths are synthesized to dissolve the first half [of the verse]. The phrase "the existence of the three original existences" explains the second half.
This concludes the central meaning of the Middle Way, which is the simultaneous negation of both [extremes] without distinction. Next, regarding the conclusion of the three truths, it says:

"The two rivers viewed in relation to one another" refers to the river of birth-and-death and the river of nirvana. If one does not know the supreme source, one will not know the depth of the bottom of these rivers.
"Fundamental and derivative are not fundamental" means that the root of birth-and-death is not the root of nirvana.
"Fundamental and derivative are not derivative" means that the derivative of nirvana is not the derivative of birth-and-death.
That which is neither beginning nor end means that the beginning of birth-and-death and nirvana is not a beginning, because the beginning is itself the end;
and the end of birth-and-death and nirvana is not an end, because the end is itself the beginning. Thus, it does not belong to the three periods of time.
Furthermore, these four modes of explanation essentially do not go beyond difference and non-difference. Why?

Because the first three explanations clarify the difference in the first half [of the verse], while the fourth, which explains through the negation of both, clarifies the non-difference in the second half.
Furthermore, regarding the three types mentioned in the sutras, one must provide a general explanation according to this principle:

if it is said that nirvana exists, then it must be stated that nirvana exists fundamentally and presently throughout the three periods of time; if it is said that it does not exist, then it must be stated that nirvana is fundamentally and presently non-existent throughout the three periods of time.
The same applies to the existence or non-existence of birth-and-death (saṃsāra) in the past and present. Moreover, Buddhas exist throughout all three periods of time.
Regarding "nature": if dharmas exist throughout the three periods of time, then such a case is possible; if dharmas do not exist throughout the three periods of time, then such a case is impossible.

This accords with the intent of the verse. As for these being the Three Truths: the first two—beginning and end—are the conventional (saṃvṛti); the second line is the ultimate (paramārtha); and the third and fourth lines are the middle (madhyamā).
The Path both obstructs and illuminates; each and every instance is both differentiated and non-differentiated, and non-differentiated and equal to differentiation.
That which is not identical to the mind is not yet the Buddha-nature, for although the Buddha-nature should encompass the present mind, it is not yet identical to it.
"One does not take sentient beings as the Buddha-mind" means that the future Buddha is not the presently deluded mind. The intent is that one must practice to attain it;
since it cannot be attained without practice, this is what is being said.
That "the mind is not itself the Buddha-nature" means that the deluded mind is not identical to the resultant Buddha-nature.
"Adorned with the six perfections" refers to the two adornments of conditions and the ultimate cause.
How could this be the same as [the case of] the "ten thousand virtues," which selects the distinct vehicles and provides the various means of deliverance?
When the Sūtra speaks of "ultimate adornment," it describes the ultimate in terms of cultivation and practice.
As for "ultimate," it is described in terms of the principle-body of Buddhahood (buddhatā), the very essence of the adorned, which is the Buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha).

Regarding the statement that there is no separate essence: if that which adorns and that which is adorned were distinct, then the essence of the subject (the adorer) would be different [from the object].
Now, that which adorns only adorns that which is adorned, and that which is adorned in turn adorns that which adorns; therefore, there are not two distinct essences.
The Sūtra states that "Śūraṅgama" refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi discussed in terms of the principle-nature (li-xing).
The Sūtra mentions five names; "Śūraṅgama" is named according to the meditative concentration (samādhi) cultivated based on that principle, while "Prajñā" is named according to wisdom.
"Vajra" is established by way of analogy, meaning that whatever it is aimed at is severed. "Lion's Roar" is established by way of discourse.

"Buddha-nature" refers to the principle-substance of the *dharmakāya*. Furthermore, regarding these five names: *Śūraṅgama* and *Vajra* derive their names from meditative concentration (*samādhi*); *Prajñā* and "Lion's Roar" derive their names from wisdom (*prajñā*);
and "Buddha-nature" encompasses all four names.
Regarding the term *ācārya*, it is called "the Great Earth. The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and desire; wisdom, mindfulness, and attention;
resolve and concentration—these are present in all minds. The commentary explains that the first three lines enumerate [the mental factors].

The fourth phrase explains the attainment of the "great ground" (mahābhūmika) dharmas. "Feeling" (*vedanā*) is that which experiences; it refers to the apprehension of the characteristics of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) is the grasping of images; it refers to the grasping of differentiated conceptualizations regarding the preceding objects.

"Volition" (*cetanā*) is the act of formation; it refers to that which enables the mind to perform formative activities. These arise in conjunction with the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness; they are capable of producing contact (*sparśa*).
Correct. "Desire" (*chanda*) refers to the longing for the task to be performed. "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the capacity to analyze and explain phenomena.
"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to clear recollection of an object without forgetting. "Attention" (*manasikāra*) means directing the mind; its nature is that which causes the mind to be awakened.
"Resolve" (*adhimokṣa*) refers to the ability to confirm an object, thinking, "This thing is thus, and not otherwise. To proceed...
The "exalted resolve samādhi" (adhimokṣa-samādhi) is here called *samāhita*. It refers to holding the mind so that it functions upon a single object;
it is also so called because it holds the mental factors (*caitta*). Regarding the phrase "the mind pervading all minds," this explains the derivation of its name.

These ten mental factors pervade all three natures, the four types of consciousness, the nine stages of the three realms, and all categories of contaminated and uncontaminated minds; therefore, they are called "great."
The "ground" (bhūmi) is the sovereign mind (citta-rāja). These ten factors arise in dependence upon the ground of the mind; thus they are called the "great ground" (mahābhūmika) factors.
As for the statement that these factors pertain to all five categories and that the number of factors arises as ten: the ten factors arise sequentially and cannot occur simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said that they are explained as ten in meaning.
Regarding the fact that the *Śāstra* names this the "Samādhi of the Heroic Aspect" (*śūraṅgama-samādhi*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 37, states:

"The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*—in the language of Qin, 'heroic aspect' (*jiànxiàng*)—is so called because it discriminates and knows the aspects, numbers, magnitudes, depths, and shallowness of all samādhis. As in the Great [Treatise]...
Because he intends to know the strength and numbers of the various forces, he is named Kṣemadarsin (He Who Sees Auspicious Signs).
"One who should speak of 'I'" refers to speaking of the true self (*ātman*).

When the Sūtra says, "I shall receive the complete Dharma from him," the term "Dharma" is used here according to the intention of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), meaning that which is within the Buddha.
For their sake, he taught of a permanent self; they then received the Buddha’s complete Dharma.
As for "harmonizing," it means that where there is existence, one speaks of non-existence, and where there is non-existence, one speaks of existence; this is called harmonizing.
Regarding the twenty kinds of form (*rūpa*): the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there are two kinds of form—first, color (*varṇa*), and second, shape (*saṃsthāna*).

Alternatively, they may be expanded into twenty, as explained in the treatise. The radiance of the sun is called light (*āloka*); the radiance of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, and various flames is called luminosity (*ābhāsa*).

Other visible forms are called shadows (*chāyā*); the opposite of this is darkness (*andhakāra*). When shapes are even, they are called regular (*ṛju*); when uneven, they are called crooked (*vakra*). "Ordinary" (*yod*) refers to a thin veil or obscuration.
The Sūtra says, "By the power of medicine," which refers to the conditions and causes of the medicinal power.
The Sūtra says, "That which is not all is called the Triple Gem," meaning that one does not perceive the Triple Gem as a single essence.
The Sūtra says, "to see even a single portion. This means that those abiding in the first stage all see a single portion of Buddha-nature.
As for the analogy of the initial moon: at the end of the previous month and the beginning of the subsequent month, although it has not yet been fully seen, one cannot say it does not exist.
Those who say it is "gradually exhausted" refer collectively to the stages from the first bhūmi upward.
As for the claim that certain functions have not yet arisen—such as the non-existence of the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth—this may indeed be the case.
If it is said that this nature does not currently exist, it would contradict the sūtras.
As for the phrase "being shrouded by delusion," this very statement already entails a contradiction. Why?
Since it says they are "shrouded by delusion," it follows that they must already be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks.
If one were to claim that seeing [the truth] occurs only upon the elimination of afflictions, this would merely establish a partial meaning and is therefore unacceptable.
Furthermore, one who has not yet realized the perfect principle has likewise not achieved complete perfection.
The Buddha-nature is neither one, two, nor three. The first three masters each cling to their own positions, falling into three distinct categories.

Although they fall into these three categories, because of their respective attachments, they cannot penetrate the underlying principle and perceive the Buddha-nature; they merely produce contentious debate.
Regarding "seeking penetration": if one clings to a single aspect while seeking what is to be penetrated, it can never be attained; therefore, he exhorts them to abandon such clinging.

This is like the saying, "one who sees an elephant. Our school’s interpretation is that this is like obtaining the body of the elephant itself; if one obtains the body of the elephant, one does not lose its head, tail, and other parts.
Between these two lands, the "Superiorly Victorious Pure Land" is established as a third land.
Those at the seventh and eighth stages who have severed their habitual tendencies (vāsanā) merely fulfill the meaning of the Shared Teaching (p'ung-gyo).

Regarding the statement that "the words for destroying afflictions do not appear": this means that only three names are mentioned, and it does not say that after destroying the afflictions, one attains the vision of nature;
therefore, it is so stated.
As for the "three contemplations" in the *Śāstra*, the passage cited from that text does not accord with the present sutra, for that [text] takes impurity as the cause of the mind of loving-kindness.

The three [factors], such as conditions (*pratyaya*), counteract the three [afflictions], such as greed. Now, having destroyed these three types [of afflictions] in this sutra, one attains the vision of the nature;

therefore, it is not the same as that [other system]. Regarding the True Dharma’s destruction of the disease of the provisional: when the mind takes the ultimate principle as its object, it destroys the disease of provisional names.

"Subduing rather than severing" refers to the meaning of destroying the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) to realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is because one must subdue the *kleśas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (*rajas-tulya-avidyā*).

"Emerging with merit" means emerging from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) into the provisional (*saṃvṛti*). The provisional is the merit of benefiting others; furthermore, it is the emptiness of all things within a single emptiness.
Below, I shall explain this by means of the three types of persons within the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
There is one person who, knowing the perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), contemplates that "one is empty and all are empty," thereby perceiving the Buddha-nature.

There is another person who, likewise knowing the perfect interfusion, should contemplate that "one is provisional and all are provisional," thereby perceiving the Buddha-nature. There is yet another person who, also knowing the perfect interfusion, contemplates only "one..."
Within all things, one perceives the Buddha-nature; thus it is said that the three truths are all empty, and so forth.

Yet even those who have not yet understood this fail to realize the depth of the refutation because the ancients did not provide exegesis based on the fourfold teaching (catuṣprakāra-deśanā). Therefore, they do not know the varying degrees of profundity in that refutation.
Regarding "this being from a distinct perspective": it is called a "distinct perspective" in contrast to the Three Teachings.
As for the previous analogy concerning the external: the moon and so forth are the external. Regarding "the mind is internal, etc.":

one should know that each branch of the twelve links of dependent origination possesses both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). For now, we shall provisionally divide form and mind into the categories of external and internal.
The ear is one such branch; it possesses all the remaining branches as well.

I [the author] privately comment that regarding the phrase "the same applies" in the text: since the sutra states this is for both internal and external phenomena, we know that "external" here encompasses both the dependent retribution (the physical environment) and the objective sensory realms.
This does not mean that the twelve [links] take objects as their domain. Rather, the sutra is primarily intended to demonstrate that each and every link possesses Buddha-nature;
it does not specifically intend to analyze the objects of contemplation.
As for "past results," this does not refer to abbreviated results or abbreviated causes, but rather refers to the two causes that give rise to them.
Regarding the five fruits [of karma] mentioned here:

as for the statement that "the seven days constitute the consciousness (vijñāna)," this interpretation is incorrect, as it would necessitate discarding the form of the intermediate state (antarābhava). At the very first moment, the defiled mind-consciousness relies upon the semen and blood of the parents;

when delusive thoughts arise—such as craving for a lotus pond and so forth—it is precisely at that point that it is designated as the limb of consciousness (vijñānāṅga). How could it wait for seven days?

The Japanese scholar obtained the name [of this text]. Next, the Master’s explanation follows that of the *Vibhāṣā*. From consciousness until death in the present body, there are ten periods in total.
There are five periods within the womb and five periods outside the womb; these are termed the "five divisions," which is identical to the current text.
"Designated as 'sentient beings'" means that sentient beings are merely provisional designations.
"Following the five fruits" means receiving the final link among these five fruits.
"Gradually increasing within conditioned formations" means gradually becoming capable of creating karma through the growth of craving and grasping.

As for the mere transference of names: one simply takes present consciousness and designates it as "future birth," and takes present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth and designates them as "future aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇa*), because the results are identical.
The Sūtra states that those who die at the stage of the *kalala* have not yet fully developed the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). These stages are: first, the *kalala*; second, the *arbuda*;
third, the *peśī*; fourth, the *ghana*; and fifth, the *praśākhā*. At the time of such development, it is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
For those who die at this stage, they possess only the first four factors.
They do not possess the feeling of suffering; among the three types of feeling, the intense feeling of suffering is excluded, leaving only the other two.
They lack intense perception and intense craving. Although these intense states are absent, because they still possess pleasant feeling and neutral feeling, they are complete with twelve factors.

Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, "The twelve divisions [of the canon]... not heard," this describes how, in the past, the twelve divisions of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) were concurrently included, yet they did not hear of Buddha-nature.
Although it was not heard in the past, one cannot say that the twelve divisions of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* likewise lack Buddha-nature.

This totals thirty-six phrases. As for the subsequent phrase, "Neither suffering nor pleasure," there is only this single instance of a double negation; this is to be understood according to the various [precedents].
Including the two phrases "suffering" and "non-suffering," there would be thirty-six phrases in total.

Furthermore, the general purport of both the topical outlines and the explanatory text is specifically to clarify that sentient beings inherently possess this principle; all phenomena are fully complete within it, and they are no different from those of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
By practicing, one attains it immediately.

The Sūtra states: "One who understands the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra. This is said because the Nirvāṇa-sūtra explains the twelve links of dependent origination, through which one attains the vision of the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the initial explanation based on both the wholesome and the unwholesome: the first section, beginning with "A certain good man," explains by means of wholesome dharmas.
The subsequent section, from "From desire there are three kinds" down to "this is called evil desire," explains solely by means of unwholesome dharmas.
From "What is great desire? onwards, it provides an explanation based on both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The claim that "liberation" is the opposite of "being burdened" lacks scriptural authority and cannot be accepted.

As for the assertion that sentient beings take the "body of response" (nirmāṇakāya) as their essence—if one were to say that the "heavenly conduct" (deva-caryā) takes "meditative concentration" (samādhi) as its essence, just as sentient beings take the body of response as their essence—then these two would never be related; therefore, such a principle does not exist.
The Sūtra states: "Now, those who have few desires go beneath the trees. This explains, by way of high and low status, the proximity to kings and others;
these are renunciants of inferior appearance.
I say that this is not the case for all [teachings]. For the present sutra takes the Great Nirvana as its essential nature; how could it employ the Small Wheel (kṣudracakra) to explain it?
Regarding those who obtain bliss through internal and external conditions: "external" refers to the Great Nirvana and the dhyāna-methods of the higher realms, as if they have come from without.
Furthermore, regarding that which is extracted from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, namely the *Bodhisattva-śīla-śāstra*—also known as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*—the second [section] asks:
"What is the meaning of 'happiness' (*sukha*)? There are five kinds of the meaning of happiness: first, the happiness of the cause, which is obtained by practicing wholesome dharmas.
Happiness in future lives is called causal happiness. Second is experiential happiness: through causes and conditions, the body attains growth and the mind attains tranquility;
this is called experiential happiness. Third is the happiness of abandoning experience: by cultivating the Noble Path, one abandons all experiences.
The Path increases and flourishes; being devoid of all sensations, it is called the bliss of severing sensation. Fourth is the bliss of seclusion:

being forever free from afflictions so that body and mind are without distress, it is called the bliss of seclusion. Fifth is the bliss of the Bodhisattva: because one experiences eternal bliss, it is called the bliss of the Bodhisattva.
From the initial cultivation of causes to the ultimate attainment of the fruit, it is said to proceed from the shallow to the profound. Thus one hears and sees.
This means hearing from the teaching.

In the "Lion’s Roar" chapter, second, regarding those who wish to hear and see: it exhorts ordinary beings to hear according to the characteristics of the teaching and to see in accordance with the teaching.
Regarding "clearly seeing the meaning": if one can observe in accordance with the teaching, one attains the meaning of seeing.
Furthermore, it is only through the four types of practice for seeing elucidated in the treatise that one attains realized vision.

The Sūtra states: "Regarding the mental characteristics of the Tathāgata: if one can perceive the characteristics of one's own mind in accordance with the teaching, then one perceives the mental characteristics of the Tathāgata.

This is precisely what is proven by the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, which says: "As one contemplates the true reality of one's own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha. This is that very testimony.
Regarding the phrase "taking up hearing, seeing, and so forth," this distinguishes [this practice] from what was explained above. Now, considering the cultivation of ordinary beings:

having heard [the teachings], one reflects and observes what has been heard and seen; thus, hearing is strong while seeing is weak. By means of the eye, one merely sees the Buddha’s body, yet lacks the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the phrase "knowing these as skillful means" and so forth: it is now based on the teaching that one knows all the manifested traces of the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body are shown as skillful means for the sake of sentient beings;
this constitutes the condition (*pratyaya*), and is therefore not the same as what was mentioned above.

Regarding the passage in the sutra that asks, "For whom does one receive a body? and so forth, it is understood that the Tathāgata manifests his body and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding the passage in the sutra that says, "one who inflicts evil physical karma upon [another]," this refers to a prior evil object inflicting [karma] upon the Buddha.
The Sūtra states that "no object is seen as having faults"; this simply means that eating food is subtle.

The Sūtra states that "one does not break the bonds of the Dharma," such as [the view that things are] like illusions or transformations; this clarifies that because of the Middle Way, they are not broken.

Regarding "both abandonments refer to these two teachings": the former two teachings merely eliminate the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; they provisionally establish the name "middle" while lacking the actual substance of a middle.
Therefore, in the first [case], one does not refute the dharmas, and thus it is termed "abandoning both."
Regarding "mutual accomplishment" as the distinct teaching (biejiao): this refers to the phrase "not saving sentient beings" and the phrase "not all things are accomplished.

These two belong to the distinct teaching; that is, the two contemplations prior to the stages (diqian) accomplish the Middle Way upon entering the stages (dengdi), which is termed "mutual accomplishment."

Regarding "shining forth both": this refers to whatever is spoken, specifically the two phrases concerning speaking not for the sake of personal gain; these belong to the category of "shining forth both. As the Sūtra says:
"Right speech" means that gentle words which accord with the Dharma are called right speech; being free from delusion and not speaking falsely constitutes truthful speech.

Speech that is without contradiction and is harmonious according to the occasion is called "timely speech" (*kālavāda*). Speech that is without frivolity or deviation and accords with the principles of the Dharma is termed "truthful speech" (*bhūtavāda*).
As for the "two kinds of causes and conditions" mentioned in the Sūtra: hearing and seeing with the eyes are named "causes and conditions. By means of these two, one relies upon the teaching.
Regarding the practice: one must necessarily perceive the mental characteristics of the Tathāgata.
As for those who are the "four reliances" (catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāni), the intent is that these four reliances may manifest as either coarse or subtle and are difficult to comprehend;
how then can one rely upon the teachings to know the mental characteristics of the Tathāgata?
The first two cases are confused with the latter two: the subtle conduct of the first person and the subtle mind of the second person are confused with that of the third person;
the improper conduct of the first person and the improper mind of the second person are confused with that of the fourth person.
The "directly established Sangha Jewel" refers to the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
As the Sūtra says, "Even Śāriputra’s shadow still trembled," this clarifies the efficacy of the precepts,
serving as a test for whether one has reached the ultimate or not.
The Sūtra says: "If one acts for the sake of the True Dharma, one upholds it with the mind of Great Nirvāṇa.
The Sūtra also says: "It is also called 'hearing and seeing. This refers to the capacity to see the Buddha-nature as being itself hearing and seeing; therefore, it says "also."
The Sūtra says that those with shallow roots have faith-roots that are shallow and easily moved.
"This is like the method of market trade" means that if there is a request for something, one exchanges it for what is valuable according to the method of market trade.

Regarding "spontaneous naturalness" (*svarasadharmatā*): it is so called because these fourteen aspects of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are established as spontaneous, proceeding from the shallow to the profound.
As the Sūtra says: "Therefore, the nature of the Bodhisattva is inherently low," which concludes the preceding thirteen phrases.
Regarding the prior reception of the intent: one obtains two fruits by means of two causes. This is truly as the Buddha taught.
As for the scripture stating that "precepts have no cause," it is because precepts are at the beginning; there is only the fruit, and no other separate dharma acts as the cause for the precepts.
Therefore, it is said they have no cause.

The Sūtra states that "Nirvāṇa has no fruit. Since liberation is the cause of Nirvāṇa, and Nirvāṇa in turn serves as the cause for the attainment of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, one might conclude that Nirvāṇa has no fruit. If it were indeed without fruit, it would be an impermanent dharma.
How then could the Tathāgata say: "By virtue of upholding the precepts, one attains the vision of the Buddha-nature and abides in Great Nirvāṇa"?

Regarding the statement that "Nirvana abides at the end of all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*): this was discussed previously in the eleventh commentary (*vṛtti*) before the section on the "phrase of Nirvana.
That [previous point] is difficult to reconcile; therefore, it is here merely referred to as being "at the end."
The Sūtra says: "It is like lighting a lamp; without causes and conditions, there would be no conditions for the lamp. Only through their conjunction do conditions exist.
That which exists through conjunction was originally non-existent and now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence; this is an impermanent dharma. Nirvāṇa is also like this;
it should therefore be impermanent."

Regarding "tying one side of the knot": this refers to not tying one side of the observance of the precepts. It should be said that if the observance of the precepts is thus, it constitutes the constant rule.
Regarding "the days of Śākyamuni being short": from dawn until midnight.

Regarding "the jar is established by means of the stand": this means that because of the jar, the stand is established; and because of the stand, the jar is established. This constitutes being mutually cause and effect.
This interpretation does not fully accord with the sutra. Our school takes only the mutual causality of the three legs of the stand as the intended meaning.
The two feet stand supported by the foot-stand; the single foot, in turn, stands supported by the two feet. The three feet face one another in succession:

one serves as the primary cause (*hetu*), and the other two serve as the secondary causes (*upādāna-hetu*). This is likewise true for the fruit (*phala*) and the subsequent fruit (*phala-phala*). [The characters] *jū* (pronounced *sǔn*) and *xū* (pronounced *jù*).

Regarding "mutually ascending and descending": when there is ascent, descent serves as the cause and ascent serves as the effect; when there is descent, ascent serves as the cause and descent serves as the effect.
This interpretation is not used in its entirety in the current admonition.
If one were to definitively establish the three periods of time, one would not take the two causes of the past and the five fruits of the present;

rather, one takes the three causes of the present and the two causes of the future to manifest cause and effect. Cause and effect are taken merely as they mutually condition one another, thereby manifesting the characteristics of causal conditions and resultant fruits.
Furthermore, regarding the refusal to employ the principles of the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā): traditionally, this school has never used such principles to interpret the present text.

The Master’s intention here is that one may merely borrow the terminology of "great birth" and "small birth" as an analogy for the cause and effect in this passage; thus, there is no fault in the meaning of cause and effect.
The Sūtra states that "arising can give rise to dharmas," which clarifies "great arising" (mahā-utpāda). This refers only to the ability to give rise to dharmas such as form and mind;
it cannot arise by itself. It is like the eye of the world, which cannot see itself and likewise cannot liberate itself because it does not arise from itself.

Through "arising-of-arising" (utpādotpāda), one clarifies this great arising; for it is through the arising-of-arising that the small arising gives rise to the great arising, as the small arising is uniquely capable of giving rise to the great arising.

Therefore, it is called "the arising of arising. The Great Arising (*mahā-jāti*) is that which is produced by this "arising of arising," and thus it is named the "arising of arising. This "arising of arising" does not arise of itself;
it depends upon the Great Arising.

By the term "arising," it is clarified that the Small Arising (*parīttā-jāti*) arises by means of the Great Arising. Although the Small Arising is indeed capable of producing the Great Arising, it cannot [arise]...
Because they arise spontaneously. Relying on the "Great Arising" (mahābhūta) to produce this [derived matter] is precisely how the scriptural text is explained.

That the "great characteristics" (mahālakṣaṇa) are the cause is because they are able to give rise to the "small characteristics" (parīttalakṣaṇa). Therefore, the small characteristics are the "cause-cause" (hetu-hetu).

Furthermore, it may also be that the small characteristics are the cause and the great characteristics are the "cause-cause," because they act as the cause for the fundamental dharma. Moreover, the great characteristics...

Regarding the eight characteristics, each possesses the capacity for all eight; yet, by citing only one characteristic, all eight are already included. This is because a minor characteristic possesses the capacity for only one, being able to produce only a single major characteristic.
Regarding the phrase "because it is a fruit of cultivation": it is a fruit of cultivation because it is obtained by means of destroying the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the phrase "there is no dependent cause": this reveals that *nirvāṇa* is established as a cause that is free from all dependence.

As for the phrase "merely a linguistic expression," it means that there is ultimately no linguistic expression at all; it is similar to non-existence, yet not identical to cases such as "at times non-existent.
Because its essence is ultimate non-existence characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity, it is not the primary intended meaning.
"Scattered in a cage" means they exist because clouds have dispersed.
The meaning of "mutual non-existence" is like a *caṇḍāla* having no *brāhmaṇa* dharma,
and a *brāhmaṇa* having no *caṇḍāla* dharma.
There is a "small portion" that is *nirvāṇa*, which is ultimately non-existent; yet it is coextensive with *nirvāṇa* as quiescence (*śānti*), though it lacks the substantiality of *nirvāṇa*.
It is fully endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Therefore, in comparison to the other five portions, it is called the "small portion."

The Sūtra states that sentient beings have parents because it is through various fetters (*saṃyojana*) that sentient beings are formed; only when sentient beings obtain parents can they achieve completion.
Therefore, parents are termed the "efficient cause" (*niṣpādaka-hetu*).
The Sūtra states that the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) are the causes of birth because they can directly give rise to bodhi.
Regarding the subsequent "horizontal and vertical" [classification]: the Eightfold Noble Path is horizontal, while the six perfections are vertical.
The world is collectively constrained by these two [positions]: if one says that produced fruits are impermanent, one is constrained by [the fact that] Nirvāṇa is permanent.
Furthermore, regarding those who employ the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, they take the *Śūraṅgama* concentration as the cause of production.
The analogy of the centipede refutes the first master; the analogy of the bird deprived of both wings refutes the next master.
Since the bird cannot achieve flight, it is like the Buddha-nature having no essence.
How could one who practices a single liberation still not be [in the state where] both are identical? This is why it is so.

Next, the Master [Sthiramati], by taking "being alone in the middle" as the definition of "single liberation," first refutes those who hold that the effect exists within the cause; this specifically refutes the view that the effect exists within the cause.
Regarding the Buddha-nature as the Middle Way: because they are conjoined [with it], it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
When people of the world seek curd, they take milk; likewise, if one seeks Buddha-nature, one seeks it within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
How can it be said that the Buddha-nature is not an internal nature when it ought to be within? For what reason is it said that the Buddha-nature is not internal?
The Sūtra says: "I do not say that there is curd within milk; nor do I say that curd already exists within milk."
As for the result, it is merely said that there is the nature of curd.
As for "milk being emptiness," the essence of milk is fundamentally and ultimately empty; it exists by virtue of causes and conditions and is but a provisional designation.

Regarding the scriptural passage stating that "all dharmas of birth and so forth," the intent of the objection is as follows: All dharmas do not depend upon causes and conditions but are spontaneously accomplished when the time arrives;
the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise so. Why, then, does it further state that it is "neither internal nor external"?
The meaning of the Buddha’s answer is this: I merely state that milk possesses the nature of curd; at no time do I say that the fruit of curd already exists during the stage of milk.
Therefore, it is said that there is no curd at the time of milk.

Regarding the essential nature of these delusions: since the very essence of these delusions arises and ceases in the same instant, there is nothing that can be bound.
When the Sūtra says, "Because of these five aggregates," etc., this passage primarily clarifies that the cause is not identical to the fruit, yet the fruit is brought about by means of the cause;
the analogy is likewise. The application in the summary text uses only the method [of the analogy], and its meaning can be understood through careful reflection.

As for the statement in the Sūtra, "I shall analyze and explain for you," it means that I shall analyze for you these aggregates (skandhas), such as whether they reach that state or do not reach that state.
Although the Sūtra mentions the five sense-faculties (pañca-indriyāṇi), when the five sense-faculties have ceased and gradually become feeble, there is no longer perception or cognition.

The Sūtra states: "In principle, there is no such thing as 'westward departure' (*xīshì*). *Shì* (departure) means to go. Since the sun sets in the west from the east, there is no principle by which it could again go toward the east.
Furthermore, this is merely a shadow; there is likewise no principle by which it could return to the west. Both interpretations are valid.
"Death and birth occur simultaneously" means that this textual combination establishes the intended meaning of the analogy.

As for the sutra stating, "As a lamp is lit, darkness is extinguished," it means that birth and extinction are simultaneous, and extinction and birth are simultaneous; there is no other intervening mind that could serve as a counterpart.
The Sūtra says, "It is like a wax seal pressed into clay. When the wax seal is between the [clay] and the [surface], it is called a "seal.

This body is not something produced from within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); this clarifies that the intermediate state body does not arise spontaneously from the intermediate state itself, but exists due to the karmic causes and conditions of the death-aggregate (*maraṇaskandha*).
The scripture states that "the characters do not emerge from the clay"; this is because the characters depend upon the wax seal.
The scripture further states that "they do not come from elsewhere"; this is also because the characters appear through the conjunction of the wax and the clay; hence these words are spoken.

Regarding the analogy of a great judicial prison: this refers to the worldly judge who, analogous to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), definitively adjudicates good and evil before one may undergo rebirth.
Furthermore, since good and evil deeds are already fixed in the past, the intermediate state merely serves to pass judgment upon those matters.
It is also said that one remains within the intermediate state for either seven days or many days; the sense of "many days" carries greater weight, as it constitutes the cause for entering the womb.
The conditions for meeting are difficult to encounter. Furthermore, the semen and blood of the parents are like mud; consciousness takes refuge therein as its father.
As for what is called "clenching" (cuǎn), it should be termed "edible food by mouthfuls" (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra). If food were mixed with water, it could not be clenched.
Thus, the term "clenched" used here is not entirely accurate.

Regarding those who possess the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), such as the locus where thought arises and so forth: that which sustains the body so that it may endure is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*).
By means of these three types of nutriment, the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is able to endure.
Regarding the ancient passage on the "four nutriments," as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: "Solid foods such as cakes, fruits, and rice are called *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (edible food).
The volitional seeking of such solid food so that life is not cut off is called *manasa-āhāra* (mental food). Sensations of cold, warmth, and so forth are called *sparśa-āhāra* (contact food)."

The mental consciousness sustains the body so that it does not perish; this is called the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*). According to the Abhidharma, all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) that sustain the body and prevent its destruction are termed edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Among the mental factors (*caitasika*), volition (*cetanā*) is the nutriment of volition (*cetanāhāra*), and contact (*sparśa*) is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
The six consciousnesses, as the sovereign mind, are called the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*). What is now explained in this sutra is for the most part consistent with the Abhidharma.

Regarding the statement that one can "skillfully contemplate and observe" (*vitarka-vicāra*): this refers to the mental activity of reflecting upon good and evil, as well as the volition regarding the place of rebirth; these are precisely what constitutes contemplation and observation.

The Sūtra states: "Regarding those who give rise to love for the mother, a male receives birth; they feel love for the mother and hatred toward the father, seeing the father as a rival for their beauty.
Regarding those who receive birth as female, they feel love for the father and hatred toward the mother."
"This is my view" means that [the five aggregates] are already mine; therefore, they belong to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding "in emptiness there is no thorn of arising": the five aggregates of death are fundamentally empty and lack the thorns of afflictions (*kleśa*); how then can one now cultivate the Noble Path to sever them?

Regarding the scriptural passage concerning "folding [the fingers]" and so forth: simply grasping the fingers constitutes folding; when the fingers are released, the folding ceases. If one does not understand this, one might think that the folding and the fingers are distinct entities.
The relationship between the aggregates (*skandhas*) and the afflictions (*kleśas*) is exactly like this: through delusion they bind, and through awakening one realizes the entirety of *dharmatā*.
Examples such as joining the palms should be understood accordingly. The explanation provided in the Commentary represents but one approach.
Regarding the statement "because retribution exists, there are bonds": these bonds are themselves liberation.
As for *ti*, it refers to that which falls from heaven as a drop. As for *di*, it refers to the substance of a single drop itself.
Regarding "nurturing": it is like a mother nurturing her child; the child relies upon the mother as its model.
Although all phenomena (*dharmas*) are ultimately empty, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) are what are termed "all phenomena."
"Unfulfilled" means not yet perfected.

Regarding those born into the families of butchers and sheep-slaughterers: it is because the evil conditions from previous lives have not been exhausted that they are born into such families; it is not due to the influence of untainted [outflows] that this occurs.
Regarding the six similes: among these six, only the first and the last are explained, while the middle four are not.
This opening of both the causes of habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*) and retribution (*vipāka-hetu*) takes the power of the Path as the cause of habituation.
Regarding those born in evil lands: they are drawn to birth in such lands by the牵引 (inducing) power of various causes for unwholesome retribution.
As for the "inferior and superior": this refers to the fact that even Bodhisattvas of the six perfections cannot be found there, let alone those who follow the later teachings.
Regarding the "boundless mind": because it takes boundless consciousness as its object, it is called the boundless mind.
Regarding the "pure aggregate": when the mental aggregate is free from manifold objects and concentrated in a single place, it is called the pure aggregate.
Regarding the "Man in the Water": in the beginning, when the world had not yet formed land and there was only water, he sat within that water.
Non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) observed him and named him the "Man in the Water."
Regarding "further extending to what precedes": this refers to the passages concerning the preceding period and the moment-to-moment [arising].
Regarding "the two past causes," one should further state that there are three present causes and two future fruits; therefore, it is not *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the presentation of the two chapter headings: there is a fault in taking them together, and there is also a fault in taking them individually; therefore, they are asked about in pairs.
The Sūtra says that "that which can be calculated" refers to those things each person obtains individually, which are dharmas that can be counted.
Because they are not one, they are not shared; because the ultimate end is attained [by each], they are not distinct.
Because they are not two, they are not separate; this is because their essence is identical.

Regarding the "essential nature of the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-svabhāva*), only the pure portion of the dharma-realm's essence is taken; the text thus excludes the five, six, or seven consciousnesses. Furthermore...
