He went forth and received the precepts within the Mahāsāṃghika community, became learned and diligent, and resided on Mount Caitya. Together with the monks of that school, he re-examined the five matters in detail.

Consequently, they led the disputes and divided into three schools. First, the Caitika school; "Caitika" means "Spiritual Temple" (lingmiao), because spiritual temples were established for offerings at all four sites:
the initial birth, the attainment of enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the parinirvāṇa.

Second, the Aparaseliya school, which is the Caitika school residing in the Western Mountains; "Apara" means "Western. Third, the Uttaraseliya school, which is the Caitika school residing in the Northern Mountains; "Uttara" means "Northern."

The Uttaraśaila school originally explained [the teachings] separately, forming nine divisions in total. Regarding the two Sthavira schools, by the third century, Kātyāyanīputra first entered the monastic order within the Sthavira tradition.
He extensively propagated the Dharma of the single flavor, while propagating the Sūtras and Vinaya to a lesser extent.
After his death, the school’s tenets were subsequently divided into two branches. Among these, the Sarvāstivāda school has two [divisions]: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)...

The three time periods [are conditioned]; the two unconditioned phenomena transcend the time periods—namely, space, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Their essence all exists, and thus they are called "All-Existence" (*Sarvāstivāda*); they are also called the "Explanatory-Cause School" (*Hetuvāda*), meaning that this school establishes its tenets by extensively producing logical reasons.
Second, the Sthavira school changed its name to the Haimavata school. Originally, the disciples of the Sthaviras propagated the scriptural teachings; the Hetuvāda school gave rise to many...

As for Mahādeva, since he was already well-versed in the Abhidharma and its principles, he was able to subdue the Sthaviras. The Sthavira school, being weakened, subsequently moved into the Snowy Mountains to avoid him;
the name [of that school] is derived from their place of residence. In the third century after the [Buddha’s] passing, a school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda named the Vātsīputrīya.
In ancient times, there was a rishi who fathered a son by a cow; since then, this has been the lineage of the rishis.
All are called Vātsīputrīya, which is a Brahmin clan name. Three hundred years later, four schools branched out from the Vātsīputrīya:
first, the Dharmottarīya; because there is a Dharma that can be ascended, it is named Dharmottara. Second, the Bhadrayānīya;
"Bhadra" is a name for a master, and "yāna" has the meaning of lineage or descendant. As they are the descendants of Arhats, they are called Bhadrayānīya. Third...

The Saṃmitīya school: this means that they provisionally establish [their tenets] through investigation and determination, naming them "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). Because their cognition is free from error, it is called "correct" (*saṃmita*).
The fourth is the Madhyāntika (Mili-lin-shan) school. This is named after the location where its founder resided, a place near a forest dense with thick honey.
Three hundred years later, another school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda, named the Mahīśāsaka.
Its founder was formerly a king who spread his transformative influence over the people and deer upon the earth; he later renounced his kingdom to become a monk, taking his name from this origin.
This is called the *Mahīśāsaka* school. Next, three hundred years later, a school emerged from the *Mahīśāsaka*, named the *Dharmaguptaka*.
It is also called the *Dharmānanda-sūtra* school; according to Paramārtha, it is called the *Dharmarakṣita* school. This arhat was a disciple of Maudgalyāyana.
After Maudgalyāyana passed away, he followed the teachings of his teacher Dharmarakṣita and compiled them into five collections (*piṭakas*): first, the Sūtra-piṭaka.
Second, the Vinaya Piṭaka; third, the Śāstra; fourth, the Mantra Piṭaka; and fifth, the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

Within the Saṃmitīya school, there is a branch that agrees with their establishment of these five piṭakas but constitutes them as a separate school, named the Dharmaguptaka. Next, during the third century, from the Sarvāstivāda school, another school emerged named the Kāśyapīya;
in Sanskrit it is called Kāśyapa, which here is translated as "Drinking Light" (Yǐnguāng).

[Regarding] the *Prabhāsa* [sect]: Kāśyapa was of noble nature. In ancient times, there was a rishi whose bodily radiance was so intensely brilliant that he eclipsed all other light, rendering it invisible.
The founder of this school was a descendant of him.
At the beginning of the fourth century, another school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda, named the Sautrāntika. These masters accepted only the sūtras as authoritative, not the vinaya.
Furthermore, regarding the Abhidharma, whatever meanings are explained therein are corroborated by the Sūtras; these are named after their respective masters.
Originally and subsequently, they form eleven distinct sections. When combined with the nine sections of the Mahāsāṃghika previously discussed, they constitute twenty sections in total.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra that mentions "faithful offerings" and so forth: this refers to faith in the three treasures as being of one essence, as well as in the causality of good and evil deeds.

If one were to interpret it according to a distinct meaning, then in the provisional teachings of the past, one could only widely proclaim and disseminate [the Dharma] for others upon reaching the stage of the ten practices;
it was only upon reaching the subsequent mind of dedication that one would see the Buddha-nature.

"Everlasting and unchanging" refers to those who have been received [into the path] but have not yet reached [the ultimate goal]; they are known in the present sutras as those who shall abide [in the truth].
These are the people of the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching within the present sutras. This stage is shared with the ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) of the four teachings;
therefore, it is called "small and great. Since both positions are contained therein, there is the need for the two explanations regarding the regression of Sudatta.

Regarding those who are practitioners of the Three Vehicles at the initial stage: they belong to the Vaipulya (fangděng) division. This refers to those who, after previously regressing from the Mahāyāna, remained undeluded by the Hīnayāna during the intervening period;
now, through this present sutra, they openly hear of the eternal [Dharma], yet temporarily take the fruits of the Small Vehicle as a place of rest.

Therefore, they do not conform to the current sutra’s treatment of the Three Vehicles. This matter relates extensively to the Small and Great Vehicles, as well as the Five Periods and Eight Teachings, which have been brought down to the present day.

The sutra further clarifies that one should know the provisional attainment of the fruits of the four stages as a state of rest within the context of eternal abiding; these cannot be definitively fixed or categorized.
Furthermore, this combined passage begins from the second person: first it cites the practice of the first person, then it sets forth the characteristics of the second person's practice.
As for the third person, it first cites the first two persons, and then, from the section "cultivating wisdom" onwards, it sets forth [the third].

The conduct of the third person: the fourth person first cites the conduct of the preceding three; then, from "next, practicing wisdom" (*tadanu prajñāṃ bhāvayati*) downward, he shows the conduct of the fourth person.
The fifth person first cites the conduct of the preceding four; then, from "next, practicing wisdom" downward, he shows the conduct of the fifth person.
The sixth person first cites the conduct of the preceding five; then, from "next, practicing" (*tadanu abhyasya*) downward, he shows the conduct of the sixth.

The characteristics of the person on the path: The seventh person first summarizes the preceding six persons, and subsequently provides a lower-level illustration to demonstrate the characteristics of the seventh person’s practice.

The Sūtra states, "dwelling upon a great high mountain. While the previous Bodhisattvas had only reached the shallow regions of causal practice, this one now dwells upon the exceedingly high and vast mountain of the ultimate stage.
Judging by this, it is the stage of Buddhahood.
Therefore, regarding the division into four persons: within the stage of the sages, the four fruits are counted as one, and the Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Buddha constitute the other three.
As for the presence of both textual accounts, these refer to the general and specific texts.
Regarding the desire to cause something to be drawn in: if the stone does not move and the iron comes of its own accord, this is called "attraction. Sentient beings are likewise;
having already possessed the Buddha-nature, if they do not practice the path-factors of non-action, Bodhi will be realized spontaneously. This principle corresponds to "attraction."
The Sūtra says: "Although it is a dharma that exists," it refers to the dharma of natural retribution. The Sūtra says:
"Those who do not cultivate the Way" means those who do not cultivate the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) factors of enlightenment; how then could they see their nature?

Regarding this "the Prajñāpāramitā manifesting" on this stage: ancient masters paired the ten pāramitās vertically with the ten stages, such that Prajñā corresponds to the sixth, the Manifesting (Abhimukhī) stage.
This is what is meant by "correspondence," which refers to a constant reckoning.

Regarding the statement "that which is done is that which is received," it should rather be said that "that which is done is not that which is received. As for "sucking up mustard seeds," it means sucking up grass and chaff.
Regarding "arising through different dharmas": through the causes and conditions of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) factors of the path, there arises permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

through the causes and conditions of evil karma, one is born into the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). To speak correctly of cause and effect, there is nothing produced by a single cause and a single condition that is not [subject to these].

They are distinct dharmas. Furthermore, because the three delusions are extinguished through the causes and conditions of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the Buddha-nature arises.

Moreover, it is precisely because the causes and conditions—such as permanence and impermanence—are each distinct that they are termed "fruition-dharmas. *Huò* (homophonous with *hù guō*; the *Guǎngyá* states that the pods of a bean are called *jié*, while their leaves are called *huò*).
The Sūtra states that as for "the existence of the Buddha," the intrinsic nature of the twelve links of dependent origination exists of itself and does not come into being through the Buddha;

only then does it exist. The Sūtra further states that the twelve links of dependent origination have no fixed abode; this is because the three paths are themselves the three virtues of Buddha-nature, and therefore they have none.

Regarding the "fixed location," the Sūtra states that the Dharma-dhātu and the Dharma-āyatana are the answer. This refers to the dharmas of the eighteen dhātus, the twelve āyatanas, and the five skandhas;
all are attained through realization and are none other than the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Therefore, they are all called "Dharma."

Regarding the absence of a single cause: there is no distinct cultivation of a single cause that constitutes the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*). It is likewise for the fire element (*tejo-mahābhūta*) and the others acting as causes.
Although there is no separate cause, the functional power of the four elements—such as the extension [of soil] and so forth—is nevertheless distinct in each case.
"Buddha-nature is also like this": when one cultivates the factors of the path of non-action and the causal conditions reach maturity, Buddha-nature is immediately manifested;
therefore, it is said that "when the time arrives, it appears.
Regarding the two phrases "immediate" and "separate": because it is immediate, it exists; because it is separate, it is absent.
Regarding the phrase "if one grasps the six dharmas, etc.": if one reckons each of these six dharmas individually as being the Buddha-nature, one is like the group of blind men.

Regarding "grasping that which is neither identical nor separate": because they are not identical, they are both simply principles; because they are not separate, one must cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) to necessarily attain [the fruit], just as a wise king or minister possesses wisdom.

Regarding the "extensive traversal of all dharmas": why should it be that only the twelve links of dependent origination constitute the Buddha-nature? It is the same for all dharmas, such as the Four Noble Truths and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
As for those who speak of "permanence and pervasiveness," they calculate that there is a self—whether of great or small form—dwelling within them.
Some say it is like a mustard seed; this is the calculation that matter is large while the self is small.
It also refutes both identity and separation: when there is no self, identity is refuted and non-existent; when there is no self, separation is refuted and non-existent.

"All are merely provisional designations" means that both "self" and "non-self" are produced through causes and conditions; they are empty, false, and unreal, existing only as provisional designations.
This is not the same as the "no-substance-but-with-function" theory established by the Kaishan school.
If sentient beings should also attain it, it ought to be called "attainment.
When the Sūtra speaks of the "Stage of the Only Son," it refers to the Buddha’s ultimate Stage of the Only Son.
To "know the faculties and conditions of beings" means to know their illnesses, recognize the appropriate medicines, and administer those medicines according to their specific ailments.
There is another so-called "name-teaching" (mingjiao), which refers to these numerical categories found within the various sutras.

As for the statement that the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) are the wisdom of contemplation (vipaśyanā-jñāna), this refers merely to the nature of the causes and conditions themselves.

Regarding the statement that there are other sources: as in this sutra, the contemplation of the wisdom of the twelve links of dependent origination differs according to the four teachings—namely, the lower, middle, upper, and supreme-upper wisdoms.
These are explained in detail within the *Four Teachings Great Text* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra Commentary*. Therefore, the commentary states "and so forth."
The Sūtra states that the "Crown Samādhi" (Mūrdha-samādhi) is so named because it is attained by Bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage.
Regarding the passage from "all sentient beings" to "are unable to know," this means that although they will attain *bodhi* in the future,
it is currently inconceivable.
The Sūtra says, "Great Nirvāṇa... inconceivable. This sūtra is able to expound upon Buddha-nature; thus it is named "Inconceivable.

[The character *xi* (序)]—as Master Pisheshong said—"is a class of characters resembling *he* (和) and *chong* (崇), and its phonetic description is like *xu* (序) and *su* (粟). [The character *li* (黎)] is pronounced with the rhyme *luo-ji* (洛嵇).
The Sūtra states, "proceeding with the wind. This means that the surging waves cause the great ocean to gradually deepen.

Why do you offer a one-sided interpretation? You should understand that when the horizontal and vertical are non-dual, the three truths are mutually identical; when duality is extinguished, both are simultaneously illumined—all of which is inconceivable.
Only then does it accord with the intent of the Sūtra. Why do you limit yourself to an interpretation of only vertical depth?
Volume Thirteen: The Chapter on Kāśyapa. The initial commentary on the *Śāstra* is divided into two parts:

first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation following the text. The first part [the explanation of the title] is further divided into three sections: first, a brief clarification of the reasons for establishing the name;
second, "Kai-sen" and below, a description of ancient interpretations; third, "Now I clarify" and below, an indication of the meaning of the chapters. The first section says "Good."
Regarding the phrase "beginning with," etc.: previously, thirty-four questions were posed whose meaning was discussed extensively; this is called a "good beginning.
Now, by asking again, one clarifies their functional significance, which constitutes their cultivation.

Regarding the previous practice of titling chapters according to their meaning: although it was Kāśyapa who posed the questions in the preceding sections, their meanings are so vast that the chapter titles were established merely in accordance with the categories of meaning; this is precisely why it does not say "Kāśyapa."
Regarding the phrase "the one who skillfully maintains the compassionate light of antiquity":
the following clarifies that the supreme function of Buddha-nature is able to encompass even Sunakṣatra and those of the most evil icchantikas, biased heretics, and outsiders.

It is through the Tathāgata’s unconditioned compassionate light that Buddha-nature is universally revealed, causing the Dharma to abide for a long time; therefore, it is called "maintaining" (zhuchi).

Regarding the meaning of the third chapter, there are two parts: first, the formal presentation of the chapter’s intent; second, from "This sutra" onwards, the differentiation of distinctions to clarify the basis for its title.
The first part follows the text. Within the first section, there are again two parts: first, stating the intent to raise the inquiry; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "One meaning.
In the explanation, the phrase "the meaning of Buddha-nature... [is] the seed" indicates that Buddha-nature itself is precisely the seed of bodhi.
Regarding the supreme function of Buddha-nature: Buddha-nature is the supreme dharma. If it were not a supreme dharma, how could there be a supreme function?

As for "proceeding from the evil five aggregates" and so forth: from the wholesome aggregates arise the untainted (anāsrava) five aggregates; from the untainted five aggregates arises the aggregate of nirvana.
Beginning with the evil aggregates of an icchantika up to those of the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), all are nothing other than the nature of fruition.
"Those who have traditionally explained it" refers to the fact that scholars of antiquity have all provided this interpretation.
Regarding "the nature of the fruit of fruits reaching the response-body (nirmāṇakāya)": the three periods [of time] manifest as the three periods.

Regarding "Buddha-nature within the causal stage being subsumed under the world": the Buddha-nature of the true cause is entirely present within birth-and-death; therefore, it is subsumed under the world.
Regarding the convergence of the three vehicles: they all reach the other shore together.
As for the statement that all six realms possess Buddha-nature, it means that each and every one is endowed with the five kinds of Buddha-nature.

The previous chapter specifically relied on the "completing cause" (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) of the myriad virtues; it extensively refuted fixed karma to demonstrate its indeterminacy, thereby causing [beings] to practice.

The "Chapter on the Path" (Dàopǐn) enables one to see the Buddha-nature; it clarifies cultivation in terms of practice, and thus belongs to the "revealing cause" (liǎoyīn). The present chapter, however, is categorized according to its universal inclusion, and thus belongs to the "conditioning cause" (yuán yīn).
Regarding the first sense: from the perspective of the primary intent of these five chapters, their titles are identical to those established for the initial major sections.

The subsequent explanation of the text is divided into three parts: first, the presentation and listing of the topical headings; second, the "Ancient Exegesis" section below which describes the views of predecessors;

third, the "Severing of the Wholesome Roots" section below which provides the formal explanation. The first part [the presentation of headings] is further divided into two: first, the listing of the headings; second, the explanation beginning with "By the power of delusion.

Regarding the meaning of the heading: as for "by the power of delusion," there is no separate delusion; rather, the Buddha-nature itself is entirely delusion. It is in contrast to the aspect of severing the wholesome roots that it is established and given this name.
Next, the exposition of the ancient [views] consists of four parts: first, the initial exposition; second, "Now, below, I shall briefly refute [them] to demonstrate the correct principle";

third, "The old [masters] say," which is a re-exposition of the ancient interpretation; and fourth, "As for the meaning," which is the extensive refutation. Regarding the first point, "the two persons alternate with one another": one person...
When one person performs good, another performs evil; when one person performs evil, another performs good.

Next, within the exposition of the correct principle, it says: "As with the seven types in the river. These seven pass through the river, either leaping over or proceeding in succession, as they encounter the three stages of the Buddha-nature.
In the commentary, it says: regarding the meaning of "connecting consciousness," the *Record of the Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* cites this master’s established doctrine.

Regarding those who have not yet aroused the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*): there is this interpretation from ancient masters found in the *Shuji* (Commentary) on the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith). [The question is:
"If even those who have aroused the four abidings are received by a Buddha and go forth to attain Buddhahood, why is it that only those who have not yet aroused them [are so described]?"

Regarding the statement in the *Catuḥśataka-vṛtti* that "eighty thousand kalpas" is given: this is identical to the outsiders' reckoning [of time] as being like a ball of thread, where one naturally attains the Way once it is exhausted.
"It should be in another place" means it should be in a place free from afflictions (*kleśa*).

The previous refutations of this doctrine are most numerous within the *Siṃhanāda-sūtra*. This conception—that [the Buddha-nature] functions by its own power, like a stone spontaneously drawing [water] toward itself—includes the beginning and the end;
that is, in all six analogies, the Bodhisattvas come first, followed by the followers of the Two Vehicles, and finally the icchantikas, establishing the meaning of their attainment of bodhi.
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, as for its correspondence with the five periods from beginning to end,
I shall for now provide a general alignment according to the text. As for the passage in the Sūtra stating,
"The meaning of the world," this includes the words *icchantika* when discussing worldly causes and effects, as well as supramundane causes and effects.

Regarding the "Householder": the Buddhas take the transformation of sentient beings as their primary task; this is why, until the very end, they do not abandon those of indeterminate nature (*icchantika*).
The principle that this encompasses all without distinction means that if there were no equality, how could there be equal teaching? Therefore, it is said to be without distinction.

Regarding the insufficiency of the elephant: if one were to discuss it in terms of specific phenomena, the power of the elephant would be exhausted by the fire, and its strength would still be feared as insufficient.
This merely serves to illustrate the analogy; the correspondence between the metaphor and the actual teaching is not exact.
The Sūtra asks: "For what reason does an Arhat [speak] regarding an Arahant? Sunakṣatra thought to himself:
"Arhat is small; Arahant is great. Why would the World-Honored One harbor a mind of envy and jealousy toward one who is greater than himself?"
As for their seeing one another so clearly: generally, humans and ghosts do not meet face-to-face.
That they are now able to see each other is proof that this is a manifestation of great expedient power (*mahopāya*).
Regarding the failure to see those who were subsequently received: it is like failing to see the asuras being taken up into the ocean by the hand of the latter [Vemacitra].
Regarding "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*): it is called unobstructed because it universally severs both mundane and supramundane wholesome states.

As for the analogy of the "unobstructed" state of the untainted (*anāsrava*), this is a partial illustration; while the untainted arises once and is never lost or extinguished, an icchantika may give rise to a wholesome mind when encountering the right conditions. Therefore, it is not a complete analogy.
Those who committed evil in the past possess only the "correct cause" (正因) of goodness; they have not yet attained the goodness acquired through cultivation (修得善).
Those who are outside the principle (理外) are sentient beings who have not yet accorded with the Buddha's teachings in their practice.
Regarding "unable to save them": because their seeds are exhausted and weak, it is said they are "unable.
Furthermore, that "Buddha-nature is permanent" refers to the Buddha-nature as the True Cause (*zhengyin*).
The phrasing "causing [them] to exert themselves" is based on the Sūtra which states, "The self-nature and Buddha-nature of sentient beings are permanent," meaning that by means of the True Self...
This reveals that the Buddha-nature and its characteristics are both eternal by nature.
The Sūtra says, "fully endowed with adornment," which refers to the attainment of the conditions and the cause [of Buddhahood].
This is what is meant by "possessing goodness. If one possesses goodness, why is such a person called an icchantika?
The Sūtra states that one who asks such a question quickly will bring great benefit, enabling sentient beings of future generations to attain correct understanding.
To speak of the fruit within the cause means that the nature of the future fruit exists within the present cause.
The Sūtra says that "to speak of the fruit as the cause" is, for example, as when it is said that the Buddha’s thirty-two marks exist within the bodies of sentient beings;
this is called speaking of the fruit as the cause.
The Sūtra says that "to speak of life as food" is, for example, as when one obtains life by means of food: the food is the cause and life is the fruit. Now...
To say that "life is called nutriment" is precisely to speak of the cause within the context of the fruit.
Therefore, the treatise says that contact is indeterminate. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Cheng lun), fascicle three, states: Question:

Are the earth and other elements, as well as fire, all without distinction in their collection of visible form, odor, taste, and touch? Answer: They are not fixed; for example, within stones and soil there are both visible form and odor.
Regarding taste and touch: sometimes there is only the tangible, as in the case of gold, silver, and so forth; sometimes water possesses color, odor, taste, and the tangible;
sometimes it possesses three—color, odor, and the tangible; and sometimes wind possesses the tangible but lacks odor, or possesses both odor and the tangible. Therefore, these are not fixed.
All of these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Because their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are dull and inferior, they belong to the indeterminate category.

Regarding the seeking of karma in contrast to wholesome volition (*kuśalacetanā*): all bodily and vocal actions performed as wholesome arise from the mind; therefore, the seeking of karma is contrasted with wholesome volition.
The Sūtra says: "Bodily action, verbal action, and mental action" refers to the basis upon which karma depends. "Engaging in karma" and "seeking karma" refer to the association with karma.

"The karma of giving" and "the karma of liberation" refer to the intrinsic nature of karma. Providing for friends and relatives, being stained by mutual affection, and serving one's teachers and elders are merely matters of human sentiment;
bestowing gifts upon outsiders is done solely to pray for a field of merit. By means of such acts of giving and the like, all...
This refers to wrong action (*mithyākarma*).
The Sūtra says that those who do not seek cause and effect do not seek the cause of Buddha-nature or Bodhi.

That their color and fragrance are not suffering means that *icchantikas* possess only the goodness of affectionate love; this is illustrated by the metaphor that their color and fragrance are not suffering.

Regarding that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): there are four types of the indeterminate. First, fruition (*vipāka*); second, the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*); third, the sphere of arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*);

and fourth, the result of mastery (*nairmāṇika*). "Fruition" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) that are the retributive results within the three realms and five destinies; they are so called because they have specifically ripened from [karmic] causes.

It is called *vipāka* (maturation) because it undergoes transformation, because it matures as a different category [from its cause], and because it possesses these three aforementioned meanings; thus, it is named *vipāka*.
Second, there are two types of *airyāpathika* (postures): first, the matter of posture, which consists of the four objects (*viṣaya*)—namely, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—as its nature;

second, the mind of posture, which is the mental consciousness whose power is so dominant that it can initiate postural movements. Although the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are inherently weak and inferior, even though they take [objects] as their conditions...
The *airyāpathika* (modes of deportment) cannot give rise to the *airyāpathika*. The seventh manas-consciousness clings exclusively to the *kliṣṭa-manas* as an internal self;
since it does not take the four objects such as form (*rūpa*) as its cognitive domain, it does not produce the *airyāpathika*.

Although the eighth *ālayavijñāna* takes the various objects such as form as its cognitive domain, its nature is weak and inferior, and thus it cannot induce the *airyāpathika*. What is called the "path" refers to the *airyāpathika*.
It is also [the basis for] walking. Third, regarding "skillful arts," this refers to all skillful crafts, namely painting, carving, and engraving;

these have the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as their substance. Second, regarding "skillful mind," this is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); the eyes and other faculties are not "dignified deportment" (*airyāpathika*), as established previously.

Fourth, regarding "attainment-fruit" (*prāptiphala*), this refers to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) attained upon realization; they are also called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) and are neutral (*avyākṛta*). Sixth, regarding "transformative matters," this refers to the alteration [of things].
Form and substance are non-existent yet suddenly appear. The Hīnayāna takes the five sense-objects as its nature; the Mahāyāna takes the five aggregates as its nature.
The two types of transformative mind are, that is to say, the mental consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "for the middling and lower types," etc., it means that there is further transformation of the middling into the upper or lower.

As for those whose roots of goodness are not fixed in their severance: if they can reform their ways and resolve their minds, they do not sever them; if they do not resolve their minds, they sever them.
Therefore, it is called "indeterminate.
If it were determinate, it would not be so; for if it were determinate, one should dwell in hell eternally. Since such a principle does not exist, we know it is indeterminate.

Question: As for those who can be seen, if they are permitted to leave the household life, this indicates that their faculties (*indriya*) are not yet known. How, then, can it be said that they possess the power of the faculties?
The Sūtra states that one who possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*) is one who possesses the fourth of these ten powers: the power of knowing the faculties (*indriyaparāparajñānabala*).
Regarding the statement that he answered on behalf of others, this demonstrates that the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the powers of the faculties (*indriya-bala*);
it shows that he does not merely know the case of Sunakṣatra, but is able to know the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings.
The Sūtra says that there are no divergent paths. Whether one commits evil or performs good, there are no divergent paths. Why is this?
If one gives rise to the bodhicitta, one will surely reach the spring of Buddha-nature; if one gives rise to the icchantika mind, one will surely reach the springs of the three evil realms.
Regarding "raising a matter to pose a question": having raised a matter as a question, one returns to that matter to provide the answer.
Regarding "conjoining with respect to the fruit": this refers to conjoining with the present body, which is the fruit.
Regarding "conjoining with respect to the cause": because the fruit is brought about by the cause, one subsequently conjoins with respect to the cause.
Regarding the statement that the teaching is not fixed: because the capacities of sentient beings are not fixed, the Tathāgata’s teaching is likewise not fixed.
The Buddha is like a clear mirror that universally manifests all images; therefore, it is said that he illuminates their faculties according to their differences.
Regarding "sentient beings who do not attain [realization]": this refers to those who have not yet obtained the profound benefit of the teachings and thus give rise to such disputes.
"This is merely a brief summary" means that because the past has already passed, it is not discussed here.
Furthermore, because past roots of goodness cause present roots of goodness to arise, one speaks of the nature of present knowledge; for this reason, it is summarized.
Regarding the phrase "when the wise first hear that existence [and non-existence] are equal," this refers to knowing them as mutually identical according to the two truths.

Regarding "hearing of existence and non-existence," when both are simultaneously illumined, one immediately realizes their simultaneous absence. When it is said that they are simultaneously absent, one immediately knows that they are simultaneously illumined, and so forth.

Furthermore, "hearing that there is" refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna. This means that upon hearing the Hīnayāna, one knows that even a single snap of the fingers or a joining of palms is no other than a cause for Buddhahood;
how much more so, then, would those of the Hīnayāna not all enter the precious island of the One Vehicle? Therefore, it is said: "Hearing that there is, one knows that there is not," and so forth.
The "first and second" and so forth refer merely to the presence or absence of dharmas. Why? Because they accord with the capacities of sentient beings.
If one speaks of existence, it exists while being non-existent; if one speaks of non-existence, it is non-existent while being existent. Therefore, it is said that no dualistic teaching is made.
Furthermore, upon hearing of existence, one simultaneously hears the other three gates.
Regarding those who do not understand the remedies (*pratipakṣa*): it is said that by asserting existence and non-existence, one remedies their attachment to existence and non-existence.

Regarding those with differing boundaries: this refers to differences in territories and variations in the customs of people. Since customs differ, their faculties and natures (*indriya-gotra*) are not the same;
it is for this reason that the Tathāgata’s teaching is not fixed, but is given in accordance with these faculties.
Only those who are permitted to eat meat may do so provided it is declared to be tasteless; only then may they eat it.
Regarding the statement that "those in the ninth stage do not see," this means that those in the ninth stage do not see those in the tenth stage.
Regarding the Buddha-nature that is realized: for the time being, this teaching is given in accordance with the capacities and conditions [of the audience].
As for the eight flavors of *nirvāṇa*, they are as explained previously in the "Chapter on Names and Merits."
Next, to explain the meaning of "one purpose" (*ekārtha*): Śakra is so called because he internally disciplines his mind through wholesome dharmas; thus, it is named "one purpose.
The Sūtra states that "Śakra" means "the Lord of Heaven who is Capable of Action."
As for Kauśika: in a past age, there was a brahmin in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī whose family name was Kauśika;
this means "original nature" (mūla-prakṛti).
As for "Jewel Summit," it is so named because of the bright jewel within his topknot.
As for "Jewel Banner," after he was victorious in battle with the asuras, he established a banner of victory, which is thus called the Jewel Banner.
Regarding "without fault" (*wúguò*): if pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*) as "Buddha," it means that the donor (*tányuè*) is free from all faults and evils.
Furthermore, when saying "surpassing all the heavens," it is pronounced with the level tone (*píngshēng*).

As for the reason why the masters of the treatises (śāstrakāra) [state this], it is simply because the knowledge of the Four Truths regarding the past and future is designated as "inferential" (*anumāna*) by comparison with the present;

thus, the primary intent here lies in that [comparison], and there is no need to rely on the treatises for its explanation. Zhezhou also said: "The Buddha knows that birth-and-death is impermanent (*anitya*);
if there were no self (*ātman*), he would know Nirvana as the Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity—these constitute the eight [attributes]."
The seventh point, "like one who practices the holy life," may be relied upon as this explanation.

As for the sūtra’s mention of the four nutriments (*āhāra*): within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) there is the nutriment of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) there is the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*); and within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) there are the two nutriments of volition (*cetanā*) and contact (*sparśa*).
Feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are not discussed here.

Regarding the statement that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) includes substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*): fragrance, flavor, and tangibility are substantial food; their nature is subsumed within the aggregate of form.

The remaining three aggregates may be understood in the same way. Regarding the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*): among the contaminated aggregates (*sāsravaskandha*), with the exception of consciousness itself, the remaining four aggregates serve as the stations for consciousness.
"Dependence" refers to consciousness abiding within form, consciousness abiding within sensation, consciousness abiding within perception, and consciousness abiding within formations.

Because there is no second consciousness, it is not said that "consciousness abides within consciousness. When the present text states "excluding only form," the intention is to indicate that the four aggregates—apart from form—are the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).

Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) that penetrate both the internal and external: edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is external, while the three foods of volition, contact, and consciousness are internal.

As for afflictions (*kleśa*), they reside precisely within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); the aggregate of formations is most manifest in its correspondence with afflictions. Furthermore, both wholesome and unwholesome aggregates belong to afflictions.
If a teacher of dharmas (*lakṣaṇavādin*) were to hear it said that afflictions are these five aggregates, they would be greatly alarmed.
I have cited this passage to show you that it is also called "the three cultivations.
This provides a further explanation clarifying that all three vehicles observe the five aggregates; by cultivating the body, precepts, and mind, one achieves the three vehicles.
The Sūtra states: "That which is called cause and effect—the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time does not transcend cause and effect.

Regarding the instruction specifically for those who are stingy: this is a teaching delivered by shifting the emphasis. It simply requires that those who are stingy practice only the other five perfections;
if they practice these other five, they will naturally and spontaneously be able to practice generosity. The same applies when any of the other five take turns as the primary focus.
The Sūtra says, "Śāriputra... [up to] the compassionate one. This citation of the disciples to manifest the Master’s unique possession of the faculties and powers (*indriya-bala*).
As for the Sarvāstivāda's reliance on facts: this refers to the fact that the Sarvāstivāda school primarily relies on manifest phenomena.
There was a skilled artisan who used this passage to corroborate the preceding *Cunda-parivarta*. From this, one knows that Cunda’s father was a craftsman;
"son" (*putra*) is a general term for a male. Therefore, ancient commentators explained [the name] as "the son of a great master."

Regarding the phrase "the substance is established by causes" and so forth: continuity is merely established by causes; it receives the name "continuity" because it is obtained across preceding and succeeding moments.

Relativity is merely established by causes; it receives the name "relativity" because it is obtained through horizontal and vertical dependence. Therefore, these two types of dependence are both termed "function."
Regarding that which is the totality of matter and mind: every constituent part possesses both matter and mind.
If this is taken as the meaning of Buddha-nature, it likewise accords with the definition of Buddha-nature established by the former master;
for we now adopt his position in order to manifest the correct principle.
The Sūtra states: "Merit" (guṇa) refers to skillfulness; that is, virtue is the cause and merit is the fruit. This is in contrast to the inferior [causes and fruits].
"Concordance" (yoga) means the act of uniting or bringing together.
Regarding those who calculate [the self] in plants and trees: since it is said that there is a self apart from the aggregates (*skandhas*), they calculate plants and trees to be the self.

As for the "six" [destinies], this is because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is added to the five destinies to make six. This refers to the school that calculates there is no intermediate state, as well as the refutation of the school that calculates there is an intermediate state.
If one were to calculate that there is an intermediate state, there would have to be six destinies; since there are not six destinies, [it is not so]. However...
There are five destinies (*gati*). It is clear from this that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not exist.
If one were to claim it exists, it would merely be that the Buddha opened [this teaching] as a special provision for certain conditions.

A sutra states that formless sentient beings have no intermediate state; furthermore, within the Abhidharma system, it is taught that with the exception of the four formless realms (*ārūpya*), the rest [possess it].
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists in all realms, because the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lacks a physical location.

Regarding "knowledge of equality" (*samatājñāna*): for the disciples of the Buddha and non-Buddhists alike, the knowledge that uses out-flowing factors (*sāsrava*) to cultivate joy and revulsion and thereby sever afflictions is called knowledge of equality.

However, regarding those who regress from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*): because they practice with a mind of longing and aversion, even if they attain the meditations of the higher realms, there is still regression.
As for this concentration being "difficult to grasp": this concentration is flickering and sharp, unable to remain long; it is difficult to seize and maintain.

Because one practices it merely with a mind of longing and aversion, if one attains two or three fruits, there is regression. If one follows the person practicing according to the gradual stages (*anupūrva-krama*) and attains [the fruit] like a flash of lightning...
Guangding: Entering the first dhyāna from the desire realm, it is not said that there is regression.
As the Sūtra says of one who frequently practices walking meditation: "The body wanders without purpose, and the mouth speaks without purpose"—this is precisely its characteristic.
The Sūtra speaks of two types of internal and external causes and conditions: first, the afflictions that lead to rebirth, which give rise to fetters such as greed at the time of birth;
second, the afflictions that obstruct the Path, which manifest as defilements that hinder the Noble Path.

In the case of those Arhats who take rebirth, the afflictions leading to rebirth never arise at all, and thus they are called "non-retrogressive" regarding them. However, it is possible for the afflictions that obstruct the Path to arise; therefore, they are said to "possess" [them].

[The practitioner] regresses. Furthermore, analyzing according to the causes and conditions of the afflictions (*kleśa*): first, they arise because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of their nature have not been severed;

second, they arise due to improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*); third, they arise through the power of external conditions. For an Arhat, the first two causes do not exist, yet they may still give rise to afflictions; this is called "non-regression.
When fetters (*saṃyojana*) arise through the power of conditions, it is called "having regression. This refers to [the case where] one perceives something as particularly superior...
The arising of greed toward sense objects is merely momentary; as soon as greed arises, one should restrain the mind and sever it so that it is extinguished.

Furthermore, when fetters are severed by impure knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*), there is regression; when fetters are severed by pure knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), there is no regression. Moreover, those of dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*) may regress, while those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*) do not regress.

The Sūtra states that there are those who are "liberated by occasion" (*samaya-vimukta*). This means they attain liberation only when they depend upon specific circumstances. There are six such circumstances: first, obtaining excellent robes;

second, obtaining excellent food; third, obtaining excellent bedding and seats; fourth, obtaining an excellent location; fifth, obtaining an excellent teacher of the Dharma; and sixth, obtaining fellow students.
Those who must wait for these six conditions are said to be of dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*). Those who attain liberation without depending on these six do not belong to this category.
"Those who have attained liberation" refers to those of sharp faculties.
"Conditioned by means of words" means that they are said to be conditioned in accordance with the teachings; furthermore, they are conditioned according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Having already destroyed the three causes" refers to the three causes consisting of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).
The Sūtra states: "The mind that moves upward" refers to rebirth in the heavens; "the mind that moves downward" refers to the three miserable realms.
The Sūtra further states: "The mind that is fixed and constant" means it is determined to exist [in those realms].

The Sūtra states that those who have attained the right path—from the stage of *srotāpanna* onwards—are all said to possess the right path. Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there is a distinction between that which obstructs and that which does not:
the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), when combined with heavy karma, constitute an obstruction to the Path; however, if the five desires are present alone, they do not constitute an obstruction.
The Sūtra states that those who definitively obstruct the true path— namely, householders who regard the first fruit [of stream-entry] as the true path—
and the five stages of preparation, which consist of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and the four [levels] beginning with "heat" (uṣmagata).
The Sūtra states that "those who distance themselves from afflictions" refers merely to the suppression of afflictions being termed "distancing.

The Sūtra further states that "the various non-Buddhists... sever the afflictions of the four dhyānas. By employing a mind of longing and aversion, they sever the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation within the four dhyānas;

this constitutes the cultivation of the "warmth" and other stages of insight, giving rise to the "worldly supreme dharma. All such practices are conducive [to the Path] and are included within the stage of "entry into the noble state."
Regarding the result:
as for the volition associated [with the act] being the primary essence, since all acts of giving are only possible through the deep faith of mental volition, mental volition is taken as the essence.
It is by means of this mental volition that one employs the body and speech as auxiliaries, thereby bringing the action to completion.
To clarify his intention:

regarding the statement that "the application of the [three] realms to meditative concentration lacks the three [unconditioned phenomena]," this is merely a teaching given according to the differing inclinations and preferences of those to be trained.

As for the existence of the three unconditioned phenomena: first is the unconditioned phenomenon of space (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*). The verse states: "Within this, that which is empty and non-obstructive is explained as space."
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has non-obstruction as its nature. Because it is without hindrance, matter moves within it; this is called space (*ākāśa*).

Second is the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The verse says: "Analytical cessation is disjunction (*visamyoga*). "Analysis" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), because by means of wisdom one discriminates the Four Noble Truths.
"Cessation" refers to nirvāṇa, which is called "cessation" because there is no further arising. The cessation obtained internally through analysis is termed "analytical cessation."

The third is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The verse states: "Ultimately obstructing that which is to arise, there is a distinct attainment called non-analytical cessation.
Regarding the term "that which is to arise" (*utpādya*): it refers to future dharmas that would arise if conditions were met, but do not arise because conditions are lacking.

At the time they do not arise, one attains non-analytical cessation. This non-analytical cessation obstructs those dharmas that are to arise, causing them never to manifest again; this is called "ultimate" (*atyanta*).

"Ultimately obstructed. Regarding the statement "attained separately," this means that non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) possesses a substantial nature; it arises as a separate attainment during the state when conditions are absent. Because it is attained, it is called "non-analytical cessation";
its attainment does not depend on analytical discernment, but is named "non-analytical cessation" solely due to the absence of conditions. As the treatise says:
For example, when the eye and the mind are focused exclusively on a single form, other [objects] such as sound, smell, taste, and touch are not seen or heard;
having passed away and ceased, they never arise again, and thus they receive the designation of "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and so forth.

The Sūtra states that "it does not arise from the condition of wisdom" (pratisaṃkhyā), meaning that it does not attain cessation through analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha); rather, it ceases solely due to the absence of conditions.
This refers to the postulation of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) known as non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The Sūtra says, "whether near or far": the past is "far" and the present is "near.
As for "subtle," "subtle" refers to the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal atom).

Speaking in terms of functional entities (*vastu*), as for what is called "form" (*rūpa*), with respect to these entities, there are both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived elements (*bhautika*), all of which are as follows: [as previously described].

The preceding text now merely provides this specific explanation for a particular capacity [of a certain type of practitioner]. It speaks only of that which can create, and does not mention that which is created.
As for the statement in the Dharmaguptaka school that "non-informative action (avijñapti) is not matter," one should likewise say it is not mind;

for that school clarifies that the substance of non-informative precepts is neither matter nor mind. The Mahāsāṃghika school refutes the position established by the former Vīra, and should instead state: "It has mind as its substance."
This was already explained in the preceding section on the precept (*śīla*).
Regarding the statement "it does not produce a mental fruit": this clarifies that non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is not a fruit of the mind. Why?
Because non-informative matter itself takes bodily and vocal action as its cause to produce non-informative matter as its fruit; it is merely a case of material cause producing material effect.
Therefore, it is not a cause-and-effect relationship of the mind.
As the Sūtra says, "Although the mind may dwell in evil," this clarifies that unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) does not belong to the mind. Why?
Because since one does not lose the precepts even when the mind dwells within the states of good, evil, or neutral, we know by inference that it does not belong to the mind.
He of Hexi says that "not producing other forms" is equivalent to not creating the causes and conditions for distinct forms.

He first mentions the sages because when sages contemplate and shatter the aggregates of ordinary beings, they realize them to be their own sage-aggregates; therefore, he says they all emerge from ignorance.

Furthermore, when ordinary beings are deluded regarding these sage-aggregates, they become ordinary beings. Moreover, if one treats the aggregates as a veil, this refers to the meaning of humans and devas.

The "shadows and veils" (*chāyā-āvaraṇa*): the shadows and veils of the three realms and the two vehicles; the shadows and veils of the outflows (*āsrava*) within the three realms for bodhisattvas; and the shadowless shadows and veils of the Buddhas.
These cover all sentient beings so that they may attain Great Nirvana.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "arising from the causal conditions of sensation," it should follow the causal conditions of craving; I do not yet dare to alter this.
First, as for what is called "those gathered by devas" (天攝), this refers to the deva lineage. Second, as for what are called "ghosts and spirits" (鬼神), these are of the ghost-spirit lineage.
Regarding the statement that "the three lower realms constitute one existence (*bhava*)," this clarifies that the three lower realms are treated as a single category.

If they were further subdivided, there would be various distinctions within the hells, such as light and heavy; among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), there would be superior, middling, and inferior grades;

and among animals (*tiryagyoni*), there would likewise be differences based on whether they dwell in water, on land, or in the air—thus they too should be divided into many existences. However, here each realm is simply taken as a single existence. As for humans, there are the four continents.
They are not the same. As for not mentioning the asuras, this is merely to account for three characters in the sutra.
Regarding cause and effect: among the twenty-five states of existence, none transcend cause and effect.
Regarding good and evil: the three wholesome states constitute good; the three unwholesome states constitute evil.

Regarding the seven stations of consciousness: the three emptinesses constitute three; the first two and the third dhyānas constitute three; and the humans and devas of the desire realm constitute one.

Therefore, these are combined to make seven. The *Śāstra* states: "One does not delight in dwelling in the three miserable realms (*durgati*), nor in the sphere of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

In the three evil existences, there is the torment and oppression of suffering, so consciousness does not find peace. In the fourth dhyāna, there is the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), which harms consciousness; thus, consciousness does not delight in abiding there.

In the single stage of neither-perception, as well as the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the mental consciousness is likewise harmed, and consciousness does not delight in abiding there."
Therefore, these are not stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Regarding the "eight blessings," Zezhou says: being wealthy and noble among humans constitutes one; the six heavens of the desire realm constitute six;
and the first dhyāna and those above it combined constitute one—these make eight. This interpretation may be relied upon.
The Sūtra states: "As for those who receive a single precept," this means that after having received the Three Refuges, one merely sets the mind upon and maintains a single precept;

at the moment of the formal declaration, merely setting the mind upon and maintaining a single precept is called "receiving a single precept. It is not necessary to say, "I receive all five together, but maintain only one."

The Sūtra states, "or for a single thought-moment," which refers merely to a single thought occurring outside of the [formal] time; it does not mean that one *kṣaṇa* constitutes a single thought-moment.
The Sūtra says, "it is not called attaining the *śīla* (precept)," because a full day and night constitute the complete portion (*śīla*).
Therefore, if one falls short of this, it is merely called attaining the goodness of the precept, but is not called attaining the *śīla*.
"Having committed a grave offense and thereby relinquishing [the precepts]" means that once a grave offense has been committed, the precepts are immediately lost.
"The two dharmas having reached extinction" means that when the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma have all vanished, the precepts are lost.

Regarding "the time when both organs arise": if the two organs transform into one another, there is no loss [of the precepts]. This refers to a monk becoming a nun; it is the same for a nun who becomes fully ordained as a monk.
This is clearly explained in the *Vinayavibhaṅga*. However, the present text specifically clarifies that the arising of both sexual organs constitutes the forfeiture [of the precepts].
The Sūtra says, "like the head of a tāla tree. This is a metaphorical expression intended to suppress [the notion of regression]; it does not mean that one has definitively lost the precepts.
The four stages of the wholesome roots, such as *uṣmagata*, serve as the causes for entering the state of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) realization.
Regarding those who receive the Way: receiving the precepts for the first time serves as the foundation for demonstrating the Way and so forth.

As for "all three and one are Mahāyāna": this refers to those who, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and after the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, heard of the three vehicles and their convergence into the One Vehicle;
all such people at the initial stage of the Mahāyāna harbor these attachments and disputes. Furthermore, if they hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...
Once the provisional teachings have been set aside to reveal the ultimate reality, such disputes will certainly cease.

Since prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there was no explicit teaching that clearly explained the principle of the three vehicles converging into the One Vehicle, we know this must be so. It is because they previously heard the teachings in secret that they gave rise to attachments and disputes.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "What is called the 'dharma of dispute'? It answers: "The Tripiṭaka is the dharma of dispute; it is rare in the Mahāyāna gate."

Regarding this matter, what is now called "dispute" (*vivāda*) mostly occurs within the Tripiṭaka. If there is dispute within the Three Vehicles—whether Mahāyāna or otherwise—it all resides in the initial stage [of practice].
As for the scriptural passage stating that a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) "does not attain the Buddha-way," this is not a general rule applicable to other lands where such attainment is achieved.
"Moderns" refers to those who have raised disputes regarding the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; they are thus called "moderns. Furthermore, since the Liang dynasty, there have also been those who held such views;
these too are called "moderns."
Regarding those who claim there is a "future fruit" and a "true deity," they are so named because of their calculation regarding what is to come.
They maintain that apart from sentient beings, there exists a mind and a sentient being; they assert that when the sentient being and the mind attain bodhi, this is called "the very sentient being."
Regarding the statement "if there are many worlds, then [they] exist": according to the Sarvāstivāda, they do not exist even in the ten directions.
This is explained in detail in the second part of the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, where the distinctions among the ten afflictions (*kleśa*) are analyzed.
The Sūtra says, "This is called attachment," referring to internal mental attachment.
The Sūtra says, "If one hears it from another," this refers to hearing it from the Buddha.
"If one seeks it in the sūtras oneself" refers to seeking it in the sūtras after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
If it was taught by another intentionally, it was heard from one at the edge of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
As for the sūtra’s statement, "first seeing the ox," this refers to a black bull.
Regarding the "three similes," these are raised as three points to pose a challenge: if one had previously seen [the ox], doubt might subsequently arise; yet the Buddha truly...
I have never taught that a stream-enterer can ever fall away.
Since you have not seen this, how could you harbor doubt regarding the stream-enterer?
Regarding the initial inquiry about *nirvāṇa*: Is *nirvāṇa* definitively existent? Is it definitively non-existent? What are its characteristics?
Such matters concern the principle (*li*), while turbid water concerns the phenomenon (*shi*).
The Sūtra says, "One who encounters turbid water. This analogy is irrational. Why?
If one had previously seen [clear water] and later sees turbid water again in another place, only then can doubt arise. Since one has never seen it before, how could there be any doubt?
The Sūtra states, "suffering is not suffering. This means that regarding sufferings such as cold and heat, one perceives Nirvāṇa—which is not suffering—as being [identical to] them;
therefore, it is said that doubt arises concerning Nirvāṇa.
"Those who can generate merit themselves" means they are able to generate merit spontaneously; this is not the same as the non-Buddhist (bāhya) doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
"Harvesting water and soil in winter" refers to the aforementioned scarcity of pasture.
The inhabitants of the three continents are weak and pliant; the people of these three continents are wealthy and joyful, yet they cling to views with inferior minds and lack firm resolve.
As the Sūtra says, there are five things [bestowed]: namely, giving to others physical form, strength, longevity, happiness, and eloquence.
The Sūtra states, "As for 'the cover being one,' this refers to the cranial vault.
Regarding the passage, "In the past there was wisdom," and so forth, this explains the causes and fruits of habituation across successive lifetimes.
"Purely ascending roots of goodness" refers to the roots of goodness pertaining to humans and devas.
Xu Puxie, who governed the people, was well able to adjudicate the right and wrong of others; yet when his own person committed an offense, he was unskilled in answering questions regarding it.
Regarding Tianzhu Yu: Tianzhu Mountain is also named Wangqin Mountain; Yu was the Chan Master Tunduo, who was assigned to Tianzhu Temple.
Later, during the reign of Empress Wu, it was renamed Daoshu Temple (and so forth).
The Sūtra states that it is not those of inferior capacity; rather, only those of sharp faculties are able to sever the roots of goodness.

Regarding "those of sharp faculties who, upon first entering [the hells]," this refers to the fact that when such individuals first give rise to fear within the hells, they possess three thoughts, as has already been explained above.
Regarding "first receiving the intent": as the Buddha stated above, the causes of goodness throughout the three periods of time can be severed, but the fruits of goodness cannot be severed.
Even a person who has severed their roots of goodness possesses the Buddha-nature. Now, one receives this intent.

Regarding the "pervasive" and "distinct" [characteristics] across the three periods of time: that which pertains to the past and below is the distinct; that which pervades the three periods of time is the pervasive. There are two difficulties here:

first, the argument from "if it were in the future" and below, which seeks to show that it is not in the future; second, the argument from "for what reason" and below, which seeks to show that it must reside in the future.
If it resides in the future, it is subsumed within the three periods of time; how then can you say it is eternal? This constitutes the difficulty regarding the present.
It is the same here. As for that which is not present: if it were present, why would it not be seen? Since it cannot be seen, how can one say it "will be"?
First, regarding the claim that this refers to the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*): because one sees the expression "that which is seen exists," it is judged to belong to the revealing cause;

there is indeed this meaning. Second, regarding what is called the "causal source" (*hetu-hetu*): because one sees the statement that the Tathāgata also spoke of Buddha-nature, it is asserted that this [Buddha-nature] exists within sentient beings.
This is precisely what is called the "direct cause. The intention here corresponds to the Buddha-nature of the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*).
If one refers to it as the "past time," this "past time" refers to the period prior to the severance of the roots of goodness in the future.

[Sūtra] (As stated at length: "What are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the Truth of the Path? There is only one Truth of the Path; when analyzed, there are thirty-seven distinct factors.
This is called 'analysis'. [Question: Is it the same for Suffering, Origin, and Cessation? [Answer: Yes, it is the same.
As for the reasons for this response, they are all merely the causes of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
As the Sūtra says regarding the "seven matters": the four, such as permanence and bliss, exist only in the fruit; the three, which are true virtues, are universal causes.
Causes belong to the three periods of time, whereas fruits are invariably not subsumed within the world of temporal succession.
Regarding the first point, "though existing, it is non-existent": although the nature of Buddhahood and equal enlightenment exists, because of afflictions, the eternal fruit has not yet manifested;
since it pertains to the three periods of time, it is said to be "non-existent."
Although it does not exist [as a present entity], it will certainly and inevitably attain its eternal fruit; therefore, it is said to "exist.
Thus, one cannot say that it is not a dharma belonging to the three periods of time, for since it is realized through the cultivation of causes, it is subsumed within the three periods.
Regarding the "future nature": the essence of Buddha-nature is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
If the Buddha-nature at the stage of fruition is invariably not subsumed within the three periods of time, then when these three meanings are fully present, the principle is thoroughly exhausted.
The "all-seeing one" of the future does not belong to the three periods of time at the moment of all-seeing.

As for the five aggregates that are wholesome, because they are the aggregates acquired as the habitual fruits of the constant and blissful state upon initial realization, they still belong to the three periods of time by virtue of being causes.

To clarify further regarding the "subsequent body" (*paścātkāya*): both its causes and its partial fruits belong to the three periods of time when discussed in terms of cultivation and realization. If one were to say that its essential substance is not subsumed under any period of time at all, this would constitute a loss of mindfulness.
For if the cause has already been destroyed, how could it be said to be "present"? Conversely, if it is present, it cannot be said to have lost its mindfulness.
"How does this differ from that of ordinary people? (and so forth).
Regarding the single point of impermanence: this is explained by way of mutual exclusion. Since permanence is absent, by definition it must be impermanent.

Regarding the scriptural passage stating that "the Buddha-nature definitely exists": if one says it definitely exists now yet is not seen, or if one says it definitely does not exist now but will certainly be attained in the future, these views are refuted so as to prevent definitive assertions;
this is termed a "set-aside" (sthāpanīya) response.
To answer by means of a counter-interrogation is simply to respond with a counter-interrogation; it is not an answer to the question posed, and its meaning is that one should set the matter aside.
When the Sūtra speaks of "stopping," it means to stop their command and prevent them from forming fixed attachments.

Regarding "the second, do not be attached": previously, when Kāśyapa asked, "I have heard," and the Buddha did not answer, this was because he was attached to signs (*nimitta*). Therefore, the Buddha rebuked him and commanded that he should not be attached.
As for "cause and effect within the causal stage," this refers to the cause of habituation and the fruit of habituation.
The Sūtra states that "it is not of the past, etc. refers to the resultant nature (*phala-svabhāva*) of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the statement that "the five aggregates of unwholesome dharmas are exclusively of the causal nature (*hetu-svabhāva*)," this does not refer only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whose afflictions, fetters, and karmic actions are not yet exhausted and who are thus termed exclusively as belonging to the unwholesome portion;
these too are called unwholesome dharmas and are exclusively of the causal nature.

Regarding the nature of the fruit of the *nirmāṇakāya*: this present body of mine is precisely the attainment of the *dharmakāya*, the eternal body, which belongs exclusively to the three periods of time.

As for the scriptural passage concerning "that which is mixed with blood and milk," it refers to the Buddha-nature being mixed with ignorance, afflictions, and karma; because it has not yet been purified, it is called "mixed with blood."
Regarding the phrase "fully present within the fruit": the *srotāpanna* and others are the fruits of practice within the cause, while the *amṛta* (the supreme cream) is the fruit of *bodhi*.
As for the statement that these exist in the future: if sentient beings already possess [marks] such as the thirty-two major signs in the present, why say they are capable [of them] in the future?
Since the roots of goodness produced in the present do not currently exist, how can it be said that they will be able to produce [results] in the future?
Regarding those who receive pleasant retribution in the present, this refers to the two types of retribution—good and evil.
As for "never producing a fruit," if a future karma arises, one then obtains its fruit; if there is no karma, one will ultimately never [obtain it].
"Unripened fruit.

The Buddha’s intended meaning in answering is this: although sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, they must cultivate the conditions and the realization [of that nature] before they can attain it.
Because the afflictions have not yet been removed by these two causes, the fruit has not yet been attained. This corresponds to the first analogy.

Regarding "not producing a fruit": if one cultivates the conditions and objects of perception in the future, only then can one obtain the fruit; therefore, it is said that the causes and conditions of Buddha-nature are able to produce [the fruit].
As for those who are stubbornly and rigidly attached—if they dogmatically cling to the *zhengyin* (direct cause) of Buddha-nature—it is like clinging to a lamp whose light has not yet emerged.
It cannot destroy darkness.
If it is a provisional designation based on causes and conditions, then once one understands that the future causes and conditions will eventually converge, one will be able to see.
This is like understanding that although the lamp or the sun has not yet arrived and has not yet appeared, one must not dogmatically insist that they cannot destroy the darkness.
The Sūtra states that "that which can produce the Buddha-nature of sentient beings" refers to that which can produce the Buddha-nature of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and subsequent stages.

The Sūtra further states: "If one says that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are the Buddha-nature, then if it is said that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, it should reside within the mind of the aggregates.
Why, then, is it said to be neither internal nor external?"
The Sūtra states: "There are those who are liberated sometimes and those who are liberated at all times. As for those liberated at all times, they enter [liberation] in the present.
How could there be anything that exists apart from the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti)? The path of karma is the conventional; the path of afflictions is the ultimate;
and the path of suffering is the middle. These three paths are thus the three truths. Therefore, the Middle Way is not external to the ultimate and the conventional.
"Furthermore, 'both being so' refers to simultaneous illumination.
'Being like empty space' refers to calculating [the nature of] the external.

'The union of sense-faculties and objects' means that arising is itself the Dharma-realm. That the sense-faculties are entirely the sense-faculties is the Dharma-realm; that the entirety of arising is the sense-faculties is sitting."
Non-duality is what is called "union," meaning that their substance is one.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "Buddha-nature is like empty space": this clarifies that when sentient beings and their environment have not yet been created, they are fundamentally like empty space;
even after being created, they are like empty space, pervading all places. Moreover, Buddha-nature is like a path in the world: there is that which has not yet been traversed...
There are those who have the desire to practice, those who are currently practicing correctly, and those who have already practiced.
Although there are differences such as those who have not yet practiced, the path itself does not have two distinct natures. Buddha-nature is likewise; it is entirely without duality.
As for "the principle is non-dual": the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time are one within the single Dharma-realm, and thus there is no duality in principle.
As for "the phenomena differ by a hair's breadth": this is because throughout a single lifetime, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.

Regarding the prior mention of the two attachments: sentient beings grasp [at things] because they do not understand them; thus, the Bodhisattva, in order to cultivate himself and transform others, eliminates the two types of attachment to extremes that arise.
The scripture states that "Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external. This is said in terms of concealing the provisional (zhēquán) to describe it as both internal and external;
it is said in terms of revealing the Middle Way by opening up the provisional (kāiquán). The subsequent passages are to be understood by this same principle.
The Sūtra states that the "vajra-body" and so forth refer to the external, while the "ten powers" and so forth refer to the internal.
To hold fixedly to either is to fall into an extreme. Therefore, the Tathāgata first negates these two extremes in each case, explaining them all by means of the *dharmadhātu*.
The Sūtra states, "Internally reflecting well," and so forth; this is explained in terms of giving rise to conceptual calculations during practice.
The Sūtra states, "Dānapāramitā," and so forth; this is likewise explained in terms of falling into extremes through fixed attachments during practice.
The Sūtra states: "Not severed" means that it cannot be severed in the present.
"Not extinguished" means that it will certainly be attained in the future. Therefore, extinction is like a lamp;
"flame" refers to taking the continuous succession of flames as a metaphor for non-interruption.
The Sūtra states that "the seasons differ," meaning the conditions of water and soil vary according to the time.
The Sūtra states that "there is the pure and the impure": if one resolves to sever afflictions, that is purity; though it may not yet be pure in the present, it will certainly be pure in the future.
As for the scripture’s statement, "arising yet not arising": when conditions converge through cultivation, one returns to this state of non-arising.
