As for the scripture’s statement, "this is called attachment": if one claims that curd already exists within milk and does not require fermentation or warmth, this is termed attachment.
The Sūtra says: "To be free from these two matters" means to be free from attachment to the false and illusory. Once one has practiced, [the result] will necessarily be attained.
Who creates the sequence? As for the sequence, it arises only through the conjunction of causes and conditions, such as that which produces curd and so forth.
Without skillful means, who could create the sequence?
When the sutra says "unequal," it simply means that because the mind is not all-pervasive, one gives rise to biased attachment.
When the sutra says "the wise," it refers to those who hear the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; such people are indeed the wise.
The Sūtra says, "clarifying desire": because desire serves as the condition for the arising of consciousness, it is called "desire.
The Sūtra says, "distinct fruits": grass is the cause of milk, and milk is the fruit of grass. Seeking curd from milk or from grass is certainly impossible.
Regarding "the absence of a categorical gate" (*amukha*): it is the absence of a categorical gate when everything is produced from a single cause.
As the Sūtra says, "by means of other conditions," salt is an auxiliary condition for that which is naturally bland.
The Sūtra says, "For example, like a seed," which is analogous to the case of salt; their characteristics are identical.
Regarding the phrase "firstly, the reprimand and the objection": "reprimand" (ze) is equivalent to "objection" (nan).
The Sūtra says, "Salt should also possess a subtle nature that is not salty. The intent of this objection is that since there already exists a general state of being non-salty...

Regarding the nature of saltiness: if salt possesses the quality of being salty, should it not also possess a non-salty nature? This constitutes a mutual refutation—refuting what currently exists by claiming it does not exist now, and refuting what does not exist by claiming it exists now.
When the Sūtra says "salt is all," it refers only to all phenomena (dharmas), using salt as a metaphor.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "because they are taught in sequence": the seeds of the internal four great elements originally exist by virtue of causes and conditions;
this is termed "sequence.
"Not from expedient means" means that the internal [elements] do not grow from the external four great elements.
Regarding the arising of the teaching based on principle: it is by virtue of the principle of Buddha-nature that the teaching arises, thereby possessing the function of verbal expression.
Since practice is established in reliance upon the teaching, the functions such as cultivating the causes are explained next.
Regarding the separate clarification of the meaning of "one's own intention": because one's own intention constitutes the primary purport of this sutra, it is explained separately.
The Sutra says, "One who knows illusion"; "knowing illusion" refers to the method, which is the cause.
One who understands illusion is one who can perform illusions.
One who understands the retribution of illusion knows that results are brought about by causes.
One who understands illusory arts knows the functional power of illusion.
"Knowing and thus killing" refers to the karmic act of killing. "One who knows the killer" refers to the person capable of killing.
"Knowing the retribution for killing" means knowing that due to the cause of killing, one falls into the hells in the next life as a distinct result (*vipāka-phala*);

in subsequent births among humans, one's lifespan is short as the concordant result (*niṣyanda-phala*); and the supportive environment one experiences is meager and lacks luster as the sovereign result (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding the fruit:
"Knowing that liberation comes through killing" means knowing that by killing the mother of craving and the father of ignorance, one attains liberation;
it also means knowing that liberation is obtained through the cause of killing.
From the killing of the five Brahmins up to those who hold wrong views—this briefly summarizes the remaining paths of action; hence it says "up to those who hold wrong views.
"Knowing" refers to the lack of faith in cause and effect.
To know those with wrong views is to know the icchantikas.

To know the retribution for wrong views is to know that when such a person dies, they fall into Avīci; this is the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*). When they are reborn among humans, their wrong views increase further;
this is the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). Their circumstantial environment and retinue are entirely deficient; this is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Regarding the "superior fruit":
one who knows the liberation from false views understands that the cause of [suffering] is false view, and through this realization, they attain the right path; this is called liberation.
Regarding "incurring immeasurable sin": King Prasenajit previously had a sincere instruction.

There are those who offend against the Buddha; their property is punished by being confiscated by the state. When such a person hears that they have committed an offense, they think, "This punishment has been brought upon me," and thus they seek to give away their wealth (and so forth).

Regarding what can be understood according to the intentions of oneself or others: to say "it exists" follows the intention of others, while to say "it does not exist" follows one's own intention. To speak in conventional terms is...

To speak in accordance with others is to follow others; to speak of true reality is to follow oneself. To speak of permanence, bliss, and so forth is to follow oneself; to speak of impermanence and so forth is to follow others. As the Sūtra says:
"Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see the Buddha-nature only slightly. This implies that even a Bodhisattva of the first abode already possesses a complete vision of the Buddha-nature.
What is now called "limited vision" among the ten stages refers merely to following the obscure inclinations of others.
Regarding the "abbreviated" aspect within each dharma: for every single practice and every single understanding, there is a corresponding pair of the abbreviated and the extensive.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that "one should not speak": it refers to that which is not in accord with either mundane or supramundane dharmas; therefore, one should not speak of it.
Regarding the term "Mṛgāramātṛ" mentioned in the Sūtra: she was the lady Viśākhā, who had a son named Mṛga.
"Non-existent yet existent" means that the original essence of the Ten Powers and so forth is like space; thus it is called "non-existent.
Nevertheless, through cultivation and severance, the Ten Powers and so forth are realized as existence by means of wisdom; therefore, it is said to be "non-existent yet existent."

Regarding "that which exists but is non-existent": "existence" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like. Now, because one abandons them through immediate knowledge, the existence of afflictions is severed and is thus no longer present.

As for the unwholesome and the indeterminate, they are omitted from the summary of the collection of wholesome states; furthermore, because the wholesome is capable of assisting toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), it is not omitted [from that summary].
It is said: furthermore, good and evil constitute the neutral resultant aggregates (*vipākaskandha*).
As for what the Sūtra says regarding "the noble and the non-noble," etc.: the noble is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), truly quiescent, neither pure nor a realm of affliction;

it is not grasping, not subject to prediction, and does not exist; it is not of the three times, not time itself; it is permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and is not form (*rūpa*) and so forth; it is not the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).

It is not an external sense-base (*āyatana*), nor is it the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Both are of the same category as "non-existence," yet there are further phrases that are of the same category as "existence-in-non-existence.

The scripture states: "The Bodhisattva in his final birth... [compared to] other Bodhisattvas. Regarding this passage, two interpretations must be maintained. If one says "final... [the text continues].

The body does not understand the Buddha-nature; this refers to the two preceding teachings [of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings] regarding those in the stage of being "ready for succession" (*upapatti-bhūmi*).
As for the remaining bodhisattvas, they are those from the stage of "ready for succession" downwards. If one provides an interpretation based on both inclusion and exclusion:

even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) within the Perfect Teaching have not yet fully exhausted the Buddha-nature of the ultimate ground of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), let alone the bodhisattvas from Equal Enlightenment downwards. However, the commentary (*shu*) primarily adopts this interpretation, which is why it says, "they themselves still do not understand. Furthermore...

Even the Bodhisattvas on the stage of "approaching" (mūrdhan) in the Separate Teaching (biejiao) have not yet been able to understand this; how much less so those below the stages of "practice" (xing) and "abiding" (zhu), who are termed ordinary Bodhisattvas.

This refers to the opening up of the causes, conditions, and karmic practices of the phenomenal world. Within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) of the Separate Teaching, the karmic practices and causes and conditions of the ten dharma-realms differ according to their respective medicines and ailments.
Furthermore, regarding the worldly conventional truth, such as the ripening of worldly flavors and virtues, neither of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) recognizes these.

The physical body that appears for the sake of the world is conventional truth; its transformations are difficult to measure and inconceivable. Therefore, it is not something that can be fully understood by those of the Two Vehicles.
This is illustrated by the previous passage which states: "Manifesting illness is the realm of the Buddha, not the wisdom of the Two Vehicles. This is precisely such an example.
Regarding the question of where the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) was taught, the intention is to ask in which sūtra it was stated. This is one interpretation;
however, the present sūtra itself states that it was taught at Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*).
There are other matters of concern, such as the five periods and eight teachings, the seven layers and two bonds, which pervade the entire span of the Buddha’s life.
Whether expanded or condensed, whether mutually inclusive or identical, and including the revelation of the ultimate truth—all of these are beyond the knowledge of the followers of the Two Vehicles.

Regarding "the nature of the objective realm" (*viṣaya-bhāva*): even though it is evil, because it is capable of being the object of the Buddha's observation, the absence of even a hair’s breadth of wisdom is called the nature of the objective realm.
Regarding "the revealing cause of the myriad virtues": that which reveals the myriad virtues is called the nature of the revealing cause.
That which is also called the "conditioning cause" (pratyaya-hetu) refers to the myriad wholesome deeds mentioned above.

Regarding the term "sentient-being nature" (sattva-dhātu): the name "sentient being" is comprehensive, encompassing both the profound and the shallow. Since it is said that they both possess the common designation "sentient-being Buddha-nature," [it follows that this applies to all].
Regarding "from one sentence to seven sentences": this refers generally to the current section where the intermediate chapters are explained together with the major sections;
hence it says "from one sentence up to seven sentences.

Regarding "both self and other, and both [affirmation and negation]": this refers to suppressing and refuting the icchantikas who currently do not possess Buddha-nature, which is termed "also non-existent," yet will [possess it] in the future.

When one comes [into being], the name "existence" necessarily exists; furthermore, previously when the mind had not yet been awakened, the name "non-existence" existed, whereas now that the mind has just been awakened, the name "existence" exists.
Regarding those who possess neither: a virtuous person lacks the side of evil, and an evil person lacks the side of goodness; therefore, it is said that their names each lack one side.
Regarding those with roots of goodness who possess the nature of non-attainment: this refers to the phrase "there is something within nothingness" and "nothingness within something.
Next, concerning those who rely solely on internal principle: this is explained by taking the internal retinue of phenomena as the basis for the dharma.
This means that he is one who is capable of understanding; others and himself consider this interpretation to be the attainment of the intended meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*): these three truths encompass all phenomena exhaustively. Because one has not yet attained the three truths, one does not reach the further shore (*pāra*).

Regarding those who lack both the Middle Way and its cause and effect: they have not yet attained the true causal factors of the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause) and the *vipāka-phala* (fruition).
As for those who mistakenly seek only substantial benefit, this refers to following toward *nirvāṇa* in order to seek liberation; it is called "following from precepts.
The *Śīla-sūtra* states that those who do not possess the path of accordance do not possess the non-action (*avijñapti*) of the meditative path.
As for the other six profound aggregates: *Gāthā* is translated here as "Verses" (or "Repetitive Verses"); *Nidāna* is translated as "Causes and Conditions";
*Avadāna* is translated as "Parables"; *Jātaka* is translated as "Birth Stories"; and *Vaipulya* is translated as "Extensive Teachings."
*Abhutadharma* (阿浮陀達摩) is translated here as "the unprecedented. Because these six profound *nikāyas* are difficult to understand, one does not believe in them.

Now, the intention [of this passage] should follow the eighth fascicle of the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), which cites Dharmatrāta as saying: "One does not believe that the six *nikāyas* are mutually interpenetrating;

that is, the *Kṣudraka* lacks the *Paripṛcchā*, the *Upadeśa*, and the *Mahā*; and the *Mahā* lacks the *Nidāna*, the *Avadāna*, and the *Arthavarga*. One should simply believe in all six *nikāyas*..."

They mutually interpenetrate; that is to say, the sūtras, geyas, gāthās, ityuktakas, jātakas, and avadānas—by means of these texts, their underlying principles are now seen to be perfectly consistent.
The Sūtra states: "Regarding those whose wisdom is not complete": from the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one seeks only the Buddha-wisdom; this is called being complete.
Apart from this, all else is incomplete (the character *niao* [鳥] is read as *huan* [喚], expressing an exclamation of wonder).

Regarding the first four preparatory practices (*prayoga*): the first is the five cessations (*pañca-vyupaśama*); the second is the two types of specific mindfulness (*viśeṣa-smṛti*); the third is general mindfulness (*sāmānya-smṛti*); and the fourth is the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

If one follows the thirty-third scripture cited below, there is a slight difference: the first is impurity (*aśubha*), the second is the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the third is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the fourth is the stage of Heat.
Regarding the statement that "the Mahāyāna encompasses the thirty minds," this is explained according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao) of the Mahāyāna.
Specifically, the stages of Abiding and Practice correspond to the remaining four types of skillful means, while the ten stages of Dedication correspond to the [remaining] stages.
The first category refers to those who have reached the other shore (*pāramitā*). The second category refers to the causes for reaching the other shore;
it takes the person mentioned in the second category as its condition (*pratyaya*).
Regarding the phrase "remaining in the stage resembling the fundamental," this interpretation is superior. "Dāocháng" (Daochang) is pronounced "Diāocháng" (Diaochang).
Regarding the phrase "this is clearly not seeing the principle": it means not seeing that which is reached on the other shore through both the general and specific teachings.

Thus, one should know that there are differences in *nirvāṇa*: the two types of *nirvāṇa*, Great and Small, are not the same. In the Small *nirvāṇa*, one does not perceive the distinction between the two deaths—the death of the segmented (*paricchinna*) and the death of transformation (*pariṇāma*).

Regarding the mutual citation of the general and the specific: the river of birth and death is specific, which only a Buddha can cross; the river of nirvana is general, being accessible to all four types of persons.
(From the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra-sijì*, Scroll Eight)
Private Notes on the Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, Transcribed in the Fourth Year of Tenpō, Fifth Month,
Fascicle Nine, Chapter on Kāśyapa, Volume Fourteen.

The "three gates of crossing" refers to the thoughts of greed, the thoughts of anger, and the thoughts of delusion; because one cultivates their antidotes, such as the contemplation of impurity, they are called "gates of crossing.
As for the "sufficient conditions," for those with much ignorance, one teaches them to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time; thus, there are three.

Because the world is a continuity, it is not eternal, as the three periods of time do not cease but rather pass into one another. Furthermore, the past refutes eternity; the future refutes annihilation;

and the present, through cause and effect, refutes both annihilation and eternity. Why? Because the twelve links of dependent origination revolve without end, with cause and effect never ceasing and moments never remaining still.
By means of this moment-to-moment impermanence, one treats the delusion of those two worlds. [The second period, the ten...]
Second, the self is refuted by means of causes and conditions. What is this? To give rise to attachment toward one’s father and aversion toward one’s mother is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

When the physical body bequeathed by the father is designated as "one's own," this is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). From the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) onward, up to old age and death, these correspond to the three time periods.
Because the two links of past ignorance and volitional formations are not grasped [as a self], it is said that the self is refuted across two time periods. By means of this investigation...

If one seeks a self within the impermanence of the present and future, it cannot be found. A single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) destroys inherent nature (*svabhāva*), for when one investigates that a single thought-moment is impermanent, it lacks substantial reality.
This is explained in detail in the third fascicle of the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), in the section on the "Excellence of the Object" (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra about "analyzing the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth," the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* explains the contemplation of the six elements—namely, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—as well as the analysis of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the thirty-six factors (*dharma*).
All of these are for the purpose of refuting the self (*ātman*); hence the use of the term "and so forth."

Regarding "the general is deep while the specific is shallow," this refers to the fourfold analysis of the relationship between object and contemplation, such as when the object is specific while the contemplation is general, or when the object is general while the contemplation is specific.
As stated in the text on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), when both object and contemplation are specific, it is called "specific characteristics" (*pṛthaglakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the attainment of the realization of emptiness through the four foundations of mindfulness: once the realization of "warmth" has been achieved through contemplation, there is already a portion of the outflow-free (anāsrava) element; this is termed the "realization of emptiness.

As for those who frequently employ the meditative absorptions of the form realm (rūpadhyāna): since the desire realm is a state of distraction, it is difficult to give rise to this contemplation therein.

Regarding "suffering, coarseness, and heaviness": that which is extremely evil and profoundly deep is called suffering, coarseness, and heaviness. That which can obstruct the higher realms is called the obstruction of suffering, coarseness, and heaviness.

When one takes delight in a higher stage, any one of the three—calmness (*śānta*), excellence (*pranīta*), and detachment (*niḥsaraṇa*)—arises accordingly. When one feels aversion toward a lower stage, any one of the three—suffering, coarseness, and obstruction—likewise arises accordingly.

The mind that feels aversion toward the lower stage is called the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*); the mind that takes delight in the higher stage is called the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Thus, there are nine grades each for the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). These suppress and sever the nine grades of afflictions of the lower stages and also enable the realization of the nine grades of unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*).

This applies to all eight stages below [the Peak of Existence], excluding only the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), where externalists may employ the six modes of practice (*ṣaḍ-abhyāsa*) to suppress and sever [afflictions].
Regarding the sixteen truths (*ṣoḍaśa-satya*), one should fully discuss the thirty-two truths consisting of the reduction of objects, aspects, and so forth.

Contemplation refers to the four aspects for each of the [Four Noble Truths]: regarding Suffering, there are the four—suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; regarding Origination, the four—origination, cause, production, and condition;

regarding Cessation, the four—cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation; and regarding the Path, the four—path, correctness, practice, and vehicle. These constitute the sixteen aspects, as explained extensively in the fourth fascicle of the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).

Furthermore, regarding the "patience with respect to the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*): this refers to the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and should not be explained as the contemplation of entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
As the Sūtra says, "the nature of Heat": Heat arises from the internal, untainted knowledge of the Truths; thus its very nature is called "Heat."

Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "Such as the 'Heat' stage and so forth": "phenomena that exist" refers to the phenomena of the three realms of existence (*traidhātuka*). "Conditioned" means that which is produced as having a fruit.
As for "these phenomena are obtained as retribution," this indicates their essence—that they are the phenomena of the three realms of existence—by way of illustrating them through their fruit.
As for these causal conditions: they can act as the cause for the five aggregates of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and bring those aggregates into being.
Regarding the mind associated with the ten wholesome paths of action: immediately after a mind associated with the wholesome, this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) arises.
As for the method, it is the method of contemplating the truths (*satya*).
As for "merely real dharmas" (*vastu-dharma*), this concentration has not yet been able to suppress or sever the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is merely designated as "real dharmas."

Regarding those who are drawn toward the first dhyāna: by means of the final grade of affliction of the desire realm, one gives rise to the concentration of the first dhyāna, which simultaneously abandons the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm.

Furthermore, regarding the use of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) to suppress the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*): the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception can only abandon the sphere of nothingness.
Delusion. Because it is a contaminated state of its own level and cannot give rise to the uncontaminated, the nine grades of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are not taken up.

Regarding the citation of Rāma: although Rāma did not give rise to the "Heat" stage (*uṣmagata*), how could a non-Buddhist from outside the [Buddhist] fold attain this meditative absorption? It is possible.
The stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) is initiated.

Regarding the phrase "that which obstructs the future": when the body, the bedding, and so forth attain the concentration of the future [dhyāna], they are able to destroy that nature which acts as an obstruction.
This "obstruction" refers to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding those who possess the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*), they are persons whose minds are associated with the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*).
As for the second interpretation concerning "the nature-obstructions" (*prakṛtyāvaraṇa*) and so forth, this explanation is superior.

Regarding the "Summit Dharma" (*mūrdha-dharma*), there are generally two meanings. First, if one regresses, one returns to the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage; however, upon advancing, one enters the "Patience" (*kṣānti*) stage.
Because it lies at the boundary between both advancing and retreating, it is like the summit of a mountain. Second, both the "Heat" and "Summit" virtues are subject to regression.
Within the category of dharmas subject to regression, the Summit virtue reaches its ultimate limit, just as the crown of the head is the extremity of the body; therefore, it is called the "Summit."

Regarding the two types of patience (*kṣānti*): one who attains the roots of goodness of patience will never again commit an immediate (*ānantarya*) evil deed, nor fall into the evil destinies, nor be born among the *saṃsvedaja* (moisture-born).

Furthermore, they will no longer undergo the retributions of being rootless, nor those of the northern continent (*uttarakuru*), the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), the neuter (*paṇḍaka*), or the hermaphrodite (*ubhayavyañjana*).
Moreover, regarding the delusions concerning principles that have attained the roots of goodness of patience—the karma and retribution of these delusions are all conditioned by the four [truths].
Roots of goodness attain non-analytical cessation; this is called the merit and excellence of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Patience does not lead to rebirth in the evil destinies"—this refers precisely to that.

Regarding the "supreme dharmas of the three times," the preceding three all take the four truths as their object. The supreme dharma of the world (*laukikāgradharma*) takes only the suffering of the desire realm as its object.

When it is now said that they "take the four truths as their object," this means that among the four, they take one aspect at a time; therefore, they are called the vehicle that takes the four truths as its object.
The first three individuals take the Four Noble Truths as their object; therefore, this statement is made. Regarding the term "supreme worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*):

the seven types of persons on the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) are all "worldly" (*laukika*) because they are still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*). This seventh person is called "supreme" (*agra*) because he is the most excellent among those in the world.
Upon attaining this root of goodness, there is the power of human effort (*puruṣakāra-bala*), which functions independently of similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) to induce the noble state.
Because it gives rise to the Path, it is called "Supreme" (*agra*). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that "the first entry into the state free from birth" (*niyāma*) is its meaning.

The term "birth" (*jāti*) refers to the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*); just as raw food causes harm when given to a person, the Path of Seeing is able to sever them, and is therefore called "free from birth."

Regarding the four types of patience (*kṣānti*) in the cessation of delusions regarding the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*): there are sixteen moments of mind consisting of eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*).

In contemplating the Four Truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*); in contemplating the Four Truths of the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*), there are four subsequent-patience (*anvayakṣānti*).

Among these sixteen, the first five moments are called the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the sixteenth moment is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and so forth. To say that "patience" is wisdom (*prajñā*) is to distinguish it [from other mental factors].

Regarding its essential nature: because within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) the vision of the Dharma is clear and the function of wisdom (*prajñā*) is intensified, it is described in this specific way.

In truth, however, its nature consists of all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). As for the statement that "it takes one Truth as its object," this clarifies the meaning of the method of contemplation;

specifically, it refers to taking the aspect of "suffering" (*duḥkha-satya*) as the focal object. Among those of dull faculties who are called "those whose conduct is driven by craving" (*tṛṣṇā-carita*), there are two types when they are about to enter the path of seeing.

Those in whom laziness predominates remain in the practice of asceticism. Those in whom pride predominates remain in the practice of impermanence. Those of sharp faculties are called practitioners of vision (*darśana-carita*).
Upon entering the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), there are likewise two types: those who are attached to "mine" (*mamakāra*) remain in the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-carita*).

If one is attached to a self, one is made to abide in the practice of non-self. Therefore, because the modes of activity differ according to the faculties and dispositions, the mind of "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and so forth perceives a steep and swift path;
it is practiced only incidentally and narrowly, failing to reach the other truths. Hence, it is said that it takes only one [truth] as its object.

Regarding the five [stages] from the first fruit up to the sixteenth moment of mind: the sixteenth moment of mind, which is the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), is the essence of the *srotāpanna*.

This is because this person possesses only a single mode of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). As for the stage of the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), it belongs exclusively to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), because it contemplates the Four Noble Truths and thus is subsumed under the aggregate of formations.
The "Single Truth of True Emptiness" (*śūnyatā-ekasatya*) refers to entering the sixteen moments of the untainted (*anāsrava*) uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) from the Truth of Suffering;
this is termed the Single Truth of True Emptiness.

Regarding the "ninety-eight proclivities" (*anuśaya*), they are collectively called "proclivities" in the sense of "driving and employing. They are so named because they drive and employ the mind of the practitioner.
The "deities" (devas) are so called because they transmigrate through the three realms; thus, they are generally designated by the term *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).

They are also called *kleśa* (afflictions), where *kṣepa* (disturbance) is the primary meaning and *raṇa* (turmoil) is the secondary meaning. These phenomena that disturb and turmoil the practitioner’s mind and spirit prevent true illumination from being developed;
therefore, they are named *kleśa*. Specifically, within the *duḥkhasatya* (truth of suffering) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ten *anuśayas* are present. First, regarding the self...

Within the aggregates, bases, and elements of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), to falsely conceptualize them as a body is called the view of a body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); it is also called the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

This refers to the reckoning of the self as being like a sesame seed, a bean, or the size of a thumb; when one is deludedly attached to [the notion] that it pervades the entire body and maintains this reckoning of a self without forgetting, it is called the view of a self.
Second is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). To calculate that the self is either annihilated or eternal is called the view of extremes. Third is the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Because one calculates [the self] as being annihilated or eternal, one does not believe in cause and effect; furthermore, one calculates this self to be spontaneous, primordial darkness, or the primal nature (*prakṛti*), which refers to the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
Moreover, one calculates that it is produced from parents, atoms, Brahmā, and so forth. To grasp these principles with a false mind is all termed false view. Fourth...

1. Grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This refers to clinging to what is false as being the path; among things that are not true precepts, one erroneously regards them as such, such as the false precepts of chickens, dogs, oxen, and so forth.
This is called "reckoning what is not a cause to be a cause" and is termed grasping at precepts and observances. 2. Grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Furthermore, because of these views, one erroneously claims to have reached the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and falsely asserts it to be *nirvāṇa*. To believe in this and nothing else is called grasping at views. 3. Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). It draws one toward and grasps at the objects of no... [text truncated]
1. *Ālaya* (Attachment): This refers to craving and desire. 2. *Pratigha* (Aversion): A mind of anger and resentment is called aversion. 3. *Moha* (Delusion):

When the deluded mind takes an object as its condition, whatever arises therein causes every thought-moment to deviate from the truth without one’s awareness; all such states are delusion. 4. *Māna* (Pride):

To rely on oneself and look down upon others is called pride. 5. *Vicikitsā* (Doubt): A deluded mind that deviates from principle and wavers without reaching a decision is called doubt. [End of] Collection.

The three views are eliminated: specifically, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are each removed.

On the path, only two views are removed: namely, the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes. These together total thirty-two. In the higher realms, for each of the four truths, one instance of anger (*pratigha*) is further removed from each category;

the remainder is the same as in the desire realm. This totals fifty-six. Thus, there are eighty-eight afflictions of the type to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*). Adding the ten afflictions of the type to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) completes the count.
Regarding the contemplations (*vitarka*): there are four in the desire realm, namely greed, hatred, delusion, and pride. In each of the two upper realms, hatred is excluded, leaving only six.

When these six are added to the four [of the desire realm], there are ten contemplations. Because all of them can moisten karma and lead to birth within the three realms, they are called "delusions of contemplation" (*vitarka-kleśa*).
Together, these constitute the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). Question: Regarding the delusions under the Four Noble Truths, by what principle or teaching are they increased or decreased?

Is this not different? Answer: According to the Abhidharma, anger does not function in the higher realms. Question: For what reason do the views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) exist only within the realm of suffering (*duḥkha*)?

Answer: These views rely upon the body; therefore, they are called the "view of self-identity. Based on the view of self-identity, one gives rise to extreme views. The other three [views] do not rely upon the body, and thus these two views do not exist for them.

Furthermore, because they are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), they are placed under the category of suffering. Question: What about the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?

Therefore, it exists only within the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*). Question: Since the grasping to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) conceives of a cause, and the Truth of Suffering is an effect, why is it included under suffering?
Answer: Because one conceives of many ascetic practices as being the actual cause, it is placed beneath the category of suffering.

Furthermore, because they are not the path to liberation, yet are falsely claimed to be the path to liberation, it can also arise in relation to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). The Truths of Origination (*samudaya*) and Cessation (*nirodha*) are different from this, and therefore the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not exist therein.

Because there is no view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there is also no view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Since [the views] of accumulation and cessation are not the path, the grasping for precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) does not arise.

Furthermore, regarding the grasping for precepts and observances that falls under the two truths of suffering and the path: those that originally belong to the inner way (Buddhism) can be abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering; those that originally belong to the outer ways (non-Buddhist paths) [are abandoned differently].

Since they are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they exist only in two [realms]. Question: Among the eighty-eight [defilements], those abandoned by the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) are exclusively delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Why, then, are there fifty-two volitions (*cetanā*) among them? Answer: These volitions depend upon the views; the views are their root.

When the views are severed, the root is destroyed and the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) withers. Volitions that are deluded regarding objective phenomena (*vastu*) are not included here. Question: Among those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), what...

Therefore, there is no doubt. [Question: It follows logically that one should have no doubt once the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) has been attained. As for the eighty-eight-headed snake dying, it died previously.

Regarding the vision of the forty-li water: the surging waves of delusion pervade the three realms, as well as the environments and the beings (*sādhāraṇa-vastu* and *asādhāraṇa-vastu*) in every place.

The innate attachments (*upapatti-āpta*) all obstruct the principle of the Truths (*satya-dharma*). This is illustrated by the analogy of forty *li* of water. Although the cultivated afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya*) pervade the three realms, they do not obstruct the principle of the Truths;

being slight and easy to sever, they are like a single drop of water. Furthermore, the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) differ from the cultivated afflictions, as they constitute only one category, thus being likened to a single drop.

The Sūtra states, "Because these three are heavy. All sentient beings who receive a body invariably conceive of a self (*ātman*). Thus, the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) subsumes the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);

the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) subsumes false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); and the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) subsumes the remaining four dull afflictions (*anuśaya*). Therefore, it is said that these three are heavy.

Those who maintain that a self exists permanently do so by viewing the aggregate of real dharmas as a whole and establishing it as a "self"; this is precisely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Those who all believe in heterodox deities include those who observe precepts through perverse seeking, such as maintaining the vows of a chicken or a dog, in the hope of attaining *nirvāṇa*;
they all rely upon the teachings of heterodox deities and heterodox teachers.

Regarding the statement that the arising of the view of self resembles right view and so forth: all three arise from within the internal mind; therefore, they are difficult to discern, which is why it is said they "resemble" them.
Regarding the statement that the view of self contradicts right wisdom and so forth: this is because the false notion of self opposes right wisdom and the like.
As for the statement in the Sūtra that "one attains the four matters," those from the second fruit onward all attain these four.
Regarding "the five faculties with faith as the foremost," they are simply the five beginning with faith and diligence.
Regarding "taking the three poisons as internal": this refers to the dullness within that which is sharp, not the three poisons within the context of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

As for the scriptural statement that they must be called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), this is a failure to revert to the Sanskrit original; the same applies to the subsequent passage concerning the "contrary flow."
The "Minor Prajñā" refers to the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the phrase "all likewise flow against the current until they reach the stage of 'not [being]" (*buzhe*): the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) is the beginning of flowing against the current; yet even they receive the name of "flowing against the current.
As for those in the other three fruits, they flow against the current most effectively. Why, then, do they not receive the name of "flowing against the current"?
If the other three [fruits] were not attained, then even a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) would likewise not attain this "flowing against the current.
As for the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "If a *sakṛdāgāmin*... and ending with "...how can he be so named," it shall first be explained in sequence:
If the *sakṛdāgāmin* and others did not depend upon the *srotāpanna*, from what then would the *sakṛdāgāmin* and others derive their attainment?

The Sūtra states, "At the time of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)... and so forth; this first provides an illustration. For example, while still an ordinary person, one already possesses a conventional name.
Just as when Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) attained the fruit of the Path, he was immediately named Srotāpanna, even though he was certain to further attain the second fruit.
That which was previously attained is called the "old" second fruit. In relation to what preceded it, it is called the "newly attained" third fruit.
In relation to the two preceding fruits, the second fruit is termed "old" and the third fruit is termed "new" (and so forth).
The Sūtra states: "First, liberation" refers to the wisdom of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*). Nirvāṇa refers to the abandonment of partial realization.
Furthermore, Master Paramārtha said: "Conditioned merit is called liberation; unconditioned merit is termed nirvāṇa. All noble ones (*ārya*) possess both of these.
Moreover, liberation is the partial attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), while nirvāṇa is [the partial attainment of] the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

One attains the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). However, while the names "liberation" (*vimukti*) and "nirvāṇa" originally referred only to the ultimate [fruit], they now extend to the first fruit (*prathamaphala*).
For this reason, the designation "one who flows against the current" (*prati-srota-āyin*) extends to the subsequent bodhisattvas as well.
Regarding the name "penetrating downward": a *srotāpanna* also seeks the bodhi of the two types of knowledge, and a bodhisattva likewise seeks bodhi.
Since the bodhi sought is identical, one should know that a *srotāpanna* is also called a bodhisattva.

The Sūtra says: "Perfectly awakening to cause and effect" means being able to realize the effect of suffering (*duḥkha*), the cause of its origination (*samudaya*), the effect of its cessation (*nirodha*), and the cause of the path (*mārga*).

The Sūtra says: "Perfectly awakening to the shared path. The name "awakening" is common to the lower [stages] and is therefore called "shared. As for the "path," it is not shared with those in suffering; it exists only in...

Regarding the Buddha, a sutra states: "One who investigates the characteristics of dharmas finds that within the Buddha's teachings there is no dharma of the non-Buddhists; therefore, it is incorrect to call [such a person] one who lacks faith. Why is this?
If one were to say that attaining the Path for the first time is immediately called *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), why would one not [be so called] from the very moment of suffering?

Is it that the first moment of patience (*kṣānti*) is already called *srotāpanna*, while the fifteen moments [of the path of seeing] are termed "approaching" (*pratipannaka*), and only at the sixteenth moment is one named a *srotāpanna*?

As for the Sūtra’s statement that one "possesses the eight knowledges," the Buddha’s intention was merely to say that attaining the Dharma at the very beginning constitutes being a *srotāpanna*. It does not [mean that one must possess all eight knowledges].
Regarding the discussion of persons, the question concerning the three fruits has not yet been answered; therefore, the subsequent inquiry arises.

One Abhidharma master explains that there is no principle for simultaneous observation, as it would properly apply to the "shared" (sādhāraṇa), yet he claims it is "unshared" (asādhāraṇa) and thus cannot be employed.
The Hexi [master] explains "shared" and "unshared," a view which our own school does not refute, as it serves to interpret the sūtra effectively. Furthermore, if...

To directly clarify the meaning of the sūtra: it should simply state that those in the stage of worthiness (*ārya*) and those who have already transcended to the fruit share the attainment of the transcendent fruit;

they no longer share it with those in the stage of preparation (*prayoga*). Furthermore, those in the stage of preparation share [the fruit] with those of the four fruits, yet the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) is not shared [with them].

Next, the first fruit is shared with the second fruit, but the second fruit is not shared. Continuing in this manner up to the fourth fruit, each preceding one is shared while each succeeding one is not.
This is not shared [with other schools]; one should provide this very explanation.
Regarding "all passing through the middle": although the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is extremely swift and thus passes through the middle, it does not grasp a fruit.
It is like a person with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): although their power is swift, the underlying principle (*nyāya*) is nonetheless not absent.

Regarding "the inferential and the manifest": "inferential" refers to the two upper realms; "manifest" refers to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) within the desire realm.
Patience is concentration (*samādhi*), while knowledge is wisdom (*jñāna*). However, concentration is not grasped [as the primary factor], because concentration is the cause and wisdom is the fruit.

Regarding "attaining each of the truths in turn": this does not mean that the faculties are not identical; there are also those who take all four truths as their object, rather than focusing exclusively on only one truth.

As for the statement that "the first fruit clarifies only the state of correctness" (*samyaktva-niyāma*): the first fruit is the beginning of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) path, and is therefore called the "state of correctness."

Regarding "one fruit and two paths" (*eka-phala-dvi-mārga*): first one cultivates the path; next, one realizes the second fruit. Having realized the fruit, one contemplates it and then practices again.
This is the path belonging to the family of these two fruits; it is the path that follows the [first] path. Therefore, it is said that this includes the path of the *anāgāmin*.
The Sūtra says: "Those who practice for the sake of food" refers to practicing by means of the untainted food (*anāsrava-āhāra*).
"Those who are born in the intermediate state" means that one attains the stage of *anāgāmin* only after being born there.

"Furthermore, those of clear faith and understanding" refers to those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) entering the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), at which point they are renamed "those of faith and understanding" (*śraddhādhimukta*). [Those of] dull faculties...

Relying on the faculties and faith, one advances toward true understanding; therefore, it is called "faith-understanding" (*śraddhādhimukta*). There are three ways for such a person to realize the fruit, namely the three fruits. Regarding those who are said to have "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*):

these are practitioners of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) who, upon entering the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), are termed "attained through vision. Those of sharp faculties personally cultivate vision through wisdom;
having seen the Dharma, they attain the principle. Therefore, they are called "attained through vision. Such a person is on the path of reflection (*cintāmārga*) in successive order.
Regarding the realization of the third fruit (and so forth), Kaishan criticized this, saying: "This distinction between the sharp and the dull does not refer to two different types of persons;
that is to say, these are not two kinds of *anāgāmin*s."

Regarding the "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin): this refers to the two types of practitioners—the one who attains through faith-understanding (śraddhādhimukta) and the one who attains through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta)—who enter the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

By employing untainted wisdom (anāsravajñāna), they sever the fetters of the lower and upper realms (avarabhāgīya- and ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana). They give rise to the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti); this is precisely the application of the foundations of mindfulness in common (sāmānyasmṛtyupasthāna).

They cultivate the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭābhibhvāyatana), and the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana), entering the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti). Regarding the three emptinesses, the phenomena, and the nature, the two obscurations [are first addressed].

Having already exhausted [the outflows], they further sever the obstacles to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and realize the principle of cessation. All mind and mental factors enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Because they have attained this attainment, they are called "bodily witnesses" (*kāyasākṣin*) who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*). What is it that enters the attainment of cessation which resembles the dharma of nirvāṇa?

He establishes [the mind] within the body and brings all the labors of the three realms to rest. Because he personally realizes the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), he is called "one who has realized through the body" (*kāyasākṣin*).
Furthermore, it is said that while only the body remains, the mind is like a fish in ice or a hibernating insect; therefore, it is specifically termed "realization through the body."

Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The Non-returner who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) through cultivation is designated as a 'Body-witness' (*kāyasākṣin*).

Since the absorption of cessation is mindless, one is called a Body-witness because it is realized by means of the body. Such a person transforms from being a Worldly Non-returner into cultivating the path toward Arhatship, and no longer emerges from that contemplation."
Having severed eighty-one grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), one has still not yet realized the fruit of Arhatship (and so forth).
As for the fact that this is not mentioned in the Mahāyāna, it is precisely to explain the present sutra; one must also state that it is not mentioned in the Mahāyāna.
This is merely a difference between extensive and abbreviated treatments, and there is no loss of principle therein.
The Sūtra states that regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the formless realm, there are two types among those who ascend through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

First, those who have practiced meditative cultivation are "those who delight in wisdom" (*prajñā-rata*); these go to Akaniṣṭha. Second, those who have not practiced meditative cultivation are "those who delight in concentration" (*samādhi-rata*).
Regarding "mixed cultivation," this refers to the cultivation of multiple moments of contaminated states and so forth.
As for "in the present body," it means that within the body of the desire realm, one immediately attains the two fruits of *anāgāmin* and *arhat*.
Regarding those who take birth throughout the four *dhyānas*, this refers to those who are "universally submerged. The remainder of the text concerns the eighteen celestial realms.

For now, we shall rely on the Sūtra’s statement concerning those who lack mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This means that while diligent cultivation of contemplative insight is called "vigor," the difficulty in manifesting a concentrated mind is termed "lack of mastery," which is to say the absence of the four *dhyāna* concentrations.
Conversely, it can be understood that one who is lax in insight may possess concentration.
"Those whose karma is dissipated" means that their contaminated (sāsrava) karma has been dispersed and destroyed.
"Not receiving a rebirth" means not receiving birth in the higher realms.

"One who has been touched by the mind of the Path" refers to one who is neither a learner (śaikṣa) nor a non-learner (aśaikṣa)—that is, one who is neither in the stage of initial fruit nor an Arhat. This is precisely [the case for] the *naivasaikṣanāśaikṣa*.
This is said because it includes those who are still training for arhatship.
"Taking the true mind as the object" means realizing the outflow-free principle.
"Cultivating the old mind" means abiding in the fruit without further progress, remaining fixed at that particular stage.

Regarding the statement that those who are called "learners" (śaikṣa) or "non-learners" (aśaikṣa) are those who have lost mindfulness: first, falling back from the fruit [of realization] is called losing mindfulness; second, emerging from meditative absorption and returning to a state similar to the distracted mind is also called losing mindfulness.

Furthermore, the phrase "one is right and one is wrong" below serves as a further judgment on the four propositions within the sūtra. The initial mention of "those who are not learners" refers to those who have received [the precepts].
1. Those born with minds that undergo the intermediate state (antarābhava). 2. Those in training (śaikṣa) possess the cause for the outflow-free (anāsrava).

Since these two are not yet nirvāṇa, it is said that "the two are not nirvāṇa. 3. Those beyond training (aśaikṣa) possess the fruit of the outflow-free. 4. Those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
This final moment of consciousness abandons the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*). As stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*:
"The Arhat’s mind of retribution-born existence and the mind of deportment, as well as the mind conforming to deportment, thus proceed toward Parinirvāṇa; these two are [the states of] Nirvāṇa."
If one later resolves [the text] below, the second master’s interpretation may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Regarding those who "constantly practice": having been born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), they practice for a long duration before finally attaining *parinirvāṇa*; they merely possess diligent cultivation.

There is neither the path of rapid progress nor the path that does not depend on personal diligence; this means that one does not await the cultivation of the path through arduous effort. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Having been born in the Form Realm, one does not undergo textual study or cultivation; through effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), one attains parinirvāṇa. Thus, both the path of diligent cultivation and the path of rapid progress are absent."
Therefore, it is said that there is "no practice.
When the masters of the treatise claim that one is "perfumed by a mind of compassion," this interpretation is irrational; thus, it is not accepted here.
First, as for the "weak and inferior": their physical strength is frail and weak, and they are unable to cultivate the Path; such is the case.
"To return to the previous point" means to establish the aforementioned meaning of gain and loss.
The Sūtra says: "As for wholesome dharmas, in their general substance, they do not go beyond the three paths; this is because they are the three virtues."

Regarding the "preparatory path" up to the "stage of the cause": this refers exclusively to the period beginning from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the stage of *anāgāmin*, all of which belong to the stage of the cause.
When the Sūtra says, "He is also called a śramaṇa," this phrase clarifies the cause, while the subsequent phrase distinguishes the fruit.
The Sūtra speaks of "seven kinds of fruits. These seven fruits are taught to manifest the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, distinguishing it from the preceding six.
The Sūtra speaks of the "fruit of equality"; this fruit is precisely the fruit of the Pure Land.

Taking the ten wholesome actions as the proximate cause, and the three calamities as the remote cause—only when the three calamities arise can sentient beings give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
"To sever lack" means to sever all forms of lack. "To sever other paths" means to sever all other paths.
All states that remain within the realm of causes are termed "lack."
The two "non-intentional" (or "not of the mind") refer neither to all [precepts] nor to all paths. Furthermore, they are neither cultivation nor fulfillment.
As for what the Sūtra calls the "fivefold dharma-body," according to the Tripiṭaka teaching, the unmanifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) constitute the body of morality (*śīla-kāya*).

The fundamental pure meditative concentration, refined through practice and cultivation, constitutes the body of concentration (*samādhi-kāya*). As for the observation of the four truths from the cessation of birth up to the realization at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)...

The Four Truths, when fully exhausted, constitute the body of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). When both the fundamental afflictions and their habitual tendencies are completely exhausted, it is called the body of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*).

To clearly know and see that the fundamental afflictions and their habitual tendencies are already exhausted, with morality, concentration, and wisdom perfected, such that one does not undergo further existence, is called the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*).

In the Shared Teaching, this is applied to the three baskets (*piṭaka*) and the five [stages] above, adding the four truths of non-offense and offense, non-distraction, non-savoring, and non-arising, up to the stage of Buddhahood.

Seeing the ultimate perfection of reality constitutes the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*). From the initial stage of seeing the ground (*darśana-bhūmi*) and liberation from the delusions of views, until the moment of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), when the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the wisdom of single-moment correspondence are entirely exhausted, one abides in *nirvāṇa* with remainder; this is called the liberation-body (*vimuktikāya*).

One clearly perceives neither bondage nor liberation, yet can see for oneself through the Buddha-eye of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); thus one abides in *nirvāṇa* with remainder, free from rebirth.

One is bound into the bondage of non-fruition; yet, seeing that all beings are without birth, one sees neither bondage nor liberation within that bondage—this is called the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*).
Both the Separate and Perfect [Teachings] rely upon the ninefold precepts, the ninefold concentrations, and the ninefold wisdoms.

When the habitual tendencies are exhausted beyond the triple realm, the Buddha-eye clearly perceives and knows, and the Dharma-body manifests. One also knows and sees the concealment and manifestation of the Dharma-bodies of others.
The sequence of stages is not disordered. These two teachings differ only in that one is sequential while the other is non-sequential, and one involves gradual entry while the other does not.

The present text, however, encompasses both the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching and the intent of the fivefold Dharma-body of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; its primary focus lies solely within the common stage of the Three Vehicles.
The Sūtra states, "Permanently severing the causes and conditions for birth throughout the three periods of time," which clarifies that its cause has been exhausted from antiquity.
It further states, "Also severing the body of the five aggregates within the three realms," which indicates its cessation. Therefore, it says, "My births have been exhausted.

According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the former refers to the knowledge of the destruction of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*); according to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the latter refers to the knowledge of the destruction of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
"The holy life has been brought to its ultimate consummation" indicates the perfection of its cause;

furthermore, "having abandoned the path of training" clarifies the culmination of its fruit. According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the former refers to the knowledge of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-jñāna*);
according to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the latter refers to the realization of cessation (*nirodha-sākṣātkriyā*).

Regarding the statement, "That which was originally sought has now been attained," this refers to those of the Hīnayāna who, being ignorant of their original aspiration, felt aversion toward the suffering of the three realms and sought only nirvāṇa.
Now, having severed the afflictions of both the paths of seeing and cultivation, they have exhausted them and realized the ultimate unconditioned nirvāṇa.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, this is the wisdom of the extinction of the lamp, wherein its fruit reaches its ultimate limit.

Regarding "those who attain the fruit through the path of cultivation," this characterizes the perfection of their realm. According to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, this refers to the wisdom of the path of cultivation;
thus it is said, "that which was to be done has been accomplished.

Regarding "the attainment of the wisdom of exhaustion," this clarifies that the cause has already been fulfilled. Regarding "the wisdom of non-arising," this manifests the cessation of the fruit. Thus, the *Śrīmālā*...
It is said: because one will not again undergo future existence after the afflictions have been severed, it is called "not receiving further existence" (*anupādāya*).
As for which category this [state] belongs to: since the Pratyekabuddha has already crossed the river of *nirvāṇa*, they too must possess a "tendency" (*pratipannaka*).

To explain what category this belongs to, the intention is that it belongs to the sixth person. Regarding the specific inclusion of this distinct case, it is explained as being situated precisely within the stage common to the Three Vehicles. Furthermore...
Now, one should follow the perfect (yuan) interpretation when explaining the scriptural text. Why?

Since it is stated that "accomplishing the six pāramitās is called reaching the other shore," and since neither the two preceding teachings nor the separate stages prior [to Buddhahood] have yet seen the Buddha-nature, they do not fully receive the name of "perfected six pāramitās.

Therefore, one should interpret them according to the perfect teaching; furthermore, the separate path of realization (*pratyekabuddha-mārga*) is identical to the perfect [teaching] and should be explained accordingly. Hence, it is called "separate" (*bie*).
There is an underlying intention. To "summarize the great principle" means merely to summarize the general meaning.

Regarding the statement that "Buddha-nature both exists and does not exist": it is called "non-existent" because its manifest function has not yet arisen; it is called "existent" because the mind will attain it in the future.

"Name also exists"—this refers to the two refutations. If one says that the icchantika attains enlightenment, it is called "deep attachment"; if one says they do not attain it, it is called "falsehood.
[The teaching] is able to refute these two extremes.

Regarding the refutation of the universal by means of the particular: this clarifies that the universal teaching does not pertain to the stage of the "causes of both," for therein one does not cultivate the immeasurable [virtues] or the three trainings, nor has the Buddha yet cultivated them;
thus, all such views must be revised. It is for this reason that they are refuted, so as to cause their views to be corrected.

The Sūtra states that those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or violate the four grave prohibitions do so because they have not yet seen the Buddha-nature; thus, these constitute the principle of "reversal" (*ānantarya*).

Regarding the phrase "crossing the river of the *Nirvāṇa* [teaching] common to all," this clarifies that these seven types of persons merely cross the river of the *Nirvāṇa* of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*). As for the following passage...
Fangyun said: "If one cultivates the three immeasurable trainings and attains crossing over the river of transformation to reach the shore of Great Nirvana,
yet says, 'This is called being stained by attachment,' or says that an icchantika need not cultivate this body to immediately attain Bodhi—
this is what is called being stained by attachment."

The Sūtra states that when mind and speech hold different conceptions and make different assertions, it is because the conceptions do not accord with correct principle, and thus cause the speech to differ.
If one were to say that icchantikas need not arouse the aspiration for enlightenment or engage in practice to attain Buddhahood, this would be called a "different assertion."
The Sūtra states: "Those who slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha" refers to slandering the Three Jewels as a single essence within one's own body.

The Sūtra further states: "Regarding what is attained by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)," if someone were to say, "An ordinary person attains the eight factors of the noble ones (*ārya-aṣṭāṅga-mārga*), yet remains fundamentally an ordinary person," one who makes such a statement is said to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
If, on the other hand, one says that these are not attained by ordinary persons, this too— [is likewise slander].
One cannot attain it merely by not practicing.
The Sūtra says: "First, those with hearts of disbelief and anger. This refers to those who, upon hearing whether an icchantika attains Buddhahood or does not, give rise to anger in every instance.
The Sūtra states: "Although one may have faith, if one does not understand the meaning, one must comprehend the principle of the Great Nirvāṇa before one can attain Buddhahood.
If one does not penetrate this, then even with faith, there is no possibility of attaining Buddhahood."
The Sūtra states: "Within a different body" refers to one who, having altered the karma of an icchantika, attains a human or celestial body;
attaining bodhi within this body is what is meant by "a different body. Because the karma of humans and celestials is not the cause of Buddhahood, such a claim leads to slander.
Regarding the scripture’s statement that "it is neither produced nor born": because it is primordially present, it is neither produced nor born.
Regarding the scripture’s statement that "it cannot be seen due to the causes and conditions of afflictions": this very statement constitutes the meaning of slander.

The Sūtra states that "all things are utterly non-existent," which clarifies non-existence; it then states "from skillful means they exist," which clarifies existence. These two statements appear contradictory, and thus constitute slander [of the Dharma].

As for the principle of Buddha-nature: if it were a categorized phenomenon (*saṃkhyā-dharma*), it would belong to the three periods of time; however, the essential substance of the principle of Buddha-nature is not a categorized phenomenon.

Therefore, regarding the statement that the cause is spoken of within the fruit: it means that one attains the vision of the Buddha-nature through present cultivation by virtue of past roots of goodness.
As for the fourth type of speech, which follows one's own inclinations, this refers to the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms.

The Sūtra asks: "What is meant by 'being like space'? The intent of the question is: Is it definitively identical to space as a substance with resistance (*sapratigha*), or is it different from this space?
If it were identical to this [space], it would then be subsumed within the three periods of time (*trikāla*).
Regarding the scriptural passage, "like flowers in the void": the entirety of emptiness is the flower; therefore, it does not belong to the three periods of time.
As for the reason it is not further analyzed: this provisional text contains a thesis, an explanation, and a conclusion, which can be clearly seen; thus, it is not analyzed.
The Sūtra states: "Regarding the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature and Nirvāṇa," the Buddha uses empty space as a metaphor for Buddha-nature.
Kāśyapa, however, posits the Tathāgata’s Nirvāṇa—as something realized and attained—in contrast to Buddha-nature, thereby causing Buddha-nature to become an existent entity.
Thus, by posing questions based on these three dharmas, he causes the analogy of empty space to also become an existent.

Regarding the scriptural passage stating that "it is not nirvana" and so forth: people of the world would never dare to say that the two vehicles are not the Tathāgata, or that afflictions are not nirvana;
they only fail to believe that walls, tiles, stones, and rubble are themselves Buddha-nature.
"Not only the primary retribution" means that while the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* belongs to the Hīnayāna, it also states that the mind creates both the primary and secondary realms.

"Nirvāṇa is fundamentally transcendent" means that Nirvāṇa is originally a dharma that transcends all relativity; however, for the sake of those with provisional capacities, it is taught as a relative dharma.
"Space is fundamentally dependent. This space is the space of the mundane world; it originally derives its name from dependence upon others.
Now, this is borrowed as a metaphor for the principle of the true cause of Buddha-nature, which is beyond all dependence; thus it is called "absolute."
"This is what is meant by 'not being comparable': it means that existence and non-existence are not comparable.

There is nothing that is not a counterpart of the four great elements; everything is simply the four great elements without distinction, because the four great elements stand in relation to the four great elements."
The Sūtra states: "Nirvāṇa is existent and visible. It is through cultivation that it becomes visible.
As for "this form," it refers to the liberation of form and the truly excellent, sublime form.
Regarding "footprints": Nirvāṇa is the ultimate destination reached by treading upon the Eightfold Noble Path.

Regarding "phrases and sentences": the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, liberation, and the Dharmakāya—these three dharmas being fully present—are called Mahāparinirvāṇa, the "Mysterious World" in the form of the letter *I*.

"This existence" refers to the sublime existence (*pranīta-bhava*). "This characteristic" refers to the absence of the ten characteristics; it is thus the characteristic of the signless (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*).
"This condition" refers to nirvāṇa acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings.
"Radiance" (prabhā) is named after its metaphor; that is, it refers to the essence of *prajñā* itself, while all other names belong to its liberation.
Third, regarding the refutation of the non-Buddhists' conception of emptiness: the emptiness perceived by the worldly eye is unfit to serve as a metaphor for Buddha-nature.
Therefore, it is extensively refuted.
Regarding the "repeated stages" (chóngshù) of the true reality (*satya*): this refutes the categories of emptiness according to their sequence.
Just as the true reality realized by the Hīnayāna is entered through a gradual progression from the shallow to the deep, they are thus called "repeated stages."
As for the scripture’s statement "extending throughout the void (up to) the waters of the ocean": it refers to the entirety of the Buddha’s void being like the characteristics of the ocean.
If one were to gather the voids of the ten directions together in a single place, this is called "perfected emptiness" (*pūrṇa-śūnyatā*).
Only that which comes to perch upon the tree is the moving entity that accords with the unmoving object;
this is precisely the identity of essence and function. For example, a person is the substance of an object, while their capacity for movement is the function of that object.
The same applies to two fingers: whichever finger one takes as the substance, its movement is the function.
Regarding the conjunction of two sufferings: it is like two hands or two fingers that have already been joined together, which are then further joined by another pair;
hence it is said, "like two pairs of fingers joined together."
Regarding the "Awakened Mind" (*citta-buddha*) and so forth, the *Śata-śāstra*, Chapter One, states: The Outsider says: "There truly exists a self (*ātman*).
As it is taught in the Sāṃkhya scriptures, that which has the characteristic of cognition (*buddhi-lakṣaṇa*) is the self. The Insider asks: "Is the self and cognition one, or are they different?

The Outsider says: "The self and cognition are one. The Insider says: "If cognition were the self, then the self would be impermanent. If cognition is the characteristic of the self, then because cognition is impermanent, the self [would also be impermanent]."
It must be impermanent. For example, heat is the characteristic of fire; because heat is impermanent, fire is also impermanent.
Now, what you maintain is identical in intent to that [example]; therefore, it is cited here.
If there is something that comes, as when an object enters into space and space is able to contain it, then one knows that space has its function;
one cannot say that it is only one thing that can be understood. Within a single vessel there is space, and there is space in all other places as well.
Therefore, it is said that emptiness is not one.
As for the statement that even a rabbit’s horn is not [existent], this is because a rabbit’s horn possesses only a name but lacks an essence; thus, it is not subsumed within the world.
Therefore, it is used as a metaphor to show that the Buddha-nature is likewise unattainable.
If one lacks this contemplation, those of the Two Vehicles and the partial Bodhisattvas will lack the contemplation of the Middle Way;
being unable to destroy the great afflictions, they consequently engage in disputes within the world.

The first clarifies the Tathāgata and the second clarifies the Bodhisattva; this distinguishes between those who have attained the fruit and those who follow the cause. Because they are entirely free from contention, they harmonize with all things;
because they accord with the capacities of beings and meet their needs, it is called "harmony" (和).
That which contradicts this intent is, for example, the twenty-one pairs of contentious arguments mentioned previously.
The Sūtra states, "First, faith," and so forth; these ten dharmas are all explained according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

One must understand that the faith and other qualities of the three preceding teachings do not accord with the literal meaning of the text. Why? Because when one gives rise to Perfect faith, birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, and afflictions are themselves bodhi.
"Ti" refers to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. The "six identities" distinguish them; thus, there is no contention. The nine dharmas below follow this same principle.

As for first clarifying existence and subsequently clarifying non-existence: these two dharmas are briefly set forth as the precepts, yet they pervade all phenomena and are universally applicable to both existence and non-existence.
The Sūtra states: "As for all transgressions," because there are the three outflows (*āsrava*), these are themselves the transgressions.
Regarding "the destruction of the Dharma-body": the Dharma-body is truly indestructible; however, when it is obscured by the outflows and thus not seen, this is termed "destruction.
Furthermore, the other two bodies depend upon the Dharma-body; if the Dharma-body is destroyed, the other two are likewise destroyed.
Regarding "observing" and "not observing": "observing" refers to the first phrase, while "not observing" refers to the second phrase.
When the Sūtra says that what is light departs of its own accord, it does not mean that it departs entirely by itself; rather, it means that which is slight and easy to sever.
The Sūtra states that these are two meanings: the two meanings of existence and non-existence.
Regarding "being free from all fetters and outflows," since these are the outflows to be remedied by the Middle Way, they pertain to both the internal and external realms.
"Causes and conditions" refers to the five external sensory objects.
