Regarding the explanation that there are minor differences [in their formation], the verse says: "If you wish to know your own faults, they all arise from conceptualization (*vitarka-vicāra*).
If you can sever conceptualization, you will no longer exist. Zhe said: "In the past, when the Tathāgata was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha, Ānanda..."

While begging for alms, there was a woman who, taking her child, went to a well to draw water. Seeing that Ānanda’s appearance and demeanor were upright and handsome, she conceived a heart of attachment;
she fixed her gaze upon him without letting go. Unaware, she tied her child to the well with a rope and pulled it out, whereby the child died.

Consequently, she gave rise to a mind of remorse and spoke this verse. After he had finished eating, he returned and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha then instructed Ānanda to receive and uphold this verse, saying:
This was proclaimed by the Buddhas of the past, whom that woman had previously heard; it was not through her own intellectual power that she was able to expound it.
Therefore, it is said that they are "slightly different.
As for the union of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*): ignorance and the afflictions of view within the three realms are combined into one.

To distinguish this from the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*): it clarifies that in each meditative stage (*dhyāna-bhūmi*) of the two higher realms, one may individually give rise to outflowing thoughts by taking objective sensory objects as conditions;

therefore, it says "excluding the conditions within the desire realm. Furthermore, in the first dhyāna, three mental factors constitute the internal [support] and four factors constitute the external [objects].
Alternatively, five factors constitute the internal and the five sensory objects of that level constitute the external. The same applies to the second dhyāna and above. Why is this so?
Therefore, as long as one has not yet seen the nature, all are termed outflows (*āsrava*).

As the Sūtra says regarding "the root of all outflows": because fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*) exists from the beginning, it deludes the truth and gives rise to falsehood, serving as the root for all outflows.

The Sūtra says, "one who forms conceptions": this distinguishes the phenomena that are objects of delusion. Because of recollective conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), an outflowing mind (*āsrava-citta*) arises; this is termed "forming conceptions.
The Sūtra says, "the cause of craving," and so forth: this is because ignorance (*avidyā*) is the root of the three poisons.
Why is there a different explanation? Why is what is said now different from what was said before?

Regarding their being mutual causes and effects: the preceding moment of thought is the cause, and the succeeding moment of thought is the effect; this applies equally to unwholesome reflection and ignorance as they mutually function in this way.
As for the statement in the Sūtra that "the son is the proximate cause," it is as follows:
because of ignorance and because of unwholesomeness, unwholesome reflection takes ignorance as its proximate cause; the same applies to the initial arising of reflection.

As for "being able to scorch the causes and conditions": through the contemplation of the Middle Way, one scorches the outflow of ignorance, causing its mutual delusions to be extinguished, so that they do not proceed from cause to fruit.

The Sūtra says: "The wise should observe the following. First, it clarifies how internal states give rise to outflows (*āsrava*); next, from the phrase "with whom one dwells," it explains how external conditions give rise to outflows.
As for "at what time," it refers to the twelve periods of the day. As for "with whom one dwells," it refers to association with evil associates (*pāpamitra*).
As for "where," it refers to arising based on the retributive environment (*niṣyanda-vipāka*).
The Sūtra says, "a single body of sentient beings," and establishes this question in order to refute those who hold wrong views.
Alternatively, regarding the statement that "craving [leads to] the grasping of signs," the intended meaning is that the term "craving" is used broadly;
it refers to wholesome craving and the Bodhisattva’s affection for the Buddha-dharma, which does not give rise to the grasping of signs.
"Great period" (*mahākāla*) refers to either falling from the womb or reaching a hundred years; all such instances are termed "great periods.
When the Sūtra asks, "Is it not within the state of abandonment? it is precisely questioning whether the fruition of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is employed for the purpose of abandonment.

Regarding the statement that "the untainted (anāsrava) has no retribution": this follows the provisional tenets of the Hinayana school. Since there is no subsequent retribution, it is said to be "without fruit.

As for the scripture stating that "the ox is itself the water and grass," water and grass are the causes of the ox, while food is the cause of the person; this is called "speaking of the cause within the fruit."

"Reaching the limit of the Brahma-heaven" clarifies that by cultivating the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) from within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one will necessarily be reborn there in the future;
this [rebirth] is designated as "the limit of the Brahma-heaven" in relation to that [upper realm].
"Concentration is mental action": when one cultivates that concentration, it is called "action" (karma) because it is brought about by volition (cetanā).
This is why it is commonly said that the form realm (rūpadhātu) is "mental"—it is simply because one constantly contemplates that realm.
The *Kāśyapa-parivarta Sūtra* states that "those who follow evil afflictions" refers to taking the most coarse afflictions as the object of contemplation.

The sūtra further states, "extinguishing those who share this doubt," because the question you have asked precisely accords with what is appropriate for the final age; therefore, the Buddha praised it.
To speak of it:
although there are slight differences in expression, their essence is the same despite these minor variations. Therefore, the preceding text states: "Compassion is itself Buddha-nature;
Buddha-nature is precisely compassion."

Regarding the practitioner who has emerged from what is produced: this further assists the intent of the question. If one realizes that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves the holy life (*brahmacarya*), then as for the five contemplations on the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*):

because the twelve links are the cause of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one subsequently contemplates the twelve links within the aggregates, thereby causing the causes of the aggregates to cease while observing the aggregates themselves.

Regarding the initial arising of consciousness at the time of nirvana: first, when consciousness first enters the womb, it is not yet capable of differentiation; second, its general nature distinguishes it from the five sensory consciousnesses.
Because sudden perception is incapable of discrimination, it belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, it is said that the five consciousnesses are, by analogy, indeterminate.

Regarding the notion of "provisional names" (*prajñapti*): perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to differentiate provisional names such as blue, yellow, red, white, and dharmas that are wholesome or unwholesome;
therefore, one must contemplate them.

As for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) being coarse and superficial: first, it is coarse and superficial; second, it is easy to understand. For these reasons, it is not contemplated [at this stage], which is merely a temporary [measure].
This is an explanation according to the sequence of the sutra text and adapted to individual capacities.

Regarding those for whom the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is predominant: because they flow from sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) into the aggregate of formations and thereby produce karmic activity, it is termed "predominance."
The three causes that arise are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).

As for the statement that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is contact (*sparśa*): since contact is a phenomenon characterized by resistance (*pratigha*), consciousness and the other factors are said to constitute contact.

Regarding the statement that "the sequential causal condition of contact as the cause and feeling as the fruit is simply the sequential cause of perception for feeling," this refers to the preceding mind of the afflictions.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Luminous, non-luminous, and neither. Its commentary explains:
"Contact associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*) is called luminous contact; contact associated with defilement (*kliṣṭa*) is called non-luminous contact; [contact] associated with existence..."

Contact associated with outflows (*āsrava*), which is neither wholesome nor indeterminate, is called "contact that is neither ignorance (*avidyā*) nor non-ignorance. Thus, it is said to be "neither of the two.
In the present text, it is precisely clarified that ignorance consists of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*). The preceding mind’s eightfold noble path is outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The preceding mind’s wholesome or indeterminate states refer to the wholesome minds of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

The Sūtra says, "There is no experiencer. This is because when one seeks the experiencer through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it cannot be found; it exists only as a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).
The Sūtra says, "Severing this conjunction. By investigating the three provisional designations through the four propositions, one brings them into accord with the principle within Buddha-nature;
this is called severing conjunction.

Regarding the claim that there is a distinct perception within the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) of the mind: it is because the influxes of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) enter into the mental formation of the mind, causing that formation to give rise to the perception of "nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya*).

Thus, there is the sphere of nothingness. This is because the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) extend only as far as the two spheres of space and consciousness. There is [a further] totality...
Perception does not exist in the sphere of nothingness; therefore, it is said that only the first two [realms] possess it entirely.

The sutra states: "Furthermore, there is great perception," and so forth, which clarifies the perception of the upper realms. From this point onward, all preceding instances refer to the perceptions arising within the desire realm.
One who is named "Wisdom-Mind" (Prajñā-citta) is so called because they are able to extinguish the conceptual mind of worldly truth; thus, they obtain the name "Wisdom.
Regarding these two intentions—skillfully approaching the good and abandoning the evil—one abandons all unwholesome dharmas and thereby attains liberation.
As for the "two types of perception" mentioned previously, it was merely a brief explanation for the sake of the context.
The Sūtra asks: "How can there be inverted perceptions among the noble ones? The Buddha’s intention was:
"If you say that [inverted perception] belongs to all noble ones, then try to explain it."
Regarding the "gate of afflictions" (*kleśa-mukha*): it is called a "gate" because one enters [into cyclic existence] through it.

As for the "ten kinds of perceptions" mentioned in the Sūtra, they are the perceptions of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch; the perceptions of arising, abiding, and ceasing; and the perceptions of male and female.
These ten perceptions arise based on the aforementioned inverted perceptions.
The "mind of equanimity in the intermediate state" is simply a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
"Naturally accords" means that it spontaneously accords with the intention to form karmic action.
The Sūtra states, "Not white... up to "...uncontaminated (anāsrava) karma. The present text briefly states that the uncontaminated is called neither white nor black.

However, according to other texts, the *sambhogakāya* realm (*saṃbhogakṣetra*) is called both black and white, while the *nirmāṇakāya* realm (*śāntaprabhāsakṣetra*) is called neither white nor black, and so forth.
One must not say that [the outflows] are "retribution," because they are untainted (*anāsrava*) and thus lack retribution.
Regarding afflictions (*kleśa*) leading to the induction of retribution: others claim only that karma can induce retribution, whereas afflictions do not;
however, this is not the case here, for afflictions are also capable of inducing retribution.
Regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and existence (*bhava*): if one speaks of them generally by way of the seven factors, they may be called both "existence" and "suffering.
However, in the present case, we follow the specific correspondence rather than the general explanation; that is why it is so.

Regarding the statement that "the latter two phrases are likewise," when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are taken as the primary term, they also possess four phrases; when suffering (*duḥkha*) is taken as the primary term, it likewise possesses four phrases.
These are explained by analogy with the preceding two phrases. When these four phrases are contrasted with the twelve phrases in the present sutra, they are simply the three paths (*trivartman*).
Regarding "old age and death" (up to its causes): for now, this shall be explained according to the twelve links of dependent origination within a single lifetime (*ekakalā*).

As for the sequential arising across these stages: for example, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) arise from afflictions (*kleśa*); formative action (*saṃskāra*) gives rise to existence (*bhava*). The remaining links should be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that there are one hundred and thirty-six hells, this has already been explained in the preceding "Chapter on Manifesting Illness.
As for ignorance being termed "lateral" (páng), ignorance refers to the residual habit-energies (vāsanā) of the Hīnayāna; therefore, it is called "lateral."
"Mutually dependent" means mutually supporting and nourishing one another.

Regarding "that which can give rise to the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way": the Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists inherently from the beginning; for what reason, then, do you say it is "given rise to"? The explanation states:

if it were not for the profound and secret teaching of the Perfect *i* (the threefold *i*) which elucidates the true nature through the cultivation of the conditions and the realization, how could one perceive this nature? It is by means of the teaching that [one realizes it].
Seeing that the teaching on the capacity for generating [the roots of goodness] can indeed produce them,

those who were previously icchantikas are now led back to the arising of wholesome roots. Because they were broken and humbled by former suffering and are now being guided and received, it is said that they "return to generate" them.
This practice is rare: because this sutra now employs the mind of the Great Nirvana for cultivation, it is praised as rare.

Regarding the praise of the Triple Gem: the teaching is the Dharma, the practice is the Sangha, and the master is the Buddha. Furthermore, the teaching elucidates the Triple Gem of the single essence.
The practices leading to the three jewels as a single essence: the Buddha is the fruit of the three jewels as a single essence.

This is not a direct inquiry into the essence of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). As stated above, the seven wholesome factors and the four immeasurables constitute the essence of the holy life through the three purities.
In the present text, the factors of the path and so forth are merely the conditions for the holy life; they are designations that describe the holy life.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra which says, "Good son, all dharmas are such," this was based on Kāśyapa’s general inquiry, to which the Buddha likewise gave a general response.
Because of this, it prompted Kāśyapa to pose a series of detailed and specific questions. Furthermore, the Buddha, in terms of revealing the provisional (kaiquan), [proceeded as follows].
Answer: Therefore it is said that all dharmas are [the One Vehicle].

Regarding "all dharmas": provisional dharmas give rise to provisional practices, and real dharmas give rise to real practices. Now, specifically concerning the opening of the provisional to reveal the real dharma, one practice gives rise to all practices;
this is precisely the practice of the Tathāgata. Hence it is said that the Perfect Teaching contains all things.
The Dharma is also that which was fully prepared with both the provisional and the ultimate by those of later generations.
As the Sūtra says, "Some speak of the wholesome and the unwholesome": the unwholesome is that which is to be refuted; therefore, it speaks of the unwholesome, wrong views, and so forth.
The sutra can give birth to practitioners. However, Kāśyapa’s question takes the entirety of the Buddha’s teachings throughout his lifetime as its subject.
As for the statement that "this *Nirvāṇa* alone is all dharmas," the general purport of this sutra contains three meanings:

first, it reveals the present reality by opening up the former provisional teachings; second, from the past until now, one has employed the mind of the Great *Nirvāṇa* to practice progressively; [and third, ...].
When practice reaches the first stage (*bhūmi*), one attains the vision of the Buddha-nature and is endowed with all dharmas.

Third, practicing the constant contemplation of *nirvāṇa* from beginning to end, the path is cultivated such that the initial and final stages are non-dual; this is called "all dharmas. The subsequent passage refers to those who are capable of being bodhisattvas from the first stage up to the tenth dwelling (*vihāra*).
Regarding "the light grade is severed simultaneously," this refers to the three delusions as being of the same substance (*ekasvabhāva*).
As for the Master Guan’s [assertion] that they are "adorned by dhyāna" and so forth, this is a position established by that master himself; it is utterly devoid of principle.
Since the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣa*) are practiced by all people, how can one judge them to be "not within the sphere of ordinary beings"?
It rejects those who harbor benevolent intentions. Even the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) are not yet the holy life (brahmacarya), let alone patience and the other perfections.

Regarding Tiantai’s [commentary] on the "many kinds": first, it clarifies that within the factors of the path (mārgāṅga), one does not necessarily require all categories of factors to be complete in order to attain the Way.

The four, three, two, five, single, seven, and eight are each their own respective paths (*mārga*). Therefore, it is said that one attains the path by relying on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

It is further said that these are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and it is further said that these are the Mahāyāna. Since this is the case for the foundations of mindfulness, it is likewise so for the other categories.

These constitute the "respective" (*pratyeka*) path-factors, rather than those that are harmoniously integrated. Second, regarding the mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*): as with the single dharma of the foundations of mindfulness, all [factors] are included therein.

Regarding the inclusion of all categories (*pakṣa*): the *Śāstra* states that since the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) include the other categories, the other categories likewise include the foundations of mindfulness. This constitutes the mutual inclusion of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Furthermore, it is not merely a matter of balancing them. Thirdly, regarding the classification by stages (*avasthā*): for example, the foundations of mindfulness correspond to their own proper stage.

Diligence (*vīrya*) corresponds to the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) correspond to the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). The five faculties (*indriya*) correspond to the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*). The five powers (*bala*) correspond to the stage of the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).

The eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) corresponds to the stage of "Seeing the Truths" (*darśanamārga*). The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) correspond to the stage of "Cultivating the Path" (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This is according to the stages; it is not yet a matter of balanced cultivation. Regarding the sequential arising of the four foundations of mindfulness: as when one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, diligence is produced; from diligence, the bases of psychic power are aroused.

The bases of power (ṛddhipāda) give rise to the five faculties (indriya). The five faculties give rise to the five powers (bala). These give rise to the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), which enter into the eightfold noble path.
This is called skillful mastery and adaptation. Precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth are all termed "right. When the pure mind is constantly one-pointed, one is then able to perceive Prajñā;
this is the arising of the faculties, and it is also mastery and adaptation. Furthermore, at the outset, one receives the Dharma from a teacher and binds the mind to mindfulness.
Mindfulness is called *smṛtyupasthāna*. Diligently practicing for the sake of seeking this Dharma is called *samyakpradhāna*. Cultivating within a single mind is called *ṛddhipāda*.
The arising of the five wholesome roots is called *indriya*. Their increase is called *bala*. The discernment of the function of the Path is called the *sapta bodhyaṅgāni*.

Walking upon the secure path is called the *āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*. One who can cultivate in this manner attains the Path; regarding the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) five aggregates, one should know [them as they truly are].
The factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*).

That which is entirely without outflows (*anāsrava*) refers to the factors of the path practiced during the stages of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*); these are exclusively without outflows.

This is the textual meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If the eightfold right path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) were placed after the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), it could also be considered with outflows.
This is also untainted (anāsrava). Why? Because entering the vision of the truths by means of the Eightfold Noble Path is itself untainted.
If it occurs prior to the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, it is exclusively untainted, as stated in the seventh fascicle of the Śamatha-vipaśyanā within the Section on the Path (Mārgavarga).

Regarding the "essence of the holy life" (*brahmacarya*): "essence" refers to that which is most honored and most essential. For the pure holy life, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are the most honored and essential.
As the Sūtra says: "If one is separated from these thirty-seven [factors], etc."—if one is separated from these dharmas, one cannot attain the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
From this point down, if one is separated from these dharmas, one cannot attain the two fruits of Mahāyāna bodhi and nirvāṇa.
The sūtra states: "Those who do not see the Buddha-nature" refers to the fruit of bodhi.
Regarding "the fruit of Buddha-nature," this refers to the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

When the sutra states that "the Brahma-conduct is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment," it means these are the combined practice of the primary and auxiliary [paths]; therefore, it says "is precisely."
The Sūtra states: "That which can destroy perversion" refers to the ability to destroy the eight *āgatis*.

"That which can destroy evil views" means that the first two [emissions] destroy the delusions of view within the triple world (*tridhātu*), while the latter two destroy the delusions of view regarding the same essence (*samāna-svabhāva*).
"One who can destroy fear" refers to one who, having entered and dwelled in the stages (*bhūmi*), is able to abandon the five fears.
Regarding the phrase in the Sūtra, "one who ultimately acts," it means that by causing sentient beings to practice, they immediately attain what is called "acting."
Regarding those who consider themselves practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*): why is it said that they cannot attain the cause of the holy life?
That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) involves a mind of grasping; the very nature of phenomena with outflows is attachment.
The inability to be "without attainment" simply means that one has not attained non-attachment.
First, let us define the thesis: is it for the sake of attaining the cause of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), or is it for the sake of not attaining it?
Those who all still possess the grasping of signs practice the five expedient means; although these serve as causes for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), they are in reality outflowing (*sāsrava*).
Those whose essence is truly non-grasping, although they are outflowing, can serve as causes for the outflow-free; therefore it is said that their essence is truly non-grasping.
"Grasping.
As for "having grasping by nature," it is called "having grasping" because one has not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding "the continuity of the resolve": the teachings on the holy life (*brahmacarya*) cause sentient beings, from their initial generation of the resolve, to seek supreme enlightenment.

"Ti. To transform sentient beings through successive moments of thought in an uninterrupted succession is what is truly called "Brahma-conduct" (*brahmacarya*). Because in this world there is only the single mind, [the sūtra] does not mention it.
As for the slighting of the latter three minds, it refers to the slighting of the three minds of sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding those who grasp an object in a single moment: this clarifies that the five consciousnesses merely apprehend objects abruptly and have not yet established the three types of conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

It is only in the second moment, through their conjunction, that they are termed "causally established" (*hetu-samutthāna-prajñapti*). The preceding moment continuing into the succeeding moment is termed "continuous conventional designation" (*samtati-prajñapti*).
Waiting for other moments of non-consciousness to know that this is a moment of consciousness is termed "relative conventional designation" (*apekṣā-prajñapti*).
Regarding the exposition of the cause by means of the effect: the five consciousnesses are the effects; because they can increase the various outflows (*āsrava*), they are termed the "cause.

As for the remaining ones, each is singular: among the nine factors, the latter seven are joy, which is the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); the eighth is tranquility, which is the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The ninth, equanimity, is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). These three each possess their own distinct essence. As for "not allowing them to be lost":
it means practicing with a mind directed toward *nirvāṇa* so as not to fall into the two extremes, thereby abiding eternally in the Middle Way of *nirvāṇa*.

The Sūtra states that the root of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is aspiration (*chanda*). This is because one aspires to seek supreme enlightenment above and to transform sentient beings below;
thus, aspiration serves as the foundation.

As for the statement in the Sūtra that "the Tathāgata previously spoke of this in this very scripture," it has already been heard previously in the *Guṇarājaparivarta*. It is difficult [to understand].
Regarding present desire, the Sūtra says:
"If one speaks of the 'cause of illumination,' it is only when one illuminates the supreme seeking without interruption that it is called the cause of illumination; this constitutes non-negligence."
The Sūtra states that "contact with clarity" (*vidyā-sparśa*) is called the cause. "Clarity" refers to the mind’s aspiration for *bodhi*.
Regarding the many phrases [that follow]: contact (*sparśa*) has the meaning of "confrontation" and the meaning of "correspondence.

In the first phrase, confronting and corresponding with faith in causes and conditions and with associating with virtuous friends constitutes "clarity"; the subsequent phrases are to be understood by this same principle.
"All can be explained" means that all can explain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as the causes for bodhi.

"The suffering of concentration has not yet been clarified" refers to the distinction between the suffering of precepts and the suffering of concentration within the sutras. The precept of the pure faculties (*śuddhendriya-śīla*) is precisely the precept associated with concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara-śīla*);
therefore, it is distinct from the previously mentioned *prātimokṣa*.
"Guarding the five faculties" refers to the unadulterated precepts, which are the precepts concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

"Abandoning all forms of wisdom" means abandoning the provisional fruits of the śramaṇa and the wisdom of the two extremes; therefore, it is said that these are "severed and eliminated," and so forth.

Regarding "extinction resembling [the preceding state]," this must be discussed in terms of meditative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and the partial realization of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), through which extinction is transmitted.
Furthermore, it is like how, from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward, one extinguishes the mind of the first stage and further attains the mind of the second stage and so forth.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "How can such nirvāṇa be attained? the intent of the question is as follows:
Is such nirvāṇa attained through cultivation, or is it attained spontaneously without cultivation? If it is attained through cultivation, what are the characteristics of that cultivation?
To speak of them by their general name is simply to refer to them collectively as "perceptions" (*saṃjñā*).

Regarding the ten perceptions in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "The nine perceptions are like binding a thief; the tenth perception is like killing a thief.

They are called "perceptions" in general because they are able to transform the mind's thoughts—that is, they can transform perceptions of permanence, bliss, and so forth, as well as various other inverted perceptions. Thus it is said.

These are called "perceptions" (*saṃjñā*). It is said that the first three perceptions are for severing the view of [the persistence of] the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*); some say the middle four perceptions are for severing the [defilements] abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
and some say the final three perceptions constitute the path of cultivation without applied thought (*avitarka-mārga*). Therefore, those who would destroy the dharmas cultivate these ten perceptions.
It is able to sever the fetters and proclivities of the three realms and realize the fruit of the untainted noble state. First is the perception of impermanence:

a perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates all conditioned phenomena as impermanent; that is to say, sentient beings and their environments are all subject to momentary arising and ceasing, and are therefore impermanent.

Second is the perception of suffering: a perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates all conditioned phenomena as suffering, which is constantly characterized by the three types of suffering.

1. The perception of suffering: the perception associated with the wisdom that views all phenomena as suffering, because they are oppressed and driven by the eight types of suffering. 2. The perception of impermanence:

the perception associated with the wisdom that views all conditioned phenomena as impermanent, because they arise from causes and conditions and lack intrinsic nature. 3. The perception of non-self: the perception associated with the wisdom that views all phenomena as being without self, because all conditioned phenomena arise from conditions, possess no self-nature, and are entirely devoid of autonomy;
when one seeks a self, it cannot be found. 4. The perception of the impurity of food: the perception associated with the wisdom that views all food and drink as impure. The world...
All food and drink arise from impure causes and conditions; therefore, [it is said... (and so forth). Fifth is the perception of the world as unlovely (*lokānabhirati-saṃjñā*):

it is a perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates all worlds as being undesirable and not to be delighted in, meaning that both sentient beings and their environments possess faults and evils, and thus nothing therein is worthy of delight.
Sixth is the perception of death (*maraṇa-saṃjñā*): it is a perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates death. If one...
The impermanence of karmic fruition constitutes two kinds of death that bring about the cessation of the exhalation and the non-entry of the inhalation.
Seventh, the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*): this is the perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates the impurity of one’s own body and those of others;

that is, contemplating that within this body there are thirty-six internal substances, while externally the nine orifices constantly flow, such that from birth until the end there is not a single thing that is pure. Eighth, the abandonment...
The perception of detachment (*viveka-saṃjñā*). This is the perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates nirvāṇa as being detached from saṃsāra.
The practitioner reflects: "If nirvāṇa is pure and free from afflictions, I shall sever the fetters and realize nirvāṇa. The perception of detachment (*viveka-saṃjñā*).
This is the perception associated with the wisdom that contemplates nirvāṇa as being detached from saṃsāra. The practitioner reflects: "If nirvāṇa is pure and detached from saṃsāra, I shall..."
The ten perceptions of exhaustion (*daśa kṣayasaṃjñā*) involve the realization of nirvāṇa amidst the flux of birth and death.
They are perceptions associated with the wisdom that contemplates the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), birth, and death within nirvāṇa. The practitioner reflects:

"If nirvāṇa is pure and the fetters, birth, and death are eternally exhausted, then I shall sever the fetters and the karma of birth and death to realize nirvāṇa. These ten exist only in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Now, regarding the ten perceptions in this sutra:

They seek exclusively for nirvāṇa; therefore, this [teaching] is cited to make them know their goal. Regarding the distinction between observational wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
the indeterminate refers to the aggregate of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta-skandha*), which is neither suffering nor non-suffering.
Regarding the four nutriments (*āhāra*): food merely sustains the body so that it may endure; this is the purpose of food. Clothing and such are the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
[The character "光" (guāng) has a sound like "似" (sì), meaning "resembling," as in "like the blue color of a single horn of a cow."]
Regarding "long breaths," as stated in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*: within a single *kṣaṇa* there are nine hundred arisings and ceasings;

that is, nine hundred arisings and ceasings constitute one thought-moment (*nimeṣa*). One hundred and twenty such moments constitute one instant (*tatkṣaṇa*), and sixty instants constitute one breath.
Thirty breaths constitute one *muhūrta*. Thirty *muhūrtas* constitute one day and night. Fifteen days constitute a half-month. Thirty days constitute one month.

According to the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), the duration of mindfulness is likewise not short; these variations in length are all for the purpose of providing diverse conditions for practice.
Regarding the scriptural passage, "This is called a śramaṇa," etc.: first, one praises such a person for their ability to extinguish evil, and thus they are named a śramaṇa;
because their brahmacarya is untainted, they are named a brāhmaṇa.

This is a praise of his sublime conduct following the description of tranquility. First, he praises his virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*): the non-arising of unwholesome karma is called "tranquility" (*śānta*);
being free from the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*) is described as "purity" (*viśuddha*); and being forever free from all suffering is described as "liberation" (*vimukti*).
This is called the wise person’s praise of their own intellectual virtue from below. One is called a "wise person" because they recognize transgressions and seek liberation;
to discern what is right and what is wrong is termed "right view," which can be understood as reaching the far shore.
"Named 'The Great Physician,' below. This praises the virtue of benefiting others and is easy to understand.

"This is named 'Skillful Understanding,' below. This refers to understanding the three kinds of speech of the Tathāgata mentioned above, such as that which accords with his own [realization], and so forth.
Regarding the seven kinds of speech of all Buddhas: from knowing superior causes to speech that accords with one's wishes, it is as previously explained in the discourse on the king’s speech.
Within these seven kinds, there are further two aspects: first, personally realizing two virtues; second, severing the nets of doubt in others by severing the seven lower [defilements].
As for the seven kinds of speech, they have already been explained above.
"Single-flavored great compassionate mind" refers to the non-referential compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*) that is of the same substance; therefore, it is called "single-flavored. Fascicle Fifteen:
*Cenru-pin* (The Chapter on Ajñāta Kauṇḍinya).
The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the formal explanation of the text. The first part is further divided into two: first, the direct explanation.
Title. Next, following the section on Kāśyapa, the purpose of this chapter is clarified. This section has two parts: first, the translation of the title;
second, the explanation of its meaning. Regarding the initial phrase "fire-vessel" (*agni-kalasa*): in full, it should be stated that this is translated as "fire-vessel.
The Brahmin caste originally served fire, and their lineage was derived from this. Fire has two meanings: illumination and burning. As for illumination, darkness does not arise. As for burning...
Thus, phenomena do not arise; this takes non-arising as its intrinsic nature. "Ajñāta" (A-jo) is a name.
This translates as "already known" or "without knowledge. "Without knowledge" does not mean there is nothing to be known; rather, it means knowing that [phenomena] are non-existent.
If one relies on the two truths, this is precisely knowing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It takes the wisdom of non-arising as its name.

Furthermore, the subsequent explanation of the meaning has two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the restatement of the intent of the entrustment, beginning with "If one were to [discuss] the transmission of the Dharma...
The initial statement, "First, let us set forth four meanings," introduces the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold truths) in their respective order: Śāriputra on the left and Maudgalyāyana on the right.
"Those who attained parinirvāṇa before the Buddha" refers to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who entered extinction in the presence of the Buddha;
there are other such examples among the remaining disciples.

The intention behind this subsequent section is twofold: first, a summary of past interpretations; second, the present correct explanation of what follows. Regarding the initial phrase, "briefly explaining the opening of the school":
from the beginning of the two chapters, "Cunda" and "Lamentation," the doctrine of permanence is opened and the meaning of permanence is briefly explained.

Those who grasp only the preceding brief meaning— if they claim this is merely answering the previous question— will obtain only the text on "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*) in the present section,

As for the portions where the text is not yet complete, they consist of three chapters in the future [recension]: first, the "Chapter on Burning the Body"; second, the "Chapter on Erecting Stūpas"; and third, the "Chapter on Entrustment.

Next, regarding the formal explanation of the text: the initial statement concerning the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold purposes) distinguishes between seeking the higher [enlightenment] and transforming those below; this refers to the worldly [purpose].
This is the realm (*dhātu*). The remaining three [realms] can each be understood by correlating them with the three [aspects] in their respective order.

Furthermore, from the beginning up to the stage where a portion of ignorance remains, all possess both the virtues of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), as well as the divisions of wisdom (*prajñā*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Second, regarding "according to what is appropriate": the present text accords precisely with the inclinations and preferences of the specific audience by teaching only that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are eternal.

This explains the cause of the body. Throughout the Prajñāpāramitā, all phenomena are traversed and described as pure, non-dual, and undifferentiated;

This is precisely the Great Treatise (Mahā-śāstra). It says: "If one gives rise to the real, this is the activity of wisdom; seeking to give rise to the real still resides in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).

It is not precluded that there may be a continuity of dependence. It is likewise not precluded that there may be accomplishment through causes.

Regarding the transformation of the consciousness of suffering into pleasure: one contemplates the conventional nature of the continuum; this very consciousness of suffering is impermanent from moment to moment.

The *Sāṃkhya* school calculates that the agent and the action are distinct, and so forth.

Regarding the fourteen difficult questions (*caturdaśa-avyākṛta-vastūni*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: 1. The world and the self are eternal; 2. The world and the self are impermanent; 3.

Regarding the statement "I am identical to sentient beings," this does not go beyond the sixteen views (*ṣoḍaśa-dṛṣṭi*). The text for these sixteen views is found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Great Chapter), where the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) provides an extensive explanation.

1. The view of being a progenitor (*janaka-dṛṣṭi*): reckoning that "I" can produce [beings], just as parents give birth to a child. 2. The view of being a nurturer (*poṣaka-dṛṣṭi*): reckoning that "I" can nourish others. 3.
The view of being a constituent (*saṃkhyā-dṛṣṭi*): reckoning that "I" possess the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).

1. The view of the elements (*dhātu-dṛṣṭi*): conceiving that "I am the practitioner. 2. The view of the four persons (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*): conceiving that "I am the one who will receive the fruit of retribution in a future body.
3. The view of the five aggregates (*skandha-dṛṣṭi*): conceiving that "I am the one who can create the worldly fruits of retribution. 4. The view of the knower (*jñātṛ-dṛṣṭi*):

conceiving that "I am the one whose five faculties know the five sense objects. 5. The view of the seer (*draṣṭṛ-dṛṣṭi*): conceiving that "I am the one whose faculties and objects can see forms and give rise to error."
1. The view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*): This refers to the arbitrary conceptualization of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as being a "self. 2. The view of a sentient being (*sattvadṛṣṭi*):

This refers to the collective grasping of the five aggregates as a "sentient being. 3. The view of a life-principle (*jīvadṛṣṭi*): This refers to the conceptualization of a life-force, fearing that this continuity might be severed.

4. The view of an agent (*kartṛdṛṣṭi*): This refers to the conceptualization that "I" am capable of performing actions; it is synonymous with the view of a person (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*). This refers to the attachment to a self held by non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka*).
13. There is the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), which conceives of a lifespan as lasting for one period;

though this is usually taken for granted, it becomes most urgent at the time of illness, when one fears the continuity [of life] will be severed or that the single period will be cut short. 14. There is the view of an agent (*kāraka-dṛṣṭi*), which means that one is driven and impelled by a self.
15. There is the view of an experiencer (*vedaka-dṛṣṭi*), because suffering and pleasure are [caused] by a self. 16. There is the view of an originator (*utthāpaka-dṛṣṭi*), which causes...

since the remaining eleven types of knowledge and vision are understood by analogy to be likewise self-annihilated, there is no need to refute them one by one.
Regarding the statement "I have two kinds," this is a phrase spoken in a state of urgency. It establishes two meanings;
however, as for the meaning that [the self] is not all-pervasive: since the self is not all-pervasive, it is impermanent. How, then, can it be conceived as permanent?
Regarding "there is no place from which it departs": if there were a place, that would be impermanent; how then could one conceive of it as permanent?
Regarding "how are the two selves different": if the two selves were different, they would be impermanent; how then can you say that the essence of the self is one?

The Sūtra says: "Thus... [up to] 'transcending the world. Here, "the world" refers to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and "transcending the world" refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Since it contradicts the conventional truth, it must also contradict the ultimate truth. Having turned one's back on both truths, how can this not be called wrong? What else could it be?
"This is the conclusion of the refutation. This very defense has already been thoroughly refuted.

Regarding "dharma and non-dharma," these refer to the dharmas of sentient and insentient beings; this interpretation is indeed plausible.

Regarding the character "karma" (業) in the subsequent text, it refers to that which is produced by karma.

The Sūtra says, "only receiving one side," meaning that one only receives the light pervading the room, and does not receive the presence of the light at the edge of the wick.

"Regarding 'there must be no real self': it means there must be no self as conceived by outsiders that is capable of seeing for itself.

"Life. This refers to obtaining the life of an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*). Furthermore, this is the correct calculation of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): the intermediate state exists spontaneously without cause;

Regarding the scripture’s statement that "all phenomena are likewise," this means that both the primary causes and effects (*hetu-phala*) as well as the secondary environmental retributions (*niśraya-vipāka*) all exist by virtue of causes and conditions.

The Sūtra states: "The cause consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth. This means the cause consists of the wholesome and unwholesome five aggregates, while the fruit consists of the five aggregates that are neutral (*avyākṛta*).

The *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The cause encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome, whereas the fruit is exclusively neutral. That is to say, by giving rise to the wholesome and unwholesome in the present, one brings about the neutral aggregates of the future.

Regarding the citation that refutes [the opponent’s] calculation: it cites the previous account of fire burning brushwood where the flames were severed, and then calculates that [the fire] has come back to refute it.
