based on this, it is all a description of the past, intended to satisfy the view of one's own body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the formation of the sixty-two [views]: this is because the "producer" and the "produced" are combined; thus, they form sixty-two. Furthermore, these four propositions all refute the preceding one;
by adhering to each single proposition, the sixty-two views are formed. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "For example, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) subsumes the sixty-two views.
As for what it means to subsume the sixty-two views, that sūtra (Chapter 14) says: "It demonstrates the root of the view of self."
The sixty-two views [regard] the world as empty. Since it is said that the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the root, these sixty-two views are subsumed within the view of self.
Regarding "broad and narrow, vertical and so forth": what is now called the "extreme" (*anta*) refers only to the vertical perspective—that is, the past in relation to the present, and the present...
They look toward the future, calculating the limits of the self across the three periods of time by means of the faculties.
To calculate that the Tathāgata is identical with the cessation of form (nirvāṇa) is to calculate that both body and spirit perish together; this is the view of nihilism (ucchedadṛṣṭi).
Regarding the phrase "if the body does not perish" and so forth: this calculates that both the body and the self (*ātman*) do not perish;
it is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). The two positions and the two negations constitute the dual calculation of what others do not perceive.

The ancient masters, based on one's own person, explained these as the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*), such as "my self comes from form," and likewise for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings.
When I do not make this statement, I have never made the statement that you conceive of as "I.
The Sūtra says: "That which is called 'view' (dṛṣṭi)"—if one makes such a statement and clings to it unshakably, this is called a "view.

That which is the objective basis for the clinging to views is called a "basis of view" (dṛṣṭisthāna). That which is capable of accumulating the fruits of future suffering is called "proclivity of view" (dṛṣṭicarita). [Thus] it is created.
Engaging in improper conduct is called the karma of views (*dṛṣṭi-karma*). Firmly clinging to an object of perception is called attachment to views (*dṛṣṭy-abhiniveśa*).

Being bound by views and constantly remaining within the three realms of existence is called the bondage of views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*). The suffering arising from views is called the suffering of views (*dṛṣṭi-duḥkha*).

Grasping what is not true as being true is called the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*). Because of views, there are the three miserable destinies to be avoided; this is called the fear of views (*dṛṣṭi-bhaya*). Being scorched by views is called...
It is the heat of views. When these fetter the mind so that one cannot leave them, it is called the "fetter of views.
Regarding those who can speak based on these views: from the perspective of the Tathāgata, this is called "inferior," referring to those who can see and can speak.
That is to say, they are able to see that saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa, and they are able to speak of seeing through errors and remaining far removed from them.
Regarding "perfectly complete and upright": because the causes are perfected and the fruits are fulfilled, the dependent and the primary [realms] are accomplished, which is termed "upright.
Furthermore, although one abides within the rational nature where the three causes are mutually interfused, all phenomena are fully present without any deficiency.

It is also called "Perfectly Complete and Upright. If it is considered in conjunction [with phenomena], it is the phrase "both existent and non-existent"; if it is considered apart from them, it is the phrase "neither existent nor non-existent.
Having refuted the four positions (*catuskoṭi*), these are provisional designations based on the conditions of the four *saṃvṛtisatyas* (the four purposes) to awaken sentient beings.

Thus, the benefits conferred upon beings throughout the preceding and subsequent stages do not contradict one another. Furthermore, the Buddha-nature is inherently present and is said to exist beforehand; it is only through the cultivation and practice of sentient beings that it is subsequently realized.
"Seeing" is termed "subsequent. The two [positions] and the two negations are to be understood by this same principle.

Regarding the "two impermanences" and so forth in the *Caturāryasatya-nirdeśa* (The Chapter on Cunda), one takes the four positions—such as the two [positions], the two negations, and the extremes—and so on, just like the four [positions] regarding "going" and so forth.
Regarding "having prior karma as the cause," it also means having the internal consciousness-mind as the cause.

Furthermore, regarding the alternative interpretation below, this master explains it in terms of the mind of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-citta*); since he agrees with the Master of Contemplation (*guan-shi*), our school now adopts the explanation of the Master of Contemplation.

The Sūtra states: "One who has severed all outflows" refers to the severing of the fetters of the "son" (the individual); "one who has severed all existence" refers to the disappearance of the fruit-fetters of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

"A small portion is called 'attaining deliverance'" refers to the *anāgāmin* (non-returner), who severs only nine grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and realizes the third fruit.
This was the beginning of the division of the four-month period for those who understand. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: There was a naked ascetic named Poṣadha who debated with Śāriputra;
he was left tongue-tied and speechless. [Śāriputra] sighed, saying, "If even one so inferior as this is thus, how much more so would one who is truly majestic?
He then went to Upananda and requested ordination. Later, when questioned on the meaning of the doctrine, he was unable to answer, and immediately [realized his error].
He thought to himself, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are foolish, ignorant, and lacking in knowledge," and he immediately abandoned the path. The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If a follower of another school comes to seek ordination, he shall dwell together for four months. When there is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) among the community of monks, the Saṃgha shall grant him the four-month probationary period.
The Buddha then commanded the bhikṣus to shave his hair for him, and he received the three refuges and the ten precepts of a śramaṇa. 4.
During the monthly offerings to the Saṃgha, the bhikṣus would say to the śrāmaṇeras: "The various non-Buddhists are evil in both their conduct and views;

they shall surely undergo bitter retribution. When they saw that the [aspirants] did not protect the non-Buddhists even when being reviled, and knew they would not regress, they conferred full ordination upon them.
This was the method for testing non-Buddhists.
"Those of various faculties and dispositions at one time" means that their inclinations and the natures of their faculties differ according to what is appropriate for them.

Regarding the mention of "stopping and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), it is because stopping and contemplation encompass all phenomena; thus, it says, "one who wishes to attain the four dhyānas," and so forth.

The Sūtra states: "Regarding the present manifestation of the Buddha’s intention to enter parinirvāṇa, it is so that all people may witness his entry into parinirvāṇa and know that it was obtained from the Buddha;
furthermore, it causes all people to take refuge in the Buddha and seek liberation."
Therefore, he entrusted this matter to the bhikṣus to convey it as a formal report.
The Buddha did not answer regarding those who do not depart, fearing that [the inquiry] would lead to an infinite regress; thus, the Buddha remained silent.
As for "craving prior to the aggregate of birth" (*upapatti-skandha*), it refers to the arising of afflictions and so forth within a previous body.
If afflictions arise again because of afflictions, then the afflictions of this present life arise again because of the afflictions of a previous life;
since afflictions arise once more upon the afflictions of the present, there is no sequence of before and after.
Regarding the statement that "clams and razor clams are completely destroyed," this refutes the argument previously cited concerning bracelets and other such ornaments.
The Sūtra says, "Their nature naturally enters the water. Here, "nature" is the cause and "water" is the condition; this is precisely cause and condition.
Why, then, do you calculate it to be spontaneous?
Regarding those who entirely lack such words—those who claim that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature—I shall now refute them by taking their underlying intent.
As for those who differ from the sacrificialists, I shall likewise rely upon their own conceptual constructs to refute them.
The Sūtra states: "As for making syrup, it refers to sugarcane syrup.
As for making honey, it means pressing sugarcane to produce honey. One should know that sugarcane and other medicinal substances [when processed] constitute stone honey (*śarkarā*)."
The Sūtra states that "there is no single nature," meaning there is no inherent, spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*).

Now, the fundamental meaning of the Buddha’s teaching is simply this: the Buddha originally taught that afflictions (*kleśa*) are the cause of the body, yet he did not speak of them as existing before or after it;
nor did he ever say that the body exists because of afflictions. Why, then, do outsiders raise this objection first?

Regarding the initial refutation of the "concomitant" [position]: although it is said that by refuting the concomitant one returns to providing the correct answer, since the opponent has already argued that the body must precede [the mind], the necessity of first refuting them to establish our own position clarifies that the Buddha never taught that the body precedes [the mind].
If you say that [the reason] exists prior [to the thesis], this is merely your own assertion; your position fails to be established and instead becomes the very point refuted by the Buddha.
Therefore, for what reason do you raise such an objection?
Setting aside that which they conceive as "simultaneity," we exclude the fixed calculation of outsiders who maintain that the effect exists within the cause and the cause exists within the effect.
Why? If one says the body definitely precedes [the cause], this is the calculation that the effect contains the cause;
if one says the body definitely follows [the cause], this is the calculation that the cause contains the effect.
Regarding "simultaneity of before and after": this clarifies that it refers precisely to the simultaneity of cause and effect in terms of temporal sequence.
Why? Because when one regards the present body in relation to its past cause, logically the afflictions should be prior and the body posterior;
yet, cause and effect have never been separated. Therefore, it is called the "simultaneity of before and after."
Regarding "simultaneous anteriority and posteriority": this is also a case of simultaneity between cause and effect.
When one considers the present body in relation to future retribution, the arising of afflictions within the present body serves as the cause for the future body.
Thus, the body comes first and the afflictions follow; this is termed "simultaneous anteriority and posteriority."
"Neither prior nor different at one time" means that by means of a single momentary cause and effect of the past, one brings about a single momentary resultant body in the present;

nor is there a single momentary [effect] that differs from what precedes or follows it. This is because the cause and effect of the present exist simultaneously, further summoning the cause and effect of a future body.
The correct meaning is that when there is a body, there is affliction (*kleśa*); and when there is affliction, there is [the body].
Within the body, cause and effect have never been separated, yet cause and effect are not lost; therefore, they are said to be simultaneous and yet sequential.

Why is this? It is because the hundred realms, the thousand suchnesses, and the three thousandfold world are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, existing solely within a single thought-moment; thus, there is no before or after.
Regarding "conditionality established by way of the fruit," the first chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, "Examination of Conditions" (*Pratyaya-parīkṣā*), states:

"Conditionality is established by way of the fruit, because the fruit, in turn, depends upon prior conditions. If the fruit does not yet exist, how can they be called conditions? Thus, the verse of the treatise says: "The fruit cannot exist within the conditions, whether it exists or does not exist.
If it does not exist beforehand, for what would they be conditions? If it exists beforehand, what use are the conditions? This is the general [explanation].
This refutes all [notions of] causes and conditions. Now, this sutra clarifies that cause and effect are established by means of simultaneity and sequence;
since their meanings differ, it is said that there is a distinct intention here.
Regarding the phrase "if one is prior," etc.: if it were said that afflictions are prior, then afflictions would have a beginning; the same applies if the body is prior.

As for saying this is taught to transform sentient beings through antidotes, this means that according to the method of transformation, in terms of actual practice, one always first destroys the afflictions and causes them to enter the Truth.
Because it is eternal, it is said that one must depend on afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to possess a body.
As for the statement "it nevertheless [involves] the principle" (*li*), the principle has no before or after, whereas phenomena (*vastu*) have before and after; therefore, it says "although."

Therefore, we know that one who speaks of the ultimate truth speaks only of the perfect and eternal. If this does not accord with the capacities of sentient beings, it instead becomes a provisional teaching of "residual" meaning.
Thus it is said:
"If one speaks of the eternal, those who receive the transformation [of the Buddha's teaching] will claim that the Buddha is the same as those non-Buddhists," and so forth.
Regarding "the substance of form and mind is one": the entirety of form is mind, and the entirety of mind is form; therefore, it is called "one.

Regarding "the principle of momentariness is equal": this simply means that phenomena are entirely the principle, and the principle is entirely phenomena; since dharmas have no dual substance, it is called "equal."

The essence lies in wearing the patched robe while maintaining its tattered state. Furthermore, following the principle of the patched robe, it is appropriate to explain that afflictions come first and the body follows.
For one who realizes that their nature is identical to emptiness, this emptiness is itself nirvana.

Who is the giver of the internal and external? The three thousand realms of the dependent retribution consist of one thousand realms that are external—the primary retribution—and two thousand realms that are internal—namely emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle—which are identical with the single Dharma-realm; therefore, there is no distinction between internal and external.
Regarding the two types of sūtra passages: because within a single moment there is one passage at the beginning, middle, and end.
These two types of sūtra passages are the definitive teaching of the ultimate principle and the essential means for resolving great doubts.
Regarding the statement that "only the wick is the lamp-vessel": oil, the pouring vessel, and the bowl are all called lamp-vessels;
they cannot be called the wick. As for the first point, "that which performs the function of moistening," Zeshou says:
from beginning to end, ignorance is ever-present, and at the moment the body arises, it must necessarily rely [upon it].
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is like a body in a dream, for it necessarily depends upon a sleeping mind.

As for the statement that it exists simultaneously, this means that the body exists in dependence upon its cause, which is affliction (*kleśa*). [Question: Upon what does ignorance depend for its arising? [Answer:
It depends on the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*). Upon what does the body-consciousness depend that it remains constant, like space, having nothing further upon which to rely? This...
Jie’s interpretation differs slightly from that of the other masters.

Regarding "moistening karma" (*karmopacaya*): when afflictions moisten karma, they can act as the cause for a body; furthermore, there are cases where one or two lifetimes have not yet repaid this karma, and thus it is called "prolonged" (*śeṣa*).
If, however, it refers to the afflictions that moisten rebirth (*upapatti*), these arise simultaneously with the body and are able to moisten it.
Birth further moistens karma to serve as the cause for the future.

Regarding "the beginning of the arising of the aggregates": this refers, for example, to the moment of initial conception in the womb, when one feels aversion toward the father and attachment toward the mother.
Furthermore, it is said that afflictions arise within the intermediate state (antarābhava) body, which are capable of moistening the body of birth.

Regarding what is expedient for the meaning, this also generally relies on that [previous] interpretation. However, if explained from the perspective of perfect interfusion, the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment have no further sequence of before or after; this is the correct meaning.
Regarding the phrase "within the aggregate of death," this refers to the present moment at the time of passing away;
it denotes the arising of craving for rebirth at the very last instant, which serves as the defilement that moistens rebirth. This is the explanation employed here.
Regarding the three meanings of simultaneous cause and effect: a cause from the past brings about an effect in the present life, and an effect in the present life gives rise to a cause in the future.
Although these are phenomena of the outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*), they possess these three distinct meanings.

Is this not a valid refutation? To the objector’s challenge, I now respond: simultaneous cause and effect, as well as the phenomena of the outflows, are simultaneous dharmas; thus, this refutes the external [opponent].
The objections raised by people—that the effect must definitely exist within the cause and the cause must definitely exist within the effect—are all refuted.
As for these three teachers, they are the Kāpila, the Sāṃkhya, and the Lākṣaṇika, as previously described.
As for "that family," it refers to the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Regarding "those who give rise to birth within the present single lifetime": these outsiders merely reckon that the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*)—from *prakṛti* (primordial nature) giving rise to *mahat* (the great one), and so forth—arise with a master and a basis as their causal conditions;
they do not say that they arise from the causal conditions of past karmic power. This is the meaning [of this passage].
Therefore, this is the causal condition and fruit of the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "the *guṇas* below," and so forth: the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*) creates the nose; water and fire create the tongue; and the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) creates the body.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Fragrance" (*Gandhalakṣaṇavarga*) in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*: at the beginning of the fifth chapter, the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Fragrance," it is asked:
"Because various fragrances such as tamāla and others are combined, their fragrance differs from the original. Does this mean that these various fragrances produce yet another distinct fragrance?
The answer is: "Due to the combination of fragrances, another distinct fragrance is produced. It is like when blue and yellow colors are mixed, green is produced. Because...

Due to various causes and conditions of karma, various fragrances arise. Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas claim that white arsenic, lead, tin, gold, silver, copper, and so forth are all substances of fire (*tejas*), yet fragrance exists within them;
therefore, one knows that fragrance does not exist in earth alone (and so forth).
Regarding the subsequent pairs: the following section is entirely from the third chapter of that treatise, the "Chapter on the Four Great Elements.
As for the statement, "If you still claim that water exists because of moist conditions," why do you not realize that earth is formed through the causal condition of cold?
Is it still called "water" by virtue of its causal conditions with water?

As for "the crisscrossing of corners": when waves and wind face one another, it is called the crisscrossing of corners. Furthermore, if one regards ice in relation to the earth, this also constitutes a crisscrossing;
if one regards ice in relation to water, or waves in relation to water, both are termed "facing one another."

Regarding the fact that the fruits and retributions differ: one should know that sometimes the possession of intact faculties is a retribution of the subsequent birth (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*), while poverty is a retribution of the present life (*upapadya-vedanīya*);
or poverty is a retribution of the subsequent birth, while the possession of intact faculties is a retribution of the present life. The same applies by analogy to wealth and other such cases.
Regarding the "two kinds of non-existent dharmas," these refer to the two previously mentioned phenomena: space and the horns of a rabbit.

"Discarding the general for the particular" means that medicine is administered according to the illness; since the methods for subverting inherent nature differ, the teaching is universally applicable throughout the entire dispensation, fitting the capacities of various beings, and is thus called "general.
The sequence of the five periods constitutes the "particular."

Regarding the frequent use of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to refute intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): as in the present text, one first employs correct dependent origination to refute the false dependent origination of the externalists' clinging to a self-nature.
Subsequently, the text employs [the marks of] impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, whereby all those externalists who submit to it come to possess the benefits of the four stages.
This is the sequential order of a single lifetime: first, the establishment of the Dharma-teachings to apprehend the characteristics of the capacities of sentient beings.
"Next, the use of the Middle Way" refers to its application hereafter.
"To shatter partiality and gradualism": "partiality" refers to the two preceding teachings, and "gradualism" refers to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

"Mutual use without fault" clarifies that the five periods are mutually applicable without fixed order, and that the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) are applied secretly and indeterminately according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "previously and subsequently refuting all internal schools and others": as previously established in the sequence of the five periods, these five periods are employed to clarify the individuals who attain the Way according to this present sutra;
thus, the horizontal and vertical dimensions [of the teaching] are self-evident.
When the Sūtra says that *nirvāṇa* is eternal, it uses profound principle to characterize a superficial phenomenon.
When the Sūtra asks, "For what causes and conditions does it speak thus?", [the answer is that] the Buddha, knowing my mind, has a further intention.
It is stated thus:
when the sutra says that begging for food is "constant," it is called constant because one begs regularly.
When it says that special invitations are "inconstant," it is called inconstant because the timing of such invitations is irregular.

Regarding "leaping over the sections" (*kua jie*): it does not rely on what [the questioner] has in mind, but instead answers by employing the profound principle that transcends the world; this is called "leaping over the sections.

Furthermore, regarding the statement within the ultimate truth that "sentient beings are inexhaustible," one asks: for what reason is it said they are inexhaustible? The answer is: if one says "sentient beings... [and so forth].
If birth-and-existence (*bhava*) were to come to an end, then nirvāṇa would also necessarily come to an end. Why? Because sentient beings are themselves nirvāṇa;
therefore, it cannot be said that it has an end. Nevertheless, the sutra answers by way of phenomena (*dharma*), while this commentary explains by way of principle (*tattva*).
This is to demonstrate that phenomena do not depart from principle; for this reason, it explains by way of principle.
Regarding the statement that Ānanda understood it: throughout his life he followed the World-Honored One, and was able to uphold all of the Buddha’s Dharma;
therefore, it does not say that he was deluded by demonic teachings.
As for what constitutes "distraction," it simply refers to being distracted by excessive speech.
Regarding the eight truths: there are four each for the upper and lower realms of the desire and form realms.
To contemplate the faults of suffering means to recognize these as afflictions; if one does not contemplate and break through them, the causes of suffering will inevitably arise.

"Contemplating the emergence from suffering" means contemplating the essential way to emerge from suffering, namely, to transcend birth and death. "Contemplating the entry into suffering" means entering into nirvana.
As for what the sutra says regarding "the manifestation of supernatural powers and so forth," this refers to the display of transformative traces.
Furthermore, if one wishes to distinguish between the teachings of Māra and those of the Buddha, [one should note that] Māra is able to speak of both provisional and ultimate dharmas.
One should ask: "Which is the provisional? Which is the ultimate? Which is that which is provisional yet ultimate, ultimate yet provisional, and neither provisional nor ultimate?
To one who asks these questions, Māra will certainly be unable to answer. By using this to test Māra, one can know whether it is Māra or the Buddha.
Regarding the "refutation of Ānanda’s true mind": it was because Ānanda might have relied on his own status as the Buddha’s personal attendant, considering himself superior to all others,
that this refutation was necessary.
Regarding those who each bear a heavy responsibility: to shoulder the True Dharma and propagate its transformation throughout the ten directions is what is called a "heavy responsibility.
To reprove those who practice according to the reality [of the teachings] is likewise merely a comparative distinction made within the first stage of abiding.

Those who propagate the profound principle extol the Great Dharma and discourse upon its depths and ultimate realization; this is beyond the capacity of the Two Vehicles, though they are designated as *śrāvakas* based on their outward traces.
Regarding those who are "unfit for bestowal or withdrawal," this refers to the process of bestowal and withdrawal conducted in relation to the Great and Small Vehicles.

If one says "to give," it is because the two vehicles have already entered from the gradual toward the sudden, and the provisional has been opened to reveal the real; thus they are fit for entrustment.
However, if we speak only of those who are near, this refers to the internal retinue within the Dharma; hence the statement.

Regarding "Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī": the intended meaning is that if one considers those who share the same rank and capacity as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, there are many such individuals who have been extensively transformed.
Nevertheless, among the various sūtras, it is specifically Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī who are singled out as most worthy of circulation.

The entrustment to the Bodhisattva Hongguang (Extensive Propagation) should likewise be understood in this way; he is not to be taken as a mere generic title, but must be a distinct Bodhisattva named Hongguang.
As for the Māra kings who have awakened their resolve, they must all have acted through the power of great expedient means (*mahopāya*).
Regarding the differences in transliterated sounds, these refer to the differing phonetic systems of the five regions of India.
As for the Sanskrit (*brahma*) sounds that incorporate multiple meanings, *pratibhāna* (eloquence) carries only the sense of "retentive mastery" (*dhāraṇī*).
Regarding the five things that sever pungency: in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), these were not severed prior to this point; it is only upon reaching this sutra that they are permanently severed.
[The characters are] *gū* (pronounced as in *li-dēng*), *pí* (pronounced as in *bó-bī*), *lài* (pronounced as in *lú-dá*), and *tì* (the pronunciation *tí* is correct).
Regarding the "Chapter on Purifying the Ground": these Bodhisattvas of the Ten Grounds possess bodies born of parents.

Because they face the fear of impurities such as venomous snakes and the like, they purify this ground by means of ten chapters of *dhāraṇīs*. Hence, it is named the "Chapter on Purifying the Ground."

Regarding those who attain birth [in the Pure Land] through the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): if explained from the perspective of the "true practice" (*shixing*), such a person has long since studied under the three preceding teachings, having thoroughly mastered the provisional gates.
Now encountering Śākyamuni and hearing the ultimate teaching of the perfect and eternal, they immediately shatter their ignorance.
This continues up to the entry into the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) and so forth. Therefore, it is called "the physical body not yet free from [defilements]. This interpretation is correct.
An interpretation based on the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is not employed here.
Regarding the fact that the names of the Three Jewels vary in various ways: although there are many different names within the various *dhāraṇīs*, they are all fully subsumed within the Three Jewels.

As for the "great fish Makara," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle seven, states: Five hundred merchants went to sea to gather treasures and encountered a...
Māgha, the king of fish opened his mouth. The ship moved with great speed. The helmsman asked those on the upper deck, "What do you see?
They replied, "We see three suns and a great white mountain; the current rushes forward as if entering a vast chasm. The helmsman said:
As for the "three days": the first was an actual day; the second was the eyes of a fish; White Mountain was the fish’s teeth;
and the rushing waters were its mouth. "We are finished," [they thought]. At that time, each person on the boat invoked their respective deity, but none produced any result.
Among them was an upāsaka who said to the crowd, "O people, we should all together invoke the Buddha. He addressed the Buddha by the name "No-... (Ananda).

Regarding those who rescue others from suffering and calamity: if all people with one mind together recite "Namo Buddha," these fish—having previously received the five precepts in past lives and having attained the wisdom of recollecting former existences—hear the name of the Buddha and immediately repent and reproach themselves. The fish then close their mouths, and the lives of the multitude are preserved.
If they hear the name of the *dhāraṇī* of the Three Jewels as one essence within this present sutra, those on the seven stages of expedient means will dwell eternally therein.
Wisdom and life shall then exist forever.
Regarding the parrot reborn in heaven, the *Sūtra on the Wise and the Foolish* states: The elder Sudatta revered and had faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, providing everything that was required.
At that time, the bhikṣus went there every day to preach the Dharma and offer instruction at Sudatta’s house.
Inside there were two parrots: one named Lati and the other named Śalati. By nature they were clever and wise, capable of understanding human speech.
Whenever the bhikṣus came and went, they would always announce it beforehand; the family members, having heard this, would prepare the bedding and seating.
Later, Ānanda went to that house and, seeing that the birds were intelligent and wise, took a liking to them in his heart and spoke to them, saying: "I wish—"
The Teaching: The two birds joyfully received the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. The verse says: *Dukha* (1), *Samudaya* (2), *Nirodha* (3), *Mārga* (4).
[These four, in the Jin language, mean Suffering, Origin, Cessation, and Path. Before the entrance of their home was a tree; having heard the Dharma, the two birds were filled with joy.
On the tree, they recited and practiced in succession, ascending and descending seven times. That evening, while staying in the tree, they were eaten by a wildcat.

Due to this wholesome mind, they were immediately reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. The next morning, Ānanda went to their house and heard that the two parrots had been killed by the wildcat.
He returned and informed the Buddha: "In the house of Sudatta, there were two parrots who yesterday were taught to recite the Four Noble Truths."
Dharma. That night he passed away, and it was not known where his consciousness had been reborn.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "Because you bestowed the Dharma upon him, he has been reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and so on up to the Sixth Heaven. He has been reborn in the heavens seven times without meeting an untimely death.
Ānanda asked again, "When his life in the Six Heavens ends, where will he be reborn? The Buddha said, "He will descend to Jambudvīpa, leave the household life, and become a Pratyekabuddha."
The Pratyekabuddhas: first, named Yummo; second, Suddhamma.
Regarding the phrase "unsurpassed mantra" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the ninth chapter, "The Chapter on the Great Mantras," states:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, if these sons or daughters of good family hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā, receive, uphold, and draw near to it..."
By reciting and correctly contemplating [this], one does not depart from the mind of *sārvajñā* (all-knowledge).

Whether one is fumigated with poisonous drugs, subjected to sorcery, cast into a fire pit, into deep water, or threatened with weapons such as knives and the like, none of these can cause harm. Why is this?
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is the Great Illuminating Mantra; it is the Unsurpassed Mantra. This is precisely the *prajñā* of the threefold wisdom within a single mind.
If one is even able to thoroughly dispel the poisons of the three delusions and two deaths, how much more so could the poisons of the mundane world cause harm?
Regarding the "Six Sublime Gates," that sutra states: "Upon hearing the six-syllable phrase of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, contemplate it with right mindfulness;
observing the mind and binding the thought to a single point within the heart-vein, one will see Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and immediately attain liberation."
One shall become an Arhat. How then may one come to see Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and hear the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions?
If you wish to see them, straighten your body and rectify your mind, ensuring the mind remains unmoving. Let the mental state continue in succession;
place the left hand upon the right hand; lift the tongue toward the palate; regulate the breath so that it is harmonious, neither coarse nor dispersed; and calmly eliminate all counting.
From one to ten, one achieves mindfulness of breathing without distraction.

This means that while in the sutra there is only the single method of counting the breaths, which is further elucidated, the other five methods were established in the commentary based on the meaning of the sutra. Why? Because it is said that the six-character phrase contains the full meaning of the six methods;
thus we know the meaning of the six gates is complete. Second, regarding the method of following: one abandons the previous method of counting and focuses the mind with single-mindedness.

Following the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, one collects the mind and takes the breath as its object. Knowing the breath enters and exits, the mind abides upon the breath-object without any distracted intention;

this is called the gate of following (*anāpānasmṛti*). Third, the gate of cessation (*śamatha*): ceasing all discursive thoughts, one does not attend to counting or following, but stabilizes the mind in stillness;
this is called the gate of cessation. Fourth, the gate of insight (*vipaśyanā*): within the state of meditative concentration, one uses wisdom to discern and contemplate the subtle.
Subtle. The characteristics of inhalation and exhalation are like the wind in the sky. The thirty-six components—skin, flesh, sinews, and bones—are as unsubstantial as a plantain tree.
Consciousness is impermanent, not abiding for even a single moment. There is no person and no self. Body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since neither person nor phenomena can be apprehended, upon what could concentration depend? This is called the gate of contemplation. As for the five gates of returning, once one knows...
Contemplation arises from the mind. If one follows and breaks down external objects, this does not reach the original source.

One should instead contemplate the contemplating mind itself. From what does this contemplating mind arise? Does it arise from a mind that is already contemplating, or from a mind that is not contemplating?
If it arises from a mind already contemplating, then contemplation already exists. If it arises from a mind not contemplating, then the non-contemplating mind must cease for it to arise.

It would follow that [the mind] arises without ceasing. If it were to arise without ceasing, then two minds would exist simultaneously. If it were a ceasing dharma that arose, then since a ceasing dharma has already passed away, it could not produce contemplation.
If one says that it arises while ceasing, or that it arises neither by ceasing nor by not ceasing, both cases are untenable.

One should know that the mind of contemplation is fundamentally non-arising from the beginning. Because it does not arise, it does not exist; because it does not exist, it is empty. Because it is empty, there is no contemplation.

Mind. If there is no observing mind, how could there be an observed object? When both object and wisdom are simultaneously extinguished, this is called the Gate of Return, the essential point of the source of the Way.

Regarding the Six Gates of Purity: because one knows that form (*rūpa*) is pure, one does not give rise to deluded thoughts or discrimination. It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
One quiets the defilement of deluded thoughts, quiets the defilement of discrimination, and quiets the defilement of grasping at a self. If one can make the mind as it was originally...

Purity. Because one cannot apprehend the one who rests, the object of rest, nor purity and impurity, it is called the "Gate of Purity. Thus, these six gates are universally accessible for the four types of practitioners to enter.
Why? Because those of the *śrāvaka* vehicle contemplate the impermanence of breath; those of the *pratyekabuddha* vehicle realize that breath is like an illusion;

those of the *bodhisattva* vehicle understand that breath is endowed with the Buddha-dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and those of the Perfect Vehicle see that breath is the secret treasury of the Buddha-nature. Having thus counted the breath...
The same applies to the other five examples. Thus, that sutra says: "I immediately practiced counting the breaths so as not to let the mind scatter;

suddenly my mind was liberated, the fetters were dissolved and subdued, and I attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi... (and so forth). In this present sutra, one knows the perfect and eternal Buddha-nature;
though one may temporarily take up the minor fruits [of the śrāvaka], one rests there only to eventually avoid stagnating in partiality. Therefore, the sutra speaks of the Māras.
Upon hearing this dhāraṇī, the king and all others resolved their minds upon bodhicitta (and so forth).
The King of the Good Devas maintains what is good so that it is not lost; the King of the Evil Devas obstructs what is evil so that arrogance does not arise.

"Arising from the back of the other [five] fetters": this conceit arises from behind the five *śaikṣa* (active) fetters. If these five active fetters are severed, this conceit is immediately eliminated.
"Attaining the lower meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*)": the concentrations of the eight lower stages are termed "lower concentrations."

"Those whose minds are particularly abundant" refers to those in the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). This clarifies that Subhadra attained the state known as the "perception-sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Regarding "those who possess pride," they are so named because they look down upon others who have attained the lower eight absorptions.

Regarding the scriptural statement, "All follow their past [actions]": outsiders merely believe that present results are summoned by past causes, but they do not say that actions performed in the present body summon future results.
Consequently, they fall into the false views of non-Buddhists, which repudiate cause and effect.
Regarding "indeterminate retribution": if one is able to cultivate the Path, one will immediately attain liberation; therefore, it cannot be said that there is fixed retribution.

As for "practicing the eight contemplations" (*aṣṭau vipaśyanāḥ*): these eight contemplations have both general and specific aspects. Generally, one uses the eight contemplations to contemplate those four [truths].
The aggregates (*skandha*) are a composite and lack substantial reality. As for their differentiation, one treats the four aggregates through principles such as impermanence:

contemplating consciousness (*vijñāna*) as impermanent, contemplating sensation (*vedanā*) as suffering (*duḥkha*), contemplating perception (*saṃjñā*) as empty (*śūnya*), and contemplating formations (*saṃskāra*) as non-self (*anātman*). One treats the four aggregates through analogies such as an abscess and a wound:

that is, contemplating sensation as an abscess, contemplating perception as a wound, contemplating formations as poison, and contemplating consciousness as an arrow. This is practiced within the context of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
The citation states: "Regard feeling as a disease, perception as an abscess, mental formations as a wound, and consciousness as a thorn.

Furthermore, one contemplates the sphere of infinite space as a disease, the sphere of infinite consciousness as an abscess, the sphere of nothingness as a wound, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a thorn.

Although their names differ, their treatment is largely the same. Because these eight exist, the mind easily gives rise to weariness and can swiftly abandon them, cultivating [the state of] non-existence.

[Regarding] the outflows (*āsrava*). Question: In the four dhyānas, one employs only three—suffering, coarseness, and obstruction—as the means (*upāya*). Why, then, must the eight [aspects] be employed for the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), such as the sphere of infinite space?
Answer: The concentration of the sphere of infinite space is subtle; the eight [aspects] are not mentioned because its defects (*ādīnava*) are difficult to discern.
Ordinary persons also have those who rely on the six practices; however, they do not equal the noble lineage which is free from them.

Regarding those who quickly attain nirvana through non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñin*), although Great Nirvāṇa is truly without conceptualization, it is verified that [the state of] falsely imagining there to be conceptualization is not nirvana.
Those who receive such an evil body emerge from the Avīci Hell and immediately receive this body.
As the Sūtra says: "How much more so for others; how much more so for those inferior to the non-Buddhist Pūraṇa Kāśyapa?"

The Sūtra says, "Severing all forms of existence (*bhava*). [In this state,] while the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) pertaining to the twenty-five existences are entirely eliminated, of the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-āsrava*), only those pertaining to the single existence of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) remain.
The Sūtra asks, "What is meant by 'the notion of reality'? I do not understand this now; please explain it for me.
As for the sūtra’s statement that "all dharmas lack self-characteristics" and so forth, this employs the practice of the Mahāyāna to investigate through the four propositions,
thereby causing one to enter the ultimate principle of emptiness, the true mark of reality.

Regarding the phrase "this emptiness dispels conventional existence": it means that through ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), one clears away the existence of the three delusions and the two deaths.
As for the statement "Subhadra attained the Way," the translators rendered only these nine characters; this was because the latter portion [of the sutra] did not yet exist at that time.

Therefore, commentators have termed this the "text on attaining the Way. Now that the latter portion exists, these nine characters should be understood as follows: [they refer to Subhadra’s realization of the truth].
This is appended after the "Text on Leaving Home" in the final fascicle.

Regarding the "Profound and Sublime Dharma of the Latter Part": having heard the aforementioned teachings such as the perception of reality (*bhūta-saṃjñā*) and so forth, one may yet attain only the minor fruits.
When the Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent," his intention was to indicate that now is precisely the right time and that he would grant whatever [the requester] desired;
thus, he praised them with "excellent, excellent" and gave his consent.
As for "a moment's grace," it refers to the single phrase "Welcome" with which one immediately attains the fruit of the Path; how could this ever be repaid?
As for "the suffering of conditioned formations pressing in," because the body remains as the basis for suffering, one cannot escape being driven by the suffering of conditioned formations.
"At this time, those who require [the teaching] shall enter parinirvāṇa as soon as these words are spoken.

"The Dharma should be thus" means that when the traces of the *nirmāṇakāya* have appeared and the conditions for conversion are exhausted, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that one should enter nirvāṇa.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching": this chapter specifically intends for the teachings to extend into the future, benefiting sentient beings inexhaustibly and never ceasing.

The three [aspects] beginning with "should be exhausted" (*kṣaya*) represent the bequeathing of the body to benefit beings, which brings about the ripening and liberation of those with indeterminate seeds through skillful means.

Why is this so? Because this present body of mine is itself the eternal body, the Dharma-body; therefore, my relics shall pervade the *dharmadhātu* to universally benefit all sentient beings. One should...
It shall not cease.

The Commentary states: "The transformative function conceals its traces. This means that not only has the Tathāgata’s period of transformative activity concluded, such that he withdraws his traces and returns to the source, but the assembly of fifty-two [bodhisattvas], having passed through the course of a single lifetime [of the Buddha's teaching] and arrived at the present sutra, likewise diminishes as they withdraw their traces and return to the source, just like the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the Bequeathed Teachings and the Bequeathed Body benefit future generations universally.
The scripture states: "At that time, the Buddha told [the assembly]... my Great Nirvāṇa. This indicates the inconceivable essence of the Dharma and exhorts its protection and maintenance.
From "From me" onwards, it explains the reason why it is difficult to obtain, thereby encouraging its cultivation for the benefit of oneself and others.
Regarding the phrase "now already revealed and taught": prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the provisional [teachings] covered the real, whether manifest or hidden.

Upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra* and this present sūtra, the provisional has been clearly disclosed so that all may equally enter the secret treasury; therefore, it is said, "now already revealed and taught."

As for all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, they are also like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which reveals the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional means, drawing together the transformations of the five Buddhas.
Thus, each and every Buddha of the ten directions and the three periods of time acts solely to lead sentient beings to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Now it is likewise; they are all identical to the Buddhas, abiding in Great Nirvana, which is eternal, blissful, and without deficiency.
"Relinquishing body and life" means relinquishing the provisional traces and leaving behind the physical form.
"The Buddhas stroke their heads" means that the Buddhas, with the hand of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), stroke the crowns of the Bodhisattvas' heads of true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).

This is the unification of the provisional and the real; only then can it be called "correctly not losing [the Way]. Consequently, they move the Buddhas so that the Buddhas constantly appear before them.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'first, those awakened externally,' this refers to those transformed by the Buddhas. In all cases, they first conform and later diverge; therefore, they are initially positioned outside.
As for 'like dry grass and leaves,' Subhadra was the foremost among the assembly of non-Buddhists;
upon a single transformation, he returned [to the truth], like dry grass cast into a great conflagration—how much more so for others who are inferior?"

Regarding "entering various realms," this does not exceed the six teachers; hence it is said that they "accept and practice heterodox teachings" (the character *yin* [音] here refers to *āyatana*, the sense bases).
As for the passage from "the bhikṣu Chandaka" to "taming," this sutra clarifies Chandaka in a manner that differs from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

That treatise instructs one to rely on the Brahma-dharma to tame him, whereas this sutra observes the twelve links of dependent origination to bring about gradual taming. Although the words differ, the underlying intent must be consistent.

Once it is accomplished and the Brahma-dharma has been administered, one must necessarily cause them to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) to harmonize their minds;
only then can they enter the Dharma. If it were otherwise, administering the treatment in vain would be of no benefit. Regarding the *śīla-pāramitā*, it refers to the Prātimokṣa.
Regarding "relying on the four foundations of mindfulness": in the present text, this refers to the foundations of mindfulness according to the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya).
As for the statement that "both of these persons possess a profound mind," it is because, first, their field of merit is superior, and second, their mind is superior, and so forth.

If the Buddha were present [up to] with his entire body, I fear that people of later generations would doubt whether there is a difference in the excellence or inferiority of merit because it is small;
therefore, I raise this question in order to eliminate their doubts.

As for the phrase "until the end of suffering": attaining arhatship is the near completion, while entering wondrous enlightenment is the ultimate completion; only then is it called the final end of suffering.
This is the Dharma of True Suchness (Tathatā), and therefore it is inexhaustible.
If one sees the relics of the Tathāgata (up to) seeing the Saṃgha, this is the Saṃgha of non-duality between the object and wisdom, which is of a single essence.
As for a Wheel-Turning King who possesses little merit, because he transforms the world through the ten wholesome paths of action, he must erect a stūpa to make offerings.
Regarding the fact that [the wheel-turning king] is within the capital city: it is because he wishes to inspire many people to resolve their minds toward awakening.
Although the wheel-turning king has not yet attained liberation, the text does not mention him next to the Arhat;
this is because, as his afflictions have not been severed, he is not permitted to wear [the robes].

Regarding the subsequent statement that "all shall succeed to the royal throne": these are all of noble lineage and great power who each protect their own domains; they do not distribute [benefits] equally among the poor masses.
Therefore, it is ordered that outside the city, all sentient beings shall be universally benefited.

Regarding the phrase "stepping [only] on a small portion of much": The Lord of Devas is a *dānapati* (patron) of the Buddha; therefore, he receives a small portion from within the great abundance, which is not the same as that of the other assemblies.
As for the difficulty of being born therein: this cites the inferior to manifest the superior. Why? Because the Third Dhyāna is the supreme bliss among the three realms.
This is the ultimate state; it is difficult to be born there. Although it is difficult to be born there, those who practice will certainly attain it.

The great assembly has encountered the Tathāgata’s final nirvāṇa and his body of true golden hue; they experience physical and mental bliss, and have further encountered these hundreds of thousands of millions of stations.
It cannot be illustrated by analogy.

The Commentary states: "To cite the cause as manifesting the fruit" means that when the cause is perfected, the fruit is fulfilled; thus, from the body of the fruit, light is universally emitted, and so forth.

"That which should exhaustively return to the source" refers to the fact that once the conditions for transformation have been fully expounded, it is termed "exhausted. One then abides in the secret treasury of virtues.
This is called "returning to the source. Therefore, the preceding passage states: "I have placed my children within the secret treasury, and I myself also abide therein.
This is precisely that meaning.

Regarding the transition from entering and emerging from the first dhyāna into the second dhyāna: according to the *Māyā-sūtra*, this constitutes an uninterrupted samādhi (*anantarya-samādhi*), and thus the character "emerging" (*chū*) should not be applied.
If one speaks of "emerging," it implies a distracted state of mind; rather, one should say that after having entered the first dhyāna, one subsequently enters the second dhyāna.

Following this sequence, one proceeds until the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Rising from the cessation of perception and feeling, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

From that state, one gradually and sequentially re-enters the first dhyāna. When both ascending and descending through these stages are performed without interruption and without passing through a distracted mind, it is called the "uninterrupted samādhi" (*anantarya-samādhi*), also known as "refined meditation" (*kṣānti-dhyāna*);
this is precisely the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*).
Next is "entering and exiting in alternation. This is the cultivation of dhyāna, also known as the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the Lion’s Unfurling Samādhi).
It is like a lion shaking off all dust; these alternating entries and exits are for the purpose of maturing the distracted mind through stillness.

Regarding "entry in forward order," one enters the nine meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in sequence from the first dhyāna up to the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Regarding "reverse order," one emerges from the attainment of cessation and re-enters the sphere of nothingness.
In this manner, one proceeds in succession until reaching the first dhyāna. Thus, whether in reverse or forward order, all involve passing through and entering a single state of distracted mind.
Regarding "transcending entry and exit in three steps": this refers to the practice of meditative cultivation known as the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* (leaping samādhi).

Having arisen from the first dhyāna, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); having arisen from that, one enters the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Having arisen from that, one enters the second dhyāna; having arisen from the second dhyāna, one enters the cessation attainment. [This continues] through the higher realms.

In all cases, one must take the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) as the primary focus. Below this, one gradually ceases [mental activity], entering the third and fourth dhyānas, the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and finally the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Having reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one returns to enter the meditative attainment of cessation; this is the "forward progression" (*anuloma*). As for the "reverse progression" (*pratiloma*): arising from the meditative attainment of cessation, one enters the first dhyāna;

arising from the first dhyāna, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the first dhyāna. Thus, the first dhyāna serves as the basis.

The Master [explains that] one gradually descends from above until reaching the second dhyāna, and then re-enters the first dhyāna. Furthermore, there are those who practice the alternating progression of the reverse and direct orders:

arising from the attainment of cessation, they enter the first dhyāna; arising from the first dhyāna, they enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they enter the second dhyāna;
arising from the second dhyāna, they enter the sphere of nothingness; arising from the sphere of nothingness, they enter the third dhyāna; arising from the third dhyāna, they enter...

The sphere of consciousness: from the sphere of consciousness one arises and enters the fourth dhyāna; from the fourth dhyāna one arises and enters the sphere of infinite space; from the sphere of infinite space one arises and again enters the fourth dhyāna;

from the fourth dhyāna one arises and enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; from the sphere of infinite consciousness one arises and enters the third dhyāna; from the third dhyāna one arises and enters the sphere of nothingness.

From the state of nothingness, one arises and enters the second dhyāna; from the second dhyāna, one arises and enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one arises and enters the first dhyāna;

from the first dhyāna, one arises and re-enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Thus, there are three modes of entry and likewise three modes of emergence; they differ only in that each involves passing through the state of distracted mind (*vikṣiptacitta*).

These characteristics are briefly set forth here based on the *Māyājāla-sūtra*, yet the phrasing in the present sūtra is concise; in its general substance, however, it is the same, and should be understood as detailed therein.
The Commentary states: "As for 'the form of the tree changes and vanishes,' withering and flourishing are neither withering nor flourishing; the Secret Treasury of Jewels is entirely ungraspable.
Since the Dharma-realm is signless, it is represented by the vanishing of form."

Regarding "the response of the capacity for cremation": speaking generally, from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* onwards, every single word and every teaching is a response to the capacity [of sentient beings].
Furthermore, in this present sutra, from the opening words "Thus have I heard" to the conclusion "and so it was practiced," everything is nothing other than a response to the capacity.
Now, specifically pointing to the proclamation of his passing into extinction as being a "response to the capacity" is intended to serve as the title of this chapter.
The Commentary states: "To manifest the distinction" means that the distinction lies in the assembly at Kuśinagara.

At that time, when the great multitude went to support the Tathāgata as he entered the golden coffin, it was through the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s equanimity that the entire assembly simultaneously supported the Tathāgata with their hands as he entered the golden coffin.
The Commentary states: "The other cities were likewise" means that the sixteen cities and so forth were all the same.
"At other times as well" means that it was the same prior to the cremation.
"Begging for exquisite fragrant wood from the devas and humans" is to manifest gratitude and offer worship.
That this site is the place where [the Buddha] dwelt clarifies that the transformative teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely identical;
they all performed the same service for the benefit of sentient beings and were all cremated at this very location.
As for the statement that "only Kāśyapa alone was enlightened": after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa remained to uphold the Buddha-dharma and should have disciplined such individuals;
therefore, he did not allow others to hear of it. Furthermore, as for placing an old cloth upon a new cloth without removing the old one:
this was done so that both ordinary beings and sages might universally receive equal merit; thus, he did not remove it.
Regarding "worshipping at one time": when a disciple serves a teacher, they should perform the *añjali* prostration by touching their feet; it is appropriate that they pay homage in this manner.
As for the "thirty-six mighty wrestlers," one should simply say "four eights" (*si ba*), which is thirty-two.
Regarding "the fire from within the chest": it refers to burning the provisional traces of the physical body and so forth with the fire of wisdom that realizes identity (*samatā-jñāna*).
Regarding "the sacred body being vast and moistening": within the equal Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), he manifests *śarīra* relics as small as mustard seeds to universally benefit all beings;
this is called "vast and moistening," where "vast" (*kō*) signifies empty space (*ākāśa*).
"A thousand sheets of fire do not burn at all" (up to) "except for one pair. This is because the Tathāgata always practices the Middle Way;
thus it is so. The commentary states:
"Regarding the eight countries in other sutras," the *Dīrgha Āgama* says: Kāśyapa emerged from the Piṇḍola Cave and hurried [to the assembly].

At the site of the cremation, the Buddha manifested his two feet. After Kāśyapa had finished prostrating, the tradition records that [the relics] were divided into three portions, namely for humans, devas, and the ocean.
Within the human portion, there was one further division into eight; as for these eight nations: first, the Malla community of the kingdom of Kuśinagara.
1. The Malla assembly from the country of Pāvā; 2. The Vṛji assembly from the country of Śūrasena; 3. The Kauṇḍinya assembly from the country of Magadha;
4. The Brāhmaṇa assembly from the country of Videha; 5. The Śākya assembly from the country of Kapilavastu;
6. The Licchavi assembly from the country of Vaiśālī; 7. King Ajātaśatru of Magadha.
The assembly of kings each declared, "I shall seek a portion of the relics there. Each prepared the fourfold army and immediately commanded the Brahmin of the Kaundinya clan:
"In my name, inquire after the welfare of the Malla people of Kuśinagara. Are you all in good health? Is your life easy? Are you strong as you go about your affairs?
Toward you all, I have always maintained mutual respect; our neighboring states have honored righteousness, and we have never had a word of dispute."
"I have heard that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa within your kingdom. He alone is the Unsurpassed Honored One; he is truly our deity.

Therefore, I come from afar to request a portion of his relics, hoping to return to my own country to erect a stūpa and offer worship. Ghaṭīkāra, having received this instruction, addressed the Mallas, saying: "It is indeed as you say.
Since the Buddha has passed away here, the people of this kingdom shall naturally provide for his constant offerings. [Those from afar...]"
"I trouble you all. You seek a portion of the *śarīra*, but in the end it cannot be obtained.
At that time, the various kings immediately assembled their ministers and said, "If [the Śākyas] do not grant us [a portion], our fourfold army is here; we shall take it by force.
Then the kingdom of Kuśinagara assembled its ministers and replied together in verse: "We dare not grant the Tathāgata’s remains. They say they will raise an army; we have them as well."

Then the one of the Gandhāra clan addressed the people, saying: "Virtuous elders, you have received the Buddha’s instructions; you recite the words of the Dharma with your mouths and submit to his benevolent transformation in your hearts.
Why then do you dispute over the śarīra and seek to harm one another? The śarīra is here before us; you should simply divide it and take your shares."

The assembly all praised this as excellent. They then spoke again, asking, "Who among us is able to divide [the relics]? The assembly proposed the one of the Xiang clan, saying, "He is benevolent, wise, and impartial;
he may divide the śarīras" (and so forth). They immediately divided the śarīras into eight portions. The ninth was for the reliquary jar stūpa, and the tenth was for the ash stūpa.
As for the hair preserved during his lifetime, the devas took it up to heaven and erected a stūpa there for worship. At the appearance of the morning star, the śarīras were thus divided.
When it was finished, there remained some charcoal. The people of Pipphalivana addressed the assembly, saying, "We beg for the remaining charcoal to erect a stūpa as an object of worship.
Everyone said, "Give it to them. Each of the various kingdoms then erected a stūpa at their own respective locations to offer worship.
To exclude those who lack the necessary conditions means to exclude those who have received the teachings of the provisional expedients and are not yet capable of receiving [the ultimate teaching].
Because they have not heard of the perfectly constant Buddha-nature, the secret "True I" (Zhenyi), it is therefore not granted to them.
The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'the text is not yet complete,' since it says 'not yet complete,' it would be inappropriate to title it as 'Part One' and 'Part Two.
